en: The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. The *Kāśikā* commentary composed by Śrī Haribhaṭṭa.
I bow to the feet of Gaṇapati, which are like two lamps for dispelling the swarm of bees that are obstacles.
They are worthy of worship by the hosts of gods and bestowers (givers of fruits) of all desired objects. || 1 ||
Having bowed to Bhairava, Śaṅkarī, Siddheśā, and the Mother of the World,
Hari composes the *Kāśikā*, a commentary on the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*.
I bow to the three sages who benefit all people and have become vessels for the ocean of knowledge;
and to my gurus, to my father Yaśaḥprakāśa—who is worthy of worship by the lords of the gods—and to my mother, the goddess.

For the sake of the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose, he first composes an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) consisting of a praise of Śrī Lakṣmīramaṇa—the Lord of the entire universe—and fixes it here for the instruction of his disciples, beginning with the words "Śrīlakṣmīramaṇam. *Śrī* is extraordinary splendor; *Mahālakṣmī*, who is endowed with that [splendor], is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all things. *Ramaṇa* refers to Viṣṇu, the beloved of her. The meaning is: "I bow to," or "I praise. Alternatively, *śrī* is as previously mentioned, or it may refer to a distinct Intellect (*buddhi*) endowed with attributes such as eternity; one who is joined with that is "Lakṣmīramaṇa. Or else:

Śrī—meaning the lover of Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī; for there is a Vedic revelation stating, "Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives. In that context, by the word "Śrī" is meant Sarasvatī and not Lakṣmī, because Lakṣmī is mentioned separately and because otherwise the use of the dual number in "the two wives" would be inconsistent; this is quite clear. Now, one might object: based on the statement, "One should perform the worship of Hari and Hara," and the sayings, "As is Viṣṇu, so is Śiva," and "Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṣṇu," [it follows that they are identical].
"He who speaks of a difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra is one of deluded intellect;
he falls downward into the terrible hells such as Raurava.

From such scriptural statements, it is established that worship must be performed through non-difference alone, and its opposite is prohibited. Furthermore, since the contemplation of difference might arise when merely praising Viṣṇu, [the author] provides the epithet "Gaurī's Lover" (Lakṣmīramaṇa) to prevent that [contemplation of difference]. Gaurī is Pārvatī, and she is also Kālikā.

"Having emerged from her, that Pārvatī became Kṛṣṇā; she is also known as Kālikā," according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, and from the lexicon [Amarakośa] which states, "Umā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Kālī. Thus, the praise of the triad beginning with Mahākālī is also accomplished. Her lover is Śiva; his form is that of her—[the goddess].

This is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is that he "fashions" (rūpayati) [the world] as Gaurīramaṇa, or grasps it as non-different from him; here the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartari*). Or again, the meaning is that he fashions or causes Gaurīramaṇa to be grasped as non-different from himself. In the former alternative (*pakṣa*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *ini* is applied; in the latter alternative, the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supsyajātau*.

What is that? It is from which—of which—this entire visible world manifests. Because it is non-dual and so forth, the suffix *tasi* is used (it would be *ādyaritvāt*). "Manifests" (*vivarttate*) means that it comes to possess the existence of an object, or rather, that it becomes the locus of an unreal transformation. As it has been said: "Real transformation is *pariṇāma*; unreal transformation is *vivarta*. And this "unreal transformation" is precisely delusion (*bhrama*). Its being the locus [of such delusion] should be understood as occurring within the world—that is, within the object—in its capacity as an object (*viṣayatayā*).

By this, it is stated that [Brahman] is the material cause of the entire world in the sense of being the locus of its illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); thereby, its fitness for praise as the most excellent of all is indicated. And that status as its material cause is established by such scriptural passages as: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter upon departing. This [status] is established in the world by this scripture...

Although the agency of maintenance and dissolution is also to be understood [as attributes of the Lord], the qualification "of the world" (*jagataḥ*) refers to the *sphoṭa*-form. *Sphoṭa* is that from which [meaning] bursts forth (*sphuṭati*); and according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), that is the very nature of Brahman, as is clear from the works of Hari and others. The meaning is that it is of that form, i.e., non-different from it. This non-difference from Brahman is established by such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman.

Furthermore, this is also a qualification of Lakṣmī’s Beloved (Viṣṇu); it is included here so that the praise of the appropriate deity may be accomplished, since the *sphoṭa* is the object of meditation for grammarians. || 1 ||

Among the triad of sages beginning with Pāṇini, he composes an auspicious invocation consisting of the glorification of the deity favored by Śeṣa—who is currently esteemed for his supreme authority and excellence—beginning with the words "aśeṣaphala-". This is for the sake of attaining all meanings of Śeṣa; that is, for the sake of the knowledge of all the meanings—both explicit and implicit—contained in the Mahābhāṣya, belonging to Śeṣa, the Great Serpent, the author of the Mahābhāṣya.

The connection is as follows: "Pray to Śiva, whose ornament is Śeṣa—that is, for whom Śeṣa serves as an ornament by way of being his [couch], or for whom Śeṣa serves as an ornament by way of being his bed—as well as to Viṣṇu, who reclines upon Śeṣa."

One might object: "The attainment of the remaining objects of desire arises from the *śeṣa* (the remainder) alone, and not from Śiva and the others; for Devadatta’s acquisition of wealth does not come from Mitrabandhu and the like. Therefore, it is the *śeṣa* alone that should be prayed to, and not Śiva and the rest. Wishing to dispel this doubt, he provides a qualification for that [word *śeṣa*], namely: *aśeṣaphala* ("the giver of all fruits"). "All" (*aśeṣa*) refers to those fruits pertaining to this world and the next, up to and including liberation (*apavarga*). "Fruits" (*phala*) refers to the results of various respective actions (*karma*). The compound is formed between the word ending in the suffix *tṛn* (denoting an agent) and the word ending in the genitive case of the *ṣaṣṭhī* (possessive) relation: "the giver of those [fruits]."

Alternatively, the compound is formed with a word ending in *tṛc* [as the prior member] and a word ending in *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) [as the latter member]. By this, the following objections are answered: that if it ends in *tṛc*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of compounding by the rule "not with words ending in *tṛc* or *aka*" (*tṛjakābhyām*); and that if it ends in *tṛn*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule "not in connection with *loka*, etc. (*na loka-*). This is because the prohibition "not in connection with *loka*, etc. applies only to the genitive case when it expresses a *kāraka* (participant in an action), and the prohibition of compounding applies only to that specific [genitive]. Furthermore, the Lord's status as the giver of results is expressed in the passage: "In whatever manner the gods act for the sake of the gods, in that very same manner the gods act for him."
"Whichever embodied being a devotee desires to worship with faith in whichever form,
I make that very faith of his firm."

"Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of the Lord; and from Him he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone for his welfare. This and other such passages are well-known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas. Furthermore, this has been explained most skillfully by the venerable teacher Śaṅkarācārya in his *Śārīrakabhāṣya* on the following Sūtras of Vyāsa: in the first pāda of the second adhyāya, "There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He is dependent [upon the karma of the souls]; for thus He shows"; and at the end of the second pāda of the third adhyāya, in the Sūtra, "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the former [view], because of the mention of a cause."

The Lord alone, in dependence upon the merit and demerit residing in each respective individual soul, is the giver of the fruit, and not karma alone. In this regard, first of all, just as rain is the common cause for the production of rice, barley, and so forth, while the specific differences among rice, barley, and the like are caused by the potencies residing in their respective seeds—potencies which are synonymous with "capacity"—so too the Lord is the common cause for the creation of gods and others, whereas the specific differences among gods, humans, and so forth are caused by the unseen merits and demerits (adṛṣṭa) residing in those respective souls.

Since causes are distinct (i.e., non-common), in this way, God is not tainted by partiality or cruelty because He is dependent upon karma, just as a king who bestows fruits in accordance with service [is not blamed]. But how is it understood that God, being dependent, creates the inferior, middling, and superior states of worldly existence?

For thus the Śruti shows: "For He alone makes him perform good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; and He alone makes him perform bad action whom He wishes to lead down. And also: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action. Smṛti also declares this in such passages as: "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them."

In the third [chapter], however, the position that "the fruit arises from *dharma* alone"—as formulated in Jaimini’s Sūtra, "But *dharma*, Jaimini [says], for that very reason"—is set aside by the word "but" (*tu*). Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit arises from the Lord (*īśvara*) alone, who is dependent upon both *karma* and the *apūrva*. Why? Because of the "designation of a cause" (*hetuvyapadeśāt*). Having stated that the Lord is designated as the cause of both merit and demerit by virtue of being their instigator, and as the giver of the fruit, the previously cited Śruti passage, "For He indeed is [Brahman]," is demonstrated; the details of this and more are found elsewhere.

One might object: "If there exist many obstacles in the form of accumulated sins (*durita*), how can the fruits of anger or non-anger be obtained? For even when a single obstacle is present, a thousand means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) are rendered ineffective. To dispel this doubt, the author qualifies [the Lord] as "the ocean of existence" (*bhavābdhi*).

*Bhava* means *saṃsāra* (the cycle of existence). The compound is formed according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsakādi* compounds, because it is consistent with the context of "crossing" (*taraṇī*). Alternatively, it is an *upamita-samāsa* (simile compound) meaning "the ocean that is *bhava*," since the act of crossing, which consists of destruction [of suffering], can logically apply there as well; and because, as in the case of the phrase "Where is the ocean of the Bhāṣya so profoundly deep?", there is no obstacle to the presence of an explicit word denoting the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) in the present instance. [Of] the ocean of *bhava*...

The word *taraṇam* refers here to a boat (*tariḥ* or *naukā*), meaning the means [of crossing]; for there is the Vedic scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (*tarati śokam ātmavit*). Amara states: "In the feminine, *naus*, *taraṇiḥ*, and *tariḥ* [mean a boat]. Thus, since it brings about the cessation of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—which consists of a multitude of sufferings that cannot be remedied by any other means—the removal of the obstructing sins will certainly follow from it; this is the sense, according to the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*).

Its status as a subordinate ornament (*śeṣālaṃkāra*) consists in its being a motivator; by means of that, through a prayer characterized by it, there is necessarily the attainment of all the remaining purposes already mentioned. Furthermore, because it is the progenitor of the Lord of Obstacles (*vighneśa*), the removal of the accumulation of obstacles is also necessarily indicated. By this, the objection—that praying to Gaṇeśa at the very beginning is appropriate for the accomplishment of the warding off of obstacles based on a collection of statements such as "The Lord of the Ganas is to be worshipped first"—is refuted. || 2 ||

He praises his own guru, his paternal uncle, who is honored by all scholars, by mentioning his name for the sake of perpetuating his fame, [saying]: "Vāgdevī... "For success"—that is, for the completion of the work he has begun to compose and for its dissemination—he says: "She dances repeatedly or with great intensity. This refers to the dancing on the tip of the tongue of the Goddess of Speech; it is a manifestation in the form of a continuous stream, sudden and uninterrupted. By this, his extraordinary scholarship and eloquence are made known.

The sense is as follows: from the root *nṛt* (meaning "to dance" or "to move the limbs"), the suffix *yaṅ-luk* is applied, followed by the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the third person singular ending (*tip*), and the elision of *śap*. Because roots ending in *yaṅ-luk* are listed among the ad-roots (beginning with *ad*) according to the rule *carkarītaṃ ca*, the augment *rīk* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *rīgṛdupadhasya ca*. Furthermore, the fact that *yaṅ-luk* occurs even in Vedic usage is known from the inclusion of the terms *hu* and *śnu* in the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*; moreover, because the term *nigama* (Vedic) is mentioned in the rule *babhūthātatantha*, it is understood that this formation is not inconsistent even in the common language (*bhāṣā*).

By introducing [the subject] as possessing such extraordinary power (*sāmarthya*), it is indicated that the praise of the initiated person—by way of suggesting his divine nature (*devāṃśatva*)—is both effective in accomplishing the desired goal and entirely appropriate. Furthermore, the divine nature of such a person is clearly stated in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Whatever being is possessed of glory, or is majestic, know that to be a fragment of my splendor. (3)

Composing the benediction consisting of salutations to the triad of sages beginning with Pāṇini—the teachers who initiated the science of grammar—and thereby indicating the fourfold preliminary conditions (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) for the engagement of discerning students, he declares his intention (for the purpose of exposition) so that the disciples may attend: "Pāṇini, etc."

Having prostrated—having performed a supreme salutation characterized by the quality of the eight-limbed (sāṣṭāṅga) gesture—to the sages beginning with Pāṇini, to my father named Raṅgojibhaṭṭa, and to Gaṇapati Ḍhuṇḍhi—I shall reveal, through reasoned arguments (upapatti), the established doctrines (siddhāntas)—namely, the tenets of the Grammarians—which have been disparaged by the commentators on the words of Gautama and Jaimini.

The construction is as follows: "I shall refute the words of those modern logicians and Mīmāṃsakas who are commentators on the utterances of Gautama and Jaimini. By the inclusion of the term "commentators" (*vyākhyātṛbhiḥ*) in the phrase "refuted by commentators," it is indicated that there is no contradiction between the sages such as Gautama and others and [the authors of] Pāṇini and so forth; this has been clarified in various places in the *Mañjūṣā*, and here too [it will be shown] in some instances.

It will be established [later]. "Pāṇinyādayaḥ" (those beginning with Pāṇini) is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing a *bahuvrīhi*: those for whom Pāṇini is the first (*ādi*) are "Pāṇini and the others," and these are also sages (*munayaḥ*). This *bahuvrīhi* is one where the qualities denoted by the members are included in the referent (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), as in the case of the rule "the words beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādīni*). By this, Pāṇini also obtains the status of being the object of salutation. The two to be understood by the word "others" (*ādi*) are Kātyāyana and Patañjali. "Raṅgojibhaṭṭa" is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose name is Raṅgojibhaṭṭa."

Gautama and Jaimini are the authors of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā Sūtras respectively; "Gautamajaiminīyāni" refers to these two [works], where the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "avṛddhācchaḥ" in the sense of "belonging to this. These are the respective statements, namely the Nyāya Sūtras and the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras, forming a *karmadhāraya* compound. The term "commentators upon them" (*teṣāṃ vyākhyātāraḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), similar to the expression "bestower of all fruits" (*aśeṣaphaladātṛ*).

He states the qualification of the Father (*pitṛ*) which serves as the ground for his being worthy of salutation: *dvaitadhvānta*, etc. *Dvīta* means "duality" (*bheda*); that which has come from this [duality] by way of being its locus is *dvaita*, i.e., knowledge [of duality]. Alternatively, as in the rule "*dvayekayoḥ*" (Pāṇini 1.4.22), the word *dvi* refers to the number two; thus, the two things denoted by the term *dvīta* are qualified by duality. That which arises from those two is *dvaita*, meaning duality. This constitutes the darkness (*dhvānta*), the gloom (*tamaḥ*), or delusion (*moha*).

That which has as its primary fruit the warding off of that [obstacle] is "of such a kind. "The deity of the state of manhood" (*puṃbhāvavādevatām*): "man" (*pumān*) means a person; "the state of him" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*) refers to his form or appearance; she who possesses that is "possessing the state of manhood" (*puṃbhāvā*), meaning she has the form of a man. And she is the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevatā*), namely Sarasvatī; the meaning is "having that form. Because the gender is not abandoned (*ajahalliṅgatvāt*), there is no contradiction in having a common substratum for the qualifier even when the genders differ, as in the expression "the woman who is the principal" (*strī pradhānam*).
By this qualification, his exceptional proficiency in the Uttaramīmāṃsā, which establishes non-duality (advaita), is demonstrated; thereby, his distinct excellence is indicated. || 4 ||

Fearing many obstacles, he again performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of salutations to Gaṇeśa and others, and records the name of himself and the work he intends to compose for the sake of perpetuating his own fame, saying: "I, Śrī Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa"—that is, I, Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, who am endowed with *śrī*, meaning the intellect known as *sphūrti* (creative intuition) characterized by ever-new manifestations—"bow to the lotus-feet of Gaṇeśa. The meaning is: of him who is the lord (*īśa*), the controller, of the *gaṇas*, namely the attendants of Śiva.

Alternatively, *gaṇānām* refers to the hosts of enemies; *iḥ* is their fortune (*lakṣmī*). He who sharpens (*śyati*)—that is, attenuates—that [fortune] is [the meaning]. This is derived from the root *śo* (to sharpen/thin), where the vowel change (*ātva*) occurs without a specific cause, followed by the suffix *ka* according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*. Or else, *gaṇānām iḥ* refers to desire (*kāma*); he sharpens—that is, cuts through—that agitation of desire. Note that "desire" is an elliptical expression for anger and the other [afflictions]; thus, the meaning is that he shatters the group of six, beginning with desire, by means of sound instruction and so forth.

The lotus-feet (*pādāmbuja*) of such a Lord—the feet themselves being the lotuses—where the singular number for "lotus" (*ambuja*) is used to indicate that they are meditated upon as distinguished by an extraordinary degree of intimacy. Regarding "the teachers" (*gurūn*): one who proclaims (*gṛṇāti*) the hidden meaning is a teacher (*guru*). According to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* "kṛgroruñca," the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *gṛ* (from the class beginning with *kryādi*), which means "to sound."

*Sarasvatī* is so called because she possesses a lake (*sara*) of nectar; for according to the *Nirukta*, "the word *sara* is a name for water, and she possesses that [water] through the root *sṛ*" (to flow). Alternatively, the meaning may be that she has a particular lake as her support. The title of the work, *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa* ("The Ornament of Grammarians"), is significant by its very name, thereby implying that it is indispensable for grammarians. || 5 ||

Regarding the term *prāripsita*: it refers to the collection (*vyūha*)—that is, the aggregate—of obstacles to that work which one intends to begin; the meaning is "for the sake of their pacification," i.e., for their destruction. By this, it is indicated that "auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not the cause of completion because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*), but rather [it is the cause] of the destruction of obstacles, while completion itself arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*)," and so forth; the details of this are explained elsewhere.

[Objection: "Even so, let the performance of the auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) occur only outside the text; its composition within the body of the work is purposeless. To this he replies: "For the sake of instructing the students" (*śiṣyaśikṣārtham*). The meaning is: when, at the time of beginning the work, the students also recite such composed verses, they too become partakers of the auspiciousness and recipients of the fruit resulting from it; it is for this purpose. "The intended work" refers to the treatise in the form of the *Kārikāvalī*. The words "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

By this statement, through the manifestation of the extraordinary power of the author of the work in the form of the *Kārikāvalī*, the necessity of studying the present work composed by him is implied. He states "otherwise" (*anyathā*) to indicate the purpose of refuting the conjectures of moderns. "Otherwise" means: if one does not refute the conjectures of moderns regarding the statements in the *Kaustubha*. "Conjectured by moderns" means: if [the *Kaustubha*] were to attain the status of being the essence [of the system], that is to say, if its status as the essence were to be established.

"Pāṇinīyānām" means those who study the treatise proclaimed by Pāṇini. In the root text, the mention of "the serpent" (phaṇin) alone, setting aside other deities, refers to the author of the science of grammar.

They say that the mention of the *muni* (sage) at the very beginning of the root text is intended to indicate that [the author] is most highly esteemed by the three sages (*munitraya*), and to convey the meaning that, unlike other commentaries, this *Vyākaraṇabhāṣya* was not composed by a modern person but by the great sage Viṣṇumitra; therefore, no suspicion of its lack of authority should be entertained regarding his statements. Furthermore, the definition of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) is presented first because of the *Nirukta* of Śākaṭāyana, which states: "All nouns are born from verbs," and "Everything is derived from verbal roots, as declared in the *Nirukta* and in the *Vyākaraṇa*, the offspring of Śakaṭa."

It should be understood that this statement from the *Bhāṣya* is made because the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the basis for all linguistic usage and is more worthy of honor than anything else, and furthermore, because in the cognition generally produced by a sentence, the meaning of the verbal root is predominant, making it the most worthy of honor. Regarding the word "verbal" (*ākhyāta*) in the phrase "born from the verbal," it refers to the verbal roots that constitute a verbal form (*ākhyāta*), which is essentially a collection of elements ending in a personal suffix (*tiṅ*). This is because of the *Bhāṣya* statement, "All nouns (*nāman*) are born from verbal roots," and because it is impossible for a noun to be born from something ending in a personal suffix. (2)

Since it is impossible for the word *dhātu* (in the singular) to be construed with *smṛtāḥ* (in the plural), because there is no agreement in number with the word expressing the substantive (*viśeṣya*), he says: *smṛtaḥ*. [He adds] "by changing the number" (*vacanavipariṇāmena*). The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) for this is "as the denoter" (*vācakatvena*).

By the dual-numbered reference "phala-vyāpārayoḥ" (of the fruit and the operation), it is indicated that there is a distinct power (*śakti*) for the fruit and for the operation separately; however, there is not a single power as maintained by the ancient logicians residing in the operation qualified by the fruit. For if that were the case, since the fruit would be merely a part of the word-meaning, its connection with other word-meanings such as the accusative case would be impossible. [This refers to] the fruit and the operation as the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*).

There is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of existence (*bhāva*), because there is no deficiency even if the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*). This is because the requirement for the cognition of a word-meaning produced from a word through its *vṛtti* (denotative function) applies only to that verbal comprehension which possesses a subject-matter distinct from the relational subject-matter (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*). Thus, according to some, the subject-matter enters into the defining condition (*avacchedaka*) of the effect as "being a subject-matter distinct from the relational subject-matter."

In reality, however, there is no inclusion [of other objects] under the status of being a "subject-matter" (viṣayatā) distinct from the relational subject-matter (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*). Even if such an inclusion were granted, once the word *ghaṭa* brings about the cognition of a jar through its linguistic function (*vṛtti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition having cloth or other things as its object. Therefore, one must state the causal relation specifically as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition characterized by having a particular thing as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and a particular property as its qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is the cognition of that specific meaning produced by that specific word through its linguistic function. And thus...

Since there is no causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) when including relational objectivity (sāṃsargikaviṣayatā), the manifestation of a relation—even one not presented through mental capacity (śakti)—is entirely unimpeded.

Furthermore, since an object presented through either primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), one must admit that both modes of presentation serve as causes for such cognition. In this regard, because it is impossible to find a single, inclusive, non-overlapping, and non-redundant property (*dharma*) to serve as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*), one must necessarily accept them as distinct causes. Consequently, since a verbal cognition regarding a specific object can still be produced by one mode of presentation even in the absence of another, there would be a logical fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore—

The proponents [of the view that the relation is not denoted] maintain that the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) must be accepted as "the state of being a verbal cognition whose object is such-and-such a meaning, qualified by the presentation of that same meaning brought about by *śakti* (denotative power)," and "the state of being a verbal cognition whose object is such-and-such a meaning, qualified by the presentation of that same meaning brought about by *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function). Furthermore, the qualification by the presentation is established through two relations: co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with itself, and immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*) to itself. Thus, since the verbal cognition whose object is the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not encompassed by these delimiters of the effect, its manifestation—even though it is not directly denotable—is free from any obstacle.
This is what others [the opponents] hold.
The Grammarians maintain that it is the relation (*saṃbandha*) that is denoted (*vācya*), while the Bhaṭṭas hold that it is the indicated object (*lakṣya*); such is the direction [of the argument].

Now, even so, one might object: according to the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "only two things presented by distinct words can have a mutual relation of semantic cognition," how can there be a mutual relation of semantic cognition between the operation (*vyāpāra*) and the fruit (*phala*), both of which are presented by a single verbal root? Nor should it be argued that such a rule is unestablished because it serves no purpose; for if it were, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of a verbal cognition involving a container-and-contained relationship (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) arising from the simultaneous presentation of Indra and a horse by the word *hari*, or a mutual relation between the meanings of "option" (*vikalpa*) and so forth arising from the particle *vā*.

If it is argued that this is not so because the attainment of awakening (*bodha*) and the cessation [of suffering] are the purposes [of the scripture], we say no. For, according to the view of others (*paramata*), since we observe the mutual cognitive connection (*anvaya-bodha*) between the meanings of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*)—namely, the agent’s effort (*kṛti*) and the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatva*)—and between the meanings of the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*)—namely, the effort and its presentness (*vartamānatva*)—such a rule of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) must be restricted. Consequently, a mutual cognitive connection between the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) is possible, and this has indeed been accepted by the Neo-Naiyāyikas as well.

The point is this: at the outset, the connection between the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) alone occurs because they are internal (*antaraṅga*); it is only after that that a connection with another meaning is experienced. For this very reason, from the sentence "going is not motion" (*gamanaṃ na spandaḥ*), there is no experience of a connection with the negation of motion (*spandabhedānvaya*), because that [negation] is understood in relation to the operation which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), whereas the result has become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that [operation]. Nonetheless, the connection of *stoka* ("a little") and so forth occurs precisely through non-difference (*abheda*), due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-vaicityāt*). Likewise, the same applies to the object-kāraka (*karmakāraka*) through non-difference; thus, there is no inconsistency in expressions such as "he cooks a little" (*stokaṃ pacati*).

In this regard, the venerable Mañjūṣākāras maintain that "the capacity (śakti) resides in the operation qualified by the result, and in the result qualified by the operation; for if one were to accept separate capacities for the result and the operation, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a cognition in which the result is the predicate (*vidheya*) with respect to the operation as its subject, and a cognition in which the operation is the predicate with respect to the result as its subject—since the separate mental representations (*pṛthag-upasthiti*) that cause such cognitions exist. However, according to the view that accepts a single capacity for the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-mata*), such cognitions do not arise, because the separate mental representations that cause them are absent. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that the capacity of a separate presentation (*upasthiti*) to cause such a cognition is unestablished; for, by the force of the non-experience of such a cognition regarding "potness" and "clothness" (or "pot" and "cloth") when they are the objects of a single presentation produced by both a pot and a cloth, one must postulate that such a presentation possesses that capacity. Nor should it be argued that there is no occurrence of such a cognition because one must postulate that the presentation of the operation (*vyāpāra*) and so forth produced by the verbal root acts as an inhibitor of such a cognition.

Because it would be cumbersome to postulate such a relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*), the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with an agentive suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*) is the regulator for the cognition of an operation qualified by a result, while the co-occurrence with an objective suffix (*karmapratyaya*) is the regulator for the cognition of a result qualified by an operation. Furthermore, one need not postulate two distinct potencies (*śakti*) for these two qualified entities; for it would be cumbersome to postulate that the two cognitions of potency and the two presentations of the qualified objects produced by the verbal root are both causes for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

This must be stated, because it is not a fault since it is based on authoritative evidence; furthermore, even under the theory of distinct powers (*pṛthak-śakti-vāda*), there is the abandonment of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*) occurs only between two items presented by distinct words, and there is the additional burden of having to postulate another linguistic rule.

Moreover, there is the complexity of postulating two sets of causal relations: that the presence of a verbal root co-occurring with an agentive suffix is the cause of a cognition in which the operation is the qualificand and the result is the qualifier, and that the presence of a verbal root co-occurring with an objective suffix is the cause of a cognition in which the result is the qualificand and the operation is the qualifier; furthermore, there is the complexity of postulating two distinct powers for the verbal root with respect to its two meanings.

Nor should it be argued that even in your own view there is parity, since one must likewise postulate the causality of two such distinct-object cognitions as well as two powers (śakti) for those two kinds of meanings; for otherwise, since the capacity to produce cognition is untenable if the word is not connected to its object, one would have to postulate two relations each defined by the two distinct [qualified] meanings within the verbal root as co-occurring with the respective suffixes, which results in a manifest [additional] complexity (gaurava). Otherwise, the very concept of *śakti* would be abolished. Thus they stated that the postulation of separate powers in other cases should also be rejected.

The root text, "phalavyāpārayoḥ," intends only that there is a single power (śakti) residing in the collection of both [the fruit and the operation]; it does not intend that there is a separate power for each. Thus, since in verbal cognition one thing appears as qualified by the other, it should be understood that the intention is that the power resides in both such qualified entities, as established by the root text itself.

In accordance with the sequence stated in the root text, [the author] explains the portion of the fruit prior to the operation as "the fruit is disintegration (*viklitti*) and so forth. Disintegration is a state of loosening, a specific separation of parts, or a specific conjunction [of parts]; and it is denoted by its specific nature consisting of the property of being disintegration (*viklittitva*), and not as a "fruit" (*phala*). This is because verbal cognition is experienced only through its specific form.

The state of being a culminating result (*niṣṭhaphala*)—such as softening (*viklitti*) and so on—is defined as: "being a qualifier (determining attribute) relative to a qualificand (predicative property) residing in the meaning of that verbal root, while being co-referential with a suffix denoting an agent, provided that it is produced by the meaning of that verbal root. Here, "being produced" (*janyatva*) is common to both actual and superimposed production. By this definition, there is no failure to establish the status of a result for things such as the absence of an activity conducive to conjunction (in cases like *vārayati*, where it refers to an activity conducive to the absence of an activity conducive to conjunction). Furthermore, in the meaning of verbs such as *patati* (falls), which consists of a conjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāga*), [the disjunction itself is the result].

The term "sat" (being/existing) is included to exclude the state of being a result (*phalatva*). Since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would remain even if one were to include merely the property of being produced (*janyatvamātra*), the object denoted by that verbal root is introduced as the determiner of the state of being produced. Furthermore, because even disjunction (*vibhāga*)—as in the case of verbs such as *gam* (to go)—is produced by some object denoted by a verbal root, the aforementioned fault would persist; therefore, the word "tat" (that) is employed [to specify the relevant root].

Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable because a conjunction produced by disjunction (i.e., a conjunction whose status as being produced is defined by itself) generates its own cause—namely, the disjunction—by means of the action it produces; for one must include either a "producedness" (janyatā) defined by a causality consisting of "contributory agency" (upadhāyakatā), or a "producedness" mediated by action. Furthermore, in order to exclude that very conjunction from being the result [of the action], the inclusion of the phrase "possessing the state of being a qualifier" (prakāratāvattva) is necessary.

The phrase "residing in the meaning of that verbal root" (*taddhātvarthaniṣṭha*) is a qualification of the "predicative objecthood" (*viśeṣyatā*) because, in the cognition produced by the sentence "the pot falls" (*patati bhavatīti*), the action of "becoming" (*bhavatikriyā*) is the object of the [inherence] relation of that [objecthood]. Otherwise, in cases such as "the rice is cooked" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate*) or "the rice is cooked" (*taṇḍulaḥ pakvaḥ*), where there is co-occurrence with an accusative suffix (*karmapratyaya*), softening (*viklitti*) and so forth would be the object of the cognition; consequently, they would not qualify as the "result" (*phala*). Therefore, the phrase "in co-occurrence with a suffix denoting the agent" (*kartṛpratyayasamabhivyāhāre*) is included.

Alternatively, if that [qualification] were not included, then the possession of such a mode (prakāratā) would be obtained under the delimitation of being verbal (*śābdatva*); and in that case, there would be the fault of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). Therefore, its inclusion is made. Thus, the possession of such a mode is an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), not a defining attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*); hence, the intention is that in the case of object-terminations (*karmapratyaya*), there is no resulting non-existence of [the mode] such as "softening" (*viklitti*) and so forth. Here, the expression was stated in that manner rather than using "in the co-occurrence with any suffix whatsoever" (*yatkiñcitpratyayasamabhivyāhāre*) in order to demonstrate the locus of such a cognition.

He defines *vyāpāra* (operation) with the words "But the operation... He explains *bhāvanā* as follows: the meaning is an operation conducive to production; this is derived from the root *bhū* (to become), which signifies production, by adding the suffix *ṇic* and then the suffix *yuc* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *ṇyāsaśrantha*. He explains *abhidhā*: it is called *abhidhā* because it "denotes" (*abhidadhāti*), that is, it produces the result; it is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*).

Thus, regarding these two designations: in the first case, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the agent by the rule *ātaścopasarge*; in the second case, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object by that same rule. Consequently, the meaning is that "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is the action being denoted as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which is another name for "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*). The statement "denoted as productive activity" (*bhāvanābhidhā*) is intended to dispel the misconception that, although activity is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is specifically the particular meaning named "productive activity" and so forth that constitutes the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*).

The expression ‘action’ (*kriyā*) is intended to demonstrate that the causative form of the verb *bhū* has the same meaning as the simple root *kṛ*. Regarding the phrase “as long as it is not accomplished” (*yāvat-siddham*): whether it be something unaccomplished in cases such as ‘he cooks’ (*pacati*) or ‘he will cook’ (*pakṣyati*), or something already accomplished in cases such as ‘he cooked’ (*apākṣīt*), whatever entity is denoted in the manner of being ‘to-be-accomplished’ (*sādhyatvena*) is called ‘action. When the question arises as to why this is so, he demonstrates the reason for its fitness (*yogya*) by means of the passage beginning with ‘resorted to’ (*āśrita*).

It is produced through the sequential arising of its parts; therefore, the meaning is that it "has a form based on sequence. The term *āśritakramarūpā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that by which a form based on sequence is resorted to" (*āśritaṃ kramarūpaṃ yayā*). Consequently, it takes the feminine suffix *tva*. When there is a desire to express the general (abstract) quality, the neuter gender is used.

"Because perception itself is the means of valid cognition. If the cognition [of the object] as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) were not admitted, then—since the cognition would be indistinguishable from that arising from words such as "effort" (*kṛti*)—there would likewise arise here an expectancy for another action, just as there is in that case. And since it is observed that only that which is already established has the capacity to preclude other actions, the absence of expectancy for another action is maintained only when there is a cognition of the object as something to be accomplished. [The phrase] "the delimiting factor of non-productivity" refers to this.

The meaning is that it consists of a specific universal (jāti) established as the delimitor of the capacity to obstruct the arising of that [action]. Regarding the phrase "that form": the sense is that once a distinctness (vaijātya) residing solely in the action presented by the verbal root is established, it is proper—on grounds of parsimony (lāghava)—to accept that very [distinctness] as being the nature of non-existence (asattva), rather than [properties such as] the lack of connection with gender and so forth. However, that distinctness is co-extensive (samānādhikaraṇa) with the lack of connection with gender and so forth, and is indeed co-extensive with the state of having constituent parts arranged in a temporal sequence (pūrvaparībhūta).

The intended meaning of the phrase "this very [point]" is exactly as stated. The term "by means of finite verb forms" (tiṅpadaiḥ) means by means of words ending in verbal suffixes (tiṅanta). It should be understood that "establishedness" (siddhatva) is a specific class-character (jāti) which serves as the delimiting factor for the capacity to arouse an expectancy for action, in contrast to this [expectancy for action].

Nor should it be argued that the conventional designation of indeclinables such as *hiruk* and others as "action-predominant" (*kriyāpradhāna*) would be undermined because they do not present their respective meanings in the form of such a [verbal] object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); for that status is based solely on their being qualifiers of action (*kriyā*). For this very reason, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of case-factors (*kāraka*) with the meaning of *hiruk* and others, since they do not appear under a specific generic property (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimitor of the fitness for connection with case-factors.

[Objection: But if this is so, then in the sentence "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, he would attain happiness," there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the act of bowing and the attainment of happiness by way of the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). [Response: This is not so; for they say that the requirement for an action (*kriyākāṅkṣā*) arises through the assistance provided by the co-occurrence with the word *cet* ("if"). In reality, however, being a goal (*sādhyatva*) is simply being something to be accomplished (*niṣpādyatva*), because it is established by experience that the cognition occurs precisely in that form. And this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rules "upapadamatiṅ," "suṭkātpūrvaḥ," and "gatigatau. Regarding the rule "upapadamatiṅ," [it concerns] the root and the upapada.

Anticipating the objection that [if] "first the verbal root is joined with its means (sādhana)," then there would be no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) for the root to be qualified by the *tiṅ*-ending first, it was resolved there that because of the prohibition "not [with] a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*), there is no formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) with a word ending in a *tiṅ*. Regarding the rules "the augment *suṭ* precedes the *kā*" (*suṭ kāt pūrvaḥ*) and "a motion [prefix] before a motion [verb]" (*gatirgatau*), it was stated that the operation between a verbal root and a prefix is internal (*antaraṅga*), and so forth; yet it was further said: "This is not the core point; for first the root is joined with its means, and afterwards with the prefix. For the means brings about the action, and the prefix qualifies that [action]."

The *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is the cognition that makes that [action] known; it brings about the action by making it known as qualified by the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). Therefore, the elders have stated that for this reason, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) prompted by it occurs first.

In the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *upapadaṃ tiṅ*, the prior mention of the relation to the means (*sādhana*) is also based on this very intention; [by the authority of this *Bhāṣya*, the manifestation of the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is accepted]. By this, the objection—that the manifestation of the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished does not occur because the lack of expectancy for an action is established solely from the very nature of the verbal power (*śabdaśakti*) when a *tiṅ*-affix is present—is refuted; this should be understood. [The phrase] "because it is established by experience" [is used].

For this very reason, when a verbal cognition arises from expressions such as "he cooks" (pacati), there is no doubt regarding [the specific action] in the form of blowing (*phūtkāra*) and so forth. Nor does it follow that there would be polysemy (*nānārthatā*), because it is impossible for a single expressive power (*śakti*) to belong to multiple denotable properties (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as blowing and the like; it is precisely for this reason that polysemy is accepted in the case of words such as *hari*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*tadādi*):

Just as, in the case of the word "that" (*tad*), a single denotative power (*śakti*) is accepted with respect to that which is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth—by means of being present in the intellect (*buddhisthatva*), i.e., by means of a particular cognition serving as a secondary qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*)—in order to account for the cognition established by experience in its specific forms such as potness; so too, in the present case, it is possible, and thus there is no contingency of polysemy (*nānārthatva*), because even though there is a plurality of delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), a single delimiter of denotability is still possible. This is the meaning.

The acceptance of that [property] as a *upalakṣaṇa* (adventitious qualifier) is for the purpose of ensuring that it does not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by that word. And being an *upalakṣaṇa* consists in not being an object of the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śaktigraha*) by virtue of being an object of the cognition produced by that specific word. The phrase "of a particular cognition, etc. means "of a cognition whose object is the blowing [upon the fire], etc. The cognition's status as the delimitant of the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*) is by way of the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*).

Regarding the non-acceptance of its being a constituent of the delimitor (*avacchedakatā*) due to its not being a regulator of function (*vṛttyaniyāmakatva*), he says "of *ādi*," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the state of being the object of a specific cognition and the state of being its delimitor are included. Others, however, maintain that while words such as *pac* (to cook) may have multiple meanings—just like the word *hari* (lion/god)—this is acceptable; but words such as *tad* (that) denote their objects only by way of a general form consisting of "being present in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*). As it is stated in the commentary on the rule *śeṣe*: "For these [words] refer to specific instances, yet they speak of them as 'offspring,' 'residence,' or 'collection.'"

Now, one might object: since the operations (*vyāpāra*) consisting of the constituent parts are manifold, perish very rapidly, and occur sequentially, it is impossible for them to exist simultaneously; and since it is impossible to intend a single action (*ekakriyā*) residing in such a collection, the established rule that "a single action is conveyed by the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātenaikā kriyā pratyāyyate*) is untenable. Nor should it be argued that such an established rule is unproven due to a lack of evidence. [The response is: No.

He refutes the objection—that "the verbal suffixes (tiṅanta) necessitate the formulation of the *ekaśeṣa* rule"—by citing the authority of the Bhāṣya on the Svarūpa-sūtra itself, stating: "In the case of the verb (*ākhyāte*)," etc. This includes the restriction (*vyavasthā*)—namely, the rule that only a single action is conveyed—as well as the [qualification] beginning with "delimitor" (*avacchedaka*).

The meaning is that [it is] by taking the identity of that specific cognition which is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*)—that is, the delimitor of the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*). And that cognition is a single one in the form of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*); thus, the sense is that such a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is based upon the superimposition of identity residing in that cognition. Alternatively, the meaning is "by taking the identity of the collection residing in such a cognition. He cites the consensus of Harisvāmin regarding the stated point with the words "And it has been said," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by those that have become subordinate" (*guṇabhūtaiḥ*): the meaning is that the term "action" (*kriyā*) is conventionally applied to a collection which—though composed of constituent parts appearing in their respective forms—is conceived as non-different by a unifying cognition whose object is unity; this collection, which is of the nature of a conceptualized difference, consists of these constituent operations that arise in succession and have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) with respect to that whole. Furthermore, the non-difference pertains to the constituent operations themselves.

In this context, the sequence of prior and posterior based on the individual parts, as well as the unity residing in the aggregate, is clearly obtained. Since the nature of being an aggregate is superimposed upon each individual part, the linguistic usage such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) is justified even during the state of a single part, such as placing the pot on the fire. Regarding this superimposition, empirical cognition itself is the basis; it should be understood that the relationship between the root (*dhātu*) and the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—in the form of their expressive power (*śakti*)—is grasped precisely through the action apprehended via superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Because there exists no primary meaning other than that [superimposed one], the [primary] meaning of the root [is not required].

If this were the case, one might suspect that [the word] is being used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense; for secondary usage applies only to that which has a distinct primary meaning, as in "The boy is a lion" and so forth.

Alternatively, the action (*kriyā*) is simply the universal (*jāti*) such as cooking (*pākatva*) residing in various such individuals; even though it lacks inherent state-of-being-as-yet-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*), that property is established through its medium of the individuals. Its manifestation occurs through moments, just as in the case of the *sphoṭa*, and its proof is the uniform linguistic usage.
And it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:

"Others say that the universal (jāti) is the action, which resides in multiple individual instances; though it is unaccomplishable in its form as a universal, it is perceived as being accomplished through the form of the individual."

Even in the case of the result (*phala*), its manifestation occurs solely as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of the superimposition of a temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) existing within the operation of its own cause; for this very reason, even in the view that "roots such as *pac* denote only the result," the designation of such roots as verbal roots (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) is maintained, and the rule that "the factors of action (*kāraka*) are construed only with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)" becomes consistent. Otherwise, since the factor of action that is the object (*karman*)—expressed by the second case ending and so forth—would be construed with the result alone, the inconsistency of that [rule] would be evident.

In this context, the delimitors of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) are the specific sequential orders (*ānupūrvī*) such as *pac* and so forth, and not "stemness" (*dhātutva*), because the latter is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*) and because understanding occurs even for one who does not know [the term "stemness"]. Regarding the phrase "the locus of the result" (*phalāśraya*): if it is argued that, since it is the initiator of the entire cycle of factors (*kāraka*) and since the aspect of activity (*vyāpāra*) is primary, it would be more appropriate to say first "the locus of activity" rather than "the locus of the result," we reply: no.

In the rule *alaḥ karmaṇi* which determines the expressive power (*śakti*), and in the root text (*mūla*) as well, since the object (*karman*)—which is the locus of the result—is mentioned first, it is more logical that it alone should be denoted at the outset; furthermore, there is no restrictive rule stating that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is always primary, because there is deviation [from such a rule] when the suffixes for the object (*karmapratyaya*) are used in co-occurrence.

One might object: "Even though there are sūtras that establish the denotative power (*śakti*) for *karman* (object) and *kartṛ* (agent), there is nothing that establishes the denotative power of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) for the substratum of the result and the substratum of the operation, since in common usage the words *karman* and *kartṛ* are well-known as referring only to motion and volition. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The substratum of the result is the *karman*. The intended meaning is that, according to the principle of the artificial and the natural (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), it is proper that these two alone should be grasped by the terms *karman* and so forth.

Since the rule "the independent one is the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.54) prescribes the designation "agent" for that which is independent and is the substratum of the primary operation denoted by the verbal root, if that were prescribed only for that which possesses volitional effort (kṛti), then the [designation] would not apply to a jar in "the jar comes into being" (ghaṭo bhavati) or to wood in "the wood cooks" (kāṣṭhāni pacanti), and so forth; such is the general direction.

One might object: "Does this not entail that the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) would also have to be denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)? This is not an acceptable consequence, because in expressions such as ‘Devadatta cooks’ (*devadattaḥ pacati*), once the blowing (*phūtkāra*) and so forth are presented by both the suffix and the verbal root (*dhātu*), their mutual connection would be untenable due to a lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*). This is because there is no expectancy for something qualified by blowing to be connected with the act of blowing itself. For this very reason, the expression ‘the action goes’ (*karma gacchati*) is not used; and the same applies to cases such as ‘the rice is cooked’ (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*) and so on. To dispel this doubt, he says "tatra" and so forth.

"Because it is obtainable through the *dhātu*. The sense is that a word's denotative capacity (*śakyatva*) belongs only to that which cannot be obtained by any other means. Now, if one accepts that the power resides in the substratum (*āśraya*), then "substratum-hood" must be accepted as the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). Furthermore, substratum-hood is the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*), and that is differentiated according to the differences in the relata (*nirūpaka*) and so forth; since these are infinite, there would be the consequence of an infinity of powers. To this, he says: "that respective power" (*tattacchakti*). This means the essential nature of the power of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth.

The point is this: although one must admit that even a *śakti* (capacity) is manifold due to the difference in its relata—otherwise, in the sentence "Having eaten yesterday, he will eat in two days or after two days," the application of the locative and ablative cases under the rule *saptamī-pañcamyau kāraka-madhye* would remain untenable even if the word *kāraka* were taken to mean *śakti*—nevertheless, there is no room for objection if that [capacity] is taken as the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) by way of a common property such as "being a substratum" (*āśrayatātva*). For this very reason, the suffix *tṛc* denotes that which is qualified by an effort (*kṛti*).

The Naiyāyikas maintain that when used in conjunction with a verbal root whose meaning is an action (*kṛtyartha*), [the suffix] has the locus (*āśraya*) as its primary meaning. Similarly, in the case of *kṛt* suffixes, since the aspect of the action (*bhāvanā*) is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), the Mīmāṃsakas hold that "only the locus is the meaning."

Now, it might be argued that there is no evidence for the substratum (*āśraya*) being denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); nor can it be said that the cognition of the substratum which arises when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is the evidence for postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) in the suffix—just as the cognition of the meaning "cow" and so forth is the evidence for postulating the power of those respective meanings in words like "cow"—because only a cognition that cannot be otherwise accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*) serves as evidence. Otherwise, one would have to postulate a denotative power even for the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) with respect to its bank (*tīra*) and such. If it is argued that in that case the understanding occurs through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, [we reply:]...

For even in the case at hand (*prakṛta*), an alternative explanation will be stated later. Nor is the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi* etc. itself the authority [for the view that verbal suffixes denote the agent], because the word *karman* in that sūtra and the recurring word *kartṛ* can parsimoniously (*lāghavena*) be taken as referring merely to grammatical properties (*dharma-mātra*), or because that sūtra actually conveys the meaning "the *l*-suffixes signify the object and so forth. Thus, since the cognition [of the agent] can be accounted for even by the method to be explained later, the sūtra does not have the function of establishing that [agenthood] as the denotative power (*śakti*) [of the suffix]; with this intention, he asks: "Now, of these two... and so on.

"Because of the cognition" means because of the cognition of the substratum of the result and the substratum of the operation. He says "by implication" (*ākṣepāt*) because, if one were to accept metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the complexity of postulating a word-function (*pada-vṛtti*). "Implication" (*ākṣepa*) is, according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); according to the Logicians (*Tārkika*), it is inference (*anumāna*). That which is not possible without something else leads to the postulation of that [other thing]. For example, in the case of "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," since being fat is impossible without eating, eating is postulated; and that [eating] occurs at night.

In the case of the prohibition of eating at night, [the injunction] concludes by taking up that very act; likewise, in the present context, because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is untenable without an agent, it postulates an agent as its substratum. Thus, the cognition of this untenability is "implication" (*ākṣepa*), which is another name for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); the resulting cognition is also designated by that same name as a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramiti*). However, according to the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), "implication" refers to the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, which generates an inference such as: "The efficient force must reside in something, because it is a quality," or "It must have an agent, because it is an effect, like a jar."

Thus, it follows that by implication—either through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference—the agent is apprehended as the object subsequent to the knowledge of the cultivation [of the action]. Since the Mīmāṃsakas accept that even what is obtained through implication can be the object of verbal cognition, its appearance in the verbal cognition produced by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is not contradictory. Likewise, the meaning is that the result (*phala*) is also implied by the action, since it would otherwise be untenable without its own substratum.

Now, since the apprehension of word-meanings (*padārtha*) produced by words through their *vṛtti* (linguistic function) is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is impossible for that which is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) to be an object of verbal cognition. Furthermore, there would be an impossibility of such a cognition being established by experience even for those who lack the knowledge of "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) and so forth; moreover, there would be an impossibility of the number denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*) co-referentially connecting with the implied [object], because it is not presented by the word through its *vṛtti*. Thus it is said: "Verbal expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is indeed fulfilled by words alone."

"Verbal" (*śābdī*) means pertaining to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) means a desire to know; it is "fulfilled by the word itself"—that is, it is removed by the accomplishment of the establishment of the object through the function (*vṛtti*) of presenting the word-meaning—such is the meaning [of the objection]. Therefore, he says "the nominative case-ending," etc. He answers with the words "To this it is said," and so forth.

One might raise the objection: "But surely this sūtra establishes the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal root with respect to the *object* (*karman*), not the *agent* (*kartṛ*), because there is no word denoting the agent present therein. Anticipating this, he says: "For here... (atrā hi). Regarding the phrase "by the word 'ca'": if it is asked how that [word] can be understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) when all instances of the particle *ca* used for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) have been rejected in the Bhāṣya, understand that its occurrence here is possible—just as in other cases—due to the commitment to the principle of self-sufficiency (*svapitṛtva-pratijñāna*) and the force of requirement (*apekṣā*).

The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the sense of *bhāva* (action/state) is neither a denoter (*vācaka*) nor an indicator (*dyotaka*) of that meaning, because that meaning is clearly understood from the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself; furthermore, it expresses number and time, since the number inherent in its meaning—namely, singularity—is capable of being construed with the action. For this very reason, it is clear from the *Mañjūṣā*, the *Śekhara*, and other works that the question of why the singular number does not arise after indeclinables (*avyaya*) was not even raised in the *Bhāṣya*.

One might object: "By this sūtra, the capacity (*śakti*) consisting in the denotation of the object (*karman*) and so forth is understood to reside in the *l*-suffixes, but not in *ti* and the others; nor can it be argued that its establishment there [in *ti* etc. follows from the principle that 'the meaning of the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indeed the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*),' because the original element, not being employed, does not produce cognition. Desiring to dispel this doubt, he says "of the nature of denotative power" (*bodhakatārūpām*), and so on. It should be understood that even under the view that the capacity is something additional (*atiriktaśakti*), that capacity is strictly co-extensive with it [the *l*-suffix].

"Having the power of *ti* and so forth" means having the power residing in those [suffixes], because meaning is understood through their employment during the state of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). "As their substituends" means as the substituends of *ti* and so forth. "Postulated" means postulated for the sake of streamlining the grammatical process (*prakriyā*) by way of parsimony (*lāghava*).

One might object: "Let it be that, instead of repeating *alasye* (for the sake of ease), the rule *tiptasjhi...* prescribes only the independent *ti*, *tas*, and so on; likewise, let the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* be stated as *laḥ karmaṇi*; and let the rules *vartamāne tiṅ*, *tiṅśit sārvadhātukaṃ*, *śatṛśānacau prathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*, etc., merely refer back (*anūdya*) to *asti* and the other verbal roots to prescribe their respective tenses. If this is argued, we say no, because rules such as *dito ātmanepadānām* would then become incoherent.

Nor should it be argued that one may attach those respective indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) to the *tiṅ* suffixes signifying those specific times—such as "the *tiṅ*s in the present" (*vartamāne tiṅ*), "the *tiṅ*s in the non-recent past" (*anadyatane tiṅ*), and so forth—so that there would be no inconsistency in rules such as "*ṭita ātmanepadānām*" (Pāṇini 3.4.79). For even so, rules such as "*liṭastabhyoreśirec*" (Pāṇini 3.4.81) and "*luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.85) would still result in being inconsistent; furthermore, it would lead to the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) by necessitating the composition of various alternative commentaries (*nyāsas*) for each of those instances. Let this suffice. [The term] *prakalpya* means having superimposed.

The sense is that, in accordance with the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the relationship between the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) exists only when both are meaningful," there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [meaning] upon the other. [In this regard, he provides a corresponding example: "by the letter *na*," etc. The sense is that since the respective meanings are understood from the letter *na* and so forth in forms such as *rāmān* and *ghadaḥ*, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides precisely in those [letters]. [Regarding the phrase] "referring to agency and objecthood": this is due to the requirement of parsimony (*lāghava*).

If the primary referent were the substratum (*dharmin*), one would have to postulate a denotative capacity (*śakti*) for both the action and the substratum, which are heavy entities; furthermore, one would have to accept that an infinite number of actions and results serve as the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), resulting in extreme complexity (*atigaurava*). However, if the action itself is the denoted meaning, there is simplicity (*lāghava*), because the delimitor of denotability is simply "action-ness" (*kṛtitva*), which is a universal (*jāti*). This is the intended sense.

According to the method of the *Darśanāntarīya*—that is, according to the Mīmāṃsaka method stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*—[it is argued that] because there is an absence of being the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the result such as softening (*viklitti*) alone is the meaning of the root, and not the operation (*vyāpāra*). This is because, compared to postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) for many roots in that regard, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate it for fewer suffixes. Furthermore, since in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is explained by the root *kṛ*, which signifies productive activity (*bhāvanā*), it is logical that the finite verb itself has productive activity as its meaning; for the explained and the explanation must be identical.

The sense is that their synonymy is already established. Furthermore, since its result is also seen to be designated by the term "action" (*kriyā*) in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, the designation "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is established even for that which denotes only that [result]. The point is that in the same way, according to your own view as well, the status of being a verbal root belongs to *pac* and so on in the sentence *pacyate taṇḍulaḥ svayameva*.

In that context—regarding the *vyāpāra* (operation)—the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for [suffixes such as] *ṇvul* and others are either the state of being an operation (*vyāpāratva*) or the state of being a blowing (*phūtkāratva*), etc. Thus, it must be supplied [to the argument]: "Even though the result (*phala*) is obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*), the rule for the *l*-suffixes would apply only to the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the form of being the locus of that [result]. For this very reason, the mention of "object" (*karman*) and so forth in the subsequent text—"there is no denotation of agent, object, and so on"—is consistent; otherwise, if the proponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*) did not admit the denotation of the object, that inconsistency would be obvious. This applies to the *kṛt* suffixes as well.

[The opponent argues: "Even for suffixes such as *ṇvul*, *tavyat*, and so on, which are prescribed [by Pāṇini] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and others, [the denotation of the agent would not be established]. The meaning is that this follows from the parity of the reasoning already stated. [The opponent continues: "But surely, by the force of grammatical rules (anuśāsana) such as ‘*kṛt* [suffixes] [denote] the agent’ (*kartari kṛt*) and ‘*kṛtya* [suffixes] [denote] those two [the agent and the object] only’ (*tayoreva kṛtya*), the fact that *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent and so forth is established; for in those [rules], the words ‘agent’ (*kartṛ*) and so on refer to the substratum (*dharmī*) [possessing the property]. To this, [the author] says: “And [as for] the rule ‘*kartari kṛt*’... The word “and” (*ca*) includes the inclusion of rules such as ‘*tayoreva*’. [This is because the opponent’s position is] equally vulnerable to refutation (*tulyayogakṣema*).

The meaning is that its capacity to convey the intended sense (*arthapratipādakatā*) is equal [in both cases]. This is the underlying point: if, out of a mere partiality for parsimony (*lāghava*), one accepts that the words "object" (*karman*) and so forth in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* refer to properties (*dharma*), then it is equally appropriate to accept that very same thing there as well; for there is no reason for such inconsistency (*vaiṣamya*).

Now, having raised the objection that the status of [the verb] as denoting the substratum (dharmin) is established by the force of the experience of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) with Devadatta and others, while the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) will be obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), [the author] replies with "Moreover" (*api ca*). It is appropriate to accept that same status in the present case as well, precisely by the force of the experience of non-difference. The phrase "of the Mīmāṃsakas" has "in their view" (*mate*) as its ellipsis. "That being so" means: if it were obtainable through implication. "It would not [be primary]" is because it is not directly expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and because of the rule that primacy belongs only to that which is directly expressed.

Otherwise, in cases such as "Bring fire," there would be the undesirable consequence that even the vessel or other implied accessories would attain primacy. Furthermore, regarding the Mīmāṃsaka tenet that in the statement "The peacock does not dance on anything other than the mountain, yet it dances," the locus (adhikaraṇa) postulated because dancing is otherwise inexplicable is established as a locus of the nature of absolute exclusion (paramatara-rūpa) due to the negation of other loci; in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence that this locus itself attains primacy.

For this very reason, it is not the reverse; for even in the case of *kṛt* suffixes, just as in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes, the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is denoted by the suffix, and thus it would result in its predominance with respect to the agent implied [by the verbal root]. [And thus there would be a contradiction with experience. Accordingly, the Bhaṭṭas have stated: "If the *bhāvanā* were understood through the agent or through the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then it would be understood as having its own form obscured, as in words such as *pācaka* (cook) or *pāṭhaka* (reader). However, because of its predominance, it is determined to be the primary meaning of the word. This is the sense.

The phrase "as in 'bring the jar' and so forth" means that just as in the case of "bring the jar," since it is logically untenable for the universal (*jāti*) to be the object of the act of bringing, the individual instance (*vyakti*) which is the substratum of that universal—which is implied by the universal—is established by experience as being primary in order to make its connection [with the action] possible; likewise, it is possible to establish that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is implied by the agent denoted by the verbal suffix, possesses primacy as established by experience. The underlying point is that the previously stated rule is subject to exceptions.

Nor should it be argued that because [the agent] is expressed by a suffix (pratyaya), the agent alone must necessarily be primary; for there is a rule that whatever is implied by the meaning of a suffix is not primary. Consequently, one might claim that the objection—that the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* would be undermined if there were a rule that everything merely implied is non-primary—has no basis. However, this is incorrect, because there is no evidence for such a rule, and because there is a counter-example (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "Bring the owner of cows" (*gomantam ānaya*), where the substratum implied by the relation denoted by the possessive suffix (*matup*) is experienced as being primary.

"Because of the observation of a paraphrase (*vivaraṇa*)," that is, because one observes the paraphrase "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) using the verbal root *kṛ*, which signifies the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). "Expressibility" (*vācyatva*) means being expressible by the suffix. "Because there is no difference in being the object of paraphrase": the paraphrase of the agent is provided by the verb "he performs" (*karoti*); since the agent is also understood from that, the sense is that it is necessary for even that which is being paraphrased to have that [the agent] as its meaning. "Intentional meaning" (*tātparyārtha*): the paraphrase refers to the agent obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), which is the object of the intention "let the understanding of the agent arise from the word *pacati*"; it does not refer to the paraphrase of the literal lexical meaning (*śabdārtha*).

[Objection: "But since only the explanation of word-meanings is observed, this [explanation of a relation] is not an explanation of a word-meaning. To refute this by showing a corresponding observed instance, he says: "pākaṃ karoti" (he does cooking). [Response: Even though one observes the explanation of a relation—which is not a word-meaning—through the explanation of its status as an object (*karma*) via the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), one might still harbor the doubt that the explanation of something other than a word-meaning has never been seen before. Anticipating this, he provides another example: "itaretaradvandva" (mutual conjunction). He adds: "the aspect of conjunction" (*samuccayāṃśa*).

The aspect of conjunction is explained by means of the two [reasons]. Regarding the phrase "because of their equality": the meaning is that even if *bhāvanā* lacks the status of being the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), its explanation remains possible according to the method stated; consequently, it would not be established that *bhāvanā* is also the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*).

One might object: "By virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is *bhāvanā* alone that is denoted by the suffix, and not the agent, because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). If that were the case, then even [grammatical] participles (*kṛt*) would have that same status.
