This should not be suspected, because in examples such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), the cognition of a coreferential relation (*abhedānvaya*) with Devadatta and so forth is established by experience. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiñca*). "Because of the observation of coreferential relation"—that is, because the coreferential relation is established by experience. "The state of having the same case-ending" (*samānavibhaktimattvam*).

The requirement is that the qualifier and the qualificand words, which denote the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) of that [relation], must possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktimattva*). This consists in either the word denoting the qualifier possessing a case-ending of the same class as the case-ending following the word denoting the qualificand, or the word denoting the qualificand possessing a case-ending of the same class as the case-ending following the word denoting the qualifier.

Homogeneity (*sājātya*) is determined by the property of being a nominative (*prathamātva*), which is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) that distinguishes the case-inflections (*vibhakti*). Therefore, because all inflections—the nominative, accusative, and so on—are not homogeneous by virtue of the general property of being an inflection (*vibhaktitva*), there is no risk of an unintended cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) arising from a sentence such as "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*). The term *nayāmaka* means "the cause" or "the determinant. The phrase "it does not exist" means that because there is no homogeneity between the nominative and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) by way of a single common form, and thus, due to the absence of the determinant for a cognition of non-difference, such a cognition is impossible; hence, the view that the substratum (*dharmin*) possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) is not tenable. This is the intended meaning.

He states that "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*) because it is impossible for the property of having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktimattva*) to be the restrictive factor due to its deviation (*vyabhicāra*). In this context, the word *soma* has an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that which possesses soma; there is a syntactic connection (*abhedānvaya*) of that which possesses soma with the sacrifice; and it is precisely out of deference to this connection of non-difference that the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is accepted here—this is explained in detail in the *Nyāyaprakāśa* and other works.

In the expression *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"), the meaning of the word *stoka* (slightness) is construed with the fruit of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha-phala*) by way of identity (*abheda*). In *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the meaning of the word *rājan* (king)—which possesses the relation of kingship—is construed with the man through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In the first two cases mentioned here, there is an absence of the qualified [relation] (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) due to the lack of homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*) between the two case-endings; however, in the last case, it is due to the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣyābhāva*).

The distinction is that [the agent] is "employed" (prayukta). This is because there would be no resulting cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*); the implication is that this is due to the absence of the condition of having the same case-ending as the verb (*aktasamānavibhaktimattva*). Thus, the intended meaning is that in the aforementioned instance, the cognition of non-difference occurs without obstacle, and for its justification, a denotative power (*śakti*) in the agent and so forth is necessary.

He raises the doubt with the words "na ceti" (if it is not so). Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in the denotation of a single substratum; thus, since the cognition of the relation of identity can be accounted for through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, the acceptance of primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that case is purposeless—this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "because of the non-attainment of denoting a substance": this is because the cognition of a substance is accomplished through indication alone. The phrase "of these and other secondary suffixes (*taddhita*)" means "of those secondary suffixes that constitute such groups as 'ityādi'. Here, the connection is made by supplying the phrase "because of the impossibility of denoting a substance" from the preceding context.

Now, since the rule "anekaṃ anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) prescribes that a *bahuvrīhi* compound denotes something other than the meanings of the words being compounded, that which is understood as residing in the constituent members (*varti*)—being subordinate (*upasarjana*) in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—is indeed the "other meaning" (*anyapadārtha*), such as the owner (*svāmin*). Furthermore, the distinction between the analytical sentence and the compound sentence consists precisely in the reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified; this is another point.

And thus, the construction is as follows: "How [could there be] the teaching that derivative (yaugika) words denote substances?"—because of the demonstration of the analysis (*vigraha*) [of the compound], one obtains the teaching [of grammatical correctness] precisely in the sense of the primary genitive (*pradhāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). By this teaching—that is, by the teaching in the form of this [rule] in the *Śāstra*—the term "by the teaching" (*anuśāsane-na*) is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the instrumental sense. "Because of the demonstration of the analysis"—that is, for the reason of demonstrating such an analysis; the meaning is: because one obtains the teaching, i.e., the grammatical justification (*sādhutva-anvākhyāna*), specifically in the sense of the primary genitive.

This word *anuśāsana* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, which denotes an abstract action (*bhāva*). Its acquisition [of the genitive sense] arises from its analysis (*vigraha*) in the sense of a genitive-terminated term. And by means of a genitive-terminated term, only the relation—which is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*)—is understood as being superimposed upon the base (*prakṛti*); therefore, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is obtained only in that context. This is the collective intended meaning. And it has been stated in the *Vārttika* on the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*:
"This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound prescribed in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*);
and the possessive suffix functions in the sense of a relation expressed as 'this belongs to this'."

[The same should be understood regarding words such as *vaiśvadeva* and others; and it is not a case of an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), as he says with the words "and so," etc. Regarding the phrase "due to the non-mention of a substance": the sense is that, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, a word such as *aruṇā* (red) is assumed to have its denotative power (*śakti*) only in respect to the quality of redness and the like, whereas a word such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) is assumed to have its denotative power in respect to the relation itself, in accordance with the method already stated. The term "in its own sentence" (*svavākye*) means: its own [efficient force], namely the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of purchasing; the meaning is that it is conveyed by words such as *piṅgākṣī* which are constituent parts of the sentence expressing that [urge].]

In this context, since redness (*aruṇya*) is formless, it is impossible for it to serve as an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the efficient force of purchasing (*krayaṇabhāvanā*); consequently, it is impossible to enjoin it with reference to that [purchase]. However, since even a word denoting a quality can, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), denote a substance, the quality of redness is enjoined as a delimiting factor with reference to the substances mentioned in the context, which are distinct from the act of purchase, in the sense that "whatever substance is used to perform something, it must be possessed of the quality of redness."

If it is argued: "Since the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the substance indicated by implication (*lakṣita-dravya*) is possible only in the act of purchase (*kraya*), why do you accept a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*)?", we say no. This is because when the purchase is already restricted by the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow), it is impossible to enjoin another substance indicated by implication. If it is further argued: "The injunction of the *ekahāyanī* itself, qualified by its specific attribute, is easy to accomplish," we say no; for once something has been enjoined by its own word (*sva-śabda*), a double injunction (*punar-vidhāna*) is impossible. Nor should it be said: "Let there be an injunction of the quality (*guṇa-vidhi*) by restating (*anūdya*) the *ekahāyanī* itself; in this way, there will be no split of the sentence. [This is not tenable.]

If that were the case, then [the word *aruṇā*] would be subordinate to the act of purchasing (*krayaṇa*) and would also have its own independent purpose; and this is not possible through a single utterance, because there is a contradiction between being subordinate and being primary. Therefore, the consequence would be repetition (*āvṛtti*). Consequently, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that one should assume a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and apply the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) to all substances mentioned in the context, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: by means of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), it is clearly understood that the quality itself is the instrument with respect to the purchase, and this is logically consistent only when mediated by a substance.

It has been stated: although, because a quality (*guṇa*) is formless, its status as a means toward the purchase (*kraya*) is not possible, nevertheless, it is indeed possible by way of delimiting the substance (*dravya*). Thus, the meaning becomes: "One should effect the purchase with a substance delimited by redness. In this way, since the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) of the directly expressed (*śrauta*) quality itself is possible, neither figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) nor a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is appropriate; and if it serves the purpose of the action, its placement is within that very substance. This has been explained by Pārthasārathi Miśra; so, enough with further elaboration.

Thus, since the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) contained in words such as *vaiśvadevī* lacks the capacity to denote a substance according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is said: "This secondary suffix expresses *āmikṣā* as being connected with the deity;
through its proximity to the word *āmikṣā*, it itself provides the object [of the sacrifice]."

Thus, one should observe the contradiction with the Bhaṭṭa school’s established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and the resulting annihilation of the *guṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning subordinate qualities) which is rooted therein. To explain: in the Vaiśvadeva section within the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* is for the Vājins. Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as follows: by the sentence "the *vājina* is for the Vājins," with reference to the Viśvedevas—who are designated by the word *vājin* through the etymological derivation "those who possess *vāja*, i.e., food in the form of *āmikṣā*"—a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) in the form of *vājina* is enjoined within the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice already commenced. [This is refuted by the Siddhāntin: because of the scriptural injunction of the [quality] taught at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*)...

Because the substance [curd] is already occupied by the *āmikṣā* and is thus free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatayā*), it is impossible for the *vājina* to be included in the sacrifice under discussion; therefore, a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaram*) characterized by that quality and having a new deity is enjoined. If the connection of the *vājina* were to occur within the sacrifice under discussion, it would have to be through the sentence expressing its production (*bhavana-vākyena*). However, since the connection with the *āmikṣā* has already been established by the stronger direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the *taddhita* suffix prior to that, there is no further expectancy. Even though there is a dependence on another word, namely the word "āmikṣā," this is still considered a purely Vedic (*śrauta*) connection because it depends on another word whose meaning is distinct from itself.

Regarding *viniyoga* (application): where there is a dependence on another word with a distinct meaning, there the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇa*) applies; thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated that there is an injunction of a different quality or action. However, according to the aforementioned method, the inconsistency of that [conclusion] is quite evident. This refers to the reasoning stated in the root-text regarding "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). [The root-reasoning proving the denotation of a substance; the unique reason: "Grammatical coreferentiality"—as in "a brown-eyed cow" (*piṅgākṣī gauḥ*) or "the curd for the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*)—is a coreferentiality established by experience. The meaning is that, according to the aforementioned method, its [the coreferentiality's] occurrence is possible through implication (*ākṣepa*) and so forth.

And thus, in the case of derivative words such as *gomat* and *piṅgākṣī*, there is nothing that proves that either the word as a whole or its constituent suffix denotes a substance (*dravya*), since the cognition of that [substance] can be accounted for through implication (*ākṣepa*) and so forth; the point is that, therefore, they would not have that denotative capacity.

[Objection: But in that case, from the word *gomattva* ("cow-possessing-ness"), there would be no cognition of a relation (*saṃsarga*), because the meaning of the suffix *matUP* is precisely the delimitor of the referent of the base (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). [Response: This is not so, for just as the denotable genus (*jāti*) is manifested from words such as *go* ("cow"), its manifestation is likewise possible here. [Objection: But in the cognition produced by the base, its manifestation is possible as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the aspect of the individual (*vyakti*) which is implied. [Response: This is not so, for the same principle applies in the present case as well.

As for the argument presented by the authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* to prove that the suffix *-matup* denotes the substance itself—namely, that the general relation (*saṃbandha-sāmānya*) cannot be the denoted meaning of words such as *gomat* or *daṇḍin*, because that would result in their becoming synonyms; nor can it be a specific relation (*saṃbandha-viśe�sha*), since the particularity therein consists precisely in the nature of the related entity (*saṃbandhin*), and therefore that must necessarily be denoted, as it is impossible for what is not expressed to function as a differentiator; and even when one of the two related entities is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since a relation is defined by both parties—[the author proceeds to state the following].

If it were necessary to provide a second designation [that is, if both were denotable], there would, on the contrary, be prolixity; therefore, by parsimony, the substance alone is the denotation of the suffix *matup* and the like. Since that [substance] is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), there is no expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the relation. And it has been said:
"In all cases, substances alone are denoted by derivative (*yaugika*) words;
for it is not possible for the relation to be the denotation, because that would involve excessive prolixity."
Furthermore:
"If a relation can be understood through the related entity itself,
who would then attribute a denotative power to that [relation] on the basis of the Vedic word?"
If it is argued that the expression of a relation would not be possible through the very sublation of the [inherent] state (*bhāva*), we say no.
For: "When no other quality inherent in its own substratum exists here as the denotable object, then, because there is no other alternative, the relation is resorted to as the denotable object."

The meaning is as follows: since the reasoning for expressing that [meaning] has been stated by this [sūtra], and because cows—which serve as qualifiers of the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*)—do not inhere in the person, it is impossible for them to be grasped by the *tva*-suffix which denotes qualities that inhere [in the same substratum]. Therefore, in the absence of any other recourse (*agatyā*), the relation implied by the sense of the word is accepted as the meaning of that [suffix]. As for the objection that such a compound must have the sense of a genitive relation (*ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha*) because of the analysis (vigraha) "one year belonging to her" (*ekam hāyanam asyāḥ*), that too is not valid.

Because, following the sense of the suffix *matup* (possessive), it is accepted that only sentences such as "this belongs to various cows" (*citragavām ayam*) constitute the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) [of the compound]; as it has been said:
"Although the denotation of a *bahuvrīhi* is said to be 'this belongs to him' (*asyeti*), nevertheless, it is understood as being equivalent to a word ending in the nominative case."

On this point, the authors of the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa* say: since suffixes such as the possessive *matup* would become synonyms if they denoted substance in general, it is necessary to accept that they denote specifically [the substance] by virtue of its equality [with other qualifiers]. In that case, the "particular" (*viśeṣa*) must be either a relation (*saṃsarga*) or the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), such as "cow. In the first alternative, since that which is not perceived and not expressed cannot function as a qualifier, its status as something directly expressed (*vācyatva*) must be accepted; and thus, the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is quite evident.

Even in the final view—that [the suffix] expresses the relation—it is not appropriate to disregard that position simply because the meaning of the nominal stem, such as "cow" (*go*), could serve as a qualifier by virtue of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For in the theory of the perception of relations, the perception of all related entities is a necessary cause; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of perceiving the conjunction between a jar and space. Thus, since a relation is defined by two relata, and its cognition cannot be established without the knowledge of the second relatum, the objection that it must necessarily express that [second relatum] is refuted.

And thus, just as from the word *gomat* there arises the cognition "qualified by a cow," the cognition "connected with a cow" is indeed unimpeded. This is due to the very nature of the power of words: just as that which is conveyed by the term *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) does not necessitate its substratum, whereas that which is conveyed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) does necessitate it, so too, although the relation conveyed by the word "relation" (*saṃbandha*) does not necessitate its substratum, it is possible for that same relation—when conveyed by a possessive suffix such as *-mat*—to necessitate its substratum.

Alternatively, even the argument beginning with "or that which is inherent in itself" (*yadvā svasamaveta*) is untenable. This is because the restrictive rule—that suffixes such as *matup* denote a quality (*guṇa*) inherent in themselves—is unestablished. Furthermore, under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, if one accepts that [suffixes] denote the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then suffixes like *matup* would not denote a relation; consequently, the suffix *-tva* would not apply to forms such as *gomattva*. If, on the other hand, they were to denote what is inherent in the meaning of the base, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*atigaurava*). Moreover, from the form *ghaṭatvatva*, there would result the cognition of *ghaṭatvatva* alone [rather than the universal].

It should be understood that even though the word *ghaṭa* (pot) denotes *ghaṭatva* (potness), the power (*śakti*) of denoting [the substance] such as a pot is necessary for the sake of primary comprehension; thus, there is no suspicion of redundancy. Therefore, since there is no fault in the relation being the expressed meaning and because it is obtainable through grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), that alone should be the expressed meaning, and not the substance (*dravya*). If it is argued that the substance is the expressed meaning of the suffix *-matup* and so forth in order to account for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then the same applies to the present case as well; this has been explained in detail in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*. With this intention, he says "in detail."

If it is argued that—on the basis of the sentence-meaning of *Pāṇini’s* rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (3.4.69) together with *tip-tas-jhi... dvacekayordvivacanaikavacane* (1.4.22), which establishes that *ti*, *tas*, *jhi*, and so forth, bearing the technical designations *ekavacana* and so on, occur in place of the *l*-suffixes when there is singularity and so on of the object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*)—it is understood from the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) that number alone, such as singularity, is the denoted meaning (*vācya*), and not the agent or the object; and that this point has been upheld by the venerable Śabarasvāmin—this is not so, because of the technical designation *ekavacana* and so forth...

By virtue of being restricted to specific substitutes (*ādeśa*), rules such as "for two or one" (*dvacekayoḥ*) form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunctions for *ti* and other suffixes alone; they do not, however, form a single syntactical unit with the rule "l-affixes [denote] the object" (*laḥ karmaṇi*), for in that latter rule, there is no mention of "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) and so forth.

Therefore, since it is impossible for the stated meaning [of the agent] to be conveyed [by the *l*-suffix], there can be no syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) between the rule for the *l*-suffixes (*lavidhi*) and the rules for the substitutes (*ādeśavidhi*); rather, there is syntactic unity at the level of the sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*), because the rule prescribing the substitutes operates by way of restating the verbal suffixes obtained from the rule for the *l*-suffixes. Furthermore, that [verbal suffix] is entirely devoid of technical designations such as "singular" and so forth. Consequently, once the comprehension of the sentence-meaning has first been effected by the rule "laḥ karmaṇi... (Pāṇini 3.4.69), and subsequently, through syntactic unity with another rule, the *l*-suffix is prescribed therein by taking up meanings such as the agent; thus, its status as the primary denotable meaning (*vācyatva*) is indeed unavoidable.

If it is argued that, by the rule "the *laṭ* [suffix] is used for the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*), it is possible to establish a syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) with respect to the suffixes prescribed therein according to the aforementioned method—even so, just as in the case of *sup*-suffixes, it would be difficult to avoid the conclusion that in *tiṅ*-suffixes as well, the agent (*kartṛ*) and other factors are the meanings of the suffix, while number is merely a qualifier thereof. Furthermore, if this were the case even in the objective (*karman*) aspect, then since the object too would not be directly expressed (*avācya*), there would be the undesirable consequence that in examples such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), the understanding of the object could not occur because the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) cannot imply it—since the operation deviates from the object (as it may also lead to other objects).

Even though there is the possibility of implying a substratum through the number associated with the meaning of the verb, the cognition [of that substratum] as possessing the capacity for the state of being an object (*karmatva*) remains impossible. Now, if the agent were the expressed meaning (*vācya*), then in the prohibition "one should not speak untruth," because direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than context (*prakaraṇa*), it would follow that this applies solely to the person's purpose (*puruṣārtha*) and not to the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Consequently, even if such false speech were uttered during a sacrifice, there would be no occasion for the expiation for the failure of the sacrifice; yet this is not an acceptable conclusion, as it contradicts the practice of ritualists (*yājñika*).

If it is argued that this is not so because it contradicts the natural sense of the Bhāṣya in the *Paspaśāhnika*, which states: "Some sages who know the distant and the near, when they ought to say 'yarvāṇas' or 'tarvāṇas', instead use 'varvāṇas' or 'tarvāṇas'; yet they do not speak thus in sacrificial rites; there were indeed sages named Yarvāṇas and Tarvāṇas," then we reply: no.

There is no fault here, because through the scriptural statement (*śruti*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is possible for [the act] to serve both the sacrifice and the person; for the consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) only proceeds when there is a conflict between two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the present case, there is no such conflict. Otherwise, in the case of the text "While yawning, one should recite 'O Mind and Vital Force!'," since the yawning person exists even during the sacrifice, your own established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that [the act] serves the purpose of the sacrifice by way of being a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) based on the non-conflicting [evidence of] sentence and context—would be undermined. This has been explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works;
enough of this prolixity.

Anticipating the objection that since the grammatical rule *nu laḥ karmaṇi-* teaches that the *l*-suffixes denote the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), the statement "but the *tiṅ*-suffixes denote the substratum" (*āśraye tu tiṅaḥ*) is incorrect, he says: "the capacity to convey" (*bodhakatā*). In this context—among the meanings such as the agent and so forth—"agent" and "object" [refer respectively to the operation and the result]. That is to say, "agent" is a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*), and "object" is a qualifier of the result (*phala*). [In the case of an object-suffix, the word "object" (*karmani*) is] understood as being connected with the word "qualifier."

One might object: "Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is presented by the base (*prakṛti*), it too is proximate; why then is it not qualified? Furthermore, since it is logical that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) should connect with the meaning of the base, and because we observe that the number expressed by a case-ending (*subartha*) connects with the meaning of the base, it is appropriate for that [suffix-meaning] to connect with that very [base-meaning]. To dispel this doubt, he states the reason for its being a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth: "because of equal proximity" (*samāna*). Thus, due to a greater degree of proximity compared to the meaning of the verbal root, the connection occurs with that [agent] alone.

This is appropriate. For this very reason, in the commentary on the sūtra *anabhihite*, it is stated that when this [word *ekatve*] is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the sūtra *prātipadikārtha*, it would be a qualifier of number alone, since nothing else is possible. Consequently, this explains quite naturally why it was said that in examples such as *pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*, the nominative case would not occur because singularity and so forth have already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). However, if that [number] were construed with the action (*kriyā*), the inconsistency of that statement would be evident.

For this very reason, the teacher Kaiyaṭa stated: "Since the singularity of the agent in the expression 'pacati' (he cooks) is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the nominative case would not occur. In the *rūpap* sūtra, they likewise explained the Bhāṣya passage—"In cases such as 'pacataḥ' (they two cook), there is a dual number dependent on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)"—in exactly this same way. Furthermore, it is impossible for duality to be non-superimposed upon the action, and there is no evidence for superimposition in all instances.

"Furthermore, among *ṭib*-ending words, some have the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) as primary, while others have the action (*kriyā*) as primary; for example, *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye* have the meaning of the case-ending as primary, whereas *ramate brāhmaṇakulam* has the action as primary. And neither of these two types of meanings is connected with gender (*liṅga*) and number (*saṃkhyā*)"—this would contradict the *bhāṣya* on the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake*. [Is this not so? Here, the view is that [the connection] is "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). By this, there is no inconsistency even when such a connection occurs in cases like *hataśāyikāḥ*.
In instances like *pacatorūpam*, the default singular number (*autsargikaikavacanam*) applies just as in *pacatirūpam*.

In reality, even in cases such as *hataśāyikā* ("those who have slept after being killed"), number does not apply to the action (*kriyā*) as an insentient entity (*asattvabhūta*); rather, the plural number used there is due solely to the authority of the Bhāṣyakāra’s statement—this is clear in works such as the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*. Others, however, maintain that in the case of verbal forms ending in a bhāva-tiṅ (impersonal passive), the singular number is the default (*autsargika*) because the action is insentient; otherwise, in instances such as *brāhmaṇābhyām āsyate* ("it is sat by two Brāhmaṇas"), the dual number and so forth would result, since a difference in agents is necessitated by the difference in actions.

Even for the Mīmāṃsakas, Naiyāyikas, and others, the connection with number is intended to reside in the *sādhana* (the factor of action) alone, not in the *kriyā* (the action itself); the only difference is that in their view this connection occurs with what is presented by another word (*padāntara*), whereas in our own view it occurs with what is presented by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "many people cook" (*anekaḥ pacati*) or "the wife cooks" (*dārāḥ pacanti*), the connection with a superimposed number is necessarily required even in the *sādhana*; for the point is that there is no evidence to accept such a thing there, since one has no other recourse.

However, in the case of a subordinate case-ending (*subvibhakti*), since its number cannot be construed with that which is presented by the same suffix (*samānapratyayopātta*), its construction occurs only with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Even if such construction were possible under the view that the object (*karman*) and so forth are denoted by the case-ending (*vibhaktivācyatāmatam*), it is certainly impossible under the view that they are merely indicated (*dyotyatāmatam*).

And so it has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "The plural is used for many": "In that case, then, [terms] such as 'singular,' 'dual,' and 'plural' are merely technical designations of words; they refer to those meanings for which the case-endings (svādayaḥ) are prescribed. For which meanings are the case-endings prescribed? For 'many' [meanings]. Which meanings are they? The object (karman) and so forth. But surely the object and so forth are not the primary meanings of the case-endings. What then? Singularity and so forth. Even when singularity and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, the object and so forth must necessarily be taken as the causal conditions (nimitta). [For instance,] in the case of an object..."

"In the case of oneness, in the case of duality of the object, and in the case of plurality of the object. Here, by the force of commencing the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"), it is intended that number is "denoted by the case-ending" (*vibhaktivācyā*), while the fourfold [categories] constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). This is the purport of the passage beginning with "Indeed, [the categories] such as object (*karman*)... and ending with "What then are oneness and so forth? [The answer is: they are the meanings of the case-endings.

They say that this is the end of the treatise (*grantha*). Others, however, maintain that this treatise intends to show that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of the five [categories] (number, gender, substance, quality, and action), because it is improper to apply the "half-old woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya*). Even in this view, they say that the [numbers] such as singularity are intended to be primary, with the intention that—given the syntactic unity with rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) when there is an expectancy for a substratum (*āśraya*) regarding singularity and so on—they serve as the cause [of case application] by virtue of being proximate and possible.

And thus, by virtue of the proximity consisting in being conveyed by the same cognition (*samānapratyayopāttatva*), the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is construed only with its other referent, namely the substratum (*āśraya*). It should also be understood that this follows because [the rules] such as *laḥ karmaṇi*, *tiptasjhi*, and *dvayekayoḥ* constitute a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*), whereby those suffixes are prescribed for the agent and so forth as qualified by singularity and the like.

In this regard, however, O venerable ones, for those [opponents], there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between sentences in the manner previously stated, not syntactic unity between words (*padaikavākyatā*). And that [unity] takes the form: "The *lakāra*s occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) and so forth, and in place of them, *tiP* and the other suffixes occur in the sense of singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. For in that case, because the second word beginning with "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) is absent, it is impossible for singularity and so forth to function as qualifiers of the object and so forth. Furthermore, there is no evidence for [the] repetition [of the rule]; therefore, the number (*saṃkhyā*) is construed only with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

When there arises the expectation, "Of what [is there oneness, etc.]?", the meaning is simply "of oneness, etc., residing in the meaning of the base (prakṛti)," because it is appropriate for the connection to be with that very base-meaning which is present [in the mind]. For in this way, uniformity is achieved between the rules governing *sup*-suffixes and *tiṅ*-suffixes, such as "for the singular and dual" (*advayekayoḥ*) and so forth. For this very reason, even the fact of being presented by the same suffix (*samānapratyayopāttatva*) is irrelevant; since [the meanings of] "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) and so forth are subordinate (*guṇa*) to the thing to be enjoined, and according to the maxim "subordinates exist for the sake of another," a connection with number is impossible for them.

Furthermore, there is no impossibility of dual number and so forth due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of the number residing in the means (*sādhana*) expressed by the suffixes inherent in their own nature (*svaprakṛtika*). Because there exists a mental certainty (*mānasaniścaya*) whose object is the means and which has that number as its qualifier—this being the very basis for the superimposition—there can be no doubt regarding that number in relation to the agent (*kartṛ*) and so on. However, in cases such as *devadattayajñadattābhyāṃ bhūyate* ("it is being experienced by Devadatta and Yajñadatta") or *supyate* ("it is being slept"), one should not expect dual number and so forth based on the superimposition of duality and so forth residing in the agent.

This is because, by virtue of the nature of *śakti*, it is accepted that the number residing in the means (*sādhana*) expressed by the suffix belonging to its own base (*svaprakṛtika*) alone is superimposed upon the action, and not the number residing in a means expressed by a separate word; and because, according to the conclusion of the Bhāṣya, it is established that in the case of "many [people] cook" (*anekaḥ pacati*), it is precisely the number residing in the means that is superimposed which conveys the meaning.

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Mahābhāṣya*, a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense. Consequently, in cases such as "it is cooked five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pacyate*), although plurality is introduced through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another word, the doctrine of word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra-pakṣa*) alone is accepted in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya-anusāreṇa*); thus, there is no contingency of using the plural number. Furthermore, by means of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the action is presented precisely as differentiated by cessation (*nivṛtti-bheda*). As stated by Bhartṛhari:

"Even though the action denoted by a verb is unitary, it is differentiated by the number residing in the substratum of the means (*sādhana*); however, that which is called gender (*liṅga*), being a locus of differentiation, is not so differentiated."

And this has been explained by Helārāja: "In expressions such as *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*, *pacyete*, and *pacyante*, the action (*kriyā*) is qualified by the duality or plurality of the substrates (*sādhana*)—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)—which are introduced by a single word; for it is by that [number] that [the action is qualified]."

It is understood that an action is to be accomplished by means of two arms; likewise, there is no connection with the gender (liṅga) residing therein, because the cognition of the word-meaning is innate and thus not accessible through logical reasoning. Thus, taking up the introductory verse of Harikārikā, "This [action] has its distinction born from the relation," Puñjarāja states: "Just as in the case of the verb *ākhyāta*, when there is a difference in the form expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*), a distinction is perceived even in the action which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) due to that relation, as in *pacataḥ* (two cook) and *pacanti* (they cook)."

In this context, the intention is that from the example ending in the dual number, unity is understood as residing in the [action] itself (*svagata*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, when the objection is raised that if the rule were not formulated, there would be the undesirable consequence of case-endings (*sup*) arising after finite verb forms such as *pacati*—since numbers like singularity are said to be expressed by the suffixes (*tiṅ*)—the objection is refuted. In your view, even though the number residing in the means (*sādhana*) is expressed, the number residing in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is the primary element, is not expressed; therefore, the arising of case-endings (*sup*) is unavoidable, because case-endings denote the number residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Likewise, in the *Rūpapasūtrabhāṣya*, having raised the objection that in forms such as *pacatirūpam* and *pacatīrūpam*, the neuter gender and the absence of number are untenable because [the verb] lacks gender and number, it is stated: "The finite verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning; and since action is one and does not possess duality or other numbers, no distinction is perceived from the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Furthermore, the neuter gender arises from its very nature. Having raised the further objection—"If action is one, how can there be dual endings and so forth in cases like *pacataḥ*?"—it is replied that "this [number] depends upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). In this regard, the interpretation that the connection of duality and so forth occurs with the *sādhana* (the agent or object) is not tenable.

Because there would arise a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*)—namely, that singularity (*ekatva*) is connected with the action (*kriyā*), whereas duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are connected with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—the intention [of the author] is this: although the singularity residing in the action is expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix, nevertheless, by means of this passage, the inconsistency in forms such as *pacatorūpam* and *pacantirūpam* is avoided. For this very reason, since the same objection would apply even in cases like *pacatorūpam* and so forth (where, because it is expressed by the *tiṅ*, there would be the occurrence of dual endings etc., just as in *pacataḥ*), once that objection has been refuted, it is stated: "In that case, even the singular number would not be obtained."

Regarding the statement "he cooks" (*pacati*), the teacher Kaiyaṭa has stated that because singularity is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the singular number (*ekavacana*) would not otherwise apply; this is his underlying intention. Furthermore, the resolution to that objection is stated immediately thereafter: "The singular number will be applied as the general rule (*utsarga*). It should not be argued that this general singular number would then also occur in forms such as *pacataḥ* (they two cook), which would render statements like "the action is one" (*kriyā caikā*) meaningless. This is because [the application of the singular] exists in accordance with the literal intent of the sūtra *dvayekayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.22).

Even under the view that the singular number is the general rule (*autsargika*), it should be understood that this [singular] is not intended [to denote the universal], because its own status as denoting the singularity inherent in the previously mentioned action is undermined. This is established by the usage of "one," "two," and "many" (where one is predicated of two or many), and by the specific mention of "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*) and "of the three" (*trayāṇām*); furthermore, in the *Prātipadikārtha-sūtra*, by the word "number" (*vacana*) and the words "one" and so forth which have number as their basis for application, it is shown that the case endings are merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*) and not [expressive of the meaning] independently.

Even regarding the maintenance of the rule (*niyamaparipālana*), here the singular number is used as the general rule (*autsargika*); this maintenance [of the singular] is due to compliance with the *lakṣya* (the actual usage) and the authority of the stated *bhāṣya*. Therefore, there is no contingency of using the dual or other numbers in cases such as *pacatorūpam*. Likewise, in the case of the abstract state (*bhāve*), the singular number is based solely on the singularity inherent in itself, and not merely as a general rule. If one does not admit its connection to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then in examples such as *pacati bhavati* or *pacato bhavati*, the number expressed by the suffix following the root *bhū* would remain unconnected [to anything]. This is not an acceptable consequence (*neṣṭāpatti*). As it is said: "The root *bhavati*, moreover, expresses the present time and singularity."

They have stated that this is because the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra establishes that it has the meaning of number (*saṃkhyā*), and so forth; the details should be consulted in the *Mañjūṣā*. [In the phrase] "having as its qualifier the number which is the meaning of the verb," one should also supply "having the agent or the object as its qualificand."

Thus, the nature of a cognition having as its qualificandum an agential object qualified by a number presented by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka); likewise, the nature of a cognition having as its qualificandum an objectial (karmabhūta) entity qualified by that [number] is also the delimitor of the effect. The nature of the presentation of an agent produced by the verbal suffix and the nature of the presentation of its object are the delimiters of the cause (kāraṇatāvacchedaka). Inherence (samavāya) is the relation that serves as the delimitor for both the effect and the cause.

Because the suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) generates a cognition whose qualificandum is the agent and so forth, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)-induced apprehension would be deviant; therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "having as its qualifier [the property] that delimits the effect-ness" is made. Since such a cognition could arise having the number expressed by the nominal suffix (*sub-artha*) as its qualifier, the aforementioned defect would remain as it was; hence, the term "verbal suffix-meaning" (*ākhyātārtha*) is used as a qualifier for "number."

Since the number associated with that [meaning] is also within the denotative capacity (*śakyatva*) of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*), the aforementioned defect remains; therefore, [the phrase "tadupasthitiparam"] refers to the presentation of that [number]. It brings about a cognition qualified by number through the cooperation of the presentation produced by it. Otherwise, because the number presented by the *su*-suffix and the number presented by the *tiṅ*-suffix would both be expressed by a single [element], the defect would persist as before.

In the sentence "The wood cooks the rice" (*kāṣṭhaḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the inclusion of the condition that the verbal suffix has the agent as its primary qualificand (*kartṛ-viśeṣyakatva*) within the scope of the effect-determiner (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is for the purpose of precluding the understanding of the number denoted by the verbal suffix as being construed with the instrument (*karaṇa*) or other factors. If it is objected: "Even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of [the number] applying to the object when an agent-suffix is used, and to the agent when an object-suffix is used," we say no. This is because one must include the status of being the meaning of the verbal suffix itself (*ākhyātārthatva*) as a qualifying condition for both agent and object. And since the meaning of that [status] is exactly as before, the aforementioned defect does not arise.

In order to exclude such a cognition [of number] arising from the presentation of the agent and so forth by means of another word, the property of being "generated by a verbal suffix" (*ākhyāta-janyatva*) is introduced as a requirement for those respective presentations. Furthermore, since the presentation of such a number exists for Caitra [in the case of *caitraḥ pacati*], the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is introduced as a constituent element of that [cognition] in order to exclude such a cognition for Maitra.

In reality, however, the property of having the agent or the object as the qualificandum need not be included in the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of the effecthood. Since the causal relation is accepted as being mediated by the relation of a qualificandumhood delimited by agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, the aforementioned defect does not arise. The cognition of the agent and so forth produced by that [word] serves as the awakener (*udbodhika*). Because the property of "belonging to that particular person" (*tatpuruṣīyatva*) is introduced into the scope of the delimiting conditions for both the effecthood and the causehood of the awakener, defects such as those regarding Caitra do not occur.

One should not suspect that there is a multiplicity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) because of the inclusion of the state of being a *tatpuruṣa* [compound], for the causal relations are fewer when compared to the inclusion of the objects (*viṣaya*), since persons (*puruṣa*) are fewer than objects. [The author] states the cumbersome complexity resulting from the causal relations according to the opponent's view with the words "the Naiyāyika," etc. He provides the reasoning for accepting the causal relations to be described with the words "the meaning of the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārtha*), etc. Thus, if that were not accepted, such a restriction would be untenable; therefore, it is necessary.

The sense is that even when [the meaning of] a word such as the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is presented, its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) [with the verb] would be impossible. The phrase "the meaning of the finite verb" (*ākhyātārtha*) is to be explained as before, and the purpose of the words is also to be understood as before. Regarding the phrase "presentation produced by [a word ending in] the first case":

in the view where [causality] resides in the object (*viṣayaniṣṭha*), the objective state (*viṣayatā*) residing in the referent of that word ending in the first case must be included as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the causal capacity. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the presence of such objective states in other word-meanings within a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), [as the specific objective state residing in the first-case referent is required].

This is because, by the statement beginning with "generated by a word ending in the nominative case," the causality of the mental representation (upasthiti) produced by another word is admitted. In this view, its greater complexity compared to one's own position is indicated. "So 'pi" (that too) refers to the aforementioned relation between cause and effect. "Like the moon" (candra iva).

Furthermore, since the moon and so forth would also be the referents of the nominative case-ending, there would arise the unwanted consequence of a cognition of the number as a qualifier in the verbal meaning—such as "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) or "goes" (*vrajati*)—in relation to the moon, eating, and so on. Nor is this a desired consequence, because such an experience is not observed. Moreover, in cases such as "the two faces are seen like the moon" (*candra iva dṛśyete mukhe*), the dual ending in "are seen" (*dṛśyete*) would be untenable, because it is impossible for duality to be predicated of the moon, which is a single entity.

Nor is there a lack of a specific subsumptive indicator (*āpādaka*) because an effect is produced by a cause; for it is the collection (*sāmagrī*) alone that possesses the nature of a subsumptive indicator. Furthermore, one must point out the failure to establish the restrictive rule that the cognition of the connection [of the word] occurs only with respect to the face and not with respect to the moon. [This refers to the phrase] "not being a qualifier of another."

In the view that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is based on inherence (*samavāya*), "the state of being the qualificand of the meaning of a nominative case-ending word that has not become a qualifier of anything else" must be included within the scope of the determinant of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). In the second view, the meaning is that "the very objective state residing in that which has not become a qualifier of anything else" is to be posited as the cognitive proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, there is no occurrence of the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*apatti*), because [in the example] the moon is a qualifier in the similarity of meaning with respect to the act of going, just as food is a qualifier in the act of eating. [The opponent objects: "This is excessive complexity (*atigaurava*)."

The point is that, according to our own view, since terms such as *candra* (moon) are not denotative of the agent (*kartṛ*), the application of number to them does not arise; therefore, the condition of "not being a qualifier of another" need not be included therein. This also refers to the aforementioned complexity; alternatively, the meaning may be that even this [condition] is simpler than the view of the opponent (*paramata*). Now, it might be argued that its being a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is improper, because it is more appropriate for the agent and the object—both of which are presented by the same suffix—to be what the number relates to.

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the recurrence of the word *dhātu* (root) [from the previous rule], when it is employed [in the definition of *ākhyāta*], since the presentness of the root is not intended to be expressed, the meaning obtained is "presentness residing in the object denoted by that [root]," and thus its connection is admitted only with the activity (*vyāpāra*). This is because, since the result (*phala*) is no different from the activity in being the meaning of the root, there would be no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for its connection to the activity alone. To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). And that—namely, the word *dhātu*—expressing the meaning of the root, i.e., making known the meaning of the root in the manner described above.

The word *ca* (and) is used because of [the relative] predominance [of the agent and object]; it serves to include [those cases] in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*). Therefore, there is no defect even in instances such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked") and *pacyamāna* ("being cooked"), where the fruit (*phala*) is predominant. Regarding the phrase "only of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoreva*): one should not argue that, by the reasoning stated previously, the [action] must necessarily be construed only with the operation (*vyāpāra*). This is because the term *anuvṛttadhātoḥ* ("of the recurring verbal root") ends in the ablative case (*pañcamyantatayā*), making such a syntactic meaning impossible; furthermore, there is no evidence for a repetition (*āvṛtti*) [of the word], and for one whose sole eye is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), there would be no perception of the actual linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). This is the intended sense.

He provides a rebuttal with the words "atīta" (past), intending to show that [the opponent's view] would have only the target as its object. Having stated the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*), he further states the failure to establish what is desired (*iṣṭāsiddhi*) with the words "apākṣīt" (he cooked). Anticipating the objection that one might simply accept the connection of that [action] with the fruit itself, and that in that case there is no occasion for the previously mentioned fault, he refutes this with the passage beginning with "nāpi" and ending with "āpatteśca. [The phrase] "prayogāpattiḥ" means the occurrence of [the action] in the form of a formal application (*prayoga*).

However, in the view that accepts the consequence of that [non-existence] in the fruit (*phala*), this fault does not arise because the fruit is not present; yet even this position is defective. Thus, since all positions are equally defective, the idea is that it is improper to resort to this particular position alone. [The phrase] "due to ignorance or non-usage" means that usage is motivated solely by the desire to communicate knowledge, as in the case of a parrot and the like.

The application [of the argument], however, is indeed accepted. Now, one might object: "Even if the effort of another is not perceptible, since inferential and other types of knowledge are possible, such an application is unavoidable. Anticipating this, he refutes it by conceding the point with the words "something" (*kiñcit*). This means "by some movement (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth"; by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), his writing and the like are included.

But authors such as Bṛhadbhūṣaṇakāra and others say: "His effort is not conducive to a result consisting of rising (*utthāna*), but rather has that [rising] as its objective; for this very reason, one uses the expression 'he strives for rising' there, but not 'he rises. This is because a specific kind of conduciveness must be accepted as the relation between the result and the operation. For this same reason, in states such as the buying of rice, the expression 'he cooks' is not used."

"Thus it is" (evaṃ ca): that is to say, since the previously stated arguments must necessarily be accepted, the "efficient force" (bhāvanā) alone is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). Now, one might raise the following objection from the Mīmāṃsakas and others: "If the efficient force is denoted by the verbal root and the agent and so forth are denoted by the verbal suffix (tiṅ), then that [force] would result in being a qualifier with respect to the accomplishment of the meaning of the suffix. This is because it is a fixed rule that, apart from number, time, and so on, the meaning of a suffix is always subordinate to the meaning of the stem. Anticipating this criticism, he refutes it with the words "even though" (yadyapi).

"Action (bhāva) is predominant" refers to the verb—the form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix—which generates a cognition in which the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) occupies the position of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), as determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix. "Substantives (nāman) have substance (*sattva*) as their predominant element" means that "substance" (*sattva*) is the category of *dravya*, which is the substratum for gender and other such properties; these [substantives] generate a cognition in which that [substance] occupies the primary position of the qualificandum (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*). This is the meaning.

Furthermore, because the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) is not required, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pacati* (he cooks), even though the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) generates a cognition whose primary qualificandum is the agent (*kartṛ*) residing in existence, which is itself determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the locus (*āśrayatva*) and number. Even if one were to avoid over-extension in that case by requiring a primary qualificandumhood determined by a mode residing in the action (*kriyā*), there would still be under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*). Thus, it is concluded that the predominance of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal root is established.

Thus, by the authority of the *Niruktabhāṣya*, a restriction of the stated rule must necessarily be admitted; rather, it is you yourselves who contradict the *Nirukta* and other authorities—this is the sense. Now, one might object: based on the etymology "that which comes into being (*bhavati*)" is a "becoming" (*bhāva*), the term *bhāva* ending in the suffix *a* denotes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) in the form of an action (*kṛti*). Since this very same thing is also denoted by the word "action" (*kriyā*), the action in the form of an effort is indeed predominant among the meanings such as time conveyed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Consequently, the meaning of a verb is defined as that which generates a cognition characterized by a subjecthood residing in the effort, which is in turn determined by a modehood residing in the meaning of the verbal root.

Furthermore, it must be stated that what has been proposed—namely, that [the meaning of the suffix] establishes the object intended by you and is contrary to our position because from expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks") there arises a cognition whose primary qualificandum is an action (*kṛti*)—is incorrect. This is because there would be no application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *ratho gacchati* ("the chariot goes") or *jānāti* ("he knows"), since in the first case an action is not perceived; and even though an action is perceived in *karoti* ("he does"), it is not the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix. Likewise, there would be non-application in the passive voice (*karmākhyāta*) such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked") and in the impersonal voice (*bhāvākhyāta*) such as *sūpyate* ("it is slept"), because an action is not conveyed there by the *tiṅ* suffix.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the cognition of an effort (*kṛti*) would not arise from a sentence such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattena pacyate*) because it is composed of those [elements], for such a cognition is possible through the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) itself. Furthermore, in that system, it is not merely "inherence" (*ādheyatva*) that is the meaning of the instrumental case.

For this very reason, from the sentence "It is cooked by Devadatta, not by Yajñadatta," there is the possibility of understanding the absence of the property of residing in Yajñadatta, where the counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*). However, if that [suffix] were to have the sense of "effort" (*kṛti*), then only the absence of effort—where the counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being produced (*janyatva*)—would need to be understood in respect to the action; yet that is not possible, because being produced is not a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*) and therefore cannot serve as a delimiter of counter-correlativity.

Furthermore, if one accepts that the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is what is manifested [in the cognition], then since such an absence remains uncontradicted even in the case of an action performed by Yajñadatta, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usage [i.e., "The rice was cooked by Devadatta" being understood as "The rice was cooked by Yajñadatta"]. Consequently, it might be argued that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case, because it is accepted that the *tiṅ* suffix itself has that meaning [of the substratum]. However, this cannot be maintained, because the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) must necessarily have that meaning [of the agent], since otherwise the cognition of the effort (*kṛti*) would not arise from the sentence "The rice was cooked by Devadatta. For this very reason, it is stated: "The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayostṛtīyā*).

Thus, this instruction also coheres well. Furthermore, since the Prābhākara-Naiyāyikas accept that even a non-restrictive relation (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) can be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence, there is no fault when a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed. In the view of the Navyas, since "being produced by an agent" (*kartṛjanyatva*) is the meaning of the instrumental case, the aforementioned fault does not arise. And so, since it is possible to convey that [meaning] by the instrumental case alone, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) lacks the capacity to convey it; consequently, the under-extension (*avyāpti*) in examples such as *pacyate* ("is cooked") remains difficult to avoid.

Even if one accepts that "the meaning of the third case [instrumental] is solely the state of being the locus (ādheyatva), and that effort (kṛti) is expressed by the verbal suffix of the object (karman) alone; whereas in the case of primary derivative suffixes (kṛt-pratyaya), the instrumental has either 'effort' or 'being produced by effort' as its secondary signification (lakṣaṇā)," the deficiency remains exactly as it was, because effort lacks primacy in the verbal suffix of the object.

Nor should it be argued that the term ‘*kṛti*’ (effort) refers merely to the meaning of *tiṅ*-suffixes as distinct from number, time, and so forth; and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as ‘the chariot goes,’ ‘he knows,’ ‘it perishes,’ or ‘it is cooked,’ because even there, the meaning of those suffixes—such as the locus (*āśrayatva*) and the like—is predominant. Even so, the lack of pervasion remains unremedied in the case of the impersonal passive (*bhāvākhyāta*), for one cannot accept that even there there is a cognition whose qualificand is the locus of the effort denoted by the *taṅ*-suffixes, since [in sentences like] ‘Caitra sleeps’ or ‘The sky stands,’ [the cognition arising from] Caitra’s state...

It should not be argued that there is the possibility of such a cognition as "an effort conducive to sleep" or "the state of being a substratum for staying residing in the sky," because logicians have stated that while such a cognition is not established by experience, the cognitions actually established by experience are rather "sleep produced by an effort residing in Caitra" and "staying residing in the sky."

In order to avoid the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "apavati" (he protects) when it produces a cognition [of the meaning of the suffix], one must state that the property of being the delimitor of the generative capacity for such a cognition consists precisely in possessing a specific sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) and so forth; and thus, there is no lack of pervasion even in the case of the verb "bhūyate" (it is being), because even in that instance, at the time when the intention (*tātparya*) regarding the objecthood (*karmatva*) is grasped, a cognition having the meaning of the suffix as its qualificandum is produced, and consequently, the generative capacity for such a cognition remains intact for that sequential order as well.

Alternatively, if the aforementioned cognition is accepted from such expressions as "Caitra sleeps" (*caitreṇa supyate*), then the passage in the *Dīdhiti* on the theory of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is consistent: "Because of the absence of a qualificand for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), number is indeed unconnected. This is because its meaning is that, due to the experience of a cognition where that [agent] is the primary qualificand, there is an absence of a cognition where anything else is the qualificand.

Since it is possible to have a cognition in which the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of the relation of being its specifier (*nirūpakatā*), the literal reading [of the opponent's position] would be inconsistent; furthermore, rather than abandoning the cognition in which the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning of the verbal root—a cognition established elsewhere—it is more appropriate to accept such a cognition in accordance with the definitions provided by Nirukta and other authorities.

In the Mīmāṃsaka system, since it is possible for the *bhāvanā*—which consists of the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the suffix—to be the primary element, the view that in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is *bhāvanā* in the form of an effort (*kṛti*) and that this alone is the principal factor is indeed correct; for this is established without any restriction on the rule governing the relationship between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). To this, he says: "Moreover... (*api ca*). Regarding the phrase "due to non-differentiation" (*abhedānvayāt*): this refers to the position where the agent (*kartṛ*) is the meaning of the suffix.

However, it should be understood that under the view that the *kṛti* (effort) is the meaning of the suffix, [the agent] is understood through the relation of being its substratum (*āśrayatva*). Regarding the phrase "the consequence of [the effort] becoming the primary element": the sense is that since the *kṛti* and so forth, which are the meanings of the suffix, would not have attained the status of being qualifiers of anything else, there would exist a causal complex for generating a cognition in which they appear as qualifiers of the meaning of the nominative-terminated word; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting such a cognition as established in the system of the Naiyāyikas.

Is it not the case that there is an acceptance of the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) regarding a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative case is the primary qualificand? For, only by accepting that [view] is the maintenance of the cognition of the connection between the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) and the predicate—where the meaning of the nominative is the subject (*uddeśya*), as established by universal experience—possible; and furthermore, under the view that the action is the primary qualificand, the maintenance of the non-arising of doubt—such as "Does Devadatta possess an effort conducive to cooking, or not?"—at the time of the cognition produced by the sentence "Devadatta cooks" would not be possible.

To dispel the objection that "only a certainty (*niścaya*) which has the same subject (*samānaviśeṣyaka*) and takes one alternative as its qualifier (*ekakoṭiprakāraka*) can remove a doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding the other alternative (its absence)," he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Regarding the *Bhāṣya*: this refers to the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* *bhūvādi* (Pāṇini 1.3.1), which provides the answer to the question, "What then is the meaning of these expressions: *pacati bhavati*, *pacasi bhavati*, *pakṣyati bhavati*?"—namely, "The actions such as cooking (*pacādayaḥ kriyāḥ*) are the objects (*kartryaḥ*) of the action of being (*bhavatikriyāyāḥ*)."

In this context, the meaning of "bhavatī" (she/it exists) in the phrase "apakṣyati bhavatī" (she will cook while existing) is that the future act of cooking exists in a subtle form. By this, the objection—that such usage cannot be justified because it would contradict the existence of a current state of being whose agent is the future act of cooking—is refuted.

The point here is that since the connection between two actions is accepted as being through the relation of action and its factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*), by the same logic, it is admitted that in the sentence "Look at the deer" (*paśya mṛgam*) as well, there is such an understanding between the two actions. Thus, in the *Mahābhāṣya*, for the purpose of refuting the Vārttika which states that the term "action" (*kriyā*) must be included in the rule "one whom [the agent] intends through the object" (*karmaṇā yamabhipraiti*), it is said: "Action is also an artificial object (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*); for an action is desired by means of an action. By what action? By an action such as seeing (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth."

In that manner, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) of the action of running with respect to the action of seeing is indeed intended. Thus, the meaning of that sentence—namely, "seeing which has the deer as its agent and the act of running as its object"—is what the authors of the Bhāṣya intend. This was also stated by Hari:

"Just as a single word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) can be an attribute of a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅnta*), so too they say that a word ending in a verbal suffix can be an attribute of another word ending in a verbal suffix."

In the verse from Māgha, "Assault the city; pluck the Nandana grove," as cited in the *Kaumudī* under the rule "samuccaye 'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 3.4.3), the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the actions denoted by the finite verbs is perfectly clear.

He states the seed of the argument regarding the impossibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) according to the opponent's view with the words "prathamānta" (ending in the nominative case). This means: "of that which is presented by the word *mṛga* ending in the nominative. By the term "of the qualificand" (*viśeṣyasya*), it is indicated that because [the deer] is the qualificand with respect to the running, and because [the accusative] is a direct qualifier with respect to the seeing, the primary grammatical operation (*pradhānakārya*) is stronger than even the "internal" (*antaraṅga*) factor. Since this is supported by the commentary on the rule *hetumati ca*, the accusative (*dvitīyā*) would override even the nominative (*prathamā*), which is "internal," [resulting in the form *mṛgam*]. However, for me, this fault does not apply, because the deer is [the agent] with respect to the running.

They say that this indicates that the first-case (nominative) formation, which arises as an internal operation due to its being a qualifier, does not cease. Regarding the phrase "because it would result in the second case": the sense is that, since the sentence "apaśya mṛgaṃ dhāvati" ("see the deer running") could indeed be possible in the sense of "you are the locus of seeing whose object is the deer, which is the locus of running," such a [desired] sentence would simply not be established.

In our own view (*svamata*), however, there is no occurrence of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). Since running (*dhāvana*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the root expressing that [action], being in the state of an object (*karman*), is not a nominal stem (*apratipadika*). Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of the second case-ending, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) of the objecthood (*karmatva*) not being manifested, on the grounds that it is not presented by a word through its function (*vṛtti*); for in the Mīmāṃsaka system, the mere presentation of the meaning is the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and thus a cognition having objecthood as its qualifier (*karmatvaprakāraka-bodha*) is possible even without a presentation generated by a word. However, in the view of those who maintain that such a presentation is the cause [of cognition]...

This is because we accept that the cognition itself possesses that relation [of the deer with running]. Nor does the same difficulty regarding the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) arise even in the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*); for in their system, it is the deer as qualified by the action of running that is construed with the act of seeing through the relation of being the object (*karmatā*), and not the deer alone. Although the qualified entity is not distinct from the pure entity, the objective state (*viṣayatā*) delimited by "deer-ness" as qualified by running is different from the objective state delimited by mere "deer-ness."

Nor is there a contradiction with grammatical usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding the direct syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root; for such a usage pertains only to the connection between the meaning of a simple noun and the meaning of a verbal root. Therefore, statements such as, "Having heard this majesty of mine, as well as my auspicious origins, I know that Sītā was born of Janaka," are consistent [with our view]. In your own system, however...

The inconsistency with the occurrence of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) from the very beginning—starting from the word for "origination" (*utpatti*)—is quite evident. Thus, it should be stated that there is no fault whatsoever in accepting a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative (*prathamānta*) is the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). For if one accepts the cognition of the objecthood (*karmatva*) of a jar qualified by "blue" and so forth, then in the expression "nīlaṃ ghaṭaḥ" ("the blue jar"), the occurrence of the second case would be impossible, and the occurrence of the first case would follow. Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *anabhihite*.

For in that context, regarding the sentence "Make a formidable, grand mat" (*bhīṣmam udāraṃ kaṭaṃ kuru*), it has been stated that if the qualified [entity] as a whole were the object (*karmatva*), then since the accusative case ending would be expressed by the suffix on the word *kaṭa*, it would not arise from words such as *bhīṣma*; therefore, the enumeration [of items] beginning with *tiṅ* (verbal endings) was provided.

Nor should it be argued that the accusative case occurs only when *karmatva* (objecthood) is intended as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the nominal stem-meaning, and not even when it is intended as a relation (*saṃsarga*), because the relevant passage from the Bhāṣya intends *karmatva* to be the qualificand; for according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, the meaning of every case-ending appears everywhere as a relation, and thus it is impossible to speak in such a manner.

Furthermore, since actions such as bringing do not have blue-colored jars and the like as their causes, there is no intention to convey a relation [of causality] in expressions such as "Bring the blue jar," "The learned Brāhmaṇa is embodied," and so forth; thus, such usages are not observed in works like the *Kāvyas* and *Purāṇas* with the aforementioned meaning. Moreover, in cases such as "Bring the blue jar" (*nīlo ghaṭa ānaya*) and "The white rice cooks" (*śuklastaṇḍulaḥ pacati*), the nominative case would not even arise—due to the grammatical rules "the nominative occurs when there is coreferentiality with a finite verb" (*tiṅ-sāmānādhikaraṇe prathamā*) and "the nominative occurs when [the agent] is already expressed" (*abhihite prathamā*)—and thus such usages would be untenable.

Thus, constructions such as "and likewise, auspicious births" (*tathā cotpattayaḥ śubhāḥ*) are to be justified solely on the grounds of being archaic (*āṣatvāt*). However, that which is not archaic is simply incorrect. In the case of the root *dṛś*, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding either a perception where the agent is one running intensely and the object is a deer, or a perception where the agent is a deer and the object is intense running; the other words serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhakāṇi*). Therefore, there is not even the slightest contradiction with etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

However, it is not tenable to claim that there is also the realization of the intended meaning—the perception of the act of the deer's intense running—without [resorting to] indication (lakṣaṇā). This is because, according to the reasoning stated above, it is improper to resort to indication when a realization can be achieved without it; furthermore, the cognition arises even without the reflection upon an inconsistency (anupapatti).

But even so, it is argued that a cognition having the action as its primary qualificand (mukhya-viśeṣya) is not tenable; rather, it is only logical that it has the meaning of the nominative-terminated word as its primary qualificand.
