For instance, regarding the rule "the third case-affix [is used] when the agent is not expressed" (*anabhihite kartari tṛtīyā*), grammarians cannot accept the meaning that "the third case-affix occurs when the agent is not denoted by a co-occurring finite verb (*tiṅ*) and so forth. This is because, since the finite verb in general is the denoter of that which specifies the power residing in the agent, the third case-affix would undesirably follow even in a sentence such as *caitreṇa pacyate taṇḍulaḥ* ("The rice is being cooked by Caitra").

Because the suffix *ya* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) is simply ungrammatical, even when there is the possibility of such usage as "caitraḥ pacyate" (Caitra is cooked), the property of being marked by *ya*, *taṅ*, and so on, does not enter into the definition of the denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) due to its complexity (*gaurava*). Nor does the meaning [of the sūtra] imply that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for an agent who is not understood; for if the sentence "caitreṇa pacyate" were to generate a cognition whose object is the agent, then all the words constituting that sentence would likewise generate that cognition, and since the agent would thus be understood from the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the aforementioned defect would remain as it was.

Nor should "the absence of expectancy useful for verbal cognition" alone be defined as that which causes its comprehension; for in the case of "pacyate" (it is cooked), the absence of expectancy that triggers its comprehension remains intact [if one were to consider only the verb], since that comprehension is possible through the third case-ending following words such as "caitra."

It cannot be argued that such an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) need not be postulated there, because the instrumental case in "caitreṇa pacyate" (is cooked by Caitra) would otherwise be unjustified. This is because from "caitraḥ pacyate," there arises a cognition whose primary qualificand is the action, with the agent Caitra as its qualifier; whereas from the simple "pacyate," there arises a cognition whose qualificand is the action, with the agent as its qualifier. Therefore, it is necessary that the expectancy consisting of the specific word-order (*ānupūrvī*) be indispensable for that verbal comprehension.

Nor should it be argued that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) need not be understood solely as co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), but rather—in the present case—it takes the form of sequential order (*ānupūrvī*), and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply; for if that were so, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would undesirably follow in expressions such as *caitreṇa pacati* ("Caitra cooks by means of [himself]"), because such co-utterance is not conducive to the cognition of that [agency]. Therefore, when there is an intention to express the agent as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the respective nominal stem-meanings, the third case ending would follow even after the word *caitra* in such instances, because there is no difference in its being the qualificand with respect to the meaning of the word *caitra*, just as in cases like *caitreṇa pacyate*.

If it is argued that, for this reason, it is proper to accept a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative case-ending alone is the primary qualificand, the following is said in response: even if one follows the aforementioned method of taking the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as the qualificand, there is no possibility of the erroneous usage "caitreṇa pacati" (Caitra cooks [with an instrument]). This is because, by virtue of the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of being expressed within a single word, the cognition of the connection with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) has already occurred at an earlier stage.

The fact that verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth do not denote the agent consists in their lacking such intentionality (*tātparya*). Since they lack that intentionality, even though the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the expression *caitreṇa pacati* is grammatically correct, the Parasmaipada is not correct because it is superseded by the Ātmanepada suffix prescribed for the passive and middle voices (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*). Thus, there is no possibility of such an usage [of Parasmaipada] occurring. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the usage *caitreṇa pacati* would occur there; for, in the absence of the intentionality regarding the agent, the suffix *śap* does not apply, and consequently, the suffix *yak* becomes unavoidable.

And thus, the final meaning is that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed by the intention to express the agent (*kartṛvivakṣā*) as being the qualificand of the respective nominal stem-meanings (*prātipadikārtha*), which are not construed with such an agent; therefore, there is no defect whatsoever. Consequently, when the third case ending or the like is intended to be prescribed for the agent of the root-meaning, the condition to be adopted is that [the agent] is not construed with the agent of that same root-meaning as presented by a co-occurring finite verb (*tiṅ*) or the like. Therefore, in the sentence *bhujjānena caitreṇa pacyate* ("By Caitra, who is eating, [something] is cooked"), although Caitra is construed with the agent expressed by the suffix *śānac*, there is no lack of justification for the third case ending after the word *caitra*.

Because there is no connection with the agent of the action (*pacikriyākartṛ*). Having taken each specific individual action denoted by the respective verbal roots as that specific individuality, one must include the property of not being connected with the agent of such and such an action and so forth. By this, in cases such as "Devadatta sees Maitra who is being seen by Caitra," there is no lack of justification for the accusative case after the word *maitra*.

In reality, the meaning of the rule *anabhihite kartari tṛtīyā* ("when the agent is not [already] expressed, the third case suffix is used") is that the third case suffix occurs after a nominal stem denoting the agent when the finite verb (*tiṅ*) and other such elements uttered in co-referentiality with it lack the intentionality (*tātparya*) to express that agent. In the sentence *caitreṇa pacyate* ("it is cooked by Caitra"), the finite verbal suffix lacks the intentionality to express the agent, whereas in *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), that suffix possesses such intentionality; thus, the employment of the third case suffix is justified in cases where that intentionality is absent. The same principle should be understood for the meaning of rules such as *anabhihite karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("when the object is not [already] expressed, the second case suffix is used").

But surely, in cases such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks") and *odanaḥ pacyate* ("rice is cooked"), since the agent and the object are respectively not expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix or a verbal suffix, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a third case ending after the word *caitra* and a second case ending after the word *odana*. And it cannot be argued that [the required condition] is simply the general absence of being expressed by a co-occurring verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth; for in the first example, the agent is indeed not expressed by a *kṛt* [suffix].

It should not be argued that even though the object is denoted by the *kṛt* suffix in the second case (the *kṛdanta*), there is no aforementioned fault because it is also denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix; for in such instances as "Maitra eats the cooked rice by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pakkam odanaṃ maitro bhuṅkte*) and "Rice is eaten by the cook Caitra" (*pācakena caitreṇa bhujyate odanaḥ*), the second and third case endings would fail to arise after the words *odana* and *caitra*, since the object and the agent have already been denoted by the *kṛt* suffix. If this is said, [we reply: no.

This is because it is not accepted that a particular case-ending is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) when the power (*śakti*) determined by the primary action is not expressed, even if the power determined by the subordinate action is expressed. As stated by Bhartṛhari:
"Where there are two distinct powers of a substance belonging to the primary and the other (subordinate) actions, and the power rests upon the subordinate, there the primary is followed."

"The capacity (*śakti*) whose object is the principal [action] is denoted by the suffix; when [it pertains] to a subordinate [action], then, although not explicitly stated, it is understood in that same way. (Kārikā 1). He elaborates upon the conformity to the capacity as determined by the principal action mentioned in the first verse with the words "pradhānaviṣayā" and so forth. The construction is as follows: when [the capacity] pertains to a subordinate [action], even though it is not explicitly stated, it is understood in the same way as if it were stated. It should be understood that, by the same logic, even if the capacity as determined by the principal [action] is not stated, it is nevertheless revealed as unspoken, since the capacity as determined by the subordinate [action] is likewise unspoken.

For this very reason, in the expression *prāsāde āste* ("he sits in the palace"), although the locativity (*adhikaraṇatva*) as defined by the root *sad-* (to sit) is already expressed [by the suffix], the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is established on the basis of the locativity as defined by the root *ās-* (to sit). This is because the term *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed") is accepted as a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *svādumi ṇamul*. For there it is stated: "The suffixes up to and including *tumun* should be prescribed when used with a verb of similar meaning (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)."

Otherwise, in the example "yavāgūr devadattena svādukāraṃ bhujyate" (The barley-gruel is eaten by Devadatta making it tasty), the suffix *ṇamul* would denote the agent according to the rule "kartari kṛt" (kṛt-suffixes [other than those denoting action] occur in the sense of the agent). Consequently, because [the agent] would be expressed [by the suffix], the third case ending would not occur after the word "devadatta. Having stated such things, [the author] refutes that statement by relying on the principle that "kṛt-suffixes following indeclinables express the action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*).

In this regard, Kaiyaṭa raises the objection: "If this is so, then in the cases 'Devadatta eats having cooked rice' (*paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*) and 'Devadatta is eaten having been cooked' (*paktvaudanaṃ bhujyate devadattaḥ*), since the agent and the object are not expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*, why do the third and second case endings not occur in relation to the act of cooking? Having raised this doubt, he resolves it as before, on the grounds that the verbal capacity determined by the principal action remains unimpaired. It is clear to those who know the subject that these two verses of Hari are intended to illuminate the purport of this very *Bhāṣya*.

Even though there is no evidence for a difference in objective status (*viṣayatā*) based on a difference in the cognition of the same form, because the capacities for the objecthood (*karmatva*) as determined by the respective acts of cognition differ, the use of the accusative case is established in the sentence "Maitra sees the jar being seen by Caitra" due to the unexpressed capacity for objecthood determined by the meaning of the root *dṛś* (to see) which serves as the base of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). However, that the objective status is the meaning of the accusative case and so forth is not established by grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*).

Since the activity conducive to the removal of an obstruction, or the activity consisting of the mind-soul conjunction conducive to knowledge—delimited by the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*)—is the meaning of the root *√jñā* (to know) as it pertains to "the visible" (*dṛśya*) and so forth, there is no impairment of the power of the objective case (*karmatva-śakti*), even though the result is differentiated according to the distinctions among actions and the like; thus, enough with this elaborate digression.

One should not suspect that "Bring the running deer" (*ānaya dhāvati mṛgaḥ*) cannot constitute a single sentence because, according to the view that the action (*kriyā*) is primary, the action cannot be the object of the act of bringing. For in my view, since it is possible for the deer qualified by running to be the object, there is no inconsistency in its being a single sentence. This is justifiable on the grounds that it is analogous to expressions such as "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*). In this very same way, the usage of "Let a hundred Brahmins be fed" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ śataṃ bhojyatām*) and so forth is consistent. Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for such a [single-sentence] unity; such is the direction of the argument.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Even if one accepts that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is a qualifier with respect to the action (*kriyā*), in accordance with the *Nirukta* and other texts stating that 'the verb has the action as its primary referent' (*bāvapradhānamākhyātam'), then in the case of 'Devadatta cooks' (*pacati devadattaḥ'), a cognition is possible where the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) is the meaning of the nominative ending—namely, 'Devadatta is the substratum of the act of cooking whose agent is one and the same [as his own]'. Therefore, let that very [cognition] be accepted. Why would there be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)? To this he says: "In the case of [the action's] being supplied (*adhyāhāre*). And [he adds]: "Because of the consequence of non-connection (*ananvayāpatteḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

And thus, because there would be the consequence of a lack of mutual syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), the intended unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) favored by the author of the Bhāṣya would be lost; this is the meaning. He concludes the refutation of the opponent's view with the words "If this is so" (*evaṃ ceti*). "In this way" means: according to the aforementioned manner, when the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is primary. "Having the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as its qualifier" means that the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffix, distinct from number, time, and so forth, is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). For this very reason, it possesses commonality with the cognitions produced by such sentences as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) and "Caitra knows" (*caitro jānāti*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause": the meaning is that, for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is the qualifier (*prakāra*) related by the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the respective nominative word, related to its respective nominative case-meaning by the relation of being the qualificand. By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) based on taking as the object a collective mental presentation (*samūhālambana-upasthiti*). Regarding the term "delimited by *bhāvanātva*": this is stated assuming that the verbal root produces a cognition in which *bhāvanātva* is the qualifier.

However, it should be understood that [the cause] is by way of having as its object that which is delimited by a specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*). Furthermore, the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) should be understood as the relation of qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). Additionally, the causal relation should be observed as follows: for a cognition in which the meaning of a *tiṅ*-suffix (such as an object) is the qualifier, the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), related through the relation of qualificandhood residing in each respective fruit (*phala*).

Now, one might object: since the verbal root-meaning (dhātvartha), which is an activity (*vyāpāra*), can only be the qualificand (*prakāra*) with respect to the meaning of a *kṛt*-suffix and not with respect to the meaning of a *tiṅ*-suffix and so on, it is necessary to establish this restriction by positing a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that "the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a *kṛt*-suffix is the cause of a verbal cognition whose qualifier is *bhāvanā*. Consequently, a cognition in which an action is the qualifier and another action is the qualificand—such as that arising from forms like *pacati*—would be impossible, because the required cause, namely the presentation produced by a *kṛt*-suffix, would be absent. To refute this doubt, he says: "Bhāvanā... [etc.].

Regarding the phrase "like the presentation produced by a verbal root (*kṛt*)," although there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—in that since the object of a word is also a content of the presentation produced by a *kṛt* (where such a presentation arises from the cognition of the word), the status of being an object of such a collective presentation (*samūhālambana*) exists even for objects like a jar—the [proposed] cause is nonetheless not [too broad], because the presentation produced by a *kṛt* functions as a cause through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the *kṛt* within the cognition that produces itself.

[Objection: This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). [Response: It is not so; for the presence of the verbal suffix (*kṛt*) brings about a presentation that has as its object the agent and so forth, which is a cognition having that meaning as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and having the suffix as its qualifier (*prakāra*) through the relation of power (*śakti*). This is because the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*)—which is defined by the qualifierhood residing in such a suffix—is present precisely in that agent and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the bhāvanā which is the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthabhāvanā*): the meaning is that there is a presentation through the relation of qualificandumness residing in the bhāvanā produced by the verbal root.

Otherwise, since existence (*sattā*) and the like, even when presented by words such as "existence," would not deviate from being the meaning of the verbal root, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result. Furthermore, the word *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is used solely for the purpose of attaining the status of being the primary qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) residing therein. As for the phrase "the direction [is shown]," its meaning has been explained at length previously.

Alternatively, the sense is that there would be a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *atiṅatiṅaḥ*, which states: "If a collection of finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) were also considered a single sentence (*ekavākya*), then the term ‘atiṅ’ [in the rule] would be redundant; for a finite verb following another finite verb cannot reside within the same sentence, and thus the prohibition of accentuation (*nighāta*) would not apply. This has been explained in detail elsewhere. "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*) means: when the meaning of the suffix—such as the agent (*kartṛ*)—is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and when the number associated with that [suffix-meaning] is a qualifier of that very agent and so forth. "One having a single substratum" (*ekāśrayikā*) means: [the number] residing in the same locus as the agent, etc.

It should also be understood that [the action] pertains to the present time. According to the view of the Navyas (modern logicians), however, the form of the cognition should be seen as "having a single agent. Regarding the phrase "conducive to cooking" (*pākānukūla*), the meaning is "conducive to softening" (*viklittyanukūla*). That is to say, the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is conducive to that softening which has a single locus. This is because, in accordance with the Nirukta commentary stating "the verb has the *bhāva* (action/state) as its primary meaning," the *bhāvanā* maintains its primacy even in the cognition arising from verbal suffixes denoting an object (*karman*).

In reality, since the primacy of the object (*karman*) with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*) is observed at the end of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, it is logical that the same [object] should possess the status of the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*) even at the end of a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. For this very reason, there is no abandonment of the rule established everywhere—that the meaning of the suffix is directly connected as a qualifier to the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*), which serves as the qualificand. Consequently, the form *putrīyati* is not used in the sense of "he desires a son" (*iṣyate putraḥ*) or "the son is desired" (*iṣṭaḥ putraḥ*), because those meanings are different; rather, it is used only in the sense of "he desires for himself a son" (*putram icchati*).

It has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *supa ātmanaḥ* that a suffix denoting the object (*karman*) is difficult to obtain after a desiderative (*kyajanta*), because [the root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Otherwise, since in both cases the primary factor is the activity conducive to desire—consisting of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*) and so forth—there would be no consistency [in the distinction made]. In my view, however, the difference in meaning is clear: in one case the activity (*vyāpāra*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while in the other the result (*phala*) is.

And thus Kaiyaṭa has stated: "When the fruit of the action (the object) is predominant, then there is only the sentence 'the son is desired' (*iṣṭaḥ putraḥ*) or 'the son is desired' (*iṣyate putraḥ*), but not a form ending in *kyac*; for that [derivative root] is intransitive, and consequently no suffix can arise in the sense of an object. Thus others have said.

Although, even when the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is predominant in relation to the object (*karman*), the number associated with it functions as a qualifier of that object, whereas in relation to the agent (*kartṛ*)—when the verbal suffix denotes the agent—it functions as a qualifier of the agent; and although the difference in meaning is thus established even by taking the connection with the substratum (*āśraya*) into account, nevertheless, the intended "difference in meaning" consists in the capacity to generate cognitions having different primary qualificands (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). That [intended] inconsistency remains quite firm.

If it is argued that "having different meanings" (bhinnārthakatva) is intended here simply as the capacity to generate a cognition of distinct types regarding some portion [of the meaning], then the point is this: since there is an absence of difference in meaning between the *vṛtti* and the sentence with respect to the meaning of the suffix indicated by the word "icchā," that [definition] would be ineffective because it fails to exclude the suffixes. Now, it might be objected that verbal roots do not have "activity" (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning.

Since [the notion that] "it arises" or "it perishes" is not experienced in such cases, he says: "In the case of 'it perishes,' etc. [He explains: "qualified by the state of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*). Because one does not employ the expression "the jar perishes" even when there is a concurrence of the causal complex for a destruction whose counter-positive is something else, the phrase "qualified by the state of being a counter-positive" means qualified by its own state of being a counter-positive. For this very reason—that is, because the verbal root *naś* has as its meaning such a causal complex—it is used in the aforementioned way.

If [the root *naś*] does not have that as its meaning, then even though the usage of "is perishing" (*naśyati*) or "will perish" (*naṅkṣyati*) would be justified, the usage "perished" (*naṣṭa*) would not be possible because the destruction would lack the quality of being past. Furthermore, even in the case of something that perished long ago, the usage "is perishing" (*naśyati*) alone would result. However, if it has the sense of "causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), since the time denoted by the suffix would only conjoin with the causal complex itself, neither the aforementioned undesirable consequence nor the impossibility arises; this is the intended meaning. And this objection applies to the view that the meaning of the suffix is "pastness," defined as being the counter-positive of a present non-existence.

It should be understood that if the meaning of that [term] were "subsisting in a time that is the counter-positive of the destruction of the present," then the aforementioned objection would not apply. "Ultimately, it is simply the substratum" means that, in reality, even the conjunction between the self and the mind can be conducive to cognition; this is the intended sense. Here, the relation that delimits the result is "objectivity" (*viṣayatā*); by means of this, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to the jar and so forth—this is how it should be understood.

Another view should be understood as follows: cognition itself is the result (*phala*), and that very same [cognition] is the operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to it; the relation delimiting its status as a result is objectivity (*viṣayatā*), whereas the relation delimiting its status as an operation is inherence (*samavāya*). Regarding the term "to be inferred" (*ūhya*): the meaning is that it is to be inferred in cases such as "he desires" (*icchati*), and so forth. || 2 ||

"The contingency of the cognition of both" means the contingency of the cognition of both the agent and the object; the sense is that the capacity [to denote both] exists in both cases. Now, one might argue: "Cognition occurs only of that for which there is a grasp of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), and not of anything else. Even if there were a grasp of the intention for the cognition of both at once, since it is unestablished that a single suffix can produce the cognition of both simultaneously, the contingency of the simultaneous cognition of both does not arise. To this, he states another refutation: "just as in the case of the cognition of the agent alone. This refers to the phrase "the contingency of cognition."

The sense is that, just as from words such as *hari* there arises at one time the cognition of Indra alone, and at another time the cognition of Viṣṇu alone; the sense is that this is because the contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*) are identical [in both cases]. Regarding the term "indicator of the intended meaning" (*tātparyagrāhaka*): the meaning is "that which indicates an eternal (beginningless) intention. And thus, although in the case of the word *pacyate* ("it is cooked") there may exist an intention for someone to understand the agent (*kartṛ*), the agent is not understood because of the absence of an eternal intention [to convey that meaning]. This is the sense.

In the *kārikā*, the word "therein" (*tatra*) means "between those two. Thus, the meaning is: "between those two, namely the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how can such conventional usages as 'the *taṅ* suffixes and others indicate the object' be justified? To this, he says, from "connected with the result" (*phalānvaya*) up to "the meaning of the aggregate" (*samudāyārtha*). Since it is impossible for them to be "indicators" (*dyotaka*) in the sense of being exciters of a [latent] power (*śakti*), he says they "cause the intention (*tātparya*) to be grasped. That is, they cause the desire for the cognition of that [object] to be grasped. This is to be understood as occurring in co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with *taṅ*, *yag*, and so forth; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *dhatte*. (3)

Thus, regarding the fact that the *taṅ* suffixes and others serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) when they follow from the fruit [of the action] and its connection to the substratum (*āśrayānvaya*). Now, raising the objection: "How can the *taṅ* suffixes and others prescribed by rules such as *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) be correct when used for the agent?"—he says, starting with *karmavat karmaṇā* and ending with *sādhanāt*. In the root text: "This is a general rule" (*utsargaḥ*). "This" refers to the previously mentioned point—that the *taṅ* suffixes and others indicate the object (*karman*) and so forth. "General rule" (*utsargaḥ*) means it is common (*prāyika*), not universal (*sārvatrika*). To answer the question "Why?", he says: "The object... (*karmeti*).

"Viparyayāt" means "from the opposite," that is, by way of reversal. "Yathāgamam" means according to scripture, or according to one's own understanding; this will be clear in the commentary. To clarify that even in cases such as "The rice cooks by itself," the locus (āśraya) is indeed construed with the operation (vyāpāra), he describes the verbal cognition here with the words "atra hi."

Regarding the expression *ekanārada*: the meaning is that there is one Nārada, or rather, knowledge having him as its object. Here, the intention is that because the object (*karman*) is denoted by the particle *iti*, the word *dvitīya* does not follow the word *nārada*. However, according to the view of the moderns (*navya*), the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) to be understood is something like "favorable to that knowledge which has the form 'Nārada'," for they do not accept that a particle ever denotes [the object], since it is stated in the Bhāṣya that only a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is counted among the *atihari* group.

The inclusion of the word *samabhivyāhṛta* (co-occurring) in the phrase "because of being a transitive root" (*sakarmakadhātutvāt*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), where, under the view that the rule *karmavat* extends the application of the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, [the suffix would otherwise apply]. To avoid over-extension in cases such as *abodhi śrīkṛṣṇaḥ* ("Śrī Kṛṣṇa was awakened"), it is specified as "common to the state of being" (*bhāvasādhāraṇā*). The phrase "yaṅ etc. includes *ciṇvad-iṭ* by the word "etc. (*ādi*). For one who lacks knowledge of the specific rules prescribing those [suffixes], context and other factors alone serve as the indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). This is likewise the case with the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes.
Otherwise, in the case of "apece," since both the agent and the object would be identical, there would be a total lack of any means to determine the intended meaning. || 4 ||

"Regarding the ineffability of *bhāvanā*": the meaning is that since it would be impossible for it to be the primary element if it were denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is therefore not denotable by it; or alternatively, the meaning is that the *bhāvanā* known as "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is simply not denotable. "In order to suggest its denotability": this indicates that the position of the ancient Naiyāyikas and others—that an activity distinct from effort (*yatna*) is neither denotable by the verbal root nor denotable by the suffix (*tiṅ*), but rather that only the result (*phala*) is the meaning of the root and "action" (*kṛti*) is the meaning of the suffix—is not correct.

Because a particular word is well-known to some [person], multiple synonyms are provided. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known that both the state of being denoted by a verbal root (*dhātuvācyatva*) and the state of being an action (*kriyātvam*) apply to common phenomena such as the effort of blowing (*phūtkāra*) performed by both sentient and insentient beings. For this very reason—that is, precisely because the operation (*vyāpāra*) is denotable in its various forms—it is "established for all. This means it is established through the experience of everyone. The implication is that the denial of what is established by the experience of everyone is improper. Thus, in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*):

It should also be understood that for this very reason, even the doubt as to whether Devadatta possesses the act of blowing or not does not arise at the time of the cognition produced by the sentence. Thus—in the manner described above—given that the operations such as blowing are denotable, [the opponent objects] "because of the consequence of complexity" (*gauravāpatti*); this is because properties such as "being a blow" (*phūtkāratva*) would have to be treated as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Regarding the phrase "that which delimits it": the meaning is that *kṛtitva* (the nature of effort), in the form of *pravṛttitva*, is established as the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatā*) of the cognition that [an action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*). Therefore, that alone is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). Consequently, the position of the ancient Naiyāyikas is finalized as follows: the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), while effort (*yatna*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix. However, the intended meaning is not that *yatnatva* (the nature of effort) is the delimitor of the denotability of the verbal root; for if that were the case, it would follow that the suffix has the sense of the locus (*āśraya*).

And that [position] is not accepted by the Naiyāyikas. For this very reason, it is also not the case that only time and number are denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*), because that too is not accepted by the Naiyāyikas. Furthermore, there would be the consequence that the effort (*yatna*) denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) could not be construed with the meaning of the nominative (*prathamānta*), as this would contradict the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root [are not directly related]. Moreover, it would contradict the sūtra "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

[Objection: But how can the cognition of "activity" (*vyāpāra*) and so forth in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), which is established by the experience of all people, be accounted for, given that effort (*yatna*) is sublated [in these cases]? To this, he says: "The chariot goes. It should be understood that "Devadatta" and so forth are the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) for the verb "knows" (*jānāti*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "desires," "perishes," and others are included. By the phrase "because it is an activity" (*vyāpāratvāt*) and so forth, the properties of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*), being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), and others are included.

It should be understood that from the statement "the jar perishes" (*ghaṭo naśyati*), because there is a contradiction regarding the locus of the destruction (*nāśāśrayatva*)—which is the operation conducive to destruction—within the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it is the very status of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) that appears there. Likewise, it is not correct to say that there is an appearance of an operation (*vyāpāra*) in the case of "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*); for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even when Caitra—who possesses the impulsion and so forth conducive to movement—is standing still on one spot, one could say "Caitra goes. [This is] because [such an operation] is possible in a heavy object.

The meaning is that since there is no difference between both power (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in their being the relation between a word and its meaning, power is possible even with respect to that which is delimited by a heavy property (*gurudharma*), just as indication is. [This is stated] because there is no reason for a disparity. Now, one might object: "The status of being a delimitor of causal efficacy (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*), the status of being a delimitor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), and the status of being a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*)—all of which consist in a specific essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*)—are possible in the case of a light property; one should not postulate them in the case of a heavy one."

For this very reason, just as in the case of a light property (*laghudharma*), the delimitation of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatā*) and the delimitation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) are postulated. For this very reason, the common saying among logicians—that the cognition "the delimitation of counter-correlativity for the absence qualified by knowability does not exist in smokiness" is established, whereas [such a delimitation] does not exist in the state of being smoke (*dhūmatva*)"—is consistent. Therefore, the meaning of the term "possible" (*saṃbhavati*) here is "that which possesses a delimitation that is possible."

And thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established as follows: that which is more complex (*guru*) than a property that possesses a possible delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) with respect to that [locus] is one that lacks such a delimitation. Possessing a possible delimitation with respect to that means being devoid of any sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding its delimitation; and a sublation consists in the lack of co-extensiveness (*asamanaiyatyam*) with the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the delimited (*avacchedya*). Consequently, it is precisely this co-extensiveness that constitutes the state of possessing a possible delimitation with respect to that.

Because two halves of a pot are included in the definition of "co-extensiveness" (*samanaiyatyam*), even a property such as "being one of those two" (*tad-anyataratvam*)—namely, being either a pot or a cloth—or "being a fire of the kitchen hearth" (*māhanasīyavahnitvam*), which is more complex than "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvam*) or "fire-ness" (*vahnitvam*), can be established as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of either a pot or a cloth, or the absence of a fire of the kitchen hearth. Co-extensiveness with respect to the counter-correlativity consists in being co-extensive with it (the delimiting property) while being the delimiting factor of the opposition to the absence that is defined by it. Therefore, there is no [such] "existence-ness" (*sattātva*) in the case of the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the absence of existence qualified by "being other than quality or action" (*guṇa-karmānyatva-viśiṣṭa-sattā*).

There is an inconsistency if "being a specific existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) restricted to that [class]" is taken as the nature [of the denotable]. If it is argued that "the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*)"—and not the delimitor of denotability through secondary indication (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatva*)—is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), we say no. For if an essential relation consists of the respective individual natures (*tattatsvarūpa*), then even the natures of heavy properties (*gurudharma*) would exist [as such relations]; therefore, it is better to simply accept [their] status as delimiters (*avacchedakatva*), since there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a positive entity [in the form of a delimiter].

If it is argued that, in other cases, only a relation is postulated for what has already been established [as a property], because of parsimony (*lāghava*), then it is more appropriate to postulate a relation for that which has been postulated elsewhere as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). This is because the status of being a delimiting factor—defined as occurring neither less nor more extensively (*anyūnānatiriktavṛttitva*)—is not lost even in the case of a heavy property (*gurudharma*); this should be understood from the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa* and other such works. [The phrase] "not by the root *kṛ*, which means effort" [is used].

The point is that since the linguistic usage of "done" (*kṛta*) and "not done" (*akṛta*) regarding a cloth and a sprout occurs at the time of reflecting upon their being produced by effort, it is necessary that the word [the verbal root *kṛ*] has "effort" as its meaning. Regarding the example "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*): if the word "chariot" were not mentioned, there would be no logical inconsistency in such a usage because an effort conducive to motion exists in Caitra and others; therefore, the word "chariot" is used. As for the phrase "the sprout is done": since this could be explained merely by taking it to mean being produced by the effort of God (*īśvara*), he says "by means of the seed, etc. This is from the *Vivaraṇa*.

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); it should also be understood that when the question "What does he do? is asked regarding effort (*yatna*), the answer "He cooks" would be untenable unless the word "cooks" (*pacati*) had the meaning of effort. The phrase "because the status of having effort as its meaning is not established" means that one should not argue that in expressions such as "The chariot performs going" (*ratho gamanaṃ karoti*), the verb "to do" (*karoti*) has a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the general sense of "activity" (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*); for the point is that while a primary meaning is possible, it is improper to assume a figurative sense.

Now, it might be argued that if [the object] possesses the capacity for activity (*vyāpāra*), then in a state where one has not cognized its being produced by an effort (*yatna*), the linguistic usage "the cloth is made" (*paṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) or "the sprout is made" (*aṅkuraḥ kṛtaḥ*) would be untenable, since there is no difference in the cognition of its being produced by an activity (*vyāpāra*). However, even when something is produced by the effort of God (*īśvara*), such usage is accepted in a state where one cognizes the absence of production by the effort of Caitra or others. As the Teacher (*ācārya*) has said:

"By the distinction between what is done and what is not done, and by the determination of the agent's nature, effort alone is 'action' (*kṛti*); in the subsequent [result], that very same thing is 'productive drive' (*bhāvanā*)."

In this regard—according to the view of others, meaning the Mīmāṃsaka position—it might be argued that even for the root *kṛ* (to do) as situated in the word "agent" (*kartṛ*), there is only a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*). If this is so, then by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), let there be denotative power (*śakti*) only for that which is delimited by the universal "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*), and let there be metaphorical indication only with respect to the "operation" (*vyāpāra*), since it is established in the systems of the Mīmāṃsakas and others that denotative power resides only in what is delimited by a simpler property. Even though, due to understanding through metaphorical indication, there must necessarily exist in that case a desire whose object is the mere existent and whose qualifier is the state of being the object of a cognition produced by that word; [The text continues: ...[the author responds]... [omitted]. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the logical structure and philosophical argumentation up to the point where the argument regarding the Mīmāṃsaka view of the root *kṛ* concludes.)

The status of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*) is admitted only for that which is delimited by a light property (*laghudharma*), and not for that which is delimited by a heavy property (*gurudharma*), because—on the strength of experience—it is postulated that the cognition of heaviness acts as an obstacle [to the assumption of such a relation]. However, in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which consists in a possible relation, its status as a relation is already established even there and need not be newly postulated; this is the distinction, and for this very reason there is no total abolition of *lakṣaṇā*. This is a point established by all experts in the systems (*tāntrika*). To this, he says: "Furthermore, regarding the *bhāvanā*... [The phrase] "in the state of not being denoted" (*avācyatve*) means that the *bhāvanā*, whose nature is activity (*vyāpāra*), is not denoted by either the verbal root (*dhātu*) or the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). The second [case]...

It might be argued as follows: if that [action] were inexpressible (*avācya*), then "karmatva" (the status of being an object) would have to be defined either as "being the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning which is in a different substratum from the operation that produces it," or simply as "being the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning. In that case, just as in the sentence "he brings about a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*), the same undesirable consequence of a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) following the word "pot" would arise in the sentence "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*). This is because in both instances, there is no difference in the fact that the pot is the locus of the result in the form of "origination" (*utpatti*), which is the meaning of the verbal root. [The phrase "due to the sublation of the technical designation 'object'"] means that the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) would be blocked [by this over-extension].

The meaning is that although the jar is the locus of the result [of the action], there is no occurrence of the accusative case because it lacks the designation *karman* (object), which is the motivator for the use of the second case. Regarding the term "universal" (*anugata*): it means common to both sentient and insentient entities. He establishes the non-agency of the jar with the words "because of being the locus of effort" (*kṛtyāśrayatvasya*); that is, because of not being the locus of the effort conducive to the result denoted by the root in question. Regarding the word "agent" (*kāraka*): it means within the circle of agents of the action denoted by the root in question. "Because of its absence"—that is, because of its insentience; the sense is that there is an absence of being the prompter of the circle of agents.

The point is this: since the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is prescribed only for one who possesses an action (*kṛti*) and so forth, in the absence of such an action, the designation "agent" cannot apply; consequently, because there is no exception to the designation "object" (*karman*), the occurrence of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would be unavoidable. Now, one might object: "The term 'independent' (*svatantra*) should be intended to mean 'the substratum of an operation conducive to the meaning of the verbal root' (*dhātvarthānukūlavyāpārāśrayatva*); and that [definition] is certainly uncontradicted in the case of a jar. To this, he says: "only a *kāraka*" (*kārakamātra*).

If [agency] were defined merely as being a *kāraka*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to all *kārakas*, because they all possess an activity conducive to the meaning of the verbal root under discussion. [Objection: But agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the prompter of the entire circle of *kārakas*, and that is determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*); therefore, there is no over-extension. For this very reason, one can even say "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*). This is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *kārake*. To this, he says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*). In order to exclude over-extension to [verbs like] *bhū* (to become) and so forth, he specifies: "having a result in its own sense that resides in a different locus" (*svārthaphalavyadhikaraṇa*).

Since even roots such as *bhū* (to become) possess an operation that has a locus distinct from the fruit of the root-meaning—such as *pac* (to cook)—the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains unavoidable; therefore, "having its own meaning" (*svārthatva*) is introduced as a qualification for the fruit. Furthermore, "having a locus distinct from the fruit" means residing in something other than the locus of any instance of that fruit, as determined by the relation that delimits its status as a fruit (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*). Consequently, there is no failure to include roots such as *gam* (to go).

By introducing the relation that delimits the result (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), even though the locus of the result—such as the earth and so forth—which is related [to the action] by a temporal (*kālika*) or other such relation, may possess a difference from the locus of its own generative operation (*vyāpāra*). Since the difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by being the locus of a specific instance of conjunction residing in both Caitra and the village does not exist in Caitra, the failure to include [the action of] *gam* (to go) and the like remains; therefore, "any" (*yatkiñcit*) has been introduced as qualifying the locus possessing that result.

Alternatively, "having a different locus from the fruit" (*phala-vyadhikaraṇatva*) means not residing in any substratum whatsoever that is the locus of the fruit; this is because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary]. Or, it may mean the operation of its own meaning (*svārtha-vyāpāra*). "Having a different locus from the operation" (*vyāpāra-vyadhikaraṇatva*) means residing in a substratum that is not the locus of the operation. The inclusion of the relation (*sambandha*) is to be understood as before.

Alternatively, "having a result that resides in a locus other than its own" (*phalavyadhikaraṇatva*) means having as its result that which does not reside in its own substratum (*svānadhikaraṇavṛtti*). Here, the referent of the word *sva* (self) is the operation (*vyāpāra*). The property of being its own substratum (*svādhikaraṇatva*) is to be understood by way of the relation that delimits the operation-ness (*vyāpāratāvacchedakasambandha*); therefore, there is no fault even though the village also possesses the operation residing in Caitra by way of a temporal relation (*kālikasaṃbandha*). Furthermore, "residing in that" (*tadvṛttitva*) is by way of the relation that delimits the result-ness (*phalatāvacchedakasambandha*); thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*). "Being denotable" (*vācyatva*) means being denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*). [The term] "any one of these" (*anyatamatva*)...
The meaning is: the state of being any one of those [properties] residing in as many verbal roots as are intended to be transitive.

And that [property] consists in being different from a collection of absences whose counter-correlates are delimited by the respective serial orders (*ānupūrvī*) of those [phonemes]. Regarding the phrase "of one alone": the meaning is "of that which possesses only a single serial order. By this, the objection that the expression "of one alone" is inconsistent—given that the two instances of the root *vah* in the two sentences "he carries a burden" (*bhāraṃ vahati*) and "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*) must necessarily be distinct from each other due to their difference in phonetic utterance and difference in meaning—is refuted. Alternatively, it should be understood that this [definition] applies even under the view that there is no difference in the word itself, despite the existence of differences in meaning and so forth.

It should be understood that even if, in this way, those verbal roots intended to be transitive are included within the delimiting factors (avacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference—where that difference consists in being any one of the various distinctions delimited by their respective individualities (tattadvayaktitva)—there is still no escape from the difficulty.

One might object: "Is it not the case that transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in a locus other than the operation (*vyāpāra*) that produces it? And this is intact for the root *kṛ*, since effort (*yatna*)—by virtue of its relation to the objective (*viṣayatā*), which delimits the nature of the result—resides in a locus other than the operation consisting of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanoyoga*) that produces it? Furthermore, intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) is the state of being different from that [transitive]; and since this is not possible for *kṛ*, the claim that 'the root *kṛ* would incur intransitivity' is inconsistent. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The point is this" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). [He explains] "the meaning" (*arthaḥ*); this refers to the phrase beginning with "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*).

The phrase "like *yat* in the sense of effort" (*yatī prayatne*) implies that it is not appropriate to describe the root as having an object (*sakarmaka*) in the manner previously stated; for if it were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the root *yat*. Rather, according to our own view, it is as previously stated: "that which has its own meaning as the fruit" (*svārthaphala*), or, according to the view of others, "that which denotes an operation qualified by a fruit" (*phalaviśiṣṭavyāpāravācakatva*). Since this [latter definition] is not possible if the root *kṛ* denotes merely effort, the consequence of it being intransitive (*akarmaka*) is unavoidable; such is the intended meaning.

One might object: "If the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone does not denote an operation (*vyāpāra*), then since it would follow that every verbal root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the specific mention of the root *kṛñ* is inappropriate. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "of *kṛñ*. Intending that being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result (*phala*), he says, "being transitive. Thus, the intended meaning is that the distinction between transitive and intransitive roots would be abolished. That—namely, the state of being denotable by all verbal roots.

By this, the criticism that there is an omission [in the definition] because the verse "vyāpāro bhāvanā" establishes that *vyāpāra* (activity) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) but fails to establish that the aspect of the result (*phala*) is so denoted, has been answered. Regarding the phrase "of the root *kṛ*" (*kṛña iti*): it was stated that if [the root *kṛ*] were to have the sense of effort (*yatna*), as in the case of the root *yat* in "yatati" (*yatī prayatne*), it would follow that it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Otherwise, since one observes usages such as "vāyur vikurute" ("the wind transforms") and "asaindhavā vikurvate" ("those who are not Saindhava horses transform"), there would be the consequence of inconsistency with the literal meaning [if it were restricted to the sense of effort].

One might object: "Even if [the root] does not denote the fruit (*phala*), the state of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*)—defined as denoting an operation (*vyāpāra*) that resides in a locus other than the fruit—is certainly intact for roots such as *kṛ* (to do/make), since they denote an operation consisting of effort (*yatna*) etc., which resides in a locus other than the fruit consisting of origination (*utpatti*) etc. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The point is this" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*): the meaning is "the meaning of every verbal root. Regarding the phrase "the consequence of the total abolition of the state of being transitive": the sense is that the definition of transitivity just mentioned cannot be accepted, because it would over-extend (*ativyāpaka*) to roots such as *yat* (to strive) and *syand* (to flow).

Now, it might be argued that, in accordance with the conventional usage of terms such as "transitive" (*sakarmaka*), even the aspect of the result (*phalāṃśa*) must be denoted by roots like *pac* (to cook); for this very reason, if the verbal root denotes only the operation (*vyāpāra*), then the result must be denoted by the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) and so forth. And thus, [in the sentence] "from Prayāga to Kāśī..."

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable application of such expressions as "Caitra sees non-Prayāga" (*aprayāgaṃ paśyati*) and "Caitra goes to non-Prayāga" (*aprayāgaṃ gacchati*), as well as "He abandons Kāśī" (*kāśīṃ tyajati*); likewise, there would be the contingency of the usage "The village flows" (*grāmaṃ syandate*). This is because the single operation denoted by roots such as *gam* (to go) produces both disjunction and conjunction residing in the preceding and succeeding locations. To avoid these contingencies, one might propose that the cognition of the connection with each specific result is caused by the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the respective verbal root; however, this involves excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Regarding the confusion that *tyaj* and *gam* are synonyms: since the production of an identical cognition arises from both sentences—"he goes to the village" (*gacchati grāmam*) and "he abandons the village" (*tyajati grāmam*)—it is impossible to postulate such a relationship of cause and effect, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Even if one were to avoid this deviation by accepting that the property of being a cognition involving the connection of various results belonging to a person at a time when that person is devoid of such a confusion is the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), it would result in extreme complexity (*atigaurava*).

It is not reasonable to claim that such a relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) is not admitted even in a state of such delusion, for it is improper to deny what is established by experience. Likewise, from expressions such as *tyajati* (he abandons) and *gacchati* (he goes), there would follow the undesirable consequence of a cognition of non-distinct moments, namely *tyāgaḥ* (abandonment) and *gamanaṃ* (going). Nor can it be argued that this consequence does not arise because one accepts a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the operation (*vyāpāra*) delimited by a specific result in those cases.

This is because it is more appropriate that the verbal root *gam* (to go) and others themselves denote the qualified object, rather than postulating a capacity (*śakti*) in various causal factors (*pratyaya*) of karma for their respective specific results, or postulating a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of *gam* and others—when not co-uttered with the causal factors of karma—to signify those same results as delimited by their respective effects.

Likewise, there is no occurrence of defects such as the impossibility of usages like "the rice cooks by itself" (pacyate taṇḍulaḥ svayam eva), because if the fruit were not denoted by the verbal root, the action would not be "resident in the object" (karmastha-kriyaka), and thus the designation of the object as the agent (karmavad-bhāva) would not apply. Similarly, even though roots such as *pac* have meanings consisting of an activity delimited by a fruit according to the aforementioned method, there is no obstacle to roots such as *kṛ* having meanings consisting solely of an activity such as effort; in that case, the conventional usage of them as "transitive" (sakarmaka) is secondary (gauṇa), based on their having meanings connected with an object.

Thus, having raised the objection that even in the absence of primary objecthood—defined as possessing a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—objecthood in the form of being an object of cognition (*viṣayatva*) is possible there, he says: "And not in the case of *kṛñ* and so forth. The sense is: "because of the impossibility of the *l*-suffixes [denoting agent or object]," according to the maxim "between the secondary and the primary [the primary prevails]. He demonstrates this very point by means of an illustration:

"No," he says. Since the aforementioned fault does not arise if the root *kṛ* signifies an effort conducive to production, he says: "And if this is so. Regarding the phrase "mere effort": the word "mere" (*mātra*) excludes the result consisting of production; thus, the intention is that signifying mere effort as intended by the opponent is indeed [also] intended by himself. || 5 ||

For this very reason—that is, precisely because the word *yatna* (effort) refers only to that [specific effort]—otherwise, there would be an obvious inconsistency, since the word *utpādana* (production) would have to mean "an effort conducive to production" and so forth. Thus, it serves as a supporting argument. By the phrase "effort and so forth" (*yatnādi*), other operations are also included, in accordance with expressions such as "the sprout was produced by the seed," etc.; for in those cases, since effort is precluded, even when that [effort] is abandoned, other operations are understood through the primary denotative power (*śakti*) itself. Now, one might object:

If it is argued that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting an operation whose locus is distinct from the locus of the result expressed by the suffix, and that "objectness" (*karmatva*) consists simply in being the locus of that same result expressed by the suffix—and thus no fault arises—this is not so. For in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), since the result is expressed by the verbal root itself (as established through presence and absence), it would be redundant to assign it to the suffix; furthermore, there is no evidence for it being the meaning of the suffix. Consequently, both definitions would suffer from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in such instances.

Furthermore, if the fruit (*phala*) were the meaning of the suffix, there would be no resulting cognition regarding the fruit in cases such as *apacati* ("he cooks"); this is the general direction of the argument. He states another reason: transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in the capacity to convey its own meaning as connected with "objectness" (*karmatva*) in a manner common to both primary and secondary [senses]. Even though the specific instances of objectness do not recur, they are subsumed by virtue of possessing the term "objectness."

Even when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is secondary, the accusative and other case endings are employed in accordance with standard usage, as seen in such authoritative expressions as *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the jar") and *karoti* ("he makes [the jar]"); just as, according to the Grammarians (*śābdika*), the instrumental and other cases are used by taking into account a superimposed agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth. It is for this very reason that such expressions as *śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ* ("O stones, listen! are logically consistent.

For this very reason, according to the view of the Bhāṣya—that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the instigator of the entire circle of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*)—the usage of expressions such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being") is accounted for. Nor should it be argued that, since it is an established tenet that the principle of the "primary versus secondary" (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*) does not apply within the section on causal factors (*kārakādhikāra*), even if the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) and others are thereby established, the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) and so forth would remain unestablished there, resulting in the impossibility of usages such as *jñāyate kriyate ghaṭaḥ*.

By the rule *svaritena*, which—through the declaration (*pratijñā*) of the *svarita* accent—carries the sense that "the subsequent [is] an extension (*adhikāra*), [or] an extension [of] an operation (*kārya*"), those [suffixes] are also established. Because the effort (*yatna*) and so forth produced by specific verbal roots (*dhātu*) serve as the determinants (*niyāmaka*) for the cognition of the connection with objects such as the accusative case and others, expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ yatate* ("he exerts himself toward a jar") do not occur when one ought to say *ghaṭāya yatate*. Alternatively, let there be only "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*) as the result (*phala*) in that case, since even that possesses the nature of being a result insofar as it is brought about by cognition and the like.

And thus, since the state of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in having the meaning of an action that possesses an object (*karman*), it is not merely the fact of having the aforementioned logical meaning that constitutes transitivity; rather, what is stated here is that it must have a meaning connected with the purpose of the technical designation *karman* according to this system. And this [meaning] is also necessary for the root *bhū*, because otherwise a suffix in the sense of the object would be untenable; therefore, the meaning is that he states another argument. Now, one might object: "Since there is no explicit statement [to the contrary], the rule 'the agent acting as object should be like the object' (*karmavat syāt*) would apply even to the *yaṅ* and other suffixes," and thus the root text would be untenable. To this, he says: "by the phrase 'it should be like the object' (*karmavat syāt*)."

"It is characterized by the *sūtra*" means "prescribed by the *sūtra*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being construed with the term "yagādi" (the suffixes *ya*, etc.). It should be understood that under the view of the transfer of operation (*kāryātideśa*), the status of being prescribed by that *sūtra* belongs directly to *ya*-suffixes and so on; however, under the view of the transfer of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), it belongs through a mediated sequence. [The phrase] "that would not occur" refers to this.

In a case where the action is equal to the action residing in the object—meaning either identical to it or having the same substratum as the operation that constitutes the result—the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), which defines such an agent as "like the object," does not apply. This is because the root *kṛ* lacks a denotation of a result (*phala*), and the effort (*yatna*) that constitutes its meaning does not inhere in the jar (*ghaṭa*) or other such objects. Nor can one simply accept the non-application of the status of being "like the object" as a desired conclusion, for that would contradict the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra.

Now, one might object: even though effort (*yatna*) does not exist in the object (*karman*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), its subsistence in that object by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*) remains unimpaired. For this very reason, just as in the expression "he knows the jar," the usage "he makes the jar" is justified; because, like knowledge and the like, effort subsists in the jar through the relation of being the object delimited by the result, and thus the jar possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, one could also say "he exerts effort toward the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ yatate*). This is because the effort presented in that context is not treated as a result by way of being its object; therefore, we do not accept that such an object-ness constitutes the delimiter of the resulthood (*phalatāvacchedaka-viṣayatā*).

Anticipating the objection that "the pot is made by itself" is thus logically consistent, [the author] refutes it with the intention that such cannot be asserted because it would lead to the absurd consequence of saying, "the pot is seen by itself," and so forth; he then establishes the example stated in the root text with the words: "Just as the pot is seen... (verse 6).

Thus, [the objection is raised] regarding the point that if the definition of "having an object" (*sakarmakatva*) consists solely of the phrase "having a result in a different locus" (*phalavyadhikaraṇa*), etc., then [it would follow that even the Lord’s cognition has an object]. Regarding the term "delimited by the object" (*viṣayāvacchinna*): the meaning is that the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) resides in the object through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*). By the word "etc. in the phrase "removal of the veil, etc.," the objective state (*viṣayatā*) is included. As for the question "Why should it not be so?": the intended sense is that, in such a case, even the definition of "having an object" in the form of "having a result in a different locus," and so forth, would not be fit to be accepted.

Furthermore, he states "thus, the village" (*evaṃ grāma*) to show that there is also the fault of the undesirable consequence of such usages as "the village is being gone-to by itself" (*gamyate grāmaḥ svayameva*). He says "desired" (*īpsita*) for the purpose of understanding the essential nature of the *nirvartya* (that which is to be produced) and other types of objects. By this, there is no harm even if there is an excess of an object distinct from those [three]. Regarding the phrase "not perceived through a distinction produced by the action" (*kriyākṛtaviśeṣa*): the meaning is "not perceived as qualified by a distinction produced by the action. Alternatively, in the analysis of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that in which a distinction produced by the action is not perceived," the qualifier may be placed first according to the rule beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31).

Although a distinction such as fainting and so forth is observed between the sight of a snake and the sight of a specific object, this is not the case everywhere. Thus, it is concluded that an action whose performance generally lacks the perception of any change produced by the act is an "attainable" (*prāpya*) action. As will be stated:
"That [action] is called 'attainable' where no accomplishment of changes produced by the act is perceived, either through direct observation or through inference."

The meaning of "it will be stated" is that [the objection] is derived from the *Vākyapadīya*. As for the statement "the over-extension is not mentioned," the reason for this is as follows: because of the inclusion of the word "by the object" (*karmaṇā*) in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), there is a restriction to those roots whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) and those whose state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*). Even without [explicitly stating] "because of being internal" (*antarangatvāt*), since the equality of action is obtained through the factor (*kāraka*) that serves as the locus of the meaning of the root in question, the [undesired application] in the example "the sword cuts well" (*sādhvasiś chinatti*) is prevented; for [in that case], the locus of the meaning of the root in question is something other than the agent (*kartṛ*).
The sense is that it is action alone. This determination of action has been stated by Bhartṛhari as follows: "Where there is the perception of a distinction, there action is established;
however, for others, the determination of action is fashioned solely by means of words."

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] has indeed already been stated. [Objection: "But in this way, [the suffixes] of verbs such as 'thinks' (cintayati) and 'sees' (paśyati) would denote the agent of the action—"

Since no distinct [result] is perceived, it is untenable for the action to reside in the agent; therefore, he states the view of others (the Siddhāntin) with the words "anyeṣām" (of others). The word "mata" (view) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Where a result common to both the agent and the object is conveyed by the verbal expression, that is an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). For example, in cases such as "he sees the jar" (*paśyati ghaṭam*) or "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the result in the form of cognition resides in both [agent and object] through the relations of inherence (*samavāya*) and objective content (*viṣayatā*); likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) resides in both through the relation of inherence. Thus...

Even in the case of laughter (*hāsa*), which is a specific modification of the mind (*cittavṛtti*), there is a state of being established in both [the agent and the object]. For this very reason, if the root *jñā* were to mean an activity conducive to the destruction of an obscuration (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, it would result in the fault that it does not have an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyakatva*), but rather would result in having an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyakatva*). Therefore, it is accepted that it means only an activity conducive to knowledge (*jñāna*). However, where the fruit resides in the agent, that is a verb whose state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), as in "he splits" (*bhinatti*) and so forth; for the act of becoming two-fold (*dvidhābhavana*) and the like can never belong to the agent. This is explained in detail elsewhere by Helārāja.

He states the reasoning for others—that verbal roots (*dhātu*) possess the capacity to denote results—by saying, "of the roots," because there is no distinction in their being denoters of action. This means that there is no distinction in their being denoters of actions belonging to the same class. For this very reason, he does not conclude that all roots would become synonyms. However, by the phrase "even [they] say," a lack of satisfaction is indicated; the seed of this [dissatisfaction] is as follows: by postulating that the cognition of a specific result through the accusative case is caused by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by that specific root, it becomes easy to exclude such usages as "he goes to Prayāga" (*prayāgaṃ gacchati*) when one ought to have used "he abandons Prayāga" (*prayāgaṃ tyajati*).

The meaning is that there is no dispute [regarding the view] because the cognition of existence (*sattā*) and so forth from words such as "it exists" (*bhavati*) is established in all philosophical systems (*sarvamata*). Dispute arises only regarding the cognition of the result (*phala*) from words such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), because it is accepted by opponents that in those cases the cognition of the result arises precisely from the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and so forth. For this very reason—that is, precisely because the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses the result—it is consistent.

In the expression "he cooks rice-grains into boiled rice" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), it is intended that the rice-grains possess the status of an object as a modification (*vikārya-karman*) and the boiled rice possesses the status of an object as a product (*nirvartya-karman*). To justify this, the passage from the Bhāṣya is concerned precisely with the fact that [the root *pac*] signifies two results consisting of production and modification. The point is that since a single operation produces these two aforementioned results, it would be clearly inconsistent to claim that it signifies two distinct operations.

[Objection: "But surely, for the sake of making verbs such as *jñā* (to know) transitive, they must denote an operation conducive to cognition and so forth; and thus one would have to say 'the eye knows,' since the contact between the eye and the mind, which is conducive to cognition, exists even in the case of the eye and other [senses]. [Reply: This is not so, because we accept this as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), just as in the case of "the pot cooks. With this intention, he says "dig" (the direction/method). || 7 ||

Having established through the previously stated arguments that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denotable, [the author] anticipates and refutes the view of those following Maṇḍana Miśra—who hold that "bhāvanā is denotable solely by a non-verbal suffix (*atiṅ-pratyaya*)"—with the words "Let it be so established," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "For upon its arrival": this refers to the Jaimini Sūtra, *śabdavattūpalabhyate tadāgame hi dṛśyate tasya jñānaṃ yathānyeṣām* ("But it is perceived as having a verbal nature; for when that [word] arrives, its cognition is seen, just as in the case of others"). In the sentence "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the singularity conveyed by the singular ending is not [connected] as an instrument (*karaṇatva*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that the connection [of number] is with the action, but rather with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), because of the grammatical rule that "suffixes [denote their own meaning] as connected with the meaning of the verbal root. Since singularity would thus not be an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice within its own form, and since there would be no deficiency in the sacrifice even in the absence of that [singularity], it would follow that it is simply not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). This is the point addressed by the following sūtra.

The meaning of that [verse] is as follows: "Like the word"—that is, unity is perceived in such a way that it is conveyed by the word; for (*hi*) when its [the word's] occurrence—namely, the hearing of the singular number—is observed, there arises the knowledge of its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), just as in the case of other [qualifiers] such as "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) or "redness" (*lauhitya*). And thus, since the qualified entity is understood through scripture to be an auxiliary, the sense is that this qualifier, which is itself conveyed by the word, is logically established as an auxiliary, just like the denotation of the word "animal."

The intended meaning is this: just as in that case [of the singular number], where unity is observed upon the arrival of the singular suffix, it is therefore accepted that the suffix has that [unity] as its meaning; likewise, when a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) such as *pacati* is heard, because an activity (*vyāpāra*) is understood, it must be admitted that the suffix has that [activity] as its meaning. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the aforementioned logic. Thus it has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "In the same way, since the parts of the base and the suffix always appear in a sequence, at the moment the suffix is heard, the nature of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is understood."

[Objection: But in this way, the previously stated distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs would be destroyed, because the operation (*vyāpāra*) would not constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), since it would be difficult to define agency (*kartṛtva*) as the state of being the locus of the operation expressed by the root, an affix could not occur with an agent such as Devadatta.
