Therefore, [the author] states that transitivity and so forth are of a different nature, beginning with the words "and thus, when connected with itself" (*evaṃ ca svayukta*); here, "itself" (*sva*) refers to the verbal root under discussion (*prakṛtadhātu*).

Since roots such as *bhū* would otherwise incur the status of being transitive (*sakarmaka*)—because they denote a result that resides in a locus different from the operation denoted by the verbal suffix associated with roots like *pac*—the term "associated" (*yukta*) is used as a qualifier for the verbal suffix. Association (*yoga*) is defined here as occurring immediately after [the root]; thus, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*) and "the jar comes into being" (*bhavati ghaṭaḥ*), even though the verbal suffix following *pac* is associated with the root *bhū*, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition.

If one were to include merely "occurring after itself" (*svottaravṛttitvamātra*), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the root *bhū* in cases such as "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) and "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadatta*). If one were to include merely "occurring immediately after" (*avyavahitottaravartitvamātra*), then even though this would include the roots *ad* and *pac* in the forms "he eats" (*atti*) and "he cooked" (*papāca*), it would fail to include those two roots when they occur within the complex forms "he will cook" (*pacati*) and "he will eat" (*atsyati*). Therefore, the second part [of the definition] is introduced. Consequently, in examples such as "he causes the jar to come into being" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*) and "he causes him to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati*), roots like *bhū* are not included, because they denote the result—such as arising—which has a locus distinct from the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

It should not be argued that since the capacity to denote [an action] such as origination (*utpatti*) resides only in the base form (*prakṛti*), such as *bhū*, and not in the causative (*ṇyanta*) form, there would be no possibility of using a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in the sense of the object (*karman*) for the causative in the expression "the jar is caused to be made" (*abhāṣyate ghaṭaḥ*). This is because there is no fault if one defines "denotative capacity" as the capacity to convey that meaning by virtue of residing in either the base itself or its constituent parts. Furthermore, it cannot be said that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the root *bhū* which is a constituent part [of the causative], for that is precisely what is intended.

Thus, "intransitivity" (*akarmakatva*) consists in being expressive of a result that is coreferential with the operation of the meaning of the [verbal] affix joined with itself; [likewise], "being joined with itself... [and so forth].

It should also be understood that "karmatva" (the state of being an object) consists in being the locus of the result produced by an operation directed toward an object. As for "kartṛtva" (the state of being an agent), it is expressed [by the suffix]; for example, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," Devadatta and others are agents; and in cases such as "Caitra causes Maitra to cook," both the instigator and the instigated are agents because they are the loci of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Likewise, in "Devadatta is cooked" and "Devadatta stands," Devadatta is the agent because he is the locus of the operation which is the meaning of the verbal suffix.

In the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth), the word "ādi" includes the previously mentioned characteristics such as being intransitive (*akarmaka*) and the like. The term "mīmāṃsakammanya" (one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka) is formed with the suffix *khaś* according to the rule "ātma-māne khaś ca. By this, it is indicated that the cognition has the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). As for the objection regarding the undesirable consequence of the cognition "he possesses going" (*gamanavān*), one should not suspect that this would apply even under the view that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are the meaning of the verbal root; for, due to its intrinsic nature (*antaraṅgatva*), it is accepted that the result is construed only with the operation.

In this way, it should be understood that there is also the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such usage as "going is not flow" (*gamanaṃ na syandaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "because it is the locus of conjunction" (*saṃyogāśrayatvāt*), the word "of motion" (*gatyādeḥ*) is to be supplied. If it is objected: "But even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), such usage would result when one intends to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the object (*karman*)," we say no. This is because the intention is that such a consequence would follow even when one intends to express the agency of the very object, such as Devadatta; or else, because suffixes such as *lyuṭ*—which denote merely the result (*phala*) or the operation (*vyāpāra*) co-referential with that result—are not employed [in such cases]. This is the underlying point (*bhāva*).

"Upon the cessation of activity"—that is, upon the destruction of the operation. "And thus there would be the consequence" means that if the verbal root does not denote the operation, then only the result (phala), which is the meaning of the word *pāka*, would be denoted; and thus the stated consequence [of over-extension] would follow, as well as the unstated consequence. The sense is that at the stage when the result has not yet arisen, the existence of the result as its agent is absent, whereas even when the operation has ceased, the existence of the result as its agent persists.

In the previously mentioned case, neither the non-occurrence nor the occurrence of the form *pacati* is possible, because it is accepted that the temporal relation (*kāla*) is connected to the meaning of the suffix—namely, the operation (*vyāpāra*)—by virtue of the scriptural injunction regarding common denotation (*samānābhidhānaśruti*). He refutes what was stated [by the opponent] regarding the removal of those objections with the words "as for what was said, 'in the sense of being' (*bhāve*). The phrase "there is no inconsistency" means that there is no impossibility of his own view, because the aforementioned defects find no scope therein.

"Like the verbal suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-ākhyāta-vat*). The meaning is as follows: just as the Mīmāṃsakas accept that, in accordance with the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, the suffixes *la* are prescribed for the action (*vyāpāra*) by taking the term "agent" (*kartari*), which is carried over from the previous rule, to refer to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), so too it is possible for *ghañ* and other suffixes to be prescribed for the action by the rule *kartari kṛt*. He states that this is not only redundant but also contradicts the Bhāṣya: "contradiction with that Bhāṣya."

The meaning is that if *ghañ* and other suffixes were to denote an action (*vyāpāra*) capable of being construed with a non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*) factor of action (*kāraka*), it would contradict the *bhāṣya* on the rule "abhāve" (Pāṇini 3.3.17). For it will be explained later that in that very context, it is established that "the meaning of *ghañ* and other suffixes is a substantialized state (*sattvabhūtabhāva*). Now, one might object: "Let the meaning of *ghañ* and others be both kinds of states; therefore, there is no contradiction with that. To this, [the author] says, "and because it would contradict that *bhāṣya*," thereby indicating the inclusion of other refutations as well.

For if the agent were not expressed by the verbal suffix, the systematic distinction between what is expressed and what is not expressed would be destroyed; likewise, if the agentive and objective *kṛt* suffixes did not denote the operation, [the distinctions in expressions such as] "the cooker of rice" (*taṇḍulānāṃ pācakaḥ*) and "cooked by Devadatta" (*devadattena pakvaḥ*) would be untenable.

The application of the sixth case (genitive) and so forth is untenable, because [the meanings of verbal suffixes] cannot be objects (*karman*) and the like. Furthermore, if those [suffixes] were also to have the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and their having that meaning would not be obtained through grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*). Nor should it be argued that, by repeating the word *kartṛ* from the sūtra "kṛt [suffixes] in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), the rule for [the suffixes] applies to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) since the term *kartṛ* denotes both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); for there is no evidence for such repetition, and even so, the impossibility of object-suffixes (*karmakṛt*) having that meaning remains constant.

Nor should it be argued that even in rules such as *tayoḥ eva kṛtya* ("the kṛtya suffixes are used after those two [roots]"), the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is carried over from the previous context so that these suffixes are prescribed for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as well; for this would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Likewise, in the case of *guruḥ śiṣyābhyāṃ pācayati* ("the teacher causes the two students to cook"), once it is established by the force of the rule *hetumati ca* that the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must be stated to be the activity of the one being prompted (*prayojya-vyāpāra*) alone. And thus, since the activity denoted by the causative suffix is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*), it can only be construed with that which is the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix.

Because the number is construed with that [object], if the number residing in the teacher (*guru*) were not denoted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a nominative case ending after the word "teacher," whereas there would be its occurrence after the word "pupil" (*śiṣya*); such details are explained at length elsewhere. "This must be accepted" means that, in order to avoid the multitude of objections stated previously, one must accept that even an effort (*vyāpāra*) other than *yatna* is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and that *yatna* is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*). "With the possibility of obtaining all activities" means that, due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), *yatna* as well must be expressed by the verbal root. "The cumbersome nature" (*gaurava*)...

The meaning is that while that [effort] may have the capacity for number, time, and so forth, it does not do so even with respect to effort (*yatna*); for since effort is obtainable through other means, it is inappropriate to postulate a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for it there. Furthermore, the meaning is that if [effort] were already obtained from the verbal root itself as an "operation" (*vyāpāra*), it would be cumbersome to postulate a capacity for the suffix to denote effort as delimited by its specific nature (*yatnatva*). For if that were the case, the cognition established by experience—such as [the effort] being a "blowing" (*phūtkāra*)—could not be accounted for; because even though the effort conducive to those respective results might be obtained, the effort conducive to the operation that is itself conducive to those results would not be obtained.

The statement of the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas that "the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) lies in effort (*yatna*) for the sake of obtaining [that effort]" is also not tenable, because such is not experienced; otherwise, since an operation conducive to the operation [itself] would not be obtained, one would have to assume a denotative power even for that [operation]. Since the meaning of the verbal root is explained as distinct from it by the verb *karoti* (e.g., "he performs cooking"), the *bhāvanā*—consisting of an effort conducive to the operation conducive to the result such as softening—is the meaning of the verbal suffix. This is because when the operation has ceased but the result remains, the expression "cooking exists" (*pāko vidyate*) is not employed.

It should not be argued that "it is necessary for words ending in *ghañ*, such as *pāka* (cooking), to have as their meaning an activity delimited by a result (*phalāvacchinna-vyāpāra*)," because the word *pāka* in the expression *pākaṃ karoti* ("he performs cooking") has as its meaning the result alone. This is because even when activities such as blowing are present at a time when the result has not yet arisen, there is still the common usage, "Cooking will take place. Thus, it is observed that in some instances the word refers solely to the result, whereas in other cases it refers to an activity delimited by a result; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. This is the intended meaning.

"How, then, is it known that *pac* and other such roots denote action? It is because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *kṛ* (to do), as in: 'What does he do? 'He cooks. Thus, the root itself expresses the action. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the *bhūvādi* sūtra is also consistent. Here, by the phrase ending in "gauravam" and by the word "tasmāt," the collection of reasons present in the mind has been set forth. From the aforementioned reasons, it follows that the root *kṛ* is merely an explanation or analysis (*vyākhyāna/vivaraṇa*) of roots such as *pac*.

He states the fundamental meaning [of the opponent's position] with the words "pacatītyasya" and so forth. The "sublating argument" (*bādhaka*) consists of the contradiction with the maxim that "between the base and the suffix, the suffix denotes the primary meaning. Their view is as follows: *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is indeed denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), because it is explained by means of the verb *karoti* ("to do"); however, it is not the case that it is merely an explanation of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), as there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [for such a restriction]. Furthermore, in our own system, the very fact that a cognition having the operation (*vyāpāra*) as its qualificand would otherwise be untenable serves as the proof. As it has been said: "The base and the suffix always express their meanings together; however, because of its predominance, *bhāvanā* is determined to be the meaning of the suffix."

This means: "the view of my own school (māmāsa). Now, one might object: "Even when the causal complex consisting of the presentation of words, word-meanings, and so forth is present, why is there an absence of the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*)? Nor should it be argued that because of the rule that 'kārakas [case-factors] must relate only to the verbal root's action (*bhāvanā*),' there is no mutual relation between them; for even if relation as *kārakas* is impossible, according to the Mīmāṃsaka method, relation in the sense of a general connection (*saṃbandhasāmānya*) is possible. To this, he says: "The point is this" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). "They express a common meaning" (*sahārthaṃ brūtaḥ*) means: they cause their own meanings to be understood as related to a single [common] meaning.

In response to the inquiry as to which of the two meanings functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and which as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), he says "of those two" (*tayor*). He states the resultant meaning with the words "for this [is the case] because... (*ityasya hi*). He explains that both possess the status of a *kāraka*—which is the cause for their mutual non-connection—as the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), by saying "cooking is the object-*kāraka*" (*pākaḥ karmakārakam*). The meaning is: "cooking" refers to the result-part; its status as an object (*karman*) is due to its being brought about by the action (*kriyānirvartyatayā*), and by virtue of the principle of "treating as the principal" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvena*), it has its own substratum as its locus.

For it has been stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* that factors of action (*kāraka*) are construed only with an action. Regarding the phrase "to be mentioned later": since the property of being an action (*kriyātva*) itself serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for their syntactic connection, they are construed only with an action qualified by that [property]; this is the meaning of "to be mentioned later."

In this regard, the only difference is that in the Mīmāṃsaka view, in such cases as "one buys Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow," all the qualifiers and the qualified are construed with the action, while their mutual connection is secondary (*pārṣṭhika*); in our own view, however, it is the qualified object as characterized by its qualifiers [that is so construed]. For this very reason, in expressions such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), the formation of a compound is justified through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). This is because, [in our view], there is no such restrictive rule [as the one held by the other school].

The meaning is that, in your view, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in such cases, the aforementioned rule itself is impossible. And as for the word "relation" (*saṃbandha*): in the case of *yajeta*, by means of direct statement (*śruti*)—that is, by the direct statement of the verbal root and so forth—the mere relation, i.e., a general relation, is stated between the meaning of the root and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Since there is an absence of case-endings such as the third (*tṛtīyā*) and others, a connection in a specific form such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is impossible; therefore, the connection is conveyed through a general relation. Upon the inclusion of one part of that [general relation]—

The meaning is that the function—the capacity—of this scripture (śruti) does not lie in making known a specific relation; for since the fitness (yogyatā) consisting in the non-contradiction of the meaning exists, the statement of its absence is inconsistent. To this he says: "anvaya... (in the context of syntactic connection), because even in his [the opponent's] view, that very [fitness] constitutes the state of being capable.

For this very reason, the sentence "he sprinkles with water" (*payasā siñcati*) is not appropriate when referring to gross water (*sthūlajala*), because the property of being a liquid substance (*dravadravyatva*) alone serves as the delimiting factor of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). This is because the word that functions as the cause for the relation denotes precisely that which delimits the relatum; for that which is delimited by something is indeed what constitutes the delimiting factor of the relatum. Furthermore, it is not the case that there would be an unwanted occurrence of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) at the time one knows a gross liquid to be a substance, even when there exists a subverting cognition (*bādhakapramā*) such as "this sprinkling is not caused by this water."

It must be stated that the capacity for the word's own form (*svarūpa-sadyogyatā*) is the cause [of its denotation]. Alternatively, the intended meaning is that even the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramā-viraha*) must be required. He states the refutation of both rules with the words "ajāśva," etc. Regarding the phrase "of femininity alone": according to the rule that "whatever is the principal [meaning] is indeed the meaning of the suffix," since the class beginning with *aṅ* lacks the status of being the meaning of the suffix, it would fail to attain primacy; rather, the intention is that it belongs to femininity alone. Under the second rule, however, this refutation is quite clear.
Now, if there is no regulator for the cognition [of the meaning] as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and so forth, then [the application] would indeed be unrestricted.

To show that there would be such an understanding, he says: "by way of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), etc. [He adds] "according to linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Thus, the intention is that since linguistic convention itself is the regulator in that case, there is no inconsistency regarding the primacy [of the object], even though the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the mental state (*bhāvanā*). He demonstrates that the understanding follows linguistic convention with the words beginning "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). [The understanding is] "only as having the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier. For this very reason: "In the Ganges there is a hamlet; indeed, a creeper is born on a mountain, but a mountain is never born from a creeper.
Now, the opposite has occurred: two mountains have been born upon the Golden Creeper (*kanakalatā*)."

In such cases, there is a cognition precisely as "Ganges-ness" or "creeper-ness," and for this very reason, there arises the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of perceiving unique qualities such as coolness and purifying power. Otherwise, what difference would there be from the expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Ganges" (*gaṅgātīre ghoṣaḥ*), and how could there be that "reversal" (*vaiparītya*) which is conveyed by the reversed words? Thus say the theorists of poetics (*ālaṅkārikas*).
"The face trembles before the face that shines; the orb of the breasts fears the breasts; the eye dreads the waist; and the lower lip is agitated by the eye."

In this context, the cognition [of the face] as "hair" (*kaca*) and so forth does not cause alarm; rather, it occurs precisely as "Rāhu-ness" (*rāhutva*), "moon-ness" (*candratva*), and so on. For this very reason, in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges," the cognition occurs through "bank-ness" (*tīratva*) and the like. Here, the word *kaca* refers to Rāhu, the word *vadana* (face) to the moon, the word *kucamaṇḍala* (breast-circle) to the pair of Cakravāka birds, the word *madhyapada* (waist-region) to a lion, the word *nayana* (eye) to a deer, and the word *adhara* (lip) to coral—all used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).

The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that the cognition of unique qualities such as coolness and purity is established simply by the word *gaṅgā* denoting [the river] through its own primary function (*svasṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "by way of reversal" (*viparyayeṇa*), it means "in the opposite manner. Regarding "those who are proficient" (*vyutpannānām*), it refers to those who possess the apprehension that such a sentence generates a cognition in which the object (*karmatva*) is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the jar is the qualifier (*prakāra*), by means of the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Thus ends the section on the Naiyāyikas.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, because the word *naiyāyika* is a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*), it would—like the words *pāṭhaka*, *pācaka*, and so on—be subject to the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) as seen in examples such as "reader" (*pāṭhaka*). [The term] "understanding" (*bodha*) refers to the aforementioned understanding. Regarding the phrase "not that" (*na tad*), the word "understanding" (*bodha*) is to be supplied here from the preceding context.

The meaning is that for those lacking such linguistic proficiency (*avyutpatti*), there arises a cognition in the form "the potness residing in the pot" (*ghaṭavṛttikarmatvam*); however, the meaning is not the non-arising of cognition in general. This is because, at a time when the certainty of incompatibility (*ayogyatā*) is absent, even for those lacking such proficiency, a cognition arises in which the pot is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and objectness (*karmatva*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). For this very reason—that is, precisely because cognition follows linguistic proficiency—it is said to be "merely a statement."

The purpose of the particle *eva* is to exclude the phrase "of the base and the suffix," because that [rule] is general and universal, whereas this [present rule] is specific; thus, the intention is that only this [latter] should be accepted. In this context, by the term *ākhyāta*, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is meant, based on the etymological derivation: "that by which the meaning, being the primary element in all cases, is expressed" (*ākhyāyate*). This is because only bases such as nouns (*nāman*) and so forth are the subject of the preceding enumeration, and because of the statement in the *Nirukta*: "Nouns are born from verbs" (*nāmānyākhyātajāni*).

For it is not possible for a name (nāman) to be produced from a verbal suffix (ākhyāta-pratyaya) or from that which ends in one; it is for this very reason that the Mahābhāṣya cites the statement, "In grammar, it is said that every name is derived from a root, as in the case of *śakaṭa* [from *kaṭ*] and *teka*," which has the same meaning as the previously mentioned Nirukta passage. Thus, the definition of a root (*dhātu*) results in being that which expresses the sense of the action (*bhāvārtha*), which is the primary element among all factors in a sentence. The mention of primacy is intended to clarify that the cognition arises precisely with that [action] as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyaka*), and not to include it within the formal definition itself—this is the path approved by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

The authors of the *Mañjūṣā*, however, maintain that in this context the word *ākhyāta* refers to a verbal form (*tiṅanta*), because it is understood as such in passages such as "a verb [is compounded] with a verb," and because the work begins with the statement, "There are four classes of words: nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. Furthermore, they cite its commentary: "The four meanings of a verb are state (*bhāva*), tense (*kāla*), grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and number; among these, state is the primary meaning," and so forth. The details should be understood from that very source.

Even in this view, it should be understood that once it has been established—by means of the arguments previously stated—that this [root] is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it serves as the regulator of its predominance (*prādhānya*). The phrase "even here" (*ityatrāpi*) includes, by the force of the particle *api*, the form *pakkavān*. "In common to both" means in common to both types of words ending in *tiṅ* (conjugational) and *kṛt* (primary derivative) suffixes. "The verbal root alone is the denoter" (*vācaka*)—the sense is that, since the root *pac* is one and the same in both cases, there is parsimony (*lāghava*); whereas because the suffixes are distinct, the theory that they are the denoters would involve complexity (*gaurava*).

"And the consequence of [the verbal suffix] becoming primary. The sense is this: even if [the verbal suffix] were accepted as denoting the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), since the agent and the object could be obtained through the implication (*ākṣepa*) by the *bhāvanā* itself, here too—as in the case of finite verb endings (*tiṅ*)—the consequence would be that the *bhāvanā* alone becomes primary. || 8 ||

"Regarding the phrase *liṅgasaṃkhyānvayeti*: the meaning is that [the agent must be expressed] so that there may be a connection with gender (*liṅga*) such as masculinity or femininity, and with number (*saṃkhyā*) such as singularity, as in examples like *pakvavān* (masculine singular), *pakkavatī* (feminine singular), and *pakkavān* (neuter plural). Regarding the phrase *karturvācyatvam* (the expressibility of the agent): this is also an illustration for the object (*karman*) and so forth in cases such as *pakvastandulaḥ* (the rice is cooked). He states the reason why a compound would otherwise be untenable in the words *puruṣaḥ*."

The meaning is that just as there is no compound in the expression *rājño bhāryā* ("the king's wife") when the intended connection is "the man related to the king [is] the wife related to Devadatta"—because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due precisely to the absence of such a connection—likewise, there would be no compound in cases such as *nakhair bhinnaḥ* ("split by claws") and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to a lack of semantic competency": since grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) connect only with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and not with one another, they lack mutual connection; furthermore, according to the opponent's view, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and other elements do not denote the productive urge. This is because [the connection] occurs through the direct connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

The sense is that even in his view, the root *kṛ* has the meaning of *bhāvanā* (productive operation) in the form of action (*kṛti*). "Succession" (*paramparā*) means a succession consisting in being produced by an action whose agent is oneself, and so forth. He raises an objection with "na ca" (and not). The sense is that in that case, there would be no connection between those two [the blue and the lotus] through the aforementioned successive relation; rather, for the sake of establishing compounds such as *nīlotpala*, they must accept a capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting precisely in having a common connection within a single action, and since that exists here as well, there is no impossibility of the compound. "Asamartha" (incapable).

In the expression *asūryapaśyā rājadārāḥ* ("the king’s wives who do not see the sun"), the Bhāṣyakāra and others maintain that this is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an "unconnected compound"), because there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of the word *sūrya* and the meaning of the negative particle *nañ*, due to the cognition of the mere absence of the action of seeing. According to your view, its status as an *asamartha-samāsa* would be undermined; for [in your view] it would mean "those who do not see the sun."

The sense is that in this case there exists the semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) consisting in the fact that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the meaning of the word "sun" (*sūrya*) are connected to a single action. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "a Brāhmaṇa who does not eat at a *śrāddha* feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*) and "these verses are not to be sung by him" (*amunargeyāḥ ślokāḥ*) are included. Regarding the phrase "because of the undesirable consequence of such [cases]": one cannot accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) even here, because the absence of compounding (*samāsa*) in those instances is accepted by everyone; for this very reason, it is stated under the rule *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ* that when the meaning is "made from the whole hide," the form *sarvacarmaṇaḥ* is a compound due to a specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*).

Now, one might object that in examples such as *kṛtaḥ sarvaḥ*, there can be no compound because [the word *sarva*] is not denoted [by the rule]; furthermore, the rule *saha supā* is not universal. For if compounds were established everywhere by that very rule alone, then the specific injunctions for compounds such as *dvitīyā śritā* would be redundant; otherwise, those various sūtras would merely be prescribing the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *tatpuruṣa* and so forth. It is precisely for this reason that the impossibility of deriving the compound through this [general rule] has been stated in various places.

Furthermore, there is no fault here, because although one might have expected the rule "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā" (Pāṇini 2.1.32) and others to state simply "with a word ending in a kṛt-suffix," the fact that a general rule was formulated, as well as the specific citation "devatrāto galo grāhaḥ," shows that the author intended to accept the compounding of a kāraka with a word ending in a kṛt-suffix by means of an instrumental capacity mediated through action (*kriyā*). This same point is also established by the force of the inclusion of the term "kṛt" [in the rule].

He states another objection with the words "Moreover" (kiṃ ca), intending the following: since the formation of the compound would be established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe* itself through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *sup*, and since even in the case of *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitaram* the compound could be prevented by the mention of the word *bahulam*, because by that very *bahulam* the compound would be established prior to the production of the nominal suffix (*sub*).

Regarding the phrase *dhātvarthaphale*: it means "having the fruit in the form of origination (*utpatti*). One might raise the objection: "But even in your view, this consequence is equal; and the resolution—that it is not so because the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) sublates the designation of object (*karma-saṃjñā*)—is also equal. To dispel this doubt, he says: "And not [in the case] of the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*). Thus, there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*): in the example, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), whereas in the thing illustrated, the meaning of the verb is the operation of the one being impelled (*prayojya-vyāpāra*).

And thus, in the expression *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he causes the pot to come into being"), since the pot lacks the status of an agent (*kartṛ*), its status as the object (*karman*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is entirely unimpeded. In the expression *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"), however, because the pot is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), its status as an object is sublated; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the event of [the pot] not attaining the status of an agent": since everything whatsoever is the locus of some activity denoted by a verbal suffix, the term "co-occurring" (*samabhivyāhṛta*) is necessary.

In the present case (*prakṛte*), the meaning of the suffix *ṇic* is not the operation of the person being prompted (*prayojya*), but rather the operation of the *ṇic*-meaning itself that is restated (*anūdyate*). For this very reason, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the prompter is established; for this same reason, because there is a rule that the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must necessarily conjoin with that which conjoins with the operation signified by the suffix, the nominative case arises after the word "guru" in the sentence "The teacher causes the two students to cook" (*guruḥ śiṣyābhyāṃ pācayati*), and the singular ending in "pācayati" is justified.

The point is that, in this way, because the prompted agent does not serve as the locus for the operation of the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyātārtha*), his status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is untenable. However, one should not suspect that this [instrumental case] is merely the "third case of cause" (*kāraṇa-tṛtīyā*); for if that were so, since the prompter—the agent—would be the cause, Devadatta would incur the status of being the cause, which would result in the impossibility of the derivation of the causative suffix *ṇic* itself. Nor should it be said that in the rule "tatprayojakaḥ," the word "tat" refers to the locus of the operation conducive to the meaning of the verbal root; for by the preceding rule, "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*).

Because the technical designation "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) is prescribed [by Pāṇini 1.4.54], it is only that which possesses the designation "agent" that is eligible to be referred to by the word *tat* [in Pāṇini 1.4.55]; otherwise, since every factor of action (*kāraka*) is the locus of an activity conducive to the meaning of the verbal root, it would follow that the suffix *ṇic* would arise even for the activity that prompts any factor of action whatsoever.

It should not be argued that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) because we observe such usages as "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pācayati*) and "he shows the Lord to the devotee" (*darśayati bhavaṃ bhaktam*); for the point is that when one intends to express the wood and so forth as the agent—meaning "the woods cook" or "the Lord sees"—such usages are desired precisely in the sense of instigating them (*tatpreraṇāyām*). [The phrase] "because it would not incur the status of being the object of the root *gam*" means that only that which is desired by the agent is an object (*karman*).

Now, even in your own system, in the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* which prescribes the technical designation of "object" (*karman*), the word *kartṛ* refers merely to that which is independent (*svatantra*), and not to that which possesses the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛsaṃjñaka*). Otherwise, in the sentence "Devadatta causes Viṣṇumitra to go to the village," the village would not attain the status of an object; for while the prompted agent (*prayojya*) receives the designation of "object" by the rule *gaty-arthādi-sūtra*, he lacks the designation of "agent."

If it is argued that there is no fault even in my view because the "instigated" (prayojya) possesses independence (*svātantrya*)—defined as being the locus of an activity conducive to connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—we say no. In this view, [independence] consists merely in being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), and not in the manner previously stated; for the latter definition would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to all *kārakas*, whereas that [former] independence does not exist in the instigated. Furthermore, it has already been stated that agency (*kartṛtva*) relative to the specific verbal root in question—which consists in being the prompter of the entire circle of *kārakas* connected to that root—is impossible in the case of an insentient entity. This is the intended meaning.

It might be argued that the village can indeed be the object (*karman*) of the causative (*ṇijanta*), and therefore the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is established from that very fact; hence, he says "the object of the root *gam*. Now, one might raise the objection: "What harm is there if that [being the object of the causative] is absent? Anticipating this doubt, he says "and so" (*tathā ca*). He provides the reason why even this would not be possible by citing the rule "gatyarthakarmaṇi. The meaning of that sūtra is: when there is movement (*ceṣṭā*), the accusative and dative case-endings are used for the object of a verb meaning "to go," provided that the object is other than a road (*adhvan*).

In his view, the state of being the object (*karma*) of a verb meaning "motion" consists in being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) when that suffix is used in co-utterance with a root meaning motion in the form of conjunction; and the state of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*) by such an agent consists in being the object of a desire [to obtain] by virtue of being the substratum of the result produced by the action denoted by the verbal suffix residing in that agent. Since this [state of being the most desired] is not possible for the village (*grāma*) according to the aforementioned definition, the sense is that even if the accusative case were established based on its being the object of a causative (*ṇijanta*) construction, the dative case would still not be established. By this, it is meant that the stated usage cannot be accounted for.

"Both" refers to both the operations of the prompted (prayojya) and the prompter (prayojaka). Regarding the phrase "is rejected": the point is that even if the aforementioned verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) were associated with a *ṇij*-affixed root, since it is not associated with a root meaning motion (*gatyartha*), the prompted agent lacks the status of being a "agent of motion"—defined as being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal suffix with which he is connected. Consequently, the status of being the "object" (*karman*) of a root meaning motion does not arise, and thus the impossibility of employing the dative case remains unchanged.

Is it not the case that, by the word *gatyarthakarma* (the object of a verb meaning "motion"), what is intended is an object distinct from [the agent] which, while being the locus of the conjunction resulting from that action, is also intended as the locus of the activity conducive to it—this being so because of the requirements of the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*)? Furthermore, the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi-* has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*; thus, there is no harm even in the absence of the status of being the object of a motion-verb, since the dative case is established just as in the expression *patye śete* ("she lies for her husband"), as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources. Therefore, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).

[Objection: Surely, even in a place devoid of a finite verb (ākhyāta), the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a *tiṅ*-suffix is necessary in accordance with the rule for the nominative case; otherwise, the nominative prescribed by the rule "the nominative occurs when coreferential with a *tiṅ*" would not be grammatically correct. And thus, in the case of "Devadattaḥ paktā" as well, the agency of Devadatta is established through the supply of "is" (*asti*) and so forth. [Response: No, because even if the agency of the root *as* were thus established, the agency of the root *pac* would remain untenable, and consequently, the suffix *tṛc* could not arise from it to denote the agent.

Now, one might argue that the meaning of the rule *kartari kṛt* is accepted as follows: "When the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal suffix—which has the verbal root as its primary cause—is apprehended as belonging to someone, then a *kṛt* suffix occurs after that root"; this is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthyāt*), and also because when someone is intended to be expressed as the substratum of the *bhāvanā* (productive activity) implied [by the verb], then [the suffix occurs] with that person as the expressed meaning. Alternatively, one might claim that the operation itself is admitted to be the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix, and thus agency (*kartṛtva*) is accepted as being simply the state of being the substratum of the meaning of the suffix. If this is argued, we say no, because it would result in an overly strained interpretation (*kliṣṭatvāpatti*).

For this very reason, out of dissatisfaction, he says: "The direction [is as follows]. The meaning of that is as follows: you must accept that both the sequence of the verbal root and the suffix (ākhyāta) and the sequence of the verbal root and the primary suffix (kṛt) serve as the delimiters of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) in a cognition whose qualifier is the *bhāvanā* related by the relation of "favorability" (*anukūlatva*) toward a result that is the meaning of the verbal root. However, for me, only the sequence of the verbal root needs to be accepted as such; thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*), and so forth—this is to be understood from the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*.

Now, one might object: by interpreting *bhūvādayaḥ* as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose beginning is *bhū*," the sense would simply be that the roots starting with *bhū* are designated as *dhātu*, and not that those items recited in the *bhvādi*-group which denote action are designated as *dhātu*; for there is no word present to convey that latter meaning. How, then, is the designation *bhūvādayaḥ* justified? Understand that the letter *va* is introduced here by way of a *nipātana* (irregularity). If it is further objected that even so, its purposelessness remains difficult to avoid, we say: No. "This letter *va* is employed after *bhūvādīnām* for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*)."

This is because the matter has already been resolved by the authors of the *Vārttikas* themselves. "For the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalārthaḥ*) means it indicates auspiciousness. The meaning is that just as in the world the acquisition of something previously unavailable, such as curd and so forth, is an indicator of auspiciousness, so it is here. Alternatively, as is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, when the letter *va* is present, the utterance of the word *bhūḥ* in its modified form brings about the recollection of the word *bhūḥ* ending in the letter *r* (as in the Great Utterance, *mahāvyāhṛti*), thereby serving as an indicator of auspiciousness.

Desiring to dispel the doubt that the Sūtra would thus fail to apply to the opponent's view, he states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words beginning "tatra bhūśca" (and there, *bhū*...). "Vyavasthā" (establishment) means an object whose first form necessarily requires a limit. "By virtue of being expressive of action"—if one were to accept similarity on the basis of [mere] phonetic nature (*śabdatva*) and so forth, then the term "vādayaḥ" (verbs, etc. would result in being non-excludent.

The sense is that if one were to accept [the term *bhāva*] on the grounds that it has the meaning of "going" (*gati*), then all roots beginning with *bhū* would not be included; therefore, based on the commentary, the point is that its acceptance is solely as that which denotes action (*kriyā*). Anticipating the objection that although words such as *hi* and *ru* function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to action, they lack the status of denoting action itself, he says: "in examples such as... The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the *taṅ* suffixes used in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāva*), such as in *śiśye*, as well as forms like *āṇavayati*. [Regarding the phrase] "the consequence of the elision of the vowel *ā*" (*ākāralopāpattiḥ*).

If it is argued that there is no elision because this form [of the root *yā*] is technical (*lākṣaṇika*), we say no; for then the form *paśuṣā* would result in being unestablished (*asiddhi*). In the sense of "he buys cattle" (*paśūn krīṇāti*), the suffix *viṭ* is applied by the rule *jana-sana-khana-ka-raṇa-jīryāṃ viṭ*. Then, by the rule *viḍ-vanor-anunāsikasyāt*, the substitution of *ā* occurs. The point is this: by the term "technical," the intention is that only the pratipadokta (directly stated) form *yā* belonging to the Bhvādi class is grasped by the word *bhvādi*, and not the pronoun *sarvanāman*. However, if one considers the following traditional verse: "Nakāra (the letter n) gives rise to anusvāra and the fifth letters (nasals) when followed by a *jhal* consonant in verbal roots; sakāra (the letter s) gives rise to śakāra; and the ṭavarga (the retroflex class) is born from the tavarga (the dental class). [In this view, the objection regarding *paśuṣā* does not hold.]

Based on the statement of the learned authorities (*abhiyukta*), it is impossible to claim that the *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā regarding forms taught by rule versus those taught by their specific definition) applies to the *dhātusaṃjñā-sūtra*. For if that paribhāṣā were to apply, it would be impossible for the letter *n* and others to be constituents of something qualified as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, it must be accepted—on the basis of such statements from the learned—that the aforementioned paribhāṣā does not operate within the *dhātusaṃjñā*. This is what is being said. If one then says, "Let the *dhātusaṃjñā* be so; nevertheless, due to the Vārttika *āto'nāpaḥ*, there is no elision of the vowel *ā* in the present case," then the introductory remark (*avataraṇikā*) beginning with "therefore he says" (*ityāha*) should be understood.

Now, one might object: "Even if the particle *vā* were a verbal root (*dhātu*), there would be no harm, since the usage *vāti* is accepted. To this, he says: "having the sense of option" (*vikalpārthaka*). The implication is that while the usage *vāti* is accepted when it has the sense of "going" (*gati*) and so forth, it is not accepted when it has the sense of option. Furthermore, if it were a verbal root, it would not attain the status of a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) due to the exclusion rule "that which is not a root" (*adhātuḥ*); and in the absence of being a nominal stem, it would fail to attain the status of a word (*pada*) because it would lack the suffix *sUP*.

By this, even though the root *han* has the sense of "going," just as the meaning of that [sense] is generally not understood from the form *hanti*, the non-understanding of the alternative [meaning] is maintained from the form *vāti*; thus, there is no flaw, as there is no harm even if it is a verbal root (*dhātu*).

The intention [of the author] is as follows: although the rule *nipātasyānarthakasya* must necessarily be commenced for the sake of assigning the designation of *prātipadika* to meaningless particles (*nipāta*), and thus, since that rule has already served its purpose by prescribing the designation for a meaningless particle, there is no evidence to override the prohibition—which is stronger than everything else. It is precisely out of this very lack of conviction that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used in the phrase "of *yāvat* etc. This is based on the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "because there is no teaching of meanings," which refers to the rule beginning with *muṇḍamiśra* and so forth.

For this very reason, the *vārttika* and its *bhāṣya* on the present sūtra are consistent with the statement: "The mention of 'measure' (*parimāṇa*) must be made [in the rule], so that it may be stated: 'this much is the limit for which the verbal designation (*dhātusaṃjñā*) applies'; for why else would the word *udbhū* have the designation of a root, while the word *punarbhū* does not? The phrase "because there is no teaching of the meaning" (*arthānādeśanāt*) means "because there is no teaching of the meaning in all cases."

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *namovarivaścitra-* that the Teacher himself illustrates this point by sometimes specifying the meanings [of roots] and sometimes not. It is for this same reason that the statement—made regarding the particle *eva* in the rule *kurda khurda krīḍāyāmeva*—that it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the fact that roots have multiple meanings, becomes consistent. Furthermore, it should be understood that this is also because the specification of meaning is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). || 10 ||

He states the purpose of filling the word-positions with the words "yathāśruta" (as heard) and "utpattau grahe vā" (in production or in apprehension). For instance, the production of Devadatta from Yajñadatta, or the production of Yajñadatta from Devadatta, is not possible. Likewise, the causality of the knowledge of the meaning of the word *it* toward the knowledge of the meaning of the word *hal*, or the causality of the knowledge of the meaning of the word *hal* toward the knowledge of the meaning of the word *it*, is not possible.

The meaning is that causality belongs only to that which is invariably and immediately prior to the effect; since this is not possible in both cases [the agent and the instrument], it follows that the status of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatva) belongs to that [instrument] alone. As for the phrase "not being any one of them": the nature of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), the state of being a verbal root's meaning (*dhātvarthatva*), and the state of being an action (*kriyātva*) consist in being any one of those things that are to be conveyed by verbal roots, nouns, and indeclinables. Therefore, there is no room for the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). As for the phrase "because it would result in futility": [this refers to the objection that if the instrument were the action, the verb would be redundant].

If it is argued that in rules such as *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ-* (Pāṇini 3.1.7), the desired result is achieved by taking only that which possesses one or another of those [conditions], and that the present sūtra exists merely for the sake of providing that familiarity—[we reply: the point is that since such familiarity, consisting of the comprehension of the meaning of this sentence, is impossible, it is impossible to include [the conditions] by way of being "one or another" (*anyatamatvena*) of them. Regarding the term *lakṣaṇam* (definition): the meaning is that it consists of the form of the sentence-meaning produced by the sūtra. The point is that there is not even a suspicion of the sūtra's redundancy if the individual components of the result are included by way of being "one or another" of them.

[Objection: But if this is so, how is it further known that *pac* and other such roots denote action (*kriyā*), given that their coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *karoti*—as seen in the usage of the *Bhāṣya* on the *bhūvādi* sūtra stating "the verbal root denotes action"—would otherwise be difficult to reconcile, since the aspect of the result (*phala*) lacks the nature of action? To this, he says: "Because it is the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatvāt*). Thus, the intention is that the usage [of the term "action"] is figurative (*gauṇa*).

Regarding this, they say: when the *laṭ* and other suffixes arise, the property of denoting an action (*kriyāvācakatva*)—even while being listed in the *bhvādi* class—is not the restrictive factor, because there is no such thing as a "universal" action (*kriyatva*). Rather, it is a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāviśeṣa*), since these are technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*). Under the view that technical terms denote universals (*jāti*), it is simply a specific universal; the rule (*sūtra*) merely serves to characterize it. In the *Kārikā*, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is understood to have its conventional power (*saṃketikaśakti*) restricted to the operation (*vyāpāra*) expressed as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); thus, only that is grasped. Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule is for the purpose of indication (*sūcanāya*).

The purpose of citing the Sūtra was to establish that a verbal root (dhātu) expresses action; however, the truth is that it was stated solely to dispel the notion that the meaning established by the aforementioned arguments was merely one's own fabrication. By this, it follows that the nature of being a root (dhātutva) should simply be "being any one of the roots beginning with *bhū*. That [nature] does not have "action-ness" as its core definition. Alternatively, the root-ness of the root *bhū* is simply "having the sense of existence (*sattā*) and so forth while being listed in the [Dhātu-]Pāṭha. In this way, the root-ness of each respective root should be inferred by taking up its specific meaning.

Furthermore, because the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is explicitly mentioned [in the definition], there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) either. Alternatively, the suggestion that the meaning of the Sūtra should be construed as "the state of being a denoter of those [words] specified by their inclusion in a *gaṇa*-list, having taken all fruits (*phala*) as being any one of them (*anyatamatva*)" is also rejected. This is because, since the matter can be resolved in the manner already stated, the positions you have proposed—which contain the notion of "being any one of them" and so forth—are overly complex (*guru*). Moreover, in the final position, it is necessary to include even the alternative (*vikalpa*) within the category of "any one of them."

By this, the view that—because whatever meaning is understood from a given verbal root in common usage, that very root is indicated as being "read in the *bhvādi* class" by its inclusion in the list [of roots] qualified by that specific meaning—is refuted; for such a determination would be difficult to ascertain. || 11 ||

Of this very [verb]—that is, precisely because it denotes action while being listed in the *bhvādi* class. "Because of the absence of such cognition" refers to the phrase "of action," and so forth; for from that [the verb], only existence in the form of a connection with various times is cognized. For this very reason, to the question "What does he do?", the answer "He exists" (*asti*) is not given, as one might say "He cooks" (*pacati*). Regarding the aspect of the substratum (*dharmibhāga*):

Regarding the portion consisting of the substratum (*dharmibhāga*) such as existence (*sattā*): since it is impossible for that which is a real entity (*vastusat*) and is to be brought about (*bhāvya*) to be useful for the cognition of its own bringing about (*bhāvanā*), he says "by way of being that which is to be brought about" (*bhāvyatvena*). The word "more so" (*sutarām*) is used because the cognition of a bringing about conducive to production (*utpatti*) is established by all experience; whereas if [the root] had the sense of mere existence (*sattā*), that cognition would occur only in some instances. However, if it has the sense of production and so forth, that cognition occurs everywhere—this is what is indicated by the comparative suffix *-tarap*. By the phrase "production and so forth," the inclusion of defeat (*parābhava*) and other such states in examples like *parābhavati* is intended.

He provides the usage from the *Rāmāyaṇa*, "rohita," as evidence for the sense of origination (*utpatti*). Regarding the sense of existence (*sattā*), there is a contradiction with experience, because in genealogical records (*vaṃśāvalī*) it is precisely origination that is experienced; furthermore, the connection of the causal sense expressed by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would be untenable. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "and because of the impossibility of the fifth case. He states "moreover" (*kiñca*) to provide another proof for the view that roots such as *as* have the sense of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) equivalent to existence. The phrase "of that very [operation]" (*tasyā eva*) means "of the productive operation itself. By the word "even" (*eva*), the aspect of the result (*phalāṃśa*) is excluded.

Regarding this, he states the proof [for his position] with the words "for the purpose of distinguishing actions. This is for the sake of differentiating its own qualified action from other actions. Since differentiation from others occurs only when time is connected to the action, the connection with time must reside in the action alone; this is because the phrase "for the purpose of distinguishing actions" is restrictive (sāvadhāraṇa), as is evident from the subsequent statement, "number belongs to everything. Thus, the point is that the very experience of the authors of the Bhāṣya and others serves as the proof.

And thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra: "Past, future, and present times are manifested by means other than [the verb] *as*; and past, future, and present times are also manifested by *as* and its synonyms. For this very reason, it is explained as "occurring in the sense of a present action. For this very reason, the status of being an action (*kriyātva*) is maintained in cases such as *asti*. The meaning of *as*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati* is self-sustenance (*ātmabharaṇa*).

The self (*ātman*) is existence (*sattā*), and existence is that form which persists through all six transformations of being (*bhāvavikāra*) and is known by the cognition "it exists. Its function with respect to its object is expressed by the two terms *ātmabharaṇa* (supporting itself) and *svarūpadhāraṇa* (maintaining its own nature). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *bhūvādi* (Pāṇini 1.3.1). It is also stated in the *Nirukta*: "The word 'exists' is the determination of an entity that has come into being. And the author of that *Bhāṣya* [on the *Nirukta*] says: "'Exists' expresses the determination of an entity that has come into being, one that possesses existence."

"He explains all categories of entities (*bhāvapadārtha*) because [the action] has the same locus as its result. Regarding "defect" (*doṣa*): it is that which renders [the action] untenable. Thus, the meaning is that, like distance and so forth, it acts as an obstacle to the clear cognition of that mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Regarding "when it is ascertained through its stability": since the question "What does it do? concerns something other than the ascertainment of an operation conducive to existence, the restriction implies that the answer "it exists" is not applicable there.

The authors of the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*, however, maintain that although it is necessary for verbal roots (*dhātu*) to denote action (*kriyā*) in accordance with the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, it is not necessary for them to denote a result (*phala*). Therefore, in the case of roots such as *as* (to be), existence (*sattā*) and the like are themselves the action. For this very reason, they state that in instances such as "Existence sees" (*paśyati bhavaḥ*) or "The rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ svayameva*), since the result—consisting of objective manifestation (*viṣayatā*) and so forth—is itself the action, the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) is appropriately established for the locus (*bhāva*) of that result. As it is said: "Roots such as *pac* (to cook) function, whether [denoting] a single part or the whole collection of operations, according to their own nature, while assuming a uniform form."

In Helārāja’s commentary on the *Vākyapadīya*, it is also stated that the state of being the action denoted by a verbal root (*taddhātvarthakriyātva*) consists in being qualified by the status of being an object of the verbal cognition produced by that root, while not being a qualifier of the meaning of that root. Consequently, in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), "he brings about a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*), or "he sees existence" (*bhavaṃ paśyati*), there is no occurrence of the accusative case; for since [the rice, pot, etc. would otherwise incur the designation of agent (*kartṛtā*) due to being the locus of the action consisting of softening (*viklitti*) and so forth, the designation of agent would sublate the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*), and thus the accusative would not apply.

In that [transitive] usage, because the result (*phala*) is a qualifier of the meaning of that verbal root, it lacks the status of being an "expressed action" (*uktakriyātva*); therefore, such usages as "the rice cooks by itself" (*ataṇḍulaḥ pacyate svayam eva*) are not possible. However, in the case of a reflexive construction (*karmakartṛ-prayoga*), since the result does possess the status of an expressed action, such usages are indeed justified. Furthermore, if the word *tat* (that) were not included within the definition of "existence" (*sattva*), then in cases such as "he cooks and exists" (*pacati bhavati*), the meaning of the root *pac* would fail to qualify as an action; hence, its inclusion is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency because, even in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), the designation of *karman* (object) does not sublate the designation of *kartṛ* (agent)—which finds its scope in examples like *pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks")—and thus [the definition] is not untenable. For in cases such as *caitro grāmaṃ gacchati* ("Caitra goes to the village") or *paśyati bhavān* ("you see"), since Caitra and others are also the locus (*āśraya*) of the result denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), they too would incur the status of *karman*, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) being applied to them.

In the expression "he causes the jar to come into being" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*), although the act of coming into being (*bhavana*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the causative root (*ṇijanta-dhātu*), it does not follow that the substratum [of that act] becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) because it would then have to be an action (*kriyā*) by virtue of being a qualifier of the meaning of the root *bhū*. This is because such a consequence is accepted. For this very reason, since there is a distinction between actions, both [agenthood and objecthood] exist; thus, the usage in both ways was established in the *Bhāṣya* by the rule: "and [the agent] of the object in a causative."

If it is argued that, in this way, since the nature of action (*kriyātva*) is constituted by the nature of a verbal root (*dhātutva*), the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) remains unavoidable, we say no; for the nature of a verbal root consists in being a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and it has already been stated previously that the rule *bhūvādi* (Pāṇini 1.3.1) is merely indicative of that. Furthermore, the state of being the fruit of the meaning of that verbal root means: being the meaning of that verbal root as qualified by its being a qualifier of the meaning of that same verbal root.

In the sentence "Look, the deer runs," the word *tat* (that) is included in the first part [of the definition] to preclude the possibility that the action of running is the result of the act of seeing on the part of the one who sees; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) after the word *mṛga* (deer). Likewise, in cases such as "The rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) and "The pot exists" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the assumption of a substratum (*āśrayatva*) as the operation and the subsequent postulation that [the verb] expresses both the result and the operation—though stated here and there—is not to be accepted.

Furthermore, in cases such as *bhāvayati*, there is an absence of experience [of the meaning] as "that which possesses an activity conducive to being the locus of becoming," because from that [verb form] one perceives only an activity conducive to becoming. Thus, according to this view, the state of being intransitive (*akarmaka*) consists in having only an activity as its meaning; it should be understood that the state of being transitive (*sakarmaka*) consists in denoting both a result and an activity.

According to grammatical rules such as *jīva* [meaning] "to sustain life," *nṛtī* [meaning] "to move the limbs," and *saṃ-sudhvaṃsu* [meaning] "to fall down," these [roots] denote merely actions such as the movement of limbs characterized by the body, or the sustaining of life characterized by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since they lack the capacity to denote both [the action and its object], and because only the qualified [action] constitutes the verbal meaning, [these roots] are not transitive. However, in the case of *dadhāti* ("he places") and similar roots, since they denote both the action of placing and the resulting conjunction (*saṃyoga*), their status as transitive verbs is established; likewise, the usage "he places the limb" (*gātraṃ dhatte*) is logically justified.

They say that because the root *pat* also possesses both meanings like *gam*, the usage of such expressions as "he falls into hell" (*narakaṃ patati*) and "he has fallen" (*patitaḥ*) is accounted for. || 12 ||

"Because of the necessity of the result" (*phalaniyatatvāt*). The meaning is that the very operation conducive to the result (*phalānukūlavyāpāra*) is the referent of the term *bhāvanā*. "Residing in that alone" (*ekamātraniṣṭhatva*) means residing in that [result] while not residing in anything distinct from its individual instances. The meaning is: "the state of residing in a locus different from the locus of either the result or the operation. He states the purpose of including the term *mātra* (alone) with the words "by that" (*tena*). In that context, he says "residing in a different locus" (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), because the qualifying portion (*viśeṣyadala*) [of the definition] would otherwise be redundant.

"Self"—meaning, bearing itself by its own nature, that is, being possessed of an activity conducive to that [existence]. The sense is that, just as in the case of *mriyate* ("he dies"), there is the cognition of an activity conducive to the abandonment of existence, here too there is the cognition of an activity conducive to that [existence]. Now, one might object: "In such cases as *ātmānaṃ jānāti* ('he knows himself'), since the result in the form of knowledge and so forth resides solely in the agent, it is impossible for the verb to be transitive (*sakarmaka*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*ātmānam*" (the self). This is as stated in the Bhāṣya.

Thus, the meaning is that the Self delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the agent, while the Self delimited by the body is the object; therefore, the difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). In this manner, verbs such as *jīvati* (he lives) do not possess transitivity (*sakarmakatva*), because of the inclusion of the qualification "provided it does not denote the locus of the result. For this very reason, the authors of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others state that although the verb *as* (to be) signifies an activity conducive to the maintenance of the self, it lacks transitivity because it denotes the self itself as the locus [of the result].

The followers of Mañjūṣā, however, maintain that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in having as its meaning an object that is related to the meaning designated as the "object" (*karman*) by this [present] treatise. By this definition, expressions such as *ādhyāsitā bhūmayaḥ* ("the lands were occupied") are justified. In this case, however, the status of "object" for the locus is established by the rule *adhiśīṅsthāsām*; furthermore, the relation is of the nature of a connection between two meanings presented separately, since the word "relation" (*anvaya*) is conventionally understood in that very sense. Consequently, there is no fault in cases such as *jīvati* ("he lives"), because in those instances, the object consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is not presented separately from the meaning of the verbal root.
And thus, they say that there is also brevity because the qualification "having the nature of not denoting an object" (aśrāvakatva) is not included. || 13 ||

"Because of contradiction with the Bhāṣya": the intention is that from such a Bhāṣya passage, one obtains the understanding [of the action] as existing solely through the *kṛt*-affix. "In cases such as 'the deer runs' (*mṛgo dhāvati*)," etc.: this is because it was stated immediately following in the *Vākyapadīya* that there is the nature of the goal and the means in the statement "look, the deer runs. "In a verbal word (*ākhyātaśabda*)" means in a collection of *tiṅ*-suffixes. "Because of the existence of two parts": thus, in that case as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the action as being in a state of completion (*siddhāvasthā*).

This example is intended merely to illustrate the cognition [of meaning] by way of being either the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Just as in the case of a verbal suffix ending in *tiṅ* (e.g., *pacati*), the root-form (*prakṛti*) conveys its own meaning as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while the suffix (*tiṅ*) conveys its own meaning as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); likewise, in the word "pāka," the action is communicated by the root as something to be accomplished, and by the suffix in the form of something already established (*siddha*). For this very reason, the singular number in the word *ākhyātaśabde* is naturally appropriate.

Others maintain that this very explanation is seen in the *Helārājīya*. "Being connected as a *kāraka*" means being connected in a form subsumed under the *kāraka*-hood that is distinct from the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) or object (*karmatva*). By this, it was stated previously that even though there is connection in the form of agent-hood or object-hood in cases such as *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks [and] exists"), there is no violation of non-existence (*asattva*). "It is not so" means that since there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*), the status of being an example is not tenable; this is the intended meaning.

In the relationship between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*), complete similarity in every respect is not a determining factor; otherwise, that [relationship] would also apply to "moon" and "face," for instance. Rather, it applies only in certain respects, and since that is present in the present case, he says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The phrase "because of being the object of knowledge" (*mānatvāt*) means that the application of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) occurs only with respect to an object perceived as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Since such a status is not present here, the status of being the object (*karman*) is untenable, and consequently, the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* is inappropriate—this is the intended meaning. Thus, he says "the genitive."

The meaning is that, even if such a connection is not perceived in the case of a word ending in *ghañ*, it is impossible to assume it on the basis of a genitive case that would otherwise be logically untenable. Now, one might object: "Since there is no connection with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix mediated by an action presented by an implied finite verb (*tiṅanta*), the genitive case is not actually illogical. Anticipating this, he says: "Not in common usage" (*na loka...*).

Nor can it be argued that the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.65] is redundant because the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) must be justified by resorting to another action, and that such justification is impossible due to the prohibition "not after [words governed by] *loka* etc. (Pāṇini 2.3.69). This is because, according to the authority of the commentary on the sūtra *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), even the suffix *ktin*—just like *tumun* and others—is merely a restatement of the meaning of the verbal root as it exists in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). Thus, rules such as *vastrasya kṛtiḥ* find their application. Likewise, in cases such as *odanapākaḥ*, a compound would also not occur, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*).

This is because the rule stating "the genitive [case-ending] connected with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded" finds its application in examples such as *vastrakṛtiḥ* ("the making of clothes"). Nor should it be argued that both the sentence and the compound are formed by the "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive alone; for if that were so, there would be no occurrence of the cognition—established by experience—in cases like *nalapākaḥ* ("Nala's cooking"), which takes the form of a cognition having "being the agent Nala" as its qualifier. Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of establishing the meaning of the sentence "The milking of cows is wonderful, [performed] by one who is not a cowherd."

They say that, by the maxim "of what follows immediately after [the word *ubhayaprāptau*]," the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* alone serves as the regulator; thus, since a genitive of the residual sense (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would be unavoidable when no word like *go* is used as an upapada, and so forth, such [objections] are to be disregarded. Now, one might object: "If this were the case, then forms such as *kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ* would result," because in the Mīmāṃsaka school, it is accepted that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verb itself as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). He dispels this doubt by accepting the consequence, stating: "In this manner."

And thus, the intended meaning of the prima facie argument beginning with "Now, [if] the action were non-existent... is that this results in exactly what is desired (*iṣṭapatti*). If it is objected that it is impossible for a single verbal root-meaning to appear simultaneously as both a contradictory state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*) and as already established (*siddhatva*), we say no. Just as a single person can be both a teacher and a maternal uncle due to the difference in their respective relations, so too, because both states are possible within a single entity through the difference in relations such as the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) and gender (*liṅga*), there is no contradiction between the two at all.

Or, just as in the case of "Look, the deer runs," where the single act of running is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to the deer and the means (*sādhana*) with respect to the seeing, so too for a single verbal root-meaning there is a mode of being as the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena prakāratā*) and a state of being as an established entity (*siddhatvena viśeṣyatā*). And because they reside in one and the same locus, their distinct apprehension is not clearly perceived in the cognition. For this very reason, textual statements such as "the *bhāva* expressed by the *ghañ*-suffix is the primary element" are consistent.

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "kartari kṛt," it is stated: "The action expressed by the suffix ghañ is external to the meaning of the root. Thus [the usage] is justified; otherwise, [there would be no distinction] among the kārakas.

The point is this: according to the rule that "conjunction (anvaya) occurs only with that which is presented as the thing-to-be-accomplished (sādhya)," even in the case of conjunction by identity (abhedena), presentation as the thing-to-be-accomplished is required; therefore, the expression *stokaṃ pākaḥ* ("a slight cooking") would not be possible. However, when there is conjunction with the operation (*vyāpāra*), the form is simply *śobhanaḥ pākaḥ* ("a beautiful cooking"), because since the operation is not an object (*akarmatā*), the accusative case does not apply to its qualifier. Furthermore, in the case of conjunction with the result (*phala*), the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* ("the [genitive] of the agent and the object [occur] with a kṛt-affix") does not set aside the accusative. This is because, due to the association with the word *kartṛ* ("agent"), the term *karman* ("object") refers only to an object that is conjoined with the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) by way of identity.
And this is clear in the commentary on the verse "By worshipping, one is worshipped," as is detailed elsewhere. || 14 ||

"In the root as the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvena*). Therein—i.e., in that which ends in *ghañ* and so forth—"is perceived" (*pratīyate*) is the ellipsis to be supplied here. He states what makes this known: "having the form of a verbal root" (*dhāturūpa*). The meaning is: that of which the basis (*nibandhana*), i.e., the cause (*nimitta*), is the form of a verbal root. Since the status of being a cause resides in the cognition and is metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) to the object being cognized, the predominance of the action is established within the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
