"The state of being established" (*siddhabhāvaḥ*) means cognition as something already established.

The phrase "thus there is no [application of the] fault" (*ityanāpattiḥ*) means that since the action presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not connect with gender, when the meaning of the word *stoka* (a small amount) is connected to it, even there the masculine gender is untenable; therefore, the sense is that the neuter gender alone would necessarily apply in the general case. "In connection with the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthānvaye*) means in connection with the fruit (*phala*) of the verbal root's meaning. "The nominative" (*prathamā*) means that, according to the aforementioned reasoning, since the accusative is not applicable, the nominative applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).

The author of the *Kātantrapariśiṣ�ṭa* and others maintain that the expressive power (śakti) does not reside in the suffix *ghañ* itself, but rather in the word ending in *ghañ*; they argue that when the syntactic connection is established through the expressive power residing in that which ends in *ghañ*, the expression "a little cooking" (*astokaḥ pākaḥ*) is indeed justified. Anticipating this view, the author refutes it with the words "na ca ghañante... ("Nor [is it the case] that...").

Furthermore, it should not be argued that even in your own philosophical system (*siddhānta*), collective denotative power (*samudāya-śakti*) is not accepted as a function (*vṛtti*); otherwise, due to the absence of "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not occur, since it has been stated that the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood to carry over into the rule *kṛt-taddhita-*; moreover, because the meaning of the suffix would only be construed with the meaning of the base, there would also be no construal of the number and other properties expressed by the case-ending. This objection cannot stand, because the collective denotative power is indeed necessary, and by virtue of the grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*), the power of the *ghañ*-affix is also indispensable; otherwise, the same would apply to the *ṇvul*-affix and others as well.

It should not be argued that "the [individual] capacity (*śakti*) is not established, nor is this an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because even there the cognition of the agent and so forth is possible through the collective capacity (*samudāyaśakti*) alone"; for this would contradict grammatical rules such as *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67). Nor should it be argued that "the inclusion of roots like *bhū* within the class [of verbal bases] serves as the regulator for the postulation of collective capacity," because that is overly complex (*kliṣṭatva*), because it contradicts the established tenets of all Tantric authorities, and because it would result in the non-occurrence of the suffix *śnu* in forms like *khaś*, leading to the impossibility of deriving names such as *janamejaya*—since the suffix *khaś* is marked with the *ṅit* indicator, which prohibits *guṇa* substitution. With this intention, he says: "dig" (this is merely a direction). || 15 ||

"Of that which ends in a vocative" means "of the meaning of that which ends in the vocative case-ending," or rather, "of that [meaning] itself by way of its referent. Regarding the phrase "because of the requirement for the *nighāta* (elision of the accent)": the idea is that only when there is a connection between "Devadatta" and the act of speaking (*bravaṇe*) does a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) become possible; it is only then that the *nighāta*—the unaccented (*anudātta*) tone—is established by the rule "āmantritasya ca," and not otherwise. Now, one might ask: why is the *nighāta* not applied even in the absence of a single sentence? To this he replies: "In the same sentence" (*samānavākye*). This means: provided that the cause (*nimitta*) and the thing caused (*nimittin*) reside within a single sentence. "The word of address" (*saṃbodhanapadam*)... [is the subject].

On this point, Puñjarāja states: "If a sentence were defined according to the *samartha-sūtra* commentary as 'a sentence is a verb with its qualifiers,' then since the meaning of the vocative case lacks the status of being a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would not apply. This matter is indeed already established: because the vocative case ending pertains to that which is already known (*anuvādya*), it is logical that it connects only with the action to be enjoined (*vidheya*). As Harivṛṣabha stated: "They know that addressing (*saṃbodhana*) is merely the bringing to face of that which is already established; for the entity, having been brought to face, is then employed in actions."

*Abhimukhībhāvaḥ* (being present before one) is the acceptance of being attentive toward grasping the meaning of the words spoken by another. Thus, in the case of "Rāma, protect me," the cognition is: "protection, which has me as its object, is the scope of an instigation directed toward Rāma who is present before [the speaker]. Here, by the phrase "saviśeṣaṇam" (with a qualifier), what is intended is a qualifierhood that is common to both direct and indirect [qualifiers], and not merely direct [qualifierhood]. Therefore, in the sense of "he stands on the bank of the river," the expression "he stands by the river" is an example accepted in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*.

In the case of "haraṇe mighātāsiddhiḥ," there is no failure of accomplishment. In the sentence "vrajāni devadattaḥ" (Devadatta, go!), the word "jānīhi" (know/understand) is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the rule stating that [the verb] "is employed in relation to actions. Since Devadatta is the one to whom the act of knowing is addressed (*uddeśya*) and the act of going is its object (*karman*), the status of being a single syntactic unit (*samānavākyatva*) is established. Through the principle of the "part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*), the cognition of the act of knowing arises from the very words heard; this alone is the meaning of the term *adhyāhāra*. Therefore, they maintain that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*) in such cases.

Others, however, maintain that *saṃbodhana* (addressing) is a desire for a cognition (*jñāna*) as its object; that there are two distinct powers (*śakti*) in the cognition and the desire; that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with the cognition by way of the relation of inherence (*samavetatva*); that the desire is construed with the cognition—already construed with the base-meaning—by way of the relation of being the object of desire (*uddeśyatā*); and that the cognition, already construed with the desire, is construed with the sentence-meaning by way of the relation of a qualified objective scope (*viśiṣṭaviṣayatā*). And thus, since the cognition inherent in the base-meaning is the object of desire, the base-meaning [is the substratum] of that which inheres in the cognition.

It is said that in such cases, the nature of being an object of address (*saṃbodhyatva*), which consists in being intended as a goal, is perceived as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); this very state of being an object of address is what is expressed by the term "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*) in the *Kāśikā* and other works. Thus, in expressions such as "O Rāma, protect me," the cognition takes a form such as: "Protection, which has me as its object, whose agent is one desiring [it], and which is the object of a cognition residing in Rāma—the subject of the desire. This, they say, is the understanding.

"Because of the existence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). This means that the definition of a sentence—as "a verb together with its qualifiers"—is present here. Regarding that syntactic unity, he cites the agreement of the author of the *Sūtras*: "A finite verb [is elided] after a non-finite verb (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*). *Ati-*...

The meaning is: "forming a *sūtra* consisting of [the word] *na-pada*. The inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not ending in a verbal suffix) serves the purpose of preventing the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for that which follows a verb ending in a *tiṅ* suffix in expressions such as *pacati bhavati*. The point is that this inclusion indicates that even in the aforementioned case—where there is an absence of sentential unity (*vākyatva*)—the author of the *Sūtra* intended that a collection of words containing a *tiṅ* suffix constitutes a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*). Regarding the term *ekatiṅ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is one *tiṅ*, i.e., one *tiṅ*-ending [word]. Thus, the meaning is that a collection of words composed of exactly one *tiṅ*-ending word is a sentence.

In this case as well, the qualification "having as its meaning an action qualified by a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭakriyārthakatvam*) must be inserted [as a condition]. By means of that, the two sentences "Devadatta stands" (*tiṣṭhati devadattaḥ*) and "Maitra cooks" (*pacati maitraḥ*) do not form a single sentence with "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*). If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the *nighāta* (elision) of the word "cooks" (*pacati*), and this is not desired, because the definition of a sentence given in the *Pāṭha* is "a verb accompanied by its qualifiers" (*āśyātaṃ saviśeṣaṇam*). For this very reason, in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, having taken the illustrative example (*pratīka*) "he cooks, he does" (*pacati karoti*), [it is stated] even without...

By the word *ca* (and), the existence of a connection is established because it brings about a conjunction; this is stated in the *Kaiyaṭīya*. It is further stated in the *Pradīpoddadyota* that "the connection [of the two clauses] as action and object is also easily expressed. In the opinion of others—meaning in that very opinion—the term *nighāta* (elision of accent) is to be supplied after *na*. With the intention that when there is agreement between opinions, it is not proper to maintain a difference of opinion, he says: "In reality (*vastutas tu*). [The phrase] "having a single finite verb as its qualificand" means...

"Ekatiṅ" means that which has a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*) as its qualifier (*viśeṣya*), in the sense that it conveys the meaning of the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). Thus, the final definition is: the state of being a collection (*samudāyatva*) composed of a single finite verb that expresses the meaning which serves as the primary qualificand.

Others, however, maintain that the rule "a sentence consists of one finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*) is useful only for specific grammatical operations within their own system, such as the suppression of accent (*nighāta*). Therefore, there is no harm even if this [definition] is absent in cases such as "Look, Nṛga is running" (*paśya nṛgo dhāvati*), because of this very point, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* ("not being a finite verb") in the sūtra *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* was rejected in the eighth book of the Mahābhāṣya. Thus, they say that in the aforementioned instance, the absence of suppression of accent (*nighāta*) for the word "Devadatta" is precisely what is obtained, since among the authorities of the Mīmāṃsakas, each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding. This is the meaning of the phrase "from that sense" (*tadarthāt*).

In expressions such as "he eats five times" (*pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte*), words like "five" (*pañca*) are intended to denote the production of that number, while the suffix merely indicates it; furthermore, it is appropriate for such a production to be construed with the action itself, because the natural sense of the rule "the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used when counting the repetition of an action" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc*) is thus preserved. In this context, the word "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) signifies repeated birth, and the resulting cognition is that [the number] pertains to the act of eating.

In this sūtra, the term *akriyā* (non-action) is for the sake of clarity; for since a substance (*dravya*) and so forth arise as a single unit, a "birth" (*janman*) suitable for counting is not established for them. However, even in the case of multiple actions, when their distinctions have ceased and they are expressed by a verbal root (*dhātu*), such a "birth" is possible. Since number (*saṃkhyā*) serves as the cause for counting—which consists in making known the possession of specific numerical values—the word "counting" (*gaṇana*) is used to include only those things well-known as numbers, such as one and so on. Consequently, words like *yugma* (pair), *ubha* (both), and others are excluded; this is clear from the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Regarding the phrase "only for those connected with an action": since the word "action" (*kriyā*) is understood from the rule *dhruvam apāye* ("that which is fixed when there is departure"), and because an action requires a producer, the phrase "that which is fixed when there is the departure [of something] from an action" results in the meaning "that which produces the action. Consequently, since a producer requires an object to be produced, it is logical that the connection occurs precisely there [with the action].

The meaning is that the technical designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) apply only to those [entities] connected with that [action]. This is because it has been stated thus. For example, in the expression "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇavad adhīte*), the word "Brāhmaṇa" refers to the study performed by that [Brāhmaṇa]. In the expression "Maitra is as beautiful as Devadatta" (*devadattavan maitraḥ sundaraḥ*), it should be understood that the verb "is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied; otherwise, the inclusion of the term "action" (*kriyā*) [in the rule] would be rendered meaningless. And in this way, it is clear that the action itself is the locus (*āśraya*) of that meaning.

In the example "The rampart in Pāṭaliputra is like that in Mathurā" (*mathurāvat pāṭaliputre prākāraḥ*), since the meaning of the suffix *vati* connects only with the rampart and not with the action, he [the author] designated this as the "first *vati*. In that case, the word *mathurā* functions [metaphorically] to denote the rampart associated with it; the suffix is applied after a genitive sense expressed by a locative ending, and not after a locative of location, because there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) with the meaning of the locative of location—this is clear from the *Śekhara* and other works, and the details should be understood from those very sources.

Regarding the phrase "because of their prescription": in the example "yāhi yāhi iti yāti" (saying "go, go," he goes), there is an *anvaya* (syntactic connection) between the meaning of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) and the action presented by the word "yāti" through the relation of general and particular.

In the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*, however, "bhoktuṃ pacati" (he cooks in order to eat) is cited as an example; although the suffix *tumun* prescribed by the rule "tumunṇvulau" is not prescribed under the governing heading "dhātusaṃbandhe" (in connection with verbal roots), its status as being caused by a connection between two actions remains intact because it is prescribed only when a word denoting an action serves as the *upapada* (governing word). Thus, the consistency of the example is maintained.

One might object: "In the case of 'The pot is not a cloth,' since the non-compounded *nañ* does not connect with the verb, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he states the intended meaning of the term "non-compounded *nañ*" as "unfit for composition" (*samāsāyogya*). Regarding the word *prasajya*: when the two words *prasajya-pratiṣedha* are compounded according to the rule *sup supā*, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *tadarhati* in the sense of "one who deserves that," meaning "fit for connection with a verb. "Unfit for connection with that" means not connected with the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound. Thus it has been said: "But the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* is that wherein the *nañ* is connected with the verb."
"That is to be understood as a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the subsequent member [of the compound].

He demonstrates the purpose of this explanation with the words "in connection with the meaning of the subsequent member. The construction is: "even though there is a connection with the meaning of the subsequent member, it is because [the compound] is not a *samāsa* (compound). He states the reason for its not being a compound with the words "by virtue of the optionality of *samāsa*."

Now, one might object: "In the case of 'the jar does not exist' (*ghaṭo nāsti*), it is the absence of the jar itself that is perceived, not the absence of an action; nor can it be said that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the absence of existence (*sattā*) having the ground as its locus and the jar as its agent, because this contradicts experience. Furthermore, where there is an absence of the relation with a jar on the ground at the time of the present, it is impossible to convey the absence of that [existence] because existence qualified by the present time and having that [ground] as its locus is unestablished. With this intention, he raises the objection beginning with "And not [in the case of] a non-compound," and so forth.

He provides the resolution with the words "But you... and so forth. [The point is that] there is a negation of the action itself; for this very reason, the use of the second person and so on is justified through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "you" (*yuṣmad*) and the like. Otherwise, just as in the case of "the absence of you exists" (*tvadabhāvo'sti*) or "the absence of me exists" (*madabhāvo'sti*), in expressions such as "you do not cook" (*tvaṃ na pacasi*), the second and first persons would be unjustified due to the lack of coreferentiality with "you" and "I," and the first person would result instead—this is the intended meaning. He states the reasoning for the perception of the negation of the action in the latter case with the words "for this very reason":
namely, because of the perception of the absence of the act of being born (*jananakriyā*).

"Even when the jar exists"—that is, even during the state of the jar's existence. The sense is that since it is impossible to communicate the absence of a jar while the jar is present, one must necessarily admit that in such a case, what is being communicated is the prohibition of an action.

Even though, in the state where [the jar] is non-existent, it is impossible to convey the absence of the jar because the status of being a locus for origination is contradicted in the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar—and therefore, even in that case, one must admit that the negation understood there pertains only to the action—nevertheless, under the view that accepts an absence capable of origination and destruction, the understanding of the status of being a locus for origination is possible regarding the absence of the jar; thus, its existence is maintained. "And so," etc.

The meaning is that, in cases such as "you do not cook," the negation of the action is necessary according to the sequence stated above. "Only the absence of existence" means only the non-existence of the being (sattā) whose agent is the jar; by the word "only" (eva), the absence of the jar itself is excluded. Now, one might object: "Even if we accept the cognition of the negation of an action due to the inconsistency in the previously mentioned case, in instances such as 'the jar does not exist,' let us simply accept the cognition of the absence of the jar and so forth, since there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka). Thus, the aforementioned rule would be violated in that very case. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For not... (na hi).

And thus, if one were to accept that [the absence of the pot's existence] in that manner, there would be a lack of uniformity (vairūpya), and that is not tenable; such is the sense. The underlying point is that even in a locus where the present existence of a pot-maker is unestablished, that [existence] exists indeed in the form of something superimposed (āropita) and so forth; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Now, one might object: "In a sentence such as 'There is no pot on the ground,' which lacks a word denoting an action, what is to be understood is simply the absence of the pot's subsistence in the ground; and thus, in that very case, the rule [of uniformity] is violated. To this, he says: "And thus, on the ground... He provides the reason for the [necessary] ellipsis (adhyāhāra) by stating: "Because of the role as a qualifier (prakāratā)."

The causal relationship (hetu-hetumadbhāva) is established as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition delimited by having the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) through the relation of being a mode (*prakāratā*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*), related [to the effect] through the relation of being a content residing in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Since such a cognition could arise through the relation of being a content belonging to the meaning of the negative particle, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); to exclude this, the content is introduced specifically as "being a mode" (*prakāratātvena*).

The *prakāratā* (qualificative relation) should be understood as being defined by the objectness (*viṣayatā*) delimited by non-existence (*abhāvatva*). Consequently, even though the *prakāratā* belonging to the cognition produced by the sentence "there is no jar" exists in the jar and so forth, there is no persistence of the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the phrase "because it is established": the meaning is that such a causal relationship must necessarily be accepted, because otherwise the aforementioned restriction would not be maintained; therefore, its necessity is established. The remainder—namely, that "superimposedness (*āropitatva*)" is what is expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*), and so on—is as previously stated. || 16 ||

Likewise, with the intention that by the phrase "yasya ca bhāvena" (Pāṇini 2.3.37) the sūtra containing those words is indicated, and by the phrase "ṣaṣṭhī ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.38) the sūtra containing that word is indicated, he explains [the passage] as: "in the case of 'yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam'... and "and in the case of 'ṣaṣṭhī cānādare'...". Thus, in the example "goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ" (he went while the cows were being milked), the locative case is applied by the first sūtra; whereas in the example "rudati rudato vā prāvrājīt" (he went forth while [someone] was weeping).

The collective meaning is that by the second [sūtra], the sixth and seventh cases are prescribed as grammatically correct only when used in connection with an action (*kriyā*). In the example "goṣu duhyamānāsu" (while the cows are being milked), the meaning of the seventh case following the word *go* is a relationship consisting of the nature of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva*).

In the case of "cows being milked" (*duhyamānānāṃ gavām*), both the status of being a signifier (*jñāpakatva*) and the status of being signified (*jñāpyatva*) with respect to the action of going are understood from the words; however, the final implication (*paryavasāna*) lies in the act of milking pertaining to them, because an action whose time is already known serves as the signifier for an action whose time is unknown by way of making known its own temporal concomitance. Similarly, in other cases such as "weeping" (*rudati*), it should be understood that an additional element—namely, disregard directed toward the son or others—is manifested.

"He will explain" means that this will be explained in the course of commenting on the verse "The incorrect [word] is established by inference," by means of the passage beginning with "the state of being uncorrupted and beginningless," and so forth. Now, one might raise the objection: since the word *kriyā* (action) is well-known to denote merely the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and since the aforementioned eightfold [characteristics] acquire the status of being correct (*sādhu*) precisely through their connection with the result (*phala*), there is no necessity for a rule that they must be connected with *bhāvanā* (productive operation). Consequently, it would not be necessary for *bhāvanā* to be the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*) in cases such as *pāka*. He dispels this doubt with the words "This is the intention," and so forth.

He cites the ninth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] as an authority for the fact that a name (*saṃjñā*) is stronger because it functions independently [of etymological derivation], stating "for this very reason. Regarding the phrase "it has been determined": in the ninth book, there arises a doubt concerning the word *uttarā* in the injunction, "If he sings on the *yoni*, he sings on the two *uttarās*. The question is whether the term *uttarā* refers to the two verses read in the *uttarā* collection which correspond to the *yoni* of the *Sāman* (the *sthantara-yoni*), or only to those read in the *uttarā* collection itself. In cases such as, "He places the most excellent (*praśastatara*) *uttara* [verse] upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," the word *uttara* [is understood in its primary sense].

Because we observe that these are relative terms, that very verse which is recited immediately after the *yoni* is the "uttarā" (the subsequent one). Consequently, since the *bṛhat-yoni* is recited in the *Yoni-grantha* after the *rathantara-yoni*, the singing of the *rathantara* occurs upon that verse; and in the *Uttarā-grantha*, since the verse "na tvā vāmanyo divyo na pārthivaḥ" is also recited after the *rathantara-yoni*, [it follows that] there is an option [as to which verse to use]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]: because the word "uttarā" refers only to those verses recited as "uttarās" in the *Uttarā-grantha* due to its usage in Vedic literature, and because [the term] lacks a necessary relative connection [to the specific preceding *yoni*], [the rule is fixed].

The certainty is that this word is conventional (*rūḍha*); therefore, by the subsequent word, there is an immediate presentation of only those two [sāmans] recited in this very *Uttarā* collection of texts. Thus, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the *Ṣaṇḍa-stotra* should be sung in that [collection] alone, and not in the *Bṛhat-yoni*.

And thus, just as in that case [of the example], the weakness of a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) is caused by its functioning in dependence upon the cognition of its respective correlate, while the strength of a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*) is caused by its functioning independently, so too in the present case: compared to a derivative term (*yaugika*) whose functioning depends on the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*), a technical name is stronger because its functioning is independent of that.

The underlying intention is that the conclusion is that the causes of weakness and strength are, respectively, the fact of causing a delayed presentation and the fact of causing an immediate presentation.

[Objection: But surely, since even the *phala* (result) is treated with the word "action" (*kriyā*) in the sūtra "like the action, by the action," and because it is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because [grammarians] establish that even in verbs like *asti* ("is") the state of being (*sattā*) and so forth constitute "action," there is no obstacle to including that [result] everywhere under the term "action. With this intention, he says: "Furthermore, regarding the portion of the result... In certain cases, such factors (*kāraka*s)—as in "Devadatta cooks the rice"—are directed toward the *bhāvanā*.

The meaning is that they have attained the status of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatā*). [The phrase] "in some cases" is used because the factors of action (*kāraka*) are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Regarding the connection of the factors of action with the productive activity, he presents the principle of the *adhikaraṇa* (topic) of the chapter on the extension of specific rules (*viśeṣātideśa*) as the supporting argument: "For it is not the case that [the word] 'sacrificer'... and so forth.

And thus, since factors of action (*kārakas*) are eternally dependent, when there is a requirement for a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), even though the portion consisting of the fruit (*phala*) is capable of such connection, the knowers of logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*) accept that it connects only with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—according to the maxim "not [just] a beggar" (*na hi bhikṣukaḥ*)—when there is a requirement for a qualificand. By parity of reasoning, it is appropriate that the factors of action also connect only with the productive urge; this is the intended meaning. And thus, in the rule that the connection of factors of action occurs only with the productive urge.

By the phrase "kārakādi" (beginning with the factors of action), the portion consisting of the fruit of the verbal root-meaning is included. "In that very [bhāvanā]" means in the bhāvanā itself which has become the qualifier; by this, the portion consisting of the fruit is excluded.

[Objection: "But surely, since there is no difference in their being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatva*), let the connection with the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) occur directly with the result [of the action], as in examples such as 'the cooking of the rice' (*odanasya paktiḥ*). And thus, in accordance with that, since the capacity to cause the cognition of the connection with a *kāraka* has already been established for the very presentation of the result, the connection with the result is not untenable even in cases such as 'the cooking of the rice' (*odanasya pākaḥ*). [Reply: This is not so, because it would follow that the meaning of the verbal root, which has become a *kāraka*, could not be connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). For a thing cannot itself be its own *kāraka*. Furthermore, if the aspect of the result were connected to the *bhāvanā* as its instrument (*karaṇa*), then in that case...

With the intention that such points as the collapse of the *vājapeya* section due to the connection with a *kāraka*, and the resulting failure of the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) to convey its meaning because of the inclusion of another instrument, should be considered in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*, he says in the *Bhūṣaṇa*: "It has been explained in detail. Therefore, it is established that the denotability of *bhāvanā* is necessary in order to establish the connection of a *kāraka* such as "of the rice" in expressions like "cooking" (*pāka*).

He states the view of other grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) who establish, by means of another method, the rule that the *kārakas* (case-factors) are invariably connected with *bhāvanā* (the efficient force), beginning with the words "some, however" (*kecit tu*). Regarding the phrase "of the comprehension of connection and the cessation of expectancy" (*anvayabodhākāṅkṣānivṛttyoḥ*), the meaning is: "of the comprehension of connection (*anvayabodha*) and the cessation of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣānivṛtti*)."

In the case of "the pot on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭa*), according to the view of the opponent (*paramata*), there arises a relational cognition (*anvayabodha*) that the pot qualified by oneness is the locus-ness (*ādheyatva*) as determined by the ground; and according to our own view (*svamate*), there arises a relational cognition that the locus is non-different from the ground. Similarly, in the case of "Devadatta [is carrying] the pot" (*devadatto ghaṭam*), although according to the opponent's view there arises a relational cognition that Devadatta qualified by oneness is the object-ness (*karmatva*) residing in the pot, and according to our own view there arises a relational cognition that the object is non-different from the pot—even so, [this applies] to all the word-meanings constituting the sentence.

It should be understood that there would be no arising of the mutual cognition of the relation [between the meanings]. Nor should it be argued that since the verbal cognition and so forth can occur simply by supplying (adhyāhāra) a meaning in the form of an action (*kriyā*), there is no need to supply a word expressing that [action]; for [the opponents] say that only the presentation of a word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by a word is useful for verbal cognition, and because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that words convey a mutual relation only when they function together. This indicates a lack of conviction [in the opponent's position]. The seed of this [objection] is that even if the [verbal cognition] is explained by the necessity of its connection with a result (*phala*), the necessity of its connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is not obtained. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "svayamupapattim" (the justification itself): since the cognition arises from the statement "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*) as "the jar is that which lacks existence on the ground," there is no requirement for a verb. Thus, in the proposition (*pratijñā*) within the logician’s syllogism stated by the Vedāntins—"The mountain ought to possess fire because of smoke, like a kitchen"—the employment of a verb is redundant. Refuting what is established in certain treatises on *tarka* regarding this, he states the justification; this is the meaning. He explains what is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the case of *nañ* etc. (*nañādiṣu*), namely, from the expression "a jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*). Regarding the rule "spṛhī with the dative": [he provides the following].

When only the dative form ‘puṣpebhyaḥ’ is employed, the Nyāyikas maintain that for the sake of grammatical correctness (sādhutva), one must supply the word ‘spṛhayati’ itself; however, they do not supply a word from another root with the same meaning, nor do they supply the meaning itself. This is what is meant by the phrase “let that be abandoned. Regarding the term *ardhajaratīyam*: it is like half of an old woman (*jaratyā ardham*), hence *ardhajaratī*; from that, the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt*. The meaning is: just as one desires half of an old woman, so too [is this]. || 18 ||

"Vivicya" means having become separate; that is to say, by not being a qualifier of the other [word]. "In this case as well"—this refers to the view that the *kta* suffix in the word *guṇabhūta* denotes the general object (*karma-sāmānya*). Even under the view that it denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*), the meaning is that it has attained the status of a qualifier in that very same place. As for the question "How is there a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) there?": the sense is that such a connection is impossible because of the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that "a word-meaning connects only with another word-meaning. "Because of the acceptance of the connection"—this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*. Hari also says: "Every relative term (*saṃbandhi-śabda*), being necessarily dependent [on another], is always compounded."

"For that mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā), which exists in a sentence, is not lost even in a compound. Thus, since according to the view of the ancient logicians there is an absence of both primary denotation (śakti) and secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) either in the compound as a whole or in its constituent prior member, [the author] proceeds to another instance—namely, "the grandson of Caitra" (caitrasya naptā)—to show that the teacher (guru) is not merely a part of the referent (padārthaikadeśa). The referent of the word *naptṛ* (grandson) is a body produced by a body produced [by Caitra]. The meaning of the genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), such as being related to Caitra, is construed with the state of being produced, which is a part of that [referent].

Nor should it be argued that the relation denoted by the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhy-artha) should simply be construed with the qualificand (viśeṣya) itself, rather than being accepted as being construed with a single part [of the complex]; for otherwise, such usage would result even in the case of "Caitra’s son" (*caitrasya putra*), since that son is also produced by the one produced by the grandfather, and is thus the locus of the relation consisting of being produced as defined by Caitra. Nor can one avoid this over-extension of usage by claiming that the relation expressed there by the genitive is merely "being employed" (*prayojyatva*), which is to say "being indirectly produced" (*paramparā-janyatva*); therefore, he says: "as in the case of 'etc. (*ityādivat*).

The phrase "and so forth" (*ādinā*) includes examples such as "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād anyaḥ*) and "separate from a jar" (*ghaṭāt pṛthak*). The intended meaning is that the relation of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the jar—expressed by the word ending in the fifth case—is desired to be construed with "difference" (*bheda*), which is one part of the referent of the word "other" (*anya*); and the relation of being the limit (*avadhitva*) of the jar—expressed by the word ending in the fifth case—is desired to be construed with "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), which is one part of the referent of the word "separate" (*pṛthak*). Although another view—that the construction occurs everywhere through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of a single part [of the referent]—is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha* Sūtra, and Haribhadra also says:
"Those things whose connection is with a whole, such as a teacher or a family... [the present view is preferred].
"Having come into contact with those parts, they are indeed joined together.

Nevertheless, because expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) exists only in a single part in the aforementioned instance, and in accordance with actual experience (*anubhava*), the first position alone has been adopted here. For this very reason, the non-arising of doubts such as "Is the teacher Devadatta’s or not? or "Is the state of being produced Caitra’s or not? immediately after the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) generated by sentences like "The teacher’s house is Devadatta’s," is naturally accounted for.

In the view that the connection [of the object] occurs with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) itself through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of a single constituent part, the phrase "connection only with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)" means that there is a direct relationship only with the productive urge. And that [direct relationship] exists either with the productive urge as the qualificand, or with one in which the relationship is already constituted. Thus, by such a rule, it should be understood that non-connection elsewhere—except through a relationship constituted by the productive urge—is excluded. He extends this stated point to other cases as well with the word "evam" (in the same way). The example given is: "cooking for the sake of eating."

The meaning is that, since the suffix *tumun* prescribed by the rule *tumunṇvulau* is ordained only for connection with another action (*kriyāyoga*), its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is to be understood as resulting from its connection with the action presented by a verbal root (*dhātu*) which denotes a non-substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*). The same point applies to the suffix *ktvā* in the example "having eaten, [he goes] to cook" (*bhuktvā pāka*).

Regarding the author of the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota*, however, the ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) of forms such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* is obtained from the *bhāṣya* on the sūtras "upapadam atiṅ" and "gatikārakopapadāt kṛd bhiḥ". For instance, in the *bhāṣya* on "upapadaṃ," after stating that the counter-example for the inclusion of "atiṅ" (not being a verbal suffix) is "kārako vrajati" and so forth—on the grounds that the rule "sup supā" applies—the term "tiṅ" is refuted [as a literal restriction]. Rather, by the term "tiṅ," the meaning of a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And thus, [the compound is prohibited] in the case of a word denoting the primary action expressed by that [verbal suffix].

The prohibition of compounding [in the rule *atiṅ*] is as follows: by the word *atiṅ*, the meaning of a *tiṅ*-ending form is grasped through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the prohibition of compounding for a word expressing the primary action denoted by that [meaning] is effected by *atiṅ*. Consequently, even though there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *sup supā*, the example "the agent has gone" (*kārako gataḥ*) will be excluded; this is the intended sense of the statement, "by *atiṅ*, there is a prohibition of its [the subordinate action's] meaning. Immediately after that, for the sake of clear understanding, it was stated that "it should be explained" (*vaktavyam*) regarding the rule *upapadam akriyaḥ*; the meaning of that too is precisely what has been stated.

Now, regarding the question, "What is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for *akriyā*?", once the counter-example has been presented, its refutation is made by stating, "This does not denote an action" (*naitat kriyāvāci*). The intention behind this is as follows: in the rule *tṛn-ṇvul-au*, it is not only *ṇvul* that is excluded; rather, since the mention of the feminine gender in the phrase *kriyārthāyām* (in the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām...*) makes it possible to obtain only the action that is the result [of another action], the explicit inclusion of the word *kriyā* (action) serves to indicate—by virtue of its own force and through proximity—that one must understand the two actions to be of the same class (*sajātīyatva*).

Since the suffixes *tumun* and others are prescribed only for words denoting an action that has attained the status of being merely something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) without relying on a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (i.e., a noun), for this very reason there is no possibility of compounding (*samāsa*) in that case according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, since the prohibition of compounding would not apply due to the absence of denotation of an action, the perceived disparity—that *tumun* and *ṇvul* occur [there] while [compounding] does not—is inappropriate.

Nor should it be argued that there can be no compound because the word *gata* lacks a subordinate element (*upapada*), since it does not primarily denote an action; nor should it be argued that there can be no compound because the verbal root (*dhātu*), having its meaning conjoined with the meaning of the *kṛt*-suffix, cannot be extracted [as a separate unit] to undergo *ekārthībhāva* (semantic unification) with another word-meaning—[for this objection is refuted by the rule] "yena vidhis tadantasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.72).

This is because it contradicts the commentary on the two sūtras "anupasarjanāt" and "samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ," for in that [commentary], it is accepted that the application of taddhita and samāsa suffixes occurs even when there is an absence of *ekārthībhāva* (syntactic unification) after extracting [the word]; likewise, in the commentary on the sūtra "yena vidhis tadantasya," regarding the meaning "the descendant of Paramagārgya," it is stated that the suffix *phak* applies by the rule "yañiñośca" due to the word *gārgya* ending in *yañ*, according to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

Regarding the rule *anupasarjanāt*, it has been stated that if this governing heading (*adhikāra*) were absent, there would be no application of the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*). Consequently, since only the word *kāra*—as part of the compound *kumbhakāra*—would end in the suffix *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīp* would be applied to that very word. Even though the restriction regarding the initial element of the compound (*tadādiniyama*) is prohibited when a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is not an *upasarjana*, the suffix *ḍhak* might occasionally still be applied to the word *kārī*.

In the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *gatikārakopapadāt*, there arises the following objection: "If the term *kṛt* (primary derivative) were not mentioned in that sūtra, then since no compound could occur with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), forms such as *niṣkauśāmbi* would be excluded by the very condition *yat-kriyā-yuktāḥ* ('joined with which action'). Consequently, since it would be impossible for a subsequent member that denotes an action to be a *kṛdanta* (primary derivative) following a prefix like *gati* etc., the mention of *kṛt* would be redundant. To this, [the answer is given]: The expression *yat-kriyā* would apply only in a case such as *prabhavanam*, because the action (*kriyā*) is the predominant factor there; however, it would not apply in cases such as *praṇāyakaḥ* or *praṇīḥ*.

Therefore, it has been stated that the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is for the purpose of including all *kṛdanta* forms that generate the cognition of an adverbial qualifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The intended meaning is that by the force of that inclusion, the rule applies even to those cases where the action functions as a qualifier.

The inclusion of the term *kṛt* [in the rule P. 3.1.91] indicates that when "action-expressing words" (*kriyāvācakaśabda*) are mentioned, only the action in its primary state as something yet-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyamātrāvasthā*) is intended; however, when the meaning in the form of action is mentioned, even such [an action] that is not of that [primary] nature is included. Consequently, case-endings denoting *kārakas* (such as the accusative) and suffixes like *kṛtvasuc* occur even with respect to an action that has attained a completed state and has become subordinate. [Objection: But if this were so, in forms such as *prapacatitarām*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would not be obtained; for if the mention of *kṛt* were absent, it would apply only to action in its state of being yet-to-be-accomplished.

Since a word ending in a causative suffix (*bodhaka-uttara-pada*) is impossible [in this context], the application of the accent here is entirely unimpeded, just as in the case of *praṇāyaka* and similar forms; for even in the word *prabhavana*, it is not only an action in its state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvasthā*) that is perceived. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "If the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix were made, the accent would not apply to a form ending in *ām*; [if you object] thus, we say no."

Regarding the statement, "The mention of *tiṅ* in the sūtra ‘tiṅi codāttavatī’ is redundant; for, by setting aside the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member—which would otherwise apply due to its higher status—the rule for the enclitic accent (*nighāta*) of ‘pra’ would take effect, making the application of the original accent of the subsequent member unnecessary; therefore, the mention of *kṛt* [in the sūtra] must be made," the entire subsequent passage beginning with "If the mention of *kṛt* is made, the accent does not apply to forms ending in *ām*" is merely a statement of doubt (*śaṅkā*). The solution (*samādhi*), however, is hidden right here.

And thus they say that even today, the expression "cooking for the sake of eating" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*) remains undesirable. Regarding the phrase "in the prior and posterior times": when a word expressive of an action is used as an *upapada* (an accompanying word), the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are prescribed after a verbal root expressing the action that constitutes the result; the sense is that the action which has become the result occurs precisely at a subsequent time. Regarding the phrase "the repetition [of the word]," etc.: by the word "etc.," examples such as "twice the killing of a goat" (*dviraṇivadhiḥ*) and "twice the sprinkling" (*dvirāvṛṣprayogaḥ*) are included. "Over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) refers to the over-extension of usage in expressions such as "two cookings" (*dviḥpākau*). [This is avoided] because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

Diti: The meaning is that from such usage, there is the cognition of a count of the occurrences (*janma*) of the action. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the phrase "two cookings" (*dvau pākau*): "Why does [the suffix] not occur here? This is not a count of actions; rather, 'repetition' (*abhyāvṛtti*) is an orientation toward activity. And that [orientation] consists of occurrence (*janma*). Thus, the sense is: "This is not a count of the occurrences of the action. If, however, it had the sense of counting the occurrences of the action, then the dual ending would result in the form "two cookings" (*dvau pākau*). For this very reason, there is no dual ending in the expression "twofold application" (*dviṣprayoga*).

"Double application" (*dviprayoga*) means "twofold utterance" (*dvirvacana*). "Application" (*prayoga*) is so called because it is employed; thus, the action (*kriyā*) presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*), which has the nature of being merely that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra-svabhāva*), resides therein. Consequently, even in the word "double utterance," which has the same meaning as that [action], the action is of the same kind as that presented by the root. However, the suffix (*pratyaya*) denotes the object (*karman*) by virtue of its frequent usage (*bāhulakāt*).

Here, the phrase "it is said" (*āhuḥ*) indicates a lack of satisfaction [with the previous view]. The seed of that [dissatisfaction] is as follows: since there is no successful application [of the rule] for such cases as *bhāvārthaka-dvirāvṛtti* (the reduplication of a verbal sense), and because we observe usages such as *dvirvacane 'ci*, it is more logical to understand the term as referring to action (*kriyā*) alone. Furthermore, it is clear elsewhere that the inclusion of the word "action" (*kriyā*) is for the sake of clarity and for the sake of subsequent rules. || 20 ||

"Of those who possess the apprehension of the verbal root's capacity (*ākhyātaśaktigrahavatām*)" means: of those who possess the apprehension of the capacity [to denote] *bhāvanā* (efficient force) in suffixes such as *tiP*. "From the cognition" means: from the cognition of *bhāvanā* arising from suffixes such as *tiP*. "Based on that" means: caused by the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*).

For example, the word *aśva* composed of the dental *s* is incorrect when it has the universal *aśvatva* (horseness) as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), whereas it is correct when it has the absence of wealth as its ground for application; however, the word composed of the palatal *ś* is the opposite in that very same sense—correct in one case and incorrect in the other.

Now, one might object: grammar is merely an explanatory account of correctness (*sādhutva*), but it does not apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) [of words]. For this very reason, it was stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now begins the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*); and further: "The relationship between word and meaning being established, and the use of words being prompted by worldly purpose, the treatise [grammar] serves as a restriction for the sake of merit (*dharma*)," rather than stating that it conveys the meaning, and so forth.
Thus: "This traditional scripture of grammar has as its object the knowledge of correctness."

Anticipating the objection that even in the *Vākyapadīya* it is stated only that [the word] "is the object of the knowledge of correctness" (*sādhutvajñānaviṣayā*), he states the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) while refuting that doubt with the words "this is the meaning" (*ayamartha*). "This" (*ayam*) refers to what is about to be explained. "In that very [word]" (*tatraiva*) means in the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) itself, by way of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*). "By way of being the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity" (*bodhakatāvacchedakatayā*). Regarding "the state of being power" (*śaktitvam*): denotative capacity (*bodhakatā*) is the capacity to produce comprehension. Since there is a rule that a generative capacity must be delimited, it is necessary to postulate a property as its delimiting factor; therefore, it is logical that this [property] alone possesses the nature of power (*śaktitva*).

The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used in the sense of "but" (*tu*). The idea is that "capacity" (*śaktatva*) and "correctness" (*sādhutva*) are one and the same; for, by accepting that cognition arises only from correct words (*sādhu-śabda*), capacity—which resides exclusively in correct words—is itself correctness. "According to that method" means according to the method of the Mīmāṃsakas.

It is precisely for the sake of determining correctness (*sādhutva*). Thus, since it is beyond dispute that grammar determines expressive power (*śakti*), the use of a *tiṅ*-suffix with the intention of denoting the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is indeed incorrect, because it contradicts the grammatical rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69); this is the intended meaning. Regarding the term "additional" (*atirikta*): the meaning is "additional to correctness. Correctness consists in being non-corrupt (*anapabhraṣṭatā*) and so forth; expressive power (*śakti*) is either a particular kind of will (*icchāviśeṣa*) or a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*).

The intended meaning is that for this very reason, linguistic usage such as "it is correct" (*sādhu*) or "it is capable" (*śakta*) becomes logically consistent. Regarding the phrase "it would indeed be so": even though the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is engaged in making known what constitutes correctness (*sādhutva*), since correctness—as established by the previously mentioned method—is dependent upon specific meanings, its capacity to determine [grammatical] capability is achieved solely through the force of meaning. Therefore, the essential point is that, due to contradiction with grammar, the suffixes *tiP* and others would indeed be incorrect (*asādhu*) when applied to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), just like the use of the instrumental case where the dative sense is intended.

[Objection: "But surely, in this way, the *smṛti* of Pāṇini would be sublated by contradiction with the sūtras of the great sage Jaimini. [Response: No, because the *smṛti* of Pāṇini is more authoritative regarding the aspect of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), since it was composed solely for the purpose of teaching what is correct. In reality, even if there were a contradiction with the works of the commentators on Jaimini’s statements, not even a trace of contradiction with his sūtras arises; for instance, in the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), the sūtra of Jaimini states: "Words denoting action have the sense of becoming (*bhāva*); from them, the action is understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined."

Verbs such as "one should give" (dadyāt) and "one should sacrifice" (juhuyāt) have the sense of becoming (bhāvārtha); that is, they primarily denote action, according to the Nirukta's statement that "the verb has becoming as its primary meaning. Therefore, from these [verbs], action is understood; it is understood primarily, for the reason of primacy.

This very point is as follows: it is the action (*kriyā*) itself that is enjoined as the object, not a substance (*dravya*). Since an action perishes immediately, it is impossible for it to produce a result occurring at a later time; therefore, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is postulated as the medium. This is the meaning of that [passage]. It should be noted that from this sūtra, one cannot derive the conclusion that the *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the suffix and not the agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth. This is the general direction. "From the context" means from the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because the statement "one should not speak untruth" (*nānṛtam*) occurs within that specific context.

And that—namely, the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) established by the context—would be sublated. Thus, if there were speaking in an improper manner during the sacrifice, it would contradict the practice of all ritualists, Mīmāṃsakas, and cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*), who perform expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for sacrificial defects; therefore, one cannot accept such a consequence, and it must be admitted that the verbal roots *bhū* and so forth denote the mental state (*bhāvanā*).

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the grammar rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) lacks authority; for although the term *vṛddhi* and others are not observed in common usage to denote the vowel *ā* and so forth, they have been defined as such within its own technical system (*paribhāṣita*). Thus, there is no fault, since grammar does not purport to determine the power of all words. Furthermore, the letter *l* itself is merely postulated, and likewise, the capacity to denote the agent or the object—though itself a conceptual construct—is possible. However, where there is a contradiction with logical reasoning (*nyāya*), [the rule is set aside].

Even in the case of worldly and Vedic [texts], there is no acceptance of the literal meaning expressed by them; yet, this much alone does not render the scripture invalid, because its authority is maintained in respect to its intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), just as in the case of *arthavādas*. Furthermore, the counter-argument—that in passages such as "One who is yawning should say: 'In me, may skill and will-power abide,'" the denotability of the agent (*kartṛvācyatva*) is necessary to establish that the sentence serves a human purpose—is also addressed.

The sense is that it is proper to rely on what has been stated by the Mīmāṃsakas, namely "no" (neti). Even though the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) functions as a qualifier, since its status as the literal meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*) is not lost, why would the prohibition not serve the purpose of the sacrifice? To explain this, he says: "For [it is] not a subordinate element," and so forth.

Since it is logically appropriate for the status of being an "auxiliary" (aṅgitva) to reside in the qualificandum (viśeṣya) alone, if the auxiliary were connected to the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), two contradictory states—primacy and non-primacy—would result. For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas have rejected the connection of *soma* with the sacrifice as its instrument in the injunction "one should sacrifice with *soma*," maintaining instead that [the agent acts] by means of a sacrifice accomplished through *soma*. Now, one might object: how can the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal root also obtain a connection with the prohibition, since that too is related to the agent who is the meaning of the suffix? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the productive activity... (*bhāvanā tu*).

The word *pradhānam* (the primary), ending in the nominative case, is a qualifier of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force). Thus, although it is impossible for something construed with one [element] as a qualifier to be construed elsewhere as a qualifier, its being a qualifier of the *tiṅ*-meaning (*bhāvanā*)—which itself is the qualificand—is not untenable; the sense is that it is indeed capable of being grasped as such. And so, because of the purposelessness of either the prohibition or that *bhāvanā*, and by virtue of the context, the sense is that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*).

The intended meaning is that only when both direct statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) are capable of establishing something as a subsidiary (*aṅga*), it is the direct statement alone that establishes it because of its superior strength; however, this is not the case in the present instance. Now, one might object: "In this way, even prohibitions such as 'One shall not harm any living beings' and 'One shall not eat *kalañja*,' would not have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārthatva*) by virtue of direct statement, since the agent, presented by the direct statement, would be a qualifier of the action."

If it is argued that because no other principal (aṅgin) is possible there, the prohibition of the agent—who has become a subordinate factor—is itself a subordinate element (aṅga), then by way of violating the stated rule, the prohibition in "one should not speak untruth" would also have to be a subordinate element of the agent; therefore, he says: "Or let it be so."

Alternatively, the weakness of *prakaraṇa* (context) has been established because it functions as an applicator with a delay relative to *śruti* (direct statement), since *śruti* possesses greater strength by functioning as an applicator prior to *prakaraṇa* without depending on anything else; therefore, in the present case as well, this resolution was made by accepting that the stronger *śruti* sublates *prakaraṇa*. However, in reality, the consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) occurs only when there is a conflict between two means of proof (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *jañjabhyamāna-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the person who repeatedly yawns), which will be explained later. This applies to the present case as well.

But he says, "Or let it be," meaning that there is indeed no contradiction between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*). "A duty of the person connected with the sacrifice" refers to the phrase beginning with "by the direct statement and the context. He provides a corresponding example: "as in the case of one who is yawning. The meaning is that just as the recitation of the mantra mentioned there is a duty of the person connected with the sacrifice due to the non-contradictory nature of the sentence and the context, so too is the prohibition of untruth (*anṛta*) [a duty of the person connected with the sacrifice] despite the presence of both direct statement and context. This has also been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "Even though [acts such as] meat-eating and the like have means for women as their purpose, they are resorted to [in the Veda]..."
"The prohibition is held to be a subsidiary (aṅga) of the sacrifice, by virtue of relying on the context.

The term "bhakṣādau" (in the case of eating, etc. ends in the accusative case; the meaning is: that which is a prohibition having those [acts] as its object. For this very reason, there is no violation of the rule—"The prohibition has the same purpose as the primary act"—in the case of "One should not speak untruth. However, in reality, it should be understood that such a rule is not universal, according to the aforementioned statement of Bhaṭṭa. [This applies to] that which is studied outside of a specific context (anārabhyādhīta).

The prohibition "one should not speak untruth" refers specifically to verbal falsehood, as is evident from the natural sense of the *Paspaśāhnika* commentary: "The sages were deceived; when they ought to have used the words *yarvāṇas tarvāṇas*, they used *yad vā na tad vā na*, and thus they became known as *yarvāṇas tarvāṇas*; however, in the sacrificial ritual, they do not speak incorrectly again. Furthermore, this is supported by another scriptural passage cited in the commentary within the section on sacrifices: "Those Asuras, uttering 'helayo helayaḥ,' were utterly defeated."

It should be understood that the prohibition "one should not speak untruth," which is recited in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), applies to both types of untruth. Making this very point clear, the author says in the *Bhūṣaṇa*: "as has been explained at length. Regarding the phrase "like corrupt forms" (*apabhraṃśavat*): just as corrupt forms, despite being communicative due to the delusion that they are correct, are nonetheless incorrect, so too, even though they convey the sense of *bhāvanā*, the suffixes such as *tiP* and others would indeed be incorrect in relation to that *bhāvanā*. This is the meaning of the statement "it would be incorrect."

Nor should it be argued that because this instruction lacks a scriptural basis, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of *tiṅ* suffixes and the like remains unimpaired even if they do not convey the existence of things; for there is the Śruti: "A Brāhmaṇa should, without motive, study and understand the Veda with its six ancillaries," and the traditional maxim:
"The great treatise of Pāṇini, which defines the correctness of words, is beneficial to all; it should be studied in its entirety, and nothing from it should be rejected."

—This is because the *Parāśaropapurāṇa* and other such texts serve as the foundational authority (*mūla*). Nor should it be argued that the status of denoting an agent and so forth is merely imagined (like the letter *l*), for in all cases, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is taught by taking the division between stem and suffix as imagined and adopting their respective meanings. That knowledge [of grammatical correctness] is not a cause [of verbal cognition], because verbal cognition is experienced even in its absence. Nevertheless, since verbal cognition does not arise when there is knowledge of incorrectness (*asādhutva*), even though that [knowledge of correctness] lacks causality, its status as a counteragent (*pratibandhaka*) must be postulated.

And thus, since [forms] such as *tib* and so forth are incorrect (*asādhū*) in their usage, how could there be a cognition of them if they were non-existent? Nor can it be argued that no cognition of them arises at all at that time, but rather that their cognition occurs only when there is an absence of the knowledge of their incorrectness; for even then, the cognition is established by experience. He refutes this objection with the words "tadvyatireke" (upon the exclusion of that). The meaning is: upon the ascertainment of the exclusion of correctness (*sādhutva*). "We shall explain" [this further on].

The sense is that since the understanding [of meaning] from words such as *gagarya* is established by the experience of everyone—even for those devoid of the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutva*) and for those possessing the knowledge of incorrectness (*asādhutva*)—the knowledge of correctness is not the cause [of comprehension], nor is the knowledge of its absence an obstacle; thus, as will be explained, all our desired conclusions are established. May there be auspiciousness! || 21 ||
In the *Bhūṣaṇa-ṭīkā*, composed by Harirāma, the son of Keśava’s brother, the determination of the meaning of verbal roots and finite verbs is complete.
Thus ends the determination of the general meaning of verbal roots and finite verbs in the *Śrīmadvaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇaṭīkā* composed by Harirāma, known by the surname Kāla.

Now follows the determination of the meaning of the *lakāra*s, "for each one. This means for every single one, because it is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Regarding the phrase "of the ten *lakāra*s": this is a compound according to the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*; the intention is that this is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for *laṭ* and the others, just as "the Seven Sages" (*saptarṣi*) is. The genitive case indicates a relationship between the whole and its parts, and it is to be construed with the word "each" (*pratyekam*). The singular number in the word "meaning" (*artham*) is intended to express the meaning in a general sense. He says "he determines" (*nirūpayati*): this is because once there is knowledge of the general meaning of the *lakāra*s, a desire to know the specific meanings of the individual *lakāra*s arises.

And thus, it should be understood that its definition is provided here by way of a relevant incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*). He defines "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) as follows: "That which has begun" (*prārabdha*). The meaning is as follows: [an action] is "present" if it is an incomplete action that is the object of an effort conducive to a specific result, which occurs at a time that is not co-temporal with the destruction of the various operations conducive to that result; and it exists at a time that is the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the final operation conducive to that result. However, for those who do not accept the category of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the meaning should be understood as: it exists at a time that is not the locus of such a destruction. Such [an action]...

The meaning is that the object consisting of action (*kriyātmaka-artha*) is the state of time (*samayatva*) characterized by its being the substratum of an action whose nature is a continuum of operations conducive to their respective results. This is because the presentness (*vartamānatva*) residing in time is established by the experience of all people; for this very reason, the common maxim that "time is the meaning of the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārtha*) is also consistent, and it is precisely for this reason that it has been stated in this very manner in the *Bhūṣaṇa* as well.

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated: "But this present tense [usage] is logical here, because the action has not yet reached its completion; for one who is necessarily eating inevitably laughs, talks, drinks, and blinks. Kaiyaṭa explains that since those [subsidiary actions] are inseparable [from the primary action], they do not constitute an interruption; thus, the usage "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*) is justified even during the state of laughing and so forth. Alternatively, Kaiyaṭa maintains that since those [actions] also contribute toward the result of the respective verbal roots, they are intended to be included within the meaning of the root *bhuj* (to eat), and therefore the present tense is appropriate.

The point is that even various activities such as eating and walking are of that same nature during the time of studying a text that requires many days to complete; for this very reason, the usage "Devadatta is reciting the *Saṃhitā*" is appropriate up until the completion of the study of the *Saṃhitā* and so forth. However, because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate that the verbal root *paṭh* and others denote such a vast number of operations, it is more appropriate that their denotative power (*śakti*) resides only in the limited operations such as the striking of the throat; thus, what was stated previously is correct.

It appears that there is no evidence for the view that various actions such as being born or being struck possess a suitability [for the designation "present"] in that sense; furthermore, since the study of the *Saṃhitā* and so forth exists at the time between the moment of eating and the subsequent moment of its completion, the aforementioned usage is maintained. The intent of the cited *Bhāṣya* is also to include such a state of being present. Moreover, the qualification "having been commenced but not yet completed" is not a mere incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), but rather a defining attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*); therefore, even in the case of past and other actions, by means of their respective temporal delimiters...

There is no risk of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of using the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) based on the existence of an action that has begun but not yet been completed; otherwise, such a consequence would indeed arise because [the condition] would not be met. This is understood from a careful examination of the *Bhūṣaṇa* text, which states that [the suffix -laṭ] denotes being characterized by an action that has begun but not yet been completed. Thus, it merely indicates those respective times, but it does not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). However, in the verbal cognition...

In reality, that time in which such "presentness" exists appears as that specific time; therefore, it is precisely as that specific time that the present tense (*laṭ*) expresses it. However, by this same logic, there would be no possibility of the pastness, non-recentness, and so forth belonging to time also appearing when the conditional (*liṅ*) and other suffixes are employed. If it is argued that these [pastness, etc. appear because they are established by the force of experience, and thus they are denoted by the conditional and other suffixes, then it appears that the same applies to the case at hand. For this very reason, authoritative scholars describe the understanding as: "the act of cooking is one whose time is the present."

Since doubt regarding [the tense] "pastness" (bhūtatva), "non-recentness" (anadyatanatva), and so forth does not arise when there is a cognition produced by [words such as] *papāca* ("he cooked"), that [pastness, etc. must be denoted; this is equally true in the present case as well. Furthermore, it would be untenable to employ expressions such as *apākṣīt devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooked [yesterday]") or *pakṣayati devadatto na pacati* ("Devadatta is cooking now, but he is not cooking [at this very moment]") with respect to Devadatta or others who were agents of cooking at a past time but are devoid of that agency at the present time.

Because the general absence of cooking performed by Caitra is sublated, whereas if the aforementioned "present" were not denotable, there would be no inconsistency in the stated usage, since the absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of being a present cooking performed by Caitra—as defined above—is not sublated; furthermore, it should be noted that the establishment of the counter-positive ultimately takes the form of a mental imposition (*āhāryāropa*).

In cases such as "fire burns," the status of being commenced (*prārabdhatva*) is understood through superimposition (*āropa*), or it should be understood as applicable to everything due to its sentience based on the authority of the Vedic text, "Listen, O pressing-stones. Alternatively, the status of being commenced should be defined as the relation to the first moment, which is a time that is the locus of an action conducive to a specific result and is not the locus of the destruction of that action. In this view, because of the complexity (*gaurava*), he states the simpler [definition] of "presentness" (*vartamānatva*): "past... and so forth.

And thus, the meaning is that "temporal existence" (*vartamānatva*) consists in having a time distinct from the past and the future. In this context, "pastness" is the state of being the counter-positive of a present destruction; "futurity" is the state of being the counter-positive of a present prior non-existence; and "presentness" is the state of existing at a time that is the locus of the current usage [of a word], such as a destruction and so forth. Furthermore, the "time that is the locus of the current usage"—consisting of a watch, a day, or the like—is situated in the intellect and must be specified in each respective case. By means of this—

Even though certain *ghaṭikā*s (units of time) included within the duration of the assault on that locus possess the property of being counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to a destruction occurring at some point during that locus's duration, there is no impossibility regarding their being distinct from the past and the future. Here, "pastness" and so forth serve merely as indicators (*paricāyaka*) for the specific time that is the counter-correlative of the difference; the denotative power (*śakti*), however, resides only in that which is delimited by "timehood" (*kālatva*) as qualified by the difference from those respective times. If one does not accept the appearance of such a difference in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then the portion ending with "difference" serves as the indicator.

It should be understood that *śakti* (potency) exists precisely at those respective times. Regarding the phrase "or distinctness," the word "or" (*vā*) indicates a lack of firm commitment [to that view]. However, the basis for that is that it is possible to state that "pastness" is the distinctness from the present and future, and so forth, since there is no decisive reason [to prefer one definition over another]. Consequently, presentness should not be defined as being constituted by distinctions such as pastness; rather, like pastness and the others, presentness itself is not constituted by the aforementioned distinctions. [This concludes the discussion] starting from "placing on the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇāt*).

When there are two *bahuvrīhi* compounds—namely, "that which has placing on the fire as its beginning" (*adhiśrayaṇādi*) and "that which has placing below as its end" (*aghaḥśrayaṇānta*)—there follows a *karmadhāraya*. The referent of the other members (*anyapadārtha*) is a collection (*samūha*). Even in the *karmadhāraya*, that same collection is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The meaning is: "in the midst of such a collection. "That" refers to the aforementioned state of being present in the *pūpa*. [Objection: But surely the Self exists?

He dispels the objection that expressions such as "the mountains exist" would be untenable—on the grounds that, because the activity conducive to self-supporting there is eternal, it lacks the status of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and thus lacks the status of being an action (*kriyā*); and because, consequently, the property of "presentness," defined as being commenced but not yet completed, is absent there—by means of the passage beginning with "ātma... (the Self).

The phrase "of that which is qualified by it" means: of the activity spoken of as having the self (*ātman*) and so forth as its agent, which is qualified by such royal action. In the expression "origination and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes completion and the distinction between their respective times. Thus, although the aforementioned activity whose agent is the self and so forth lacks origination and the like due to its eternality, it is easily established that it possesses the aforementioned "presentness" because it possesses origination and the like when qualified by those various temporal royal actions; this is your [the opponent's] position.

In this regard, he cites the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vartamāne laṭ* as authority, stating: "And it is said in the *Bhāṣya*: 'The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the root *sthā* [is the time]'.
