Even if [the property] was not previously present, there is no fault; for by the aforementioned relation, the absence of being a delimitor of the counterpositiveness of an absence that is co-locative with heaven is an absence of a particular such delimitingness, rather than an absence of its general form. And this [particular absence] is indeed uncontradicted in the case of *jyotiṣṭomatva* (the nature of being a *jyotiṣṭoma*) and so forth. Since the absence of such delimitingness is construed with the *jyotiṣṭoma* and so on through the relation of "possessing the *jyotiṣṭomatva* which is its own locus," there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule that "a word-meaning [is connected] with a word-meaning."

In the view that the property of being a guru (gurudharma) serves as the delimitor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), it is accepted that even from the sentence "there is no [thing] possessing a single neck and so forth," there arises a cognitive apprehension (*anvayabodha*) of the absence—the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—in relation to the potness-delimited counter-correlativity. For this very reason, the use of such a sentence in a location where some pot exists is not considered valid. Furthermore, they resolved the issue by maintaining that the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) concerning having a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*) applies specifically to cases involving the co-occurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

Modern logicians (*navyatārkika*), however, maintain that the causality of heaven consists precisely in being the cause of heaven such that it possesses a property which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its necessary posteriority (*niyatottaravartitā*) and is not itself delimited by any other property that accounts for its being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*). Such a property is a specific universal (*jātiviśeṣa*) to be postulated at a later time; it appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) by way of the general property consisting in being the delimiting factor of necessary posteriority. And such causality of heaven is certainly uncontradicted in the case of yoga, as the status of being the delimiting factor of necessary posteriority belongs to the [yogic] cause.

The state of not being a delimiting factor (*anavacchedakatva*) for the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā*) delimited by the moment of origination (*utpattikṣaṇa*), which is qualified by the locus-hood of the absence of either that [effect] or its operation as delimited by the property that delimits it; and the qualification of the locus-hood [is determined] by the relation: "residing in its own substratum, delimited by the moment immediately following the moment that delimits itself."

For such a state of being a delimitor of the necessity of following immediately after the staff indeed exists in "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva); because, while there is a qualification of the locus-hood of the pot residing in the potsherd delimited by the moment of production by the locus-hood of the absence of either the staff itself or its operation as delimited by "staff-ness," the status of not being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (nirūpakatā) with respect to the locus-hood of the pot and so forth delimited by the moment of production remains well-established in "pot-ness" even according to the aforementioned relation.

Alternatively, the causality of heaven consists precisely in possessing a property that is the delimitor of the invariable antecedence delimited by the dharma residing in heaven; and being the delimitor of invariable antecedence is as follows:

The state of being a delimitor (avacchedakatva) [of the causal capacity] is understood as follows: by means of either the relation of being its own locus (*svāśrayatva*) or the relation of being an operation (*vyāpāratva*) as determined by its own locus, there exists a spatial pervasion (*daiśikavyāpakatā*) consisting in the property of not being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in the locus of that [effect], at a time delimited immediately prior to being delimited by the dharma characterized by the duty (*dharma*) culminating in heaven; and such a state of being a delimitor of that kind of pervasion, by means of either of those two relations, is to be understood as the state of occurring in no more than the extension of that kind of pervasion (*tathāvidhavyāpakatānatiriktavṛttitva*), etc., by means of that same relation.

Since the property of being a *jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth possesses the status of being a delimitor of such pervasion residing in the operation consisting of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), by virtue of its relation as an operation defined by itself, the status of being a delimitor of the invariable antecedence defined by properties residing in heaven is indeed unimpeded. By this, it must be admitted that, on the view that the meaning of the injunction is causality characterized by invariable posteriority and so forth, the apprehension of such causality residing in the sacrifice is to be accepted as the cause of inclination toward action.

In view of that, the objection—that if the cause were a cognition whose object is heaven and which has as its qualifier the state of being achievable through sacrifice (consisting in possessing a property that delimits the status of being a necessary subsequent member of that [sacrifice]), and if such achievability were the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*), then there would be parsimony (*lāghava*)—is refuted. This is because the causality involved in the definition of pervasion (*vyāpakatā*) does not consist in achievability; thus, by virtue of parsimony, it is possible for [the injunction] to function as an instigator of activity (*pravartaka*) and so forth, provided that the meaning of the injunction is the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Since the nature of being a means (sādhanatā) consists in the inclusion of the determinant of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) precisely as the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedakatva*), there is no impossibility of grasping causality from verbal testimony in cases where that [determinant] is not specifically presented, and the cause is instead characterized by a property that is either too narrow or over-pervasive. However, even so, it might be argued that activity prompted by a desire for a specific mode [of the result] is necessitated by a cognition of the means-nature as determined by that specific property; [this is not the case], because from such sentences as "In the Jyotiṣṭoma... [the means-nature is understood generally].

If it is argued that even when there exists a cognition of being a means (*sādhanatā*) as determined by a specific universal (*vaijātya*) characterized by "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*), an activity motivated by a desire having "heaven-ness" as its qualifier would be impossible due to the absence of a cognition of being a means as determined by "heaven-ness" itself—this is not so. For it is an empirical fact that even from a desire having "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) or similar properties as its qualifier, an unerring activity occurs when grass and other materials are present; furthermore, even those seeking abundant happiness who are free from error engage in specific actions [based on such cognitions]. This is because of that property...

For an activity prompted by a desire for a result characterized by a particular property, there is required only the cognition of a means-hood (sādhanatā) as determined by that which appears under the aspect of that very property. Indeed, [universal properties] such as *vahni-tva* (fire-ness) are not the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being produced from grass and so forth, because they exist even in fire that arises without grass and the like. Furthermore, [properties] such as multiplicity (*bhūyastva*) do not serve as delimiters of the state of being produced for anyone, since they arise merely by the force of the circumstances. Moreover, one who desires an object delimited by *ghaṭa-tva* (pot-ness) would also act toward threads and the like, since threads and so forth are also [causes].

One should not suspect that [the injunction] is based on the possession of a means-ness (*sādhanatva*) delimited by substance-ness (*dravyatva*), as qualified by produced existence (*janyasattva*) and indicated by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth; for the certainty of the non-production of the result acts as an independent inhibitor. Since the status of being a means consists in the production of the result, and this is the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, there can be no such usage as "one desiring a jar should employ a thread. Thus they say; enough of these elaborations. He provides an example of the rule "the optative suffix is used to express cause and effect" (*hetuhetumator liṅ*) with the words "he who [should strike] a Brāhmaṇa..."—*avagoraṇaṃ*.

The raising of a staff or similar weapon for the purpose of killing [is the meaning]. The dative case in "brāhmaṇāya" is used because of its status as a *saṃpradāna* (recipient), just as in the expression "patye raiḥ" (wealth for the husband). Thus, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is as follows: "The hundred-fold torments, performed by the agents of Yama, which have as their object such a person (the Brāhmaṇa) whose cause is the raising of a staff or similar weapon by an agent directed toward a Brāhmaṇa."

The connection of such an action—specifically an action qualified by a *kāraka*—with an action in the form of a torment occurs through the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), but the optative suffix (*liṅ*) does not have the meaning of "cause" and so forth. This is because the meaning of the rule is that the optative suffix follows a verbal root whose meaning is an action standing in a cause-and-effect relationship with another. Since the purpose of the rule is fulfilled simply by its serving to grasp the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the cognition of the connection through that relation, it is improper to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for it in that regard.

Regarding the phrase "in the mere element" (*bhūtamātre*): intending that the word *mātra* signifies restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he says "in the generality of elements" (*bhūtasāmānye*). The meaning is that there is an intention to refer to it by the general property of being an element (*bhūtatva*), and not by way of its specific forms. He provides the authority for this, saying "having introduced [the topic] with 'in an element'. The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood as referring to the time when the action is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

However, on the view that *bhūtatva* (pastness) is the meaning of the suffix, although the previously mentioned usage ‘*abhūt ghaṭaḥ*’ (the pot came into being) can be accounted for as having the sense of origination, there would also have to be such a usage with the sense of existence (*sattā*) when [the pot] is present; for at that time, the pot possesses the property of being present, which consists in its occurring within a time-period relative to its counter-correlate. But there is no fault if it is construed with the action (*kriyā*), because that [presentness] does not exist in the aggregate of all the operations extending as long as the substance—which constitute the pot’s agentive maintenance of itself—since such pastness [of the action] is absent.

This is because, according to the Buddhist view, the relation of locus and located is accepted as applying only to the collection of parts denoted by the word "element" (dhātu). Furthermore, even if "origination" (utpatti) were the intended object [of the verbal suffix], one must observe that the usage "the jar existed" (*ghaṭo 'bhūt*) would be untenable in the moment immediately following origination, if one were to accept its application to the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "iti bodha" (thus the cognition): in the view that "the state of occurring at such a time is the nature of being past," the cognition to be understood is of the form: "that which occurs at a time that is the counter-positive of a destruction existing [at that time]," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "yamatra": "this" refers to what is currently under discussion and will be explained. The word "saṃgraha" (compendium) is to be connected with the word "draṣṭavya" (should be seen). Regarding the word "ādya" (first): it means "of today. Regarding the word "bhedāt" (due to the difference): thus, in the first case, all three types of usage are observed—namely, "Devadatta cooked" (*apākṣīt*), "he cooks" (*pacati*), and "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*). The "last" one is "non-today" (*anadyatana*).

Regarding these two—the past and the future times: some say that the word *laṅ* [in the rule] means "when intended" by the rule *liṅnimitte*. However, in reality, since the cognition of both "pastness" and "non-recentness" (*anadyatanatva*) is established by experience, the interpretation "intended as non-recently past" alone is appropriate. Otherwise, the expressive power (*śakti*) for "pastness" would not be established; for there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one accepts the meaning as: "the *lṛṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root whose meaning is an action occurring at such a past time in actual fact."

The phrase "another logical argument" (yuktayantaram) should be understood as previously stated. In that very context: "when the state of being non-recently past is intended to be expressed," [the suffix] "bhaviṣyat" is used; this means "future non-recently past."

"In the past regarding the future" means: when there is a relationship of cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*), that is, when such a relationship exists between the past time and the future time. He states the authority for this with the words "when there is a condition for the *liṅ*," and so forth. Regarding "good rain": the occurrence of good rain is the cause (*hetu*) of the occurrence of abundance (*subhikṣa*), and the occurrence of abundance is the effect (*hetumat*). Therefore, the *lṛṅ* suffix is used by both verbal roots (*dhātu-vyakti*) that convey these two meanings.

The causal relation (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) is the cause by virtue of its own nature (*svarūpasat*), but even there, it is not a denotative power (*śakti*), because it does not appear in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Likewise, the accomplishment of an action (*kriyāniṣpatti*) is also understood through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and is not directly expressed (*vācyā*).

Now, one might object: "In the cases of a good rain and the state of abundant harvests, since their production is prevented by a deficiency in the causal conditions (*sādhanavaikalya*), their non-arising is understood by oneself and thus explained; in those cases, non-arising occurs due to the future nature [of the effect]. That which has already arisen is called 'past' through the sequence beginning with existence (*sattva*); and that which is capable of arising when the collection of causes is present is called 'future. Therefore, because the causal conditions are absent, even though its arising was possible, it does not occur. If this is argued, we say no. For even in the cases of "it did not exist" (*abhūta*) and "it will not exist" (*abhaviṣyati*), there are indeed the states of having been past and being future.

There is no fault [in this], because the two [terms] are superimposed as the counter-correlates of the negation; for it is precisely for one who conceives of good rainfall as the cause of a state of abundance that this [statement] is uttered, and thus the accomplishment of the action is established. In this case, even though there exists a certainty regarding the absence of pastness and so forth, a cognition characterized by pastness and so forth must necessarily be admitted as being of the nature of a voluntary superimposition (*āhāryāropa*).

Otherwise, if the certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*) were not an obstacle to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then even a non-artificial superimposition (*anāhāryāropa*) would be possible. This is indeed logical; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of denying the verbal cognition established by experience in cases such as the metaphor of identity (*abhedopamā*) "The face is the moon," or in farces (*prahasana*), despite the presence of a certainty of sublation. Furthermore, in cases such as quarrels, since false speech is uttered, verbal cognition would be untenable; and if verbal cognition were to follow in those instances, anger would be inexplicable. Likewise—this [is the case].

If one does not accept that verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) arises from sentences such as "the son of a barren woman goes," then the resulting aesthetic delight for the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) would be inexplicable. Now, one might argue: "In cases such as 'The face is the moon,' the word 'moon' is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean something similar to the moon; and its non-difference (*abheda*) from the face is indeed uncontradictedly understood. Likewise, in cases of false accusation such as 'This is the son of a barren woman,' once the word-meanings are presented by the words, there occurs a mental (*mānasa*) qualified cognition; thus, there is no inconsistency regarding the arising of anger and so forth. If this is argued, we say: No. For if that were so, [in the case of 'The face is the moon'], it would simply mean "something similar to the moon..."

In the two sentences "The face is the moon" and "The face is not the moon," there arises the impossibility of generating distinct cognitions established by experience; furthermore, if one were to accept mental cognition in cases such as curses and the like, then since that would apply everywhere, it would result in the total destruction of verbal testimony (*śabdaprāmāṇya*). For this very reason, the author of the *Khaṇḍana* also stated:
"Indeed, even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent, a word produces a cognition."

Nor does this lead to the untenability of the cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) as a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), for such a consequence is accepted [by us]. Nor does it follow that verbal comprehension would occur even when there is a certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), such as "irrigation has fire as its instrument," for such a consequence is also accepted; moreover, since others—who do not accept the status of a certainty of sublation as an inhibitor of verbal comprehension but do accept the status of the cognition of semantic competency as its cause—also admit verbal comprehension from an artificial (*āhārya*) cognition of semantic competency, this being the case, [there is no fault].

Activity is fit to be induced by the ascertainment of sublation, because in that case, activity is generated only by a cognition whose lack of validity has not been apprehended through the production of a knowledge of invalidity regarding the awareness [of the means]. Enough with this prolixity. When there is the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*), the meaning of the verbal root or of the conditional suffix itself is also "non-existence" (*abhāva*); this non-existence is construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the meaning of the verbal root, and the two non-existences are construed with each other through the relation of the instigator and the instigated (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*). With this intention, he says: "In this case, [the word] 'not different from fire' (*vahnyabhinna*)," and so on. "Even in another sense," etc.

The meaning is that, according to the rule "laṭ sme" (Pāṇini 3.2.117) and others, the *laṭ* and other suffixes are seen even in the past tense (*bhūta*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "according to the system of another school" (*darśanāntararītyā*): in his own system (*svamate*), however, there is only direct denotation (*śakti*) for every stated meaning, not figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); it is in order to convey this that he says "according to the system of another school. Incidentally, he states the rule governing the sequence of *laṭ* and the other suffixes with the words "of these" (*eteṣām*). "Of these" refers to the *lakāra*s. "Only the sequence of the *anubandha*s" means [the sequence] of the *anubandha*s, such as the letter *a* and so forth.

He corroborates the aforementioned point with the usage of the Mīmāṃsakas as well, stating "for this very reason. However, at the beginning, the *ḍit* [suffixes] were not enumerated, because Pāṇini first specified only the *ṭit* [suffixes] in rules such as "the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*). Regarding "the *lakāra*s": the meaning is that they denote the specific senses of the *lakāra*s, such as *laṭ* and so forth. || 23 ||
Thus ends the determination of the specific meanings of the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) in the *Kṣipravaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra-vyākhyā*.

"He states the meaning of *sub* [suffixes]"—the sense is that after the determination of the meaning of *tiṅ* [suffixes], which is the motivator for the status of being a word (*padatva*), there follows the determination of the meaning of *sub*, which is the motivator for that [word-status]. Now, one might object: "The fact that objects such as the *karman* (object) are the meanings of [case-endings] like the second case is obtained through the force of grammatical rules such as 'the second case is used for the *karman*'; however, this is not the case for *ākhyāta* [verbs], because of the absence of such an injunction. Desiring to dispel this doubt, he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and that" (*tac ca*): "that" refers to the *karman*; the particle *ca* has the sense of *tu* (but/rather).

Regarding the phrase "the most desired by the agent" (*karturīpsitatamam*): since the technical designation *karman* (object) is prescribed for that [thing] by the rule *karturīpsitatamam-*, one might object: "Since the word *īpsita* (desired) is conventionally established in the sense of 'intended,' it can only convey the meaning of being 'exceedingly intended' (*atiśayitābhipreta*), and not the sense of 'substratum' (*āśraya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "produced by the action" (*kriyājanya*).

Furthermore, from the root *āp* (to obtain), with the suffix *san* added in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*), the word *īpsita*—derived as a past passive participle (*kta*) in the sense of the object according to the rule "after [roots] meaning cognition, thought, or honor" (*amatibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*)—is employed here as a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), not as a conventional term (*rūḍhaśabda*) meaning "intended. If it were the latter, then in cases such as "he eats milk," etc., even the milk would incur the designation of "object" (*karman*), because since the specific act of eating is intended, it would be impossible to say that it is not intended; for this very reason, even one who has already eaten may eat again out of a desire for milk.

It is established in common usage that [an action] "proceeds" (*pravartate*). Thus, if one respects the term *kriyā* (action) [in the definition], then when there is the intention to express merely the state of being a preeminent benefactor (*prakṛṣṭopakārakatva*), even though [the object] is the locus of the fruit produced by the action, it does not incur the status of an *karman* (object), because it is not intended as such; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra and other sources. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "vāraṇārthānām-" (Pāṇini 1.4.27), it is explicit that this is a word denoting action (*kriyāśabda*). In the rule "kartur īpsitatamam" (Pāṇini 1.4.49), the word "kartuḥ" (of the agent) is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67).

The genitive [in *kartuḥ*] is used; thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that the *kāraka* which is most desired to be reached—that is, connected—with the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) co-occurring with the agent (*kartṛ*) is designated as the *karman*. Furthermore, the connection of the agent should be understood as mediated solely by the action which serves as the qualifier of the referent of the word "agent," because it is what is immediately present [in cognition]. And that [connection] consists in being the locus of the result produced by that [action]. Consequently, "being most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*) means being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) by virtue of being the locus of the result of the action denoted by the co-occurring verbal root, as brought about by such an activity.

[The discussion] concludes as follows: the inclusion of the term "being prompted" (*prayojyatva*) results in the establishment of the status of "object" (*karmatva*) for milk and the like, provided that verbs such as *duh* (to milk) signify an operation conducive to an operation conducive to [the primary action's] result, such as separation; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Now, one might object: since a relationship such as being the prompter of an action—which is constituted by the action itself—exists in other *kārakas* as well, how can such a specific result be obtained? To this, he says: "produced by the action" (*kriyājanya*). The point is that, because another technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed and because we must follow what is desired [by the grammatical system], only the aforementioned relationship is accepted here.

Alternatively, having raised the objection: "But surely, since the desire [denoted by] *san* (the desiderative suffix) is understood through the term *īpsitatama* (that which is most desired), the object of pursuit is already obtained as possessing such a result; therefore, the mere statement that [the object] is the substratum of a result produced by the action is inconsistent," he says: "produced by the action. The meaning is this: "of the object itself"—that is, of that very thing which is the substratum of such a result. Thus, the fact that the agent pursues something as possessing such a result is useful only for the sake of that specific grammatical designation (*saṃjñā*), but it does not mean that the object is included within the range of the primary denotation (*vācya*). This is the point.

Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "and likewise [the case] is so joined," etc. By the word "etc. (*ityādi*), there is the inclusion of [rules] such as *gati-buddhi-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52). The intention is that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the accusative and other cases resides precisely in the non-destruction of such a result, for the sake of establishing a commonality with the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) prescribed by those sūtras. As for "from the compendium" (*saṃgrahāt*): when the result itself is intended to be expressed as a cause, the ablative case is used. In the same way—there is only the postulation of the stated meaning for the accusative and other cases.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to claim that [the object] appears in verbal cognition precisely because of [the presence of] the desire to obtain (*īpsā*) and so forth, he says "īpsita" (desired). This means: regarding the states of being desired and not desired. Now, one might raise the doubt: even so, the expressive power (*śakti*) is obtained only for a substratum (*āśraya*) qualified by a result produced by the action, and not for a mere substratum; he refutes this with the words beginning "tathā ca. That is to say: "tathā ca" means when the substratum of the result produced by the action is the object (*karman*).

Others, however, maintain that since the status of being intended (uddeśyatva) as the locus of such a result must also necessarily be expressed, for this very reason, in cases such as "he eats rice with milk" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), substances like milk—which are indeed loci of such a result—do not possess the status of an object (*karman*) because they lack that specific kind of intendedness. Now, one might object that since the nature of being a locus varies according to differences in its relatum (*nirūpaka*) and so forth, there would be an infinite number of expressive powers (*śakti*); to this, he says: "And its essence... (*tattvaṃ ca*). This means: "And the nature of being a locus... (*āśrayatvaṃ ca*).

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the *Bhāṣya*, which holds that "there is indeed a difference in the capacity" (*śakteḥ bheda eva*), it should be understood that there is a unification (*anugama*) of the various loci (*āśrayatā*) by way of their being "locus-ness" (*āśrayatātva*). However, in the view of the moderns (*navya*), it should be noted that the locus is the denotatum (*śakya*) by virtue of possessing the capacity in the form of "objecthood" (*karmatva*). In expressions such as "because it is the locus of origination," the term "objecthood" (*karmatā*) is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) for the connection. This is because origination is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); this has been explained previously.

He addresses the objection that, since verbs such as *jñā* (to know) denote merely the act of knowing and since objects like a jar (*ghaṭa*) lack the status of being the locus of a fruit produced by an action, they cannot attain the status of an object (*karman*)—and he refutes this by relying on the view that these verbs signify an operation conducive to the removal of the previously mentioned obscuration, stating: "In the case of *jānāti*... [and] "the jar..."

The meaning is "in [statements] such as 'he knows,'" with the words "of the jar, etc. being understood as the ellipsis. It is untenable for the past and the future to be the locus (*āśraya*) of the fruit, because that which is non-existent lacks the status of being a locus. Nor should it be argued that, although the destruction of the veil produced by that [knowledge] is absent in the past and future jar at the time of the knowledge itself, its status as the locus remains intact when delimited by the time of that jar, etc.

He dispels the doubt—namely, that an operation (*vyāpāra*) cannot possibly initiate a result either subsequent to itself because it is empty of its own nature at that time, nor can it initiate a result prior to itself—and does so with the words beginning "past" (*atīta*).

The sense is this: although it is impossible for an operation to initiate a result at a different time, it is accepted that the substratum of the result—consisting of the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*)—is produced by the operation at the very moment immediately following it; just as the Naiyāyikas accept that past and future objects serve as the substrata of knowledge by way of being its objects (*viṣayatayā*).

Otherwise, the undesirable consequence (āpatti) would arise in both systems that "I do not know as before," because at that time there exists the absence of the destruction of the veil and of knowledge, whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of identity with their own nature (svarūpa-viṣayatā-sambandha); and because there also exists the absence of past jars and so forth, whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relations of being located in (ādheyatva) and objectness (viṣayitā), with respect to the destruction of the veil and the knowledge.

In our own system, it is held that a negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the absence of an action qualified by its factors (*kāraka*). Thus, even though it is impossible to cognize the absence of [actions] such as the "shattering of an obstruction," since it is possible to cognize the absence of an action qualified by its factors—which is itself conditioned by that absence—there arises the undesirable consequence (the *prayogāpatti*) of such usage. In that context, although the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) exists, there is a dispute regarding whether knowledge has that objecthood as its locus; therefore, he says "satkārya" (the effect exists).

For this very reason, in the expression "the jar is born" (*ghaṭo jāyate*), the status of being a *kāraka*—defined as the capacity to produce an action—and the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) are both logically established for the jar; otherwise, if it were non-existent, those would be untenable. Regarding this, he cites the consensus of Bhartṛhari, saying: "And it has been said. That [nature] itself is of the nature of concealment (*tirobhāva*). Non-existence (*nāstitā*) means the state of not having come into being. "Obtained," etc.

The meaning is: "when such a disappearance (*tirobhāva*) has occurred for that by which the sequence has been attained. The conventional usage "it perishes" (*naśyati*) is based on the presentness inherent in its production; immediately after that, the sense is "it has not perished" (*anaṣṭa*). By the phrase "by which the sequence has been attained," its nature as an activity (*vyāpāra*) is indicated. By the word "is perceived" (*pratīyate*), perception is stated to be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Disappearance (*tirobhāva*) is simply remaining in a subtle form; thus, there is no inconsistency in its being the locus for the removal of concealment (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). This should be understood in the same way regarding the future as well.

"Because it is the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatvāt*). It should also be understood that this means "because it is intended as the locus [of the action]. Regarding the phrase "even though the action is in use (*prayoge’pi*)," the sense is that since the inclusion of the result within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is not required, the action itself would incur the designation of *karman* (object), because it possesses the result in the form of separation (*vibhāga*). Regarding the phrase "by the sublation of the technical name *karman* (*karmasaṃjñāyā bādheneti*)," the meaning is "by sublation due to its being of higher priority. The sense is that because these two technical names fall under the rule *ākaḍārād ekasaṃjñā*, there exists a relationship of sublation and sublated between them.

Now, one might ask: what is the reason that, between the status of being the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*) and the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it is the designation itself that serves as the regulator? Furthermore, why not simply let the very status of being the locus of such a result—which is necessarily required by the regulation of the designation—be the regulator of the second case (*dvitīyā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the production of the second case. He then states the refutation of the view that the status of being the locus of the result is the regulator.

"Otherwise" means that the accusative case would result after the word *kṛṣṇa*. The meaning is that since Kṛṣṇa is the locus (*āśraya*) of the fruit—which consists of an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*) and is prompted by the activity denoted by the verbal root *pācayati*—the form ending in the accusative would be grammatically correct. The example "he causes Kṛṣṇa to go" (*gamayati kṛṣṇam*) is cited to refute the objection that this consequence does not arise because it is accepted that being the locus of a fruit prompted by the activity denoted by a verbal root in its non-causative form (*aṇijanta*) alone is the regulator for the use of the accusative.

And thus, if the previously mentioned position were accepted, the point is that even in the case of "he causes Kṛṣṇa to go" (*gamayati kṛṣṇam*), the accusative ending would not be grammatically correct. Now, one might raise the objection: "I am not asserting that the accusative ending is correct in the aforementioned instance; rather, I am asserting that a verbal cognition arises from such usage. To ward off this objection by granting it as a desired consequence, he says: "verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha*). Verbal cognition is a cognition of the form "the going has Caitra as its agent and Caitra as its object," and so forth. [The phrase] "in the case of *caitraścaitram*" refers to this.

The meaning of "Caitra goes to Caitra" is as follows: "for those who are thus proficient" means for those who have grasped the capacity of that sentence to produce such a cognition. Anticipating the objection that the verbal cognition described from such a sentence is not established by experience—and thus that the "admission of the desired consequence" (iṣṭāpatti) is improper—he offers a rebuttal with the words "or let it be said. This means "let it be accepted. Regarding the phrase "by the relation of being a qualifier" (*prakāratā-sambandhena*):

the relation of being a qualifier is the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), whereas the delimiting condition of the cause (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the locus of the agent which is not the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root.

And thus, the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is established as follows: "The cognition of such a result [as the object] through the relation of being a qualificand (prakāratāviśeṣyatā-sambandha) has the presence [of the object] brought about by the case-ending (vibhaktijanyopasthiti) through the relation of being such a qualificandum (tādṛśaviśeṣyatā-sambandha) as its cause. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "in a locus other than the operation denoted by the verbal root" (dhātvarthavyāpārānadhikaraṇe) serves precisely to demonstrate this aforementioned relation; for in the sentence "Caitra goes to the village" (caitro grāmaṃ gacchati), there is the presence brought about by the accusative case-ending (dvitīyājanyopasthiti) in the locus consisting of the village through the relation of being such a qualificandum. Therefore, in that case...

The realization of the result, which consists of the connection with the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), is achieved through its relation as a qualifier (*prakāratā*). Since the condition of being produced by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is included in the requirement for semantic presence (*upasthiti*), there is no deviation from the rule of coreferential connection (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) in the case of "the village being reached" (*gamyamāno grāmaḥ*). He demonstrates the exclusion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of "Caitra [is] Caitra" (*caitraścaitraḥ*) by stating: "In the present case, of Caitra... (*prakṛte caitrasyeti*).

Because it has already been largely stated—that is, because it has already been largely stated by the phrase "the locus of the fruit produced by the action"—the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is employed here since the phrase "the fruit of the verbal root's meaning" was not explicitly mentioned there. For this very reason, when a horse is tied in a bean field for the purpose of eating beans so that they may fatten, then in the expression "he ties the horse among the beans," the beans do not possess the status of an object (*karman*), even though they are the locus of the fruit consisting of eating, which is prompted by the act of tying.

The statement regarding the impossibility of *prayāga* being the object (*karman*) is made with the intention that "separation" (*vibhāga*) is not the meaning of roots such as *gam*. However, if it were its meaning in the manner to be explained later in the section on the *apādāna* (ablative), then the aforementioned defect would be avoided, because the relation residing in the limit (*avadhi*) would not be the delimitor of the result (*phala*).

He introduces the view of the Naiyāyikas—who seek to avoid the fault in two ways through an alternative formulation—in order to refute it: "The Naiyāyikas, however," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "inherence in another" (*parasamavetatvam*): the first syntactic connection is that they adopt "inherence in another" as a denotation of the second case-ending in order to avoid the first fault; the second syntactic connection is that they adopt "being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakatvam*) as a qualifier of the result (*phala*) in order to avoid the second fault.

Since separation (*vibhāga*) is not the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the meaning of the verbal root *gam*, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the usage "He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī. Furthermore, being a delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root consists in being a qualifier within the portion denoted by the root's primary power (*śaktyaṃśa*). Even if the property of "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*), which is expressed by the accusative case, were construed with the result (*phala*) or its locus, the aforementioned fault could not be avoided; for [the result of] conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the village (*grāma*) reside in Caitra's distinct [locus]. Therefore, he says: "residing in another."

"It follows upon the action denoted by the verbal root" means that it follows upon the action denoted by the verbal root which is mentioned in grammatical co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with the producer of the result. The term "its own word" (*svapada*) refers to that specific individual which is intended as the object by virtue of possessing that specific result; therefore, in the sentence "Maitra goes toward Caitra who is cooking," there is no lack of justification for the accusative case after the word "Caitra," even though the cooking action inherent in Caitra and the action conducive to conjunction [in Maitra] do not both reside in someone other than Caitra.

In the second case, although there is an absence of inherence in something distinct from itself within the action that produces the conjunction denoted by the verb *gam* (to go) as co-uttered [with the verb], there is no inconsistency, because such [inherence] remains intact in the action that produces a specific instance of conjunction where Maitra is the counter-correlative and Caitra is the substratum.

"Other" (*para*) means that which possesses difference (*bhedavān*), that is, the state of being inherent in that [difference]. In the sentence "Caitra goes to the village," due to a peculiarity of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), the village—the meaning of the base of the second case—conjoins with "difference," which is a single part of the state of being inherent in that which possesses difference, by way of the relation of "substratum-ness" (*anuyogitā*) as determined by "correlativity" (*pratiyogitā*). Furthermore, because it is inherently relational, even though it is a single part of a word-meaning, its conjunction with "difference" is not untenable; this is just as in expressions such as "Devadatta’s father," where "being related to Devadatta" conjoins with "paternity"—which is a single part of the meaning of the word "father"—as the sense of being a progenitor.

The inherence (*samavetatva*) of that which possesses the difference associated with it [the action] occurs in the action through the relation of being its locus (*āśrayatva*). In the sentence "The village is being gone to by Caitra" (*caitreṇa grāmo gamyate*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is "inherence in another" (*parasamavetatva*). Where there is a suffix denoting the object (*karman*)—which is the locus of the result—the village and so forth enter into the "difference" that constitutes that [inherence] as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogitā*). Nor is it the case that the expression "Caitra goes to Caitra" (*caitraścaitraṃ gacchati*) would be unavoidable, since a difference from Caitra exists in Caitra himself by virtue of [his] duality and so forth.

If one accepts that the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) is construed with the difference (bheda), which is the meaning of the accusative case, by way of the relation of having a counter-positive delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedakāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*), then such expressions as "Devadatta goes to a substance" (*devadatto dravyaṃ gacchati*) and "One wrestler goes to another wrestler" (*mallo mallaṃ gacchati*) would be untenable; for in Devadatta there is no difference whose counter-positive is delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*), and in a wrestler there is no difference whose counter-positive is delimited by wresltorhood (*mallatva*). Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is no possibility of the sentence "Caitra goes to Caitra" because it is accepted that only the state of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*)—which is not delimited by a property that is either specific (*vaiśiṣṭya*) or co-extensive (*vyāsajyavṛtti*)—functions as the relation; for such a counter-positiveness can only be delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), and thus the anomaly remains in cases such as "Devadatta is a substance. [To this] we reply: No, because [the relation is] by way of having a counter-positiveness delimited by the respective individuality (*tattadvayaktitva*).

Since the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is admitted as being construed [with the suffix], the aforementioned defect does not arise. Thus, in the sentence "The village is gone to by Caitra" (*caitreṇa grāmo gamyate*), the meaning of the passive verbal suffix (*karmākhyāta*) is both "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) and "locus" (*āśraya*); furthermore, it should be understood that in the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), "being a locus" (*āśrayatva*) is the meaning of the passive verbal suffix. The village or other object of the action (*karman*) is construed with the difference (*bheda*)—which is a constituent of "residing in another"—by way of the relation of having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by its own individuality (*tadvayaktitvāvacchinna*). Consequently, there is no undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) such as "Caitra is gone to by Caitra," nor [is there the consequence] of "by Caitra... [in the case of *caitreṇa*].

The point is that there would be an inconsistency in such expressions as "the substance is gone" (*dravyaṃ gamyate*) or "the wrestler is struck by the wrestler" (*mallo mallena gamyate*), because the grammatical rule—that the relation [of the negative particle] consists precisely in having a counter-positive delimited by the delimitor of the coreferentiality (*anvayitāvacchedaka*)—applies specifically to the object of the verbal cognition of the absence presented by the negative particle (*nañ*).

Nor should it be argued that in a case of conjunction produced by the actions of both parties, the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable because the action residing in Maitra—which generates the conjunction having Caitra as its locus—is unassailably characterized by "inherence in something other than Caitra. For even though an action residing in another (Maitra) possesses the property of inhering in one distinct from Caitra, the property of being the substratum of an action residing in another (Maitra) which—inhering in one distinct from Caitra—generates a conjunction residing in Caitra, is absent in Caitra; thus, [the expression] "Caitra goes to Caitra" [is avoided].

Since there is an absence of inherence in anything other than Caitra within the action whose agent is Caitra, and since the state of possessing a conjunction produced by an action that does not inhere in Caitra is absent in Caitra himself, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that "Caitra is being gone by" is untenable; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Alternatively, the meanings are difference (*bheda*) and location (*ādheyatva*). In that case, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) connects with the difference as before; the difference [connects] with the operation (*vyāpāra*) through the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and the meaning of the base [connects] with location. And thus, from the sentence "Caitra goes to the village," the understanding is: Caitra is the locus of that operation which produces a conjunction residing in the village and which is coreferential with a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the village.

In the case of "The village is being gone to by Caitra" (*caitreṇa grāmo gamyate*), the understanding is that the village is the locus of the conjunction brought about by an operation that is co-located with a distinction from Caitra and has Caitra as its substratum.

[Objection: But surely the relation of "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) would only be construed with the result (*phala*) and so forth; and if that were the case, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would remain as before. To this he says: "In the same way, the effect... etc. The meaning is that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is such that, with respect to the cognition residing in the action (*kriyā*)—which is the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so on and resides in another—the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), related through the relation of being its own qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). The mention of "by the second case" is illustrative of all nominal case-endings (*subvibhakti*); therefore...

Just as one says "Caitra goes to the village" (*caitro grāmam gacchati*), one would likewise say "Caitra goes for Caitra" (*caitraścaitrāya gacchati*); and just as one says "the going of the village by Caitra" (*caitreṇa grāmasya gamanam*), one would likewise say "the going of Caitra by Caitra" (*caitreṇa caitrasya gamanam*). With the intention that, according to this view, the definition of the object (*karmatva*) results in being the locus of a fruit produced by an action inherent in another, he presents that [definition] with the words: "And thus, Caitra [is the object of] the rice."

The mention of "the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*) is intended to demonstrate that softening (*viklitti*) possesses the status of being a delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root; however, it should be understood that there is no manifestation in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) by means of that specific form, because the primary denotation (*śakya*) does not exist as delimited by that [form], and because no such cognition is experienced through that form. Now, one might object: "In order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), one must indeed postulate a linguistic power (*śakti*) for the cumbersome property of 'being inherent in another' (*parasamavetatva*). To this, he says: "Over-extension. This is because that [objection] remains as it was—that is, because the over-extension of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) to undesired instances remains just as it was.

Since the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the case of "Caitra goes to Caitra" is impossible according to the method already stated, he states another over-extension in the example "He causes Kṛṣṇa to cook. Regarding the phrase "due to this consequence": the meaning is that since Kṛṣṇa—the one being prompted—possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*), defined as being the locus of a result consisting of the action denoted by the base [of the causative verb], which is delimited by the meaning of the root of the causative (*ṇijanta*) verb and is produced by an action inherent in a prompter distinct from himself, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*). The citation of the example is as before.

He demonstrates the over-extension of the accusative case when [the action] is the agent (*karmakartṛ*) with the words "viklittyanukūla... (conducive to softening). The meaning is as follows: the meaning of the verbal root *pac*—which consists of the contact with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) that is conducive to softening and which inheres in something other than the rice—is the fruit produced by that [contact]. This critique is offered with the intention that, in this context, the contact with fire is intended to be expressed as the primary meaning of the verbal root.

It should be understood that this objection does not apply to the position where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the mere result in the case of a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), or where the meaning of the root is the activity residing solely in the rice-grains conducive to the *iṣ* (desire) suffix. Regarding the phrase "desired connection" (*iṣṭānvaya*): the state of being "other" (*paratva*) is understood as having only the referent of the second-case base (*dvitīyādi-prakṛtyartha*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and not as having any other thing as its counter-correlate; furthermore, the property of "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) is construed only with such an action and not with anything else. This is for the sake of avoiding two kinds of restrictive rules (*niyama*).
The meaning is that there would be an excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating various specific relations of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for each individual case.

Since knowledge characterized by a general form is the cause for the desire to know [the object] in its specific form, when there is a desire for knowledge in its specific form, he divides the *karma* (object) by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*), stating: "And this is of seven kinds. Regarding "that which is to be produced" (*nirvartya*): the construction is that the *karma* most desired (*īpsitatama*) is considered to be of three types—*nirvartya*, *vikārya*, and *prāpya*. As for "but the other": it refers to that which is distinct from the "most desired."

He states its fourfold nature with the words "by indifference" (*audāsīnyena*): the meaning is that which is to be reached when there is neither the state of being desired (*īpsitatva*) nor the state of being detested (*dveṣyatva*), that is, the locus of the fruit produced by the action. "Not desired" (*anīpsita*) means detested. "By other designations" (*saṃjñāntaraiḥ*) means by designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so on. "Not mentioned" (*anākhyāta*) means not intended to be expressed; thus, by the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, it receives the designation of *karman* (object). "Preceded by another" (*anyapūrvaka*) means...

[An example] preceded by another designation: as in "he becomes angry at the cruel one" (*krūram abhikrudhyati*), where by the rule *krudhadruhe*rṣyā* [Pāṇini 1.4.37], the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) would otherwise apply. He states the definition of the triad beginning with the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*): "that which is non-existent" (*yadasat*). Regarding "the destruction of the material cause" (*prakṛtyuccheda*): it means that the destruction of the self, which constitutes the material cause, has come about—has been reached (*bhū*).

The suffix *kta* here denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), [the agent] of the base—such as wood and so forth. He states the examples in sequence, beginning with "he makes a jar. The first is the *nirvartya* (that which is to be produced): in the view of the Naiyāyikas, the jar arises from a state of non-existence; however, in the views of the Sāṃkhyas and in our own view, it arises from that which already exists. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "The state of non-existence prior to production is based on a mental state;
it is not distinct from that which is existent, for the agent of birth [acts upon what is already present]."
Or, when the cause abides in the form of the effect,
it then acquires the designation "effect" and arises as an effect.
"Just as the coiling of a snake or the coming together of those who were scattered,
so do some declare the nature of birth for the existent ones."

He states the definition of the *prāpya* (attained) object with the words "produced by action" (*kriyākṛta*). Regarding the phrase "from perception" (*darśanāt*), it means from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In the case of an *nirvartya* (produced) object, the specific quality consisting of the acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*) is cognizable through perception; likewise, in the case of a *vikārya* (modified) object, there is sometimes the acquisition of its own nature, and sometimes the acquisition of another quality. This is known through inference, as for example when a son experiences happiness; here, indeed, the inference of happiness occurs through the brightening of his face. And this is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* and other sources. The second [type] is the *vikārya*.

In this context, it should be understood that while wood and gold alone possess the status of being the object of modification (*vikārya*), the ash and the earring are intended to be the transformations (*pariṇāma*) of the wood and gold respectively; thus, even for these two [the ash and the earring], the status of being the "object to be produced" (*nirvartya*) is maintained. Some, however, state: "That whose transforming material cause (*prakṛti*), whether existing or non-existent, is not relied upon, is declared to have the status of being the 'object to be produced' (*nirvartya*)."
"But when there is a desire to express the material cause (*prakṛti*), some [grammarians] describe the object (*karman*) differently:
as that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and as that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*)."

Thus, from the *Vākyapadīya*: in the expression "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), although the clay is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the jar, it is not intended to be expressed as undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*); therefore, the jar is merely something to be produced (*nirvartya*). In the expression "he makes ashes" (*bhasma karoti*), the material cause of the ashes—namely the wood—is not present in the state of being ashes; since it is intended to be expressed as such, the ashes are merely something to be produced (*nirvartya*). Likewise, in the expression "he makes a jar out of clay" (*mṛdaṃ ghaṭaṃ karoti*), when the transformation of the material cause is not intended to be expressed, [they have accepted that the jar is merely something to be produced].

In expressions such as "he turns wood into ash" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasma karoti*) and "he makes gold into an earring" (*suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ karoti*), the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is an operation conducive to the production [of something] preceded by an operation conducive to a transformation (*vikāra*). This is because of the cognition: "transforming the wood, he produces ash. Therefore, the status of both [wood and gold] as objects (*karman*) is maintained. In the first case, the transformation consists of destruction; in the other, it consists of a specific form, as in the case of a jar.

In order to dispel the doubt that—if independence, which consists in not being dependent on another, were required [as the sole criterion for agency]—then in cases such as "Devadatta causes Mitradata to cook," Devadatta would fail to be designated as the agent because he is dependent on the instigator (prayojaka), the author states the intended meaning: "And independence... and so forth.

Regarding the term *dhātūpāttā* (included in the verbal root): it means "included in the root under discussion," because [the inclusion] does not exclude anything that is included in any verbal root whatsoever. Furthermore, the primary operation (*vyāpāra*) must be understood [as the meaning of the root]. Therefore, in the case of the root *nī* (to lead), since its meaning is an operation conducive to an operation conducive to conjunction, in the sentence *devadatto grāmam ajāṃ nayati* ("Devadatta leads the goat to the village"), the goat does not possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no application of that [accusative] designation because it is sublated by the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*); for in examples such as *caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("Caitra cooks the rice"), since the designation "object"—defined as "that which is most desired by the agent"—has already found its scope in the rice and so forth, it lacks the status of an exception (*apavāda*). Furthermore, because there is no priority [of the latter rule], on the contrary, the designation "agent" (*kartṛsaṃjñā*) itself would be the sublater due to its priority. Moreover, when the intention is to express agency (*kartṛtva*), the rule *akathitam* does not apply. [The following applies: "In the case of the roots *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *pracch*, *bhikṣ*, and *ciñ*, the cause of the utility (*upayoganimitta*) is designated as the object (*karman*) when the rule is not previously established."
"Whatever is associated with the qualities of the roots *bruvi* (to speak) and *śāsi* (to command) is called *acarita* (conduct) by the poet"—this is stated in the *Parigaṇanavārtika*.

Furthermore, because roots such as *nī* (to lead) are not included [in that list], and because primacy (*prādhānyam*) consists in not being the locus of the subjecthood (*prakāratā*)—which is defined by the objecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of a particular root as understood from a cognition produced by that root when it is co-occurrent with a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛpratyaya*)—there would otherwise be no status of agency for Devadatta in the sentence "The rice is cooked by Devadatta," since the operation (*vyāpāra*) is a qualifier relative to the result (*phala*). Therefore, the phrase "when co-occurrent with a suffix denoting an agent" is specified.

He states the proof for the fact that the word *svatantra* has the meaning [of independence] as it is etymologically derived: "The agenthood of a factor whose action is expressed by the verbal root is always accepted" (*dhātunoktakriye kārake kartṛtā nityam iṣyate*). This is the construction [of the verse]. Now, if such independence were adopted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that in expressions such as *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in a pot"), the pot and so forth would also be agents, because they are the substrata of the activity consisting of holding [the food], which is conveyed by the verbal root *pac*. To this, he says: "For this very reason, when... (*ata eva yadā*). "For this very reason" means precisely to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the pot and so forth in the aforementioned instances.

Nor should it be argued that the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the designations of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) and others because they are without scope; for the intention is that even within the domain of the designation of "agent," the designation of "locus" would also apply, and since that too would be without scope, there would result the contingency of [the two] being synonymous. When one accepts that "he who is the substratum of the activity expressed by the verbal root is the agent at that time," then since both agency and objecthood are possible for a single entity, one raises the objection regarding the contradiction with the *adhikaraṇa* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) which states "due to the designation as agent or object," and then refutes it with the words "nanvevam" ("But if this were so...").

Thus—regarding the acceptance of both agency and objecthood for the same [entity]. "Of that" (tasya): the connection is that the designation of [the self] as both agent and object in such scriptural passages as "he goes from here to him" (etamitaḥ pretyābhisambhavitāsmi) is contradictory for one endowed with qualities such as consisting of mind (manomaya). "Him" (etam): this refers to the Self under discussion, who possesses qualities such as consisting of mind and is being meditated upon; it designates Him as the object, specifically as the object of attainment, in the phrase "I shall attain Him."

The embodied self is designated as the agent of the act of worship because it has attained agency; for the phrase "I shall attain" (abhisaṃbhavitāsmi) means "I shall reach" (prāptāsmi). Regarding the statement in Śaṅkara’s commentary, "And when a [distinct] destination exists, it is not proper to designate one and the same thing as both object and agent," the connection here is with the word "designates" (vyapadiśati), which must be supplied after "as the agent" (kartṛtvena) in the phrase "I shall attain. This is so because... [the destination exists].

By the passage beginning with "having gone" (*gatāv*), it is indicated that the conceptualization of a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—as in the view that "the self kills itself by itself"—is untenable. Regarding the form "I shall come to be" (*saṃbhavitāsmi*), the verb *bhū* (to become), which is inherently *ātmanepada* and signifies attainment, takes the *parasmaipada* ending in place of the *luṭ* suffix due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*). Although a single entity may possess two different names at different times, it cannot do so simultaneously. The intention [of the author] is that in the present scriptural passage (*śruti*), the simultaneous perception of two distinct operations resulting from the application of two names is contradictory.

It is explained by the words beginning with "samādhatte" (he answers) and so forth. Regarding "jñeyatve" (in the state of being knowable): this means when [the Self] is understood as an object of knowledge through the passage beginning with "manomaya" (consisting of mind). "Karmatvaṃ vācyam" (the status of being an object must be expressed): the sense is that the status of being an object must be expressed by the word "etam" (this), because the pronoun *etad* refers back to what has been previously introduced. "Bādhāt" (because of sublation): the sense is "because of its superiority" (i.e., the superiority of the genitive case over the accusative). Furthermore, he states another objection regarding the agent being the same as the object in the phrase "karmakartṛtāyām" (in the case of the object-agent identity).

The point is that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in "I shall come into being" (*saṃbhavitāsmi*) does not denote a pure agent (*kartṛ*), but rather a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). Thus, since the one previously designated as the object in the preceding sentence—"having departed from here"—is now the agent, there is no simultaneous occurrence of two grammatical designations; consequently, there is no contingency for the application of the *yak* suffix and so forth. The phrase "contingency for the *yak* suffix and so forth" means the contingency for the application of the *ātmanepada* suffix, which is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). The underlying intention is that it is not proper to accept such a [reflexive] designation when the matter can be resolved without any grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*). Regarding the phrase "the cause of distinction": [it refers to the distinction between the agent and the object].

The meaning is that this is the reason for the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, it is established that by the term "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, the Supreme Self alone is indicated; therefore, there is no contradiction with the aforementioned section (*adhikaraṇa*). This is the intended sense. Furthermore, if agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal root, then the statement of the author of the *Kalpataru*—that in the expression "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the pot itself is the agent because it possesses the definition of agency as the locus of the activity belonging to the pot—is also consistent.

For this very reason, in the *Bādhalakṣaṇa* section on the *asthiyajña*, under the *Kratvarthābhyuccaya* sub-section, it is established that agency does not depend upon consciousness, since even pieces of wood possess agency in acts such as burning; rather, "he who possesses the inherence of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in relation to others is the agent. Therefore, it was concluded that the ritual acts beginning with the touching of the *śukra* vessel must be performed by means of bones.

In passages such as "The sacrificer takes hold of the parrot," where the sacrificer is subordinate, if someone among those performing a *sattra* sacrifice dies, the rite must be performed by the others who have commenced the *sattra* along with that person's bones; for even in that case, the agency characterized by independence—which was previously mentioned—is possible. This is the purport of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) therein. This is clear in the first section of the tenth chapter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*. [This concludes] the section on the "Circle of Kārakas."

The meaning is: "a collection [of factors] whose activity consists in the sense of the verbal root (dhātvartha) as co-uttered [with the suffix]. And since, in examples such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," that [collection] belongs to Devadatta alone, the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) is applied to him alone.

Intending to show brevity by means of what has already been stated, he says "kṛti" (effort). The meaning is that being the locus of an effort conducive to the operation of the meaning of the verbal root in question constitutes "agency" (*kartṛtva*) with respect to that verbal root's meaning. By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by taking an effort conducive to the operation of something else; furthermore, "locus-ness" (*āśrayatva*) is to be understood as [inherence] (*samavāya*). Therefore, even though the pot possesses the status of being a locus—by way of a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*)—with respect to an effort conducive to cooking, there is no undesirable consequence such as "the pot cooks" (*ghaṭaḥ pacati*) or "it is cooked by the pot" (*ghaṭena pacyate*). [The opponent objects: "It is under-defined (*avyāpta*)."

The meaning is that [the definitions of] "agency" (*prayoktṛtva*)—consisting in being the instigator of the circle of causal factors (*kārakacakra*)—and "possessing volitional activity" (*kṛtimattva*) are both sublated in the case of insentient things such as a staff. Here, although the objection—that on the view where "agency is the possession of volitional activity," since the substratum portion is obtainable from words such as "Devadatta," one must admit that the meaning of the case-ending is merely volitional activity, and thus there is no possibility of the case-ending having power over it because volitional activity is already manifested by the verbal root itself—is indeed possible, it has been set aside; for even if the volitional activity conducive to the result is obtained from the verbal root, [there remains the need for the case-ending to express] the volitional activity conducive to the operation (*vyāpāra*).

Because the capacity for case-inflection is possible there even without [the explicit mention of] the object, the claim that "an effort conducive to that [action] does not appear" must be settled by oath. Alternatively, since effort is already obtainable from the verbal root, if one accepts that the meaning of the instrumental and other cases is simply the locus (āśrayatva), then this very objection is stated because the aforementioned defects would not apply.

Others, however, maintain that independence (*svātantrya*)—as intended by the *Bhāṣya*—is simply the status of being the instigator of the entire circle of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*). This [independence] is unimputed (*anāropita*) in the case of Devadatta and the like, while it is imputed (*āropita*) in the case of a jar and the like; it is precisely through the imputation of the status of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) that the usage "alms cause one to dwell" (*abhikṣā vāsayati*) and so forth is justified. As it was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kārake*: "In its connection with the primary factor, the pot is dependent. But what, then, is the primary factor? The agent. How is it known that the agent is the primary factor? Because, when all the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are present..."

"He becomes the agent, the instigator. Thus, independence (*svātantrya*) also consists in having the capacity for engagement or withdrawal according to one's own will; and this is possible for the person being prompted (*prayojya*), through their engagement or withdrawal based on the presence or absence of their own purpose, even when the prompter (*prayojaka*) is present. This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*).

This [agency] is also superimposed upon the pot and so forth, but it is not superimposed upon Devadatta and others; rather, it is simply the state of being the locus of the operation that constitutes the primary meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because the term "independent" (*svatantra*) is not defined there [in the *Pāṇinian* technical rules], and because in common usage that term applies only to those things whose meanings have already been expressed [by other words]. For this very reason, when there is a doubt regarding the impossibility of agency for the prompted agent (*prayojya*) due to its lack of independence, it is established that [agency] consists in having the power to initiate or cease activity according to one's own will. It is with reference to this very thing that the operation residing in the locus of such independence is expressed by the verbal root. Intending precisely this, [the author says]:
There is no contradiction with that [statement], because it was stated by Hari [in the *Vākyapadīya*]: "A root is that which has not yet had its action expressed," and so forth.

For this very reason [it is said]: "Because [the word] acquires its power from something else prior [to the sentence], because it brings about a state of subordination, because the activity of those [words] already active depends upon it, and because it causes those already active to cease."
"Because no substitute is seen, because [the action] is not observed when there is separation [from the agent],
and because it provides assistance even from a distance, the independence of the agent is asserted."

Thus it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. Its meaning, however, is as follows: the agent acts for reasons other than the instrument and so forth—such as desire and the like—even prior to the existence of the instrument; the instrument and the rest have their activity and cessation dependent upon that [agent]; furthermore, a substitute is observed for the instrument and the rest (e.g., because a sacrifice can be performed even in the absence of *vrīhi* rice), whereas no such substitute exists for the agent, since it is well known that when there is a difference in the agent, it is simply a different action altogether; moreover, this agent is observed even when other factors (*kārakas*) are not employed—it is precisely here that the purport of this passage lies, they say. In this regard, the following should be understood: [of all the *kārakas*...]

By means of their respective intermediate actions (*avāntarakriyā*), they bring about the accomplishment of the principal action; for this very reason, they are construed with *bhāvanā* alone. Furthermore, since there is a rule that a factor requiring something to be produced must be construed with that which produces it, it is appropriate that they be construed with *bhāvanā* specifically. It should not be argued that because the word *kāraka* and the word *kartṛ* (agent) have the same meaning, the usage "the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a *kāraka*" is untenable—just as saying "the agent (*kartṛ*) is the agent (*kāra*)" would be—and that such usage would result in tautology. For it is said: "In every case, agency (*kartṛtva*) exists in a *kāraka* simply by virtue of its production [of the effect].
When there is a requirement for a distinction of operations (*vyāpāra*), the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth becomes possible."

Thus, because the resolution is provided by Harigraṇtha himself: since all [factors] possess agency (*kartṛtva*) by virtue of being independent producers of the principal action through their respective operations, they possess the status of a *kāraka*; therefore, the conventional usage "the instrument is a *kāraka*" is justified, as the general property of being a *kāraka* exists even in specific cases. Likewise, in such instances, although the ablative (*apādāna*) possesses agency just like the object (*karman*) and other factors, the expression "the village comes" (*grāma āgacchati*) does not occur due to non-utterance (*anabhidhāna*), because the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) applies only to the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) and so forth.

Because [the agent] does not exist [independently], there would be the undesirable consequence of applying linguistic conventions such as "instrument" and "agent. Since independence (*svātantrya*) is already obtained by the very mention of the word "kāraka," the further inclusion of the term "svatantra" (independent) is for the purpose of obtaining the specific meaning: that this designation applies only to that whose independence alone is intended to be expressed, and not to that which possesses an independence associated with dependence (*pāratantrya*). Therefore, that [designation of agent] does not apply during the state of being an instrument or other factors. However, the technical designation of "kāraka" proceeds on the basis of the mere presence of actual independence, due to the capacity of the rule for enjoining instruments and so forth. Alternatively:

Because they possess independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to their own respective operations such as burning and so forth, those operations are denotable by verbal roots (*dhātu*). Consequently, in instances such as "the fuel cooks" (*edhāḥ pacanti*), the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) is established by taking up a temporary agency (*kartṛtva*). Furthermore, by way of their own operations, they possess the status of instruments (*karaṇatva*) and so on, due to their contributing to the accomplishment of the principal action. Even for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), the status of being a *kāraka* is achieved precisely by taking up independence with respect to their own operations; thus, even in the absence of actual usage such as "the Brahmin gives" (*vipraḥ dadāti*) or "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), [their status is secured]. As it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*:

"It has been sufficiently demonstrated that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of instruments (*karaṇa*), loci (*adhikaraṇa*), and objects (*karman*) serves as an illustration for the demonstration of the agency of the ablative (*apādāna*). In examples such as "the tree becomes the limit" (*vṛkṣo 'vadhibhāvam upagacchati*) and "the Brahmin consents" (*vipra anumanyate*), agency is observed in those [factors] because they are engaged in their respective operations; however, it should be noted that the verbal root *pat-* does not express that operation, as there is no rule prescribing it.
