Furthermore, the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) that serves as the basis for the various technical designations (*saṃjñā*); this is clear from the Bhāṣya.

Alternatively, since independence—defined as the state of possessing an operation inherent in its own constituent elements (dhātu)—does not exist during the states of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and its status as a *kāraka* remains exactly as before. Enough with this elaboration.

He analyzes the agent (*kartṛ*) with the words "and this. It is threefold—that is, it possesses three properties. He states the examples in order with the word "by me" (*mayā*). This [agent] possesses a pure agency (*śuddhakartṛtva*) whose locus is not co-extensive with the status of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) or the status of being an object (*karmatva*); the status of being an instigator and the status of being an object are to be understood as determined by the respective meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātu*), so there is no lack of established instances. Alternatively, pure agency is the agency that is the object of the intention [of the speaker] at a time when the status of being an object and the status of being an instigator are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*). "By the effect" (*kāryataḥ*).

From the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *kṛ*, the suffix *saṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmani*), followed by *yak*; here, Hari is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartā*). [In the sentence] "He causes Kṛṣṇa to go" (*gamayati kṛṣṇam*), because the rule "gati-buddhi-" prescribes the technical designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) for Kṛṣṇa—who is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative form (*aṇau*)—Kṛṣṇa is the "agent-object" (*karmakartā*). Thus, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both an object and an agent. Although the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the designation of "object," there is no loss of the status of being an agent in the sense of being the substratum of the activity conveyed by the verbal root in its original form, even in the absence of that [technical] designation.

"An activity conducive to service (*sevanānukūlo vyāpāraḥ*). Service (*sevā*) consists of such acts as massaging the feet or affection; according to the Navya school, however, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) to be understood is "service consisting of the object Hari, produced by an activity whose locus is non-different from me," and so forth. Similarly, in the case of "He is made to act by Hari" (*kāryate hariṇā*), the cognition to be reflected upon is "the production (*utpādanā*) produced by such an activity."

Now, one might object that there is no evidence for the locus (*āśraya*) and the process (*vyāpāra*) being denoted by the instrumental case in the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), since the designation "instrument" is prescribed only for that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). To this, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Regarding the phrase "without intervention" (*avyavadhānena*): the meaning is "that which possesses an operation which produces the result without intervention."

The meaning of the third case (instrumental) in the word *avyavadhānena* is "distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭya*); thus, the meaning is "time qualified by that [absence of intervention]," and this [qualification] connects with "production. Since the action—the result—is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is conventionally treated as an "action," just as in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*. The point is that when both the substratum and the operation constitute the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*), the sūtra *sādhakatamam* serves as the authority.

And thus, the intention is that in the root [sūtra], the term "substratum" (*āśraya*) is also an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the operation (*vyāpāra*). In the expression "Vālī was killed by an arrow," the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), namely the arrow, is construed with the substratum as the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) by way of identity; that [substratum] is then construed with the operation—the other meaning of the third case—by way of being the locus (*ādheyatā*); and that [operation] is construed with the operation denoted by the verbal root or with its result, which consists in the separation from life, by way of the relation of being produced (*janyatva*).

Others, however, say: "The meaning of the third case is not the power (*śakti*) residing in the operation; rather, the power of exhaustion itself is connected [to the result] through a relation such as being produced by an operation that resides in its own locus. Still others say: "The meaning is the power of instrumentality (*karaṇatva-śakti*); the connection is as before. He clarifies the purpose of the phrase "is intended" (*vivakṣyate*) with a verse: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*). That—namely, instrumentality—is "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*), i.e., because it resides in a specific entity, "indescribable"—meaning it is impossible to describe.

Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "for not" (*na hi*). For (*hi*)—that is, because of the reason that it is not established as a real entity (*vastu*), nor is it restricted solely to a particular real entity like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. He states the reason for its not being restricted solely to a particular real entity with the words "by the pot" (*sthālyā*).

Even though the cooking pot (*sthālī*) is the object of the determination of its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), it assumes the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) by virtue of its thin-walled nature when so intended. Although, according to the aforementioned reasoning, all [factors] possess the status of an instrument, there is no simultaneous intention to express the instrumentality of all of them; thus, one should note that the undesirable consequence of the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not arise in every instance. Having raised the objection regarding the contradiction with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) if the instrumentality of all factors were accepted through such an intention, he refutes it with the words "And it is not so," etc., [referring to] the *mīmāṃsādhikaraṇa*.
In the section located in the third pāda of the second adhyāya, [the sūtra] states: "The individual soul (jīva) is the agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless.

The meaning of this sūtra is that scriptural injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" and "one should offer oblations" become meaningful only when there is agency; for it is only when agency exists that one can teach the performance of sacrifices and other rites, and not otherwise. [This is followed by the phrase: "Because of the reversal of capacity."

The individual soul (*jīva*) must be the agent distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*); for if the intellect (*buddhi*), which is denoted by the word "consciousness," were itself the agent, there would be a reversal of capacities: the intellect’s capacity as an instrument (*karaṇa*) would be lost, and it would incur the capacity of being an agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, if the intellect possessed the capacity of being an agent, it alone would become the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), and so forth—as established in Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the phrase "of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇasya*): the internal organ is a modification (*pariṇāma*) of the intellect; since there is no difference between a modification and that which undergoes modification (*pariṇāmī*), there is no contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being an instrument": the intention [of the author] is not that the status of being an instrument for all [entities] is merely a matter of linguistic intent (*vaivakṣika*), as might be suggested by the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, and so forth. Rather, having raised the objection that even though the status of being an instrument is well-established in the case of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is no obstacle to intending agency in other cases—since it is only the simultaneous intention of both [agency and instrumentality] that is contradictory—he says: "But in reality... [and] "in the Bhāṣya itself."

The agency of the individual soul (jīva), established by reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures, is not innate but rather adventitious (aupādhika). If it were innate, liberation would be impossible, because agency is of the nature of suffering; for if it were the very nature [of the self], its separation from the self would be impossible, just as heat cannot be separated from fire. The Teacher states this very point: "And as the carpenter, in both ways."

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). Just as a carpenter with tools such as an axe in his hand becomes miserable, while one devoid of them is clearly seen to be happy—by this illustration it is stated clearly in Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya that agency is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). And thus, the sense is that the previously mentioned reversal of power is indeed of the nature of a further corroboration (*abhyuccaya*). And that [is] also designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

One might object: "Even if the locus (*ādhāra*) is the meaning of the locative case, how can the substratum (*āśraya*) be the primary meaning (*śakya*) of the locative? For there is a difference between being a locus and being a substratum. Anticipating this objection, he says: *tatvaṃ ca* ("and its essence"). This means "and the state of being a locus" (*ādhāratva*). He says: "the state of being a substratum" (*āśrayatva*). The sense is that since there is no evidence for the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*) as something distinct [from the state of being a substratum], there is no difference in name nor in reality. He says: "merely by virtue of being a substratum" (*āśrayatvamātreṇa*). This means it is prescribed by taking only the state of being a substratum into account. He says: "the technical designation 'locus'" (*ādhārasaṃjñā*).

The term *ādhārasya saṃjñā* means "the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the locus (*ādhāra*). It cannot be argued that the designation *ādhāra* itself is being prescribed for the locus, because [if that were the case], the expression as it stands would be incoherent due to the non-prescription of the *ādhāra*-designation; furthermore, since the locus has already been previously indicated, it is only that which follows [the mention of the action] which can be a designation. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the *Vṛddhi* rule. Moreover, it would result in the incoherence of rules such as *stamyadhikaraṇe*. By those—namely, the designations of *karman* and so forth—there would be sublation (*bādha*).

And thus, since those [definitions] are without scope, it is indeed appropriate that they should supersede the technical designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locus); the sense is that there is no possibility of the designations of *karman* (object) and so forth being reduced to the designation of *adhikaraṇa*. The phrase "only when the action itself is exhausted" (*kriyākṣaya*) means "directly when the action is exhausted. By the word "only" (*eva*), there is an exclusion of things like mats (*kaṭa*) which have Caitra or others as their substratum (*āśraya*). Consequently, the technical designation would apply either to such an agent (*kartṛ*) alone, or to the object (*karman*) which is the substratum of the result (*phala*), but not to the mat and so forth; this is the intended meaning. "Directly" (*sākṣāt*).

Since the designations *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object) are prescribed for that which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action, [the author] replies with the words "nevertheless, here... with the intention that, by process of elimination, there is the apprehension of the substratum of the action through its being the immediate substratum of the action. With the intention that "action" is obtained here because it falls under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *kārakas*, and that this action also possesses a result (*phala*), he says "by means of the agent and the object. "The state of being its substratum" (*tadāśrayatvam*) means the state of being the substratum of the action consisting of the operation and the result residing in the agent and the object. To support the stated point, he cites the consensus of Hari: "separated from the agent and the object."

The meaning is: "that which resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth residing in itself. "That which assists" (*upakurvād*) means that which brings about the accomplishment of the principal action by means of its own action; this is obtained from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the case of a *kāraka*. Regarding "proximate" (*aupaśleṣika*): "proximity" (*upaśleṣa*) is a connection (*śleṣa*) in close vicinity (*upa*), and that which is produced by that is "proximate. It is also called "proximate" even when the connection occurs through the delimitation of a single part (*ekadeśāvacchedena*). This is because the etymological derivation is possible there as well: "proximity" (*upaśleṣa*) is that which is near (*samīpa*) to the connection (*śleṣa*), and [the term refers to] what is produced by that. Among these, the first type is clearly explained in the commentary on the sūtra "In a *saṃhitā*" (*saṃhitāyām*) regarding the rule "A semi-vowel replaces an *iK* vowel before an *aC* vowel" (*iko yaṇ aci*).

Regarding the statement "the month in which [a gift] is given is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of that gift by way of proximity (*aupaśleṣika*)," this is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *tatra ca dīyate*. Furthermore, this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *tadasminn adhikam*. "Locus by way of domain" (*vaiṣayika*) means a locus distinct from both the proximate (*aupaśleṣika*) and the pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*). "Pervasive" (*abhivyāpaka*) means a substratum of the relation with the located (*ādheya*) through the delimitation of all its parts. For example: "oil in sesame seeds" and "ghee in curds."

In this case, since the relation between oil and clarified butter exists in every part of the sesame seeds and the curd respectively, the status of being a pervading substratum (*abhivyāpakādhāratā*) is established. This alone is the primary locus (*mukhyam adhikaraṇam*); everything else distinct from it is secondary (*gauṇa*), as is clear from the commentary on the *sūtra* "svaritena—" (Pāṇini 1.3.72). Regarding the example "he dwells with the teacher" (*gurau vasati*): when there is an intention to express dependence upon the teacher, one says "he dwells with the teacher. Others, however, say that the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is that which possesses the power of being an ablative (*apādānatva*) co-extensive with such a state of being a limit (*avadhitva*).
This [example] and "he desires boiled milk" (*mīkṣe icchāsti*) are examples of the objective locus (*vaiṣayika*).

He cites the rule as the authority for the fact that the ablative (*pañcamī*) has the sense of the limit (*avadhi*): "The fifth case-affix is used in the sense of the *apādāna*. Now, one might ask: even if the rule establishes that the *apādāna* is the meaning of the ablative, how is it established that the limit (*avadhi*) is its meaning? To this he says: "And that" (*tac ca*). This means "and that *apādāna*. The construction is: "the limit (*avadhibhūta*)," according to the rule "That which remains fixed during separation is the *apādāna*. Thus, the intended meaning is that the limit possesses the status of being the meaning [of the ablative] because its technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed by the aforementioned rule.

Others, however, say that the meaning of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is the power of being an *apādāna* (ablative point) that co-occurs with such a status of being a limit (*avadhitva*). The sense is that although causes (*hetu*) and so forth are designated as *apādāna* by rules such as "bhītrārthānām-", they possess this denotation (*vācyatva*) there, whereas elsewhere it is merely a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In reality, however, since the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected (pratyākhyāna) the rules beginning with "bhūtrārthānām-", the designation of the *apādāna* (ablative) applies only to that which serves as a limit (*avadhi*). Thus, this [statement] intends to convey that the meaning of the fifth case in the context of *kāraka*s is precisely the limit; consequently, there is no harm even if that [fifth case], prescribed in connection with words such as *anya* and others, or that prescribed by the rule "vibhāṣā guṇe," also signifies the cause of the relationship (*saṃbandha-hetu*). "Departure (*apāya*) is separation (*viśleṣa*)"—separation means division (*vibhāga*).

Intending that the term *apāyapada* refers to an action that produces separation (*apāya*), he says: "in the action producing that. This object which serves as the limit (*avadhi*) is called the "stable entity" (*dhruvapadārtha*). "Stable" (*dhruva*) means firm; and that [stability] consists in not being a substratum for the action, which [action], by virtue of proximity, is that which is expressed by the verbal root under discussion. The sense is that, in this way, this [object] is indeed the limit. Regarding the reading *ubhayakarmaka* in the verse of the *Vākyapadīya*, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has both actions as its producers," i.e., produced by the action of both [the agent and the object].
The reading *ubhayakarmaja*, however, is straightforward.

Regarding the phrase "that which is neutral (udāsīna) in separation" (*apāye*), the intention is that the term *apāye* refers, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the action that produces disjunction; with this in mind, he explains it as "the cause of disjunction. The meaning of the word *dhruva* (fixed/constant) is expressed by the word *udāsīna*. Intending that neutrality (*audāsīnya*) consists in not being the locus of that [action], he says: "neutral means non-locus. He states the resulting meaning: "and so," which means: when, by the expression "fixed in separation," there is the intended expression of neutrality toward the action that produces disjunction. "The state of being the locus of disjunction" means the state of being the locus of the disjunction that is the meaning of the verbal root; this too is obtained by implication.

This inclusion [of the condition "that which remains fixed"] is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Kāśī and the like in examples such as "Devadatta goes from the village to Kāśī. Although one might argue that since the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) is superseded by the designations of *karman* (object) and so forth due to their higher status in the hierarchy of rules, there is no risk of over-extension, nevertheless, the intention is that this [condition] is stated to convey that the power (*śakti*) of *apādāna* is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with separation (*vibhāga*). "To avoid that" means to avoid the designation of *apādāna*. The phrase beginning with "the first part" (*satyantam*) refers to the meaning of the term "fixedness" (*dhruvatva*).

If that [the *apādāna* designation] were not applied, there would be an exclusion of the *kartṛ* (agent) designation itself; for the sense is possible that in the context of separation (*apāya*), whatever is the *kāraka* that serves as the substratum for the action whose form is separation is called the *apādāna*. The intention is that the scope for the *kartṛ* designation is such cases as "Caitra cooks" (*pacati caitra*). By this, the objection that "this is inconsistent because the *kartṛ* designation, being of higher priority, sublates [the *apādāna* designation]" is refuted. Now, one might argue: let the word *apāya* mean simply "separation"; then "in separation" (*apāye*) would be a locative absolute, and the verbal root is obtained from the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning *kārakas*.

And thus, if one accepts the meaning of the sūtra as "that *kāraka* which, while being the substratum for the division of the meaning of the verbal root under discussion, is the *apādāna*," then this technical term (*saṃjñā*) would not be an exception to the term *kartṛ* (agent), because it would already find its application in cases such as "the village" (*grāma*). And in this way, since it would be sublated by the subsequent term *kartṛ*, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the agent. If this is argued, they say that even though the previously mentioned sense is possible, the [sūtra] was stated solely for the sake of clarity.

Now, one might object: "Since the over-extension [of the definition] to the agent (*kartṛ*) can be avoided by intending to express that [the cause of separation] is not the substratum of the action denoted by the root in question, what is the use of including the condition of being the 'cause of separation'? To this, he says: "running" (*dhāvataḥ*). One might suspect that when it is said, "He falls from the horse," such usage would be justified only in a state where [the horse] is not the substratum of the action; therefore, the inclusion of the qualification "running" is for the purpose of excluding that [case].

The point is that, given the aforementioned intended meaning, the impossibility of such usage on the grounds that [the tree] is merely the substratum of the action of running denoted by the root in question (*dhāv*) remains firmly established. However, since running is both deviant and otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), it is not the cause of separation; thus, the stated defect does not persist. It is precisely for this purpose that the term *apāye* (in separation) was included in the Sūtra. Otherwise, since the word *dhruva* would result in the apprehension of only that which is stationary, there would be the undesirable consequence of the aforementioned usage being untenable. [The phrase] "that which produces disjunction" (*viśleṣajanaka*)...

The meaning is that there is a separation between the horse and the wall, even though [the horse] is the locus of the falling that produces that [separation]. While it is true that if one takes "separation" in its general sense, the status of the horse as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) would be untenable in the case mentioned, there is no fault if one takes "separation" in its specific sense. This is because the falling residing in the horse, like the horse itself, does not produce a disjunction from that [wall]; such is the intended meaning of the resolution, which he states as "tadviśleṣa" (that separation). The meaning is: "the state of being the limit of a particular instance of separation is [the definition] for that particular instance of separation. Regarding "aśvaniṣṭhā" (residing in the horse): the meaning is "an action residing in the horse that produces the disjunction between the horse and the wall. [He says this] because there is an absence of non-residence in the action; for [the action] belongs to both members of the pair [of sheep], etc.

The intended meaning is that [the substratum] is the locus of the action that produces separation from that [other object]. By this, it is indicated that in a case of separation produced by the action of one of two [objects], there is no inconsistency in the statement "one ram moves away from the other ram," because it is possible for the non-locus of the action producing that separation to reside in the other [ram]. From the words "both are indeed unstable" up to "there is separation," a doubt is raised; the resolution is provided by "but the actions are established as distinct therein. It should be understood that this very point has been clarified by the passage beginning with "of the two rams."

In that regard, he provides a corresponding example concerning the locus of disjunction produced by the action of one of two [objects], beginning with "just as the immovable" (*yathā niścala*). This means: from that ram which is immovable, i.e., which is not the substratum of the action that produces the disjunction. Regarding "moving away" (*apasarad*): this means the second ram, which is moving away and is the substratum of such an action. To dispel the doubt that—despite the fact that neither ram is the substratum of the other's action—the definition is untenable because there is no absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the destruction of the action producing that disjunction in the case of each respective ram, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). He explains: "the state of not being the substratum of that action."

And thus, by taking each individual action that produces the separation from that [object] as a specific instance (*tadvayaktitvena*) and stipulating that it must not have that [object] as its substratum (*anāśrayatva*), there is no inconsistency; for each single arrow does not serve as the substratum for the action inherent in another arrow that causes the separation from that same object—this is the intended meaning. Others, however, maintain that although a difference in actions exists due to a difference in agents, that difference is not perceived, because the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) presents the action as one whose differences have ceased once it has been denoted by the root (*dhātu*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sarūpasūtra*: "Verbal suffixes do not necessitate the formulation of the *ekaśeṣa* rule."

And thus, it is not possible to avoid the aforementioned logical inconsistency; rather, the consensus is that by relying on a difference in denotation based on a difference in words—since agency belongs to those two things presented by the word *meṣa* (ram) insofar as they are the substrata of such actions, while ablativity belongs to those same two things presented by the word *paraspara* (mutual) insofar as they are not the substrata of such actions—it is appropriate to accept a difference even through a difference in words, just as a difference is accepted through the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

[Objection: But surely, in a case where a disjunction is produced by the very action of the tree, the usage ‘the cloth falls from the tree’ (*vṛkṣād vastraṃ patati*) would be untenable; for the tree lacks the status of being a non-substratum of that action which produces the disjunction between the tree and the cloth. To this, he says: “And here, the action [is the meaning of the root]” (*kriyā cātra*). Regarding the phrase “the meaning of the verbal root”: thus, since the tree is not the substratum of the meaning of the root *pat*—which consists of an operation conducive to conjunction—the status of the tree as an ablative (*apādāna*) is established.

[Objection: "But surely, since such a meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) does not produce disjunction (*vibhāga*), and because it is impossible for that [meaning] to be the locus of the non-existence of a root-meaning that produces separation, the [definition of *apādāna*] is even more impossible. [Reply: This is not so. One should include merely the state of not being the locus of that specific root-meaning by taking each respective root-meaning in its particular individuality (*tattadvayaktitvena*), but one need not include the property of being the cause of separation within the root-meaning itself. For by that much alone, in the case of "He falls from the running horse" (*dhāvato'śvāt patati*), the horse's status as the *apādāna* is established, since it is not the locus of the falling which resides in the person [who falls]. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning to be understood is that whatever serves as the locus of the respective meanings of those verbal roots which cause separation possesses the state of being distinct from that [locus]. In the example "Devadatta falls from the tree," the intended sense is that Devadatta and others alone are the well-known counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) who are the loci of the aforementioned verbal root-meanings. However, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning a separation produced by the action of both is not accepted; for in the case of "from each other" (*parasparasmāt*), both possess the status of the limit (*avadhitva*) and the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*), whereas here, one possesses the status of the limit and the other possesses the status of the agent.

This treatise is introduced to indicate a distinction [from other views], namely that agency (*kartṛtva*) is [the meaning of the ablative]. Now, one might object: if the latter part of the definition (the absence of a substratum) were not denotable, then in the sentence "Devadatta comes from the village," there would be the undesirable consequence of using the form *devadattāt* (with the ablative suffix), because Devadatta is indeed the substratum of the separation (*viśleṣa*). To this, he replies: "The meaning of the second case has been stated."

The intended meaning is as follows: just as in the usage "Devadatta goes to Devadatta," there is no undesirable consequence despite [the object] being denotable because it is the supreme [referent], since the technical designation *karman* (object) is sublated by the subsequent designation *kartṛ* (agent); likewise, it is appropriate that the one possessing the capacity of being a limit (*avadhi*) is what is denotable by the designation *apādāna* (ablative), due to its sublation by the designation *kartṛ*. "Even so" means: even when usages such as "Devadatta [goes] to Devadatta" are excluded. Regarding the example "He moves from the tree": [this is used to illustrate the necessity of the limit].

Even in that case, since the tree possesses the state of being the locus of the separation produced by that [action], while not being the locus of such a verbal root-meaning, this undesirable consequence (āpatti) applies even to the view that the meaning of the "satyanta" portion [of the definition] is the denotable meaning (vācya). He dispels the suspicion that the aforementioned usage would result from accepting this consequence by stating, "He has moved from his seat. He introduces a refutation of the solution proposed by some to avoid the aforementioned usage with the words, "By this... (etena).

"In the cognition of the status of an ablative (*apādānatva*)" means in a verbal cognition where the status of an ablative is the qualifier (*prakāra*) by way of the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā*). Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) where the status of an ablative is the qualifier. "The state of being a cause" (*hetutvam*) means the state of being a cause by way of the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). However, in the case of a verbal root such as *spand* (to vibrate), which is used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇika*) to mean an operation conducive to conjunction, or when it is the object of a misconception regarding its power (*śakti*), the point is that in such usage, the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) is simply accepted. The verbal root *pat* (to fall) is transitive (*sakarmaka*).

This is because [the root *pat*] signifies an activity conducive to a conjunction that has its locus in a downward direction. For this very reason, the compound *kūpapatitaḥ* ("fallen into a well") and others are established by the rule "dvitīyā-śrita-" (Pāṇini 2.1.24). Consequently, there is no inconsistency in such usages as *aśvāt patati* ("he falls from the horse").

Alternatively, according to the view that there is a single power (*śakti*) for the operation qualified by the result—on the basis of the principle that "the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a cognition residing in an operation delimited by a result that does not reside in the locus of the operation" (as expressed by the phrase *sakarmakadhātujanyopasthiteḥ*)—or according to the view that there is a separate power for each, the cause is the mental presence produced by a cognition that apprehends the subordination (*avacchinnatva*) of the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) residing in the conventional understanding (*saṅketīyabodha*) to the state of having that [specific] result as its object; and [in the case of the second view], it is the mental presence produced by the apprehension of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) whose object is the operation qualified by such a result.

The intended meaning here is "cause. Therefore, since there is no difference in meaning, there is no fault even if there is a difference in words; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "is rejected": the point is that if one accepts the aforementioned relationship of cause and effect (hetu-hetumat-bhāva) in order to prevent the usage *vṛkṣāt spandate* ("it moves from the tree"), then the desired usage *āsanāc calitaḥ* ("he has moved from his seat") and others would not be accounted for. Thus, such a relationship of cause and effect should not be accepted, and consequently, it is appropriate to accept the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) even in the case of the usage *vṛkṣāt spandate*.

Regarding this, they say: since the root *spand* signifies mere movement (*kampana*) and does not convey the notion of separation (*vibhāga*), and thus lacks the character of an injunction (*avidhi*), the usage "vṛkṣāt spandate" (it moves from the tree) is not appropriate; rather, only "vṛkṣe spandate" (it moves on the tree) is correct. However, because the root *cal* signifies an operation conducive to separation and so forth—as evidenced by the usage "calitaḥ" (having moved)—the same meaning is accepted for *spand* as well, and thus the aforementioned usage is indeed desired. Others, however, maintain that it does not have that meaning at all.
However, the present text should be understood with the intention that even the roots *calati* and *kampati* have that same meaning. Regarding the phrase "it is unavoidable":
since the tree possesses the state of not being the locus of an operation delimited by disjunction (*vibhāga*), the technical designation of *apādāna* (ablative) would apply [to it].

Regarding the term "by the designation of object" (*karmasaṃjñayā*): the designation of object applies to the tree because it possesses the status of being the locus of the fruit, which is disjunction (*vibhāga*), by way of the delimiting relation of inherence (*samavāya*) that defines the nature of the fruit. In expressions such as "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), since the verb "comes" signifies an activity conducive to a conjunction produced by disjunction, disjunction itself lacks the status of being the fruit; furthermore, since only an inherence residing in the agent serves as the delimiting relation for the fruit, there is no possibility of the village and so forth being designated as the object.

He dispels the following doubt: "Even though the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) lacks grammatical correctness because the designation of 'ablative' (*apādāna-saṃjñā*) is precluded by the designation of 'object' (*karman-saṃjñā*), a person might still employ such a construction due to the error of thinking it is an ablative, which would result in the cognition of a relation with a limit (*avadhi*). This is addressed by the words beginning with "due to error" (*bhramāt*). [The word] "cognition" (*buddhiḥ*) means "mental presence" (*upasthitiḥ*). It must be stated that [this presence] is the cause. Nor should it be argued that, in a state where there is an error regarding the synonymy of the roots *tyaj* (to abandon) and *pat* (to fall), such usage would still lead to the non-cognition of the status of being an ablative.

The intended meaning is that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); or rather, one should assume the purport of the present text to be that the cause [of the verbal cognition] is the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by roots such as *tyaj* (to abandon), provided it is not grasped as a synonym for *pati* (to go) and so forth. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. The attempt to prevent such a cognition by postulating that the cause is the presentation of an action (*vyāpāra*) not delimited by a separation (*vibhāga*) is not correct; for in the case of a connection with *pati* meaning "conjunction produced by motion" (*gatijanya-saṃyoga*), such a cognition would not arise. This is the underlying point.

In this context, by the word "yadi" (if) in the phrase "if the absence of cognition is established by experience," it is indicated that such a cognition is indeed intended [as a premise]. Now, an objection is raised: in the expression "it flashes from the cloud" (*balāhakād vidyotate*), the status of the cloud as an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is untenable, because motion (*gati*) is not present, and it is precisely motion that constitutes an *apāya* (separation). To this, he says: "from the cloud" (*balāhakāt*). [The ellipsis is] "having emerged" (*niḥsṛtya*). He supplies the missing words (*adhyāhāra*). Here, the verbal root functions with reference to the flashing preceded by that [emergence]; the author himself will explain this shortly thereafter.

That which is called a "cloud" (*balāhaka*) is a combination of smoke, light, water, and wind. Since there is no intention to express a distinction between the lightning—which is of the nature of light—and the cloud, which consists of such a collection, the cloud serves as the point of reference (*avadhi*). However, when that [cloud] is intended to be the substratum of the light, then the locative case is used, as in "lightning flashes in the cloud" (*balāhake vidyotate vidyut*). It should be understood that when there is no intention to express a distinction between the composite whole and its parts, the nominative case is used for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha-mātra*). This is clearly explained in the *Kaiyaṭa* and other works.

Regarding the phrase "form is separate from taste," one might raise the objection that in the case of form, there is a contradiction with the notion of "emerging" (niḥsaraṇa) as an activity conducive to disjunction following conjunction. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Form... [and] "conceptualized by the intellect. The intended meaning is this: in the rule *dhruvam apāye* ("that which is fixed when there is a departure"), the word *apāya* (departure/separation) includes difference (*bheda*) just as the word *vibhakta* does in the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* ("the fifth [ablative case] is used when there is separation"). Furthermore, the meaning of the word *pṛthak* (separate) is indeed difference itself, and not some other distinct quality, precisely because of the usage [of the word in such contexts].

Even the state of being the object of the cognition of difference (*bheda-jñāna*) is grasped by the word "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇa*), as in the rule *abhidir vidāraṇe*. This is because even in that case, there exists a "tearing apart of the intellect" (*buddhi-vidāraṇa*) when that which was previously known as one is subsequently known as having difference as its object. Thus, just as in expressions such as "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād bhinnaḥ*), here too the ablative case is applied by this sūtra [Pāṇini 1.4.29] through the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) according to the rule *apādāne pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.28). However, in the sūtra *anyārāt...*, the term *anya* is not taken as a synonym for "difference" (*bheda*), because the word *itara* is mentioned separately. [This refers to] the tearing apart of the intellect consisting in the state of being the object of a cognition whose object is difference.

It is stated that [the quality of] being dependent implies being conceptually constructed by the intellect. Here, one should not suspect that because the word *pṛthak* does not denote an action, it cannot function as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant in an action); for the intention is that there is no fault, since one may supply the verb *bhavati* and, given that verbal roots have multiple meanings, accept that its meaning is the state of being separate (*pṛthagbhāva*) characterized by differentiation.

To avoid this fault, he states the fifth [kāraka], "pṛthak-vinā," by means of another sūtra. Others, however, explain the meaning of the sūtra as follows: when there is a specific movement (gati) toward a state of separation (apāya), that which remains constant as the point of reference (avadhi)—provided that no other operation (vyāpāra) is required for the application of the status of a point of reference beyond that—is the *apādāna*. In examples such as "the leaf from Vṛtra out of fear" (*trāsāt vṛtrāt parṇam*), there is no deviation regarding the utility of being a point of reference; thus, even though the utility of being a point of reference exists in the present case, there is no fault because it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatva*).

For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya, the doubt regarding the example "the horse has fallen from the tree" (*atrastādaśva*) is resolved by not intending to express non-permanence (*adhrauvya*). However, the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) is the *apādāna* when there is departure" (*dhruvam apāye*) is intended to preclude the status of *apādāna* that would otherwise apply—by virtue of being a causal agent of action according to the actual state of things—to a tree in examples such as "the leaf falls from the tree. In that context, he explains that the meaning of the word "in departure" (*apāye*) is "when [the thing] is intended to be expressed as a causal agent of action."

They say that the inclusion of the word *dhruva* (fixed) is for the purpose of making known that the operation of the *apādāna* (ablative) consists solely in its attaining the state of being a limit (*avadhi*), and not in some other operation as in the case of other *kārakas*. This should be understood in detail elsewhere. He analyzes that [term] as "having the indicated object" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*). With the intention that the word *viṣaya* here refers to the motion (*gati*) which serves as the cause, he says: "where [it is] directly," meaning without the aforementioned ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). "By the verbal root" (*dhātunā*) means by a verbal root well-known for having the sense of motion.

It is pointed out—that is, it is established. "Where a root meaning movement is pointed out" means where a verbal root denoting motion is indicated. He defines that which has its object grasped: "where there is another root-meaning. This means: the meaning of another root—such as *niḥsarati* (to go out)—is the "meaning of another root"; that is the "limb"—the qualification—where [the action occurs]. Having stated this meaning, he applies it to the example: "having the limb of going out" (*niḥsaraṇāṅga*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning: "that in which there is a going characterized by separation. "Required" (*apekṣita*) means "expected" (*ākāṅkṣita*).

With the intention that desire (*ākāṅkṣā*) arises when there is no [explicit] grasping (*anupādāna*), he says: "as from what? The sense is that even an action (*kriyā*) that is merely implied requires the employment of a case-ending for its *kāraka*. It should be understood that both the question and the answer sentences require an implied action. He states the proof for the fact that the dative signifies the intended recipient (*uddeśya*): "For thus... Although the status of the dative as signifying the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established by the Sūtra, he dispels the doubt that this does not establish the status of the intended recipient itself by saying: "And that... "And that" refers to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

From the sūtra, "That which one intends [to reach] by means of the object (*karman*) is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)," the connection is that [the recipient] is the intended object (*uddeśya*). He states a qualification—beginning with "by means of the object" and ending with "having this meaning"—which serves to establish the recipient's nature as the intended object and its function as the indicator [of that status]. By the phrase "as an instrument" (*karaṇabhūtena*), he dispels the misconception that the instrumental case in "by means of the object" (*karmaṇā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*), as well as the misconception that the instrumental case is otherwise incoherent.

The status of an object (*karman*) as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) occurs through its being a constituent of the relation that forms part of the intention (*abhiprāya*), which consists of a desire directed toward a specific relation; this is mediated by existence and other such factors. Thus, the final meaning is that the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is that which is intended as the goal (*uddeśya*) by virtue of possessing a relation such as being the determiner of a result—like ownership (*svatva*)—which resides in the cow or other such objects.

This is the sense. "This very thing" means precisely the state of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). Regarding that, he states the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas: "the desire whose object is that [thing]" (*tad-uddeśyakecchā*). Thus, the sense is that the specific objective state belonging to a desire is the state of being the intended object. "In this section" (*ity adhikaraṇe*) refers to this particular section located in the second quarter of the fourth chapter of the *Pūrvatantra* (Jaimini’s *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*). It has been "determined" (*niṇīṃta*).

For in that context, after prescribing the giving of the staff to the initiated person, it is further stated: "When the Soma has been purchased, he hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa. This handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa, enjoined by this sentence, is a ritual of disposal (*pratipattikarma*), because the staff, having served its purpose in being held in the hand of the initiated person, stands in need of disposal.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that because the second case-ending indicates his (the Maitrāvaruṇa’s) predominance and not that of the gift, the staff must be placed in the hand of the Maitrāvaruṇa, [the author] refutes it: since the fourth case-ending denoting the recipient (saṃpradāna) reveals the predominance of the Maitrāvaruṇa characterized by being the intended object (uddeśyatva), the giving of the staff is for the sake of the Maitrāvaruṇa; thus, the staff is the motivator (prayojaka) of the act. Indeed, the staff serves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha) as a support for him while he stands reciting the directions (praiṣānuvacana).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even when the initiated sacrificer performs the *nirūḍhapaśu*—which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya-paśu*—the acquisition of the staff for the sake of the Maitrāvaruṇa is accomplished; this is the meaning. Thus, the sense is that because the Maitrāvaruṇa, who is designated by the dative case, is understood to be primary in relation to the staff, which is designated by the accusative case, the desired result is achieved.

For this very reason, they say that in the expression *ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati* ("he leads the goat to the village"), the village does not possess the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) because it lacks the quality of being the beneficiary (*śeṣitva*) with respect to the goat; however, if the leading of the goat is for the sake of preparing the village, then even though that [quality] exists in the village, there is no fault because the designation of "object" (*karman*) prevails due to its higher priority and thus sublates [the designation of recipient].

One might object: "In that case, the usage *rajakāya vastraṃ dadāti* (he gives a cloth to the washerman) would result [as a correct application], because the operation of the root *dā* (to give) consists of an intention conducive to washing, and the washerman is intended by the cloth, which is the object of that operation. Anticipating this objection, he dismisses it by accepting the point with the words *rajakāyeti*. He provides the evidence for the acceptability of such usage with the word *khaṇḍika*. The meaning is "the teacher of a young boy. This is because it is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya.

In this context, since the root *dā* (to give) signifies an operation conducive to a specific result [of giving], if one were to accept the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) only when it is in construction with that primary sense of "giving," then the usage cited in the Bhāṣya would be untenable. [The term] *capeṭā* refers to the palm of the hand extended forward.

Nor should it be said that this usage is merely figurative (*bhākta*); for the authors of the *Bhāṣya*, by rejecting the rule "the term *kriyā* must be included" and by accepting that the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is etymological (*anvartha*), have admitted the primary (*mukhya*) status of the aforementioned usage as well as usages such as *rajakāya*. In this same way, the statement "one should not give knowledge (*mati*) to a Śūdra" is also consistent for this very reason. In that context, the verb *dadāti* means "to impart understanding," and the word *mati* refers to the Vedas and other scriptures which produce that understanding.

In the sentence "He gives a cow to the Brahmin" (*viprāya gāṃ dadāti*), the understanding is that there is an act of giving which has the Brahmin as its recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the cow as its object (*karman*). The author states the view of the Vṛttikāras—who accept the etymological significance (*anvarthatā*) of the term *saṃpradāna*—with the words "The Vṛttikāras, however... [and so on]. The phrase "up to the cessation of one's own ownership" (*svasvatvanivṛttiparyantam*) means up to the operation conducive to the cessation of one's own ownership. This is stated with the intention that the production of another's ownership does not occur through the mere act of giving, but rather through the act of acceptance (*pratigraha*).

Otherwise, however, the meaning is that [the action] extends up to the operation conducive to the mere cessation of one's own ownership and the arising of another's ownership. The term "mere" (*paramātra*) is stated because of the usage in the expression "he gives in joint property" (*saṃsṛṣṭidhane dadāti*). Since no further ownership can arise in that which already possesses ownership, the destruction of ownership must be admitted even in this case. In that regard, although common ownership (*sādhāraṇasvatva*) arises, there is no arising of "mere" ownership; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, ownership is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*), destroyed by giving and so forth, and produced by acceptance and so forth.

In such injunctions as "one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ śrāddhaṃ dadyāt*), although the ownership (*svatva*) characterized by the ancestors is sublated, there is no fault because the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) remains intact, since the ancestors are still the intended objects of the gift. "Explaining the meaning" means explaining the sense of the phrase "for the sake of the aforementioned act of giving," and so forth. The expression "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates the underlying sentiment (*rasa*). The reason for this has already been stated. "And this" (*idaṃ ca*) means that this recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is also threefold.

He states the reason for its threefold nature with the passage beginning "because of non-rejection" (*anirākaraṇāt*) and ending with "from the *Vākyapadīya*. Because the agent does not reject that which is most desired through the action (*īpsitatama*), because of the non-rejection—that is, the non-refusal—of the gift, and because of instigation and consent (namely, instigation and consent regarding the object of giving), it is a constituent part of the relinquishment (*tyāga*), meaning it effects the relinquishment. By this, its status as a *kāraka* (participant in action) is indicated; thus, the construction is that such a *kāraka* attains the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

Alternatively, the triad beginning with "because there is no rejection" (*anirākaraṇāt*) connects with the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatā*) as its cause. Thus, the meaning is that [the recipient] is of three kinds: the non-rejecter (*anirākartṛ*), the instigator (*preraka*), and the consenter (*anumantṛ*). Regarding the phrase "not here in the case of the sun": this is to indicate that in the case of the sun, there is no rejection of the prayer or consent, because it is not occupied by those forms [of agency]. He describes the cognition of the syntactic connection between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the second and subsequent kārakas in the phrase "in all these cases," referring to examples such as *hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari"). This refers to the meanings of the base and the suffix.

The meaning is that the sense of the base (prakṛti) functions as a qualifier for the sense of the suffix (pratyaya) by means of the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*). Nor should it be argued that the sense of the base is never observed to function as a qualifier for the sense of the suffix through the relation of identity; for this is observed in the case of *taddhita* suffixes denoting deities according to the Mīmāṃsā school. As it has been said:
"This *taddhita* suffix indeed expresses *āmikṣā* as qualified by the deity."

In that context, the second case-meaning, which is substratumhood (*āśrayatva*), is construed with the result (*phala*) by way of the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatā*). The third case-meaning of the agent (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) is construed with the activity (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root; and the third case-meaning of the instrument (*karaṇa-tṛtīyā*), due to the peculiarity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*), is construed with the activity conveyed by the third case-ending itself. And that [instrumental activity] is construed with the activity denoted by the verbal root and with the result conveyed by it by way of the relation of being produced (*janyatā*). Alternatively, the activity is not the meaning of the third case-ending at all.

However, it should be understood that the locus (*āśraya*) is either endowed with the capacity for instrumentality (*karaṇatva-śaktimān*), or—by means of the relation of being produced by the operation residing in its own [locus]—it is connected to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through the locus denoted by the locative case, and [further] to the agent and the object; this applies respectively to the operation residing therein and to the fruit (*phala*). There is a rule that when a verbal root having the sense of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is used in co-utterance, the relation that delimits the status of being a fruit (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is precisely ordinary objective manifestation (*laukika-viṣayatā*). Otherwise, even when there is a cognition of fragrance and so forth that has been removed [from the senses], there would result the undesirable application of such expressions as "he perceives fragrance" (*saurabhaṃ paśyati*).

And thus, one should not raise the objection: "How can such a mode (prakāratā) be accepted here as the delimitor of the resulthood? For such a rule is accepted only in cases where the object of perception is not conditioned by its content (*viṣaya*). [As stated: "The book..."

In the expression "jighrati" (he smells), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation conducive to olfactory perception (*ghrāṇaja-pratyakṣa*). However, the odor (*gandha*) is not included within that [operation] as its object. It should be understood that the odor possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) because it is the locus of such a result—namely, the perception—in relation to the delimiting relation of ordinary objective domain (*laukika-viṣayatā*). In the expression "puṣpaṃ jighrati" (he smells the flower), the meaning of the verbal root is an operation conducive to a perception characterized by ordinary objective domainness (*laukika-viṣayitā*) as determined by the odor.

The status of the flower as the object (*karmatva*) is established by virtue of being the locus of such a result—namely, a perception—through a relation that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka-sambandha*) for that result; this relation consists of a specific objective state (*viṣayatā*) characterized by a mode (*prakāratā*) determined by an objective state that is both inherent and adventitious. In the verse "O Lord of the Earth, fragrance [is] on his face" (*tadānanaṃ mṛtsurabhi kṣitīśvara*), the face possesses the state of being the locus of such a mode belonging to the cognition "fragrance is in the face"; thus, the status of the face as the object is logically justified.

In the case of the relational role (*saṃbandhaghaṭakaprakāratva*), one must include the property of being "determined by a qualificand-ness residing in fragrance" (*gandhaniṣṭhaviśeṣyatā-nirūpitatva*). By doing so, even if one takes the role of the qualifier (*aprakāratā*)—which is determined by the relational object-ness (*sāṃsargikaviṣayatā*) belonging to the locus-ness (*ādheyatva*) determined by the qualificand-ness in the flower at the time of the perception "there is fragrance in this flower"—with respect to time, the aforementioned fault does not arise; because locus-ness is qualified by its being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, the expression "one smells time" (*kālaṃ jighrati*) is not employed. This is the direction of the argument.

One may entertain the error that "fragrance" exists in time, but one should not conclude that the defect [of the definition] remains as it was; for such an error lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*). For this very reason, in expressions such as "fire smells" or "color smells," there is no true cognition (*pramā*) having time as its qualifier by way of the relation of locus-ness delimited by temporal connection.

Objection: It is not possible to accept the connection of the substratum of the second-case meaning with the fruit of the verbal root-meaning by way of the relation of *ādheyatā* (inherence), because it is unestablished that such a substratum—which is non-different from the referent of a noun such as "rice" (*haryādi*)—can be connected to the verbal root-meaning through a relation of difference (*bheda*). Otherwise, in the case of "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), there would be the undesirable consequence of such a connection even through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*). Response: This is not so. The grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) is simply this: there is no mutual connection between the referent of a noun and the referent of a verbal root without the mediation of a case-meaning (*vibhaktyartha*).

In the present case, there is no obstacle to such a connection [of the meaning of the suffix] through the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). Now, one might object that a relation of identity between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not possible, because case-endings denote only properties (*dharma*). To this, he says: "of the case-endings, the property... The second case-endings and so forth appropriately have their denotative power (*śakti*) restricted to properties alone, such as "objectness" (*karmatva*), on account of parsimony (*lāghava*); in that case, the meaning of the base is construed as being inherent (*ādheyatayā*) through a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*).

He refutes the view of others—that [the accusative case] relates to the fruit of the verbal root-meaning and so forth through the relation of being its qualifier (*nirūpakatā*)—with the words "only a property" (*dharmamātra*). By the word "only" (*mātra*), the substratum (*dharmin*) is excluded. The phrase "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is used because otherwise there would be an undesirable violation of the natural force of rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and "the third case is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*). Otherwise, he would have formulated the rule as "the second case is used when there is the state of being an object" (*karmatve dvitīyā*), rather than "for the object" (*karmaṇaḥ*).

The meaning is not that "when the object (*karman*) is to be expressed" (*vācye*), and so forth; rather, the meaning is that "the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) [is used] when the object is to be understood (*bodhye*). And the justification for this is that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). In this way, there is no violation of its natural semantic force (*svarasabhaṅga*). Nor is it the case that even when the base-meaning, such as Hari, is construed with the relation of being a locus (*āśrayatva*), the cognition is merely "the locus-ness qualified by Hari," and not "Hari who possesses locus-ness"; how then [could there be a problem]?

It must be stated that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) functions to convey the fulfillment of the action (*karmabodhanirvāhakatva*); for when there is a cognition of the relation of the base-meaning—such as Hari—as the locus (*āśrayatva*), it is possible for the cognition "Hari is the locus" to arise.

Just as from the statement "Devadatta is a friend of the king" (*rājasakho devadattaḥ*), there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of Devadatta’s friendship with the king, and one grasps that the king is a friend of Devadatta; likewise, the assumption that the rule (*sūtra*) which teaches the denotative power (*śakti*) [of a suffix] in respect to an object (*karman*) actually teaches a power residing in the locus (*āśraya*) alone—this assumption remains unavoidable even in your own view, because it would entail a violation of the natural sense of the rule. If you argue that, since the result (*phala*) is obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*), the power should be assumed in the locus alone, and that this is equally the case in my view due to parsimony (*lāghava*) in assuming it in the property (*dharma*) [rather than the substance], he says: "In the sense of the accusative case, etc. (*dvitīyādyarthaka*).

Regarding the term *dharmivācakatā* (denotative of the substratum): in the case of the compound *prāptodaka* ("one who has reached water"), the meaning of the compound is "a village that is the object of an action of reaching whose agent is water. To account for the experience of a cognition in which this meaning and the word *grāma* ("village") stand in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is necessary that the accusative case-ending possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the object (*karman*). Otherwise, since even a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose meaning is the referent of the accusative would result in denoting the state of being an object (*karmatva*), the impossibility of coreferentiality would follow.

He states that "supām karmādayo" (Pāṇini 2.3.2) is also a proof for [the suffixes] denoting the substratum (*dharmin*). The intention is that, according to the opponent's view, this would result in a violation of the natural sense [of the rule]. Nor can the word "karma" here be taken as referring to the property of objecthood (*karmatva*), because that would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in numerous instances.

Now, one might argue: even if there is a necessity for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in words such as "object" (*karman*) in expressions like *karmaṇi*, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to maintain that the second case endings and so forth denote only the property (*dharma*). Let it be granted, then, that even a *bahuvrīhi* compound denotes only the property, and its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the head noun can be established through secondary indication; furthermore, the usage of terms like *prāptodaka* in their primary sense occurs in cases such as *prāptodako 'sti*. To this, he says "dig" (the direction). For if [the compound] were to denote only the property inherent in that object, then how could even a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix—such as *tavya*—be established as denoting the possessor of wealth?

If it is argued that [the suffix *kṛtya*] functions in this way because of the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "rice" (*taṇḭula*) and so forth in expressions such as *paktavyās taṇḍulāḥ* ("the rice is to be cooked"), we say no; for that is accounted for by the very manner already stated. If it is argued that the cognition of mere objecthood (*karmatva*) from words such as *paktavya* contradicts experience, the point is that the same applies to cases such as *prāptodaka* ("to whom water has come").

Furthermore, the accusative case endings (*dvitīyādi*) do not have a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the substratum (*āśraya*), because—just as the result and the operation are obtained through the verbal root—the substratum is also obtained through the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the base; rather, they denote merely the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) and so forth, since that is not obtainable through any other means.

And because there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), the designation "object" (*karman*) and so forth is not untenable; for this very reason, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that holds that the accusative and other case-endings denote the capacity (*śakti*) such as "objectness," the status of denoting the substratum—as in the case of *prāptodaka* ("one who has obtained water")—is maintained for *vrīhi* ("rice"), since it is precisely a capacity that has acquired a distinction through a difference of capacities that is expressed by the case-ending.

However, since the substratum (āśraya) is understood from forms such as *pacati*, *paktā*, and *pakva*—which consist of verbal roots and suffixes—and because the linguistic usage expressed in the rule "when *yuṣmad* is a coreferential subordinate term" (*yuṣmadyupapade samānādhikaraṇe*) requires it, it is appropriate that the substratum possesses a denotative power (*śakti*). With this intention, he says, "of the substratum also," and so forth. The syntactic connection is: "Since the substratum is obtained by the base itself (*prakṛti*), it is not denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Regarding "not by the case-ending": the meaning is that it is not denoted by case-endings such as the accusative (*dvitīyā*) and others.

Now, if "being a substratum" (āśrayatva) is what is to be expressed [by the word], then one must accept that "the property of being a substratum" (āśrayatvatva) is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka); and in that case, there would be prolixity (gaurava), because that [property] consists in residing in all substrata while not residing in anything other than those substrata. To this, he says:

"That very [thing]" means "the state of being the locus (āśrayatva) itself. By the word "only" (eva), the state of being the locus-as-such (āśrayatātva) is excluded. Having raised the objection—"How can that which resides in it (tadvṛtti) be the delimitor of denotability residing in that [locus]?"—he says: "By way of identity" (tādātmyena). The point is this: although identity is not a regulator of occurrence (vṛttyaniyāmaka), relatedness (saṃbandhitva) is certainly possible through it; thus, since the state of being the locus is related to itself by way of identity, there is no inconsistency in its being the delimitor of denotability residing in itself.

Even if one accepts that the property of being a substratum (*āśrayatātva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), there is no complexity (*gaurava*) even if it serves as its delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*). Nevertheless, if the property of being the substratum of the result (*phalāśrayatvatva*) and so forth were the denotation of the accusative case and other such suffixes, then since the property of being a substratum (*āśrayatātva*) is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*), it cannot serve as its delimiting condition. Furthermore, because the property of being the substratum of the result consists of multiple results, the state of complexity remains unchanged. Moreover, if one posits a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that which is qualified by the property of being a substratum, then because that power must be postulated for both the attribute and the substrate, there is no economy of thought (*lāghava*) compared to the previous alternative; this is the intended meaning.

"Operation (vyāpāra)" means even the operation that constitutes instrumentality (*karaṇatā*). By the word "also" (*api*), the status of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) is included. "Of the six" means of the six case-terminations (*kāraka-vibhakti*) [denoting the kārakas].

Since [the term] "of the six" (*ṣaṇṇām*) is used because the case endings are derived as being prompted by the six *kārakas*, there is no room for the following objection: "If one intends to include those case endings that lack the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), then even though there are six of them, the genitive *kāraka*-case ending would not be included; whereas if one intends to include those case endings that do possess it, then since there would be seven such endings, there would be the undesirable consequence of including a case ending characterized as the seventh. Thus, the statement "of the six" is not inconsistent. Furthermore, by this, it is indicated that the case endings of the *upapada* have "relation" (*saṃbandha*) as their meaning.

Now, the meaning of case-endings (*vibhakty-artha*) is examined in certain grammatical applications (*prayoga*). Among these, regarding the case-endings used with *upapadas* (governing words), since no specific distinction is stated here and because the relation to that [word] is perceived in those instances, they possess that [general] meaning. In cases where there is a prescription for a specific relation, and where there is a fixed expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward a related entity (*saṃbandhin*) by virtue of that relation, those endings have their meaning as a specific relation; for example, in rules such as "anur lakṣaṇe" (Pāṇini 1.4.84) and in expressions such as "antarā tvāṃ māṃ hariḥ" (between you and me is Hari).

In the expression "he rained upon the chanting" (*japamanu prāvarṣat*), the relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣyalakṣaṇabhāva*) expressed by the accusative case is not merely suggested (*dyotya*), but is actually denoted (*vācya*). This is because [the particle *anu*] is a *karmapravacanīya*. By demonstrating its etymology—"those who have expressed an action (*karman*) are *karmapravacanīyas*"—it is shown that while they previously manifested a specific quality residing in an action, they are now prescribed as having that designation precisely when they manifest the relationship between a nominal meaning and an action.

However, where that [general rule] is sublated, there the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) occurs by virtue of the power of the specific injunction, as in the case of *adhi* and others in the rule "adhi-parī anarthakau" and so forth. This is clear from the Bhāṣya and other works on the rule "karmapravacanīyāḥ. In the expression "japam," because the instrumental case ending sublates the instrumental of cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*), it also expresses the sense of cause; and in the present context, its being the object of indication (*lakṣyatva*) consists in its being the object of a cognition produced by another cognition.

For recitation (*japa*), being known as having a specific time and so forth as its instrument, possesses the character of an indicator by virtue of its being qualified by a time subsequent to its own substratum-time. By this, the objection that—because recitation lacks pervasion by rain—it is impossible for rain to be indicated by recitation, is refuted; for an action whose time is already determined can indicate an action whose time is not yet determined through its qualification by a specific time. For this very reason, it is appropriate for [the statement "recitation has occurred"] to serve as an answer to the question, "When did it rain?"

Furthermore, whether the cognition of the specific qualification of time is produced by that sentence or by another means of knowledge (māna) is a separate matter. The resulting cognition is: "The raining is the object of a cognition produced by a cause non-different from the recitation. And it has been stated by Hari:
"This [particle] is not an indicator (*dyotaka*) of the action, nor is it an expresser (*vācaka*) of the relation;
nor does it imply (*ākṣepin*) the verb, but rather it is a differentiator (*bhedaka*) of the relation."

The meaning of that [statement] is as follows: in cases such as *prajayati*, the prefix *anu* does not indicate a specific quality—such as intensity—belonging to the action, unlike other prefixes (*upasargas*). Furthermore, in cases such as *prādeśaṃ viparilikhati*, it does not imply a verbal root, just as the word *vi-* does not imply a verbal root in *vi-mā*. For the word *vi-* implies the action of measuring; for this very reason, *prādeśa* has the status of an object (*karman*), because the sense is "having measured the *prādeśa*, he traces around it. This being so, the use of the second case ending is established on the basis of the implied action.

Otherwise, the rule "karmapravacanīyayukte" would be rendered purposeless; rather, [the particle] indicates that specific relationship produced by a qualified action which is expressed by the case-ending, whereas in the present instance, the aforementioned relationship is produced by the action of hearing (niśamana).

Others, however, maintain that *lakṣaṇa* means "differentiation" (*vyāvartana*). In the present context, the act of raining is intended to be understood as occurring subsequent to the recitation (*japa*), and the recitation serves as the differentiator. Furthermore, they argue that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) need not express the causal basis for the relationship consisting in the state of being posterior in time to the recitation. Their view is that the resulting cognition is: "raining is posterior in time to the time which is the locus of the cause non-different from the recitation."

The formulation of specific case endings depends on the specific relationship; when a relationship is intended to be expressed in its particular form, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is used, as established in the Bhāṣya on the rule *caturthī* (Pāṇini 2.3.73). For there, it is stated that in the example *guroridaṃ gurvartham* ("this is for the teacher"), the genitive is employed because the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) is intended as a general relationship. Consequently, in the expression *tava mama cāntarā kamaṇḍaluḥ* ("the water-pot is between you and me"), the accusative does not occur after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, because the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is intended as a general relationship, and not specifically as the state of being a limit.

Because the state of being "middle" (*madhyatva*), which is denoted by the word *antarā* and constitutes the locus within a delimited interval, necessarily requires a correlate related to it through the relation of being a limit (*avadhitva*); and because the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is precisely that which is delimited by the property of being a limit (*avadhitvatva*), the second case is not applicable here.

For this very reason, there is no room for the following objection: "Even if the use of the genitive case is justified when the word *kamaṇḍalu* is uttered with the intention of referring to its own relation—namely, the relationship between 'you' (*yuṣmad*) or 'I' (*asmad*) and their respective owners, based on the desire to express a relationship of owner and owned—nevertheless, such usage is untenable when it intends to refer to a *kamaṇḍalu* that has no owner. Furthermore, the word *antarā* also has the meaning "absence," as in examples such as *antarā hari na sukham* ("There is no happiness without Hari"), where the word *hari* serves to indicate the intended meaning.

Alternatively, there is the manifestation of that [relation] as a specific instance of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*). By this, the following objection is refuted: "If pure counter-positiveness were the denotable meaning, then even in one who possesses devotion to Hari, since an absence having that [devotion] as its counter-positive exists by way of duality and so forth, the expression 'Hari is within [him] happily' would result. [In our view,] the word "exists" (*asti*) is supplied; and in the absence of existence whose agent is the happiness of the assembly, the connection occurs through the relation of inherence (*ādheyatva*) with the absence of devotion to Hari.

Nor should it be argued that such a syntactic connection is impossible because it contradicts the grammatical derivation [of the word *antarā*] as "between name and object" (*nāmārthayoḥ*). This is because the term is qualified by the exclusion of particles (*nipātātirikta*). Alternatively, the meaning of the word *antarā* is simply absence (*abhāva*). Its connection with such an absence occurs through the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In either of the two cases, it results in the fact that the absence of devotion to Hari is the cause of the absence of happiness and so forth. Or, in the second case, the connection is with that very [absence] through that same relation.

Although it is possible for the meaning of the base (prakṛti) to be construed with [the suffix] through relations such as counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) due to the qualification "other than particles" (*nipātātirikta*), nevertheless, since its meaningfulness is possible, it is improper to accept that it serves merely the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). This is because, like the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it must necessarily express the aforementioned meaning. Furthermore, according to the view of the author of the *Mañjūṣā*, since particles lack the status of nouns (*nāman*), there is no need for the inclusion of the qualification "other than particles" in his system.

In this way, the word *antareṇa* also has the same meaning as this [word *vinā*]. Even when used in conjunction with it, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied by the rule "antarā-antareṇa" (Pāṇini 2.3.4), as in the examples "Hari is between you and me" (*antareṇa tvāṃ māṃ hariḥ*) and "there is no happiness without Hari" (*antareṇa hariṃ na sukham*). In those cases as well, the aforementioned method should be followed. Thus...

The word *vinā* also signifies non-existence (*abhāva*) or has non-existence as its meaning; in that case as well, the same principle applies.
