In expressions such as "the lightning flashes toward the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut*), the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*), which is to be illuminated by the prefixes *prati*, *pari*, and *anu*, is expressed by the case-ending. For, when a tree is seen in dense darkness, the flashing of lightning in a specific location near it is inferred. The meaning of the case-ending is the state of being the object of a cognition produced by another cognition. The resulting understanding is: "The flashing of lightning is the object of a cognition produced by a cognition whose object is the tree."

In expressions such as *bhakto viṣṇum prati*, the relation termed "devotion" (*bhaktatva*)—which pertains to one who has attained a certain state—is indicated by the term *prati* and others, which are designated as *karmapravacanīya*. According to the rule *itthaṃbhūtākhyāne*, these *karmapravacanīya* markers like *prati* signify that state, and the case-ending expresses it; however, it is not the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) that is thus expressed, because it is more appropriate for the "state of being a devotee" (*bhaktatva*) itself, as mentioned in the sūtra, to be the one so characterized.

Nor should it be argued that, because the object [of the action] is denoted by the nominal stem (*bhaktapadopātta*), there is no possibility for the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) to have its own expressive power, on the grounds that the meaning of a word must be something not obtainable through any other means. This is because, even when the object is established as being understood as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*), the power of the case-ending is necessary to ensure its understanding as a relation (*saṃsargatayā*). This is observed in instances such as "Caitra’s son" (*caitrasya putraḥ*), where the meaning of the case-ending, though denoted by another word, appears as a relation; for it is only the produced [son] who can possibly function as the relation within the qualificand denoted by the word "son."

The meaning is that a word-meaning [as a whole] cannot be related to another word-meaning [as a whole], because such a relation would contradict the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*); for it is improper to regard as a "relation" something produced by only a part of a word-meaning when that [whole] has already been determined. In examples such as "Lakṣmī belongs to Hari," the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*), denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), and indicated by the preposition (*pra*) and so forth; the cognition is: "Lakṣmī has Hari as her owner."

In expressions such as *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("he waters tree after tree"), in the context of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) is indicated by the reduplication. The word *vṛkṣa* refers to a tree qualified by pervasion, and the particle *prati* and others serve to indicate the intention that this [tree] is to be construed with the pervader (*vyāpaka*) through the relation of pervasion. The relation delimiting pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is identity (*tādātmya*), while the relation delimiting pervasiveness (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*)—in the case of watering, which consists of an activity conducive to conjunction with a liquid substance—is the conjunction produced by that [activity].

In the case of such a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), however, when pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is manifested, it is [the relation of] inherence (*samavāya*). Within the definition of pervasiveness, either "lack of coreferentiality with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*)—in the form of being unconditioned occurrence—or "pervasive occurrence" (*vyāpyavṛttitva*) should be introduced. Consequently, because action and conjunction are non-pervasively occurring (*avyāpyavṛtti*), even though their absence exists in a tree that possesses them, there is no loss of pervasiveness. Thus, even if a particular act of watering were to be pervasive across all trees on the surface of the earth, there would be no fault.

Since the word "tree" (vṛkṣa) refers to a specific tree by virtue of being present in the intellect, it follows that pervasion—which is established as the state of possessing such properties as "being the act of watering performed by Caitra"—is a relation consisting in being the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of an absence that resides in such a tree and is non-co-referential with its own counter-correlate; it is not, however, the mere state of being devoid of the counter-correlativity of such an absence.

Because such an act of watering would possess the property of being the counter-positive of an absence—which is non-co-located with and delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity residing in such a tree—it would follow that it could not be the pervader; this is the general direction of the argument. The ancients say that since the action of watering is transitive, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs only for the object (*karman*), while the purpose of designating it as a *karmapravacanīya* is merely to prevent the designation of it as a prefix (*upasarga*) or a motion-word (*gati*), thereby ensuring the absence of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.

In that view, when [the object] is the object of the act of sprinkling (*secanakarmatva*), its pervasiveness—either by way of essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) or identity (*tādātmya*)—appears respectively as being related to the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛtyartha*), but not to the sprinkling and so forth. This is because it is impossible for the meaning of the verbal base, which is already construed as a qualifier of the case-meaning, to be further construed as a qualifier of the sprinkling and so forth. Others, however, hold that the purpose of the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* is also to establish the use of the second case (*dvitīyā*) when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not intended to be expressed.

For this very reason, in expressions such as *pratyarthaṃ śabdābhiniveśaḥ* ("the adherence of words to each object"), although the object (*artha*) functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) determined by the action of "entering" (*niveśana*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is presented in the Bhāṣya and other works simply as *arthaṃ arthaṃ prati*. However, if one were to accept that trees and the like possess the status of the direct object (*karman*) of the action and thereby admit that this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) serves to justify the use of the accusative case, then an analysis using a word ending in the locative case would be more appropriate in the present context; consequently, there would be a contradiction with the aforementioned Bhāṣya.

If such a designation (saṃjñā) results in the second case (*dvitīyā*), however, there is no inconsistency; for when one intends to express the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the object, the second case is governed by the relation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). For this very reason, even in cases such as "darkness in every tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati śyāmatā*) or "odor in every jar" (*ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ prati gandhaḥ*), the second case is established as being governed by the relation of possessing an operation produced by an action (*kriyājanitavyāpārakatva*).

Because the repetition [of the word] indicates pervasion (*vyāpyatva*), and because of its co-occurrence with words meaning "to sprinkle," that which pervades each [individual] appears as a qualifier in the form of being pervaded. However, if one does not accept a single recurring property of "being pervaded" (*anugatavyāpyatvatva*), then what would be the evidence for the meaning of "tree" and so forth residing in "pervasion" (*vyāpyatva*)? For instance, even when there is a desire to cognize pervasion in the present context, since the verb *āp* (in *prāpnoti*) is preceded by the prefix *pra*, it aims at the cognition of that [pervasion]; yet, because the desire itself is not cognized through the use of the doubled expression, "pervasion" cannot have that [desire] as its meaning.

Thus, when there is a desire to understand pervasion (*vyāpti*), the meaning of the sentence culminates in the statement "there is a double expression" (*dvirvacanam*). Nor should it be argued that the verbal root alone should express the sense of pervasion, while the case-ending should serve merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); for since a direct relation of difference between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root is unestablished, it is impossible for [the tree] to be construed with pervasion and so forth through relations such as being the locus of the definition (*nirūpitatva*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as *caitraḥ pacyate* ("Caitra is cooking"), there is no cognition of the relation of being the agent (*kartṛtā*) of Caitra with respect to the act of cooking through a relation such as "qualifier of" (*nirūpakatva*). In the case of *śobhanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks well"), the word-meaning "beautiful" (*śobhana*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of difference (*bheda*). In cases such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), the rice and so forth are construed directly (*sākṣāt*) through the intermediary of the case-meaning (*vibhaktyartha*).

In the example *māsam adhīte* ("He studies for a month"), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is applied by the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*, which means that when there is an uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*)—that is, a continuous relation—between a time or distance (the *anuyogin*) and an action, substance, quality, or state (the *pratiyogin*), the second case is used after words denoting time or distance. Through the etymological derivation "a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that has transcended (*atikrānta*) an end (*anta*) or cessation," the sense of an uninterrupted connection is obtained.

The mere phonetic form (*śabdasvarūpa*) as it presents itself does not possess the status of a *prakṛti* (base), because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule prescribing compounds—namely, *kālāḥ* and *antantasaṃyoge ca*—which employs the plural number. The meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). When one accepts the manifestation of pervasion as determined by "month-ness" (*māsatva*), which is the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), then the relation that constitutes the factor of pervasiveness (*vyāpyatāghaṭakasambandha*) is either inherence (*samavāya*) or identity (*tādātmya*); and its nature consists in being thirty days and nights, which is the essence of "month-ness."

The state of being a locus whose property is not a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of an absence that is non-co-locative with its own counter-correlative. And the relation constitutive of pervasion is the one consisting of temporal qualification (*kālika-viśeṣaṇatā*). Furthermore, the word "month" (*māsa*) refers to a collection of thirty days and nights that is not distinct from its constituent parts, but does not refer to a gross duration persisting for that long. For if it were so, the expression "he studies for a month" would incorrectly apply even to one who studies for only a single day or so.

Since his study also possesses the property of being a "study by him" (tadīyādhyayanatva), which is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of an absence that is non-coexistent with its counter-correlative and resides in such a period consisting of thirty days and nights, it is possible for it to pervade the month and so forth; thus, because the absence of his study is non-coexistent with its counter-correlative, the aforementioned fault does not arise. Furthermore, the "day and night" constituting that period is nothing other than a collection of moments and the like, existing from the limit of sunrise until the subsequent sunrise.

Therefore, since—even at the place of study for thirty days—the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable when one introduces an absence that is non-co-instantaneous with its counter-positive (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇābhāva) within moments and the like that constitute the locus of the month during the intervals of sleep and so forth, that introduction is made in order to exclude such a defect. Furthermore, non-co-instantaneousness with the counter-positive (pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya) consists in residing in a locus different from that which possesses a non-co-instantaneousness with respect to those things delimited by the delimitors of the counter-positivehood as conceived by the relation intended to be the delimitor of pervasion (vyāpakatāvacchedaka).

However, it is not the case that, by virtue of that relation, the property of "not occurring in the locus of the delimitor of the agenthood" applies to studying and so forth; for since studying occurs non-pervasively (avyāpyavṛtti) during the day, its absence exists even at times that are its own loci, being delimited by certain moments and so on. Consequently, because there is an absence of "not occurring in the locus of the counter-positive," there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using the expression "he studies for a month" even for one who has studied for only a single day within that month.

Even when there exists a mountain or the like within only a portion of a *krośa*, the absence of that [mountain]—whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the relation of conjunction residing in a location other than that [portion] which is pervaded by the *krośa*—is present in that very place pervaded by the *krośa* by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*). Since the locus of the counterpositive (the mountain) exists there, the qualification of "not subsisting in the locus of the counterpositive" is absent; therefore, it is only the past instance of that [mountain] whose counterpositiveness is not delimited by such a counterpositive-inherence-disjointness (*tādṛśa-pratiyogi-vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the *krośa*.

Since existence (*sattva*) resides in the mountain itself, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "the mountain [extends] for a *krośa*. Therefore, the locus of the counter-positive must be defined as non-residence with respect to the relation that constitutes pervasion (*vyāpakatā*). For instance, when Devadatta does not observe a fast in Kāśī for one day, two days, or more, but instead fasts outside of Kāśī during the remaining days and nights within the month, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Devadatta’s absence of eating [occurs] in Kāśī for a month" in such a case.

Since the absence of Devadatta’s eating, qualified by being delimited by Kāśī, is identical to the absence of such eating that is not so delimited, the absence of that absence of Devadatta’s eating as delimited by Kāśī—though it exists in another day which is the locus of that month—is not "residing in a locus other than the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) with respect to that other day belonging to that month; for that day is the locus of the counter-positive, namely the absence of Devadatta’s eating. Rather, it is simply another absence; its counter-positiveness...

This is because the property of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) exists in the absence of Devadatta’s eating as delimited by Kāśī. Likewise, if Devadatta did not stay outside for two days within a month, but stayed in Kāśī for the remaining twenty-eight days, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Devadatta’s absence was in Kāśī for a month. This is because, although the absence of the absence of Devadatta as delimited by Kāśī resides in the days covered by the month, it lacks the property of having a different locus from the speaker (*prayogivyadhikaraṇatva*).

Because it is co-located with its counter-positive, which consists of the absence of Devadatta qualified by being delimited by another location; for a qualified entity is not distinct from the pure entity itself. Therefore, there must be the inclusion of the condition of non-co-location with that which is delimited by the counter-positive’s delimiting property (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).

This being the case, since the property of not having as its locus that which is delimited by the delimitor of counterpositiveness—namely, the nature of the absence of Devadatta’s eating restricted to Kāśī—exists on other days that constitute the locus of the month, even absences such as the absence of Devadatta’s eating restricted to Kāśī are counter-positive-locus-different (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa); thus, the aforementioned over-extension does not occur.

In this regard, the following should be understood: the second meaning [of the suffix] is not "pervasion" (*vyāpakatva*). This is because pervasion—being an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) property that cannot be defined independently of its specific correlate (*vyāpya*)—is difficult to express; furthermore, since there would be an infinity of such pervasions, it would entail an undesirable consequence of an infinite number of word-powers (*śakti*). Moreover, because the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*) would lack expectancy for the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would be impossible. Therefore, the denotative function (*vṛtti*) applies distributively (*khaṇḍaśaḥ*) to the absence qualified by the "non-co-referentiality with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), to the counter-positivehood-delimiter (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), and to the absence itself.

In the absence of the first [negation], the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), such as "month," is construed with the [second] negation by way of the relation of locus (*ādheyatva*). The property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of that [first] negation is then construed with another negation—the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*)—by way of the relation of having a counter-correlativity delimited by such a delimiting factor. And that [second] negation is construed with Caitra’s studying by way of a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of its own non-existence (*svābhāva*), which is defined by the state of being Caitra’s agent of studying (*caitrakartṛkādhyayanatva*).

Alternatively, let it be that the accusative case possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the state of not being the locus of each respective counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and that this [counter-correlate] functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) due to a peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). To this, they reply: "If one accepts a primary denotative power there, there would be an infinity of powers; if one accepts figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it contradicts the established doctrine that 'there is no indication in an inflectional suffix' (*vibhaktau na lakṣaṇā*), and there is also the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). [To this we say: Since there is no other way, the infinity of powers and so forth is accepted.

Thus, power (*śakti*) is also accepted as being included within each respective non-pervasive [property], such that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with the qualified pervasiveness (*viśiṣṭavyāpakatva*) alone through the relation of qualifierhood (*nirūpakatva*), and not with the month-ness (*māsatva*) and so forth that constitute the pervasiveness itself. Therefore, there is no room for the objection that, because [the base] lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) regarding the substratum-ness (*ādheyatva*) of month-ness in that which possesses month-ness, an impossibility of construal (*ananvaya*) would result.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that if power (*śakti*) were admitted to reside in parts, then—due to the absence of the causal condition consisting of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by distinct words—the comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would be impossible. Furthermore, since it is established by experience that the cognition occurs precisely as a relation (*saṃbandhatva*), there is no risk of an infinite regress of powers either.

Others, however, maintain that there is no need to include "absence of coreferentiality with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*) within the meaning of the case-ending, nor is there a need to include the "pervaded" (*vyāpya*), because the analysis is consistent by accepting the following: the meaning of the base (the month) is construed with the absence—which constitutes the pervasiveness—via a relation of "inherence" (*ādheyatā*) qualified by being the counterpositiveness residing in the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of the difference residing in itself. Thus, they say, there is no prolixity; this is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, "month-ness" (*māsatva*) [is determined] by the difference between those months.

It is clear from the *Vyutpattivāda* and other works that there is no such lack of syntactic validity (*anupapatti*) in expressions like "he has studied for one month," provided that the study has occupied at least one single locus (day) within that period. In phrases such as "he sleeps during the day," the word "day" refers to the collection of moments (*kṣaṇasamūha*) beginning from sunrise and ending with the next sunrise; therefore, such an expression is not used when one sleeps for only a single *daṇḍa* or similar duration.

In the expression "a mountain for a *yojana*," there is an absolute connection with a substance (*dravya*); in "the river is winding for a *krośa*" or "it is beautiful for a *krośa*," there is an absolute connection with a quality (*guṇa*) such as windingness; and in "the absence of food for a month," there is an absolute connection with an absence (*abhāva*). Therefore, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) follows words such as *yojana*.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as in examples such as *māsam āste* (he sits for a month), *godoham āste* (he sits while the cows are being milked), *māsa āsyate* (a month is sat through), and *godoha āsyate* (the milking-time is sat through), the accusative case is established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam karma* ("that which is most desired by the agent is the object")—since we accept that the verbal root (*dhātu*) extends its function up to the resulting action (*vyāpāra*)—so too in the case of *māsam adhīte* (he studies for a month), the accusative would be established by that same rule. Thus, the sūtra *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* ("in connection with time and distance when there is continuous contact") would be redundant. As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "When time, state, path, and place are connected with all intransitive verbs, their status as an object (*karmatva*) arises through the inclusion of another [implied] action."

In this regard, although it was stated [in the Bhāṣya] that "only intransitive verbs" are intended, there is no obstacle to accepting that even transitive verbal roots may have such a function provided that the object is included within their meaning, as the underlying logic remains the same. For this very reason, the doubt regarding the redundancy of this sūtra—on the grounds that "this is merely the natural (prakṛta) object"—was raised in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra. If one were to accept the aforementioned rule [of inclusion] only for intransitive verbs, then the doubt would be inconsistent, since the sūtra would still be necessary to account for usages such as *māsam adhīte* ("he studies for a month").

Nor should it be argued that such usage is simply not desired because of the subsequent commentary (*parabhāṣya*) containing such a doubt; for otherwise, the suspicion of the futility of this very sūtra—which provides the justification for the two types of usage, namely *māsam āste* and *māsam adhīte* under the rule "apavarge tṛtīyā"—would be untenable. In this sūtra, there exists only the type of usage involving intransitive roots, such as *āsyate māsaḥ* (the month is sat through) and *śayyate krośaḥ* (the league is slept through).

However, constructions such as *māsam adhīte* ("he studies for a month") consist of transitive roots, such that one would have to assume the inclusion of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) even there; this is because such usages are indeed accepted, as evidenced by the usage *māsam adhīto 'nuvāko na cānena gṛhītaḥ* ("the lesson was studied for a month, but it was not mastered by him"). For this very reason, the usage *māsam odanam pacati* ("he cooks rice for a month") also occurs when there is an intention to express the object as being pervaded.

Since time and the like are external objects (*bahir-aṅga*), the *la*-affixes (the terminations of the first four lakāras) do not apply to them; rather, they apply to the internal object (*antar-aṅga*), which is the substance (*dravya-karman*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya-pradīpodyota*. Following this very principle, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the rule "in the case of continuous connection [with time, etc.], [the verb] should be treated like [a verb having] an object" (*atyanta-saṃyoge karmavat*) need not even be formulated. Furthermore, the expression "by means of roots that have no object" (*akarmaka-dhātubhiḥ*) does not exist in the *Bhāṣya* at all. As stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *akathitaṃ ca*: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are indeed designated as the object (*karman*) for intransitive verbs (*akarmaṇām*)."

Thus, even this is a statement of an established fact (*siddhārthakathana*) and not something previously unknown (*apūrva*), as is clear from the *Śākhara* and other works due to the use of the particle *hi*. In that context, time and the like are the primary objects (*pradhānakarman*), while the substance (*dravya*) is the secondary object (*apradhānakarman*), because time and the like connect with the action only by way of the substance, serving as its substratum. Therefore, if it is argued that the Sūtra is redundant, we say no; for the *Bhāṣya* itself provides the resolution: "This must be stated for the sake of those cases where there is a connection with an action [other than the primary one]."

If it is asked, "How then is 'māsam adhīte' (he studies for a month) an illustration [of *atyantasaṃyoga*]?", the intention is that the explanation given in the Bhāṣya is appropriate: since this [term *atyantasaṃyoga*] is necessary both to prevent the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is a desire to express a general relation and to ensure connection with an action, it serves to express *atyantasaṃyoga* (absolute connection) in cases where there is no desire to express the relation between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*).

Although in the example "the river is winding for a *krośa*," the introduction of the verb "is" (*asti*) is necessary because the nominative case cannot be justified without it, nevertheless, this [sūtra] is intended to establish the accusative case when one intends to express that the windingness itself qualifies the *krośa*; thus, there is no inconsistency with the *Bhāṣya* or other texts.

In this regard, due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), there is a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) either with a portion of the object such as "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*) and so forth, or with the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by that [portion]. Others, however, maintain that the function of every verbal root extends up to its pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, even in cases such as "the river is crooked for a *krośa*" (*krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī*), the second case ending is justified. Nevertheless, they argue that in an expression like "he sat for a month" (*māsi māsam āsita*), the genitive case prescribed for connection with a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) would apply rather than the second case; therefore, they say this [rule] is necessary for that purpose. Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the second case.

"One infers fire by means of smoke" (*dhūmena vahnimanuminoti*); here, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). On the view that the cognition of smoke and so forth is the instrument of inference, words such as "smoke" refer to the cognition of that smoke. However, on the view that what is being cognized is the instrument, they retain their primary meaning. Since the mental operation (*vyāpāra*) consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which apprehends the qualified presence of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the status of the cognition of smoke etc. as qualified by pervasion as the instrument is thereby established.

Because it is accepted that the relation of being produced by the cognition of smoke and so forth is construed with respect to the universal of inferential cognition (*anumiti*) where fire is the property to be inferred (*vidheya*) and the delimitor of the subject (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), there is no such usage as "inference of fire" (*vahnyanumiti*) [in this context], nor is there the usage "one infers a pot by means of smoke. [Objection: This is possible in the system of the Logicians (*tārkika*), but not in the system of Grammarians (*śābdika*). For in their system, the meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyārtha*) is the *vidheyatā* (the state of being the property to be inferred), which is identical to *vidheyitā* (the state of being the property to be inferred). That [state] is construed with the inferential cognition through a relation such as being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*).

In an inference qualified by such a property as being the object-to-be-prescribed (*vidheyatā*), there is the possibility of "being delimited by the correlate" (*anvayitāvacchedakatva*) for properties such as having fire as the object-to-be-prescribed, because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the fact of having the cognition of smoke as its instrument. However, according to the view of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), the meaning of the verbal root is the operation conducive to inference, and the relation of being the object-to-be-prescribed is that which delimits the result. In this way, it is quite clear that "the state of having fire as the object-to-be-prescribed in an inference" lacks the status of being delimited by the correlate.

If it is argued that, even so, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains unavoidable in this view, we say no; for by accepting the connection of the instrumentality of the knowledge of smoke and so forth with the fire delimited by the inference—through a relation of "predicability" (*vidheyatā*) that stands in place of [the usual] predicability—the aforementioned over-extension becomes impossible. But even then, in a case where there is an inference of fire based on the mark of smoke, and that inference involves the apprehension of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth through the cognition of a jar, the use of a sentence containing the negative particle—as in "one does not infer fire by means of a jar"—would be untenable.

In the case of the aforementioned inference based on a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) of fire, it is impossible to communicate the absence of that aforementioned inference—which is qualified by being caused by the cognition of a pot—through the sublation of the absence of having the cognition of a pot as its instrument; for [one cannot say], "This inference of fire is by means of smoke, not by means of a pot."

Even in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is untenable. One might argue that while it is possible to convey the cognition of absence in the previously mentioned case—where there is the possibility of a misconception regarding the pervasion of fire by the jar at the time of an inference of fire based on the cognition of a jar as the instrument (in the first-case-noun referent)—it is impossible here. If this is said, we reply: no. For when the aforementioned inference consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) exists, the path of the formal argument—"This inference of fire has smoke as its instrument, not a jar as its instrument"—must be demonstrated here, just as follows:

They say that such an application is not accepted by the Tathāgata, and thus even the two previously mentioned applications are not accepted. Others, however, maintain that even under the view that [words] are instruments of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇatā*), terms such as "smoke" (*dhūma*) retain their primary meaning; for since the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is impossible according to the rule *'hetau'* (Pāṇini 2.3.23), the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) in the form of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) is common to all [causes], including those that delimit the generative capacity (*janakatāvacchedaka*). Thus, it remains intact in the case of smoke and so forth, which delimit the generative capacity of an inference with respect to its object (*viṣayitā*).

The meaning of the instrumental suffix (*tṛtīyā*) is either *prayojakatva* (the state of being a motivator), which consists in being the delimiting factor of the producedness (*janyatāvacchedakatā*), or *prayojyatva* (the state of being motivated). Its connection with the meaning of the word ending in the case-suffix in "fire" (*vahni*)—namely, the property of having fire as its qualificandum (*vidheya*)—is accepted as occurring through relations such as *nirūpakatā* (the state of being a relatum). Consequently, there is no possibility of the erroneous usage "with a pot, fire" (*ghaṭena vahniḥ*), because the property of having fire as its qualificandum lacks the state of being a relatum of the motivatorship residing in the pot. Furthermore, since the absence of being motivated by the pot is uncontradicted in that context, the usage "with a pot" (*ghaṭena*) and so forth is logically justified.

The validity of such formal expressions as "by smoke [one infers] fire" (dhūmena vahnim) is established because the state of being the object-to-be-prescribed (vidheyitā) is both the determinant of the causality residing in smoke and the effect of that causality. According to the Grammarians' view, since there is no secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) in case-endings, the state of being the object-to-be-prescribed cannot be the meaning of a case-ending. Consequently, to account for the derivation of the aforementioned expression containing the negative particle (nañ), one must necessarily accept that the verbal root *minoti* itself—preceded by its specific sequence of phonemes (*anupūrvī*)—possesses a secondary signification denoting an inference where fire is the object-to-be-prescribed, while the word ending in the case-suffix, such as *vahnim*, functions merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

And thus, there is no possibility of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of using the expression "one infers fire by means of a jar" with the intention that the inference here is one having a collective object (samūhālambana). However, they say that the expression "one does not infer fire by means of a jar" is to be accounted for only by accepting the connection of the third-case meaning [instrumentality] with the property of being the qualificandum (vidheyatva) of fire, which is a part of the meaning of the verbal root; for it is possible to convey the absence of a qualified inference—caused by the absence of the state of being prompted by the cognition of the jar—in respect to that property of being the qualificandum of fire which is to be produced.

In the expression "the father has come with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā*), the instrumental case ending is used according to the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* ("when joined with *saha*, the subordinate [participant takes the third case]"). The meaning of the word *saha* is "concomitance" (*sāhitya*). This concomitance consists in the connection with an action or the like that is simultaneous with the action or the like denoted by the word uttered in close proximity [to *saha*]. Furthermore, this state of being connected is precisely the same kind of relation as that which is perceived between the action or the like connected to the concomitance and the word denoting the action or the like uttered in close proximity. In examples such as *putreṇa*, that [relation] takes the form of agency (*kartṛtva*).

In examples such as "he eats rice with milk" (*payasā sahaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*) or "rice is eaten with milk" (*payasā sahaudano bhujyate*), [the word *saha*] denotes the object (*karmatva*). In "he was killed by an arrow together with a sword" (*khaḍgena saha bāṇena hataḥ*), it denotes the instrument (*karaṇatva*). In "a sacrificial fee is given to the teacher together with the pupil" (*śiṣyeṇa saha gurave dakṣiṇā dīyate*), it denotes the recipient (*saṃpradānatva*). In "the gods are in Kāśī together with Prayāga" (*prayāgeṇa saha kāśyāṃ devāḥ santi*), it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). In cases such as "he is stout together with his son" (*putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ*), the relation is one of substratum (*ādhāratva*) and so forth; even in instances like *putreṇa*, although it is the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*), it is indeed simply agency (*kartṛtva*) and the like.

The agency qualified by the son (putrānvita-kartṛtva) is construed with the act of coming (*āgamana*), which constitutes a component of the meaning of "together" (*saha*), via the relation of being the relatum (*nirūpakatā-saṃbandha*). This agency, whose sense is "coming at a time other than that of the arrival," is construed with the father through the relation of being implied by the meaning of "together. Thereafter, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*)—qualified by that [agency]—is construed non-differently (*abheda*) with the agent of the coming. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) due to the identity between the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*).

Because agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth are included within the sense of "together" (*saha*) precisely as relations, there is a lack of syntactic expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) only when the delimitors of the referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) are of a single form; since that is absent in the present case. Alternatively, the meaning of the word *saha* is simply the state of being related to a thing that is simultaneous with its relatum. And the relation—agency and so forth—is to be included as a relation, as before, and constitutes the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) following the word "son."

The agency [of the teacher] is determined by the action of coming, which is understood through the force of the connection with the meaning of the word "saha" (together). For this very reason, there is no inconsistency in the Bhāṣya’s statement that in examples such as "he came together with the pupil," the matter is established by the third case ending itself expressing agency.

Since it is established that even a connection with an implied action serves as the motivator for the use of a case-ending denoting a *kāraka*, once the cognition "the state of being related to such an object [e.g., arrival] which is related to the son" has occurred, the relation of the son—who is perceived as connected to the arrival—cannot be accounted for without his own relation to that object. Consequently, that relation must be mentally conveyed in respect to the son as well; thus, the meaning of the word "son" stands in a relation of being the qualificand (*nirūpaka*) of the agency (*kartṛtva*) residing in itself, as expressed by the third case-ending.

In the case of *sahārtha* (the meaning of "together with"), there is a connection with that which possesses the relation constituting the [co-occurring] object. For example, in the sentence "He eats rice with milk" (*payasā sahaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), there is a connection with the son through a relation consisting of the accusative case [ending] defined by the action being perceived. Alternatively, *sāhitya* (concomitance) is a distinct, indivisible category of meaning that is co-extensive with the state of being connected to such referents. The rest is as before. In this interpretation, there is not even the suspicion of identity between the delimiting condition of the locus of predication (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the property to be predicated (*vidheya*).

Because such co-presence (*sāhitya*) alone serves as the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) [of the object]. Thus, there arises the cognition: "The father, who possesses co-presence with the son, is distinct from the agent of the going," and so forth. In this view, the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with co-presence by way of the relation of being "characterized by" (*nirūpitatva*). As for the word *saha* within the compound *saputra*, however, it refers to the substratum (*dharmiparatva*). For this very reason, its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "father" is established. It is precisely for this reason that the rule prescribing the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the form *tena saha* (together with him) becomes meaningful.

Since there is no absence of the referent of another word (*anyapadārthatva*) in the case of "possessing concomitance" (*sāhityavat*), the rule *anekam* does not apply. However, by accepting that [the term *sahita*] has merely concomitance as its meaning, the authors of the Bhāṣya refute that rule. Alternatively, *sāhitya* means "togetherness" (*saha-artha*). And that is simply the state of being a word simultaneous with words such as "coming," which are presented by the words uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*), because it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the meaning of that [concomitance] is either the state of occupying the same location (*samānadeśatva*) or an indivisible attribute (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) co-extensive with it.

And its (the third-case suffix's) positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is with the coming and so forth, which are presented by the words *āgata* and the like. Furthermore, when there is a co-utterance with a verb, the relation that is perceived as belonging to the action in the primary [meaning] is precisely that [relation denoted by the third case]; namely, in the case of agency and so forth, it is the very same relation—such as the relation of owner and owned—that is perceived through the force of the connection with the meaning of "together" (*saha*), being determined by the respective actions perceived through the force of the connection with the meaning of "together" when there is a co-utterance with a substance and so forth. And that [relation] has its positive concomitance with the coming and so forth, which are the meanings of the verbal root and the like.

In expressions such as "sthūlaḥ putreṇa saha" (fat with his son), through a peculiarity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of the word *saha*—namely, simultaneity with the fatness—is construed with the fatness that constitutes a part of the referent of the word *sthūla*.

And thus, in cases such as *putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā* (the father has come with his son), *putreṇa saha piturgauḥ* (the cow belongs to the father together with the son), and *putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ* (he is stout together with his son), the understanding occurs respectively in this manner: "the locus of an arrival simultaneous with the arrival whose agent is the son," "the cow possessing ownership by the father simultaneous with ownership by the son," and "the one possessing stoutness simultaneous with the stoutness residing in the son. However, in expressions such as *saputraḥ* ("with a son"), there is no lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), because such actions and so forth are included within the meaning of the composite whole.

In the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), the word *saha* as a constituent of the compound has, by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning "one who possesses an arrival simultaneous with [the speaker's] own arrival. The word *putra* has the meaning "the state of being the agent of the son," and this relates non-differently (*abheda*) to the act of arriving. Alternatively, the son relates to the act of arriving (which is the meaning of *saha*) by way of being the qualificand of the agency residing in himself. In the expression "stout together with the son" (*putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ*), the word *putra* has the meaning "that which has the son as its locus," and the word *saha* has the meaning "one who possesses stoutness simultaneous with [the speaker's] own stoutness."

The relation (*saṃsarga*) is the non-difference (*abheda*) of the meaning of the prior member with the grossness inherent in the meaning of the subsequent member, and the son is construed as being the locus of that [grossness]. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. Out of necessity, it is accepted that the analytically expanded (*vyasta*) and the compound (*samāsa*) sentences produce cognitions of different forms; furthermore, in examples such as *saputra āgataḥ* ("he has come with his son") and *saputraḥ sthūlaḥ* ("he is stout with his son"), the relation of the suffix *ri* (the genitive case) is understood in two ways toward the father and so forth.

The elders have accepted the opponent's position with the intention that, in the case of "He falls together with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ patati*), the dual manifestation of that [action] is redundant; for, according to the method to be explained, in a sentence containing the negative particle (*nañ*), it is necessary that there be a manifestation of simultaneity with actions such as coming whose agents are the sons, precisely within the action presented by the verbal root (*prakṛtadhātu*). The sense is that where sesame seeds are sown after the sowing of beans in a field, there is a connection of the beans with the sesame seeds.

In this context, its meaning is the state of occupying the same location as the meanings of the words uttered in proximity [to it]. Therefore, it is like the previous case. Now, one might object that the purpose of the sūtra is already served by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). Nor should it be argued that the sūtra exists for the sake of overriding the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by connection with a *kṛt* suffix—as in the example "Devadatta’s going together with his son" (*putreṇa saha gamanaṃ devadattasya*)—because in that instance, what is intended to be grasped is precisely the agent and so forth, which are the meanings of the *kṛt* affix, even without the utterance of another word [in proximity].

Nor can it be argued that the instrumental case for the agent is not applicable because it is not prescribed by the *kta* suffix; for even in such cases, the agent is indeed denoted by the *kta*. If this is said, we reply: no, because according to the aforementioned reasoning, that [denotation] is necessary for meanings such as "he is fat along with his son. However, this must be understood: in the previous view, in expressions such as "he does not come together with his son," when used in conjunction with the negative particle (*nañ*), the meaning of the word "together" (i.e., simultaneity with the action of coming) must be admitted to connect only with the action and so forth expressed by the verb with which it is co-occurrent.

Otherwise, in a case where a father has not come with his son, although the father's accompaniment by the son is sublated, the absence of the act of coming performed by the father is not sublated; thus, while the usage "the father does not come with the son" would be justifiable, usages such as "the father did not come with the son" or "the father is not fat with the son" would be inexplicable. In those cases, one must maintain that there is a cognition of a difference in the agent of the act of coming and a difference in fatness residing in the father who possesses accompaniment by the son.

And that [cognition] is not possible there because of the understanding of the co-presence with the son and the aforementioned difference. However, if one accepts the connection (*anvaya*) of the simultaneity of the action expressed in proximity (the verb) with the son as its agent, then in the stated instance, the usage is sustained by the non-sublation of the father's meaning—namely, the difference between the agent of the departure simultaneous with the son’s departure, and the difference from one possessing stoutness simultaneous with the stoutness residing in the son—through the assistance of the presentation of the words uttered in proximity.

In this context, "non-predominance" (aprādhānya) consists in the absence of connection with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth; and that [absence], being a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) caused by the absence of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*), resides in the son and others. In such expressions as "the she-ass carries the burden together with ten sons," where there is a connection with the word *saha* expressing coexistence, there is also a qualified absence caused by the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—which is of a nature other than the action and so forth.

They say that even when joined with the word *saha* (together) in such cases, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs because there is no determining factor [to prefer one interpretation over another]; the meaning is: "even though sons of such a number exist. Their intention is this: the word *saha* ends in an elided locative case (*luptasaptamyanta*), and that is a locative absolute (*satisaptamī*). Furthermore, the word *api* (even/though) is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). Thus, the stated meaning is obtained. Others, however, maintain that the words "existing" (*vidyamāna*) and so forth are to be supplied; and they have established that in this way, the sense of concomitance (*sāhitya*) is maintained as being prompted by the action of "existing" (*vidyati*).

One might object: "In such passages as *'Sumitrā gave birth to Śatrughna of noble deeds together with Lakṣmaṇa'*, since there is an absence of simultaneity between the births of Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, it is impossible for the meaning of the word *saha* (together) to be the simultaneity of two actions. This is not so; for even in that case, simultaneity defined by a broad period of time (*sthūlakāla*) is possible. Likewise:
"One should not perform the *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) while the mother of the infant is pregnant..."

This should also be understood from such Smṛti passages as: "If one should perform [the rite] together with the bringing [of the boy], then no fault exists. In that context, the word "day" (dina) is included within the sense of "together" (saha). Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency regarding the sequence of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) and the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), as they lack a single point of time in the form of even a few *ghaṭikās* [if "day" were not included]. [Objection: If this is so, then in the case where someone arrives before the arrival of his son, the expression "this person has arrived, but not with his son" would be untenable; for even there, by taking a gross period of time such as a day, there is indeed a state of being simultaneous. [Response: This is not so.

In this regard, because time is subsumed within the meaning of the word *saha* precisely by virtue of its being a moment (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth, the details are explained elsewhere. In the examples "A jar [is produced] by means of a staff" (*daṇḍena ghaṭaḥ*), "He is stout from drinking milk" (*payaspānena sthūlaḥ*), and "Hari is seen through merit" (*puṇyena dṛṣṭo hariḥ*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is applied by the rule *hetu* (Pāṇini 2.3.23), and not by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.18) for the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because, although the staff possesses activity (*vyāpāra*), it lacks the status of an instrument since it does not produce the action; for only that which possesses activity and produces an action is an instrument. If it is argued that the status of producing an action remains intact because the verb "exists" (*asti*) must necessarily be supplied, we say no.

The phrase "due to the absence of being a producer of action" means "due to the absence of the intention to designate it as such a producer. Furthermore, since a jar continues to exist even in the absence of a staff, the staff is not its producer. Although a milk-nurse possesses the activity (*vyāpāra*) of bringing about the growth of a parrot, this consists in producing a quality (*guṇa*) such as stoutness, rather than producing an action (*kriyā*). Likewise, although merit (*puṇya*), which is of the nature of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of a supreme *apūrva*, produces the action of seeing, it lacks [any intermediate] activity.

If, however, the word *puṇyapada* refers to acts such as giving (*dāna*), then the instrumental case alone is used. Causality (*hetutva*) is a specific property residing in an operation that is distinct from the operation producing any one of substance, quality, or action, and which exists even in the absence of another operation. As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"The cause whose object is a substance and so forth is an instrument (*karaṇa*) when its action is restricted;
but when no operation is relied upon, the cause is intended as the efficient cause (*nimitta*)."

Thus, the elders have stated that because there is a distinction between being a cause (*hetutva*) and being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), two sūtras are necessary to ensure the proper comprehension [of these roles] in their respective forms. Others, however, argue that in the absence of an injunction for the third case (*tṛtīyā*) to denote the instrument, in examples such as *śaraiḥ śātitapatraḥ* ("one whose leaves were cut by arrows"), the compound would lack grammatical correctness due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). This is because the action of cutting (*śātana-kriyā*), which constitutes a part of the compound, would be dependent on its connection with the arrows as its cause (*hetu*). For the third case denoting the instrument is a "case-ending of an agent" (*kāraka-vibhakti*), and as such, it applies according to the rule: "Whatever is other than the word expressing the counter-correlative (*pratiyogipada*), and whatever is other than [the word expressing] the agent (*kāraka*)."
"In the etymological derivation [of the word *vṛtti*], its connection with a portion of the word *vṛtti* itself is not intended.

Thus, because the exclusion of *kāraka* (in the rule *kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā*) implies that the instrumental case-ending is a *kāraka*-case-ending, even though it depends upon the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not arise.

Thus, in the expression *dhanavatā ṛṇena baddhaḥ* ("bound by debt because of wealth"), the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) after the word *ṛṇa* is untenable; for that third case, which would otherwise be prescribed as a causal third case (*hetutṛtīyā*), is sublated by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) taught by the rule *akartary ṛṇe*. Therefore, the grammatical prescription of the third case in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*) is indeed necessary; they say that when this [prescription] exists, the third case is established when the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is intended. It should be understood that even in this view, the result is simply that those two [words] convey distinct modes of cognition (*vibhinnaprakārakabodhakatva*).

But surely, in a case where a single act of cooking is accomplished by Caitra using firewood and by Maitra by throwing in husks, there would be the following untenable usage: "Caitra does not cook with husks, but only with wood. This is because, since that act of cooking possesses the state of having Caitra as its agent, having husks as its cause, and having those [husks] as its instrument, the absence of the action qualified by all those attributes is what must be conveyed by the negative particle *nañ*, due to the sublation of the existence of such a qualified action. However, in the Nyāya system, this fault does not arise.

Since the state of having husks as the cause exists in the cooking already mentioned, even when there is a cognition of its absence [in the husks], the definition of "instrumentality" (karaṇatva)—which consists of an operation dependent on the operation of the agent expressed in grammatical coordination—and the state of possessing an operation in the agent exist in that agent; therefore, in order to avoid over-extension (atiprasaṅga), one must intend to exclude the husks. Consequently, the absence of having those [husks] as the instrument, which is uncontradicted in that cooking, [is established].

[Objection: Since [the definition] is possible through the awakening [of the cognition], one might argue that to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the agent—who is the substratum of an operation dependent on the operation of the agent in the form of an effort (*kṛti*)—one must include "difference from the agent" (*svabheda*) within the definition of "agent. [Reply: This is not so. Because the action of cooking (*pākakriyā*) is also differentiated by the difference of agents, there is no contradiction in the absence of having chaff as its instrument (*tuṣakaraṇakatva*) in a cooking performed by Caitra; for the absence of a present cooking performed by Caitra with chaff as its instrument remains unimpaired (*akṣata*) in that case, and thus there is no fault.

And thus, they say that in such cases as "Caitra cooks with wood" (*caitraḥ kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*) and "Maitra cooks with husks" (*maitraḥ tuṣaiḥ pacati*), a difference in sentences is indeed intended. In the case of "He dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*), the third case ending is used when there is an intention to express the cause (*hetu*)—namely, that study, though its fruit is dwelling, is the cause of dwelling by way of its own knowledge. The understanding is: "Dwelling has a cause non-different from study," or "The dwelling has a single agent [who is also the agent of study]. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtras beginning with *pratyayaḥ* and *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau*.

[Objection: But in this case, since Kāśī and the like are also causes by virtue of being the locus (*vāsa-hetu*), would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) of the third case ending when one intends to express them as causes? [Reply: No; for when the intention is to express them as the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), they are superseded by the seventh case ending, which is higher in the order of precedence. However, when that [locus-ness] is not intended, then—just as when one intends them to be instruments (*karaṇatva*)—the desired result follows as a matter of course (*iṣṭāpatti*). Others, however, maintain that in this sūtra the word "cause" (*hetu*) includes the "result" (*phala*) as well. For this very reason, the experience-based cognition that "residence generates the result consisting of study" is successfully accounted for. Nor should it be argued that there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that instance.

This is because metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not admitted in the case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). In that context, the fruit is the meaning of the case-ending by virtue of being the result. Therein, the meaning of the stem is related to it [the fruit] as its qualifier through non-difference, and that [fruit] is related to the act of residing (*vāsa*) through the relation of being a generator (*janakatā*). By this, it is understood that the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) is mediated solely by cognition. For this very reason, the experts (*tāntrika*) admit that words such as "smoke" (*dhūma*) possess metaphorical indication with respect to the cognition thereof. Thus, they say that the objection—"How can there be an instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) here?"—is refuted.

Even if one does not resort to the condition of being caused by the door of knowledge (*jñānadvārakanimittatva*), and even if the fruit (*phala*) is not included under the term "cause" (*hetu*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denoting causality or denoting the sense of cause is established from the word *adhyayana* by the rule "hetau" (Pāṇini 2.3.23). In the case of causality, the relation is that of being characterized (*nirūpitatva*) by the study with respect to that object; in the case of the residence, the relation is that of being the locus (*āśrayatva*). With respect to those objects which are of the nature of causes, the relation is that of having causality characterized by itself.

One should not suspect that the understanding [of the sentence] is such that its denotative function (*vācaka*) consists in the fact that "residence" (*vāsa*) is qualified by being the cause for the culmination of study (*adhyayananiṣṭhāhetutva*). This is because the required meaning is already obtained through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), which dictates that when a suffix denotes a relation such as causality, it must denote the substratum of that relation. For this very reason, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) prescribed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayostṛtīyā* never occurs after a word denoting an action (*kriyā*), but only after a word denoting an agent (*kartṛ*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*). Otherwise, in examples such as *devadattena bhuktam* ("it was eaten by Devadatta"), the third case would have to occur even after words like *bhukta* (past passive participle).

Nor should it be argued that, because of the Nirukta statement "names have action as their primary meaning" (*karmākhyātāntare 'sattvapradhānāni nāmāni*), the suffix-meaning is construed with the primary meaning precisely by virtue of the action being primary; and thus, since an agency defined by that [action] is impossible, there is no contingency for a third-case ending (*tṛtīyā*) to arise from that.

Even so, if one intends to express the meaning "Devadatta is the agent of eating," the genitive case would unavoidably apply by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, resulting in the undesirable usage *bhukteḥ Devadattaḥ* (Devadatta [is] of the eating), whereas the intended form is precisely *Devadattasya bhuktiḥ* (the eating of Devadatta). Nor can it be argued that the nominative will prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules, thereby avoiding the aforementioned consequence; for since the genitive is *antaraṅga* (more internal/essential), it can be stated that the nominative is actually an exception (*apavāda*) to it.

When there is an intention to express the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), the dative case also occurs in such expressions as *adhyayanāya vasati* ("he dwells for the purpose of studying"). In this context, the meaning of the dative is "being a benefactor" (*upakāratva*). Here, the relation of being "defined by" (*nirūpitatva*) is the semantic link between the base-meaning [of the verb] and [the dative]. Thus, the cognition is: "the dwelling is a benefactor defined by the act of studying. Alternatively, it may be accepted that the meaning of the dative is "the state of being the beneficiary and the benefactor. In this view, the base-meaning is construed with the beneficiary through the relation of difference (*bheda*). In the example *dāsyā saṃyacchate kāmukaḥ* ("the lustful man bestows [favors] upon the maidservant"), the third case ending is used in the sense of the dative.

This is because of the statement beginning with "in the practice of the unrefined" (*aśiṣṭavyavahāre*). Here, the verbal root [√*dā*] has the sense of enjoyment preceded by giving. The meaning of the third case is the capacity for being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*). The sentence-meaning is the enjoyment preceded by giving with a female slave as the recipient. By the rule *'dāṇaśca sā cet'* (Pāṇini 1.3.55), which prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the use of the third case in the sense of the fourth case is indicated; furthermore, by the word *cet* ("if"), its non-obligatory nature is indicated. Thus, the portion "in the practice of the unrefined" is established. It is clear from that very rule in the Bhāṣya that the "practice of the unrefined"—those who follow prohibited conduct—is of the nature of an action. May there be auspiciousness!

In the expression *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"), the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) applies according to the rule: "that person whom one intends through an action [is the recipient]. The meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the capacity (*śakti*) of being a recipient. The resulting cognition is: "lying down having the husband as its recipient. According to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, the action is considered a non-artificial object (*akṛtrima-karman*). It is an object because it is desired by the agent of that action, being defined by the initiating activity (*ārambhakriyā*) produced by the acts of seeing, requesting, and resolving. Thus, they say that the designation *saṃpradāna* would result from the very rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti* ("whom one intends through an object"). [The verse states: "Seeing [leads to] requesting; immediately after that, resolving..."
Likewise, resolve serves as the means for undertaking an action.
"That which is the action in the former [stage] is itself considered the means (sādhana) in the latter.

Here, "vision" (saṃdarśana) is the resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the fruit; it is either knowledge or desire. That [vision] is the cause for the prayer, which consists of the means to the fruit. "Determination" (vyavasāya) is the ascertainment that a specific operation, such as cooking, is the means to a particular fruit. In this context, the immediately preceding prayer is the cause, because such a determination arises when there is desire. And determination is the cause for the undertaking—that is, for the activity in this [stage]. The primary action being brought about by that [determination] becomes the object (karman). "In the former"—that is, at the prior time.

"In the other"—that is, in that which occurs at a subsequent time. According to this view, the understanding is that "lying down" consists of the action of undertaking the act of giving pleasure (*rati*). They say that because there is no such designation [of the object], there is no over-extension (as there would be) in cases such as "he makes a pot. In the expression "He sacrifices to Rudra with an animal" (*paśunā rudraṃ yajate*), the power of being an instrument (*karaṇatva-śakti*) resides in the desire for the fruit, while the power of being the object (*karmatva-śakti*) resides in the intended recipient. This is due to the rule: "The object receives the designation of instrument, and the recipient receives the designation of object. The literal meaning is: "A sacrifice having an animal as its instrument and Rudra as its object."

The meaning [of the sentence] is: "An operation conducive to the cessation of the ownership residing in the animal, having Rudra as its intended object. This very [meaning] is considered the literal (śābda) meaning according to the view of others; it should be understood in the same way in other cases as well. In the expression *haraye rocate bhaktiḥ* ("Devotion is pleasing to Hari"), the meaning of the root *ruc* is "an operation coreferential with that [devotion], which is conducive to pleasure (*prīti*). Pleasure (*prīti*) is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And that [pleasure] consists either of a cognition whose content is an object and whose qualifier is "belonging to me" (*madīyatva*), or of a desire in the form "May this [object] be one that experiences the desired [state]."

Even though the pleasure residing in Hari is eternal, because its object is non-eternal, the objective determination (*viṣayatā*) that delimits the result is non-eternal; thus, by superimposing the state of being produced upon the pleasure through the relation [of inherence], its being conducive (*anukūlatva*) is established. In the view of those who do not accept such superimposition, however, the referent of the word "pleasure" is simply knowledge and so forth qualified by that result through the relation of determinative-ness (*nirūpakatā*). And in this way, just as in the expression "the crested one (the peacock) is destroyed," the state of being a determiner of conduciveness is established by taking the result of the qualifier.

Precisely because the state of being an object (*viṣayatā*) is the delimiting factor of the result, the root *ruc* is not transitive. In the expression *prīyamāṇaḥ*, the suffix *śānac* is applied to the present participle (*laṭ*) of the root *prīñ* in the sense of "to satisfy" (*tarpaṇa*), and not to the root *prīṅ* meaning "to love" (*prīti*) belonging to the *divādi* class; for that [latter] root is intransitive. For this very reason, one says, "May the Lord Īśa be pleased. This being the case, the meaning of the rule must be accepted as follows: the designation [of "object"] applies to the substratum of the operation which constitutes the meaning of the root *prī*.

It should not be argued that even if [the definition] were thus, since Hari and others possess the state of being the locus of an activity conducive to that [pleasure] which is co-referential with pleasure (*prīti*), the designation would be established in those cases; and furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to things that are not loci of such activity. This is because it would contradict all the treatises to claim that the designation applies to the object of the root *prī* (to please), and because, by virtue of its association with the term "one who is being made to know" (*jñīpsyamāna*), the suffix *śānac* is appropriately used only for the object. Moreover, the relation that delimits the result of the root *prī* is inherence (*samavāya*).

For this very reason, constructions such as *hariṃ prīṇayati* ("he pleases Hari") are not established [by that rule]. By the rule *rucyarthānām-*, the status of recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) belongs to the substratum of pleasure (*prīti*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Since the root *prī* does not have the meaning of "liking" (*ruci*), the status of recipient does not apply in its connection [with the object]. For this same reason, the mention of *prīyamāṇa* (in the rule) is justified. In the absence of this rule, the genitive case would apply to words such as *hari*; therefore, the dative serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive. Others, however, maintain that the root *ruc* has the same meaning as the root *prī*.

And thus, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is intended as an exception to the general notion of "action" (*karma*). They argue that because of the specific mention of "one who is pleased" (*prīyamāṇa*), this designation does not apply to the locus of pleasure (*prīti*) denoted by the verbal root *prī*. According to that view, there is an unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), since one must rely on the specific mention [of *prīyamāṇa*] just to exclude the application of the designation when it is in conjunction with the root *prī*. Furthermore, the meaning of the verb *abhilaṣyate* is an activity conducive to pleasure that is not co-locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) with the pleasure itself; the relation that delimits the result is "objectness" (*viṣayatā*).

For this very reason, since *sa* (he) is not the object of the desire (*rucyartha*), Hari does not have the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) in the expression "he desires devotion to Hari" (*haribhaktim abhilaṣati*). They say that since Devadatta and others—who are the substrata of the fruit in the form of happiness—would otherwise have attained the designation of "object" (*karman*), this [designation of recipient] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

In this view as well, the aforementioned prolixity remains. Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the root *ruc* is pleasure consisting of desire (*abhilāṣātmaka-prīti*), while the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is agency (*kartṛtva*) in the form of being an object; thus, the dative case is a substitute for the genitive by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and the resulting cognition from the sentence "The quarrel is pleasing to Nārada" (*nāradāya rocate kalahaḥ*) is: "The quarrel possesses the state of being the object of the liking related to Nārada. Still others, the logicians (*tārkika*s), [hold a different view].

They say that because quarreling and the like are the substrata of the verbal activity—which consists in being the generator of the meaning of the root under discussion (namely, the generation of pleasure)—they possess "agency" (*kartṛtā*), which is to say, "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*). This [substratum-ness] is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), while the relation consisting in "being dependent upon" (*āśritatva*) is the meaning of the dative case. Even according to this view, the dative serves as an exception to the genitive; however, since the root *prī* does not have this meaning, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise.

In the sentence "The gopī, out of love, praises, conceals, stands [in defiance], or curses Kṛṣṇa," the person being informed receives the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) by the rule "ślāghahnuṅsthāśapām-. By the word *jñīpsyamāna* ("the one being informed"), there is a choice between taking either the object of the causative (*ṇyanta*) or the object of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). Because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is predominant, its object is taken; however, due to the natural consistency of the sense, the object of the base meaning is also accepted.

Otherwise, he would have simply said "being made known" (*jñāpyamāna*). Since the object of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely Kṛṣṇa—is also the locus of the result produced by the activity that is the object of the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), it follows as an object of the desiderative form; thus, the production of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) there is not contradictory, and such a designation is justified. In the case of "praising" (*ślāghā*) and so forth, the purpose is to make [the other] understand [one's own state] preceded by affection through praise. For example: "By means of praise, he makes Kṛṣṇa understand his own devotion. Similarly, in the case of "concealing" (*hnuti*) and so forth, the meaning is "he makes that Kṛṣṇa understand [his state]. "Concealing" (*hnuti*) consists in placing [the object] in a location where it is capable of being unseen by others.

This designation [of the object] is one that sets aside the conventional notion of an action; however, the fact that it pertains to the domain of affliction (vādhi) and follows the self is understood from the context and other factors. The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "An activity preceded by praise and so forth, caused by love (*smara*), conducive to a cognition whose object is affection for the self, and directed toward Kṛṣṇa as its recipient. If the object is taken as the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), the sense is: "By means of praise and so forth, she makes Kṛṣṇa aware of her own circle of friends."

In the expression *devadattāya śataṃ dhārayati* ("He owes a hundred to Devadatta"), the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) by the rule *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ*. The suffix *-tama* has the sense of "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*). The suffix *ām* does not apply because the excellence pertains to the substance (*dravya*). The term *uttamarṇa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has an excellent debt. Precisely for this reason, by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the past participle ending is placed at the end of the compound. A creditor is the owner of wealth. The root *dhṛ* (to stay) belongs to the *divādi* class; from it, with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the meaning of the root *dhārayati* is "an operation conducive to the state of staying [of the debt]."

The subsistence of a hundred [coins] in the debtor is by virtue of a specific connection with the bad karma (*duradṛṣṭa*) produced from the non-payment of his own debt. For this very reason, even when there is no contact or other relation between Caitra and the debtor until the debt is cleared, and even in the absence of contact, the usage "Caitra owes a hundred" is justified; likewise is the usage "Caitra owes a hundred to Devadatta. Indeed, the usage "he causes to cook" does not occur during a state in which the activity of the one being caused to act is absent.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "hetumati ca. The operation conducive to that [debt] consists either of the non-clearance of the debt or the acceptance of wealth given by another after promising to give one's own wealth. Nor should it be argued that at the time subsequent to the act of acceptance, the term "he prevents" (*vārayati*) would not apply because the act of acceptance no longer exists; for in a subtle form, through its connection with a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by itself, that act persists until the point of clearance.

Alternatively, it is because even though that [act of lending] has perished, there is an intention to express its "presentness" in the form of an uninterrupted continuity of activity. Here, although the creditor is the prompter of the act of holding [the debt] by means of the act of giving, nevertheless, since no verbal root (*dhātu*) expressing the action is heard, the designations of *hetu* (cause) and so forth do not apply; thus, the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would result. It should be understood that whenever a specific form is not intended to be expressed, but rather the mere fact of being the cause of an action is intended, the status of being a "residual" (*śeṣa*) applies. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "In cases such as those involving the roots meaning 'to please' (*ruc*), whether the factor is designated as an object (*karman*) on account of being a cause, or as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the scripture prescribes for it the technical name 'recipient' (*saṃpradāna*)."

Debt (*ṛṇa*) is the taking of another’s property given by them, preceded by an agreement to accept such like-substance; or it is a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) residing in the debtor produced by that act. The designation "debt" applied to the object being taken is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), based on its being the cause [of the debt]. For this very reason, even when one consumes food and the like that has been received, the expression "I have a debt" is logically consistent. If it is argued that the primary sense of "debt" should belong to such an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) rather than to the act of taking itself, we say no.
