By the rule *ṛṇam ādhamarṇye*, that [term *ṛṇa*] is a nipātana (irregular formation) specifically for a state such as existence residing in a debtor; therefore, it is appropriate that its denotative power (*śakti*) resides only there. Furthermore, in the Amarakośa it is stated: "Trade is *satyānṛta* (truth-and-falsehood), while *ṛṇa* is *paryudañcana* (recovery/repayment)."

If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) is in no way [an object] for Him, and since you have such a poor vision regarding that matter, how can there be an illustration of Him "bestowing liberation upon His devotee"? To this they reply: because it must necessarily be given, even in that case there is the conventional usage of the term "debt. Thus, the activity conducive to the maintenance of liberation—consisting of such things as being the object of service directed toward Hari—is what constitutes the debt. Consequently, by virtue of being the locus of the benefit consisting of service, the devotee becomes the subject of the conventional designation "creditor" (*uttamarṇa*).

The author of the *Vyutpattivāda*, however, maintains that the meaning of the root *dhṛ* (to owe) is a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) produced by the taking of property given by another, preceded by the acceptance of the giving of another substance. The agency associated with the act of giving, which is a constituent of that [action], is the meaning of the dative case. Nor should it be argued that only the non-clearance of a debt produces demerit (*duradṛṣṭa*), since that very act is enumerated among the minor sins (*upapātaka*).

Although the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) is the cause of that [non-clearance], it is counted among the minor sins (*upapātaka*) with the intention of showing that the failure to clear the debt leads to the production of results in the form of hell, thereby making its clearance the means of destroying that [debt]. They explain at length that it is more appropriate to postulate the non-payment of debt itself as the cause for the production of bad karma (*duradṛṣṭa*), rather than the failure to clear a debt already incurred, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). In the expression "he longs for flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*), the root *spṛh* denotes mere desire.

By the word *īpsita* ("desired"), there is an understanding [of the object] as the locus of the result produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root; however, this does not imply that the result itself is the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the dative case (*caturthī*) triggered by this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) serves as an exception to the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The resulting cognition is "the desire whose recipient (*saṃpradānika*) is the flower"; however, its actual sense (*ārtha*) is "having the flower as its object. Furthermore, this verbal root expresses either a desire delimited by a result, or it expresses an operation such as a mental contact (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*) conducive to desire.

The fruit of desire (*icchā*) is either the objectness (*viṣayatā*) or the inclination (*pravṛtti*). When that [desire] is connected [to an object], if there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) to express it as the locus of the fruit intended by that [desire], then—by virtue of its higher status—the designation "object" (*karman*) applies, and consequently the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and so forth follow; this is explained in detail elsewhere. *Haraye krudhyati*, *druhyati*, *īrṣyati*, or *asūyati*. "Anger" (*krodha*) is a particular state of mind produced by an activity conducive to killing and the like; such is the meaning of the root *krudh*. Since the meaning of the root *duh* is specified as "the desire to harm" (*jighāṃsā*), "malice" (*droha*) is the meaning of *duh*.

And that [root] is a specific modification of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) which produces a specific action that generates suffering. Because their objects are subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), these two roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*). When used with a single [object], the genitive case would have been required; however, for the object related as the locus of the anger—which is the basis of the meaning of this verbal root—the designation "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is prescribed by the rule *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānām*. Thus, the understanding is: "anger directed toward Hari as its recipient," or "malice directed toward Hari."

The meaning of *īrṣyā* (envy) is a specific mental state (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) that produces an activity conducive to attributing qualities contrary to excellence. The meaning of *asūyā* (malice) is a specific mental state conducive to attributing defects—such as being fabricated by hypocrisy—to objects that possess virtues like purity and proper conduct. These [emotions] are rooted in anger (*kopa*), which is a specific mental state. Since it is precisely anger in its fully developed form that constitutes the referent of the term *krodha* (wrath), even in those cases, the status of being rooted in anger remains without exception.

In connection with verbal roots having meanings such as envy (*asūyā*), the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) applies to the substratum of the result of the respective root-meaning, as qualified by being the object of the underlying anger (*kopa*). By the phrase "the anger directed toward whom," only the object of that anger is obtained; nevertheless, for the sake of conforming to actual usage, the qualification "the substratum of such a result" has been included. The purpose of this qualification, however, is to exclude the wife from being designated as the *saṃpradāna* in the sentence "he envies his wife" (*bhāryām īrṣyati*).

In this context, there is no anger toward the wife; rather, it is the inability to endure her being seen by others. The meaning is that, in the case of having only one wife, there is no locus for the result consisting of the attribution of the root-meaning of *īrṣy* (envy). The cognition [of envy] is a particular mental state conducive to the attribution of qualities contrary to the excellence of the recipient, Hari. However, in the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), anger (*krodha*) is a specific form of hatred or a specific kind of cognition; malice (*droha*) is the desire for harm, which is to say, the desire for the welfare of an enemy. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is intolerance, consisting of hatred directed toward the excellence of another.

Envy (*asūyā*) is a specific activity consisting of the revelation of faults in one who possesses virtues. It should be understood that [qualities such as] being the object of envy and so forth constitute the meaning of the dative case. Because there is an absence of being an object of desire due to Hari’s anger and malice, the designation [of the recipient] by the rule "the one toward whom [the agent] acts through an action" (*kriyayā yam*) is not established. In examples such as *mitrāya druhyati pratāpo’pi* ("Even Pratāpa bears malice toward his friend"), one should understand it as a metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) of sentience. They say that forms such as *kupyati kasmaicit* ("he is angry with someone") are simply ungrammatical, or that the status of the recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) might apply here according to the rule "the one toward whom [the agent] intends through an action" (*kriyayā yam abhipraiti*).

He deliberates or examines regarding Kṛṣṇa (*kṛṣṇāya rādhyati īkṣate vā*). Here, the roots *rādh* and *īkṣ* have the sense of deliberating upon or examining the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the object of inquiry. Because [Kṛṣṇa] is related to that object of inquiry which is the purpose of the action, he receives the status of a *saṃpradāna* (recipient) according to the rule: "The one connected with the object intended for that [action] is the *saṃpradāna*. Thus, the dative case is used in the sense of "deliberation regarding auspiciousness and inauspiciousness having Kṛṣṇa as its recipient. Therefore, in the expression *tasmā idam* ("this is for him"), the meaning of the case ending is either the state of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*)—derived from the etymology "the state of being for the sake of that"—or the nature of being a benefactor and a beneficiary (*upakārakatva* or *upakāryopakārakabhāva*).

In the first case, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is related to the meaning of the suffix (*vibhakti*) as that which is delimited (*nirūpitatva*); and its relation to the wood (*dāru*) is the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatva*). In the latter case, the meaning of the base is the property of being located (*ādheyatva*), and its relation to the state of being assisted (*upakāryatva*) is the relation [of inherence]. Alternatively, the meaning of the suffix is the state of being assisted; in that case, the relation of the meaning of the base is identity (*abheda*), and it connects by way of the relation of assistance as determined by the state of being assisted residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhopakāryatānirūpitopakārasambandha*). Expressions such as "merit for heaven" (*svargāya puṇyam*) are indeed intended [in this sense]. For this very reason, [one says] "sin for hell" (*pāpaṃ narakāya*).

This accounts for the usage in Smṛti and other texts such as *bhavati*. In expressions like *yāgāya yāti* ("he goes for the sake of sacrifice"), since the sense of being for the purpose of something (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the suffix *dhañ* (which has the meaning of the infinitive suffix *tum*), this [usage] would not be established by the present rule; thus, the sūtra *tumarthācca* is commenced. In cases such as *brāhmaṇāya dadhi* ("curds for the Brahmin"), the instrumental case is established either through the indirect benefit to the Brahmin provided by the curds—which assist in the act of eating performed by the Brahmin—or through the metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) of "being beneficial to the Brahmin" onto that which is actually beneficial to the meal.

In expressions such as *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), because the relationship residing in the cause is understood through the dative case suffix itself occurring after a word denoting the effect (*kārya*), the third case does not apply to words like *dāru*, even though causality (*hetutva*) is present. *Bhaktir jñānāya kalpate* ("Devotion conduces to knowledge"). Here, the dative case is applied by the rule *klṛpi saṃpadyamāne ca*. The meaning of that rule is that the dative case is used after a word signifying that which is being produced (*saṃpadyamāna*) when it is in construction with a verbal root having the sense of *klṛp*.

And that [understanding] is the cognition that "the production [of the self] has as its agent non-differentiated knowledge through devotion"; in the phrase "it transforms into the nature of knowledge," the word *ātman* refers to the attributes residing in knowledge. Thus, since it does not denote a modification (*vikṛti*), the fourth case is not used there; rather, the third case is used because it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*. Its meaning is "distinction" (*vaijñiṣṭhya*); the understanding is that the attainment of another state characterized by the nature of knowledge has devotion as its agent. The attainment of another state is the meaning of the verbal root.

When the distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) is intended, the fourth case (*caturthī*) does not apply because the relationship of material cause and modification is not perceived; rather, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) applies by virtue of the status of "ablative" according to the rule *janikartuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30). Regarding the expression *bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpyate*, Kaiyaṭa clearly states in the *Mañjūṣākṛt* that, due to its proximity to the word *jñāna*, the first case (*prathamā*) alone is used—both because it is more powerful than the fourth case required for the sense of "purpose" (*tādṛrthya*) and because of the rule *upapadavibhakteḥ kārakavibhaktirbalīyasī* (the case ending denoting a kāraka is stronger than a case ending based on a secondary word).

Others, however, hold that when a distinction is intended, the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) is used after a word denoting a modification (*vikṛti*). The meaning of "is fashioned" (*kalpate*) is "undergoes transformation" (*pariṇamate*). Although the fourth case-ending expressing purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*) would suffice when a distinction is intended, this usage is nevertheless necessary to ensure the proper comprehension of the relationship as a connection (*saṃbandha*). Otherwise, if such a distinction were intended, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would occur. But when non-distinction is intended, the first case-ending (*prathamā*) alone applies because it is of higher priority, as in: "Devotion is knowledge; it is fashioned."

In a sentence containing the fourth case (caturthī), the understanding is that there is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) identical to knowledge, having devotion as its agent. In one containing the first case (*prathamā*), however, the understanding is that there is an origination (*utpatti*) having knowledge non-different from devotion as its agent. They say that when the status of an ablative (*apādānatva*) is intended, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used, as in *phalebhyo yāti* ("he goes for the sake of fruits"). Here, the fourth case is applied by the rule *kriyārthopapadasya-* ("of that which has a word expressing a purpose as its adjunct"). The meaning of this is: the fourth case is used for the object of a verbal form ending in *tumun* etc., provided that it expresses a "resident" (*sthānin*)—that is, something understood as having a word expressing a purpose as its adjunct; specifically, it is used for the object of the action presented by the verbal form ending in *tumun* etc. (i.e., the action for the sake of which one acts).

Just as in examples such as *brahmaṇāya dadhi* ("curd for the Brahmin"), the dative case occurs in the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthye*) because the curd assists the Brahmin by way of assisting his meal, so too the same dative would apply to the assistance toward the fruit by way of assisting the act of fetching the fruit. Nevertheless, this sūtra is necessary to ensure the grammatical correctness of the dative in a cognition where the fruit is the object of the act of fetching—specifically, in the understanding that "the vehicle has the fetching of the fruit as its result" (*phalakarmakāharaṇaphalakaṃ yānam*), wherein the fruit is the object (*karman*) characterized as the mode (*prakāra*). This is explained in detail elsewhere.

In such instances as "The tawny lightning [forebodes] wind" (*vātāya kapilā vidyut*) and "The very red [lightning forebodes] heat" (*ātapāyātilohinī*), the dative case signifies the relationship between the indicator (*jñāpaka*) and the indicated (*jñāpya*). This is because of the rule stating "and when [something] is indicated by a portent" (*utpātena jñāpite ca*). The meaning of that rule is that the dative occurs when it expresses an object indicated by a portent (*utpāta*), which is a modification of the elements (*bhūtavikāra*) that signals the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of living beings. The resulting cognition is: "The tawny lightning is the indicator of wind."

In the expressions ‘brahmaṇāya hitam’ (beneficial for Brahmins) and ‘brahmaṇāya sukham’ (pleasure for Brahmins), the dative case is employed in connection with the words *hita* and *sukha* by virtue of the rule prescribing compound formation: ‘caturthī tadarthārtha-’ (Pāṇini 2.1.36). Furthermore, the specific mention of the dative in the rule ‘tasmai hitam’ (Pāṇini 5.1.5) should be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this usage]. The meaning of the word *hita* is "that which is a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhana*). The meaning of the dative case consists in the state of being the locus (*ādhayatva*) of the desire that is a constituent part of that [means], or rather, it is a mediated relation (*paraparā-sambandha*) consisting of the desire that is conjoined with the means to the desired.

For this very reason, it is consistent that one might say "this is beneficial for a Brahmin" with the intention of [offering] another's medicine and so forth; such is the general direction. *Namaḥ* (salutation) to Hari. Here, the dative case is used by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-*. The meaning of the word *namaḥ*, as listed among the group beginning with *svar*, is an activity conducive to the communication of the cognition of being inferior. This is because, when the word *namaḥ* is employed, there is the empirical fact of its making known the cognition of inferiority residing in oneself.

However, when such [inferiority] is not directly experienced, the meaning of that word should be understood as an activity conducive to the cognition of inferiority. For this very reason, it was stated exactly thus in the *Bṛhacchabdenduśekhara*: "Inferiority is perceived as residing solely in the independent speaker and as qualifying the object of salutation; the activity, too, is perceived as residing only in the speaker, due to the inherent nature of the power of words, since the word *namaḥ* uttered by one person does not convey the salutation of another."

The operation (*vyāpāra*) consists of the conjunction of the hand with the head and so forth, as well as the employment of a sentence containing the word *namaḥ*. The meaning of the dative case is "being the intended object" (*uddeśyatva*). The resulting cognition is: "such an operation has Viṣṇu as its intended object. [As in: "This offering is for Śiva."

In expressions such as *namaḥ* (salutation), the meaning of the word *namaḥ* is "renunciation" (*tyāga*). Renunciation is an operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of a desire conducive to the cessation of one's own ownership. The meaning of the dative case is "status as the intended object" (*uddeśyatva*), which consists in being the object of a desire that has [the recipient] as the locus of ownership. Thus, the cognition is: "The offering (*arghya*) is the object of renunciation directed toward Śiva. If it is thought that the very desire whose object is the cessation of one's own ownership also takes the other's ownership as its object, then in that case, "being directed toward that [recipient]" should be understood as the state of being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the status of being the intended object in the manner described above.

If, however, it is accepted that the very desire which produces the act of giving apprehends that [object], then it should be understood that the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*), whose nature is *uddeśyatā* (the state of being intended), appears as a relation characterized either by indirect (*paraṃparayā*) determinacy (*nirūpakatva*) or by being the object of a desire dependent upon a desire that determines itself.

Furthermore, renunciation (*tyāga*) is understood as being specifically qualified by having its object indicated by the Veda and by being performed by oneself, due to the very nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). This is because the utterance of the word *namaḥ* by one person does not result in the perception of a renunciation associated with another. By the phrase "indicated by the Veda" and so forth, it is excluded that the word *namaḥ* is employed in the case of a renunciation whose object is not so indicated—such as the casual, non-devotional renunciation of food by one’s own whim—and also in the case of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who performs such an utterance after first superimposing ownership upon the sacrificer’s property.

Even though the property-ownership (*svatva*) of Śiva and others is sublated when their substance is [taken], there is no inconsistency in the injunction "one should not take the property of Śiva" (*śivasvaṃ na gṛhṇīyāt*), because its meaning is that it has been relinquished for the sake of a specific recipient. In the expression "he pays homage to the gods" (*namaskaroti devān*), the verbal root *kṛ* alone conveys the aforementioned sense; the word *namaḥ* is a particle (*nipāta*) belonging to the *ūrjādi* group, serving as an indicator (*dyotaka*) of that sense. According to the maxim "the case-ending of the subordinate term [prevails]," the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The relation that constitutes the fruit (phala), which is of the nature of inherence (samavāya) and is qualified by its subsisting in that [object] by virtue of which inferiority is understood, is the delimiting relation of the fruit (phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha). Therefore, they say that by this relation, agency (karmatva) belongs only to the gods, who are the substrata of the fruit consisting of such cognition, and not to a neutral bystander who is the substratum of the said cognition through mere pure inherence. It should be understood that the dative case here is obtained simply by the connection with the meaning expressed by the word *namaḥ*.

In the expression *namaskurmo nṛsiṃhāya* ("we pay homage to Nṛsiṃha"), the dative case is understood according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.14) because of the cognition that [the act] is for the purpose of propitiating Nṛsiṃha; this is clear from the *Kaumudī* and other works. Here, if the word *namaḥ* is denotative (*vācaka*), the dative is applied by the rule *namaḥsvasti* (Pāṇini 2.3.16). Others maintain that even when it is indicative (*dyotaka*), the dative sets aside the genitive—though the status of the object is not intended to be expressed—and thus the dative is used. In the phrase *na tvāṃ tṛṇāya manye* ("I do not consider you as a blade of grass"), the dative is used in the sense of the object by the rule *manyakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.17).

In this context, the word *anādara* (disrespect) does not merely indicate the absence of respect; rather, because the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses the opposite, it signifies that which is contrary to respect, just as *adharma* (unrighteousness) is the opposite of *dharma*. Since the rule for the fourth case (*caturthī*) following the word *anādare* prescribes it only when the word denotes an object that indicates disrespect, the fourth case is not applied here to the pronoun *yuṣmad*. Furthermore, although one could have simply said "in contempt" (*kutsite*), the inclusion of the term *anādara* is intended to make known that this particular case-ending is employed only when one wishes to express an intensity of disrespect.

It is precisely for this purpose that the negative particle *nañ* is employed in the example; for by conveying the understanding "I do not consider it even equal to a blade of grass," it expresses the excellence [of the other]. For this very reason, the authors of the commentaries have declared the ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) of such usages as "even the joy of the Raghus, having considered him as a blade of grass" (*tṛṇāya matvā raghunandano’pi*). However, if one intends to express the form ending in the suffix *śyan* (i.e., *manye*), then its ungrammaticality is not tenable, because the dative case would not apply in connection with a verbal root ending in a *viṅ* suffix or similar affixes. The mention of the suffix *śyan*, moreover, is intended to exclude roots belonging to the *tanādi* class.

Therefore, in the expression "he does not think of you," it is quite clear that the fourth case (*caturthī*) is not used; this is the general direction [of the argument]. "May there be well-being for the Brahmins. The word *svasti* means either "welfare" or "auspiciousness," and the relationship [between the two] is the meaning of the fourth case; enough of this elaboration. May there be auspiciousness!

In the sentence "Devadatta is separated from the caravan" (*sārthād dhīyate devadattaḥ*), the caravan (*sārtha*) functions as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) because it serves as the limit for the division [of space] implied by the verbal root. Now, an objection might be raised: since the caravan is the locus of the activity (*vyāpāra*) expressed by the verbal root, it should—by virtue of being the higher-ranking factor—be designated as the agent (*kartṛ*). However, if it were not the locus of that activity, then Devadatta, being the locus of it, would be the agent; and if he were the agent, there would be the undesirable consequence that he could not be denoted by the accusative case-ending (*lādi*) and so forth.

If it is argued that since the caravan (*sārtha*) becomes the object (*karman*), there would be the over-extension (*prāpti*) of the rule "the caravan is abandoned by Devadatta" (*devadattena sārtho hīyate*), the following is said in response: There is no fault, because even though agency (*kartṛtva*) would otherwise be obtained, the status of being the point of departure (*apādānatva*) is made known by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*. Otherwise, since the caravan would lack the status of being the point of departure, the suffix *tas* (forming the word *jahatas*) would not apply; what then would be the purpose of the prohibition "not [in the case of] *hīya*" (*ahīya*)? That indicated status of being the point of departure applies specifically to the domain of the verb root *jahāti* when followed by an object-case suffix (*karmapratyaya*), as indicated by the mention of *hīya*.

Therefore, in examples such as *devadattaḥ sārtham jahāti* ("Devadatta abandons the caravan"), [the designation of object] does not apply. In the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* ("that which is most desired by the agent"), the word *kartṛ* (agent) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇika*) to mean "the locus of the primary operation expressed by the verbal root"; thus, Devadatta's status as the object (*karman*) is established. This is also the intended sense of Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule for the technical term *saṃpradāna*. In the case of *adharmāj jugupsate* ("he feels disgust toward unrighteousness"), the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) is established by the rule *jugupsā-virāma-pāpa-varaṇārthānām bhayahetuḥ*.

The meaning of that [Vārttika] is this: if disgust (*jugupsā*) and the like are intended as the object (*viṣaya*), then that is the *apādāna*. Disgust, which consists in the cognition of something as a means to an undesirable end, is the meaning of the root *jugupsati*. The sense of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "being the object" (*viṣayatva*) and so forth, or it is the power of being an *apādāna*. By accepting that the verbal root has a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the cessation preceded by such disgust, the status of *apādāna* is established by the rule itself, "That which is fixed when there is separation" (*dhruvamapāye*). It is the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya that for this very reason, this Vārttika and the subsequent rules need not have been composed.

The meaning of *viramati* (he abstains) is an activity conducive to the absence of contact with action (*kṛti-saṃsarga*). Here, "conduciveness" is understood in the sense of both *yoga* (acquisition) and *kṣema* (preservation). Furthermore, this conducive activity consists precisely in indifference (*upekṣā*) toward the object that is dharma. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "This person who possesses an atheist's mindset perceives: 'There is such a thing as dharma in the Veda; I shall not perform it. Having reached [that conclusion] through his intellect, he then desists."

By this it is understood that even for one who has never at any time performed [the action], that [non-performance] is intended as the *prayoga* (preparatory effort). By this, the meaning of *virati* (cessation) is established as the state of being non-causal immediately after the causal action. And that is the destruction of an effort (*kṛti*) which is co-located with the duty (*kṛtya*) and delimited by the period of life. In both cases, the effort has the same object. Therefore, since it is co-located with efforts such as eating, there is no impossibility regarding the general category of the destruction of effort delimited by the period of life.

Because the qualification "being delimited by the period of life" is introduced [in the definition] regarding destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), the expression "he desists from dharma" (*dharmād viramate*) does not occur by taking into account the destruction of an action occurring at the time of death or the like. Life must be understood as being related to the agent himself; therefore, since the state of being delimited by the period of another's life exists in the destruction of Caitra’s own action occurring at the time of his death, that fault does not remain.

In order to prevent the undesirable consequence that one would cease from dharma even when not performing it during the time of a *ghaṭikā* (twenty-four minutes) or similar duration—despite having practiced dharma in the preceding and succeeding times—the qualification "co-located with the effort" (*kṛtisamānādhikaraṇatva*) is applied to the destruction of the effort (*kṛtidhvaṃsa*). This [qualification] consists in being different from that which is co-located with the effort by way of being delimited by a body belonging to the same class as the body that delimits the effort itself; this is the intended meaning regarding the object of dharma.

In order to avoid the impossibility of such usage—since even the destruction of an action would reside in the same locus as an action delimited by a future body—the qualification "residing in the same locus as an action delimited by a body belonging to the same class as the body that delimits itself" is added.

If one were to include "being delimited by such a body" [in the definition], then because bodies differ according to their various states, even when a person performs a religious duty (*dharma*) while delimited by a youthful body, the destruction of an effort delimited by an infant body would not be delimited by the very body that delimits that effort. Consequently, since it would not be non-co-referential with the effort within its own delimiter, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the expression "he desists from the duty" being applicable [even though he has not actually desisted]. Therefore, "being delimited by a body of that same class" is included [in the definition].

Homogeneity (*sājātya*) is determined solely by the nature of Caitra-hood and so forth as presented by words such as "Caitra," and not by earth-hood, human-hood, and so forth; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not persist on the grounds that the body of another life is also homogeneous with it in terms of earth-hood or human-hood. In that case, since the present body is not the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for such an effort (*kṛti*), it cannot be the delimiting factor for its co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus, the stated defect does not arise. If it is objected that the defect remains just as before because of the co-location of the effort delimited by the former body, we say no.

This [objection] is also refuted by including "being delimited by the time delimited by its own restrictor" (*svāvacchedakakālāvacchinnatva*) within the definition of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For if one never practiced the Dharma at any time, such a usage [of the term "Dhārmika"] would not result [as intended]. [Objection: But surely that usage is not intended there; for such a usage occurs only when all people have practiced the Dharma and subsequently fail to do so. Furthermore, the aforementioned Bhāṣya can also be understood as referring to one who previously practiced the Dharma but later became an atheist (*nāstika*). Therefore, [the objection does not hold]. [Reply: No, because there is no evidence (*māna*) for such a restriction. Even one who has turned away from the Dharma...

Furthermore, [this is so] because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (anāpatti) of [the term] "re-engaged" (*punar-pravṛtta*) and so forth. Now, an objection might be raised: "In your view, first there is indifference (*upekṣā*) regarding the object of duty, and immediately thereafter there is the activity of sleeping and so on; at that time, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usage [of the term 'engaged'], since the operation consisting of indifference conducive to the absence of effort (*kṛti*) exists then. In your [opponent's] view, however, there is no such consequence, because at that time the destruction of each respective effort (*kṛti-dhvaṃsa*) is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that respective effort. If this is argued, we say: no.

For at the time when such an application is authoritative, it is accepted that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is precisely the indifference (*upekṣā*) residing in that specific time. It is for the sake of clarifying this very point that it is stated in the *Mañjūṣā* that "it is a particular kind of indifference. Now, one might object: the meaning of "non-performance after performance" is not what has been stated; rather, its meaning is an activity conducive to the absence of performance, qualified by performance through both the relations of immediate succession and coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And this activity is exactly as previously described. Alternatively, it is the aforementioned activity conducive to the destruction of the performance.

If it is argued that even in the case of "one who is thus averse to dharma" (*dharmād virataḥ*), the aforementioned fault does not apply because it is in consideration of a lack of refinement (*apariṣkāra*), and because there is no heaviness (*gaurava*) in this [formulation] compared to the meaning stated by you—this being the sense of the alternative "or else" (*athavā*)—we say no. This is because the aforementioned fault remains as it was (the fault of *kadāpi*), and because the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*) as defined by having an origin (*utpattimattva*) is more cumbersome than the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. The meaning of the verbal root [in *pramādyati*] is a lack of attentiveness (*anavadhānatā*), which consists of a cognition whose qualificandum is a desired means (*iṣṭasādhanaviśeṣyaka*) and whose qualifier is the state of being a means to the undesired (*aniṣṭasādhanatvaprakāraka*). One becomes negligent regarding dharma (*dharmāt pramādyati*).

The meaning of the fifth case (pañcamī) is either the state of being an object (*viṣayitva*) or the state of being a source (*apādānatva*). Others, however, maintain that [the meaning] is the absence of activity preceded by non-recollection, or non-recollection itself, which constitutes inattention. That alone is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); recollection has as its qualifier such properties as "being something to be done" (*kartavyatva*), and the state of being an object is the meaning of the fifth case. Thus, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is either the absence of activity directed toward dharma caused by the absence of recollection having dharma as its object and "being something to be done" as its qualifier, or the absence of such recollection itself.

In the examples "he fears the thief" (*corād bibheti*) and "he protects from the thief" (*corāt trāyate*), the thief is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) by the rule *abhitrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*. Fear (*bhaya*) is the apprehension of an undesirable outcome; protection (*trāṇa*) is an activity conducive to the removal of that undesirable outcome. In the sūtra, the word "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the undesirable outcome (*aniṣṭa*), which is a constituent part of fear. Thus, the meaning is: that which is the cause of an undesirable outcome is termed *apādāna*. According to the author of the *Mañjūṣā*, the cognition takes the form "the cognition of an undesirable outcome having the thief as its *apādāna*" (*corāpādānakamaniṣṭajñānam*), and so forth. According to other views, the cognition takes the form "caused by the thief" (*corahetuka*), and so forth.

According to that view, since the state of being caused (*prayojyatva*) is the meaning of the ablative case, it is construed with "the undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*). And by proximity, this undesirable is something related to the agent that is likely to occur. It should not be argued that, in a case where someone has an undesirable event dependent on thieves that is not well-known, yet he suspects his own misfortune will be caused by them, the expression "he fears the thieves" (*corād bibheti*) would be incorrect; for in such a case, the fact that his undesirable event is caused by the thieves would be contradicted [by its lack of renown]. This is not so.

This is because the stated formulation is sustained by superimposing the state of having a thief as its cause upon another's undesirable [result] which has that [other person] as its cause, or upon that person's own undesirable [result]. Where the fear produced is not well-known to anyone, if such a formulation is intended, one must resort to superimposition alone. Here too, when the thief and so forth are intended to be expressed as possessors (the relation), the genitive case occurs; for this very reason, the usage in the *Rāmāyaṇa*—"Of whom, when enraged in battle, do even the gods stand in fear?"—is consistent.

They say that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) should be accepted as "of whom in relation to the conflict" (*kasya saṃyuge*). The logicians (*tārkika*), however, maintain that the meaning of the ablative case is "the state of having the quality of being the object of the instigation" (*prayojyatā-prakārakatvam*). Since this remains intact within the context of apprehension (*saṃbhāvanā*), the validity of even such a sentence as "he fears even a friend through the delusion that he is an enemy" is established. Thus, they say that when used with a verbal root meaning "fear," the *apādāna* is that which is apprehended as the cause of fear; whereas when used with a root meaning "to protect," it is that which causes the undesirable—this constitutes the two distinct meanings of the sentence.

In the expression *adhyayanāt parājayate* ("he fails because of study"), the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *aparājer asoḍhaḥ*. The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the absence of an effort directed toward that [object], which co-occurs with a cognition whose mode is the impossibility of accomplishing the action through effort. Here, the "status of the ablative" (*apādānatva*) consists in being the object of that [effort]. This is because the term *asoḍhaḥ* (unendurable) signifies an object for the meaning of the root, which is the form of such non-endurance. Thus, it follows that this serves as an illustration only when the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

*Utsāha* (zeal) is a particular state of the mind designated by the term "joy," or else it is a particular mode of activity. The understanding is that there is an absence of such zeal whose source (*apādāna*) is study. Others say that the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "object-hood" (*viṣayatva*), and that this object-hood of study is construed with the zeal. Still others, however, hold that the meaning of the word [denoting the source] is "the state of having the property of cessation dependent on aversion. The meaning of the ablative is "subject-hood" (*viṣayitva*), which is construed both with that aversion and with the cessation.

They say that the understanding is either "the cessation of specific activities motivated by aversion toward the subject of study" or "one who possesses such [aversion]. Thus, in both the immediately preceding view and this present view, the term is understood as *sakarmaka* (transitive). However, this appears incorrect because it is established by direct experience (*anubhava-siddha*) that what is actually perceived is merely the absence of engagement (*pravṛtty-abhāva*) and so forth. In the expression *śatrūn parājayate* ("he defeats the enemies"), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation conducive to humiliation (*tiraskāra*).

The enemies possess the status of the *karman* (object) because they are the substratum of the result consisting of being treated with contempt. Because of the expression "unable to endure" (*asoḍha*), there is no status of *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) here. In the examples "He drives the cow away" (*gāṃ vāsyati*), "He wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), and "He keeps the blind man away from the well" (*kūpād andhaṃ vārayati*), there is the status of *apādāna* by the rule "Of roots meaning 'warding off,' [the desired object is so called]" (*vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ*). The meaning of that rule is: when in construction with a root meaning "warding off," that which is the object of desire—by virtue of being the substratum of the specific result of the meaning of that particular root—is designated as *apādāna*. And the desire belongs to the cow or other [creature] being warded off.

By the term *īpsita* ("desired"), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the agent who is the substratum of either the primary or secondary activity. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on this very sūtra. The meaning of the root *vārayati* is an operation conducive to the absence of an action that is favorable to contact with eating and so forth. The resulting sense is that when a particular action is prohibited, the word [denoting the agent] signifies an operation conducive to the absence of that specific action. The cognition is: "The barley and so forth are the operation conducive to the absence of the operation [of the cow] which is favorable to the contact below the throat of the cow, who is the agent of the eating and so forth."

It is to be undertaken because it is conducive to the common security and well-being (*yogakṣema*). Therefore, even though antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like are not produced, there is no failure of the stated application in preventing what has not yet occurred. This is because the *Bhāṣya*—in the passage, "If these cows go there, there will certainly be destruction of the crops; from that destruction follows demerit and fear of the king; having perceived this with his intellect, he turns [them] back"—establishes that this [prevention] is indeed desired.

Conformity (*anukūlatā*) should be understood as consisting solely in the capacity for the essential nature (*svarūpayogyatā*), and not as being characterized by the actual attainment of the result (*phalopahitatva*). Consequently, even if one eats a cow or similar animal immediately after a prohibition, the usage of the verb "he prevents" (*nivārayati*) is justified; for although the person does not actually turn [the animal] back, the action of preventing remains. According to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, since such an action of preventing—which is conducive to the absence [of eating]—is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established precisely by the rule "that from which there is a departure of something not fixed" (*adhruvam apāye*).

In his view, because there is no cessation of activity imposed upon an insentient object, the claim that "it does not ward off the heat from the flowers" is unestablished; furthermore, even the falling into a well is an object of desire for a blind person insofar as it is a movement toward a location in front of him.

This being the case, they say that even if the object is not the object of desire in its capacity as an "object" (*viṣayatva*), it may still be the object of desire in its capacity as "food" (*bhakṣaṇatva*). Thus, when there is the contingency of eating poison as an unavoidable consequence, the resulting usage—"Yajñadatta wards off Devadatta from poison"—would follow; however, this is to be avoided by accepting it as an intended result (*iṣṭāpatti*). [In the phrase] "Kṛṣṇa hid himself from his mother," the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *antardhau yena-*.

The meaning of the sūtra is this: "the state of staying in a remote location, which is conducive to the absence of a perception of one's own object caused by another agent, is the *apādāna* when one desires that absence of perception caused by a particular agent. The sense of concealment (*antardhi*) is expressed by the verbal root *līṅ*. In the example, the desire is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), and the fact that the perception is performed by the mother is obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

And thus, the understanding is that the activity—consisting in remaining in such a place—is performed by Kṛṣṇa and is conducive to the absence of that seeing which has the mother as its agent (by virtue of the sense of "from") and has herself as its object; [that is, it is conducive to the absence of seeing her]. Others, however, hold that agency is the meaning of the ablative case, and that it connects with the seeing—which is a constituent of the verbal root's meaning—via the relation of being the qualificand (*nirūpakatva*). Thus, the understanding is that the activity is of such a kind as to be conducive to the absence of that seeing which has the mother as its agent and has herself as its object.

In the Sūtra, the word "yena" (by which) is employed so that [the result] would belong only to one who desires the absence of such a vision in the absence of that [vision]. Now, an objection is raised: since the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) prescribes the genitive case for the agent and the object, the use of the instrumental "yena" is untenable. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, by supplying "ātmanaḥ" (of the self) as the object, the restriction "ubhayaprāptau" (Pāṇini 2.3.66) applies, thereby preventing the genitive.

This being the case, even in the expression "atha śabdānuśāsanam" (Now, the instruction on words), since the teacher’s name is well-known, its necessary ellipsis would trigger the application of the restrictive rule "ubhayaprāptau" (when both [agent and object] are present); consequently, the prohibition of compounding by the rule "karmaṇi ca" (and when the object is present) would result. In reality, however, the operation of that restrictive rule occurs only when both [the agent and the object] are explicitly mentioned, as is clear from the commentary on the sūtra "ātmamāne" (in the sense of self-praise). Thus, in the present instance, there is no fault, as the word "ātmanaḥ" (of oneself) is not to be supplied. This is well-established.

In the expressions "he studies from the preceptor" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*) and "he hears the Purāṇa from the scholar" (*paṇḍitāt purāṇaṃ śṛṇoti*), the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *ākhyātopayoge*. The meaning of that rule is that when there is the acquisition of knowledge (*vidyā*) preceded by a formal restriction (*niyama*), the speaker is the ablative. The meaning of the root *iṅ* (in *adhīte*) is an activity conducive to the acquisition of a text, occurring after its utterance and preceded by a restriction such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*). The meaning of the root *śru* (in *śṛṇoti*) is an activity conducive to the perception of hearing preceded by a restriction.

If it is accepted that the utility consisting in the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a formal rule (*niyamapūrvaka*) serves merely to designate the actual existence (*svarūpasattā*) [of the action], and not even its appearance (*bhāna*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then the state of being "preceded by a formal rule" need not be included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In that case, the resulting cognition would be: "such an activity having the teacher as its source (*apādāna*)."

Others, however, hold that the meaning of the ablative is dependence upon the agent of utterance, or merely dependence upon utterance itself. In the former case, the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) is construed non-differently with the agent included within the meaning of the ablative; in the latter case, [the base is construed] with the utterance and so forth through the relation of being uttered by its own agent.

They say that [the relation] in the sense of the verbal root *rūp* (to produce) is by way of the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*). Regarding the statement "creatures are born from Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ prajāḥ prajāyante*), the status of being an ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *janikartuḥ*. Here, the compound *janikartuḥ* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* meaning "the agent (*kartṛ*) of birth (*janiḥ*)," where birth is defined as production or origination. Since the word ends in the suffix *tṛn*, there is no prohibition against such a compound. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the prohibition on the genitive case by the rule *na loka-*; for the established doctrine is that that prohibition applies only to the genitive used in the sense of a *kāraka* (case-role), and thus there is no obstacle to the application of the "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive.

In reality, however, it should be understood that a compound with a word ending in *tṛc* is easily available even with a genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*); this is clear in the *Manoramā* and other works. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is: "The *apādāna* is the material cause (*prakṛti-rūpādāna-kāraṇa*) which is the locus of origination. This is because the word *prakṛti* is well-known in that very sense [of material cause]. That Brahman, variegated by *māyā*, is the material cause of the world is established as the settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vedāntins. For this very reason, [the sūtra] is established for the purpose of showing that Brahman is the material cause of the world, as in [the scriptural statement]: "From which indeed these... (*yato vā imāni*).

In expressions such as *putrāt pramodo 'jāyata* ("joy was born from the son"), the usage is justified by superimposing the status of the material cause (*upādānatva*). The author of the *Vṛtti*, his followers, and others state that, in accordance with usages like *putrāt pramodaḥ*, the term "base" (*prakṛti*) in the rule refers to the cause in general. Nor should it be argued that, just as in *dhūmād agnimān* ("he has fire because of smoke"), the ablative case is already established here by the rule *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 2.3.25), so what is the need for this specific sūtra? For this sūtra is necessary to ensure that the cognition is conveyed specifically in the form of the "ablative relation" (*apādānatva*).

Others, however, say that this [mention of *bhū*] is necessary both for the establishment of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) when there is a cognition of dependence on a specific relation whose nature is distinct from being a cause (*hetutva*), and for the purpose of ensuring the comprehension of causality in its general form as a "relation" (*sambandhatva*). In the expression "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is established by the rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ*. Here, *bhū* means "originating" (*bhavanam*); the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because the root belongs to the *saṃpadādi* class. Furthermore, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*), even though it is part of a compound, is understood here due to its being marked with a *svarita* accent.

And likewise, there is the "source" (*prabhava*) of the agent of origination. The meaning of "source" is that from which something originates—that is, the ablative case (*apādāna*) as the locus of the first manifestation. As the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *prabhava* may mean the source of water, the cause of birth, prowess, or the initial locus of knowledge. In the expression "it originates" (*prabhavati*), the meaning of the verbal root is the first manifestation in the form of the first perception. The root *bhū* in the sūtra also carries this very same sense.

The state of being an object of a cognition consisting of manifest perception, or such cognition alone, by way of the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā-sambandha), belongs to the Ganges and so forth, which are the substrata thereof; this constitutes their agency.

The "priority" (*prāthamya*) residing therein consists in being qualified by the non-existence of its own destruction, related through the relation of simultaneity (*samānakālikatva*). Such knowledge is possible only for someone situated on the earth's surface who is simultaneous with the manifestation of the Gaṅgā. Even when one coming from the South first sees the Gaṅgā at the Vindhya mountain, the expression "the Gaṅgā originates from the Vindhya" is not employed, because that perception lacks the qualification of being characterized by such a non-existence of its own destruction.

And that knowledge, by virtue of its intended meaning (*tātparya*), pertains exclusively to what exists in the world of mortals. Therefore, there is no logical consequence of the usage "the Gaṅgā flows from Vaikuṇṭha" based on taking the gods as the objects of such knowledge. The author of the *Mañjūṣā* holds that the meaning of the ablative case is the power of being an *apādāna* (point of departure). Others hold that the meaning of the ablative is the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). The author of the *Vyutpattivāda* holds that its meaning is dependence upon a relation.

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is "visibility delimited by a location that is not separated from a location delimiting the absence of visibility. The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamyartha*) is identity (*tādātmya*). This [identity] is construed with the second location, which is a constituent of the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, according to the author of the *Tārkikaratnākara*, the cognition is: "The Gaṅgā possesses visibility delimited by that location which is non-different from the Himālaya and is not separated from a location delimiting the absence of visibility."

According to Kārakavādaka, however, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the first conjunction with the external; in the present context, the referent of the word "external" (*bahiḥ*) is the netherworld (*rasātala*). The meaning of the ablative case suffix (*pañcamī*) is the state of occurring at the moment immediately following the destruction of that conjunction. The meaning of the verb ending (*ākhyāta*) is the locus (*āśrayatva*).

And thus, the meaning of the fifth case (pañcamī) is "occurring in the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction whose relatum is the Himalaya," while the meaning of the verb suffix (ākhyāta) is "substratum. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "The Gaṅgā is the substratum of the first conjunction with the earth occurring in the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction whose relatum is the Himalaya. The inclusion of the terms "immediately following" (avyavahita) and so forth is for the purpose of excluding such usages as "the Gaṅgā originates from Vaikuṇṭha" or "from Kāśī."

They say there is no fault because the conjunction with the earth does not occur at the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction with Vaikuṇṭha; and because the conjunction with the Gaṅgā and the earth, which occurs at the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction with Kāśī, lacks the quality of being "first. In this context, the meaning of the verbal root is the first manifestation consisting of the first cognition, as is obtained from the Viśvakośa lexicon stating that "cognition" resides in the "first place" (*ādimasthāna*). [The form] *upalabheta*...

This is also evident from the commentary on the usage of the word *prabhavati*. Here, in the expression *āsanāt prekṣate* ("he looks from his seat"), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule *lyablope karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* ("when there is an elision of a *lyap*-ending [gerund], the case endings for the object and the locus are used"). "Elision" (*lopa*) refers to the non-occurrence of a word because its meaning is already understood. Thus, the meaning of the rule is that when a verbal form ending in *lyap* is not expressed due to the understanding of its sense, the case endings apply to the object (and locus) of the action denoted by that *lyap*-ending verbal root; such is the sense. However, the phrase "when there is no utterance of the *lyap*-ending form" is not the actual meaning of the rule *lyablope*, because "elision" (*lopa*) is a technical term specifically applied to the absence of the perception [of the word].

It is clear from the *Bṛhacchabdaratna* and other works that the act of seeing (*dṛśi*) lacks the nature of an act of utterance (*uccāraṇakriyā*). The meaning is: "having sat down on a seat, he looks. In the expression *prāsādāt prekṣate*, the meaning is: "having ascended the palace, he looks. In sequence, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the object (*karman*) are the meanings of the ablative case. The manifestation of actions such as sitting down occurs by way of the maxim of the "single part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "The act of sitting, which has a seat as its locus, is immediately followed by an act of looking, having the same agent," and so forth. In the expression "the village is one *yojana* from the forest" (*vanād grāmo yojane yojanaṃ vā*), the ablative case and others are prescribed according to the rule: "When distance or time is measured, the fifth [ablative] case is used; it should be stated that after a word denoting distance associated with that [measure], the first and seventh cases are used, and after a word denoting time, the seventh case is used. Thus, the ablative and other cases are enjoined.

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed when the creation or delimitation of either a path (*adhvan*) or time (*kāla*) is expressed by depending on something as its limit. From that which is connected with such [an ablative]—that is, from a word denoting a path to be delimited that is semantically connected with a word ending in the fifth case—the first (*prathamā*) and seventh (*saptamī*) cases occur. In the rule concerning "time" (*kālāt*), the phrase "connected with that" (*tadyuktāt*) is also understood by ellipsis; thus, its meaning is "from a word expressing such a sense of time. The meaning of the ablative suffix here is "immediately following."

The relation is with the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) through the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva), and its connection occurs through the relation of substratumhood (āśrayatva). The meaning of the nominative and locative cases is "occurring immediately after. This [meaning] connects as the substratum in the village.

And thus, the understanding is that the village is located in a place immediately following the one immediately following the forest. In the expression "The Āgrahāyaṇī [full moon] is a month from the Kārtikī," the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is "being composed of parts [of the interval]," while the locative (*saptamī*) means "occurring in a time immediately following. The base-meaning, which is the form *Kārtikī*, connects by way of identity (*tādātmya*) with the "part" that constitutes the meaning of the ablative. The resulting cognition is: "The Āgrahāyaṇī occurs in a time immediately following the month that is composed of parts of the Kārtikī."

In the preceding case, as well as here, the meaning of the first and seventh cases—and specifically of the seventh case—is merely "immediately following. This [meaning] connects with the village (*grāma*) by way of the relation of locus (*āśrayatva*). Because the expression "from the forest to the village" (*vanād grāmaḥ*) is not used when there is an intervention of more than a *yojana*, the aspect of non-intervention is included within the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in that instance. For this same reason, it is also included in the meaning of subsequent case endings beyond the fifth. Furthermore, its inclusion within the meaning of the seventh case in the example "in a month" (*māse*) is precisely for this purpose.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the expression] "the month following Kārttikī" applying even to Pauṣī; for the property of occurring in a month subsequent to the one containing Kārttikī exists in Pauṣī as well. Furthermore, in the ablative case "from Kārttikī" (kārtikyāḥ), the meaning is not "immediately following," as in the case of "from the forest" (vanāt). This is because the property of occurring in a month immediately following the month immediately after Kārttikī is impossible in Agrahāyaṇī, which would render the aforementioned usage untenable. Therefore, in both cases, the meaning of the ablative is "limit" (avadhi).

The grammarians (Śābdikas) maintain that the resulting cognition is of the form: "a village exists in a location immediately following [and not separated by] a distance measured in *yojanas*, having the forest as its limit. The point is that there is no impossibility [of such a construction], because once the meaning of the *yojana* and so forth is known, there is invariably a requirement for a limit (*avadhi*). Nor is there a lack of semantic consistency even in cases such as "from the Kārttikī," because that which possesses a particular property can also serve as the limit for that same property; this is the sense of the rule *abhividhau*. In expressions such as "other than the pot" (*ghaṭād anyaḥ*), the meaning of the ablative case is the relation of difference whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is itself.

Through that relation, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed with another [word]; for this very reason, there is no possibility here of a partial construal (*ekadeśānvaya*). For this same reason, grammarians (*śābdika*) accept that in expressions such as "Devadatta’s son" (*devadattasya putraḥ*), the state of being produced (*janyatva*) and so forth is the meaning of the genitive case. The lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) understood from words such as "other" (*anya*) does not function as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*); for if that were understood, there would be a lack of expectancy precisely because of that [understanding], and thus there would be an absence of the lack of expectancy required for understanding [the relation] as a connection (*saṃsargatayā*).

The phrase "having its own counter-correlate" (svapratiyogikatvam) means "having a counter-correlativity delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of the base" (prakṛtyarthatāvacchedakāvacchinnapratiyogitākatvam). By this [definition], the undesirable consequence that one might say "the pot is different from the pot" does not arise, even when taking another pot as the counter-correlate within the pot itself. Furthermore, even if one takes that specific individual qualified by potness (ghaṭatva) as the referent of the word "self" (sva), the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable because one could still take a difference having that [pot] as its counter-correlate by way of duality (dvitva) and so on; thus the objection is applied. Others, however, hold that the meaning of the ablative case (pañcamī) is either counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) or possession of a counter-correlate (pratiyogimattva).

In the case of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—which is itself connected to the meaning of the base by the relation of being a locus delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning—conjoins with the difference (*bheda*) by the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*); or, in the second view, it conjoins with that which possesses such a difference by the relation constituted by that [determiner], within the nature of the negative correlate (*anuyogitā-svarūpa*).

When there is the possession of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with [the counter-correlate] by way of the relation of being "determined by" (*nirūpitatva*) that which is delimited by the delimitor of the meaning of the base; and that [delimitor] is construed, by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatva*), with the difference (*bheda*), even though it is only a part [of the whole], due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpattivaicitrya*), just as in the case of *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ*, where, due to the peculiarity of convention, [the quality of] clarity is construed [with the excellence of the cloth].

Precisely for this reason, because there is an absence of primary grammatical coreferentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the compound is not a *karmadhāraya* according to the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), but rather a *sup-supā* compound, as indicated by the evidence in the rule "words such as *vispaṣṭa*" (*vispaṣṭādīni*). This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the sūtra "compounding occurs prior to *kaḍāra*. Others say that the word "different" (*bhinna*) is construed with that which possesses difference through a relation constituted by that [word]. It is for this very reason that the usage "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād bhinnaḥ*) is established, since the meaning of "other" (*anya*) is understood.

However, in the expression "the difference of the jar" (*ghaṭasya bhedaḥ*), there is no application of the ablative case. This is because [the rule] specifically refers to that which signifies an object qualified by difference, and the word *anya* (other) has such a qualified meaning. It was with this very intention—that the mention of *itara* (the other) is merely indicative of this same purpose—that it was stated in the *Kaumudī*: "for the sake of elaboration."

For this very reason, the ancients maintain that there is no such contingency in the case of "the pot is not" (*ghaṭo na*), because they accept that [the particle *na*] functions as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*). However, in the view of the modern grammarians (*navya-śābdika*), the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is unnecessary, as it is not stated in the Bhāṣya. As for the justification of the ablative case in "different from the pot" (*ghaṭād bhinnaḥ*), it has already been explained previously; so, enough of this. In the expression "misery without Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇād ṛte duḥkham*), the word "Kṛṣṇa" is used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean his devotee. The meaning of the word "without" (*ṛte*) is the absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*).

That [absence], which is connected with the meaning of the base (prakṛti) through the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā-sambandha), is connected with the suffering residing therein through the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya). In the case of absence, the condition of "counter-correlativity being non-co-located" (pratiyogi-vaiyadhikaraṇya) must be introduced; otherwise, since devotion—which consists of a cognition having "being worthy of worship" as its qualifier—is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), its absence would co-occur even with pleasure. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "pleasure exists apart from Kṛṣṇa" (kṛṣṇād ṛte sukham). In some cases, however, the connection occurs precisely through the relation of being employed (prayuktatva).

For this very reason, it is not the case that "there is happiness without rain. Otherwise, even though rain exists in the field and so forth, since its absence exists in the self, such a formal application [of the argument] would be possible. This is because the cognition of the intended meaning in expressions such as "Devadatta has suffering due to the departure of his enemy from his own country" is established by experience and is therefore necessary.

Otherwise, even when an enemy has departed, since that absence exists in Devadatta, it would be unavoidable [to claim] that the suffering caused by his illness and so forth possesses co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with such an absence of departure. Likewise, for this very reason, there is no possibility of such usage as "there is no jar without a donkey," just as there is "no jar without a staff. This is because, while the fact that the absence of the jar is caused by the absence of the staff remains uncontradicted, the fact that it is caused by the absence of the donkey lacks such uncontradicted status.

If, however, the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) were taken as the relation of connection (*saṃsarga*), then the aforementioned undesirable consequence would indeed follow. As for the restrictive rule that its [the absence's] connection occurs only through the relation of being employed (*prayuktatva*), that is untenable because it is impossible in cases such as "there is no absence of the form of the mountain except for fire. Enough of this.

In the sentence "The tree falls in the absence of wind," the meaning of *ṛte* (without/in the absence of) is either non-existence (*abhāva*) or that which possesses such non-existence (*tadvān*). When the relation [of non-existence] is understood as qualifying the tree with respect to its falling, the resulting understanding—either that the falling lacks being produced by that [wind], or that the tree lacks being the producer of that [falling]—is an implied (ārtha) sense. Since it is impossible for something not presented by the word "being-produced" (*janya*) to appear as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a non-existence, and since "being-produced" is not a relational determinant (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), it is also impossible to have a cognition of the non-existence of wind whose counter-positiveness is delimited by that [relation of being-produced].

However, if the word *vāta* is taken as having the secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being produced by wind," then resorting to that very [meaning] is a fault. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *ṛte* can also possess difference (*bheda*), as in the example: "There is no archer other than Rāma" (*rāmād ṛte na dhanurdharaḥ*). Here, the cognition is: "one who is different from Rāma is different from the archer. Every method explained in the case of "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād anyaḥ*) should be understood here as well. Moreover, the accusative case is also used in conjunction with this [word], because of the inclusion of the term "seen" (*dṛśi*) in the rule: "It is seen elsewhere than that" (*tato 'nyatrāpi dṛśyate*). For this very reason, the followers of Candra formulate the rule: "The accusative is also [used] after *ṛte*."

For this very reason, the usage "without the propitiation of the Person" (*puruṣārādhanam ṛte*) is also correct. By that [same principle], the expression "the tree falls without the wind" (*ṛte vātaṃ vṛkṣaḥ patati*) is also possible. In the phrase "the lake is east of the village" (*pūrvo grāmāt taḍāgaḥ*), the ablative case is used by the rule *anyārāt-*. Here, although the word "east" (*pūrva*) functions as a direction (*diś*), the inclusion of the term "word" (*śabda*) in the rule allows for the inclusion of anything perceived merely as being in a direction. Thus, the referent of the word "east" is a location adjacent to the mountain of sunrise (*udayācala*). The state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is the meaning of the ablative case.

Priority (*pūrvatva*) is a non-specific property that requires a limit (*avadhi*). It is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). Posteriority (*paratva*) and so forth are likewise. The cognition occurs in such a sequence as "that which possesses priority whose defining relation is not determined by the village as its limit," and so on. In the expression "Phālguna is prior to Caitra," it is precisely the time that is not the locus of either the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) or its destruction that appears, aided by the co-occurrence with the word expressing that respective limit. The cognition is: "Phālguna is one who exists at a time possessing priority relative to Caitra. This excludes [the possibility] of being one who exists at a time that is merely not the locus of its destruction.

If [the word "prior"] were denotative in the form of "priority" (*pūrvatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Caitra is prior to Caitra. If [the word] were denotative of that which exists in a locus not occupied by its own counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) alone, then, if one were to accept a denotative power (*śakti*) that includes the beginning of the counter-correlates such as Vaiśākha and Caitra, there would be an infinity of powers. If, on the other hand, it were included merely in the form of "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*) and so forth, there would be the fault of non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*). For fear of such defects, the denotative power is accepted for that which exists at such a time precisely in the form of "priority."

Since time (*kāla*) functions solely as a delimiter of action, there would be no connection with [months] such as Phālguna; therefore, its inclusion is within that [category of time]. In this case, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) and so forth. However, in the absence of such indication, the usage would simply be "Phālguna is prior to Caitra. This indeclinable (*avyaya*) primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). There is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a verb such as "exists" (*asti*). Others, however, maintain that in the expression "prior to the village," the meaning of the word "prior" is that which is the substratum of posteriority relative to the Eastern Mountain (*udayācala*), while the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is the state of being the determiner of that posteriority.

And thus, the understanding is that [the word "east"] denotes the locus of that posteriority which is delimited by the mountain of sunrise (udayācala) and is characterized by being directed toward the activity of the village. In the example beginning with "Caitra from the sun" (*caitrād ādityāt*), the word "prior" (*pūrva*) signifies the locus of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). The ablative case (*pañcamī*) has the sense of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*). However, if prior non-existence is not accepted, then the meaning of the word "prior" is the counter-correlate of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). The meaning of the ablative is the property of being the substrate (*ādheyatva*), and this [property] is construed with destruction.

They say that the cognition takes such a form as "Phālguna is the locus of the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) whose counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is Caitra. In this view, since prior non-existence and the like lack a limiting relation (sāvadhikatva), the word *pūrva* (prior), which denotes such a non-existence, would not have the sense of requiring a limit (avadhi-ākāṅkṣā). Consequently, in the absence of such a fixed relation, its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) would not be established. Nor should it be argued that its status as a pronoun is justified simply because there exists a requirement for a counter-correlative (*pratiyogy-ākāṅkṣā*).

The grammarians (Śābdikas) say that there is no inconsistency in my view because the meanings of "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*) and "limiting point" (*avadhitva*) are distinct, and because "priority" (*pūrvatva*) is necessarily relative to a limit. In the expression "Vaiśākha is posterior to Caitra," the meaning of the word *para* (posterior) is that which exists in a time that has Caitra’s destruction as its locus; the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of being a limiting point (*avadhitva*). In such examples as "To me, the Gaṅgā is further than the house, but Kāśī is closer to me," the words *para* and *apara* denote, through priority and posteriority, those situated in distant places and those situated in proximate places respectively.

The cognition proceeds in the following sequence: "The Gaṅgā [is] characterized by a relation to a house that serves as its limit," and so forth. The relation residing in the term "further" (*para*) consists in being the substratum of a series of conjunctions with what is conjoined to itself, or being dependent upon it; whether the intervening house is related to itself or related to something else is another matter. This is because, when there is an expectancy for that object, the case-ending caused by it is accepted as belonging only to that which expresses it, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, it is quite clear that words such as "further" (*para*) have a fixed expectancy only toward a limit (*avadhi*).

The terms *prāc* and so forth have been explained by [the analysis of] *pūrva* and so forth. However, in cases such as *sadhyuṅ caitreṇa* ("facing east with Caitra"), it is accepted that only a word denoting a direction (*digvācaka*) with *añc* as its final member serves as the cause for the fifth case (*pañcamī*), by virtue of its association with the meaning of the fifth case. In the expression *grāmādbahiḥ* ("outside the village"), the term *bahiḥ* is used to denote, through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the form "being outside," that which is not the locus of the property delimiting the referent of the co-occurring word (*samabhivyāhṛtapadārthatāvacchedakānāśraya*), as well as that which resides therein. By the phrase "an unobstructed space" (*anāvṛtadeśa*), this very same meaning is intended. For this reason alone, expressions such as "a quality (*guṇa*) existing outside of a substance (*dravya*)" are justified.

Regarding the phrase *kāśīto bahirbhūtam idaṃ gṛham* ("this house is outside of Kāśī"), the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) here is indicated by the rule for compound formation involving the word *bahiḥ*. They say that because what is established by a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) is not universally applicable, the expression *karasya karabho bahiḥ* ("the forearm is outside of the hand") is thereby justified. In the examples *apa hareḥ* and *pari hareḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("the cycle of existence is away from or around Hari"), the words *apa* and *pari* have the same meaning as the word *ṛte* ("except for"). By the rule *apaparī varjane*, they receive the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*. Consequently, the ablative case is applied by the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*. Here, the word *hari* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean "devotion to Hari."

Samsāra—meaning birth and so forth—is either co-located with the absence of devotion to Hari or is caused by it. Others, however, maintain that the meaning of these two [words] is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), while the meaning of the ablative case is the property of being the locus (*ādheyatva*). This [locus] is construed with the absolute non-existence, and the absolute non-existence is construed with samsāra as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogitā*). Thus, the cognition is: "Samsāra is the counter-correlative of the absolute non-existence residing in Hari. They argue that this is because one has such an experience in cases like "the absence of smell in water" or "the absence of smell in earth."
