Their intention is this: it is not possible to accept the cognition that "the existence of odor has the same locus as the absence of earth," because it would then follow [absurdly] that "there is an absence of moisture in water" and so forth.

If it is argued that the cognition "the absence of smell is caused by the absence of earth" is accepted, while the absence of oiliness (*sneha*) and so forth is not caused by that [absence of earth], and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then [we reply]: since only the absence of the cause as delimited by its own causal-relation-delimiter (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is the instigator of the absence of the effect, it is impossible for the respective absences as delimited by relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) to function in that way. It should be understood, however, that if one accepts the cognition that [the absence of smell] is caused by the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of earth, then the aforementioned fault does not arise.

"Until liberation (āmukteḥ) is saṃsāra. Here, the prefix *āṅ* has the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). This limit is twofold, according to the distinction between time and space. Regarding the temporal nature of the limit: it is the state of not being the locus of that which is co-referential with the term mentioned, existing throughout the entire duration of time that is the locus of both its own subsequent non-existence and the prior non-existence of its successor. The word "liberation" (*mukti*) refers to the time that is the locus of that [non-existence]. The meaning of the ablative case is the relationship of the limit and the limited (*maryādā-maryādibhāva*), and this alone is what is expressed by the prefix *āṅ*. The resulting cognition is: "Saṃsāra has liberation as its limit."

The understanding of that pervasiveness—which is qualified by the occurrence in a time other than the time of liberation and the time prior to its non-existence—as defined by the prior non-existence of the time of liberation and so forth within the context of *saṃsāra*, is indeed implied (ārthika).

The mention of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that subsequent time is made solely for the purpose of ensuring the fulfillment of the implied understanding of "subsisting at such a time. Furthermore, it must be included that at the time which is the locus of such a prior absence, there is no being a non-locus of the prior absence of the time expressed by the co-occurring term. By this, in the usage "Sāvitrī [is to be recited] when the solar disc has half-set until the appearance of the stars," the manifestation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*)—which is not determined by such a prior absence residing in the recitation—is secured; otherwise, it would not be established.

This is because the absence of that [property] exists even at the time when the sun has half-set, and thus its non-pervasion [of the locus] is sublated, making it impossible to establish [the definition]. Here, in reality, that which is qualified by such a qualifier—the co-occurring word-meaning—is its "non-residence" (tadanadhikaraṇatva), which consists in the difference from its own substratum. This is expressed either in the form of being different from the substratum of the difference from the co-occurring word-meaning, or as a relation; thus there is no infinity of powers (*śakti*). Furthermore, "limitation" (*maryāditva*) is the state of being the determiner of such a limit-nature (*maryādātva*).

Bodhayam explains that the absence of simultaneity (*samānakālikatvābhāva*) and temporal non-interruption (*kālikamavyavadhānam*) are conveyed by the prefix *a-* (in the word *apratibaddha*). Such non-interruption consists in being a moment belonging to a moment that is the locus of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [action], while not being the locus of the prior absence of the moment that is the locus of the prior absence of that [action]. However, for those who do not accept the existence of prior absence (*prāgabhāva*), the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*)—namely, "being the counter-positive" (*pratiyogitvam*)—consists in occurring at a moment that is the counter-positive of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) arising at a moment which is the locus of that [action].

And thus they say that the cognition is: "The transmigratory state (saṃsāra) is separated from liberation, because it possesses the absence of a time simultaneous with liberation. In this view, it should be understood that the fact that the transmigratory state does not occur at a time subsequent to liberation is obtained as a matter of logical implication (ārthika). Nor should it be argued that there is no deficiency even if that [simultaneity] is not manifested; for if one were to study after midday or before it, there would result the improper usage: "He studied until midday," implying a cessation in the middle.

In the case of one who studies every day until evening, expressions such as "he studies until evening" (*ā sāyaṃkālāt*) and so forth are to be explained by taking the verbal root to refer to those specific acts of study. Alternatively, the term "subsequent time" (*uttarakāla*) may be intended to mean a specific point in time immediately following [the action]. In this view, however, it should be noted that if one were reciting at dawn—which is indeed a time preceding the subsequent time of evening—the usage "he recites starting from dawn until evening" (*prātarārabhyā sāyaṃkālāj japati*) would result as an unintended consequence.

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the prefix *aṅ* is simply prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which constitutes the essence of a limit (*maryādā*). The word "liberation" (*mukti*) refers to the time of liberation, and the ablative case (*pañcamī*) expresses the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*). Thus, there is the acquisition of a prior non-existence whose counter-positive is the time that serves as the locus of liberation. This [non-existence] is construed with "saṃsāra" (the cycle of worldly existence) through a relation of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) conjoined with the property of not occurring at its own time or at any subsequent time. They say that in expressions such as "It rained from Prayāga up to Kāśī," the limit is of the nature of a place (*deśa*).

The nature of a limit (*maryādātva*) is the state of residing in all locations situated between Kāśī and Prayāga, excluding those that are not substrata for the referent of the word co-uttered [with the limit], which resides in its own respective subsequent location. However, the meaning intended by others is that the nature of a limit residing in that [subsequent location] is the state of being a non-substratum for such a co-uttered referent while not residing in the subsequent location itself. By including the status of being a non-substratum in the subsequent location, there is no risk of such usage occurring even when rain exists in the region to the east of Kāśī.

If there is rain in the eastern region from Pāṭaliputra, and there is no rain in the interval between Kāśī and Pāṭaliputra, then when there is rain in the Madhyadeśa (Middle Country) between Prayāga and Kāśī, the aforementioned usage is authoritative. In that case, by the word "uttara" (northern/after), the immediately adjacent northern region is to be understood. Alternatively, the word "vṛṣṭi" (rain) may refer to a specific type of rain, and the ablative case after the word "prayāga" is used in connection with the sense of "starting from" (*prabhṛti*). Thus, the understanding is: "The Lord is the cause of the rain extending from the limit of Prayāga up to Kāśī."

The meaning is as follows: it refers to the agent of that rain which is the locus of the counter-positive of the absence residing in all regions situated between Kāśī and Prayāga—starting from the initial locus of Prayāga and extending up to Kāśī—and which is defined by [the absence] residing in the region north of Kāśī. Since the nature of being a limit (maryādātva) constitutes the meaning of the ablative case, one must, due to the lack of any other recourse, accept that the state of not being the locus of the meanings of the co-referential words is included within the region north of Kāśī. This being the case, the intention is that there is no undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) even if there is multiplicity of meanings.
In reality, however, *maryādātva* (the state of being a limit) is a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) that conforms to both types of limits.

Thus, there is no contingency of multiple meanings; for this very reason, the learned demonstrate the understanding [of the term] as "one who is a limit of Kāśī. If the state of being a limit as a specific property were not accepted, then the aforementioned method should be applied here as well. The intended meaning is the sublation of that pervasiveness—which is qualified by the non-existence in a specific region of abundant food—defined relative to the region west of Kāśī, such as Prayāga and so forth; for such pervasiveness is not presented by the word itself.

It cannot be maintained that the solution is achieved by accepting the ablative case (*pañcamī*) following the word *kāśī* as having the sense of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), because pervasiveness is difficult to define when it is not constituted by a specific pervaded (*vyāpya*). If one were to accept a separate power (*śakti*) for each of the constituent elements of that [pervasiveness], there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*), and furthermore, the desired result could not be established in the absence of the presentation of the specific pervaded. It should be understood that if the power were to include the specific pervaded, there would be an infinity of powers (*ananta-śakti*) and so forth. "Limit-inclusive" (*abhividhi*) means complete pervasion up to that point; the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the limit.

And that fifth-case meaning is expressed by the prefix *ā*. Furthermore, "pervasion up to that limit" consists in being related to everything other than that [limit], while simultaneously being its pervader. And this [pervasion] appears, depending on the intended meaning (*tātparya*), sometimes as the nature of being a pervader, and sometimes as identity, conjunction, and so forth. Sometimes it is merely the state of being a pervader, as in: "Everything up to Hari is knowable" (*ā hareḥ prameyatvam*). Here, regarding knowability, there is understood the state of being a pervader of everything other than Hari, while it is simultaneously a pervader of Hari.

"From the atom (ā paramāṇoḥ) [extends] the earth": here, the word *paramām* refers to the atomic constituent of earth (*pārthivaparamāṇu*). It should be understood that through identity (*tādātmya*), there is the non-pervasion of that [atom] by [the earth], as well as the relation of identity with what is other than it, and so forth. "From the whole (ā sakalāt) [extends] Brahman": here, the meaning is merely pervasiveness (*vyāpakatvamātra*). The cognition is: "Brahman is the pervader of the whole. Furthermore, the relation in the form of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) is of two kinds: temporal and spatial. An example of the former is: "The cold lasts from the full moon of Kārttika until the full moon of Caitra."

The understanding is that "cold" is that which pervades the period beginning from the full moon of Kārtika and ending with the full moon of Caitra; here, the word *caitra* refers to the time ending with Caitra. As for the latter [type of pervasion], for example: "It has rained from Kāśī as far as Pāṭaliputra. In this case, the pervasiveness of the rain over the region beginning at Kāśī and ending at Pāṭaliputra is perceived. According to the learned, by virtue of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), what is understood in these two cases is a pervasiveness qualified by the property of not occurring in a time other than that [specific period] and a pervasiveness qualified by the property of not occurring in a place other than that [specific region]. Thus it has been stated by the authorities.

The intended meaning is as follows: pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) is the referent of the second case-ending (*dvitīyārtha*), and the word *yāvat* is its indicator (*dyotaka*). Due to the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), qualified by the meaning of the other words, with that pervasion through the relation of being determined by the time ending with Caitra. Furthermore, pervasion must be understood as consisting precisely of those things which are not pervaded; therefore, it is not unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Alternatively, the referent of the second case is this pair—namely, the state of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a difference, and non-existence (*abhāva*)—both of which are constituents of pervasion and consist precisely of the pervaded.

The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), as qualified by the other word-meanings, is construed with "difference" (*bheda*) through the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatva*); by the force of that very [construal], its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is obtained. Alternatively, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word *caitra* signifies the period of time beginning from the full moon of Kārtika and ending with the full moon of Caitra—just as the word *caitra* [signifies the month itself]—whereas the meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyārtha*), as before, serves to capture the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the phrase "from the Kārtika [full moon]. This should be understood in the same way for the expression "from Kāśī. However, in the view where the word *yāvat* functions as a denotative term (*vācakatva*), the meaning of the second case-ending is "being located therein," which is construed with the "difference" that constitutes the meaning of the word *yāvat*; the rest is as before.

Alternatively, the meaning of the second case (accusative) is pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) and its connection with that which is other than it; and by way of proximity, that "other" is precisely the time beginning with the month of Kārtika, while the "connection" appears in the form of pervasiveness—this is the general direction [of the argument]. Although, even in the case of an example of a limit (*maryādā*), the cognition of pervasiveness can be accounted for in this manner, nevertheless, the account of the cognition as having the specific form of a "limit" is possible without such laborious effort; thus, that [pervasive interpretation] was set aside there.

In this case, however, the understanding of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) has been accepted according to the stated sequence, even without [the prefix] *ā* being present. When there is the intention of "complete pervasion" (*abhivyāpti*), examples such as "from Kārttikī until Caitrī it was cold" should also be understood as illustrations of temporal inclusive limit (*kālikābhividhi*). Here too, the same method previously described must be followed. The distinction is that what constitutes the meaning of the accusative (*dvitīyā*) in those cases is here the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*), while the prefix *ā* remains the same.

Others, however, hold that in the expression "from Kārttikī until Caitra," the meaning of the word *yāvat* is the priority of the subsequent time; and in "from Kāśī to Pāṭalīputra," it is the posteriority of the eastern region. The meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*), which is construed with the meaning of the word *yāvat*. The priority of the subsequent time is construed with the act of experiencing cold through the relation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). Within the locus of the priority of the subsequent time—which constitutes the factor of pervasion—one must include the difference from the preceding times of the Kārttikī and so forth mentioned in the same sentence.

In the second [definition] as well, the state of being in the eastern direction and the western direction is related to the rain by way of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). Here too, within the locus of the state of being in the eastern direction and the western direction—which constitutes the factor of pervasion—the distinction from the western direction, namely Kāśī, must be included.

When such pervasiveness (vyāpakatva) is manifested, it follows by implication that [the action] does not occur prior to the time of the Kārtikī full moon; enough with this excessive detail. They say that all of this should be understood even in the case of examples involving the prefix *ā*. As for the ablative case in *kārtikyāḥ*, it is caused by its connection with the sense of "starting from" (*prabhṛti*). The indeclinable *prabhṛti* has the meaning of "beginning from. The fact that the statement "this should have been used here, but was not used" exists in the *Mahābhāṣya*—intended to refute the *Vārttika* "yataścādhvakāla" (*Pāṇini 2.3.29*)—indicates the existence of such a rule.

Therefore, even when that [action] is not expressed, the establishment of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is secured; its meaning is "taking as a limit" (*avadhimādāya*). That is to say, it means "accepting as a limit. Regarding the word *ārabhya*, there is an apprehension of both that meaning and the mere sense of beginning. In the first case (when it means taking as a limit), the ablative occurs; in the second case (when it means beginning), as in "starting from the morning time" (*prātaḥkālamārabhya*), the accusative occurs because of its status as the object (*karman*). Furthermore, in the expression "Hari is to be served from birth onwards" (*bhavāt prabhṛti sevyo hariḥ*), the state of being a limit depends upon the time ending with death, which is the referent of the co-occurring term; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Thus, the state of being a limit is the meaning of the ablative.

In the phrase *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati*, the word *prati* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ. By the rule "pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt," the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed. The meaning of the rule is that when a substitute (*pratinidhi*) or a counter-gift (*pratidāna*) is connected with a *karmapravacanīya*, the fifth case is used for that which relates to it—that is, its correlate (*pratiyogin*). The sense of the rule is that the fifth case is used after a word denoting the object of such a connection, where the relationship is one of being a correlate. Thus, the meaning of the fifth case in the rule is the relationship characterized by being a correlate.

The word *prati* has the meaning of "similarity. In the expression *kṛṣṇāt*, the meaning of the ablative case is "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*); the resulting cognition is that [the subject] possesses a similarity whose counter-correlative is Kṛṣṇa. In the expression *tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati māṣān* ("He gives back beans for sesame seeds"), *pratidāna* (giving back) consists of a return preceded by a prior taking. In this context, the meaning of the verb *yacchati* as it occurs in conjunction with *prati* is a gift consisting of the destruction of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by a debt previously incurred. The resulting cognition is: "A giving back having beans as its object, preceded by the taking of sesame seeds. Here, the relation of being the object (*karmatva*) is the meaning of the ablative; it connects with the "taking" which is a constituent part of the verbal root's meaning.

The authors of the *Tārkikaratnākara*, however, maintain that the meaning of the prefix *pra-* is "the producer of the destruction of debt-ness" (*ṛṇatvadhvaṃsajanakatva*), which is construed with "taking" (*ādāna*) by way of its substratum; the meaning of the ablative case is "being produced by taking," which is construed with "debt-ness"; and "debt-ness" (*ṛṇatva*) is either a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*) or a specific kind of demerit (*pāpa*). Thus, they accept the resulting cognition to be of such a form as: "The act of giving beans is the producer of the destruction of the debt-ness produced by the taking of sesame seeds. In the expression "bound for a hundred," the ablative case is used according to the rule: "The ablative is used for debt when [the creditor] is not the agent."

The meaning of that [rule] is that the fifth case ending occurs after a word denoting a debt (*ṛṇa*) which is distinct from the agent and serves as the cause (*hetu*). The meaning of the fifth case is either the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) or the state of having a cause (*hetumattva*), in the form of a causal relation (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). The understanding is: "the act of binding has a hundred as its cause. They say, however, that while the nature of being a debt (*ṛṇatva*) is a real objective condition (*vastusan nimitta*), it is not included within the range of what is directly expressed by the word. Others say that its status as a directly expressed meaning is not tenable due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) and because such a cognition is not experienced.

In the counter-example *śatena baddhaḥ* ("bound for a hundred"), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) after the causative (*ṇic*) derived from the root *bandh* with the causal suffix *ṇi*. Here, "a hundred" is the debt (*ṛṇa*), which is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*); and by the rule *tatprayojakaḥ*, it receives the technical designation of "cause" (*hetu*). In the case of *jāḍyād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of dullness"), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is optional according to the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe*; in the alternative, the instrumental of cause (*hetutṛtīyā*) is used. The understanding here is that [the person] is the object of the act of binding caused by dullness. Regarding examples such as *dhūmād agnimān* ("possessing fire because of smoke"), the authors of the *Mañjūṣā* state that the ablative is used because the relation of produced-to-producer (*janya-janaka-bhāva*) residing in cognitions is superposed (*āropa*) upon the object.

According to this view, the understanding is that "fire has smoke as its cause" (*dhūmahetuko vahnih*). By this, the objection regarding the impossibility of using the ablative case (*pañcamī*)—on the grounds that smoke and the like are not the *producers* (*janaka*) of fire and the like—is refuted. However, it is not correct to claim that the word "cause" (*hetu*) includes that which is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because the lexicon (*kośa*) defines the word "cause" as "reason," "instrument," or "seed," thereby establishing that the word "cause" signifies a causal factor (*kāraṇa*). Furthermore, such usage is not observed in common worldly practice. According to the *Laghuśekhara*, the word "smoke" (*dhūma*) refers to the cognition of smoke, while the word "possessing fire" (*agnimat*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean the object of its own cognition.

According to this view, the cognition is: "the mountain, which is the object of the cognition of fire caused by the cognition of smoke. However, according to the author of the *Maṇi*, the word 'fire' (*vahni*) is used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) for the cognition of fire, and the word 'smoke' (*dhūma*) is used metaphorically for the cognition of smoke; the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is causality (*hetutva*), in the form of being a generator (*janakatva*). That [causality], which is qualified by the cognition of smoke—the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—is construed with the cognition of fire, which is the referent of the word 'fire,' through the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā*).

The meaning of the possessive suffix *matup* is either the state of being an object (*viṣayatā*) or the object itself; or the meaning of *matup* is that which possesses the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*), with the word "fire" (*vahnipada*) functioning as a *lakṣaṇā*. Alternatively, they accepted that the word "fire" is *lakṣaṇika* (indicative) of fire as being known (*jñāyamāna-vahni*), and the meaning of *matup* is "that which is in conjunction" (*saṃyogin*). Between these two views stated in the *Mañjūṣā* and the *Śekhara*, it appears that the position according to which the object is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the relation of produced and producer residing in the cognition is the correct one.

The authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others, however, maintain that being made known by a cognition is the meaning of the ablative case, while the word "smoke" (*dhūma*) retains its primary sense. For this very reason, in sentences such as "the rising of smoke," it is not smoke alone that possesses the capacity to indicate [fire].

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and so forth is now demonstrated. In this way, even the word "fire" (*vahni*) retains its primary meaning. For this very reason, it expresses that which is intended to be known (*jijñāsitābhidhāna*); since it is fire itself that is sought to be known, and not the cognition of fire, they say so—enough of this prolixity. Furthermore, the "cognition" (*jñāna*) that constitutes the meaning of the ablative case and so on must be of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Consequently, even when an inference arises—such as the cognition of smoke possessing fire based on a fallacious object like the pervasion—the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of using such expressions as "by means of fire" (*vahninā*) or "fire's [possession of] smoke" (*vahneḥ dhūmavān*) does not occur.

It should be understood that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being different from whatever is not smoke; thus, even in the erroneous cognition "fire is pervaded by smoke," there is validity regarding the aspect of "fire" and so on, and therefore the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not remain. Furthermore, although smoke and the like are not qualities (*guṇa*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used due to the rule *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 2.3.25), which allows for a separation of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*). For this very reason, they say that in the expression "there is no jar because it is not perceived," the ablative is used despite the feminine gender of the word *anupalabdheḥ*.

Others, however, state that the two qualifiers are merely *prāyika* (occasional) because of the usage in the *vārttika* on the sūtras "The [suffixes] *uṇ* etc. are manifold" (*uṇādayo bahulam*) and "Due to the observation of the base-form in many instances" (*bāhulakaṃ prakṛtestanudṛṣṭeḥ*). This is because it is accepted that the relationship between the signified (*jñāpya*) and the signifier (*jñāpaka*) is perceived by way of the delimiters of the concomitance (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), such as the nature of fire (*vahni-tva*) and the nature of smoke (*dhūma-tva*); therefore, expressions such as "the mountain possesses fire because it is a substance" (*parvato vahnimān dravyatvāt*) or "because it is a substance-in-general" (*dravyatvena vā*) are not valid usages.

Otherwise, however, since fire is also indicated by "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth as being a substance (*dravyatva*), and since it is indicated as a substance qualified by the form of "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*), the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prayogāpatti*) would indeed be unavoidable. In this way, because one accepts the rule that "knowability" and so forth appear only in respect to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the positive concomitance (*anvayitāvacchedaka*)—such as "mountain-ness" (*parvatatva*)—of the possession of fire that is to be indicated, there is no such consequence for [inferences like] "The mountain possesses fire, because it has kitchen-hood (*mahānasatva*), or because it is known as having kitchen-hood."

Furthermore, there would be the following logical inconsistency in such formulations as "the mountain possesses fire because it is a substance" or "because it is a kitchen": according to any philosophical system, since the property of being known by a cognition qualified by "substance-ness" (dravyatva) delimited by "knowability" (prameyatva) and so forth exists in fire, and the property of being known by a cognition of "kitchen-ness" (mahānasatva) exists in the kitchen, it is impossible to convey the absence of these properties on the mountain. This is because the absence of the property of being known by a cognition of "substance-ness" (as prompted by those reasons) and the absence of the property of being known by a cognition of "kitchen-ness" on the mountain are themselves unestablished (aprasiddha). Thus, the communication of their absence cannot be achieved.

If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: no, because in the cognition of a non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no requirement for the actual existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), but rather merely for the knowledge of the counter-positive. And that [knowledge] can take the form of a superimposition (*āropa*) even in the present case; it should be understood that there is a superimposition of "being delimited by fire-ness" (*vahnitvāvacchinnatva*) upon what is made known by the knowledge of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), and a superimposition of "kitchen-hood" (*mahānasatva*) upon the aspect delimited by "mountain-ness" (*parvatatva*), and so forth.

For this very reason, from such sentences as "One should not pile [the fire-altar] in the intermediate space" (*nāntarikṣe cinvīta*), there is the successful establishment of the cognition of the absence of the action consisting of piling with the intermediate space as its locus; and for this very reason, even when the cooking of milk in a specific house is unknown, or when mere cooking by Caitra is unknown during his state of deep sleep, there is no semantic incoherence (*ayogyatā*) in a negative sentence such as "Caitra does not cook milk in this house," which intends that specific house as its locus.

Even though the effort conducive to the cooking of milk located in such a house is unreal, it is possible—according to the aforementioned method—to convey both its absence and the absence of the cooking qualified by the grammatical factors (kārakas) co-referential with Caitra; for even if the absence of being located in such a house can be conveyed regarding the act of cooking, it is impossible to convey an effort existing at the present time that is conducive to such cooking as qualified by that kind of absence, because such an effort is sublated (bādhitā) in Caitra. Therefore, in sentences of this type, [the meaning] is not "the blind man does not [see] the sky."

If it is argued that [the statement] "it sees" is likewise non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), then the sentence "the mountain possesses fire because it is a substance" and so forth would also have to be accepted as non-authoritative; however, the followers of the Navya-nyāya explain the validity of such an application in this way.

In cases such as "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke" (*parvato vahnimān dhūmāt*) or "by means of smoke" (*dhūmena*), the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and others denote being caused by a cognition, which consists in being the delimiting factor for the state of being produced by that cognition; this is qualified by the objective-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) of the co-occurring subject, such as the mountain, and it is split into two distinct semantic scopes regarding the property to be predicated (*vidheyatva*). The smoke and so forth are construed with the cognition through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatva*); the state of being caused by the cognition of smoke is construed with the property to be predicated, and that [causality] is construed with the fire and so forth. Thus, in the aforementioned instance, within such a property to be predicated—

The absence of being caused by the cognition of substanceness (*dravyatva*) or kitchenness (*mahānasatva*) is what is conveyed [by the word ‘therefore’], and that [absence] is indeed uncontradicted. Furthermore, being caused by that [cognition] is well-established in the case of a predication delimited by knowability (*prameyatva*) and in the case of a predication qualified by the subjecthood residing in the kitchen. [Objection: But then, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the following formal usage: “The mountain possesses fire, because of smoke”? For [in this case], the property delimited by various instances of fireness (*vahnitva*), which is not a delimiting factor for the state of being produced by the cognition of smoke, [would be the probandum]. [Response: Regarding the mountainness (*parvatatva*)— (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the full argument would typically proceed to show how the specific nature of the locus and the specific nature of the probandum are established through the inferential process.)

If it is argued that this is not so because the property of being the predicate (vidheyatā), as determined by a qualificandumhood (viśeṣyatā) delimited by [the absence of smoke], exists in fire as well, we say no; for we accept that there is a cognition of the connection of the absence of being prompted by the knowledge of smoke, etc., with respect to that very nature of being the predicate (tathāvidheyatātva). This is because the predicatehood [in question] is [delimited] by a relation that delimits the state of being the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha).

Therefore, the meaning of the fifth case (ablative) and subsequent cases must be accepted [as denoting the locus of the absence]. Consequently, in the case of the inference "He possesses knowledge because he is a self," since the property of being caused by the knowledge of "substance-ness" exists within the predication residing in knowledge—which is qualified by the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) located in the subject (pakṣa) as delimited by the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā)—it is impossible to convey the absence of that [causality] with respect to the delimitor; thus, the objection regarding the impossibility of the usage "not substance-ness" and so forth is refuted.

In the cognition that constitutes the meaning of the fifth case (ablative) and so forth, one must include the property of having a qualifier delimited by each respective relation that serves as the delimitor of the causehood (*hetutāvacchedaka*). By this means, there is the justification for such usages as "This [place] possesses fire because of its color, not because of smoke," when the intended meaning is that the causehood is based on the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). In the examples "separate from the village" (*pṛthag grāmāt*), "without the village" (*vinā grāmāt*), or "apart from Rāma" (*rāmeṇa* or *rāmam*), three different case endings are prescribed by the rule beginning with "pṛthag-vinā" (*Pāṇini 2.3.32*).

Alternatively, the third and fifth case endings are prescribed by that [sūtra], while the second case ending occurs even when there is no direct connection with the word "ṛte," as seen in the example *ṛte vātam* ("except for the wind"). In this context, the meaning of the fifth case and so forth is "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*). According to the view that "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) is a quality (*guṇa*), its meaning is "limitation" (*avadhitva*). However, in reality, separateness is not a quality, but rather simply "difference" (*bheda*). For this very reason, the cognition of separateness occurs even in the case of color and so forth, as in *rūpaṃ rasāt pṛthak* ("color is separate from taste"), because one quality cannot exist within another quality.

Nor should it be argued that [the quality] residing in its substratum appears in color (*rūpa*) and so forth through a relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For this appearance is established by experience as being due to a relation of inherence (*samavāya*), just as in the case of "the jar is separate from the cloth. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "that color is separate from that color," because separateness delimited by that [second] color exists in its own substratum. Moreover, there would be no such consequence for the cognition "color-ness is separate from taste-ness," since separateness is possible in the form of a quality within the substratum of that [taste]. This has been explained in detail elsewhere.

In the expression *stokena stokād vā muktaḥ*, the meaning of the case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Since the word *stoka* denotes a property (*dharma*) in the form of "smallness," it lacks coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a substance; consequently, it is unfit to be referred to by a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) and possesses the nature of a non-substance (*asattvarūpatva*), just like the conjunction (*samuccaya*) and other relations presented by the particle *ca*.

It should be understood that a property (dharma) presented by words such as *stoka* is unfit to be referred to by a pronoun (*sarvanāma*). Its "insentient nature" (*asattvabhūtatva*), which consists in not being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so on, is also [to be understood]. Words like *stoka*, like words like *śukla*, refer to the property alone. The causality of the property is mediated through its substratum; and according to the force of the rule *akaraṇe ca stoke* (Pāṇini 3.4.28), grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) applies only in such a sense. For by that rule, the third and fifth case endings are prescribed here. This is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *aluguttarapade*.

"Having gone far from or not far from the village. Here, by the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* ("from words meaning 'far' or 'near,' the second case is used, and optionally the fifth and others"), the fifth case and so forth are prescribed in the sense of the mere nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*). According to the commentary, the word *dūra* refers here to that which exists in a distant location. Thus, the understanding is: "the act of going that exists in a location distant from the village. This should be understood similarly in cases such as *grāmasyāntikam* ("near the village").

By the rule "saptamyadhikaraṇe ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.37), "and the seventh [case-ending] [is used] after words meaning 'far' and 'near' when expressing the locus," four case-endings occur in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, it should be understood that in the rule "saptamyadhikaraṇe ca," because there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.34) together with the three preceding case-endings, all four case-endings are prescribed for these words when expressing the locus. However, in the expression *dūraḥ panthāḥ* ("a distant path"), the application of the second case and the others does not occur.

By the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "of that which does not denote a sentient being" (*asattvavacanasya*), the suffix *tasi* is prescribed only after words denoting "far" or "near" that are not in grammatical apposition with a substance (*dravya*). This is illustrated by the example: "Far from the dwelling [is] the urination; far [is] the washing of the feet. Thus concludes the investigation into the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

By the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed for a relation distinct from the meanings of the *kāraka* (participant in an action) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), such as the relation between owner and owned; and that relation is understood either as a "relation" in its general form or in its specific form according to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Its meaning is understood in its specific form in some cases and as a "relation" in its general form in others. Furthermore, the relation between an action and its participant (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is also its meaning; for this very reason, even though a garment may possess many relations such as being contemporary [with other objects], the expression "this is not Caitra’s" (*nedam caitrasya*) is used.

[Otherwise,] it would not be possible; for otherwise, due to the absence of a relation with Caitra and the absence of a distinction [from him] therein, its impossibility would be quite evident. However, if the meaning of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is a relation characterized by those respective forms, then since a distinction qualified by the possession of ownership and so forth exists in the clothes belonging to another, there is no inconsistency in the aforementioned usage. Precisely because it is denotable in those respective forms, there are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive; thus [it is said], "the genitive..."

The commentary on the *sūtra* "sthāne" is thus justified. However, if its status as the meaning of the genitive case were based solely on its being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*), then that [commentary] would be untenable, because the single power delimited by the property of being a relation would be one and the same. Furthermore, in accordance with experience, from the accusative case and others, there is a cognition specifically in the form of particularities such as "objectness" (*karmatva*) and "actionness" (*kriyātva*), which constitute the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*).

Regarding expressions such as *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), the modern grammarians (*śābdikas*) and logicians (*tārkikas*), including Miśra and others, maintain that if one accepts the relation between action and its factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*) to be understood in the form of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of requiring a second accusative case ending; therefore, they hold that this relation is understood solely as a "relation" (*sambandha*). The ancient authorities, however, maintain that even here, the relation—whether it be the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), or the state of being a cause (*nimittatva*)—is perceived either as a "relation" in general or in its specific form, which is rooted in the action-factor relationship. For this very reason, it is said:
"A relation is distinct from the [six] factors of action (*kārakas*), and it is preceded by the action-factor relationship."

By the statement, "It is expressed in relation to an action, whether that action has been heard [previously] or not," Bhartṛhari asserted that the nature of a relationship is rooted in the relation between an action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva). For everywhere, indeed, a relationship is based upon that. In the expression "the king’s servant" (*rājñaḥ pūruṣaḥ*), the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is preceded by the relation between an action and its factors. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources: "Since the king gives wealth to the servant, he consequently becomes the master of that servant."

For it is clear from the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and other works that action (*kriyā*)—which possesses its own established nature—effects a connection between substances (*dravya*) that would otherwise not relate to one another in the absence of action, acting like a ladder. They say that in cases such as *bhāti* ("shines") or *smarati* ("remembers"), the action is explicitly heard (*śruta*), whereas in cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the action is not heard (*aśruta*) and must be inferred (*anumīyate*) as being [an act] such as giving. The detailed explanation, however, should be sought in the *Mañjūṣā*.

Although a relation such as that between owner and owned resides in both relata, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is introduced only after the word denoting the qualifier—such as *rājan* (king)—and not after the word denoting the qualified—such as *puruṣa* (man). This is in accordance with the principle that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) is predominant over the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*). For instance, the king is the qualifier in the relation, and that [relation] is the qualifier in the man; this is because the cognition arises as "the man who has the relation of being the king."

Even according to the view of the Bhāṣya—that the relation denoted by the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha) appears solely as a relational object (saṃsargatayā)—the status of being primary (prādhānya) remains intact. This is because, since a mode-object (prakāratā) is defined by both its relatum (nirūpaka) and its qualificandum (viśeṣya), it possesses a subject-object relation (viṣayatā) that serves as the definitor of the mode-object. Indeed, this [status of being primary] is not established when the genitive occurs after words such as *puruṣa* (person). Furthermore, they say that since the qualificandum, such as *puruṣa*, must necessarily be either a kāraka or the meaning of a nominal stem (prātipadika-artha), the genitive does not occur after a word expressing that [qualificandum], because it would then lack the status of being a "remainder" (aśeṣatva).

Others, however, maintain that due to the very nature of the power of words, the relation is perceived as being manifest only in the qualifier; thus, the genitive case is employed. As it was stated by the followers of Hari:
"Even though this [relation] belongs to both [terms], because it exists for the sake of another, it is distinguished among the qualifiers;
and while being expressed therein, it also serves the primary [term]."

"Because they are for the sake of another"—this means that qualities (*guṇas*) are intended as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to another [substance]. The underlying point is this: in systems that do not accept non-difference (*abheda*) as a relation within the mode of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*), there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the blue pot. Therefore, the accompaniment of difference (*bheda*) is pursued. Since that which is accompanied by difference is necessarily a relation, the expectancy for it arises only in the case of a qualifier; thus, the relation is perceived as manifest only there, and it is precisely there that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) finds its footing.

However, when the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not in proximity to another word, it lacks the expectancy for a relation that would determine its status as a qualificand precisely because it is self-contained (*svaniṣṭhatvāt*). Self-containment means either appearing as a qualificand determined by the ground for the application of its own meaning, or possessing that state. In the case of a subordinate element, a relation—though partially brought into the path of cognition by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth—is also useful for the primary element, since such a relation resides in two relata.

The meaning is that [the genitive case-ending] assists the predicatedness (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the king or other [referents] which are implied when there is co-occurrence with words such as "king" (*rāja*). Only when the word "king" ending in the genitive case is present does [the referent] possess the predicatedness determined by that [king's] meaning, or rather, become an object of cognition by virtue of possessing such predicatedness. The distinction is that in cases such as *rājñaḥ* ("of the king"), even in the absence of a word like "man" (*puruṣa*), there is the cognition of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) as determined by a general relation that is supplied through ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*).

The lordship of the king, being understood by this much alone, leads to the inference of ownership in the person through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, because the relationship is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) while [ownership] is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) to the person, the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*) alone [is used]. For this very reason, since the collection of ownership, lordship, and so forth constitutes the relationship itself, that [collection] alone is the meaning of the case-ending.

It is not [the relation] of ownership (*svatva*) and so forth alone, because that lacks the property of residing in two relata (*dviniṣṭhatva*). One should not argue that ownership is unexceptionally established as such by virtue of its being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*) and thus residing in the owner; for since being a qualifier does not entail a fixed mode of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmakatva*), it is impossible for the owner to possess it. And all of this is clear from the commentary on the present sūtra and other works, so they say.

When there is a desire to express the *puruṣa* as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the genitive case indeed occurs after it, just as in the expression "the king of the limbs" (*aṅgānāṃ rājā*). However, the attempt to prevent the genitive from the word *puruṣa* by accepting that the term *śeṣa* (remainder) signifies what is non-primary (*apradhāna*) is not correct; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the genitive occurring after words such as "white" in expressions like "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*). It appears, however, that this fault does not arise if one prioritizes primacy in the form of a qualificative relation (*viśeṣaṇatā*) delimited by a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*).

In this regard, the following should be understood: the locus-factor (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*), by virtue of its relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*), is not intended to be expressed as a relation [in the sense of a genitive]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on that sūtra that the locative case is prescribed in the rule "tadasyāstyasmin—" for the sake of establishing usages such as *vṛkṣavān parvataḥ* ("the mountain possesses trees"), whereas the genitive case is used for the sake of forms such as *gomān devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta possesses cows").

One might object: "In the expression *adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ* (the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta), the locative case of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) is accepted in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yasmād adhikaṃ...* by means of the passage beginning with *ādhṛtās te tatra bhavanti*. Likewise, here too, the locative case will apply in the sense that 'cows exist in this [place]' (*gāvaḥ santyasmin*). Why, then, is the genitive case employed? If this is asked, the answer is no. For even when one intends to express the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), the genitive is adopted in order to establish forms such as *gomān* ("possessing cows"). This is explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā*. [Example: *annasya hetor vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food").

The genitive case here is prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* ("the genitive occurs when the word *hetu* [cause] is employed"). The meaning of that rule is that the genitive is used after the word *hetu* itself and after words in apposition with it. If the rule had simply stated *hetoḥ*, the genitive would have applied only after the word *hetu* itself, and not after its coreferential modifiers; therefore, it was formulated as it is. The relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) is the meaning of the genitive. The resulting cognition is: "the dwelling has food as its cause. In this context, the word *hetu* serves merely to indicate the intended sense (*tātparya-grāhaka*). The same should be understood for examples such as *annena hetunā vasati* ("he dwells because of food").

The case-ending (*vibhakti*) expresses the purpose (*prayojana*) and the cause (*hetu*) according to their respective roles; others hold that it conveys a cognition characterized by the nature of being a purpose and so forth.

In the examples "the action of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ*) and "Kṛṣṇa is the agent of the world" (*jagataḥ kartā kṛṣṇaḥ*), the genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. Its meaning is "agent" and "object. The resulting cognition is: "an action whose agent is Kṛṣṇa" and "that which is the locus of an action whose object is the world. According to the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), the meaning is "agency" (*kartṛtva*) and "objecthood" (*karmatva*). The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is connected there through the relation of "inherence" (*ādheyatva*); it is connected to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through the relation of "being the determiner of agency" and so forth.

The understanding [derived from the sentence] is: "The effort which characterizes the state of being the agent of the action of making black cloth is the locus of the effort which characterizes the state of being the object (karmatā) consisting in the objective status of the world. This grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) serves only to establish the primary denotative power (*śakti*), and not to establish secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for there is no grammatical rule anywhere that establishes secondary indication—this is explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works. However, in cases such as *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), the genitive case is not applied to the word *kaṭa* etc. by this rule.

By the force of the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule], the genitive is prescribed only for the agent and object of an action that is the object of a mental presence (*upasthiti*) prompted by the apprehension of the power residing in any *kṛdanta* [word] whatsoever. Otherwise, since the prohibition "not with *tiṅ*" (*ana loka-*) would already establish the genitive only in connection with *kṛt* [words], the mention of *kṛt* would clearly be redundant; this has been explained in detail by Kaiyaṭa and others.

In the present case, however, it is not the apprehension of the power of the mere *kṛt* suffix that causes the presentation of the action; rather, it is the apprehension of the power of the *taddhita* suffix. For instance, in the word *kṛta*, the suffix *kta* does not denote the object (*karman*), because otherwise the accusative case in *kaṭam* would be unaccounted for; instead, since the object is not intended to be expressed, the root is treated as intransitive, and the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, this [suffix] occurs only in the scope of a *vṛtti* (compound or derivative formation), as in examples such as *katapūrvī* and *adhītī*. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "When there is a sentence, there is no suffix; when there is a suffix in a general sense, then there is a *vṛtti*."

Regarding the phrase "there is no suffix for the state [of being] at that time," the meaning is that there is no suffix in the sense of a state (bhāve) at that time, because [the root] is transitive (*sakarmaka*). Regarding the phrase "when there is a suffix," the word "in the sense of a state" (*bhāve*) is to be supplied as the remainder, according to the maxim that "every sentence [is incomplete until it is understood]. Regarding the phrase "then there is the occurrence (*vṛtti*)," the meaning is "then there is only the occurrence. And he states "in a general sense" (*sāmānyena*) to show that this [occurrence] is not by means of a suffix ending in *kta* used with an object. The meaning is: by means of a suffix ending in *kta* derived from a verbal root whose expressed meaning is devoid of an object, according to the method already shown.

Thus, it has been stated quite clearly that such a compound does not occur in a sentence. Furthermore, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the relationship between "kṛta" and "kaṭa," which takes the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), ceases once the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix has been produced. By this, it is implied that as long as the *taddhita* suffix has not been applied, the form remains simply "kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ. For this very reason, the expression "kaṭaṃ kriyate" (the mat is being made) is not used.

Then, in the sense that "this was done by him previously," while the rule *apūrvādiniḥ* is still in force, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *-ini* is applied by the rule *sapūrvācca*. Subsequently, when there is an expectancy for a locus (*āśraya*) for the result, it connects with specific objects such as a mat (*kaṭa*). Nor should it be argued that the secondary derivative would not arise due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*); for at the time of its production, such a lack of competency is absent. Thus, it is clear that the action of the base is prompted precisely by the apprehension of the power residing in the word ending in the secondary derivative. Furthermore, it is quite evident that the connection with a factor of action (*kāraka*) occurs even with respect to an action that has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*). As it is said: "Just as an action like 'going,' which is not expressed as a separate word (*avigraha*), is connected with objects such as a village..."

"In the same way, the state [of being] in words such as *kṛtapūrva* is connected with the action"—thus it is stated in the *Harikārikā*. "Without a separate form" (*avigrahā*) means that it becomes the object of presentation precisely as a qualifier of the agent. They have also stated another alternative: "Even when the connection with a specific object is expressed by the *kṛt*-suffixes and so forth..."
Another [type of] word, "kṛta," functions independently of any specific distinction.

"Only when [the root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*) and thus ends in a *kta* suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*), does the connection with an agent possessing action (*kriyāvat*) as an object (*karman*) occur. Here, "attainment" (*nirbhāga*) refers to the acquisition [of the meaning], and it should be understood that this occurs within the sentence (*vākya*). However, in the case of *taṇḍulānāṃ pācakataraḥ* ("one who is a better cooker of rice"), there is no lack of justification for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because even in the separate usage of the word *pācaka*, the cognition of the power residing solely in the *kṛt*-suffix serves as the cause for the presentation of the action (*kriyā*). If, by the term *kṛti*, one were to accept the exclusion of only the additional *taddhita* suffixes, then according to the aforementioned method of the Bhāṣya, the desired result would follow.

The fault consisting in the logical inconsistency of the usage "taṇḍulānām" (of the rice) and so forth is indeed manifest. Since the author of the Bhāṣya, instead of providing the counter-example "taṇḍulān pācakataraḥ" (a better cooker of rice), offers the laborious counter-examples such as "kṛtapūrvī," it is understood that in the case of "taṇḍulānāṃ pācakataraḥ," the author intended the genitive case alone.

Regarding the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā...* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the prohibition by the word *na* does not apply here [to the present case]. This is because that rule prohibits the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) only for an agent or an object that is connected with an action whose presence is triggered by the apprehension of the suffix's capacity as being merely a *niṣṭhā* (past participle) ending. In this instance, however, they say that the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is intended as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), and that the *Bhāṣya* is authoritative. By postulating such a meaning, the prohibition does not apply to the present case, thereby establishing the meaningfulness of the mention of *kṛt*.

Nor is the mention of the *kṛt* suffixes thus rendered useless, because counter-examples such as "the agent previously [engaged] in the mat" (*kartṛvyapūrvī kaṭam*) and "the one previously [engaged] in cooking" (*paktavyapūrvī odanam*) are indeed possible. Even in those cases, the suffix *tavya* can occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the method already stated. Nor should it be argued that such an assumption is invalid because this specific counter-example does not appear in the Bhāṣya; for others have said that even so, the difficulty of finding a practical purpose (*prayojana*) remains unavoidable.

It appears reasonable that even in the absence of an explicit purpose, one should postulate such a meaning on the grounds that otherwise the various noble examples found in the Bhāṣya would be inexplicable. However, in cases such as *kaṭaṃ kṛtavān putraḥ* ("the son made a mat"), the prohibition certainly does apply, because the action is presented by means of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*). Furthermore, if—as per the aforementioned method—it is established that [the son] was preceded by the act of making the mat (*kartavyapūrvī*), then let that too indeed serve as a counter-example.

Others, however, on the authority of the Bhāṣya—which provides the counter-example *kṛtapūrvi kaṭam*—accept that the prohibition applies when there is a connection with a past participle (*niṣṭhā*) or similar suffixes that have not entered into a state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*). "Not having entered into semantic unification" means not being the locus of the semantic unification that depends upon the other [word], since otherwise an impossibility would arise. And thus, in the present case, there is no possibility of the application of that prohibition.

The purpose of such a restriction on the prohibition [of the genitive] is as follows: in the case of *gata ivācarati* (he behaves as if gone), the suffix *laṭ* is applied after the *kvip*-derived form *gata*. In the expression *grāmasya gatatī*, the genitive case for the object (*karman*) is thus established. Furthermore, the prohibition "not [the genitive] when there is a connection with a substitute of *l*" (*lādeśayoge na*) need not be suspected here; for that prohibition is accepted only for the agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) of the primary action (*mukhyaviśeṣyakriyā*) which is presented by the base (*prakṛti*) of *l* and so forth.

Thus, when the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the word *gata* following the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), and when the suffix *ac* from the *pacādi* group is applied, the result is that the genitive case is established in the forms *grāmasya gatakaḥ* and *grāmasya gataḥ*. This is the intended fruit [of the rule]. However, one should not suspect that this results in the application of the genitive case triggered by *ṇvul* and other such suffixes; for a prohibition is stronger than a mandatory injunction, as its very nature is to uproot the possibility of the latter. And they say that all of this is inferred from the examples in the Bhāṣya involving the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), such as *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*.

In the *Tarkaratnākara*, however, it is argued that in expressions such as *pakkapūrvī sūpān* (“one who has previously cooked soup”) and *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* (“one who has previously made a mat”), the meaning of the suffix *-in* alone is the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) conducive to the act of cooking and so forth; the form ending in *kta* (*pakva-* and *kṛta-*) is, on the other hand, devoid of meaning. This is because of the force of the inclusion of the word *kṛti* [in Pāṇini 2.3.65]. Otherwise, since the object would already be expressed by the *kta*-suffix, the genitive case—which applies only when the relation is not already expressed—would not apply, making the inclusion of *kṛti* clearly redundant. Furthermore, the use of forms such as *sūpān* would be untenable, as it would entail the occurrence of the accusative case [if the object were not expressed by the suffix].

In the expression *kṛtapūrvi kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), since the root *kṛ* is transitive, it is difficult to justify the suffix *kta* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the form *gamyate grāmam* ("the village is being gone to"). Nor is the usage of the suffix ending in *kta* redundant, because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) [the suffix *-in*] expresses that very meaning.

Because [the mention of *kṛt*] is meaningful as that which makes the intended meaning (*tātparya*) apprehensible; and thus, since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise be applicable due to the non-expression of the object of the action, the inclusion of the term *kṛt* is purposeful, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is established, and there is no application of the prohibition occasioned by the *niṣṭhā* suffixes—since it has been stated that the prohibition of the sixth case applies only to those [words] whose objects are construed with the action denoted by the base of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes due to proximity—it is clear to those learned in the subject that this is inconsistent with the *Mahābhāṣya*.

Furthermore, the use of the accusative case after words such as *sūpa* (soup) would be untenable, because the aforementioned operation (*vyāpāra*) does not constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and thus lacks the quality of being a result that delimits the meaning of the root. As for the use of the *kta* suffix in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), this has already been established; moreover, following the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities, any over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has also been prevented. Enough of this prolixity. The cognition produced by a sentence such as *kṛtapūrvī* ("one who has previously made") is: "the locus of an operation conducive to the production [of a mat] occurring in the past, having the mat as its object. This rule is non-obligatory (*anitya*), according to the indication in the rule *tadarham*.

Thus, the usage by Bhaṭṭi, "tenādhāyairāmodamuttamam" (having deposited with him the highest fragrance), is justified; such details are explained at length elsewhere. In cases such as "jagat kurvan" or "kurvāṇa," the genitive case is not used, because of the prohibition "na loka-. This concludes the determination of the meaning of the genitive.

In the expression *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("one who has studied grammar"), the locative case is used according to the rule *ktasyenaviṣayaḥ*. This means that the word ending in *-in* (*innanta*) is the "domain" (*viṣaya*), which is to say its sphere of application (*vartanabhūmi*). Alternatively, by the word *viṣaya*, the base (*prakṛti*) is implied; in this view, there is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound: *inaḥ viṣayaḥ*. Here too, as in the case of *kṛtapūrvi*, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract action (*bhāve*). The suffix *ini* is added according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaśca* to denote the agent (*kartari*). The meaning of the locative is [the object, etc. (*karmatvādi*). The resulting cognition is: "one who is the agent of the study having grammar as its object."

In such examples as "one kills the leopard for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*) and "one kills the elephant for its tusks" (*dantayor hanti kuñjaram*), the locative case is used according to the rule *nimittāt karmayoge*. The meaning of this rule is that the locative case occurs after a word denoting a *nimitta* (motive or cause) when there exists a relationship with an object (*karman*) characterized by either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). In this context, the relationship with the object is the actual motive, but it is not included within the denotative scope of the locative case itself.

Thus, the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the seventh case (*saptamī*). It is construed with the action of killing whose object is the leopard and so forth, by way of a relation such as being the specifier of its own status as a fruit. In that context, there is inherence (*samavāya*) between the leopard skin and the antelope horns, while for the other two [the tiger skin and the rhinoceros horn], there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore, the status of being a fruit of the killing for the skins and so forth consists in being the object of a desire that motivates a desire directed toward oneself. The desire that motivates the desire to kill is the desire to obtain the skins and so forth; thus, the status of being such a fruit in the case of the skins and so forth remains intact.

In the system of the logicians (*tārkika*), the meaning of the locative case is either "being the fruit" (*phalatva*), "being the instrumental cause" (*nimittatva*), or "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). They say that this [latter view] alone is correct because of its parsimony (*lāghava*) and because it does not contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). In the examples "He went while the Brahmins were studying" (*brahmaṇeṣv adhīyāneṣu gataḥ*) and "He went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*), the locative is used according to the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*. The meaning of that rule is: when one action (*bhāva* = *kriyā*) is characterized—that is, made known—by another action, then the locative case is applied to the word expressing that [first action].

Since both words, *brāhmaṇa* (in *brāhmaṇeṣv adhīyāneṣu*) and *adhīyāna* (in *adhīyāneṣu*), denote the substratum (*āśraya*) of an action, the locative case (*saptamī*) is applied after both. An action whose time and place are already known serves as a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) for an action whose time and place are unknown, by means of making known its time and place. Thus, this locative case—which sets aside the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—expresses the relationship of indicator and indicated (*jñāpaka-jñāpya-bhāva*) between the agent or object that denotes an action having an unknown location and so forth, and [the action itself].

In this context, since the verbal root denotes merely the action (*kriyā*), there is no contradiction in the object (*karman*) also being its locus (*āśraya*). Among these, some action delimits another action by means of the time that constitutes its own locus, as in the examples cited above. Some [action delimits another] by means of the time immediately preceding its own locus, as in "He went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu dhokṣyamāṇāsu gataḥ*). Some [delimits another] by means of the time immediately following its own locus, as in "He went after the cows had been milked" (*goṣu dugdhāsu gataḥ*).

Furthermore, the relationship between the signified (*jñāpya*) and the signifier (*jñāpaka*)—intended precisely as being understood through those respective words—is the sole cause for the operation of this treatise; it does not depend on apprehension by other means of knowledge (*māna*). Therefore, there is no requirement for repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). For this very reason, the use of the locative case is justified in the aforementioned instance. Otherwise, it would apply only in cases such as "When the sun has risen, darkness is destroyed," and not here. It should be understood that while a connection between the *godohana* vessel and the act of going performed by a specific person may occasionally occur at the same time, it is not an invariable rule.

An example with a locative adjunct (*sadeśodāharaṇa*) is found in such cases as "when there is quality, there is substanceness" (*sati guṇe dravyatvam asti*). Here, the status of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*), which is perceived through the locative case in expressions such as "while the Brahmin is studying," ultimately results in being mediated by the time and other factors of the action that serves as its own qualifier. It should be understood that in cases such as "while the cows are about to be milked" (*goṣu dhokṣyamāṇāsu*), it is not contradictory for even a future event, such as the milking of the cows, to possess the aforementioned status of being an indicator, provided it has ascended to the level of cognition (*buddhyupārūḍha*). [This applies] to an object established by another means of knowledge (*mānāntarasiddha*) regarding time—

This sūtra operates only in those instances where there is an intention to convey a specific relationship (viśeṣasaṃbandha) and so forth, according to the natural intent of both the sūtra and the bhāṣya. Thus, in the case of the injunction "one should bathe during an eclipse of Rāhu" (*rāhūparāge snāyāt*), the term *rāhūparāga* indicates by implication (*lakṣyate*) the time that serves as the locus for its own meaning; here, the locative case is indeed one of locus (*adhikaraṇasaptamī*). Similarly, in the injunction "one should perform the *nāndīmukha* rite at a wedding" (*vivāhe nāndīmukhaṃ kuryāt*), the term *vivāha* indicates the period of time preceding it; the locative case here is just like that in the word *rāhūparāga*, as is explained in detail elsewhere.

Others, however, maintain that in the aforementioned context, [the action] is intended to be understood as being simultaneous with actions such as going or milking; thus, they claim that simultaneity is the meaning of the locative case. Consequently, they argue that through the connection of the milking and so forth—presented by the verbal root *duh*—as the relatum (*nirūpaka*), one obtains the simultaneity of going and so forth with the milking. This, however, is not logically tenable, because it is impossible for an action such as milking, which has become a qualifier of the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix, to be connected with simultaneity.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the locative case-ending to convey its own meaning as unconnected with the meanings of the base (prakṛti), such as "cow" and so on. Therefore, the meaning of the locative is simply the action—such as milking—that is co-occurrent (samabhivyāhṛta) with it. In that context, when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix functions as a qualifier, the meaning of the base is construed with it through the relation of being the determiner of the object (*karmatva-nirūpakatva*). However, when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix denotes an agent—as in "among Brāhmaṇas who are studying" (*adhīyāneṣu brāhmaṇeṣu*)—it should be understood that the construal occurs through the relation of being the determiner of the agent (*kartṛtva-nirūpakatva*). And this [action denoted by the locative] is construed with the act of going and so forth through relations such as simultaneity (*samānakālikatva*).

In that regard, they say that when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix denoting a present object, the relation is simultaneity; in the case of a *kṛt* suffix denoting a future object, it is existence at a prior time; and in the case of a *kṛt* suffix denoting a past object, it is existence at a subsequent time, and so forth. However, others maintain that the previously stated view alone is correct, as it accords with the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, and other authoritative texts.

In the expression *rudati rudato vā prāvrājīt* ("He went forth [into homelessness] while [his son] was crying, or as he was crying"), the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings are applied by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* ("The sixth [case ending is used], and also the [seventh], in the sense of disregard"). The meaning of this rule is the relationship between the indicator (*jñāpaka*) and the indicated (*jñāpya*). The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is "going forth" qualified by disregard. In that context, the sixth and other case endings convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Furthermore, by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the disregard pertains specifically to the son and others. The qualification by disregard is established through two relations: co-referentiality with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇya*) and being subsequent to it (*svottarakālikatva*).

And thus, the understanding is that the renunciation is characterized by disregard, as indicated by the son and others who are the agents of the weeping. In examples such as "Among men, the twice-born is the best," the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41) applies; its meaning is that when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)—consisting of the separation of a single part characterized by a genus, quality, action, or name—from a whole (*yataḥ*), by means of a property that distinguishes it from other members of that same whole, then the sixth and seventh case endings occur.

The sixth and seventh case endings (*ṣaṣṭhī* and *saptamī*) are prescribed here. Furthermore, "separation" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*) consists in making something the object of a cognition whose qualifier is a distinct property; it culminates in an operation conducive to a cognition that has such a single part as its qualificand and such a property as its qualifier. "Being other than itself" (*svetaratva*) means being the locus of a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the property that serves as the delimitor of the referentiality residing in itself.

For this very reason, in such expressions as "the best among men" (*naraṇāṃ naraḥ śreṣṭhaḥ*), although it is possible to effect a separation—by means of which the quality of being "best" in one person consisting of a twice-born (*dvija*) is distinguished from the collection of persons consisting of Śūdras and others by way of a difference delimited by their status as twice-born and so forth—it is nonetheless impossible for that [person] to be the object of the aforementioned selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). This is because there is a contradiction in attributing to the quality of being "best" a state of being excluded from those who possess a difference delimited by humanity (*naratva*); [such an exclusion would imply that the "best" is not a human].

Nor is it for this very reason that the usage "Among men, the twice-born (dvija) is the best" would be impossible—given that a difference relative to a twice-born person could exist even within a twice-born person, making it impossible for "being excluded from a group composed of such a twice-born person" to be possible in the case of "excellence. Rather, the purpose of including the condition of "being a constituent of the group itself" is to prevent such usages as "Among Kṣatriyas, the Brāhmaṇa is the best."

In the expression "There is a best among men, O best of the twice-born" (*asti ca narāṇāṃ dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ*), when the intended meaning is as follows: there is a cognition regarding a *dvija* (twice-born) which has as its qualifier "excellence" that excludes those such as *śūdras* who are members of a group composed of men and possess a difference delimited by being a *dvija*; thus, such usage is justified. In this way, the meaning of the ablative of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-vibhakti*) is the relation of "exclusion. Furthermore, the word *nara* (man) refers to the collection of men other than the *dvija*, either by way of the general form of "manhood" (*naratva*) or by way of a specific form.

And thus, the cognition is that "the twice-born (dvija) possesses excellence as excluded from such a collection of human beings. In the expression "among men, valor resides in the Kṣatriya," the term "among men" refers to the highest among the collection of human beings. And thus, the cognition is that "valor, which resides in the Kṣatriya, is excluded from such a collection of human beings."

Patañjali has stated quite clearly in the commentary on the sūtra "kārake" that, because one intends to express the distinction between the parts as being predominant within the whole, the plural number alone is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) in this context; thus he says, "In the case of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), one should say 'among the *kārakas*' (*kārakeṣu*).
