For this very reason, the authors of the commentaries (*nibandhakāra*) have stated that in the sūtra "midaco'ntyāt," the singular number in "acaḥ" is correct by virtue of being a Vedic or technical usage (*sautratvāt*). This is because, due to the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti-vaicitryāt*), the meaning of a case ending—namely, the state of being excluded (*vyāvṛttatva*)—can apply even to a single part of the referent of a word (*padārthaikadeśe*).

The connection [of the exclusion] occurs either with the excellence (*śreṣṭhatva*) and so forth, or else it occurs with the locus itself through the relation of "possessing that which delimits the category of the object which is its own substratum. By this, the objection—that in cases such as "A jar is that which possesses a conch-like neck," the property of jarhood (*ghaṭatva*) cannot be connected as excluded because the delimitor of the connectedness (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), namely the nature of jarhood (*ghaṭatvatva*), is not presented—is refuted.

One should not raise the objection that, in cases such as "existence (sattā) resides in things possessing a genus (jātimat)," it is impossible to convey the sense of exclusion because existence and the like are contradicted by the absence of a general inherence (*vṛttitva*) defined by anything other than that which possesses a genus; for this reason, the inherence (*samavetatva*) defined by that [other] would be unestablished, and consequently, its absence would also be unestablished. This is not to be feared, because the intended meaning is the absence of inherence delimited by a direct relation (*sākṣātsambandha*). Within the definition of a direct relation, one must include the condition of being distinct from temporal relations (*kālika*) and the like.

Otherwise, since odor exists—by virtue of the relation of temporal succession—even in substances such as water that are distinct from earth, the linguistic usage "substances [in general] have odor" or "earth has odor" would be untenable.

Alternatively, they say that in cases where there is a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word whose denoted object is the predicate related by identity (*tādātmya*), the absence of relation to anything else through identity connects precisely with the referent of words such as "best" (*śreṣṭha*). In cases where the predicate is related by the relation of difference (*bheda*), as in "The excellence among men is in the twice-born" (*narāṇāṃ dvije śraiṣṭhyam*), the absence of occurrence delimited by the previously mentioned relation is conveyed in the excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) and so forth; thus, there is no contingency of partial inherence (*ekadeśānvaya*).

Others, however, maintain that in cases where there is co-referentiality with a word expressing a predicate that is non-different [from the subject], the state of being excluded—consisting in being the counter-positive of a difference—is conveyed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). In cases where the predicate is construed as different, that which is the counter-positiveness of the absolute absence delimited by the relation through which that [difference] is construed is made known in the predicate. It must be admitted that this [counter-positiveness] is construed under the delimitation of the delimitor of the predication-ness (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*).

Therefore, there is no fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in such applications as "Devadatta is the most brave among men," "the jar is the most fragrant among things on earth," and so forth. This is because, although the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the various types of difference residing in the "most brave" and so on exists within the "most brave" itself, it does not exist with respect to the delimitors (*avacchedaka*) such as "most bravery. This is because that [delimitor] is not the delimitor of the locus-ness (*dharmitā*) of such a difference. Alternatively, one should include as qualifiers in the case of difference the property of "not occurring in the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogyavṛttitva*), and in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), the property of "non-coexistence with the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), and so on; by doing so, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

In the case of negation (*bheda*) and so forth, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the property of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*), which is qualified by a negation delimited by the delimitor of the denotatum (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*)—such as *kṣatriyatva* (the state of being a Kṣatriya)—of the word "man" (*nara*) etc., and which is related through the relation of being a substratum (*ādheyatva*) that pervades the delimitor of the denotatum of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), such as *naratva* (the state of being a man). By this much alone, since the exclusion of men other than Kṣatriyas is obtained within the predicate (*vidheya*), the word "man" retains its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*).

In expressions such as *dravyāṇāṃ kṣitipāthasī rasavatī* ("Among substances, earth and water are flavorful"), the relation for the base-meaning in the form of a substance (*dravya*) with respect to the meaning of the case-ending denoting distinction (*bheda*) is the state of being a locus (*ādheyatva*), which is determined by a substratum that pervades the nature of substance and is qualified by the two distinctions delimited by "earthness" and "water-ness. In the case of the predicate, such as "most brave," it is precisely the identity (*tādātmya*) qualified by "manhood" (*naratva*)—which is the delimitor of the base-meaning of the selective case-ending (*nirdhāraṇavibhakti*)—that appears as the relation.

Therefore, they say that there is no undesired consequence (āpatti) regarding the usage of "rākṣasa" and so forth for humans. Others, however, maintain that the venerable author of the Sūtras did not intend for "exclusion" (vyāvṛttatva) to be the meaning of the case-ending. This is because the Sūtra "na nirdhāraṇe" teaches that exclusion is included within the category of meanings expressed by the case-ending; furthermore, there is no evidence that the word "nirdhāraṇa" in that Sūtra has the meaning of "exclusion."

Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that the genitive and locative case endings are used when there is a separation (*pṛthakkaraṇa*)—based on a specific property that excludes [the item] from other members of the aggregate, from that aggregate which consists of its own class and is qualified by genus, quality, action, or name, and which contains a portion thereof. In this context, the referent of the case ending is the state of being the object of the aforementioned selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), as well as the relationship of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*), both of which are coreferential with the item being selected.

The cognition is: "A twice-born person (*dvija*)—who is a member of the group of humans—is the object of a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) characterized by excellence, which excludes non-twice-born humans from the group of humans. The first relation is accepted as the meaning of the case ending in order to exclude such usage as "Among humans, the *śūdra* is the best" (where the excellence does not pertain to the specific category of twice-born), and the second is accepted as the meaning of the case ending in order to exclude such usage as "Among humans, the *rākṣasa* is the most heroic" (where the excellence pertains to a quality other than caste).

Since even a Śūdra possesses superiority in relation to those of the lowest castes and so forth, there would be no way to prevent the occurrence of such usage [i.e., "the Śūdra is the best"] based on the cognition of that [superiority]. Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) that constitutes the relation must be understood as being precisely of the nature of "superiority" and the like. Consequently, there is no possibility of the usage "among men, the Kṣatriya and others are the best. Otherwise, since the Kṣatriya and others would also be objects of the act of separation (*pṛthakkaraṇa*) having "being the most heroic" and so forth as its instrument, such a usage would indeed occur.

In the expression *nṛṇāṃ madhye dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("Among men, the twice-born is the best"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of "in the midst of" (*madhyayoga*). However, the locative case (*saptamī*) in that construction is not correct. Nor should it be argued that even when [the word *madhya*] is present, the locative of specification (*nirdhāraṇasaptamī*) is indeed correct because the sense of "in the midst" is not intended to be connected [to the genitive]. For when that [word *madhya*] is present, its meaning necessarily requires a limit (*avadhi*), and it is therefore more appropriate for it to be construed with that [limit] alone. This is especially so in cases involving the locative of specification, such as in terms like "most excellent" (*śreṣṭhatama*).

The cognition of the exclusion of non-twice-born persons and others, however, when one says "Devadatta with his left eye," occurs only mentally—just like the cognition of the absence of seeing with the right eye as the instrument; for even in a sentence containing the locative case of location, such as "the one remaining in the assembly of the twice-born is the best," such a [mental] perception is necessarily required.

The cognition of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) occurs only when there is the proximity of the delimiter (*avadhi*), the object being selected (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), and the cause of selection (*nirdhāraṇahetu*); therefore, only in such cases does the case ending of selection apply and the prohibition of compounding (*samāsaniṣedha*) hold. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa on the rule *dvivacanavibhajya-* states that in the expression *puruṣāṇām uttamaḥ*, the genitive is the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), and thus the compound *puruṣottama* is grammatically valid. Thus they say.

In the example "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra," however, because there exists a distinction (*bheda*) between the item being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*) and the basis of the selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhi*), the ablative case is applied by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* ("the fifth [ablative] case is used when there is a division"). In that context, the word *vibhakta* signifies "distinct"; thus, the meaning of the rule is that the ablative is used after a word denoting the basis of selection where there is indeed a distinction between the item being singled out and that basis. The restrictive sense is obtained through the force of the inclusion of the term *ibhaktāḥ* ("those who do not eat"). Therefore, this rule does not apply when there is non-distinction in any form whatsoever.

In this context, the meaning of the case-ending is the state of being the object of a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) where the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a property (*dharma*) that distinguishes [the subject] from those excluded by a specific limit (*avadhi*). The understanding is: "The Mathurans are more wealthy than the Pāṭaliputrakas," which means they are the objects of a selection whose instrument is their greater wealth, distinguished from those limited by the Pāṭaliputrakas. Regarding the expressions "one should invoke the Goddess at Mūla" or "one should dismiss her at Śravaṇa," or simply "at Mūla" and "at Śravaṇa," the locative case is used here by the rule *nakṣatre ca lupi*. By the word *lup*, the meaning of the suffix that has been elided (*lupta-pratyaya-artha*) is indicated through the technical designation *lup*.

And thus, the meaning of that [sūtra] is that when words denoting constellations (*nakṣatra*) are used in the sense of such a locative relation (*pratyaya*), the seventh case (*saptamī*) and the third case (*tṛtīyā*) are applied. The term "locative" (*adhikaraṇe*) is obtained through *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from a previous rule). Its purpose, however, is to exclude the application of the seventh case and others in examples such as *adya puṣyaḥ* ("today is Puṣya"), for otherwise, due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*), the suffix would apply only in the sense of the nominal stem itself (*prātipadikārtha*). In the case of *mūlena*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* ("time joined with a constellation"). Therein, by the word "constellation," the moon situated near it is expressed.

The suffix *aṇ* [in the word *mūla*] undergoes elision (*lup*) by the rule "elision when no distinction is intended" (*lubaviśeṣe*). When there is elision (*lupi*), the meaning of the suffix that is being elided is conveyed by the base itself, according to the maxim: "that which remains conveys the meaning. The locative case and so forth denote the sense of the locus (*ādhāra*) and other such relations. Thus, the resulting cognition takes the form: "the invocation having the Goddess as its object, which has as its locus the time associated with the moon situated near the *mūla* constellation," and so on.

"Having eaten today, he will eat in two days or after two days. In this instance, the seventh and fifth case endings are prescribed by the rule *saptamī-pañcamyau kāraka-madhye*. By the term *kāraka*, the capacity (śakti) such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth is denoted. From the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*, the words *kālādhvanoḥ* are understood to carry over [as anuvṛtti]. Thus, the meaning of that [rule] is: the seventh and fifth case endings occur after a word denoting time or distance when those [time or distance] lie between two capacities. The meaning of the case ending is the state of occurring at a time subsequent to [the reference point].

The property of having "this day" (*adya*) as its locus is construed with the act of eating; furthermore, the meaning of the current case-ending is also construed in that very same place—namely, with the act of eating denoted by the absolutive suffix (*ktānta*) which is so construed—by way of both the relation of occurring at a time subsequent to it and the relation of having the same agent.

The meaning is as follows: this [act of eating] is that which has the day as its locus, occurs subsequent to a meal, shares the same agent as such a meal, and takes place at a time immediately following the second day after that day. The fact that "two days" (*dvayahe*) occurs immediately after "this day" is obtained by the force of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). Moreover, even that is not expressed by the words (*śābda*), but is rather implied (*ārtha*). For example, in the sentence "Standing here, one should pierce the target at a *krośa* or from a *krośa*," the meaning of the case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is the state of being located in a space immediately adjacent [to the speaker].

In this context, the locative relation (*adhikaraṇatva*) denoted by the word *iha* (here) is construed with the act of staying (*sthiti*). Such a state of staying resides in the locus of the meaning of the *kṛt*-suffix; that [locus] resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); that [agent] resides in the action of piercing (*vyadhanakriyā*); and in that very action resides the property of having as its object that which is situated in a place one *krośa* beyond the present location. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The piercing—which is the object of possibility—is performed by an agent who is the performer of a stay whose locus is this place, and it has as its object that which is situated in a place one *krośa* beyond this place.
This should be inferred in other cases as well. Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the locative case.

Having thus described the meanings of the well-formed case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*), he explains the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—which consists of all the *kārakas* together with their mutual relations—in accordance with that [description], beginning with the words "In this way" (*evaṃ ca*). "In this way" means: when, according to the stated method, the substrata (*dharmin*) are the meanings of the case-endings. "Having as its locus that which is non-different from them" (*tad-abhinnāśrayaka*) means: the intention is that the cow is construed as non-different from the locus of the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*). "The producer of separation" (*vibhāga-janaka*) means: the intention is that the root *dā-* (to give) functions in the sense of giving preceded by separation.
"Likewise, of the *tiṅ*-suffixes" means: the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffixes is the agent, the object, and number. "Restriction" (*niyama*) refers to the restriction of the meaning.

This is the meaning. And thus, even from an indeclinable (avyaya) whose meaning is devoid of [grammatical relations] such as objecthood (*karmatva*), the derivation of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is established. Regarding the view that the rule concerns the suffixes (*pratyayaniyamapakṣa*), he states the establishment of the case-ending therein: "The restriction (*niyama*) applies to those under discussion. The restriction is in relation to the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth which are under discussion; by the restriction such as "the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs only for the object," the second case and others are excluded from the agent and so forth, but not from that which is devoid of objecthood and the like. This is the meaning.

One might object: "Under the view that [the rules] are restrictive (*niyamapakṣa*), the rules such as *svaujasamauṭ* and *tiptasajhi*—which prescribe the suffixes *su*, etc., and *ti*, etc.—cannot be understood to convey the denotative power (*vācakatā*) of those suffixes with respect to the object (*karman*) and so forth, because the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (and its like) is absent there; nor can the rule *karmaṇi* (and its like) be so understood, since it functions as a restrictor (*niyāmaka*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). [This occurs] through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatayā*), meaning through the unity of the entire sentence (*vākyaikavākyatayā*), not through the unity of individual words (*padaikavākyatayā*).

If that [view] were accepted, then the understanding would necessarily proceed in this sequence: when there is a singularity residing solely in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which is capable of expressing "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, the nominative singular suffix *su* occurs; when there is a singularity co-referential with the capacity for "objectness" and so forth, the accusative singular suffix *am* occurs, and so on. And in this case, it would be impossible to justify the application of [suffixes] elsewhere, such as in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*).

In the case of syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*), however, suffixes such as *svādi* arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and since they occur when [the number] such as singularity is understood as residing solely in the meaning of the nominal stem, the form of cognition arises as "and so forth. This being the case, it would be possible to justify the application [of suffixes] to indeclinables (*avyaya*) and the like by means of the first sentence. Furthermore, in this way, there would be the total abolition of the restriction on meaning (*arthaniyama*), the restriction on suffixes dependent on the contextual meaning (*prakṛtārthāpekṣapratyayaniyama*), and the restriction on pure suffixes (*śuddhapratyayaniyāmaka*).

In the case of words such as *ekavacana* (singular), one must resort to a future designation—like the expression "a cloth made of threads" (*sūtraśāṭaka*)—in order to avoid mutual dependence; furthermore, this involves complexity. Therefore, by the term *ekavākyatā*, it is precisely the unity of the sentence within a larger sentence that is intended.

[Objection: But in this case, how is it possible for [the suffixes] prescribed by each preceding rule to convey meanings such as "action" (karman) and so forth? Nor should it be argued that since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, that [conveying] is indeed possible; for if that were so, then even in the absence of syntactic unity within a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), when a rule such as *dvayekayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.22) effects the understanding that the singular number is used precisely for the sense of oneness, it would be possible to understand it as having the meaning of oneness, and thus the prioritization of syntactic unity between sentences (*vākyaikavākyatā*) would be pointless. [Reply: This is not so.

In the view that they form a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), a sentence-unification (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with the rule for case-endings (*svādi-vākya*) alone is accepted based on the aforementioned reasons, and not with rules such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) or "for the singular and dual" (*dvayekayoḥ*); rather, there is word-unification (*padaikavākyatā*). And thus, by virtue of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) in the form "the singular number of the second case ending occurs only when there is singularity residing in the object," this [result] is obtained here.

However, in the absence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), there would be two contradictory rules: that the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) occurs only for the object (*karman*), and that the singular number (*ekavacana*) occurs only for singularity (*ekatva*). This is untenable; such is the general direction of the argument. In either case, [the rule] would contradict an established restriction. In this regard, the lack of contradiction with the restriction on suffixes—namely, that "the accusative occurs only for the object" and so forth—is evident upon accepting *viṣayatā* (objecthood) as the defining characteristic [of the relation]. It should be understood that even under the view that the restriction pertains to the meaning (*arthaniyamapakṣa*), there is a contradiction with the restriction that "only the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs for what remains (*śeṣa*)" because objecthood is a type of remainder (*śeṣatva*).

Regarding the point thus stated, he cites the agreement even of the ancient Naiyāyikas with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason), and so forth. Thus, it is indicated that the position of the modern Naiyāyikas not only contradicts grammar but also contradicts their own established tradition; therefore, their statement is to be disregarded. The same applies to the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the determination of the meanings of case-endings (*subarthanirṇaya*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra-vyākhyā*, composed by Harirāma, the son of Keśava Dīkṣita, who bears the surname Kāla.

With the intention of first defining the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*) which constitute the basis for all nouns, then the meanings of *tiṅ*-suffixes derived from them, and by extension the meanings of *su*-suffixes, he now defines the meanings of nouns (*nāman*) according to the logical sequence of the occasion; thus he says, "the meanings of nouns" (*nāmārthān*). This means "the meanings of nominal stems" (*prātipadikārthān*). To dispel the suspicion that words such as "one" (*eka*) might refer to unintended meanings due to their common usage, he states the specific meanings intended in this context, beginning with "one is a genus" (*ekaṃ jātiḥ*), and so forth. [He gives the example] "cow" (*gauḥ*), etc.

The meaning is that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) in multiple individuals, or in postulating it in the universal (*jāti*), or in postulating the property of being the delimitant of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) therein. Nor should it be argued that even under the theory of the power residing in the universal, one must admit the property of "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) and so forth as the delimitant of denotability; and thus, since that [delimitant] necessarily possesses denotability in the form of "being inherent in all cows while not being inherent in anything other than cows," the complexity is actually reversed. For here, just as even that which is not the primary object of definition (*alakṣya*) can serve as the delimitant of the definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), so too even that which is not directly denoted (*aśakya*) can possess denotability.

Nor can it be argued that there is an unnecessary complexity (gaurava) resulting from the acceptance of a cumbersome delimitor (*avacchedaka*), because the word and its meaning are identical (*tādātmya*); thus, it is the genus (*jāti*) residing in the word itself that serves as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). Alternatively, the property residing in that [genus] is of the nature of a specific property belonging to the realm of ignorance (*āvidyaka-dharma-viśeṣa*). This is clear from other sources: in expressions such as *gotvatvam* ("the state of being cow-ness"), it is precisely that [genus] which is the meaning of the suffix *-tva*, and not a property consisting of "not inhering in anything other than cows," due to the latter's complexity.

"In the case of another individual through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)"—the ellipsis is "if it were accepted," and such acceptance is necessary because it would otherwise be impossible to account for the cognition of another individual. "'Inhering in itself'": the meaning of the word *sva* (itself) is a specific individual intended to be the denotable object (*śakyārtha*). "Thus there is parsimony" (*lāghavam*): the point is that this aforementioned parsimony serves as the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*), and therefore there is no lack of a deciding criterion. Furthermore, he states that it is logical that the universal (*jāti*) alone is the denoted meaning because it is that upon which [the cognition of the individual] depends, beginning with the words "not without having grasped... (*nāgṛhītā...*).

The core of the maxim is: "A cognition that has not apprehended the qualifier does not reach the qualificand. Since the knowledge of the qualifier is the cause for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), a cognition of this kind whose qualifier has not been apprehended cannot have as its object a qualificand qualified by that qualifier. By the two negative particles (*nañ*), it is first indicated that the apprehension of the qualifier is necessary. This very point was stated by the Bhaṭṭas:
"The denotative function (*abhidhā*) cannot proceed to the qualificand once its power is exhausted in the qualifier."

[Objection: In that case, there would be no cognition of the individual (vyakti). Nor should it be argued that it is obtained through implication (ākṣepa), as in the case of "Fat Devadatta [is here]" implying "he eats at night"; for in cases such as "One should give a cow," the connection of the objecthood (karmatva) and so forth with the individual would be untenable, since the individual is not presented by the function (vṛtti) of the base (prakṛti). This is because of the linguistic rule (vyutpatti) that suffixes are connected with the meaning of the base. Furthermore, in that case, there could be no connection with other word-meanings, because such connection occurs only with the qualificand (viśeṣya) of the grasp of the function (vṛttigraha). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such connection even with ether (ākāśa), which is presented [to consciousness] by way of inherence (samavāya). For it has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*: [text follows].

"Furthermore, no qualification (viśeṣaṇa) is ever observed for an object that is currently being traversed [i.e., an action], whether by another word or by a case-ending, as in the expression 'this smoke is burning. The meaning of "qualification" here is either the exclusion that serves as a qualifier, or the presentation of something as possessing a cognitive objectivity termed "qualificative-ness" (viśeṣaṇatā). Moreover, even an implication (ākṣepa) in the form of a logical necessity (āpatti) is not possible; for we observe comprehension from statements such as "one should give a cow" even without the cognition of an inconsistency (anupapatti). The teachers (Guravaḥ) maintained that implication consists precisely in being cognized through the same act of awareness (samānavittivedyatva).

And as it has been stated by them: "To whatever extent the cognition of a universal (jāti) takes an individual (vyakti) as its object, therefore, the very causal complex that manifests the universal must be admitted to manifest the individual as well. Since there is no perception of the universal without the perception of the individual, this restriction is determined precisely therein; and thus, it follows that the knowledge of the word's power (śakti) regarding the universal is itself the cause for the verbal cognition which has the individual as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) and the universal as its qualifier (prakāra). But even that is not correct.

This being the case, since there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition qualified by "cowness-ness" (gotvatva) from the statement "cowness exists," others maintain that the meaning of the word [cow] as implied by the definition (lakṣaṇā) is precisely what is intended. And thus, the connection with the meaning of the case-ending and so forth is indeed possible within the individual (vyakti) presented by that [definition]. Others, however, do not accept this, because since a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) depends upon the knowledge of the impossibility of the connection between the primary meaning and the context, it is swallowed up by the aforementioned defect; therefore, he says: "But the cognition of the individual... [The phrase] "by way of metaphorical indication" means by way of a conventional or established metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā).

The point here is that there is no requirement for the cognition of the impossibility of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. By the term "by way of secondary indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*), the non-difference (*abheda*) between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) is also implied. As it has been stated by the Bhaṭṭas:

"Therefore, because the connection with the action is understood through the individual indicated by that [universal], either the non-difference of the individual and the form (*ākṛti*) is intended in the meanings of sentences."

It is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *taddhitārtha-*: "Alternatively, due to distinction (*vyatireka*), there is the bringing of the substance [as distinct] from the substance's form. However, a word such as *gotva* (cowness) possesses the power (*śakti*) for a property residing in cowness; therefore, no cognition having an object qualified by cowness arises from it. Now, one might object: "This is inconsistent with the principle that 'metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs when the denoted object is known through a form other than its own.'"

If it is argued that, by this rule, a cognition having the denoted *gotva* (cowness) as its qualifier and a particular individual as its object cannot be established through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), we say no; for there is no evidence for such a restrictive rule. Furthermore, since a cognition having the denoted white color and so forth as its qualifier and a particular individual as its object arises from expressions such as "bring the white [cow]" (*śuklam ānaya*) through secondary signification, the proposed rule is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). With this in mind, he says "the direction" (*dig iti*). It is precisely with this intention that the Vārttika—"The mention of *aṇ* in the rule for homogeneous letters (*savarṇe*) is not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*), because of the inclusion of the generic form (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*)"—is consistent.

It is also stated in the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa-sūtra*: "Vājapyāyana [holds that the word denotes] the form (*ākṛti*). However, other Mīmāṃsakas argue that just as in the view that the power (denotative capacity) resides in the individual (*vyakti*), the power or its delimiting condition (*avacchedakatā*) with respect to the aspect of cowness (*gotva*) and so forth is undelimited (*niravacchinna*), so too in the view that the power resides in the genus (*jāti*), that [power] is likewise undelimited. Consequently, there is not even the slightest suspicion of the complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the inclusion of "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) and so forth. For this very reason, even in this view, the manifestation of cowness and so forth in their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) is established within verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

[Objection: "But surely, even if the property of being 'cowness-ness' (*gotvatva*) and so forth lacks the status of being the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is unavoidable; for in the causal factor for grasping the denotative capacity, the property of being 'cowness-ness' must enter as the object characterized by the relation called 'delimitor of the subject' (*dharmitāvacchedakatāviṣayatā*). This is because, in the theory that the individual possesses the denotative capacity (*vyaktiśaktivāda*), only the delimiting-ness residing in 'cowness' and so forth, taken in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), is introduced [as the object]. [Reply: No.

This is because it is accepted that the cause [of verbal cognition] is precisely the knowledge of the word-potency (*śaktijñāna*), which takes the form "the word 'cow' has the potency [for the cow]" or "the word 'cow' is the cow"; this knowledge has as its qualifier the word "cow" (which functions as the qualificandum) and as its qualificandum the potency, with the property of cowness (*gotva*) as its mode by way of the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*). Furthermore, in that case, the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of cowness and so forth does not enter into the causal structure.

They stated that there is no such rule that "only through inherence (samavāya) is there being a qualifier by way of its own nature (svarūpataḥ)," because in the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) "I know the jar," one accepts that jar-ness and so forth are qualifiers in the portion of the cognition itself by way of the relation of being a qualifier (prakāritā), even though they exist by way of their own nature; such is the direction of their argument. Raising an objection against this view and stating the proof for the position that the word's power resides in the individual (vyakti), he says "or else" (yadvā) to establish that a single word refers to the individual. "The individual alone" (kevalavyaktireva): the word "alone" (eva) excludes the universal (jāti).

The word *kevala* (alone) serves as a clarification for the sake of clarity, since the exclusion [of other views] is already established by that very term. It refers specifically to the position that the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the meaning of the word. However, according to the view that the meaning of a word is the individual qualified by a universal (*jāti*), the capacity (*śakti*) is grasped as having a qualificandumhood delimited by that universal. Consequently, because the cognition of the word—delimited by the nature of being a word—is a cause for a cognition whose qualificandum is the locus of that universal and whose mode (*prakāra*) is that universal, it would be possible to grasp all individuals that are the loci of universals such as *atva*. Thus, the mention of the letter *a* in the rule *aṇudit* would be redundant.

However, according to the view that the suffix possesses only the power to denote genus (*jāti*), its redundancy is quite evident. The word "of the mention of *aṇ*" (*aṇgrahaṇasya*) is to be construed with "by the introduction" (*ārambheṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "and of *ekaśeṣa*": the meaning is by means of the formulation of the rule "of those that are similar" (*sarūpāṇām*). The formulation of *ekaśeṣa* serves as the proof for the view that the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning, but not for the view that the individual alone is the word-meaning; for even if the word-meaning were an individual qualified by a genus (*jāti*), the formulation of that rule would still be necessary. Alternatively, it should be understood that since it will be explained later how multiple objects unified by a particular genus are conveyed by a single word, this [formulation] establishes that the individual alone is the word-meaning.

Nor should it be argued that even if a universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, the formulation of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule is necessary to justify expressions such as "akṣāḥ" (dice), since there is no single universal common to dice, beans (*māṣa*), and ropes (*pāśa*)—and thus one would have to intend multiple universals such as "bean-ness" and "rope-ness. This is because the word "akṣa" is derived from the root *aś* (to pervade); therefore, we accept that the universal consisting of "pervasiveness"—which resides in the meaning of the root—is denoted by the word "akṣa" in relation to beans, ropes, and so forth, through a mediated relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) consisting of inherence-in-that-which-is-inherent-in-itself (*svasamavāyi-samavāya*).

And so it has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the *Sarūpa-sūtra*: "The [term] *akṣa* is established there because of the generality (*sāmānya*) of the action in the root *aś*. This means the generality residing in the action. Others, however, say that the meaning is: the generality invariably concomitant with such an action is inherent in the three things denoted by the word *akṣa*. And thus, since such a genus is possible, the aforementioned fault finds no place; having stated that the scripture is the authority even for that position—the view that the word denotes only the individual—he also provides reasoning as proof for it, saying, "And this is logical."

"Only in the individual" means that the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs only with respect to the individual, because the power is grasped through the subsequent practical activity (*vyavahāra*)—such as bringing a jar—performed by the person being prompted immediately after the utterance of the sentence "Bring the jar. Now, one might object: even if the apprehension of the power is initially formed with respect to the individual, it is later sublated (*bādhyate*) on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). Sublation, defined as the apprehension of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyagraha*), is seen when a previously perceived astronomical fact regarding the moon’s orb, for instance, is sublated by the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), and not merely by parsimony; thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that even a previously established determination of a *karmadhāraya* compound would be sublated later for fear of postulating an unprecedented (*apūrva*) meaning, and thus there would be a contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati* section [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras], we say no; for that which was previously established...

Because sublation is impossible on the basis of mere parsimony (*lāghava*). Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in the injunctions "one should cause a Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice" and "one should give a cow," since, according to the view that the word's power resides in the genus (*jāti*), the giving of the genus *gotva* (cowness) and so forth is impossible. Nor is it correct to argue that this is resolved by taking the individual denoted through secondary indication (*lakṣita-vyakti*), because no relation with the primary power (*śakya*) can be apprehended in one individual, and a relation apprehended with respect to one individual cannot produce the cognition of another individual.

Otherwise, from the apprehension of the relationship between a mahout and a single elephant—where "elephant-ness" is the delimiting property of the subject—one would incur the undesirable consequence of remembering another elephant upon seeing a mahout at a later time. Furthermore, there would be the burden of postulating two distinct functions (*vṛtti*) in sentences such as "Bring the cow. For this very reason it is said: "No one indeed intends to express the existence or non-existence of a universal;
for these two [properties] are qualifiers of the individual, which is indicated by the universal because it is eternal."

Thus, even what was stated by Maṇḍana Miśra is refuted. If it is argued that the connection with the act of giving [the cow] occurs because there is no difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), the implication is that the denotability of the individual has already been accepted. Now, if it is objected that since individuals are infinite, this would entail an infinity of linguistic capacities (*śakti*), and that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the capacity resides in only a certain individual—[we reply: if that were so, then even when an individual whose capacity has not been grasped is understood, the capacity-grasping (*śaktigraha*) would fail to be the cause of verbal cognition due to its lack of invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, since there is no difference in their not being objects of the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti*), it would follow that even things such as *taṭa* (a riverbank) could be understood from the word *ghaṭa* (pot). As it has been stated by the Mīmāṃsakas and others: "Because of [the faults of] infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and because of the defect of having multiple denotative powers (*śakti*)."

Dispelling this doubt, he says: "of the delimitor of relatedness" (*saṃbandhitāvacchedakasya*). This means "of the delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakasya*). The construction is: "of that which consists of a universal" (*jātirūpasya*). And thus, because it is precisely the delimitor of relatedness that is intended as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the neuter gender is justified. Otherwise, one would have to say "of the female [delimitor] of relatedness" (*saṃbandhitāvacchedikāyāḥ*); this is how it should be understood. "Only one" (*ekaiva*).

The point is this: although the individual instances (*vyakti*) capable of being denoted are infinite, they are unified because the genus (*jāti*), such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which serves as the secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), is one; thus, there is unity [of the denotation]. This is just as, although the individuals that serve as the locus (*āśraya*) and the relatum (*nirūpaka*) of a causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*) are many, there is unity [of the capacity] because the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), such as "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), is one. Furthermore, since the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*)—which has as its object a substratum delimited by a particular property—is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdatva*) delimited by having that property as its qualifier and that substratum as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even if it is impossible for the apprehension of power to have all individual instances as its object.

The point is that, since the specific individualities (*tattad-vyakti*) are not included within the scope of the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and "being a cause" (*kāraṇatva*), there is no contingency of a cloth or the like being understood from the word "jar," nor is there the contingency of a jar appearing as having "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) as its qualifier. He raises an objection: "And not thus... That is to say, if "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth were the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). [The response continues: "...because of being the delimiter of denotability."

The point is that since being the delimitor of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka) residing in the object grasped by the apprehension of the word's power (śaktigraha) constitutes being the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatva) when denotability is possible, it follows necessarily that even "potness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth must be denotable. "That alone is the denotable" means that, in this way, the position that only the individual (vyakti) is denotable is utterly destroyed by its own impossibility; such is the intended meaning. "Even though it is not the object of definition" (alakṣyatve 'pi).

Just as in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) characterized by the qualifier *tīratva* (bankness) is achieved simply through the apprehension of the relation of the denotatum—namely, the flowing current—to that which is delimited by *tīratva* (the bank); for it is the very apprehension of [the current] as the delimitor of the relatum-ship (*saṃbandhitāvacchedakatva*) that serves as the cause for the object's presence (*upasthiti*) and so forth, and not the fact that this [delimitor] is also part of the collective intended meaning (*samuditatātparyārtha*).

The objection that even if [the property] is the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), it might still be accepted as the delimitor of the relation to that [property] even when devoid of a relation consisting in occurrence (*vṛtti*)—is thus refuted. Furthermore, this example belongs to the system of the Naiyāyikas; however, in the systems of the Alaṃkārikas and others, there is indeed *lakṣaṇā* (indication) even with respect to the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Thus it has been said: "When the primary meaning is sublated, and there is a connection [between that primary and another], another meaning is indicated either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*); that is *lakṣaṇā*."

"It is indicated" (*lakṣyate*) means "it is known. And thus, there is no self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, they say that since this [indication] consists in the presentation of the impossible through the possible, its existence as an object (*viṣayatā*) within the delimiting property of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is likewise beyond dispute; such is the direction of the argument. To support the stated point, he cites the statement of Bhaṭṭa found in the *Uṇādi* section: "Even though there is infinity," etc. "Of entities" (*bhāvānām*) refers to things like jars (*ghaṭa*), which are intended to be denotable. "One" (*ekam*) refers to a universal such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which is connected to many individuals. "A connection that is easy to establish" (*sukarasambandhaḥ*)— [...]*Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

The apprehension of the relationship is easy; "relationship" here means in the form of a *śakti* (potency). And the intended meaning of the phrase "it will not deviate" has already been stated. Regarding the expression "of that whose referent is the *ākṛti* (form/class-character)": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that for which the *ākṛti* is the word-referent. This is from the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, this is the *Bhāṣya* located in the *Sarūpa-sūtra*. "The qualified [entity] is the denotable object": the meaning is that the cow and so forth, as qualified by the universal (*jāti*), are the denotable objects of the words "cow" and so forth.

For this very reason, there is no violation of the rule that the word-form (*śabdarūpa*)—as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) equal in status to the object-meaning (*arthapramāṇa*)—grasps only its own related object, such as when one says "the denotable object of the words 'eye' and so forth."

Others, however, argue that the Bhāṣya—stating, "For it is not the case that for one for whom the universal (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, the substance (*dravya*) is not the word-meaning; nor is it the case that for one for whom the substance is the word-meaning, the universal is not the word-meaning; rather, both are the word-meaning for both, such that for some one is primary and the other is secondary"—indicates by its description of the universal as a qualifier in the theory where substance is the word-meaning, that even in that view, the *ekaśeṣa* (the single-remainder formation) need not be commenced. This is because, through a single word alone, the cognition of multiple individuals qualified by that genus is possible.

They say that it is also indicated [in this context] that in the theory where the genus (*jāti*) is the denotatum, the individual (*vyakti*) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), whereas in the theory where the individual is the denotatum, the genus is the delimitor of the denotative capacity. Now, one might object: "If the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is the meaning of the word, then the term 'one' (*eka*) would be contradictory. To this, he says: "And as for the term 'one'... The particle *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tu*). "This" refers to what is about to be stated. "The genus alone" means: in the causal efficiency residing in the knowledge of the denotative power (*śaktijñāna*), the genus alone is the delimitor with respect to the objective relation (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), and not the individual; the point is that there is no causal efficiency based on the knowledge of the power having the individual as its object.

In this view, it should be understood that the meaning of "one" in the phrase "one [name] has one object" is that the universal (*sāmānya*) alone serves as the delimitor of such causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). He clarifies this very point with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Regarding the phrase "not having another as its qualifier in the aspect of potness" (*ghaṭatvāṃśe'nyāprakāraka*): by this, there is no resulting cognition of a qualified pot from the statement "potness exists. The same applies to the statement "the universal exists. By this, the objection—that in order to prevent such a cognition from arising from the statement "potness exists," it is necessary for the causal capacity to reside in the knowledge of a qualified power (*viśiṣṭaśaktijñāna*)—is refuted.

Since the word "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) has its denotative power (*śakti*) restricted solely to that which is delimited by the property of pot-ness, it is possible for there to be a cognition of power whose mode is precisely that [property] regarding the aspect of pot-ness. This very view is called the "theory of crooked power" (*kubjaśaktivāda*) by the Mīmāṃsakas. There is no evidence for the restrictive rule that "only that object regarding which a cognition of power is a cause [of comprehension] possesses denotability"; thus, the denotability of the individual (*vyakti*) is established. If it is objected: "Due to the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*), let the cognition of power have as its object the individual itself, and let it be a cause for such comprehension simply by virtue of having the individual as its object," we say no. This is because individuals are infinite; if one were to include "having all infinite individuals as objects" [in the definition of the cause], it would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no complexity [in the theory] because one should simply stipulate that the objectivity consists in being a particular that is the locus of some universal; for if even the cognition of the word-potency (śakti) for words such as ‘substance’ were to have causality solely by virtue of having a particular that is the locus of the universal ‘substanceness’ as its object, then it would follow that from the word ‘pot’ (ghaṭa), too, there would arise a cognition having ‘substanceness’ as its qualifier.

Intending to state that such matters as the impossibility of accounting for a cognition qualified by "substanceness" (dravyatva) through other synonymous terms—which would necessitate accepting the knowledge of the word *dravya* itself as the cause—should be seen in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*, he says: "It has been explained at length in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. This [objection] is to be resolved, as before, by accepting the meaning that [the word] is the delimiting condition of such causality through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*). Otherwise, there would be an obvious contradiction: in the previous view, only one [of the two] is the meaning of the noun, whereas in this view, both are so.

In the previous case, the contradiction regarding the qualified entity being the word-meaning was resolved; here, however, that [contradiction] is resolved by both [the gender and the number] being so. Now, one might object: "Femininity and the like, intended [by the definition] as a specific configuration of parts—as in the statement 'a woman would possess teeth and hair'—cannot sustain the technical system of this grammar. For if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of the *natva* substitution in forms such as *dārān*. Nor is it tenable to resolve this through superimposition (*āropa*), because such superimposition is impossible for those who perceive the specific reality."

Nor should it be argued that such a non-noble [entity] is impossible; for even in its absence, such usages are accepted. For this very reason, having raised the objection that the definition of "femininity" and so forth provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya* in the rule *striyām* is untenable, he follows the method stated in the *Bhāṣya* by saying "in existence" (*sattve*). [Objection: But surely, since contradictory properties such as increase and decrease cannot coexist in one place, forms such as *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam* would be untenable.

Nor is it correct to argue that this [usage] is established by prioritizing the momentariness of the qualities (*guṇas*); for even so, the impossibility of such simultaneous conventional usage remains difficult to avoid. Furthermore, since accumulation and the like are impossible in that which is changeless, usages such as "Brahman is the Self" would be untenable. If one insists on superimposition (*āropa*), then the disregard for worldly indicative marks (*liṅga*) would be groundless; therefore, he says: "resting upon those respective words.

Now, even in this view, the problem of the impossibility of multiple contradictory marks in a single word remains as it was; to this he replies: "that very same [word], though contradictory... He says: "they differ," and thus:

There is no room for the aforementioned objection. [Objection: But if this is so, then the conventional usage [expressed in grammatical works] such as "the word *taṭa* [is used] in three genders" would be untenable; therefore, he says, "of some. [The phrase] "on account of similarity" refers to the cause for the superimposition of non-difference (*abhedāropa*). [The phrase] "and thus" means: and when gender is inherent in the word itself. Others, however, maintain that because the three states—accumulation and so forth—are universal, this gender is a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayi*), since usages such as "this is a substance," "this is an individual," and "this is an object" proceed unimpededly, being established by all people.

And that [gender] is based on the object (*arthaniṣṭha*). For the *Bhāṣya* states: "Because there is a difference in words for a single object, a difference in gender is observed, as is a difference in grammatical components (*avayava*). The teacher Kaiyaṭa explains: "The meaning is that because we observe various words such as *puṣyatārakā*, *tārakā*, and *nakṣatra*, gender—which is distinct from things like breasts or hair—is based on the object; and because we observe a difference in gender when the component letter *r* is added, as in *kuṭī* and *kuṭira*. For this very reason, it is stated in the introductory *Bhāṣya*: "For color, taste, smell, touch, and sound, the feminine and masculine genders are based on solidity (*styāna*) and productivity (*prasava*)," since color and the other qualities do not reside in the word itself.

If it is objected that, in this case, the conventional usage "the word is masculine" would be untenable, we say no; for such usage is possible either through the metaphorical attribution of identity (*abhedopacāra*) between the signified and the signifier, or because [the term *puṃliṅga*] ends in the suffix *ac* (as in *darśa*). Furthermore, the establishment of usages such as "the Self is Brahman" is possible because everything is superimposed upon Brahman, and because [Brahman] exists as a continuous, beginningless reality through a traditional lineage (*saṃpradāya*).

One should not say that "forms such as *taṭaḥ* and *taṭī* are untenable because mutually contradictory properties like augmentation (*upacaya*) cannot coexist in a single locus," for there is no contradiction at all, given the authority of the lexicons (*kośa*), the Bhāṣya, and other sources. It should be understood from the lexicons and similar authorities that one word denotes an object qualified by a single gender, while another denotes an object qualified by two genders, and so forth. In this regard, although it would have been more appropriate to assign a short technical designation (like *ṭi*, *ghu*, or *bh*) rather than a long one, the fact that a long designation was employed implies that even worldly gender (*liṅga*) is accepted as a causal factor when rules concerning nasality (*natva*) and other grammatical operations are to be applied.

Just like the designation of numbers, although the technical designations such as *puṃs* (masculine) and so on serve the purpose of including additional cases, they do not serve to exclude meanings established by common worldly usage (*lokaprasiddha*). When a worldly meaning is not possible, then only the technical (*śāstrīya*) [designation] applies, and there is no application of terms like *natva* (the substitution of *na*). However, when that worldly meaning is possible, it is only the worldly one qualified by the technical [rule] that applies, and not the purely technical one alone; for through the grammatical operation such as *natva*, there is the cognition of the worldly gender (*liṅga*) residing in the object itself. "Manifestation, disappearance, and persistence—these properties, which are ever-present in all material forms, are established as the basis for gender."

Thus, even from the *Harikārikā*, it is determined that its [the gender's] status is restricted solely to the meaning (*arthaniṣṭatva*). Here, by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that when possible, even worldly gender (*laukika-liṅga*) serves as the cause for the application of suffixes such as the feminine marker *ṭāp*; this and more was established in the *Mañjūṣā*. Now, an objection is raised: if that [gender] were restricted to the word (*śabda-niṣṭhatva*)—that is, if it were denotable by the word itself—then since its connection to the meaning would be impossible, one could perform even with a goat the sacrifice enjoined by the rule "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). To this, he says: "And that gender... [and so on]. [The phrase] "by way of delimiting the meaning" (*arthaparicchedakatvena*)...

The meaning is: "by way of being its qualifier. Since it is established by the science of grammatical gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) that only that which is qualified by a specific gender expresses a specific object, it is logically consistent for [gender] to be a qualifier of the object through the relation of being expressed by its own substratum.

And thus, since it is precisely a male animal (*paśu*) qualified by masculinity that is enjoined, there is no contingency of the he-goat (*chagī*) being its instrument. The point is this: the masculine gender of the word *paśu* denotes only a male individual; otherwise, the assumption that it functions as a qualifier of the meaning through a mediated succession would result in its own uselessness. [The phrase] "stated by words such as *paśu*" has the ellipsis: "masculinity follows as a delimiter of the meaning of the word *paśu*. [The statement] "the animal does not exist in the female" [is explained as follows].

If the word "animal" (*paśu*)—which occurs within the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal"—does not apply to a female because it conveys masculinity through its absence [of femininity], then for that reason the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" does not enjoin goats and the like as subordinate elements; the meaning is that it does not include them. Now, one might object: if there were a rule that the masculine word "animal" denotes only a male individual, then what was stated would be possible; however, anticipating that this is not the case, he raises the doubt with the words "not so" (*na ca*).

Regarding the phrase "denoted by words such as 'individual' (*vyakti*)": just as the gender denoted by words such as "individual" is common [to both sexes]—in that it is connected to males and so forth through the relation of being denoted by its own substratum—and for that very reason serves to distinguish those respective objects, so too the gender denoted by words such as "animal" (*paśu*) would likewise not be a distinguisher, because it is connected to female individuals through the aforementioned indirect relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*). This is because only that which is restricted to [one sex] alone can serve as a distinguisher, whereas that which is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) cannot.

This is the collective meaning [of the passage]. The term "of the gender" (*liṅgasya*) is to be supplied here as referring to that which is expressed by words such as *paśu* (animal). He provides the rebuttal—starting with "Because the word *vyakti*..."—that although the word *vyakti* is common [to both genders] due to its feminine suffix *-ktin*, the word *paśu* is not common because there is no evidence for it being eternally feminine; rather, it is eternally masculine. As for the phrase "because it is seen in the Veda," the intention is that since the form *paśv-* and so forth is observed, the word *paśu* occurs even in the feminine gender. It is quite clear that if it were masculine, the stated form would be unestablished due to the application of the substitute [nasalizing] *n*.

Likewise, due to the application of *guṇa* by the rule "a-gher ṅiti," the form *paśve* would remain unestablished. Now, one might object: even in the feminine gender, the failure to establish the aforementioned form remains just as it was due to the application of *guṇa*. Nor can it be argued that the designation *nadī* applies by the rule "ṅiti hrasvaśca," thereby precluding the designation *ghi*; for if that were so, the aforementioned defect would persist because the augment *āṬ* would apply. To this we reply: no, because the augment *āṬ* does not apply since the word ends in *ch*, which is easily accounted for. This is the intended meaning.

One should not suspect that the usage [of the masculine] is established by the rule "In the Veda, there is an option regarding *jas* and so on" (*jasādiṣu cchandasi vāvacanam*), for even in the feminine gender, the explanation is possible through the aforementioned method without resorting to that rule. This is because the intention is that, since the irregularity of the grammatical rules (āgamaśāstra) is observed in cases such as "desirous of crossing the ocean" (*sāgaraṃ tarttukāmasya*), one need not rely on its being Vedic (*chāndasatva*) for the application of the prefix *āṅ* in those instances. He also states another reason proving the other gender: "In the Mīmāṃsā," meaning in the fourth chapter (*caturthe*).

This is to be understood in its first quarter. One might object: "The claim that there is no evidence for its being invariably masculine is inconsistent, because grammar itself—specifically the rule that 'words ending in the suffix u are masculine'—is the very authority [for this]. Anticipating this objection, the author states "But in reality" (*vastutas tu*) to preclude the possibility of selecting a female goat (*chāgī*) by another means, even though there exists evidence for the word *paśu* being invariably masculine. This is based on the statement: "It is not the absence of an absence."

And likewise, the point is that even if the word *paśu* were restricted to the masculine gender, constructions such as "and [the animal] of the beast" (*paśośca*) would still be untenable. "Due to the determination of its constant masculinity" means "due to the determination of its constant masculine gender. And thus, the point is that because masculinity is common [to both genders], it cannot function as a differentiator.

And likewise, even if the aforementioned reasoning that excludes the female individual is untenable, he shows another reason for excluding her by citing the sūtra of the final section of the sixth chapter: "Or rather, the goat [is meant], because of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*). For there, it was determined in the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" (*agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta*) that the word "animal" (*paśu*) does not refer to a horse or other such creatures, but specifically to a goat, on account of the wording of the mantra "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*). Similarly, the meaning is that the male gender is also determined from that very same source.

Just as in the section "But when there is doubt, [the decision is] from the remainder of the sentence" (Yathāsaṃdigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt), where a decision regarding an injunction in case of doubt is made on the basis of the remainder of the sentence—just like [the determination of] number and so forth—as in the case of the statement "There are two rams for Sarasvatī," where a doubt arises as to whether the base word of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is masculine or feminine, it was concluded by means of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "This indeed is a divine pair," that both genders are included through the principle of *ekaśeṣa*.

[Objection: Let it be so for the aforementioned case; nevertheless, since the gender residing in a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is common to both sentient and insentient beings, as well as to females and males, it would follow that the *adhvaryu*-priest’s injunction, "Bring the firewood for him" (*prāsmā agniṃ bharata*), would apply even to a female [victim]. Nor is this a desirable consequence, as it contradicts the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine. However, there is no such fault under the view that worldly gender (*laukika-liṅga*) is the denotation [of the pronoun], because when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one, and thus even metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) is impossible. [Reply: This is not so.

Because words such as *asmai* (to him) and *enam* (him), which present the object in its previously established form, bring to mind animals qualified by masculinity (*puṃstva*) and so on—just as they bring to mind those qualified by "goat-ness" (*chāgatva*) and so on—it is possible that these [words] would not apply to a female sheep (*mेषी*). With this intention—that the details should be sought in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*—he says: "It has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. Even under the view that gender resides in the object itself, it should be understood that only the male individual is to be taken, according to the principle of "the goat, indeed, [is the animal] for the mantra," etc.
The Vaiśeṣikas, however, hold that masculinity and the like are universals (*jāti*), as stated by Harisvāmin: [text follows].
"Thus, these three types exist for some [thinkers], coexisting without contradiction alongside contradictory types such as 'cow-ness,' 'buffalo-ness,' and so forth.

The meaning is that these [three] exist in mutual non-contradiction with mutually contradictory types such as "cowness," "buffalooness," and the like. Helārāja states: "For some—namely, the Vaiśeṣikas."

The intended meaning is as follows: if there were no mutual exclusion between universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, it would follow that the linguistic usage of "cow" and the like would apply even to buffaloes and other animals, and conversely, the usage of "buffalo" and the like would apply even to cows and other animals. Even if one accepts their mutual exclusion, however, there is no contradiction because linguistic usages such as "this is a male," "this is an individual," or "this is an object" are universal. Thus, there is no conflict.

Regarding the phrase "that is what is expressed": "that" refers to the triad beginning with gender (*liṅga*). "From that alone" means from the suffix alone. Or rather, it is the base (*prakṛti*) itself that possesses the expressive power (*vācakatva*). Nor can it be argued that there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the base in that case, because comprehension occurs even without the recognition of an inconsistency (*anupapatti*). Furthermore, the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) for infinite bases does not constitute a fault, as it is "aimed at the result" (*phalamukha*); moreover, for one who has grasped the power residing in the base, the cognition of gender and so forth arises from the base alone.

Furthermore, because we observe that the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) pertains exclusively to the base (*prakṛti*), for this very reason, the status of rules such as "dvayekayoḥ" [Pāṇini 1.4.22] as restrictive (*niyāmaka*)—once it is established through the maxim "those whose referents are not explicitly stated [refer to the base]" (*anirdiṣṭārthāḥ*) that they denote number and so forth—is consistent with the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya.

As for the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), they say it is to be avoided by noting that no other restrictive factor, such as speaker's intention (*tātparya*), is heard in the rule. However, some maintain that number alone is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), while the other four factors are the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). As it has been said:
"The case-endings may be either expressive (*vācikā*) or indicative (*dyotikā*) of duality and the rest."

In this regard, the following should be understood: in a word such as *ghaṭa* ("pot"), distinct powers (*śakti*) denoting gender, number, and so forth must be admitted; yet, even though these meanings are presented by a single word, they are mutually connected due to the variety of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Among these, gender and number function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*), while the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) functions as the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Alternatively, even that [number] is indeed a qualifier because it is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). If the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were to possess the power (*śakti*) to denote an object qualified by gender, number, and so forth, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating powers for objects qualified by singularity, as well as for those qualified by duality and the rest. Furthermore, in cases such as *gorūpam* ("the form of a cow"), the cognition of an object unqualified by number and so forth would be untenable; however, under the view that word-meanings are presented in isolation (*viśakalita*), such a cognition is established through the absence of any factor to restrict the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Others, however, maintain that the capacity (śakti) resides only in what is not distinct from the *dhātu* (verbal root), because they accept a separate capacity even for that which is qualified merely by *ghaṭatva* (potness) and so on; thus, they claim that the production of a cognition not having number (*saṃkhyā*) as its object is thereby accounted for. Now, one might object: "If all five [number-genders] are indeed the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then principles such as 'the cognition of the meaning of a nominal stem qualified by [another property] is caused by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by case-endings (*sub*) and so forth' would be rendered obsolete. To this, some reply: "That is not so, because those principles remain valid when the meaning manifested (*dyotya*) by the case-ending is taken into account."

Others, however, say that even if that [denotative power] were to dissolve, it would be an instance of "accepting what is desired" (iṣṭāpatti), because such a cognition—given that the indicated meaning (*dyotyārtha*) functions as a qualifier—is as non-existent as a sky-flower; for it is logical that denotative power resides [only] in suffixes, which are fewer in number than nominal stems (*prātipadika*). The sense is that it is appropriate to postulate denotative power only in those elements that are fewer in number relative to the nominal stem. He clarifies the purpose of using the general term "śāstra" by stating "in the śāstra," and [he notes] "in many. || 25 ||

One might raise the objection: "Since we do not experience that a word such as 'pot exists' is the object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by a sentence like 'the pot exists,' the root text beginning with 'If even the word [is perceived] as distinct'—which aims to prove that each word is the denotatum of itself—is inconsistent. To dispel this doubt, the author cites the experience of the most eminent scholar Bhartṛhari as proof for the fact that a word is indeed the object of verbal cognition: "There is no such thing... "Accompaniment by the word" (*śabdānugama*) means the manifestation of the word. "As if permeated" (*anuviddham iva*) means as if connected through identity (*tādātmya*).

The word "as it were" (iva) is used to indicate that the identity with the word is superimposed upon cognition. The appearance of the word in all cognitions, such as perception and the like, is justified by the identity between the word and its object. However, some maintain that even though there is a difference between the word and its object, on the strength of experience, it is postulated that the causal complex for cognition in general (*jñānasāmānyasāmagrī*) alone causes the manifestation of the word; thus, its justification is established.

It is not tenable to claim that a word, presented by its object-cognition (*arthajñāna*) as a means of awakening [memory], appears as a qualifier (*prakārībhūya*) regarding the object-component in perception and other cognitions, because there is no subverting evidence and because such is experienced; for it is impossible for that word to appear within the object-cognition that presents the word itself. Rather, they say that its appearance can only be established in the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), according to the manner previously described.

In this context, taking words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), it is established that they are the objects of the respective verbal cognitions (*śābdabodha*). This is done by means of the reason consisting in being indicated by the statements of such experts as being objects of the cognition of every member of the class [of words denoting jars]. It should be understood that there is no lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*), because being the object of the cognition of every member of a class is not possible without being the object of the cognition of at least one member of that class.

When the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is presented specifically as being the object of the respective verbal cognitions with respect to words like "jar," [it is established] by the cognition produced by sentences such as "the word exists," etc.
By taking "being the object of verbal cognition" as the probandum, there is no proving of what is already established.

"Without the word as its object" means without having the form of words such as "Viṣṇu" as its object; the final meaning is "without having words as its object. Because there is no difference in their capacity—that is, because they are equal in terms of expressive power—and because an beginningless intention (tātparya) is required in both cases, natural secondary indication (svārasikalakṣaṇā) finds no footing, due to the absence of a specific purpose. He demonstrates a case where secondary indication is simply impossible with the example "jabagaḍa," etc. [He says] "by not grasping the primary meaning," etc.

The meaning is: although the denotative power (*śakyārtha*) of each individual phoneme is established by the authority of works such as the *Ekākṣarakośa*, it is not apprehended [in that context]. Now, one might object: "Even if the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) is not apprehended there, let there still be a cognition of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), since the causal complex consisting of the secondary function is present. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "and of that which is unknown" (*ajñātāyāśca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). "Because of its uselessness" (*anupayogāt*): because the presentation of the meaning is impossible without the knowledge of that [secondary function]. "From the attainment of correctness" (*sādhutāsaṃprāpteḥ*): from the acceptance of grammatical correctness. And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule for the vowel *ṛ*.

Anticipating the objection that "even there, indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—in the form of a relation with its own signified—is indeed possible," he says: "In the other system" (*paranaye*). This means: in the system of the Naiyāyikas. Thus, while it may be possible in the Mīmāṃsaka view—which accepts that indirect indication is a relation with its own signified—it is necessary to accept a primary power (*śakti*) in that case according to the Naiyāyika system, which does not admit that such a relation constitutes indirect indication; otherwise, no cognition would arise.

The sense is that, due to the absence of "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*)—defined as the capacity to produce a cognition of meaning through its own function (*vṛtti*)—there would be no designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), nor would there be grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). "In some cases" refers to when one intends to express the distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*). He explains the meaning of the word *tathā* found in the root-text as "the meaning of the nominal stem. The word *siddhaḥ* is glossed by *upasthitaḥ*. [The term] *arthavat* [is explained as follows].

The fundamental meaning is that when the object (*artha*) appears, the word (*śabda*) also appears because it is present; the resulting sense is that "it appears as if it were the object. However, there is no compound between the word *artha* and the particle *iva*; for if such a compound were formed, the rule "a compound with *iva*" would require the case-ending to be heard [in the compound], which is not the case here.

[Objection: Since it is necessary to accept a function (*vṛtti*) regarding the verbal element for the presentation of the object to be imitated (*anukārya*) even in both positions—that of difference and non-difference—is it not improper to state in the root-text that such necessity exists only in the position of difference? [Response: To explain his intention, he says in the commentary, "This is the sense": "In the case of the difference between the object to be imitated and the imitation.
