The sense is that when their difference is intended to be expressed, the difference between the imitation and the object to be imitated—such as in "paṭad" (imitation) and "kuru" (object to be imitated)—is established through the connection with contradictory properties, such as consisting of sound (*dhvani*) versus consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*).

"Because of the non-presentation of the word" means "in the absence of expressive power," and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that because the object of imitation cannot be presented from the word due to the absence of expressive power, its status as an object of verbal cognition would also not be possible. Otherwise, even the status of being an object of verbal cognition would not occur, because only the presentation of a word-meaning generated by a word through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*) is the cause of verbal cognition.

He states, "In the view of non-difference, [the object] becomes the object of verbal cognition even without an additional power," by saying "in the case of perception under the view of non-difference. Regarding the phrase "because of being the cause": this is the reason for the fact that the presentation [of the object] is produced by the word. Regarding the phrase "to avoid over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*): the meaning is that it is for the purpose of preventing the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that ether (*ākāśa*), which is the object of the presentation produced by words such as "pot" through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), would become the object of the verbal cognition produced by a sentence such as "there is a pot."

The intended meaning is as follows: the cause [of word-meaning apprehension] is precisely the presentation of the word (*padopasthiti*) produced by its *vṛtti* (linguistic function), and since that [presentation] does not exist in the present case, it is impossible for the object of the verbal cognition arising from the sentence "gavityayamāha" (he says 'go') to be the [word] *gauḥ*. An objection might be raised: even if the possession of the *vṛtti* in the form of *śakti* (denotative power) exists [in the word *gauḥ*] by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*), it does not exist by way of the relation of specifier (*nirūpakatā*); therefore, the status of being an object of verbal cognition remains unestablished, because it is precisely the existence of that [power] by way of the relation of specifier that acts as the causal factor for the manifestation of the word in verbal cognition. Anticipating this, he says: "nirūpakatā... (the relation of specifier...).

"Of that which possesses occurrence (*vṛttimat*) alone" means: not [of that which possesses occurrence] by way of being a relatum (*nirūpakatayā*), but rather of that which possesses occurrence [as a related term]. "Is postulated" means: the intention is that, in accordance with experience, even though there is complexity (*gaurava*), one postulates that the existence of such a relation is the condition for its manifestation in verbal cognition (*śābdabhāna*). "Because it is determined by both"—that is, because it resides in both; for a relation indeed touches upon both [terms].

For this very reason, the usage of the elders, such as the logicians (*tārkika*), consists precisely in the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*) or the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*). "By way of making that known" means by way of making the meaning known. By this, it is indicated that *śakti* (potency) is a relationship in the form of the relation between the signified and the signifier (*bodhyabodhakabhāva*), since the word (*śabda*) itself is the locus of that [relationship]. And thus, because there exists the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) through the function (*vṛtti*) of the word, there is no impossibility of its manifestation; this is the intended sense.

The point is this: in the view that there is a distinction [between the original and the imitation], the status of being the locus of a power determined by an object belongs only to the *anukārya* (the original) and not to the *anukaraṇa* (the imitation). Therefore, for the sake of bringing the *anukārya* to mind through the *anukaraṇa*, it is necessary to postulate a separate power (*śakti*) in the latter. This meaning is also accepted by Pāṇini himself, who composed the sūtra "svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya" (A 1.1.68). He provides the authority of Hari’s statement for his own position with the words "uktaṃ ca" (and it has been said). "Of light"—meaning of lamps and the like. "These"—meaning these two powers: the capacity to be perceived (*grāhyatva*) and the capacity to perceive (*grāhakatva*).

The point is this: it is undisputed that contact with light (*āloka-saṃyoga*) is the cause for the visual perception of a substance, since otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving jars and other objects even in the dark when they are in contact with the eye. And so, just as the contact between a jar and the light of a lamp produces the perception of both the jar and itself, likewise, a word—aided by the power (*śakti*) residing in it which has the object as its domain—produces the perception of both the object and itself.

Just as in the absence of contact between the jar and the eye, that very same contact with light produces a perception whose object is only itself, so too, when there is an absence of intentionality (*tātparya*) toward an external object and intentionality resides in the word, the word—by virtue of that very [intentionality]—produces the cognition of itself alone. The inclusion of the distinction between substance and light is not necessary, due to both complexity (*gaurava*) and the lack of purpose. And thus, because the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) occurs through its presentation by the auditory organ (*śrotra*).

By this, the following fallacious objections are refuted: (1) that when it is said "utter the word *go*," there would be the consequence of uttering the *vikṛta* (the modified form) because only that is presented to the ear; (2) that since the word [itself] is not the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), the application of case-suffix meanings to it would be untenable; and (3) that in cases such as "the cow exists" (*gaur asti*), because the word itself is more rapidly presented by perception, there would be the consequence of only the word appearing [rather than its meaning]. This is because, through the assistance of the apprehension of intention (*tātparya*), the unmodified word itself is presented precisely by means of a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). Otherwise, it would be more reasonable to hold that [the word] is directed toward the meaning alone.

Therefore, it is established that when the determination of the intended meaning (tātparya) has occurred, the word itself appears as the primary element; however, in its absence, it appears merely as a qualifier of the meaning. This detail should be investigated in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*. || 26 ||

He provides the explanation of the word "ataḥ" with the passage beginning "gavityayam," etc. "They do not differ" means they are not intended to be expressed as having [independent] reality (*tattvena*). Thus, since imitation words (*anukaraṇaśabda*) lack meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), the intention not to distinguish them from the original (*anukārya*) is the cause [for their non-difference]. By the phrase "meaningfulness, etc.," the inclusion of properties such as being a *kṛdanta* derivative is intended. "In the case of the non-application of these [rules]" means because they lack meaningfulness in the form of conveying a meaning through a grammatical function (*vṛtti*). It follows that "correctness" (*sādhutva*) is applicable.

The meaning is that, since there is no lack of correctness (*asādhutva*) according to the method to be explained, its correctness remains unimpaired by virtue of usage by the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*) and other such factors. Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of non-difference (*abheda*), why is its correctness not [accepted]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Otherwise," [referring to] the rules "the suffix" (*pratyayaḥ*) and "and following" (*paraśca*).

Since the fifth case (pañcamī) is specified in the rule for the formation of suffixes (*pratyaya*), the suffix is already established as following the base (*prakṛti*) by the very application of the *paribhāṣā* "from that [the subsequent]," which states that when a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used to denote a portion, it refers to what follows. Therefore, the sūtra *paraśca* ("and subsequent") serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning that the base must be employed only when followed by a suffix. It is with this very intention that it is recited: "A base alone should not be employed; a suffix alone should not be employed."

Thus, it should be understood that according to the view that restrictive rules (*niyama-śāstra*) function by way of prohibition (*niṣedha-mukhena*), the transgression of the prohibition is explicit; whereas, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Bhāṣya—that they function by way of injunction (*vidhi-mukhena*)—it is a transgression of an implied prohibition (*ārthika-niṣedha*).

The point is this: under the view of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), because there is an absence of *prātipadika*-hood according to the method already stated, and because there is an absence of "stemness" (*prakṛtitva*)—defined as being occupied by the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of the rule prescribing the suffix—the prohibition "not alone" (*na kevalā*) does not apply. Furthermore, since the prohibition "what is not a word is not [used]" (*apadaṃ na*) applies only to that which is devoid of word-status (*padatva*) while otherwise being fit for word-status, the second prohibition also does not come into operation. It should be understood that even though there is a communication of meaning through the function (*vṛtti*) under the view of non-difference, there is no *prātipadika*-hood because there is an absence of the communication of meaning regarding a specific denotative power (*śakti*).

Others, however, maintain that when there is an intention to express non-difference based on similarity, the original object (*anukārya*) is presented by the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) through the very relation of similarity. Since the defining property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for verbal cognition produced by an imitation is simply "being a verbal cognition not generated by an imitation," it is possible for what is thus presented to be an object of verbal cognition. Furthermore, because it lacks "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*)—defined as the capacity to convey meaning through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*)—it does not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding the rule "one should not employ an *apada*," the meaning of *apada* here is "that which is not finalized" (*apariniṣṭhita*). Finalization is established by such grammatical indications as "the root *bhū* is used in the sense of existence. Thus, they say that since an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) lacks this state of being non-finalized, it does not fall within the scope of the aforementioned prohibition.

These two positions are established like the positions regarding genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*); therefore, the applications of Vedic scriptures such as "On the full moon day, one sings the *rathantara* in the *kavatī* verses" (*vārtaghnī paurṇamāsyāṃ kavatīṣu rathantaraṃ gāyati*), as well as the applications of grammatical rules such as "eruḥ," "eco'yavāyāvaḥ," and "raṣābhyāṃ noṇaḥ," are rendered consistent. If only the position of non-difference (*abheda*) were accepted, then because a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would arise from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the application of the aforementioned scriptural usage—"in the *kavatī* verses"—would be untenable. Likewise, the inconsistency of the application of the grammatical rules is also evident. By resorting to both these established positions, all that is desired is accomplished. || 27 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of nouns in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra-ṭīkā*. 4.

Regarding the term "compounds" (*samāsān*): being a compound consists in possessing the designation "compound" through a relationship with the convention of Pāṇini and others. [One might object that] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this definition to jars and the like, since they possess the designation "compound" through a relationship with the convention of another person—such as the thought "a jar is to be understood by the word 'compound'"—therefore the phrase "Pāṇini and others" is used. This means "the sages who composed the grammatical treatises. Furthermore, such a convention regarding such a person does not exist, because there is a lack of evidence for it.

This is because they do not employ [such terms] elsewhere, and because those who are experts do not employ them in such a way. For this very reason, the status of being a compound (samāsatva) does not consist in having the nature of words like "ghaṭa" through a relationship with some arbitrary convention made by a person, since experts do not employ them in that manner. Rather, a compound is a collection of nouns (*nāma*) in which the preceding member is not the object of a cognition whose qualifier is the state of occurring immediately prior to a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that results in the understanding of a meaning.

Even in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), although there may be a recollection of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) for the word "king" (*rājan*) with respect to some person, there is neither impossibility nor lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because that [recollection] does not result in the cognition of the meaning [of the compound]. Furthermore, in cases such as *dadhi sundaram asty ānaya* ("Bring the beautiful curd"), since verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is accepted only when there is a recollection of the respective case-endings, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) there either. However, it is not correct to argue that in the case of compounds (*samāsa*), there is no fault because verbal comprehension is accepted even without a recollection of the case-ending in the prior member (*pūrvapada*).

In cases such as "dadhi sundaram" (the yogurt is beautiful), there would be over-extension [of the definition], because understanding arises even for one who does not know the case-ending (*vibhakti*) word. If it is argued that there is no over-extension because understanding is not admitted to occur without the recollection of the case-ending, we say no; for since there is no evidence to the contrary, the same could be asserted for compounds (*samāsa*) as well, which would result in the definition being impossible [to apply].

Nor should it be argued that, because in a compound (*samāsa*) the immediate sequential relation between two words constitutes *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) and the knowledge thereof is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is appropriate to accept a cognition even without the consideration of case-endings (*vibhakti*); whereas in a non-compound (*asamāsa*), since *ākāṅkṣā* consists precisely in the knowledge of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as being immediately preceded by a case-ending, the consideration of the case-ending is necessary therein. For such a claim is refuted by the counter-example (*vyabhicāra*) of compounds with elided endings (*aluk-samāsa*), where there is no knowledge of such an immediate sequential relation.

Because [the suffix] cannot function as a cause (*hetu*), one should not argue that there is no fault since the entire complex "the son of a female slave" (*dāsyāḥ putra*) and so forth constitutes the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in those cases. Even so, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of *aluk*-compounds such as "the son of a female slave" (*dāsyāḥ putraḥ*) and "Kāla on the neck" (*kaṇṭhekāla*), because the cognition of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) which forms part of the complex also generates understanding; therefore, what must be included there is the quality of generating understanding by way of presenting the meaning (*arthopasthiti*), so that there is no over-narrow definition in those instances, whereas in the other case, the case-ending lacks the capacity to present the meaning.

If it is argued that for this very reason there is no cognition of plurality in the case of *goṣucara* despite the presence of the plural suffix—as is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *samartha*-sūtra—even so, the under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *paryabhūṣat* and *pacatabhṛjjata* remains unavoidable. They say that the resolution by treating these as non-examples (*alakṣya*) is not appropriate; such is the direction of their argument.

Other logicians, however, maintain that a compound (*samāsa*) consists of such a sentence in which a suffix such as *tva* or *tal* following the sentence generates a cognition possessing a subject-object relation whose own object is determined by the subject-object relation of a certain meaning; in other words, being a sentence that conveys such a meaning is what constitutes "compound-hood. This is because, in cases such as *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*, the suffix following it generates a cognition of its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the second member, as qualified by the meaning of the first member.

Sentences such as "the cooker" (*pācaka*), which express a meaning consisting of the agent of the act of cooking, are not "great sentences" (*mahāvākya*) because they lack the quality of expressing a meaning that is obtainable through multiple names contained within themselves; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to such cases.

If it is objected that there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as *upakumbha* ("near the jar"), because the word *kumbha* itself, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), has the meaning "in proximity to the jar," we say no. This is because [the definition] includes the property of being "great" (*mahattva*), which consists in the incapacity to convey a relation with the meaning of the suffix as delimited by the meaning of the base alone. For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the part "nīlaghaṭatvam" in the expression "nīlaghaṭatvam," since it lacks the status of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) as previously described. Nor is the word "alone" (*mātra*) redundant.

Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *kṣīrapāyī* ("one who drinks milk") and *haritrāta* ("protected by Hari"), even though these [words] generate a cognition whose object is the meaning of a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) qualified by the meaning of the verbal root which serves as their base (*prakṛti*), they do not possess the quality of being a cause for a cognition of the meaning of the primary derivative suffix qualified by the meaning of the base alone; rather, they generate a cognition of an agent or other [case-role] qualified by an action such as "drinking" (*pāna*) conjoined with "milk" (*kṣīra*). Therefore, since that [specific condition] exists, there is no over-extension.

From expressions such as "the king's manhood" (*rājñaḥ puruṣatvam*), it is understood that the state of being a man resides in the king alone; the suffix *-tva* does not denote a man who is qualified by a relation to the king. Similarly, in cases such as "I shall become your sonhood" (*tava putratvam eṣyāmi*), the meaning of the genitive case—the state residing in the son—is construed with the property of being defined by the referent of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*). This is because of the grammatical rule that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) convey their own meaning as related solely to the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*).

In this context, if *tvādi* (the suffixes *tvā*, etc. or *taddhita* (secondary suffixes) were introduced merely as general categories, then in examples such as *arājñaḥ putrīyaḥ* ("belonging to the son of a non-king"), since the son qualified by the relation to the king would be construed with the meaning of the suffix *-cha*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the portion "the king's son. Therefore, *tvādi* and so forth are specified individually; for even when there is a syntactic connection (*ekādeśa-anvaya*) due to constant dependence (*nityasāpekṣatā*), there is no obstacle [to the application of the rule]. Furthermore, the grammatical maxim (*vyutpatti*) that "secondary suffixes [denote] the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*) must be restricted to refer to specific types of secondary suffixes.

For this very reason, there is consistency with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "yena vidhis tadantasya" regarding the derivation of *phak* from the word *gārgya* in the sense of "the descendant of Paramagārgya"; otherwise, since [the suffix] would convey its own meaning as related to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) and further related to the meaning of the base as qualified by *para*, the inconsistency would be evident. Alternatively, [the term *tadantavidhi*] may refer to a base-meaning that is distinct from meanings involving relations (*sasaṃbandhikārtha*).

It should be understood that if, in that case, the relation with the king is construed—through a mediated sequence—with the meaning of the suffix itself as qualified by the meaning of the base, then there is no harm even when "taddhita" is mentioned in general. Regarding the phrase "the wealth of the king’s servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam*), they say that because the person related to the king is construed with the meaning of the genitive (such as ownership), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the portion "king’s servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣa*); therefore, the mention of "suffix" in general is disregarded [in that specific context].

In this view, although there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as *apibatakhādata*, *pacatabhṛjjata*, and so forth, nevertheless, in the case of *dāsyāḥ putratvam* ("the sonhood of the maidservant"), the meaning expressed by the genitive ending—which is the relation with the maidservant—is construed only with the meaning of the suffix in the word *putratva* (sonhood), and not with the referent of the word *putra* (son).

For this very reason, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the portion "the king's son" within the phrase "the king’s son-ness" has been refuted; for there is no restrictive rule that such a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs only when words are used separately. Furthermore, since [words like] *pradāya* and so forth connect only with the action, and since [words like] *paryabhūṣat* and so forth lack the suffix *tvā*, the aforementioned definition is impossible there; because the meaning of those [forms] connects only with the meaning of the first [word], and although they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), they lack the status of being in the genitive case, as the subsequent case-ending is devoid of meaning.

Understand that the avoidance of these cases on the grounds of their being *alakṣya* (unfit for definition) is not striking. Others say that there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in examples such as *pradāya*, *prasthāya*, *anuvyacalat*, and *paryabhūṣat*; however, enough of this prolixity. Regarding the phrase "even both words": by the word "even" (*api*), compounds consisting of three or more words are included. Consequently, there is no failure to include compounds such as *dvayahnajātaḥ*, *citrājaradguḥ*, and *hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ*. Thus, the intended meaning is that the defining characteristic (*vibhājakatāvacchedaka*) is the state of being composed of multiple *subanta* (inflected nominal) elements. As for the example "the king" (*rājā*): *The king, having given his daughter to the sage, went away; Having gone, he returned again, and adorned her completely.* In this verse, the words *pradāya*, *prasthāya*, *anuvyacalat*, and *paryabhūṣat* are instances where the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap* are elided. Since these are not *samāsa* (compounds), they would otherwise fall outside the scope of the definition. Therefore, the author states "even both words" to show that the definition applies even when two words are combined in this manner. By extension, this also includes cases involving three or more words. Thus, the definition is established as being applicable to all such instances.

It should be understood that, by virtue of the authority of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *upapadam atiṅ*, and because the paribhāṣā *gatikārakopapadānām* applies even in cases such as *dvitīyāśrita*, which does not consist of multiple *subanta*s, the maxim of "that which presents itself first" (*prathamopasthita*) is not adopted in this system—since the mention of the number three in *nijāṃ trayāṇām* indicates its non-application here—and furthermore, due to its being the most well-known example; thus, setting aside compounds like *kṛṣṇaśrita*, the example *rājapuruṣa* is presented.

Regarding the form *paryabhūṣat*: in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, there is the phrase *devān kratunā paryabhūṣat*. Here, the compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) from the word *saha*. In this case, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule *samāsasya* is set aside; and although the accent of the original form of the first member (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable would apply under the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthāvyaya-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), that is further superseded by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139). Consequently, by means of the original accent of the second member (*uttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), the accent of the suffix *aṭ* remains. This is because the author of the Vārttika [Kātyāyana] included the term *kṛt* (primary suffix) in that specific rule.

Because of its rejection. Now, one might object: "Since the *Bhāṣya* establishes this compound through the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) of the word ‘*saha*’, it lacks the status of a *tatpuruṣa*; therefore, how can the accent prescribed for a *tatpuruṣa* apply here? To this they reply: "In the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*, the term ‘*nityam*’ is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga*, thereby accepting the status of this compound [as a *tatpuruṣa*]; thus, the aforementioned fault does not arise. However, in cases such as *yatrā naro devayanto yugāni vitanvate*, if one assumes the status of being a *tricakra* (three-wheeled) compound, etc.—

It should be understood that there is no final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) here. In this regard, if the term *kṛt* were not included [in the rule], the [acute accent] would apply only in cases such as *prabhavanam*, where the action is predominant, but not in cases such as *praṇīḥ*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *kṛt* must indeed be made for the purpose of encompassing all *kṛt*-derived forms; however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*), it should be understood—on the basis of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*) alone—that the initial acute accent of the second member occurs in forms such as *paryabhūṣat*. For further details, one should consult Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa*, Uddyota, and other works.

One might object: "Since the Bhāṣya states that because of the mention of *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes), both [the terms] *sup* and *supā* are excluded by the rule *sup-supā*, the statement *supāṃ nāmnā* ('of nouns with case-endings') is inconsistent; for the compound formation occurs even before the case-endings (*sub*) arise in both words. To dispel this doubt, he says: "In this context, regarding the subsequent word" (*atrottarapade*). This means: "The statement *supāṃ nāmnā* is not inconsistent"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Because of the exclusion of *atiṅ*, only the term *sup* ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], whereas the term *sup* ending in the first case (*prathamānta*) certainly does carry over.

The Bhāṣya, however, intends that [the term *sub*] does not recur [to the subsequent rules]. Even though it recurs in one case, there is no inconsistency in its intended meaning, because the absence of its recurrence in both cases remains unimpaired. Alternatively, since the exclusion of forms such as *edhān āharakaḥ* and *vrajati* is established by the recurrence of *sub* alone, let the statement in the Bhāṣya—that by the mention of *atiṅ* both [terms, *sub* and *atiṅ*,] are withdrawn—be taken exactly as it is heard.

Thus, because the technical term *mahāsaṃjñā* (great designation) is applied by stating that "a word uttered in proximity [is an *upapada*]," one relies on its etymological meaning; consequently, the compound occurs immediately after the case-ending (*sup*) has been produced in the prior member. Furthermore, since the suffix *ṇini* in the rule *supyajātau-ṇiniḥ* can only occur after the case-ending has been produced, there is no fault, as the status of being an *upapada* would not exist without that [suffix].

There is no fault even in cases such as *nirgata* and so forth; the point is that because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the case-ending (*sup*) arises before the connection with another word, and once the *suk* augment has been added, the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) occurs only after the connection with the other word. He states the purpose of the aforementioned explanation with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). "Otherwise" means if the compound were to apply even to the preceding member before the case-ending had arisen; [the fault would be] that the elision (*lopa*) would not occur because of the absence of the status of being a "word. Regarding *kaṭaprūḥ*: it is one who moves toward a mat (*kaṭaṃ prūḥ*), hence *kaṭaprūḥ*.

From the root *prūṅ* in the sense of "going," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the agentive sense (*kartari*). Regarding *āyatastūḥ*: the meaning is "one who stretches" (*āyataṃ syauti*). In both cases, there is lengthening of the root vowel according to the rule *kvibvacipracchiśraśrṛṇupṝkvāḥ*. Regarding "from the Vārttika": the compound is formed by means of a specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the Vārttika. Regarding *pibata*: the meaning is that action in which "drink and eat" (*pibata khādata*) is continuously expressed is called *pibatakhādatā*. Regarding "a verbal form" (*ākhyāta*): the meaning is that when continuity—that is, uninterruptedness—of an action is to be understood, a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is compounded with another word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. Regarding "from the Sūtra": here the word "compound" (*samāsa*) is supplied as a remainder.

Regarding *jahistambam*: the meaning of the compound is "one who strikes a pillar. Regarding *jahikarmaṇā*: the word *jahi* (an inflected verbal form) is compounded with a *sub*-ending word that expresses its object (*karman*), provided that the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is understood and the compound is intended to express an action for the benefit of the agent (*kartrabhiprāyaka*). This is the meaning.

Its classification—that is, the classification of compounds—is stated in the root text: "That which begins with 'pūrva'. This discussion regarding the predominance of the meaning of the first member—the discourse that "an *avyayībhāva* is that in which the meaning of the first member is predominant," and so forth—is also merely a general statement; the meaning is that it is "mostly applicable" (*prāyika*). He states the reason for the general applicability of the division mentioned by the ancient authors with the words beginning "bhūtapūrva. [He says] "because of non-inclusion": because those compounds are excluded from the technical designations such as *avyayībhāva* and the rest.

In the case of *tatra bhūtapūrvaḥ*, there is a compound according to the rule *sup supā*. In *āyatastūḥ*, the form is established by the nipātana (irregular derivation) in the Vārttika *kvibvacipracchi...*. In *vāgarthāviva*, there is a compound according to the rule *ivena samāsaḥ*. Regarding the term *pūrvapadārtha*: the meaning is "that in which the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant. Thus, the final definition is: an *avyayībhāva* is that which generates a cognition in which the primary qualificandhood (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the first member.

Therefore, even in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), although there is the generation of a cognition whose qualificandhood resides in the king and is determined by a modehood residing in "kingship" (*rājatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there, because the king lacks the primary qualificandhood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) belonging to the cognition produced by that [compound]. This should be understood similarly for what follows. As for the avyayībhāva compound *upakumbham*, which has the form "near the jar," there is consistency with the definition because it generates a cognition in which the meaning of the prior member is the primary qualificand. Regarding the phrase "the meanings of both members": [this refers to the dvandva compound].

The meaning is that [the compound] has multiple word-meanings as its primary referent (*pradhāna*). By this, there is no failure to include compounds composed of three or more words. Regarding the term "mutually" (*paraspara*): because of mutual deviation—that is, because the delimitors (*avacchedaka*) characterized by the definition reside in loci where each other is absent. He demonstrates this deviation with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). "Non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*) refers to the non-pervasion of the definition of the *avyayībhāva*. He states the indicator for the primacy of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) with the words "and in the case of the external referent" (*anyapadārthe ca*).

The phrase "due to being a compound" (*samāsāt*) is the reason for the predominance of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). This is because of the existence of the predominance of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*). The meaning is that it generates a cognition in which the object denoted by the final member—specifically in the form "a trace of connection with a *sup*-ending word"—is the primary qualificand. Now, one might object: since in the rule prescribing the *avyayībhāva* compound the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is mentioned first [by the term *prathamānirdiṣṭa*], how can the indeclinable here be considered the final member? To this, he says: "By the rule *sup-pratinā*."

Regarding the term *pūrvapadārtha* (the meaning of the prior member): because the cognition arises from [the understanding] "half related to the *pippalī*," the commentators maintain that, according to the maxim "words are seen to apply to the whole," words such as *pippalī*, *kāya*, and so forth refer to the parts beginning with the *pippalī* and the body, respectively; thus, in cases such as *ardhapippalī* and *pūrvakāyaḥ*, there is only a *karmadhāraya* compound.

And thus, the three rules beginning with "arthaṃ napuṃsakam" need not be formulated; for this very reason, [the rule] concerning "ūrdhvakāya" and so forth has been established. In that view, although there is no deviation because the meaning of the subsequent member (uttarapada) is predominant, one must observe a deviation in all systems regarding the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type compounds—such as "rājāntaram," which conveys the sense of "another king"—where the predominance of the meaning of the prior member (pūrvapada) is understood.

Since the word *antara*, which denotes "division," is neuter, the compound takes the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) due to its inclusion in the *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* and other such groups (*gaṇa*). By this, the objection—"How can there be the gender of the final member here, given that in the Bhāṣya on the rule *paravalliṅgam*, the example *ardhapippalī* and others were shown to be *tatpuruṣas*; yet by accepting them as *karmadhārayas* and assuming the predominance of the meaning of the second member, one could justify them otherwise, thereby dispensing with the mention of *tatpuruṣa* in that rule?"—is refuted.

In this context, the relation to some counter-positive residing in the cognition of that which is the substratum of the property delimiting the meaning of the prior member is obtainable through the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Likewise, one should observe the deviation in cases such as ‘*nṛsomaḥ*’ (man-moon) and ‘*prasannena dṛgabjane*’ (with the clear lotus-eyes). In ‘*dṛgabjena*’ and similar instances, the compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group; for that very reason, it takes the gender of the final member and has the meaning of the prior member as its predominant sense. This is because [the predominance of the prior member] is not observed in compounds formed with that [term] in expressions such as ‘*rājāntaram*’ (another king).

Because a word expressing a general quality (*sāmānyavācaka*) is employed here, the compound "that which is compared with [words such as] *vyāghra* and the like" (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*) does not apply. Since it is clear from the tenth chapter of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* that the meaning is "only an expressed attribute (*upāttadharma*) is the cause of similarity when that [attribute] is employed," it is incorrect to claim that similarity here is based on an unexpressed attribute (*anupāttadharma*). Furthermore, in examples such as "the city-moon is full" (*purenduḥ sakalaḥ*), similarity cannot possibly exist through an unexpressed attribute.

Furthermore, this sūtra would apply only when there is identity of gender and number; otherwise, it would result in the inconsistency of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *aparavalliṅgam*, which asks, "Which [compound] causes the Tatpuruṣa to function [as such], namely the Ekadeśisamāsa, as in *ardhapippalī*?", as well as the Bhāṣya intended to reject the mention of *Tatpuruṣa* by means of the *Nyāsa* rule *dvandvaikadeśinoḥ*.

This is because even in cases such as *dṛgabjena* (lotus-like eye), there exists a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the meaning of the prior member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*) and which takes the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*). Furthermore, in examples such as *mukhacandra* (moon-like face), the designation of a "metaphor" (*rūpaka*) based on the form of the moon occurs precisely because of this [definition], since the meaning of the prior member is predominant; and its taking the gender of the subsequent member follows from that very same reason, as is clear in the *Mañjūṣā*. The phrase "due to the predominance of the meanings of both members" refers to the fact that from a term like *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), an understanding arises of "either two or three. The expression "over-extension to *dvandva* compounds" means over-extension of the definition to those [dvandva] compounds.

The same applies to what follows. "Because of another [word] whose form is a collective" means because of the predominance of that other referent which consists of a collective (samāhāra). "And there would be non-pervasion of *dvandva*"—the sense is that in cases such as *dhavakhadirau* (a *dvandva* of *dhava* and *khadira* trees) involving mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), it is not possible for the resulting cognition to have both word-meanings as its primary qualificands.

In reality, however, upon a careful examination of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "cārthe dvandvaḥ," it is understood that even in the case of *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection), the primary significance belongs to the collection of meanings denoted by "ca" (*cārtha*), just as it does for the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in a *bahuvrīhi*. For in that context, having raised the objection that since the meaning of "ca" is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), the compound expressing it would likewise lack gender and number, a resolution is provided based on its inherent nature: that the meaning of the compound, like a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), depends upon a substance (*dravya*), and thus adopts the gender and number of that substance.

The resolution has been stated. For this very reason, this commentary does not intend [the term] as a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound), because such a compound lacks the capacity to convey that meaning. In this regard, the distinction is as follows: in an *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) compound, there is a collection (*samūha*) in which the difference between the members is manifest; whereas in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, the members are unmanifest. The state of having manifest differences between members consists in possessing a number that is superimposed upon the members. When the number belonging to the members is not superimposed, there is a lack of manifest difference between members; this is precisely what is meant by "the concealment of the difference between members. This and other points are explained in detail elsewhere.

In this view, however, one should understand that the aforementioned definition is impossible [to apply] and that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *bahuvrīhi* into the case of *dvandva*. Thus, having refuted the definitions of *avyayībhāva* and so forth as stated by the ancients—namely, "that in which the meaning of the first member is predominant" and so on—he states the definitions according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words "But in the established doctrine... (*siddhānte tu*).

"Under the heading of *avyayībhāva*": the meaning is that it is a compound prescribed by a rule falling within the jurisdiction (*adhikāra*) of *avyayībhāva*. By this, there is no defect even if compounds such as *upakumbha* are not explicitly mentioned under that specific heading, nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substitutes (*ādeśa*) and the like read under various headings, because those lack the status of being compounds; and since the nature of a compound has already been defined previously, there is no fault. However, others maintain that the definition of each [type of compound] is simply the possession of the term "avyayībhāva" and so forth, through the relation of a technical convention (*saṃketa*) established by Pāṇini and others.

Others have declared that being the object of linguistic usage such as *avyayībhāva* and so forth is not the definition [of a compound]. Regarding the term *bhautapūrvya*: "that which existed previously" (*pūrva-bhūta*) is *bhūtapūrva*; *bhūtapūrva* itself is *bhautapūrvya*, with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in the sense of the base meaning (*svārthe*). Because of the reason—that prior to the formation of the compound (*vṛtti*), there existed the capacity to generate a cognition having the meaning of the first member as its qualificandum—for that reason, even that [usage], namely the general rule (*utsarga*), is established—meaning it is accepted—just like [the usage] regarding *gavaya* and so forth. By the phrase "due to *bhautapūrvya*," the possibility of such a statement is expressed.

"Not being a definition of the compound" means as follows: just as a line-drawn gavaya (rekhāgavaya) or the like, because its tail and other features do not actually belong to a real animal, cannot be a definition of a real animal; likewise, since the capacity to generate such-and-such a cognition does not reside in those respective compounds themselves, it cannot be a definition of those respective compounds. The point is that by accepting a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) [in the whole], the individual parts would be rendered meaningless. "The capacity to convey meaning is exactly like that."

The point is this: just as the tail and other features belonging to a *rekhāgavaya* (a line-drawn gavaya) convey the knowledge of a real animal by means of conveying the knowledge of the tail and other features belonging to that animal through similarity (*sādṛśya*), so too, when a certain thing is perceived as having the status of a specific word-meaning prior to the application of a grammatical operation (*vṛtti*), that compound conveys its substratum by generating a cognition whose qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is that specific meaning.

"Easy to state" (*suvacam*): the sense is that, accordingly, the definitions stated by the ancients are not impossible to maintain. Regarding "abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*): the sense is that the state of abandoning one's own meaning is precisely *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), whereas the state of not abandoning one's own meaning is precisely *vyapekṣā* (mutual dependence). In the view of *ekārthībhāva*, since the presentation of the qualified meaning is possible through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) alone, the individual parts do not present their own meanings, as that would be redundant.

The sense is that, since mutual expectancy—in the form of a requirement for syntactic connection—is impossible without the non-abandonment of their own meanings, the constituent parts (*avayava*) must, according to the view of expectancy, necessarily present their own respective meanings. "The aforementioned rule" means the established rule such as: "the *avyayībhāva* has the preceding member as its primary meaning," and so forth.

"It is not impossible" means that its occurrence is possible in compounds such as *upakumbham* (near the jar), which are avyayībhāvas. Just as in examples like *sūpapada*, even though there exist defects in the form of under-extension (*avyāpti*) or over-extension (*ativyāpti*), the meaning is that what was immediately mentioned—namely, impossibility—is indeed impossible here. "The words abandon [their original meanings]" refers to the fact that, by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of the locative case in the rule *saptamī viśeṣaṇe*, a bahuvrīhi compound occurs in some instances even for words that have different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*). This is the intended sense.

Others maintain that a compound may also consist of coreferential (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) words, such as *jahatsvārtha*, which means "that [compound] in which the meanings of the constituent words are abandoned. This implies that in a compound, the individual words lack meaning (*padānām ānarthakyam*). The underlying idea is that if one does not accept the lack of meaning for the words constituting a compound—just as one accepts it for the phonemes constituting a meaningful word (*śakta-pada*)—then even the phonemes constituting those words would not be devoid of meaning.

One might object: "Even though the individual phonemes constituting a word are meaningless in isolation because they do not convey any meaning, there is no possibility of meaninglessness in the case of words such as 'rāja' (king), since they convey meaning within a sentence, and because in a compound (*samāsa*), they produce the understanding of the meaning observed in the sentence. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The point is this" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "qualified by the king" (*rājaviśiṣṭa*): the meaning is "a person qualified by the king through a relation such as ownership (*svāmitva*) and so forth. Even in the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the relation appears solely as a *saṃsarga* (relational adjunct); thus, the identity of meaning between the derivative form (*vṛtti*, i.e., the compound) and the sentence is maintained.

However, if one accepts that the relation (*saṃbandha*) functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by a sentence, then it must be admitted that the complex expression "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and the like conveys a man qualified by a relation with the king. Regarding the phrase "if possible" (*saṃbhave sati*): [the meaning is] "if such a possibility exists. Regarding "conveying that" (*tadbodhakatvam*): it means "conveying the king and so forth. As for the word "to be postulated" (*kalpyam*): the syntactical connection is "it is not to be postulated" (*na kalpyam*). The underlying intention is that this would be purposeless and would lead to the undesirable consequence of a repetitive cognition (*bodhāvṛtti*).

[Objection: "Surely, by the maxim that 'if there is a combination [of two means], one of them is redundant,' there is no risk of the repetition of cognition—just as with two cakes—and thus there is no obstacle to the words constituting the sentence expressing their respective meanings. To this, he says: "vṛṣabha... (the bull).

The point is this: although the word *vṛṣa* has the same meaning as the word *vṛṣabha*, it is established by experience that the *vṛṣa* occurring within the word *vṛṣabha* does not convey that meaning; the same applies to the word *yāva* occurring within *yāvaka*. Thus, one must necessarily accept that the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) which is not included within the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is itself the delimitor of expressive power. Consequently, how could there be any possibility of the words constituting a compound (*vṛtti*) being expressive? This is the underlying sense.

Now, although words such as *vṛṣa* and *vṛṣabha* are synonyms, and thus the word *vṛṣa* contained within the compound *vṛṣabha* lacks independent denotative power, this is not the case for the two words *rāja* and *puruṣa*.

Because there is an absence of *samānārthatva* (having the same referent), there is no evidence for the meaninglessness of the constituent word "king" (*rājan*) in a compound; furthermore, the rule that "only in cases where there is a single referent does [the meaning] not enter into the delimitors of the denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*)" does not apply here, thus there is no fault. Moreover, in the case of words like *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), which possess both etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍha*), the sequential order of the parts enters into the sequential order of the whole which is the delimitor of the denotative power; therefore, such a rule [of non-entry] is impossible.

Thus, having raised the objection that this lack of restriction does not apply only to compounds but rather to words in general, [the author] states the counter-argument against the capacity of the constituent parts to convey meaning: "by the word *rāja*," etc. Otherwise—that is, if the constituents of a compound were to convey their own primary meanings independently—this undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would also follow. However, under the theory of *jahatsvārthatva* (the abandonment of one's own meaning), there is no fault, because the meaning of *rāja* and so forth is presented only as a qualifier for the person (*puruṣa*) and the other members of the compound.

"Na jahati" (they do not abandon): this is a neuter nominative plural form (*jas*) derived from a present participle (*śatṛ*). Here too, the compound should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*: "that [compound] in which the meanings are such that they do not abandon their own [meanings] (*ajahatsvārtha*). One might object: "If the cognition of a person qualified by a king and so forth can occur through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) alone, then the constituent parts cannot, according to the previously stated reasoning, bring about the presentation of their own individual meanings. Thus, the position that [compounds] 'do not abandon their own meanings' (*ajahatsvārthatva*) is impossible. To dispel this doubt, he states: "The intention is this... (*ayam abhiprāyaḥ*).

One might object: "Is it not the case that the very cognition of the relation [between the king and the servant] is what postulates [the possessive suffix], and that its appearing as a relation is not contradictory even for that which is not [otherwise] presented? It should not be said [that this is so], because the cognition of two nominal stems (nāmartha) through a relation of difference is contrary to linguistic convention (vyutpatti). To this, he says: "klupta... [and] "...gauravaparāhatatvāt. The meaning is that the linguistic convention regarding two nominal stems applies to cases other than compounds; thus, a cognition having possession (svatva) and so forth as its relation is not untenable.

Since there would be the burden of adding the qualifier "other than that which constitutes the constituent of the complex" (*vṛttighaṭaketaratva*) in the process of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he says: "whose power is already established" (*klaptaśakti*). [Objection: But this position is not accepted by the Sage (Pāṇini); therefore, he says: "this very one. This excludes the alternative view that the word *rāja-* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "one related to a king," and that there is a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between that person related to a king and the [word] *puruṣa*. [He says: "as another opinion. Thus, in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* regarding semantic competency (*samartha*), it is stated: "Some hold that semantic competency is mutual expectancy (*parasparavyapekṣā*)."

Even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), since the referent of the whole is the external object (*anyapadārtha*), the cow—conjoined with "brindled" and so forth—is connected [to that object] through a relation such as owner-and-owned; thus, even there, the possibility of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) exists. In a *dvandva* compound as well, since the referent of the whole is a collection (*samūha*), the meanings of the constituent members are connected [to it] through the relation of part-and-whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*); thus, even there, that possibility exists.

The proof for the fact that the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) and so forth constitutes the denotation of the composite whole (*samudāyaśakyatva*) is to be understood from the rules: "When there are many [words], [the compound is formed] in the sense of the referent of another word" (*anekamanyapadārthe*) and "A *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of the *jar* [suffix]" (*jārthe dvandva*). Precisely because of the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is no compound in cases such as "the king's wife" (*rājño bhāryā*) or "Dēvadatta’s man" (*dēvadattasya puruṣaḥ*), in the words *rājapuruṣa* and so forth. [Regarding the objection] that "there would be the consequence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being construed [with the other member]," this is because its cause—the presence of an independent presentation (*svātantryeṇopasthiti*)—exists. [This is stated] according to the *Vārttika*.

The sense is that the undertaking of this statement is simpler than the assumption of a separate power (*śakti*) in the case of compounds and so forth. "The systematic arrangement is easily established" means that even if there were instances of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and the like, there would be no impossibility (*asambhava*). Furthermore, this position is necessary.

If the *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) were included in the definition of *samartha* in the *Samartha-sūtra* by virtue of the capacity of the form itself, then there would be an inclusion of the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). This is because *ekārthībhāva* is impossible in that case, and such an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) is not desired. For if that were so, just as in the example "yatte divo duhitarmartabhojanam" the vocative elision (*āmantritanighāta*) occurs for "divaḥ" due to its status as being like a subsequent member, so too would it occur for "ṛtena" in the example "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhāvṛtaspṛśā."

There would be the undesirable consequence of the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatā*) for the vocative by virtue of its being treated as part of the preceding word (*paraṅgavadbhāva*), because the grave accent (*nighāta*) prescribed in the eighth [chapter] does not apply due to the absence of being after a word (*padāt paratva*) and because it stands at the beginning of a *pāda*. However, in the view that semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) constitutes grammatical capacity (*sāmarthya*), once the technical rule regarding "capacity" (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) is applied, the word *ṛtena* is construed only with the action expressed by the verb *ānaśāthe* (which is derived from the root *aś* meaning "to obtain"), and thus there is no semantic expectancy with *mitrāvaruṇābhyām*; consequently, the aforementioned defect does not arise. This is clearly explained in the Vedabhāṣya and other such works; so it should be understood.

"Both types of function" (dve api vṛttī) means that both types of function—namely, *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) and *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning)—are present. Since the word *bheda* is observed to be used in the sense of "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) as well, he says: "Difference (*bheda*) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)."

Now, if difference (*bheda*) were the denoted meaning, would the difference of the referent of the word "king" (*rājapada*) reside in the man? Or would the difference of the man, or rather the difference of the man qualified by the king, be perceived in the king? It cannot be the first [alternative], because it is impossible for that [difference]—which has become a qualifier of the man—to be construed as a qualifier when it is itself a difference; furthermore, since the difference of the king exists in every man related to the king, such a difference would fail to serve as a differentiator (*avyāvartakatva*), and it would also fail to accomplish the purpose that will be stated later. Nor can it be the second [alternative], because [the difference] would have as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) that which is delimited by the delimitor of the relation (*anvayitāvacchedaka*), namely the nature of being a man (*puruṣatva*).

Because difference (*bheda*) is sublated in the case of the king, and because a difference having that [king] as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) does not serve to exclude [others]; and because, even though a difference having as its counter-correlate that which is delimited by "wealth-ness" (*dhanatva*) exists in the prior member of compounds such as *rājadhanam*, the cognition of that [difference] is of no utility. For this very reason, the third alternative is also not tenable, since the cognition of that [difference] is useless. To dispel this doubt, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is: "and when difference is included within the denoted meaning. "Such a cognition" (*iti bodhaḥ*) means: "the cognition that [it] is not related to one distinct from the king."

However, the view that the form of the cognition is "as heard" (yathāśruta) is not tenable; for since such a cognition has as its qualifier the difference from one who is not related to the king, it would act as an inhibitor only with respect to a cognition of the form "not related to the king," and not with respect to a cognition of another relation. Consequently, there would be no way to prevent such usages as "the king's man is Devadatta's" (rājapuruṣo devadattasya ca).

In the compound *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the whole as denoting one who is distinct from a person related to the king; here, "related" (*saṃbandhī*) should be understood according to the specific context as involving relations such as that of owner and owned. For this very reason, when the intended relation is one of being an object of affection, the usage *rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāḥ* ("the king's man [is] of his wife") is indeed possible, because the cognition produced by the compound—having the form "one whose owner is distinct from the king"—does not act as an obstacle to the comprehension of that [affectionate relation]. If such usage were in every respect undesirable, then...

The relation in general (*saṃbandhasāmānya*) alone should be accepted as the denotable meaning. However, the natural sense of the subsequent text—“but [the word] even when there is no owner”—is understood to favor the former alternative (the view that the relation is the denoted meaning). Furthermore, the natural sense of the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, which states, “The king turns away the man from others,” supports this position. It should be understood, however, that the cognition “the man is related to the king” arises subsequently (*pārṣika*) in the form of an inference based on such distinctions as the fact that [the relation] resides in a particular individual. As for the phrase “and the contingency of usage”: [The text continues: ...[the contingency of using the singular number would arise]. Even though the relation is one, it is expressed by the singular suffix because it is a single entity; yet, since the relation is not a substance (*dravya*), the singular suffix cannot be applied to it. Therefore, the singular suffix is applied to the possessor (*svāmin*), who is a substance, and through the relation, it is understood as applying to the relation itself. Alternatively, since the relation is a quality (*guṇa*) residing in a substance, the singular suffix is applied to the substance, and through the relation, it is understood as applying to the relation. Or again, since the relation is a property (*dharma*) of the substance, the singular suffix is applied to the substance, and through the relation, it is understood as applying to the relation. Thus, the contingency of usage is avoided. This is the view of the *Kāśikāvṛtti*. But this is incorrect. For if the relation were the denoted meaning, then in the case of "the king's men" (*rājñaḥ puruṣāḥ*), the plural suffix would be impossible. Why? Because the plurality of the men is not connected to the relation. If it were connected, then the relation would be many, and consequently, the singular suffix would be impossible. Therefore, the relation is not the denoted meaning. Rather, the possessor (*svāmin*) is the denoted meaning. And the relation is understood through the force of implication (*ākṣepa*). The point is that even in the case of something ownerless (*asvāmika*), there exists a distinction between having no owner at all and having an owner other than the king. "Both" means both difference (*bheda*) and relation (*saṃsarga*). Others, however, maintain that what is called *jahatsvārthā* (the theory where the word abandons its own meaning) refers to the fact that the subordinate members of a compound do not present their own meanings; thus, due to the proximity of words such as "king," it is the word "man" itself that conveys a man related to the king. This is like the common usage of expressions such as "a bundle of campaka flowers" or "a bundle of jasmine," which occurs even when the campaka or jasmine flowers are absent from the bundle, because they take on the association of fragrance. In the same way, the meaning of the word "king" [is understood] in the context of the man.

Thus, the linguistic usage [of the term] *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) is justified. For this very reason, Helārāja states in his commentary (*Helārājīya*) that the meaning of the compound *jahatsvārthā* is: "that [compound] in which the subordinate words (*upasarjana*) abandon their own primary meanings" (*jahati upasarjanapadāni svārthaṃ yasyāṃ sā*). And so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*: "Alternatively, it becomes a qualifier through association (*anvaya*), as in: 'This is a jar of jasmine,' 'This is a jar of campaka. Even when the flowers have been removed, it remains a qualifier through association, as in: 'This is a jar of jasmine,' 'This is a jar of campaka.'"

Alternatively, "capacity" (sāmarthya) consists of difference and connection; for instance, in a compound, due to the proximity of the word *rāja-* (king), the word *puruṣa-* (person) itself conveys only a person whose owner is the king and who is distinct from other kings. Therefore, the king has no separate relation with another [person], because the word *rāja-* lacks its own independent meaning [in that context].

Therefore, there is no such usage as "the king's man-horse" (rājapuruṣo'śvaḥ), analogous to "the king's man and horse" (rājñaḥ puruṣo'śvaśca); nor is there a relation of the man with another owner, because even in the form of "man-ness," there is a contradiction with the cognition of that specific individual, and the implication is that even the cognition of him [as a mere man] is opposed to the understanding that "this man has Devadatta as his owner."

Just as in the Vedāntic view there arises from sentences such as "That thou art" a cognition of an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) meaning, so here too there is a cognition of a specific individual by way of the form "man. However, it is not logical that difference (*bheda*) should be the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*), because it is not experienced [as such]. Regarding the statement that "either difference or relation is the capacity (*sāmarthya*)"—made in the context of demonstrating that a word's function (*vṛtti*) is "leaving its own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*)—what, then, is this difference or relation? In the case of the expression "the king's," all property is implicated; when "the man" is said, every owner is implicated.

In this context, when it is said, "Bring the king's man here," the king excludes [the man] from other masters, and the man also excludes [the king] from his own [subordinates]. Thus, when both sides have been excluded, if he should abandon his own primary meaning (svārtha), let him do so; for by this statement in the *Bhāṣya*, it is precisely the non-denotability (*avācyatva*) that is obtained. Here, by the expression "from another master," the non-exclusion of the master in the form of the king is obtained, thereby expressing his connection (*saṃsarga*); and by this, it is indicated that neither difference (*bheda*) nor connection (*saṃsarga*) is an object of direct denotation (*bodha-viṣayatva*).

If [the king] were the object of the cognition [of the compound], it would be necessary for the referent of the word "king" to be connected as the counter-correlative of the difference in relation (*saṃsargabheda*); since this would entail the abandonment of the stated objection regarding its non-presentation, such a consequence would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of the specific relation [of the king] with the man should arise from the word "man" alone, and thus there would be no inconsistency in mentioning it; for otherwise, this would result in no distinction from the previous alternative (that the relation is expressed by the word "king"). Furthermore, by stating that "the man excludes the king from his own [other] attendants," it is precisely those two [exclusion and relation] that are obtained as the denotable meanings; for indeed, neither the cognition of the relation of the man with the king nor the cognition of the exclusion of the king from others who are not the man is accepted by anyone.

Thus, they say that establishing the cognition [of the meaning] in the case of *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds is indeed impossible according to the aforementioned method; however, there is no such impossibility in this view, because the intention is that the compound conveys a collective as the "referent of another word" (*anyapadārtha*) precisely in that manner. This intention—that even from expressions such as *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*, one is understood as "one who has resorted solely to Kṛṣṇa" by way of the form of "having resorted"—should be understood in detail from the *Vivaraṇa* and other sources; enough of this digression. Regarding the statement "the connection [is established] through relation," in the previous alternative and in this alternative, in cases such as *mahādevaḥ*, the application of suffixes like *ātva* occurs by taking the meaningfulness [of the compound] based on its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

Just as in the Vedāntic view, regarding the sentence "The moon is that which possesses supreme luminosity" used as an answer to the question "What is the moon?", the meaningfulness of the word *prakṛṣṭaprakāśa* (supreme luminosity) lies in its conveying—through the actual nature of things—that it refers to the cognition of such a luminous entity, while the word *candra* (moon) causes one to grasp that [luminosity] in the form of the property of being the moon; so too, in the present case, the meaningfulness of the word *rājā* (king) and so forth should be understood as consisting in their causing one to grasp that the word *puruṣa* (person) refers to such a specific individual.

The meaning is that according to the Vedāntic view, from the statement "the moon is pre-eminent light," there arises a cognition of that which possesses such light as being the moon—both by way of its being the moon and by way of its possessing the word "moon"—but not merely as possessing such light. In this regard, the *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) consists in the coalescence of meanings (*ekārthībhāva*), and thus the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.1] becomes more unified; this is the sense of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *Samartha-sūtra*.

Kaiyaṭa states that the mention of the comparative suffix (*tarap*) is intended to indicate that, although the *sūtra* would have to be split into two distinct sentences if one were to accept both types of capacity (*sāmarthya*), and even though the *sūtra* remains undivided in the view where there is only one type of capacity consisting of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), nevertheless, because faults exist in that position, the position of "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) alone is correct. The phrase "based on that" means based on the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*). He says "compound" (*samāsa*) in order to avoid the charge of deficiency [in his own statement]. [He says] "as mere *vṛtti*."

The meaning is "the function of derivative forms (kṛdanta) and so forth. Because they are the substrata of a function consisting of the power of a composite whole that generates a single presentation, they are designated as having a "function" (vṛtti). He explains the term *samartha* [in the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*] by means of the word *vigraha* ("analytic statement"), because this is obtained from the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the term *kṛttaddhita*: by the word *kṛt*, that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix is understood; by the word *taddhita*, that which contains a *taddhita* suffix is understood. Consequently, there is no failure to include [the examples] *bahupaṭuḥ* and *sarvaka*. Due to the application of the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) concerning *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes, in the case of "he makes a cloth" (*paṭaṃ karoti*) and "bring the jar" (*kumbham ānaya*), the suffix *aṇ* is not applied [to form *pāṭaka* or *kaumbhya*]; and in the case of "the offspring of the wealthy Upagu" (*ṛddhasyopagor apatyam*), the *taddhita* suffix is not applied [to form *aupagava*]. Semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) is the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) of words that possess separate meanings. As in the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the meanings are separate; however, in a compound (*samāsa*), they become unified.

This is because of the *Samartha-sūtra-bhāṣya*. In that context, the meaning is that since non-existence cannot be established even by a hundred statements, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of that which is qualified by semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) is what is being enjoined. Thus, it is concluded that "integration" (*ekārthībhāva*) consists in the fact that words observed in common usage—which, according to [the Naiyāyikas], have as their objects distinct meanings presented separately by whatever words may produce them—generate a single presentation of a single denotatum (*śakya*) with respect to a qualified object. The nature of such words, however, is to be understood through similarity.

But in the theory that words denote the completed action (*kārya*), the production of the application [of a word] is caused by the sentence, or rather, by the cognition [of it]. The inclusion of the phrase "of those seen" at the end is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the case-ending. For, just as the meaning of a case-ending is understood through that very case-ending and not through any other word, there is no over-extension regarding the end of such a form, because a case-ending does not possess such a [independent] meaning.

The inclusion of the term *yatkiṃcit* (whatever) is for the sake of including examples such as *aupagava* (the descendant of Upagu); for in cases like *upagor apatyam* (the offspring of Upagu), it is observed in common usage that the meaning in the form of "offspring" is the object of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the word "offspring. Thus, its inclusion is achieved. The mention of the suffix *cvī* is intended to indicate that "oneness of meaning" (*ekārthatva*) is figurative (*gauṇa*). It should be understood that just as the linguistic usage of "existence" regarding words—which are themselves non-existent—is figurative, so too is their usage as having "one meaning. This is explained in detail elsewhere. [The phrase] "compound and single-remainder" (*samāsaikaśeṣa*)...

In this context, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member) does not constitute a *vṛtti* (compound formation), because the aforementioned *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) is impossible, as it lacks the capacity to present its own meaning as connected with the meanings of other members; for it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the remaining word manifests the respective collective meaning through its own function (*svavṛtti*)—as is evident in the *Śekhara* and other works. Furthermore, rules such as *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) are also included, as they indirectly have words as their objective (*uddeśya*).

One who studies grammar is a *vaiyākaraṇa*; one who cooks is a *pācaka*. In these cases, there is no impairment of the capacity to denote the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*), because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—which conveys the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or a primary derivative (*kṛt*)—generates a cognition in which the agent is the qualificand. Now, one might object: "Since the word *paṅkaja* is also a compound (*samāsa*), even according to the opponent's view, it is not accepted as having a [unitary] expressive power (*śakti*). Therefore, its inclusion as an example is inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of those who do not accept [unitary] expressive power."

The phrase "in this [context], 'avṛttau' etc. refers to the following: the point is that, according to the manner about to be explained, this serves precisely to establish *śakti* by way of refuting the views of others. Regarding the expression "yogād eva": the meaning is "by means of *yoga*, which is the power residing in the individual parts (*avayava-śakti*)."

In that context, due to the diversity of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of the noun *paṅka* (mud) is also construed as the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) with respect to the production (*utpatti*) denoted by the verbal root *jan*, and such a production is construed as the substratum (*āśrayatā*) within the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the meaning of the suffix *-ḍa*. Thus, since the understanding "that which is the substratum of a production whose locus is mud" is established, the notion is that a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) [of the whole word *paṅkaja*] would be redundant. That [collective power] is postulated as a capacity consisting of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). This is because [the parts] present themselves in the form of the state of being mud (*paṅkatva*).

Thus, because it is impossible for there to be a presentation [of the object] under that form (as *pajha-ness*) without a denotative power (*śakti*) delimited by *pajha-ness*, the point is that the cognition of a word's occurrence (*vṛtti*) as delimited by a particular property is the cause of a presentation that has that property as its qualifier.

"Regarding the phrase *svāmitvenopasthitaye* (for the sake of presentation as the possessor): the meaning is for the sake of presenting the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) in the form of a possessor. It should be understood that without another mode of operation (*vṛtti*), the presentation of the substratum (*dharmin*) in any form whatsoever is impossible. Regarding *lakṣaṇayā* (by means of indication): the meaning is either by indication of the whole (*samudāya-lakṣaṇā*) or by indication of the suffix *ḍa*. He states *evam* (thus) to indicate that the word *paṅkaja* is an illustration of other words that are both etymologically derived and conventional (*yogarūḍha*). Regarding the phrase *sthakārapade 'pi* (even in the case of the word *sthaka*)."

The phrase "the power of the whole [word] would not be established" is to be connected here by way of ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). One might object: "Let there be no power of the whole in that case; for in that instance, comprehension is experienced precisely in the form obtainable through the power of the parts, namely, as the agent of the production of the action of a chariot. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "And so it is. The meaning is that the word *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) can indeed convey the sense of a Brāhmaṇa and others, because based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "one who makes a chariot," it is possible for it to denote a Brāhmaṇa and so forth.

Regarding "in the case of birth": since Brahmins and others possess the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), they are eligible [for the rites]; thus, the injunction prescribing the laying of the fires (*adhānavidhi*) fulfills its purpose through them as its performers. Regarding "the postulation of that": it refers to the postulation of a specific power (*śakti*) delimited by a specific class (*jāti*) within the aggregate. Regarding "of the specific class" or "qualified by a specific class": [as stated in the text]—"From a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya woman bears a Māgadha, and from a Vaiśya, a Kṣattṛ."

Thus, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, it should be understood that one born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is an *anuloma* caste known as a *rathakāra*. The phrase "the assumption of a novel [scriptural] injunction" refers to the Mīmāṃsakas; [to assume such a thing] would be highly improper.

The point is that because the term *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*), this sentence does not concern Brāhmaṇas and the like, but rather concerns those of the *anuloma* castes; since such persons cannot study the Veda, the Mīmāṃsā tenet—that the Vedic study required for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) prescribed by the Veda must otherwise be inferred—would be contradicted. [Regarding the phrase] "there would be a qualifier": thus, just as one uses the expression "the king's man," one might also use the expression "the rich king's man."

He states the reason for the connection with the qualifier by saying, "by the word *rāja*.
