Regarding the term "independent" (*svatantra*): the meaning is that in cases such as "the jar is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), in order to prevent the cognition of the connection of the meaning of the word "eternal" with the jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so on, an appearance (*upasthiti*) is postulated as the cause for the cognition of the connection with a qualifier, by way of the relation of being the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). However, if one were to postulate a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), then by virtue of that [power], the word *rāja* and so on would present an object qualified by its own meaning; thus, because the appearance having itself as the primary qualificand is absent there, [there is no such problem].

The intended meaning is that there is a connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇānvaya*). Since the person is presented [in the mind] precisely through its distinction from the king (*rājavaiśiṣṭyena*), the expression "the king’s man and the wife" (*rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāśca*) does not occur; for it is unestablished by linguistic convention (*avyutpannatvāt*) that a connection with another [word] occurs through a relation of the same kind as the one by which some distinction was presented. For this very reason, the expression "the pot’s substanceness" (*ghaṭo dravyatvasya*) does not occur, because once the pot has been presented through its distinction from potness (*ghaṭatvavaiśiṣṭyena*) by way of inherence (*samavāyena*), there is no connection of substanceness with it by means of that same relation.

The expression "the king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣo 'bhirūpaḥ*) certainly occurs, because there is no factor that would cause it to be understood [as a compound]. Nor does the expression "the king’s man horse" (*rājapuruṣo 'śvaḥ*) occur; for that which has been presented as a qualifier in one instance cannot function as a qualifier in another. Regarding the restriction of compounds (*samāsaniyama*): since the use of a sentence would necessarily have occurred [otherwise], a compound being introduced would invariably exclude the sentence. However, under the view of "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), since the compound is established when there is integration of meaning and the sentence is established when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), the governing rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) need not be formulated. This is because, due to their having distinct domains, there is no possibility of the compound subverting the sentence.

Thus, the word *vā* (or) found in the rule *asamarthānāṃ prathamādvā* need not be included; likewise, the mention of *vā* in the context of prescribing the suffix *san* need not be made. This was stated in the Bhāṣya: "The mention of *vā* is useless because [the desired result] is established by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva-siddhatvāt*). The lack of congruence in gender (*liṅgāyoga*) should be observed in certain instances, such as *kukkuṭāṇḍam* ("a hen's egg") and *mṛgakṣīram* ("deer's milk"), but not everywhere, since it is seen in cases such as *kumārīputraḥ* ("the daughter's son"). Others, however, maintain that this [lack of congruence] is not necessitated by *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), because even in sentences intended to exclude other classes (*jātyantara-nivṛtti*), such as *chāgasya māṃsam* ("goat's meat"), no specific gender is observed.

Thus, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra* that no specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*) manifests in the subordinate member (*upasarjana-padārtha*) of a compound; rather, a specific number such as singularity (*ekatva*) is perceived merely as "numberness" (*saṃkhyātva*), and not in its specific form as "singulartiness" (*ekatvatva*). This very point is expressed by the statement that "non-dual singularity" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) is what is perceived. "Difference" (*bheda*) refers to a specific form.

The meaning of that [phrase] is "the number one in the form of its absence. It should be understood that the expression "in the form of its absence" means "in the form of the absence of the cognition of that [number]. However, the number which serves as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) and is conveyed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is perceived in cases such as *dviputra* ("having two sons"); therefore, when that [number] is not conveyed [by the stem], it is not perceived. There is no evidence for interpreting the Bhāṣya through such a restriction, for in instances such as *tvatputraḥ tāvakīno māsajātaḥ* ("your son, born a month ago, belonging to you"), a single individual appears in the form of each respective basis for application.

However, in expressions such as *yuṣmatputraḥ* ("your son") or *yauṣmākīṇaḥ* ("belonging to you"), there is the manifestation of multiple individuals through that very form; for this very reason, in cases like *goṣucaraḥ* (meaning "cock" or "indragopa insect") or *varṣāsujātaḥ*, even though the plural suffix is present, there is no manifestation of plurality. Thus, they say that here, by the superimposition (*āropa*) of plurality, there is merely a formal adjustment of the word, but there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of that [plurality] with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). For this reason, in expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), the cognition of number is not caused by the absence of the case-suffix (*sub*), because even when that suffix is present [in the compound], it is not cognized.

The detailed exposition should be sought in the *Bhāṣyapratīpodyota* and other such works. For this very reason—namely, because the concept of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is accepted as the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). || 32 ||

He himself states another purpose for the *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) as explained by the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and others: "In the same way, *dhava*... In expressions such as *dhavakhadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), there is a sequential connection through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and so forth. Thus, in a *dvandva* compound like *dhavakhadirau*, according to the rule "a *dvandva* occurs in the sense of *ca* [and]," multiple *sub*-ending words are employed in the sense of *ca*, and that [compound] receives the designation *dvandva*. One would have to effect the communication of the meaning by accepting a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This results in prolixity (*gaurava*). Likewise...

Even in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, one should understand that the meaning is assigned by means of a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*), according to the rule "prefixes such as *nis* [and others] [form compounds] with a word ending in the second case when they signify 'gone beyond' (*krānta*) and so forth. This indicates that a compound consisting of a prefix like *nis* followed by a word ending in the second case occurs in the sense of "gone beyond" and receives the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa*). However, regarding instances such as *goratha*, one would have to postulate a separate rule for each specific meaning, which results in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). In that context, in the case of *goratha*, the meaning is "a chariot joined with a cow" (*goyukto rathaḥ*), which is a sense of conjunction (*yuktārtha*).

In the case of "ghṛtaghaṭa" (a jar of ghee), the meaning is "a jar filled with ghee," where the sense is that of being full (*pūrṇa*). In "guḍadhānā" (molasses and grains), the meaning is "grains mixed with molasses," where the sense is that of being mixed (*miśra*). In "keśacūḍa" (a tuft of hair), the meaning is "one whose tuft consists of a mass of hair," where the sense is that of a collection (*saṃghāta*). In "suvarṇālaṅkāra" (gold ornament), the meaning is "an ornament made from gold," where the sense is that of a transformation (*vikāra*). In "dvidāśā" (twelve), the meaning is "ten repeated twice," whereby the suffix *suc* is elided. In "saptaparṇa" (seven-leaved), the meaning is "one who has seven leaves [on each branch]," whereby a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is understood.

Others, however, maintain that [the addition of] *nir-* and so forth has the meaning of "transgressing" (*krānta*) and the like, but this does not belong to the composite whole; thus, this distinction is not caused by *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning). For this very reason, it is not counted among the distinctions produced by *ekārthībhāva* in the Bhāṣya. Even in the case of *dvidaśāḥ*, they say that the operation occurs because the first member has the sense of *su-* as its internal meaning through the natural power of the word, and not from the power of the composite whole; for the understanding is that "ten" is the object of the operation in which the number two arises. [The phrase] "because of the word *ca*" in the root text [refers to this].

In examples such as *dhava-khadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), the use of the particle *ca* (and) would follow the pattern of a sentence; its prohibition—namely, its elision (*lopa*)—is what must be prescribed. However, in the view that there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), since there is no separate presentation [of the meanings], the conjunction (*samuccaya*) based on separate presentation is not perceived, and thus the use of *ca* does not arise; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "of *iva*, etc.": here, the word "elision" (*lopa*) is connected [to these]. Regarding the phrase "of those previously mentioned": this means the inclusion of the elision of words such as *krānta* in cases like *niṣkauśāmbi* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī").

The analysis of the compound *haṃsagamana* is "one whose gait is like that of a swan" (*haṃsa iva gamanaṃ yasya*). However, in the view where there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*) is included within the meaning of the whole compound; therefore, it is not used [separately]. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "it is already established. He says "the agent of attainment" (*prāptikartṛ*) because, if one were to first assume a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *udaka* as "related to water," then the agent of the attainment of the object—which has already been reached as a part of the water—could not be syntactically connected [to the action]. He says this because the intended meaning would not be obtained.

In the case of indication based on relation (*saṃbandhilakṣaṇā*), there arises the very cognition that "the village is related to the water, which is non-different from the agent of the attainment. Although the nature of being related is simply the state of being the object of the attainment whose agent is oneself—so that the cognition occurs as the state of being the object of attainment—and likewise in examples such as *ūḍharatha* ("one who has brought a chariot"), even when there is indication based on relation in the word *ratha* and so forth, the desired meaning is indeed obtained because the nature of being related consists precisely in being the agent of the act of carrying whose object is oneself; nevertheless, [it is understood] specifically as a relation.

The intended meaning is that the manifestation [in cognition] would be as "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, but not as "the nature of objectness" (*karmatvatva*) and so forth; this is the underlying point.

Regarding the phrase "the object of attainment" (*prāptikarma*), it means that there would be a cognition such as "water is non-different from the object of attainment. This refers to the word *prāpta*.

Since the word *udaka* (water) is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*) and [the agent] is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), it is more appropriate for water itself to be the qualificand; thus, although the desired connection of water as the agent of the attainment (*prāpti*) would not occur, it is stated in that way to indicate that [the connection] is rather by non-difference (*abheda*) with the object of attainment. It should be understood that the intent lies precisely in the point that the desired connection would not otherwise occur, and not in the necessity of the aforementioned cognition of the connection. "Otherwise" means: if one were to accept the connection of water with the attainment through the relation of agency (*kartṛtā*).

"Co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) means that the referents of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) possess the same case-ending. "And because of the lack of syntactic connection" (*anvayāsaṃvāt*)—the sense is that, according to the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root can only be connected directly through identity (*abheda*). "Otherwise"—that is, if such a rule is not accepted—"because of the non-occurrence of non-connection" (*ananvayānāpatti*): since it is possible for Devadatta to be connected with the act of cooking by way of the relation of agency (*kartṛtā*), it would be untenable to maintain that such a sentence possesses a non-connected meaning, which is what [the opponent] desires. "Related to that" (*tatsambandhī*).

The meaning is "the action of attainment. Regarding the phrase "of the qualificand-ness in the agent," the meaning is "of the qualificand-ness as determined by the agent"; thus, the point is that the aforementioned cognition would be impossible. He states the reason for this impossibility: "in the base [word]," etc. Furthermore, one should observe the contradiction with the statement: "Nouns (nāman) have substance (sattva) as their primary meaning."

One might object: "In cases such as *pacati* (‘he cooks’), let there be a renunciation of the established predominance of the suffix even in a compound (*vṛtti*), and likewise, let the statement ‘they have substance as their predominant meaning’ (*sattvapradhānāni*) also refer to nouns that do not participate in the formation of a compound. Anticipating this objection, he says: “by being the meaning of a noun” (*nāmārthatvena*). This means: by being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by a noun. The point is that the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) occurs only between the two things that are the qualificands of the cognition produced by a noun, and that relation occurs precisely through identity (*abheda*); this follows from the sense of the rule beginning with “the meanings of two nouns” (*nāmārthayoḥ*). [He adds: “and because it would result in an identity-relation” (*abhedānvayāpatteśca*).

The meaning is that if *prāpti* (attainment) were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there would be no possibility of a cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the water and the agent (*kartṛ*) who has become the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If one does not accept that the ascertainment of semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) is a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābda*), then let it be exactly as stated in the literal text. He states "in the same way, *ūḍharatha*" [to show] that there is not only a failure to provide a solution through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in a *bahuvrīhi* where the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the meaning, but also in a *bahuvrīhi* where the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and others are the meanings. From the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*) "one by whom a chariot is carried" (*ūḍho ratho yena*), the cognition is: "that which has the act of carrying as its object, and whose agent is such-and-such."

In the sentence "upahṛtaḥ paśuḥ yasmāt" (from whom the animal was offered), the meaning understood from the sentence is that the animal is the object of the act of offering directed toward [the deity] *yat*. In the sentence "uddhṛtaḥ odanaḥ yasyāḥ" (from which the rice was taken out), the meaning understood from the sentence is that the rice is the object of the act of taking out relative to [the vessel] *yat*. In the sentence "bahavaḥ pācakāḥ yasyām" (in which there are many cooks), the meaning understood from the sentence is that the agents of cooking are those distinct from many [individuals] residing in [the place] *yat*. Here too, even if one resorts to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the relationship with that [place] after first understanding the syntactic connection of the denoted meaning—that the chariot is non-different from the object of the act of carrying—the construction of the singular cognition "the agent of carrying" and so forth is not achieved.

The collective intended meaning is that objections such as the impossibility of [the object] being the qualificand with respect to the meaning of the suffix—since the vehicle (*vahana*) and so forth constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*)—should be understood as before. The point is that even if the aforementioned multiple instances of the breakdown of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) do not apply to the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a related entity (*saṃbandhin*), the stated cognition cannot be accounted for; this should likewise be observed in what follows. Furthermore, in the case of *bahupācika* ("one who has many cooks"), if there were a metaphorical indication of a related entity, the cognition would arise only as being related to that [entity], and not as being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). This is the sense.

It should be understood, however, that this objection does not apply if one accepts a lakṣaṇā (metaphorical indication) qualified by the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). Regarding the phrase "just as in the case of the word *ghaṭa*": the point is that just as the word *ghaṭa* brings about the cognition of a thing qualified by the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) through its own qualified power (*śakti*), so too the compound *prāptodaka* brings about the cognition of a thing qualified by the state of being the object of the action of reaching (*prāpti*) having water as its agent, through its own qualified power; thus, there is no lack of logical consistency [in the theory of *samartha-samāsa*]. This is because the grammatical rules such as "the meaning of two nouns" (*nāmārthayoḥ*) have as their scope cases of separate presentation (*pṛthag-upasthiti*). || 33 ||

In the rule *aṣaṣṭhyarthe bahuvrīhau*, the word *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the locative (*saptamī*) as well; for, just as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* with a genitive sense, there is no necessity to postulate a separate etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) for a *bahuvrīhi* with a locative sense. Regarding the phrase "one might postulate" (*kalpayet*): the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a deliberation (*saṃpraśna*), according to the rule *vidhinimantraṇa-*. Having raised the alternative—whether the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the first member (*pūrvapada*) or in the second member (*uttarapada*)—he states that it is not the former: "For that [indication] is not [possible] in *citra*" (*sā hi na citre*). This refers to the example: "The cow whose owner is Citra" (*citrasvāmī gauḥ*).

Even if the cognition of the cow itself is secured by the word *citra* (variegated) through its proximity to the word *go* (cow)—since it possesses a variegated form—there arises the following difficulties: first, the cognition of the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the owner by that which is qualified by "cowness" as conjoined with "variegation" would be untenable; second, there would be the consequence of a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the owner of the variegated [cow] and the object presented by the word *go*. Likewise, in cases such as *jaraccitraguḥ* (the old variegated-cow-owner) or *śobhanacitraguḥ* (the beautiful variegated-cow-owner), if each individual word were to indicate its own meaning as the owner of the cow, the resulting cognition would be "the cow is non-different from that owner of the cow who is non-different from the old one," and not a cognition of the object "oldness" etc. as being related to the cow.

It should also be understood that [the word] functions through mediation (*vyavadhāna*). The word *citra* (variegated) indicates the owner of the variegated [cow], and the word *go* (cow) indicates the owner of the cow; there is the manifestation of only a single individual by way of its variegatedness and its cowness, according to the maxim that "words denoting individuals refer to the individual present [in proximity]"—however, this is not [the case] for such a cognition.

In cases such as "bhavācchobhanacitraguḥ" (you are the owner of beautiful brindled cows), the connection with the word "beautiful" (*śobhana*) is untenable, and thus [the interpretation] is inadmissible. Furthermore, if the word "beautiful" were to indicate the "owner of the beautiful," it would contradict direct experience; these points should be understood. The intended meaning is that there would simply be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) for the referent of the word "cow. He states "not the latter" (*nāpi*) [to refute the second alternative]: "The cow's owner is brindled" (*goḥ svāmī citraḥ*) is to be explained as before; the cause [for rejecting it] is the apprehension of the absence of any intention (*tātparya*) toward such a meaning.

[Objection: But surely, when there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) between the cow and the "variegated" (*citra*)—which is a part of the referent indicated (*lakṣyārtha*) by the word "variegated"—there arises a cognition such as "the owner of the variegated [cow] who is non-different from the cow," or "the owner of the cow who is non-different from the variegated. And thus, the undesirable consequence of a cognition in the aforementioned form does not follow. To this, he says: "of the mere 'variegated' etc. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), the owner is excluded. "Because of the impossibility of syntactic connection" (*anvayāyogāt*): because it would contradict the grammatical rule that "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning" (*padārthaḥ padārthe na*). "After the cognition of the syntactic connection" (*anvayabodhottaram*):...

The meaning is as follows: because of their proximity, the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between those two [the cow and the quality of being variegated] occurs first through the causal complex consisting of the presentation of word-meanings and so forth. Subsequently, when there is the apprehension of a cognition of a cow non-different from the variegated one, the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*)—namely, the owner—is indicated by the word "cow" in the form of being the owner of a cow non-different from the variegated one. Furthermore, such an initial cognition is necessary for the presentation of the ownership of a cow qualified by variegation and so forth. And it is precisely by virtue of producing such a cognition that the word "variegated" (*citrapada*) is rendered meaningful. This is the sense [of the phrase] "direct connection" (*sākṣātsambandha*).

In this context, the meaning is as follows: the "possible relation" (*śakyasaṃbandha*) is a direct relation consisting of ownership (*svāmitva*) as determined by the substance (*sattva*). On the other hand, since the word *citra* denotes a quality (*guṇa*), the relation—either a secondary relation (*paraṃparāsaṃbandha*) consisting of ownership as determined by subsistence (*samavāya*) in that which possesses its own power, or a relation consisting of indication (*lakṣaṇārūpa*) involving the substrate substance—is what must be expressed; thus, there is prolixity (*gaurava*). However, this is stated according to the view of others; in our own system, it should be understood that since the word *citra* also denotes a substance qualified by a quality, a direct relation is possible for that [word] as well.

Regarding the term *kṛtaviśva*: by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "one by whom the universe (*viśva*) has been made," the referent of the compound is understood either as the creator whose activity has the universe as its object, or as one who possesses an action directed toward the universe. Here too, the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is indicative of the locative (*saptamī*) as well; for there is also a bahuvrīhi with a locative sense, as in *citragur grāmaḥ* ("the village possessing brindled cows"). Regarding the phrase "as having the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth": in *prāptodakaḥ*, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent; in *kṛtaviśvaḥ*, it denotes the object (*karman*).

In examples such as *snānīya-cūrṇa-pātra*, the meaning is that the *kṛt* suffix has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth. The mention of "derivative words" (*yaugika*) is made because a restrictive factor (*vinigamaka*) is possible; it is intended to exclude words like *śukta* which are based on conventional usage (*rūḍha*).

This is an elliptical illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). In the case of possessive compounds (*bahuvrīhi*) expressing the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), such as *pāṭhakaputrakaḥ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta, whose son is a teacher"), *vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ* ("a village whose men are heroes"), and *pācakapuruṣakaḥ* ("one whose men are cooks"), as well as in those expressing the sense of the locative (*saptamyartha*), there is sometimes a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) because words like *vīra*, *pāṭhaka*, and so on, denote the substratum (*dharmin*) and are thus equally directly connected [to the compound]. However, it should be understood that the phrase "not the sense of the genitive" (*aṣaṣṭhyartha*) was stated to indicate that while there is always a lack of a determining factor in the case of possessive compounds expressing the sense of the accusative and other cases, this is not the case everywhere in other instances.

"Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in both words" means that in the case of *citrapada* (the word "variegated") and *gopada* (the word "cow"), there is indication of the owner of the variegated cow. "The Naiyāyika" refers to the ancient Naiyāyikas. "Mutually" means that when there is indication of the owner of the variegated cow in *citrapada*, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *go* acts as a regulator by apprehending the intention toward such a meaning; and when there is indication in *gopada*, the co-occurrence with the word *citra* acts as the regulator. [This is stated] because the state of lacking a decisive reason for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*) remains as it was.

The meaning is that there is no determining factor (*vinigamanā*) here as to when or in which single word the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs, because it would result in a state of uncertainty. "Because of the impossibility of *lakṣaṇā*" means that it is impossible for *lakṣaṇā* to occur in a single word at one and the same time; furthermore, in cases such as *śobhanā citraguḥ* ("one who possesses brindled cows is beautiful") or *śobhanā jaratī citraguḥ* ("the brindled cow is beautiful"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the word-meaning "beautiful" (*śobhana*) being unable to connect [with the rest of the sentence].

Because it is impossible for [the word *citra*] to have a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) there as being a part of the same referent (*ekadeśatva*), and because even in the case of words such as *śobhana*, if one accepts that they indicate (*lakṣaṇā*) the owner of the brindled cow characterized by "beautiful," then all three words would indicate such a qualified object; thus, there is no room for parsimony (*lāghava*) compared to the assumption of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*). Furthermore, in this alternative, one must recognize the cumbersome complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the acceptance that the three presentations (*upasthiti*) produced by the three words are all causes of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) [to prefer one over the others].

He introduces [the following] to refute the doctrine of the modern Naiyāyikas, beginning with "na ca" (and not). "Sā" refers to *lakṣaṇā* (indication). "Saṃnihitapadārtha" means the meaning of the immediately preceding word; otherwise, in the case of "rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ" (the king's man), there would be the undesirable consequence of the relation denoted by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha*) being construed with the meaning of the word "puruṣa" as well. And in that case, one might also perceive [the meaning] "a king who is related to the man."

And likewise, the point is that even in cases such as *prāptodaka* ("water-reached"), it is accepted that the lakṣaṇā (metaphorical indication) resides specifically in the word *udaka* (water), signifying the water as the agent of the action of reaching (*prāpti*). Now, one might object: "The status of denoting the meaning of another word consists in being conducive to the cognition thereof; and that..."

Since a word becomes conducive to that cognition by presenting its own meaning through its own function and by serving as a grasper of the intention (*tātparya*) of the other words, he states another objection with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). Regarding the phrase "this being so": it means when one accepts that the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) resides only in the final member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The point is that if expressiveness (*vācakatā*) belonged to the final letter alone—because that letter is immediately followed by the suffix and because of parsimony (*lāghava*)—then expressiveness would have to be attributed to that alone; yet this is not an acceptable consequence, as it contradicts established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*).

Furthermore, it should also be observed that the cognition of a jar or the like is established through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the final phoneme itself, which takes the form of the suffix *ac* (the nominalizing suffix) in words such as "ghaṭa" and "paṭa. Now, one might object: "By the authority of the lexicons (*kośa*) and other sources, the denotative power (*vācakatva*) of a word like 'ghaṭa'—which consists of a collection of several phonemes—is accepted. However, in the present case, since the matter can be explained by the secondary function of the final word alone, there is no proof for a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) [of the whole word], especially because such lexicons do not exist here, and because the meaning of a word must be something not obtainable through any other means (*ananyalabhya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The details are elsewhere."

"Elsewhere"—that is, in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa* and other works. Regarding "in detail": the acceptance of the etymological rule that suffixes (*pratyaya*) are applied to what is proximate and precedes [the base], and so forth, is not possible, because there is a deviation in cases such as *sarvakaḥ*. Furthermore, in cases such as *dadhīyaddadāti*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the meaning of the suffix *vatup* (possessive) being construed with *dadhi* (curd). Moreover, in the case of *dadhivahupaṭurdadāti*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the meaning of the suffix *bahuc* (intensive) being construed with *dadhi*, and the undesirable consequence of its not being construed with *paṭu* (clever).

Furthermore, according to the grammatical rule that suffixes such as *su* (the nominative case-ending) occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of the object (*karmatva*) and so forth, there is obtained through proximity the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meanings as connected with the meaning of the stem. If [one were to claim] that the meaning of the suffix is connected only indirectly [to the stem], this would result in the subversion of the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of both the stem and the suffix, since the latter member alone is not a stem. Moreover, in cases such as *citraguḥ* ("one who has spotted cows"), if one assumes that the first member possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of its own expressed meaning, then its role as a facilitator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhakatva*)—as seen in examples like *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* ("a hamlet on the Ganges")—would be undermined.

The meaning is that one must observe that if the established [meaning] were to be abandoned, it would lead to a logical fallacy; however, if another etymology is accepted, it is more appropriate to assume a specific power (śakti) [of the word]. Regarding the phrase "by the aforementioned reasoning," the meaning is: by the reasoning consisting in the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) in cases such as *prāptodaka*. He explains "abandonment of what is established" as "by means of the established power. And regarding "abandonment of the etymology," the meaning is the abandonment of the restriction that the matter is resolved by the established power alone; for otherwise, the cognition that "the water is the object of the attainment whose agent is [the river]" would be impossible.

"What then is the capacity? [The author] explains this as being conjoined with "completion" (*pūraṇa*). "What then is the capacity in every compound?"—thus, because the cognition [of meaning] is established. That is to say, even if one were to set aside the capacity of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*), since the cognition of the relation is accomplished through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *rāja-* as "related to a king," the postulation of a capacity for the whole based on the inexplicability of that specific cognition is to be questioned, because it would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, the sense is that there is no lack of "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) in the form of conveying meaning through a linguistic operation (*vṛtti*), nor is there any impossibility of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) simply by virtue of being a compound.

In this context, if one were to accept indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the relation itself, there would be an inconsistency with the linguistic rule that "the meaning of a noun [is construed] with the meaning of another noun," because the relation could not then be construed with the person by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*). Therefore, one resorts to indication with respect to the relatum. For this very reason—that is, precisely because indication is accepted with respect to the relatum—the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "not even the connection with qualifiers such as 'beautiful' (*na śobhanasya*)," etc., carries the sense of "also. Thus, there is no construing of the qualifiers.

In cases such as "the cowherd settlement on the beautiful Gaṅgā," however, it is the word *gaṅgā* itself that indicates the beautiful bank of the Gaṅgā; therefore, just as there is the connection of "beautiful" with the Gaṅgā—which is a part of the indicated meaning—there is no room for the objection that here too the connection of "beautiful" should apply to the king or others, who are merely parts of the indicated meaning.

In the case of *ghanaśyāma* ("dark as a cloud"), the referent of the word *ghana* ("cloud") is construed with the referent of the subsequent member (*śyāma*) by way of the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*). In *niṣkauśāmbi* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"), it is by way of the relation of being the point of departure (*niṣkramaṇāvadhitva*). In *goratha* ("ox-cart"), the referent of the prior member is construed with the referent of the subsequent member by way of the relation of being yoked to it (*svayuktatva*). With this in mind, the author raises an objection, beginning with "na ca" (if it be argued), based on the following intention: even if words such as *iva* express [the relation] as a mere connective element (*saṃsarga*), the employment of words like *iva* remains unavoidable for the sake of producing a cognition in which similarity and so forth function as qualifiers (*prakāra*). This is stated by the phrase "by virtue of expressing the aforementioned meaning."

The meaning is that in a compound, a word such as *ghana* (cloud) possesses the stated meaning by virtue of indicating (*lakṣaka*) something similar to it; otherwise, due to the contradiction with the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) "the meanings of two nouns [are connected]," there would be an impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through a relation such as similarity. [This concludes the explanation of] "the restriction of usage."

The point is that there is no possibility of sublation of the sentence by means of a compound (*samāsa*) and so forth, because they have distinct objects of cognition. In a *karmadhāraya* compound such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), is there a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the coexistence of the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), or regarding the coexistence of the blue and the lotus? In the first case, the cognition would be "a blue lotus possessing a collection of the properties of being blue and being a lotus. In the second case, however, it would be "a lotus that is non-different from that which is co-locus with the blue."

In the view of the Grammarians (Śābdikas), the absence of expressive power in the aggregate is accepted for this very reason; however, in a sentence, that conjunction is conveyed by two *ca* particles. Therefore, there is a distinct domain for both the compound (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), and the same should be understood regarding the copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Others, however, hold that in the sentence "that lotus is blue" (*nīlaṃ ca tad utpalaṃ ca*), the meaning of the case-ending following the word "blue" (*nīla*) and so forth is non-difference (*abheda*); this [non-difference] is construed with the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*) through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*). In a compound (*samāsa*), however, non-difference from blue and so forth is conveyed by the word "blue" itself through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, there is the possibility of a systematic distinction: a compound occurs when there is an intention to convey such a meaning through secondary signification, whereas a sentence occurs when there is an intention to convey it through a case-ending. This is even the case for the term "single integrated meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), which refers to a meaning composed of the word-meanings observed in the corresponding sentence.

They stated that the meaning is that "only the secondary indicative function (lakṣaṇā) is expressed. In the same way, it should be understood that in words such as *aupagava*, the word *upagu* and so forth possesses a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to its connection [to the descendant]. Regarding the phrase "establishing the primary power" (*śaktisādhikā*), the meaning is "that which establishes the primary power in all grammatical operations" (*vṛtti*). To the question, "How can the non-apprehension of the component powers (*avayava-śakti*) act as a sublater (*bādhaka*) in the apprehension of the secondary indicative function? he says: "And there is no non-apprehension of the power. The construction is "and it is not possible. The meaning of "not" (*na ca*) is "indeed not" (*na hi*).

The point is that without the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*), there can be no presentation of the denotable meaning; and in the absence of such presentation, it is impossible to grasp the *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which consists in a relation to the denotable. Thus, the intended meaning is that even in a state where the apprehension of the power of the individual components is lacking, the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) is necessary to account for the experience-attested cognition of the lotus as qualified by the property of "lotusness" (*paṅkajatva*) arising from the word *paṅkaja*.

In the same way, it should be understood that even in the case of the word *rathakāra*, the acceptance of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) is necessary; thus, there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned section (*adhikaraṇa*). Now, one might object: "If this were so, then in a situation where the power of words such as *rāja* (king) has not been grasped, the cognition 'a person related to a king' would not arise. To this, he offers a rebuttal by accepting the objection as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), stating "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: precisely because the knowledge of the power of the individual parts (*avayavaśakti*) serves, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as the cause for the cognition of the qualified meaning.

"Not [the] cognition" means as follows: at that time, when there is an absence of the apprehension of the component meanings (*avayava-śakti*), it is established by experience that such a cognition simply does not occur; the point is that since there is no cognition, the non-arising of cognition is precisely what is desired as the conclusion. "The destruction of many linguistic conventions" has already been explained in this very work in the main text (*mūla*). He states the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) for why the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) applies only to the final member (*uttara-pada*) in the phrase "of the first member" (*pūrvapadasya*). "Of its signification" means "of the apprehension of the signification of the first member. "Root and suffix," etc.

The meaning is that both the verbal root and the suffix, as well as their respective meanings, are to be accomplished through knowledge; the point is that since the knowledge of the meaning cannot arise without the knowledge of the root and so forth, the knowledge of the root and so forth also serves as the cause for grasping the definition (lakṣaṇa) by way of the knowledge of the meaning.

Now, it might be argued that there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the composite whole "prāpta," because, since that whole lacks denotative power (*śakti*), figurative indication—in the form of a relation to the denoted—is impossible; rather, [the indication] occurs only in the *kta* suffixes that constitute those respective words. And thus, [the action] would be accomplished merely by the knowledge of those respective meanings, and not even by the knowledge of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and its meaning. Even in the case of figuratively indicating the object of the agent's attainment (*kartṛ-prāpti-karman*), there is indeed equality [with the other view], as it too is accomplished by the knowledge of the word "water" (*udaka*) and its meaning.

[Objection: Surely, when the suffix *kta* is present, one must admit that the knowledge of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with such a verbal root serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) for the definition [of *prāpta*] as having water as the agent and attainment as the object; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And in this way, the fact that [the understanding of the compound] is to be accomplished by the knowledge of the verbal root and its meaning remains unimpaired. Furthermore, according to the Mīmāṃsā view that "metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in a relation with what is understood by itself," since metaphorical indication is impossible in the entire aggregate "prāpta," it is quite clear that being accomplished by the knowledge of those respective meanings is beyond dispute. [Response: If this is argued, [we reply that] in the word *udaka*, such a meaning—

In the case of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), it is impossible to deny that it is established by the knowledge of the verbal root, the suffix, and their respective meanings, since the co-occurrence of words not [directly] obtained serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This is because, without knowledge of the object of attainment (*prāptikarma*), it is impossible to grasp the secondary signification consisting of its relation [to that object]. Therefore, regarding secondary signification based on the final member of a compound, he states another determining factor: "of the suffixes" (*pratyayānām*). "Proximate" (*saṃnihita*) means belonging to the meaning of that word which is proximate.

In this regard, in the expression "Bring the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), the objecthood (*karmatva*) denoted by the suffix does not connect with the king; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a dual number ending. Furthermore, at a time when one perceives that the man lacks the status of being the object of bringing, if there were an intention to convey the connection of objecthood with the king, it would result in the improper usage "Bring the king’s man. Moreover, once the cognition of that meaning has arisen immediately after hearing such an expression, it would follow that the king himself must be brought. By this, the argument that one might simply accept such a connection [of objecthood] with the king is refuted.

The phrase "in words such as 'ghaṭa'" refutes the objection in the form of a counter-argument (pratibandī) stated by the Grammarians (Śābdikas), namely that by parity of reasoning, the denotative capacity (vācakatva) would belong solely to the final phoneme within a word like 'ghaṭa'. The phrase "an additional power" (atiriktā śaktiḥ) means a power distinct from the powers of the verbal roots and other elements constituting that word, or distinct from the power of a word whose own power has already been apprehended, or a power distinct from the mere capacity to convey meaning (bodhakatva).

It is postulated in the qualified [word]; that is, it is postulated in the qualified [word] alone. Because it is conventionalized—because it is understood through convention established by lexicons and the like. Now, one might object: "The power (*śakti*) consisting in the capacity to convey meaning must reside in the final phoneme alone; moreover, even if a power distinct from that were to be postulated on the grounds of its inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), it would ultimately resolve to that very same [final phoneme]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even of the capacity to convey meaning" (*bodhakatvasyāpi*). This means: even of the state of being the locus wherein the generation of cognition is fully resident (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatva*).

Therefore, there is no harm even if the status of being the basis for the cognition [of the meaning] exists in that [the first member]. Now, one might object: "In the present case as well, since the cognition 'the owner of Citragu' cannot otherwise be accounted for, the secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) being postulated must be assumed in the first member just as much as in the second member, as there is no distinction between them. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And in the present case... "That is postulated" means that the secondary signification is to be postulated. "The distinction" refers to...

The point is that since the final phoneme is not experienced as having expressive power even when the conditions for its cognition are fully present, it is postulated that the entire collection [of phonemes] alone possesses the capacity to denote meaning. As for the phrase "and it is accepted": the implication is that if the final phoneme alone were the denoter in words such as *ghaṭa*, this would simply result in the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "by those who consider themselves Mīmāṃsakas": by the rule *khaśi arurdviṣad...* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), the suffix *mum* is applied. The meaning is "those who consider themselves to be Mīmāṃsakas. By this, a lack of satisfaction [with the author's position] is indicated; its basis, however, is the contradiction with lexicons (*kośa*) and other authorities. Regarding the phrase "the technical name (*saṃjñā*) and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), the subsequent production of a case-ending from the entire compound, and the application of the rule *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158) are included.

If one accepts that "possessing meaning"—defined as the capacity to convey a meaning through the assistance of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors—is also a condition for the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, this is impossible in cases such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), because it is only the word *go* ("cow") that conveys the qualified meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor should it be argued that "possessing meaning" should be understood as being a word that is the object of a cognition which generates the comprehension of a meaning; and that this [definition] applies without hindrance to the aggregate [of words] as a whole—whereby one word [the first member] functions through secondary indication and the other [the second member] functions by making the intended meaning known.

The sense is this: since it would result in the application of case-endings (*vibhakti*) to each individual [element], the objection cannot be avoided by the maxim of "doubling of a single vowel" (*ekāca-dvirvacana-nyāya*), because that maxim applies only where a collective operation benefits its constituent parts. Furthermore, if one were to avoid this by means of the rule "the first [element] consisting of a single vowel is doubled" (*ekāco dve prathamasya*), it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*). This is what is meant by the statement: "Therefore, there would be great complexity. By the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*), the term "that" (*sā*) refers to the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*).

And thus, the intention is that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, one might object: even if it lacks the status of being a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is no harm; furthermore, since terms such as *asūryapaśyāḥ* ("those who do not see the sun") and *śaśaśṛṅgam* ("the horn of a hare") lack meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), it is impossible for [the rule] to function as a restrictive rule by way of prescribing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "because it has been clearly established in the *Bhūṣaṇa*."

Even in cases such as *asūryapaśyā* ("one who does not see the sun"), the status of being "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is established by the rule itself through the assumption that the word *asūrya* denotes "that which lacks the act of seeing the sun. As stated by Kaiyaṭa on the *Samartha-sūtra*: "Even in an 'asamartha' compound, because both [members] meet in an action, there is indeed a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) by means of that [action]. "Both" refers to the two words *nañ* and *sūrya*.

Even in the case of words such as *śaśaśṛṅga* ("hare's horn"), it is well known that the [constituent parts] are dissociated and that a superimposed relationship (*āropitasaṃbandha*) is possible; therefore, the application of the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.45], "that which has a meaning" (*arthavat*), certainly occurs. Furthermore, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) for the element *asūrya-* is established by the authority of the rule "asūryalalāṭayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.36), which apprehends the very entity that possesses the nature of a compound. For it is clear in the technical treatises (*nibandha*) that the status of being a subordinate word (*upapadatva*)—defined as the state of being a word uttered in proximity—cannot be maintained without the status of being a nominal stem and the subsequent production of a case-ending (*sub*).

It is clearly stated in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works that even things such as a rabbit’s horn have a denotable meaning (*vācyārtha*) according to the Buddhist view. Thus, in my opinion, the fact that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*) is well-established. Furthermore, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources that in the rule *kṛttaddhita* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), the term *arthavat* is carried over (*anuvartate*) in order to obtain the application of the rule to that which ends in those suffixes (*tadantavidhi*). Consequently, if one does not admit a primary expressive power (*śakti*) in compounds, that [application] cannot be established even by the mention of "compound."

However, it is not correct to say that "the term *arthavat* [in Pāṇini’s definition] relates only to *kṛt* and *taddhita* derivatives, and not to compounds (*samāsa*)," because if that were the case, the *dvandva* compound would result in being grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*). This is because, if only one member were learned, there would be no usage such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are both learned. For it is accepted that a *dvandva* is grammatical only when the meaning of the other word is connected to the meanings of all the members constituting the *dvandva*, and not when it is connected to the meaning of just some part of those members. If, on the other hand, grammaticality is postulated based on its being a *sūtra*-formulation (*sautratvāt*), then...

It is precisely for the sake of respect [for the rule]. Even if the mention of the term *samāsa* (compound) were intended as an injunction (*vidhi*), in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, because there is an absence of *arthavattva* (meaningfulness), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) would not apply by the rule *arthavat*. Consequently, by the statement *citaḥ saprakṛteḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) conditioned by being a *cit* suffix would fall on the vowel *a* following the word *vāk*; however, what is desired—as is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources—is that it should fall on the vowel *a* following the suffix *ṭak*. In the final view (*siddhānta*), however, by the maxim *antaraṅgān api*, the first-generated *jas* [is applied].

It is established that the accent proceeds precisely according to the rule *luguttara* (P. 2.4.82); for if one were to initiate the statement *bahucpūrvasya* (P. 6.2.173), there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor should it be argued that the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies here by the rule *kṛttaddhita* (P. 1.2.46) because the word *taddhita* refers to that which is qualified by a *taddhita* suffix; for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pacatakī*, and also in the sentence *bahupaṭavastiṣṭhanti*.

The point is that there is no evidence for taking the very same combination of base and suffix as qualified by the *taddhita* suffix when that suffix has been prescribed; furthermore, it would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate such a separate statement.

By this, the view that the item qualified by the *taddhita* is taken through a relation of either immediate precedence or immediate succession—thereby avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases like *pacatakī*—is refuted. This is because such a restriction is not stated in the rule, and there is no authority for postulating a meaning contrary to the maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "when a suffix is mentioned, that which ends with it is understood."

Similarly, in the case of "mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte" (he eats with radish as a side-dish), by the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of *kṛt*-formed words, the compound "mūlakenopadaṃśam" would otherwise result in being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, the radish possesses the status of the object of the act of side-eating (*upadaṃśana*), while in relation to the verb "to eat" (*bhuj*), it possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Since the instrumental case-ending is applied solely on account of its instrumentality toward the principal action, the status of the radish as a factor of action (*kāraka*) in relation to the side-eating remains intact. Thus, there is no loss of its status as the object of side-eating.

Nor should it be argued that such a sentence lacks the status of a *prātipadika* by virtue of the rule "from the third case onwards" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīni*), which prescribes composition optionally, since the result of that rule is merely the occurrence of case-endings. For there exists the specific phonetic result of a difference in accent: in a compound, there is the natural accent of the final member (*uttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), whereas in a non-compound, there are two acute accents (*udātta*). Furthermore, in the case of "dadhi upadaṃśam," there is also the possibility of the result being the application of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-composition) rule "iko'savarṇe" [Pāṇini 6.1.127].

By this, the charge that the rule prescribing the option for compounds would be redundant—given that the accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*) is already subject to option—is refuted. However, the attempt to establish that redundancy on the grounds of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*) is not tenable. Nor should it be argued that because the *paribhāṣā* "in the case of the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛdgrahaṇe*) is established by a *jñāpaka* and is therefore not universally applicable, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *na mūlakena* in the rule *kṛttaddhita-* due to its repetition; for it is improper to resort to such a desperate expedient (*agatikāśrayaṇa*).

In the Siddhānta, however, because of the restriction established by the inclusion of the term "compound" (samāsa), there is a sublation [of the previous rule] due to its higher status; thus, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when *kṛt* is mentioned" does not apply at all in the rule *kṛttaddhita*. This should be understood from the Bhūṣaṇa and other works; enough with excessive detail. "In a compound sentence" (*samāsavākye*) means "in a sentence consisting of a compound. "Because even the possession of a secondary meaning (*lākṣaṇikārthavattva*) is impossible"—this is said in response to the Naiyāyika.

The point is that even if [the relation] were possible in the view of the Mīmāṃsakas—who maintain that the definition [of a word] consists in its connection with its own meaning—nevertheless, because established secondary signification (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) is equivalent to primary denotative power (śakti), the position favored by the Grammarians is established. Regarding the phrase "established in the Bhāṣya": this means it is established in the Bhāṣya on the *Arthavad* Sūtra, as in: "'If it is argued that [the suffix] is not a suffix, then a prohibition must be stated regarding the single-substitute (ekādeśa) for *ti*; for example, in *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, because [the substitute] has the status of being the end (antavat). Enough said."

The meaning is that the two sūtras beginning with *arthavat* need not be commenced; rather, the two sūtras *prātipadikam* and *samāsaśca* should be formulated. As for the phrase "of the compound (*samāsasya*) also": since a compound is distinct from that which ends in *tip*, and because the technical term *pratyaya* (suffix) being employed [in the definition], the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) "from whatever [a suffix is prescribed]" (*yasmāt*) applies to it—this is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "because of the necessity of being meaningful" (*arthavattvāvaśyakatvena*): the meaning is that the qualification "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is necessary. Now, one might object: since there is an absence of number, object, and so forth, a case-ending (*sup*) will not arise from each individual phoneme; furthermore, even the general rule (*autsargika*) for word-formation is clearly applicable only when there is a signifier (*gamaka*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṅyāp-*, the possibility of case-endings arising after verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) was raised in the absence of that specific rule, and it was resolved by stating that it is not so, because [number] such as singularity and the rest have already been mentioned.

If it is argued that, because there is thus no meaning [in such cases], the designation of *prātipadika* will not apply to each individual phoneme either, even so, the qualification "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is necessary in order to exclude unconnected groups of sounds such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*) or "six cakes" (*ṣaḍapūpāḥ*). For it is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources that if these were *prātipadikas*, the suffix would be elided by the rule "sūpo dhātu-" (Pāṇini 2.4.71).

However, it is not possible to achieve the desired exclusion by means of the mention of the compound (*samāsa*) for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), because a restriction depends on its own class (*sajātīya*); thus, it would exclude only a collection of words whose meanings are mutually connected. For this very reason, it is clear from the *Śabdenduśekhara* and other works that the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) does not apply to a collection [of words] such as in the example "He says 'go'" (*gavityāha*).

Regarding the phrase "there would be over-extension to compounds": the sense is that if the definition of a compound were intended as an injunction (*vidhi*), then the multitude of defects previously mentioned would necessarily follow. If it is argued that a third rule—"not [for] a non-compound sentence"—must also be formulated, the sense is that this would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Here, [the discussion concerns] those ending in *samā* and so forth.

However, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has not been established [for these], because even if that status were granted, the undesirable consequence of case-suffix (*sup*) production from them would arise, as it would be blocked by the rules for *apād*, *asti*, and so forth. Now, one might argue that even if the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is intended as an original injunction (*vidhi*), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of "mūlakena" has already been prevented by the sequence previously stated; therefore, he states another fault: "Moreover, in this way," etc. "In this way" means: if the expressive power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) is not admitted. "In cases such as *ardhapippalī*" and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [compounds] such as *apūrvakāya* and other types of *dvandva* is intended. One should observe that even in a *dvandva*, there is a deviation [from the rule] because the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth can be construed with a word-meaning that is separated [by other members]. However, the point is that if one were to ensure that the grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) has a scope exceeding those [specific types] by including distinctions such as *avyayībhāva* and others, there would be the burden (*gaurava*) of having to include numerous distinct categories.

If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] because in *nanupakumbham* the word *kumbha* itself denotes the sense of "near the jar" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and likewise in *ardhapippalī* and so on, the words *pippalī* etc. themselves denote the qualified meaning—this is incorrect. For when the connection [of the sentence] can be established by secondary indication applied to the qualified meaning, it is improper to accept [secondary indication] for the individual members. This is precisely why the rule "the *avyayībhāva* is predominant in the meaning of the first member" is consistent. Furthermore, the point is that the deviation in the case of *dvandva* compounds remains firmly established.

It should be noted that, according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, although there is no deviation [from the rule] in cases such as *ardhapippalī* because it is a *karmadhāraya* compound where the meaning of the final member is predominant, the deviation in cases such as *upakumbha* remains entirely unimpeded. [The rule applies] only after a word that is being compounded.

The "word being compounded" (*samasyamānaṃ padam*) refers to the words constituting a compound—whether they be the first, the last, or the middle. Thus, in an *avyayībhāva* compound, it is the indeclinable; in an *ekadeśisamāsa*, it is the word denoting the single part; and in a *dvandva*, all the words are being compounded. Consequently, the case-meanings (*vibhaktyartha*) are construed with their respective meanings. It should be understood that by rules such as "in an *avyayībhāva* and other compounds, an indeclinable is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix," it is taught that only the indeclinable and so forth function as the object (*karma*) of the act of compounding, and not the [other] word.

Thus, regarding the fact that in a compound (samāsa), the syntactic connection (anvaya) occurs sometimes with the meaning of the prior member, sometimes with the meaning of the subsequent member, and sometimes with the meaning of all the members constituting the compound, the point is that the grammatical rule (anuśāsana), along with factors such as semantic compatibility (yogyatā), serves as the regulator. "Only after the specific [compound]" means "only after the aggregate in the form of the compound. By the word "eva" (only), the constituent words of the compound are excluded.

Regarding the statement "from the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*)": the intended meaning is that because of the instruction—"suffixes such as *sva* and others occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)"—that same instruction is indeed unestablished when applied to the word following a compound member (*samasyamānapada*). Nor should it be argued that a distinct grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇabheda*) must be postulated for each specific instance (*pratilakṣya*), based on the status of the nominal stemhood residing in the form of the compound member, such that the suffixes *sva* and others occur [only] from that; for the very instruction that "suffixes such as *sva* occur after what is the locus where nominal stemhood is fully resident" (*prātipadikatvaparyāptyadhikaraṇāt*) is established by the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, and not otherwise in this context.

There is no evidence for such an assumption; for if it were so, the whole would fail to be a subordinate member (*aṅga*), while its constituent part would incur that status. If that were the case, in examples such as *devasya puruṣaḥ* (the servant of the god) = *devapuruṣaḥ*, and *tasyedaṃ* (belonging to him) = *daivapuruṣam*, the *vṛddhi* substitution would not apply to the beginning of the whole compound, but would instead apply only to the beginning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). If it is argued that the rule "from the [beginning of] a subordinate member ending in /ṛ/" and others serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution will indeed apply to the beginning of the whole, the point is that following the expressive power (*śakti*) of the whole is more appropriate than resorting to such a strained assumption.

In this way, one should also observe that in cases such as *upakumbham*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) of not hearing a case-ending after the entire compound. "It is postulated" means that it is not postulated that the meaning of the case-ending is construed with an object that is the locus where the status of being a base (*prakṛtitva*) is fully resident; rather, the sense is that since the status of being a base resides in both the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and the prior member (*pūrvapada*), the aforementioned fault does not arise. "The contingency of [unwanted] construction" means the contingency of the objecthood of the act of bringing being construed [with the wrong element].

But this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because even when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), such a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is never experienced without *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Furthermore, it would lead to the absurdity (*prasaṅga*) of bringing up mud. Regarding the undesirable consequence in another instance, he says "aghaṭam" (not a jar). The point is that while in the previously mentioned case, if there were a syntactic connection with the action in something qualified by a staff and so forth, there might occasionally be an acceptable consequence regarding the connection with the qualification—the staff itself; however, in the present case, no one ever experiences a connection of the action of bringing as having the jar as its object (*karmatva*).

The phrase "not there as a qualifier" means that, according to the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of an inflectional suffix (*vibhaktyartha*) must be construed with that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the base word (*prakṛti*), [the possessor] is not so construed here. However, since the owner of the "variegated cows" (*citragu*) is indeed the qualificand of the cognition produced by the base word, there is no logical inconsistency in his being construed with the meaning of the suffix. The phrase "construal with bringing, etc. refers to the construal with being the object (*karman*) of the act of bringing, and so forth. The phrase "of the state of being produced" refers to that which constitutes the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The phrase "non-construal with form, pleasure, etc. [indicates that these are not the qualificands].

Because blue color and pleasure lack the status of being the objects of the specific cognitions produced by the words "blue" and "direction," since the word "blue" refers to that which is qualified by blue color, and the word "pleasure-possessor" (sukhin) denotes that which is qualified by it; thus, in one case—

If it is argued that the relation with another [term] as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*) is simply unestablished (*avyutpanna*), whereas the relation as a qualificand (*viśeṣyatayā*) is not, and therefore there is no unwanted consequence of the relation of being the object of worship (*pūjanakarmatva*) in cases such as "one should worship the staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinaṃ pūjayet*), nor the impossibility of the relation of being produced by cooking (*pākajanyatva*) in "blue from cooking" (*pākānnīlaḥ*), etc.—we say no. For if that were so, there would be the unwanted consequence of the relation of a qualifier such as "to be worshipped" (*pūjya*) with the trident (*śūla*) in cases like "the trident-bearer is to be worshipped" (*śūlī pūjyaḥ*). Furthermore, when duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are sublated in the trident-bearer, one would have to perceive two tridents in the case of "see the two trident-bearers" (*śūlinau paśyata*).

The phrase "such applications would result" indicates the general direction of the argument. "Mere being an object of cognition" means that it is not the state of being an object of the cognition produced by the base (prakṛti) through its own function (vṛtti). Here—in cases such as "the owner of a brindled cow" (*citragu-svāmī*), which is indicated by the initial part of the subsequent compound—[the objection applies]. "By way of inherence" (*samavāyena*) means for the purpose of precluding the connection of the meaning of the accusative case (karmatva), which follows the word *ghaṭa*, with the ether (*ākāśa*) as presented [in the mind] by way of inherence. "Being the meaning of the base by way of its function" means being the object of the cognition produced by the base by way of its function.

Because it is necessary—that is, because it must necessarily be included. In cases such as "the pot" (*ghaṭam*), in order to prevent the relation of objecthood (*karmatva*) from being construed with "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, one sets aside the general property of being an object (*viṣayatāsāmānya*) and introduces [the property of] being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). For this very reason, in expressions such as "see the man with a staff" (*daṇḍinaṃ paśya*), there is no such relation [of objecthood] with the staff and so forth. Nor is there such a relation with space (*ākāśa*), because the phrase "occurring in the word preceding the suffix" must also be inserted [into the definition]. This is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "in Kṛṣṇa, the meaning of the third case" [is explained as follows].

The point is that if [the suffix] were to reside in a portion without an intervening element, then in examples such as *upakumbham*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the meaning of the case-suffix (*vibhaktyartha*) being construed with the meaning of the preceding member (*pūrvapadārtha*). Similarly, one should observe that there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *bahupaṭaḥ* and *sarvakaḥ*, and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in *dadhiyaddadāti* and the like. However, if one were to include the condition "provided that it is that after which a particular suffix is prescribed," then in *citraguḥ* and similar instances, because the status of being "that after which [a suffix is prescribed]" is absent in the final member (*uttarapada*), it should be understood that the aforementioned defects remain as they are. [This refers to the phrase] "in accordance with established etymological derivation" (*klaptavyutpatti*).

The meaning is that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is "the suffixes [occur] when conjoined with the meaning of the base. Now, one might object: "In the case of complex aggregates consisting of multiple compounds, it is not more burdensome to postulate a distinct etymological derivation and abandon the established derivation than it is to postulate a new power (*śakti*). To this, he says: "The direction [is indicated by the word *dig*]."

The meaning of this is as follows: In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), although the application of a qualifier like "beautiful" (*śobhana*) to the servant (*dāsī*) is avoided by resorting to a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) that identifies the king as a part of the whole [of the compound], in compounds where the elision of the case-ending is not applied (*aluk-samāsa*), such as *dāsyāḥ putraḥ* ("the daughter of a slave"), there is no evidence for such a signification. Consequently, the application of qualifiers like "beautiful" to the slave-girl and so forth would be unavoidable. Even if one were to assume a signification based on relationship (*saṃbandhi-lakṣaṇā*) there as well, the resulting cognition would be of "one related to the slave-girl," which is not desired, as it contradicts universal experience. Furthermore, in the context of *aluk*-compounds, the case-ending does not bring about the presentation of its own primary meaning; therefore—

In expressions such as *apsucaraḥ* ("moving in water") and *agoṣucaraḥ* ("not moving in cows"), there is no cognition of plurality; likewise, even when the word *dāsī* (female slave) is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "one related to a female slave," the resulting cognition—characterized by the relation of the king, having the relation as its mode of connection, and having the king as the qualifier and the person as the qualificand—is established by the Bhāṣya and other authorities as arising from the compound *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* just as it does from the sentence. It should be understood that this [cognition] is not possible if the indication were merely of the "related one" (*saṃbandhin*). This is because [the required properties] would be absent.

The meaning is that [the word *taṇḍula*] lacks the status of being an object of a presentation (upasthiti) generated by an inflection (*vibhakti*). Now, an objection is raised: in cases such as "the white rice" (*śubhraḥ taṇḍulaḥ*), a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*)—such as "white"—as its qualifier arises with respect to the rice (*taṇḍula*) and so on, in the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*). Yet, in that case, there is no presentation generated by an inflection as the qualificand. Thus, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the aforementioned causal relationship is impossible. Furthermore, in order to prevent the aforementioned cognition in the case of "the rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), one would have to resort to the necessity of postulating that a presentation generated by a verbal root (*dhātu*) acts as an inhibitor.

Alternatively, one might postulate that the cause [of semantic cognition] is the presence (*upasthiti*) produced by distinct *dhātus* (verbal roots). In this way, there would be no obstacle to the comprehension of the relation (*anvaya-bodha*) in cases such as "the king's servant" (*rājapuruṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "In cases such as 'white rice' (*taṇḍulaḥ śubhraḥ*)," etc. Regarding the phrase "the nominative [case-ending] whose meaning is the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthakaprathamā*): the meaning is that it refers to the meaning of that nominative case-ending which has the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its own meaning.

The meaning of the rule *prātipadikārthamātre prathamā* is that the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs when the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is to be expressed. In examples such as *pākaḥ*, the meaning of the nominal stem appears in two ways, just like the action (*vyāpāra*). Since that [meaning] is presented by the inflection (*vibhakti*) in the form of a non-substantial entity (*asattvarūpa*), there is the possibility of a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) due to the existence of this "dissimilar presentation" (*virūpopasthiti*). Thus, the intended sense is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the stated causal relationship.

[Objection: But even if deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is excluded here, in cases such as ‘śubhraṃ taṇḍulam’ (‘white rice’) and ‘śubhreṇa taṇḍulena’ (‘with white rice’), deviation remains unavoidable; for the accusative and other case-endings are not prescribed [by Pāṇini] with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). To this he says: “In ‘śubhreṇa taṇḍulena,’ etc. [He explains: “The meaning is non-difference (*abhedārtha*). The point is that since the non-difference of the object (*karman*) and so forth—being of the nature of the object itself—is the subject matter of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). In this very way, there is no deviation in cases such as ‘stokaṃ pacati’ (‘he cooks slightly’). [Objection: But since the meaning of the object and so forth is already conveyed by the case-ending following the word denoting the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), [what is the need for the suffix after the word denoting the qualifier?]...

Anticipating the objection that "the case-ending serves solely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), and thus the connection between the object *śubhra* and *taṇḍula* must be stated [separately], so that the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was," he says: "or by way of implication (*pārṣṇika*)."

The intended meaning is as follows: it is not correct to say that the case-ending is used for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) by the rule "the accusative occurs only when there is an object" (*karmaṇy eva dvitīyā*); rather, it denotes the very status of being an object (*karmatva*). This is because, according to the *Bhāṣya*, "the mat is also the object, and the terrifying [quality] and so forth are also the object," the status of being an object exists even in the qualifier. Thus, since there is a rule that "kārakas connect only with the action," they must connect with the action.
