Consequently, because there is no mutual connection between the qualifier and the qualified, there is no deviation (invariable concomitance). Nor does deviation arise simply from their connection with the action.

Since it is accepted that the connection [of the adjective] occurs only through the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), there would be no exclusion of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the absence of mutual connection; thus, even when it is said, "One should worship Śiva with white rice," there would be the possibility of worshipping with any rice whatsoever—even black rice—provided it is white. Likewise, due to the lack of semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*), compounds such as *śubhrastaṇḍulaḥ* (white rice) or *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus) would not be possible. To avoid these defects, a simultaneous mutual understanding of the connection between the two is accepted, and that is as follows:

[The cognition] is either verbal or mental. Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of semantic capacity (sāmarthya), a compound is formed by the force of the prescriptive rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (Pāṇini 2.1.57) and so forth; for the point is that it is more appropriate to assume an implicit understanding (pāṣṇikabodha) based on the force of that very rule.

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is not the denotation of the nominative case, because this would lead to the undesirable consequence of its repeated cognition, and because it is impossible for two things presented in a single form to enter into a syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Furthermore, such a cognition is never experienced in distinct forms; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is accepted as simply this: when a specific meaning is intended by a particular nominal stem, the nominative case follows it. Thus, there is no evidence that the case-ending of an attribute denotes non-difference (*abheda*) as its meaning; even though the non-difference of an object (*karman*) is of the nature of the non-difference of the action (*karman*).

Since it is established by the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) that [the case ending] must be expressed solely as *karmatva* (objecthood) and so forth, one might ask: "How then can the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) follow from words such as *śubhra*? Regarding this, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* on the *anabhihita* rule state: "Because the qualified [entity] is desired through the action, there is objecthood; thus, the second case ending occurs in both instances. Their intention is that objecthood residing in the qualified entity cannot be conveyed without the presence of identical case endings.

In this view as well, from the qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇa*), there arises the apprehension of an objecthood (*karmatva*) that is not qualified by [the specific attributes of] "fearful" and so on; however, because it is perceived as being characterized by those [attributes] through the qualified [word] (*viśeṣya*), there is the cognition of a single objecthood belonging to the qualified whole. Consequently, they have established that "the mat is also the object, and the 'fearful' and so on are also [the object]."

In this view, the qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇapada*) conveys its respective power (*śakti*) as distinct [from the substance]; however, because that power is non-different from the substance, it is grasped specifically through the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). In this view as well, the connection of the action (*kriyā*) occurs only after the mutual connection between the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, there is no violation of the rule regarding the necessary connection of *kārakas* with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*): those factors that directly produce the action connect directly with the *bhāvanā*, whereas those that produce it by means of a substance connect with it precisely by means of that substance.

Because the rule [of the accusative] has been accepted; however, there is no occasion here for the maxim "and because qualities exist for the sake of another," since, according to the aforementioned reasoning, there is an inequality between substance and quality. Therefore, they conclude that the qualificand alone possesses the status of the object (*karman*), and by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, the second case ending is applied even to words such as *bhīṣma*.

Regarding this, the teacher Kaiyaṭa [states] that just as friends of a king, though themselves poor, partake in the fruits of wealth solely through that king’s wealth because they are dependent on him alone, so too—since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in the cognition of a single meaning and numerical unity, is untenable without the qualifier possessing the same capacity as the qualificand—the qualifier must indeed possess the same capacity as the qualificand; and since that [capacity] is merely superimposed (*āropita*), the derivation of case-endings is thereby accomplished. This is the intended sense.

"In this view as well," they say, "only the mutual connection between those two is obtained. The detailed exposition, however, should be understood from the *Mañjūṣā* and other sources; it is not elaborated here for fear of excessive length.

And thus, in cases such as "white rice" (*śubhra-staṇḍula*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is difficult to avoid; if, for the sake of excluding that, the property of having a name-meaning as its qualifier (*prakāratā*)—delimited by the relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*)—is inserted into the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the semantic presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the case-ending, then it appears that there is no obstacle to the cognition of the king's relation-bearer through difference. It should be understood that the subsequent passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*) was stated precisely because of this lack of satisfaction (*asvarasa*).

Now, one might object: "Does not having the same meaning as a compound mean being the generator of a cognition whose object is the same as the object of the cognition produced by the compound? And this is unimpaired in the present case, because 'the king's man' (rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ) generates a cognition whose object is the relation of the king, which is the object of the cognition produced by the compound. To this, he says:

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if the capacity to generate only the aforementioned cognition were of the nature of a *vigraha* (analytic expansion). Therefore—due to the *vigraha*-nature of the explanation (*vivaraṇa*)—there would be no determination of the word's expressive power (*śakti*). For the determination of expressive power through an explanation is possible only under the rule that the explanation and the item being explained must have identical meanings. However, if one accepts that even what is stated without identical meaning can be an explanation, then such a rule would be violated, and consequently, there could be no determination of expressive power from the explanation provided by the learned authorities. And thus, [it cannot be determined] by the verb *karoti*, which signifies the result (*phala*).

The point is that [if this were so], the view that the verb has the power (*śakti*) to denote effort (*yatna*), as established by the *Vivaraṇa*, would be undermined; or else, the point is that the well-established empirical fact (*anubhavasiddha*) that the analysis (*vigraha*) "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) determines the meaning residing in the compound would be lost. Regarding the phrase "by way of occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*): the point is that since the connection with sovereignty (*rājya-sambandha*) is the meaning of the noun, its cognition as being construed with the "servant" would occur only through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), and not through the relation of substratum (*āśraya-sambandha*).

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*) is the necessary condition for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda*) between the meanings of two nouns? Since that is absent here, how can there be the cognition ‘the person [is] related to the king’? To this he replies with the words "viruddhavibhakti... (regarding the absence of contradictory case-endings). The point is that because there are counter-examples such as "beautiful curd" (*sundaraṃ dadhi*) and "water that sprinkles" (*secanakṛdvārī*), it is impossible for having the same case-ending to be the determinant for the aforementioned cognition; therefore, the absence of contradictory case-endings alone must be accepted as the determinant.

Furthermore, this requirement—that there be either a cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) or the absence of a certainty regarding incompatibility (*ayogyatāniścaya*)—should be understood as applying only when such states actually occur; however, it must not be forgotten that, according to our own view, it has already been established that neither the cognition of compatibility nor the certainty of incompatibility functions as a cause or an inhibitor [of verbal comprehension].

Now, it might be argued that the causal relation—namely, that "the semantic representation produced by names devoid of conflicting case-endings is the cause of a cognition of non-difference where the qualificandum is the meaning of a name as derived from its etymological analysis"—is untenable, because it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *caitrasya sutasya dhanam* ("the wealth of Caitra’s son"). If this is said, we reply: no, for we accept the aforementioned causal relation with respect to a cognition consisting merely of the connection between the meanings of names, without including the meaning of the case-ending within the scope of the relation. The point is that a cognition in which Caitra alone is the qualifier and the relation is identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*) is indeed intended [as the result].

"Contrary case-ending" (*viruddhavibhakti*) means a case-ending with a contrary meaning, that is to say, a case-ending with a different meaning; the absence of such a case-ending is the governing factor in the aforementioned cognition. However, in the expression "the king's son's wealth" (*rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam*), the two case-endings do not have the same meaning, because in one instance [the genitive] has the sense of being produced (*janyatva*), while in the other it has the sense of ownership (*svatva*). Others, however, maintain that even in the expression "the king's man's wealth" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam*), although both genitives have the sense of ownership, there is no fault because those two instances of ownership are distinct.

If it is argued that we accept another etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) for the compound, then the establishment of a distinct expressive power (*atirikta-śakti*) remains unimpeded; having all this in mind, he says: "This has been explained at length in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*."

For this very reason—that is, precisely because of the acceptance of a collective denotative power (*samudāya-śakti*) which serves as the cause for the absence of separate presentation. "With reference to the *bhakṣa*" means: having a single form. "Because of the consequence of a breakdown" means: since that would result in an obstruction of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), there would be no compound; for in a compound, all the word-meanings must function either as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) or as the predicate (*vidheyatva*), as in the examples "The *dhava* and *khadira* trees are beautiful" or "These two trees are the *dhava* and *khadira*."

However, due to the aforementioned fault, one cannot posit that the meaning of one word within a compound is the subject (*uddeśya*) with respect to the meaning of another word within that same compound; thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) found in the third chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra—that "the eating is qualified by the first [part]"—should be understood. This is expressed as: "The *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] is performed with the three parts."

By the injunction "In the animal sacrifice, one first cuts off [a portion] of the heart," and so forth, the offering of eleven limbs is established; since the principle of "the modification is like the archetype" (*prakṛtivadvikṛti*) applies, the offering of eleven limbs would follow as a matter of course. It is with this in mind that the present statement is commenced. Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, by way of referring back to the limbs (*aṅgānuvāda*), the number three is enjoined. However, because of the aforementioned defects, it was established in the tenth chapter that this is an injunction of another limb qualified by the number three. And this occurs precisely through a qualified power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), just as from the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), both the jar and its jar-ness [are understood].

The overall meaning is as follows: because the "first" qualified by the act of eating and the "three" qualified by the limbs are simultaneously present, it is impossible for them to be construed in the relationship of subject and predicate within the sentence-meaning; thus, [the formation of a compound] is consistent. However, if the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) were not admitted, then even in a compound, such a construction would occur—as in the case of "the first eating with three limbs"—and this would contradict the established *adhikaraṇa*.

Nor should it be argued that because the conditions for being the subject (*uddeśyatā*) and the predicate (*vidheyatā*), such as "connection with *yadvṛtti*" (the word *yat* occurring in the relative clause) and "primacy" (*prāthamya*), which are established by the statements of the learned—"Connection with *yadvṛtti*, primacy, and so forth are the characteristics of the subject"—are absent here, there can be no injunction of primacy and so on by way of restating the act of eating; for [if that were true], such a status would not arise even in cases like "the first eating" (*prathamo bhakṣaḥ*). For this very reason, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the definition of the subject—"Connection with *yadvṛtti*, primacy, and so forth"—is employed to indicate that these criteria are not strictly fixed.

Nor is it correct to argue that because predication (vidheyatā) resides only in the substantive (viśeṣya), primacy (*prāthamya*) and so forth cannot be the object of predication; for since only what is unknown can be the object of predication, it is possible for such qualities to function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) just as they function as substantives, and there is no evidence for such a restriction. For this very reason, in the case of "the first [portion] is to be consumed" (*prathamo bhakṣaḥ*), there is the experienced cognition of primacy and so forth as being the object of predication. Furthermore, since the mental representation (*upasthiti*) produced by distinct words in a compound is a cause for such verbal cognition, [primacy] cannot be [predicated] merely by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "consumption" (*bhakṣa*).

It should not be argued that this results in the undesirable consequence of [the word] being treated as an injunction regarding primacy and so forth; for such a cognition would not arise in cases such as "the four-armed one clad in yellow garments" (*pītavāsāścaturbhujaḥ*) or "the first consumption must be performed" (*prathamabhakṣaḥ kartavyaḥ*). Nor should it be argued that there is no fault at all by positing the aforementioned causal relationship (between the cause and the effect) after inserting into the compound word denoting the counter-correlate of the difference the property of consisting of both the expression of the subject and the expression of the predicate; for the intention is that, rather than positing such a cumbersome causal relationship, it is more appropriate to posit the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

Others, however, maintain that in cases such as "The priests proceed wearing red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*) and "The sacrificial post of the Vājapeya is seventeen *aratnis* long" (*saptadaśāratnir vājapeyasya yūpo bhavati*), the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine is that the redness and the state of being seventeen-fold are enjoined with reference to the turbans and the sacrificial posts respectively. Consequently, when a compound is employed with the intention of such a connection, it is indeed desired that such a cognition arises after one has reflected upon the fact that [the members] have already been established [by other means]. For this very reason, in usages such as "An *apṛkta* is a suffix consisting of a single phoneme" (*apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ*) and "There is elision of the reduplication" (*abhyāsalopaśca*), the corresponding meaning is experienced. Therefore...

Thus, according to the Alamkarikas, in examples such as "This is a great insult to me that the enemies... and so forth, even though the word *idam* (this), which expresses the subject (*uddeśya*), is not the primary referent (*aprakṛta*), there is a delayed cognition [of the intended meaning]; whereas in a compound (*samāsa*), such cognition does not occur. Consequently, the seed of defect is either the violation of this general rule (*utsarga*) or the distress of sensitive readers (*sahṛdayodvega*). Similarly, this [use of *idam*] is not incorrect because of the usage found in the Sutra; nor is it the case here that, since the dimensions of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) are obtained through extension (*atideśa*), the instruction [of the specific measure] is stronger than the extension, and thus [the measure] is first established by sentences such as "seventeen cubits long" (*saptadaśāratni*).

It must be stated that this is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Since the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the priests (*ṛtvij*) are already obtained through extension (*atideśa*), this injunction pertains to the archetype (*prakṛti*) only after the process of extension has been considered. However, in the case of the phrase "first drinker" (*prathamabhakṣa*), because direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are stronger than name (*samākhyā*), there is no injunction for a different drinking at the outset; thus they have established in the *Mañjūṣā*. It has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

It is heard in the scripture: "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow. Here, a doubt arises: should the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) be separated from the sentence and applied to all substances within the context? Or, having entered into a relationship with the act of purchasing (*krīṇāti*), should it be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that act specifically in relation to the one-year-old cow? In this doubt, because it is impossible for something formless to function as an instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*) in an action, the redness is separated from the action. It is then connected by means of a sentence—constructed through the context and completed by a portion [of the injunction] inferred from what is heard—to the quality of redness.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was argued that because the injunction takes the form "one should effect the delimitation of the substance which serves as the means for the *apūrva* relevant to the context," all substances within the context would be subordinate (*aṅga*) to it. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached as follows: The knowledge of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is not the sole cause of verbal comprehension; rather, the certainty of semantic incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) merely acts as an obstacle to it. Consequently, when such a certainty is absent, the comprehension of the connection of redness (*āruṇya*) with the action is possible. As for the "heel" (*pāṣṇika*) [the subsequent word], its connection is with the substance; therefore, there is no suspicion of a disjunction from that [action] based on that [subsequent connection]. Thus the conclusion was established.

In this case, there is no possibility for the opponent's (pūrvapakṣa) argument to arise; for even if a qualified potency (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) is not accepted, since the words *piṅgākṣī* and *ekahāyanī* would also have to denote yellowness, eye-ness, oneness, and one-year-old-ness respectively, these too—being incorporeal—could not possibly serve as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of purchase. Consequently, since the instrument [of purchase] could not be obtained from this sentence, it would be impossible to interpret the word *aruṇā* as a reference (*anuvāda*) to the instrument already present in the context; thus, the very suspicion of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is untenable. Furthermore, since the injunction of a substance indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣita-dravya*) is possible in all three cases, the suspicion of a syntactical split has been dispelled.

Since there is no distinction among the three [terms] regarding their being defined by their specific characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*), and because there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that the dual number applies only to the two *bahuvrīhi* compounds and not to the word *aruṇa*, these and other points have been examined in the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

Now, according to the Mīmāṃsaka tenet that the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes an extracted power (*niṣkṛṣṭa-śakti*), let there be no restatement (*anuvāda*) of the substance functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Even though the nominal stem *aruṇā* (red) denotes a quality, it is indeed possible for it to convey the substance through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And the substance thus conveyed appears as the instrument due to its connection with the third case-ending; in this way, the cognition of an instrument qualified by a quality is established. Thus, the substances are understood as being instruments.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—that the quality (guṇa), which consists of the qualifier defined by the subject (viśeṣya) being restated, is enjoined as a delimiting factor such that whatever action is performed with a substance is performed with that substance characterized by the quality of redness—is indeed plausible.

By this, the prima facie argument is also refuted: namely, that it is impossible for redness to be included in the context through syntactical split (vākyabheda); for it cannot be connected with the actions of the context because it is immaterial (amūrta), nor with the substances because it is a factor of action (kāraka), and how could substances already restated [by other injunctions] enter into a connection with a quality?

Intimating this very point, he says: "Let the details rest. Here, the contradiction with the Jaimini-sūtras by the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas) is utterly inappropriate; thus, it was stated that [this view] must necessarily be accepted even by the Jaiminīyas, so enough of this elaboration. || 34 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Has it not been stated immediately after establishing the power of the composite (*samudāya-śakti*) that 'the verbal suffix [is used] for the sake of *taddhita* and *kṛt* suffixes,' and so forth? That [statement] is inconsistent with the preceding text. To dispel this doubt, he states the connection by means of the words "In cases such as *rājapuruṣa*," and so on. "‘And he is the king’ (*rājā cāsau*)": the meaning is that even though the word *rāja-* resides in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), it refers to that which is related to the king; thus, because the analytical statement possesses the same meaning as the compound (*samāsa*), there is no loss of its purpose. "The analysis is exactly as follows" (*ityeva vigrahaḥ*).

The word "eva" (only/indeed) serves to exclude the well-known analysis "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Now, if it is argued that even when the analysis is made with a genitive ending, the word *rāja-* indicates (*lakṣaka*) "one related to the king," and that the identity of meaning is maintained by accepting that the genitive case has non-difference (*abheda*) as its meaning—[we reply: this does not resolve the loss of identical meaning. This is because, in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), the non-difference expressed by the genitive appears primarily in relation to the one related to the king, whereas in the compound (*samāsa*), it does not appear in that way; thus, the loss of identical meaning remains unaddressed. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the genitive case having non-difference as its meaning.

If it is argued that the genitive case is used for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and thus there is no loss of the same meaning as the compound, this is not so; for the genitive is prescribed only in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*), and its employment for the sake of mere correctness is untenable. [The phrase] "this belongs to the cow" (*gavāmayam*) is used; the word "analysis" (*vigraha*) is to be supplied. This is because of the rule "the *bahuvrīhi* is the remainder" (*śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*). The meaning is that the "remainder" refers to those triplets of cases for which a specific compound has not been stated, and such a triplet is indeed the first triplet beginning with the nominative (*svādi-trika*). "Ending in the nominative" means consisting of a word ending in the nominative case.

"It is obtained in one alternative" means that the compound is optional; this is the intended sense. Regarding "because they have different meanings": from the compound *rājapuruṣa*, there arises a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*) characterized by connection with the king; whereas from the compound *citraguḥ*, there arises a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the constituent members (*vartipadārtha*) and whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*), taking the form "the owner of cows who are variegated. From the analytical sentence *citragavo yasya* ("he to whom there are variegated cows"), however, there arises a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the external member, taking the form "the variegated cows of which he is the owner. Thus, [the meanings] of the constituent members...

The sense is that because the cognition has a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is a difference in meaning [between the two cognitions]. Regarding *ākṣika*: by the rule "one who plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied to denote the agent of playing. Regarding *kumbhakāra*: by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* after an object" (*karmaṇyaṇ*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. "Conducive to the jar" (*kumbhānukūla*) means an activity conducive to the production having the jar as its object; the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the activity conducive to production. Regarding "even for the Mīmāṃsaka": the word "consent" (*saṃmati*) is to be supplied. It is not a sublater of the nature of being an explanation (*vivaraṇatva*).

The point is that even if there is a reversal of the status of the qualifier (*guṇa*) and the qualified (*pradhāna*) in the explanatory sentence (*vākya*) that demonstrates the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or a primary derivative (*kṛt*), it is still possible for that sentence to function as an analysis (*vivaraṇa*), just as in the case of the sentence "one whose cows [are many]" (*yasya gāvaḥ*). Thus, the essential requirement for an analytical sentence (*vigraha*) is simply that it generates a cognition having the same object (*viṣaya*) as the cognition produced by the derived form (*vṛtti*); it is not required that it generate a cognition having the same mode (*prakāra*) as well. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the statements of the Sage (Pāṇini), such as: "In the case of *citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*, the *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of possession (*matvartha*); [in] *kartṛkarmavacanenāprathamāyāḥ*, the *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of a non-nominative case-ending; and 'the remainder is *bahuvrīhi*', where 'remainder' refers to that which is left after the three [other compounds]. Nor should it be argued that this contradiction does not arise because only words ending in the nominative case enter into the *alaukika-vākya* (pre-grammatical stage), for in the *alaukika*, those very case-endings that are present in the constituent words must remain in the final, established form (*pariniṣṭhita*).

The objection—that because it is appropriate to enter [the compound] for the sake of conveying the worldly meaning when possible, a *vigraha* (etymological analysis) containing a genitive case-ending is not logical; and that even in a non-genitive *bahuvrīhi*, such a thing is impossible due to the lack of semantic equivalence; and that from the *vigraha* "this belongs to the water that has arrived" (*prāptasyodakasyāyam*), there does not arise the universally experienced result of a compound-generated cognition in the form "the object of the arrival whose agent is water," but rather a cognition in the form "related to the water which is the agent of arrival"—is not correct.

The argument of the modern Mīmāṃsakas—that because only a relation characterized as the agenthood of water and the objecthood of attainment (prāpti) is manifested, the status of having the same meaning as the analytical compound (*vigraha*) is maintained—is refuted, as it contradicts the aforementioned words of the Sage (Patañjali). Others, however, explain that regarding the rule *tatra dṛṣṭo viparyayaḥ*, the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) generates a cognition where the agent and so forth are the primary qualificands (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) in the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*); whereas those ending in secondary derivatives generate a cognition where the verbal root's action (*bhāvanā*) is the primary qualificand; and those [sentences] generate a cognition where a particular entity is the qualificand, with the meaning of the suffix serving as the qualifier.

The final meaning is that [the definition] results in being a generator of a cognition whose object consists of a relationship between a qualificand and a qualifier that is the reverse of that [usual order]; this does not apply to a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*), because the meaning of the term "error" (*viparyaya*) is precisely the relinquishing of a previously perceived quality followed by the acceptance of another quality. This is because, even if there were a reversal of the status of the qualificand and so forth, such a reversal would not reside in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Rather, it refers to the fact that a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) used in common worldly usage generates a cognition in which the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is the primary qualificand, and it is not the case that it generates such a cognition [in the context of the definition].

The meaning is that even for that [compound] which resides within a *vigraha*-sentence, there is the capacity to generate a cognition whose primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) is the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, just as in the case of words ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and the like; and thus, there is no violation of the principle that the compound and its analytical sentence possess the same meaning. This verse by Hari has been explained in exactly this way by Puñjarāja as well; and by this, it is indicated that, according to the same logic, the same applies everywhere in sentences that demonstrate the meaning of a compound.

And likewise, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *tadvahati*, it is stated that the prescription of suffixes after words such as *ratha* in the sense of "carrying" is purposeless, because [the form] is already established by the rule *tasyedam*. Having raised the objection—on the grounds that "voḍhā" (carrier) has substance as its primary meaning while "vahati" (he carries) has action as its primary meaning, and thus one word means "he carries the chariot" while the other means "the carrier of the chariot," and therefore [the desired form] is not established—it is concluded that [the form] is established due to the identity of the underlying meaning; for the very same meaning that "he carries the chariot" is identical to "the carrier of the chariot. Thus, the redundancy [of the sūtra] is made firm.

In the case of *dvirathya* and similar forms, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states that the suffix *ya* is used so that the *luṅ* (elision) might not occur; however, if the suffix were *yañ*, then because it would belong to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, there would be elision by the rule *dvigor luk*. But since this [suffix *ya*] is not *prāgdīvyatīya*, there is no elision. Regarding the phrase "that very same meaning" and so forth: the meaning that exists in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "it carries a chariot" (*rathaṃ vahati*) is the very same meaning that exists in its analytical statement "the carrier of a chariot" (*rathasya voḍhā*). However, in a *tiṅ*-ending word that is not part of the analytical statement, there is indeed predominance of the action (*kriyā-prādhānya*).

In accordance with the requirement that the derivative (vṛtti) and the analytical sentence (vigraha) must have the same meaning, it is accepted that even the analysis "he whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) generates a cognition in the form "the owner of variegated cows. Similarly, the compound *prāptodaka* produces a cognition specifically in the form "water as the object [of the action] whose agent is the reaching. However, since it is a logical contradiction for water—which is the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—to be the locus of the relation of being an object (*karmatva*), the final meaning settles upon the qualifier "reaching," just as in the case of the expression "the crested one is destroyed" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*).

For this very reason, there is no complexity resulting from the assumption of a relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) in words such as *prāpta* and so forth. For this same reason, they say that there is neither a violation of the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) between the preceding and following members—which is the basis for forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound—nor does the rule for masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) fail to apply; the details of this are explained elsewhere. || 35 ||

Likewise, the analysis (*vigraha*)—such as "one for whom there are brindled cows" (*citrā gāvo yasya*)—is the form of the analysis. Regarding the "established conclusion based on the subject matter" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*): the established conclusion in that context is that the term *niṣādasthapati* is a *karmadhāraya* compound due to its parsimony (*lāghava*), rather than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, because it lacks figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meaning is that the establishment of that [conclusion] would not occur if one were to accept a specific denotative power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), since the denotative power would be no different in either case.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the claim regarding "internalness" (*antaraṅgatva*) and so forth in the apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) is inconsistent, since the apprehension of meaning occurs at the same time in both cases? To this, he says: "The point is as follows. [Regarding the example] *niṣādasvāmike*: the meaning is that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the *sthapati* (architect) is the *niṣāda* who is the owner (*svāmī*). The word *sthapati* is a synonym for "owner. [He says] "because it is expressive in all cases."

The point is this: if there is an intention (*tātparya*), a cognition of the ownership belonging to the *niṣāda* and so forth would also arise; therefore, a primary denotative power (*śakti*) must necessarily exist even in that case, because according to the opponent's own view, it is accepted that such a cognition can arise through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when an intention is present. This he will state immediately following this very passage. "In the assumption of that" means in the assumption of the intention. "Only the meaning already previously presented" is said because, in the case of the *sthapati* who is a *niṣāda*, the presentation of that [meaning] occurs first, precisely due to its connection with the *niṣāda*.

And thus, in the apprehension of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) which determines the expressive power (*śakti*), factors such as "internalness" (*antaraṅgatva*) result; it should also be understood that the apprehension of the expressive power of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) than the apprehension of the expressive power of a *karmadhāraya*, because it possesses an additional object in the form of the meaning of the genitive case. By the phrase "upasthityādi," etc., other factors such as "proximity" (*upasthiti*) are also to be included. Jaimini also said: "The *sthapati* would be a *naptṛ* (grandson/nephew) due to the capacity of the word."

The meaning is this: the *sthapati* (chief) who is non-different from a *niṣāda* is precisely what is conveyed by the compound *niṣādasthapati*, because of the capacity in the form of a power (*śakti*) conducive to generating a rapid mental presentation of such a meaning due to its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*). Now, one might object: "In the Mīmāṃsā view, since there is no semantic power (*śakti*) in a compound, how can it have multiple meanings? To this he says: "Of others" (*pareṣām*). "When there is an intention" (*sati tātparye*) means: when there is an intention toward the sense of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* or other such compounds. "Like 'Bring in the staff-bearers' (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya')"—in that case...

Just as in the case [of the word "staff-bearer"], even in the absence of an impossibility of connecting with the primary meaning, there is indeed figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) due to the impossibility of the intended sense (tātparya), so too in the present case, even though there is no impossibility of connection, figurative indication is unavoidable due to the impossibility of the intended sense in the meaning of a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, etc.; this is the meaning. The word "incongruous" (*asaṅgatam*) is to be supplied after the word "considered" (*cintyam*).

The word *sthapati* is an adjective (*guṇaśabda*), while the word *niṣāda* denotes a specific caste born in the natural order (*anuloma*), according to the traditional definition: "An *ambaṣṭha* is born from a Śūdra woman, as is a *niṣāda*, also known as a *pāraśava*. Thus, one should not suspect that the compound *niṣāda-sthapati* would result in the *sthapati* being placed first [as per Pāṇini 2.2.36], because it belongs to the class beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31), which requires the latter member to be placed first.

If it is argued that, because there is a constant expectancy regarding the element of relation, a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound is more appropriate, we say no; for Jaimini states another reason in the words, "And because an indicative mark is seen" (*liṅgadarśanācca*). And the indicative mark is indeed seen in the passage, "The *kūṭa* is the sacrificial fee" (*kūṭaṃ dakṣiṇā*). For the *Śābarabhāṣya* explains that the *kūṭa* belongs exclusively to the Niṣādas. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 36 ||
Thus concludes the examination of the expressive power of compounds.

"Of that"—that is, of the *śakti* (potency). Regarding the phrase "it is understood as having no beginning," the meaning to be understood is "that which has no beginning (*an-ādi*). "That very [is] the *śakti*" means that the *śakti* consists precisely in the nature of being the cause of cognition. However, others [argue]: "The nature of being a generator of cognition cannot belong to the relationship in the form of *śakti*—which is postulated because it is otherwise impossible for a word unconnected to its object to produce a cognition whose content is that object—since this would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*)."

If it is argued that there is no such fault in the assumption that *śakti* (potency) is postulated as being of the nature of the causality consisting in the suitability for producing verbal cognition—since this is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*) by the fact that it brings about the fruit, which is verbal cognition itself—even so, it is improper to postulate such a status for "causality" (*janakatva*) here. This is because, among the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇas*), it is already established that only a relation distinct from and inclusive of "causality" serves as the instigator of valid cognition (*pramiti*). Otherwise, one would have to conclude that the very status of being the cause of the inference of fire, residing in smoke and the like, constitutes the relation between fire and smoke.

There would have to be a relation; for a relation is defined precisely as that which determines a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*), and since the capacity to produce (*janakatva*) does not determine such a cognition, it cannot possibly be a relation. Furthermore, it should be understood that because neither the desire [to speak] nor its object determines a qualified cognition, they cannot be relations. Therefore, they say: "Power (*śakti*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). The Naiyāyika raises an objection with the word "nanu. This doubt should be understood to apply even to the position that "power is a distinct category."

"Modern"—that is, indicated by a modern convention. "Due to its absence"—due to the absence of primordial power (*anādi-śakti*); and thus, from that [convention alone], there would be no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Now, one might object that there is no proof for the absence of power in that case; therefore, he says: "Otherwise. "Otherwise" means: if power were present there. "Convention by a father, etc."—[this refers to the objection].

If there were power (*śakti*) in that [conventional meaning], then since the knowledge of the convention established by the father and others—and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for its apprehension—is present, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of its apprehension. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because it would lead to the occurrence of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through a causal complex composed of the very cause that consists in such apprehension; this is the meaning. Thus, the point is that the non-apprehension of what is otherwise capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is itself the proof for its absence. Regarding the term "indicative" (*lākṣaṇika*): the meaning is that since that too generates cognition, it would follow that there is beginningless power (*anādi-śakti*) even in that case. Regarding "knowledge of the convention" (*saṃketajñāna*): [this refers to the aforementioned consequence].

Although the property of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges" exists in the bank (*tīra*)—which is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the convention consisting of God’s will—it is not accepted that God’s will has the property of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "Ganges" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the bank in the form of "the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word 'Ganges'. Rather, it is accepted [as its qualifier] simply in the form of pure "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*). This much alone does not contradict the Lord’s will having all things as its objects; and thus:

The point is this: since it is accepted that the knowledge of a convention—consisting of the Lord’s will—characterized by a qualifier-nature (*prakāratā*) delimited by the property of being the object-nature (*viṣayatvatva*) of the cognition produced by that word [is the cause] in the apprehension of power (*śakti*), there can be no such knowledge of convention in the case of a word used in a secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*). Consequently, because the apprehension of power is impossible [there], the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā* is postulated as the cause for the occurrence of verbal comprehension. Thus, due to the absence of any means of grasping power in the case of a secondary meaning, and the lack of evidence for its existence there, it follows that there is no power (*śakti*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "by the father and others in the modern [context]": in that case, because there is no divine convention (*saṃketa*) such as "let there arise an object of cognition produced by the word 'Caitra' and so forth," and because there is an absence of lexicons or other means for grasping such a convention, the convention—"on the twelfth day, the father shall give a name"—is not specifically directed toward each particular word; thus, it is of no consequence. The point is that power (*śakti*) is merely convention. Regarding the phrase "the cause by its own nature": the meaning is that it is a cause by virtue of its own form (*svarūpa*).

"From that whose capacity has not been grasped" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the word refers to something other than its own constituent members. The meaning is that even from a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose capacity has not been grasped, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because the causal capacity for such cognition exists. "Known in a general way" means known by some form or another. "In the knowledge of that" means in the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) of God (*Īśvara*) and so forth. "Linguistic" (*laukika*)... [etc.]

The meaning is "both worldly people and the Mīmāṃsakas and others. By the term "worldly," common folk and atheistic Mīmāṃsakas are to be understood here; by the word "and others," Buddhists and so forth are included. Now, one might object: even if the knowledge of that [word] as a convention is possible for them through its being a convention of God, the knowledge of it as a convention is indeed possible [for others too]. To this he replies: "only for those who possess the apprehension of its being the generator of the cognition of such-and-such a meaning."

The meaning is that there is an exclusion of the cognition of a mode [of being] as a convention (*saṅketa*). Thus, since verbal cognition arises from the aforementioned cognition even in the absence of the cognition of it as a convention, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, even the cognition [of it] as a convention is not the cause. [This concludes the discussion on] "the capacity to produce the cognition of an object."

The meaning is as follows: the capacity to produce comprehension (*bodha*) is the fitness for producing comprehension; and that [fitness] consists in possessing a property that delimits it (*tadavacchedakadharmavattva*). And since that [delimiting property] is already established, it is simply the convention (*saṃketa*) of God and so forth. Even though knowledge [of the convention] cannot be the cause [of comprehension] because it would involve deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to its being merely a convention, it is nonetheless possible for knowledge to be the cause by virtue of being the delimiting factor of the capacity to produce comprehension, as there is no deviation in that case. "Knowledge of that" refers to the knowledge of the convention. "By way of parsimony" (*lāghavena*)— [End of excerpt]

There is parsimony [of theory] because the property of being the delimitor of the generativity of the cognition of that meaning is not included within the scope of the delimitor of the generativity [of the word]. "From the knowledge of the convention alone": the word "alone" (eva) excludes the apprehension of the status of being the generative cause of the cognition of that meaning. "Of this": of the apprehension of the status of being the delimitor of the generativity of the cognition of that meaning. "By way of encompassing."

The meaning is as follows: according to the rule that "in whatever respect a cognition of desire and the like possesses a particular objective mode (prakārakatva) regarding its own object, in that same respect it possesses that objective mode," there is no impairment of the fact that such a cognition of desire possesses the objective mode of being a generator of the understanding of meaning with respect to the word. Regarding the term "independently" (*svātantryeṇa*): this means "without being a qualifier of anything else. However, in this case, it [the word] functions as a qualifier in the respect of being an objective mode; for the reason is that the property of having "being a generator of understanding" as its objective mode resides within the desire.

"Otherwise"—that is, if the cause were merely the cognition of that [word], common to both independent and non-independent [words]. "The consequence of grasping that" means the consequence of grasping the object; for even there, one apprehends the capacity to produce a cognition characterized by the absence of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). "By sublation" means by the certainty that the word lacks the capacity to produce a cognition. "Regarding the word" means even for one who possesses the knowledge: "This person possesses the knowledge that 'this word is the producer of the cognition of this object. "Grasping that" refers to...

The meaning is that the apprehension of a word's capacity to generate the cognition of its object does not arise [in that case]. "Otherwise" means if one were to accept a cognition that apprehends the presence of that [object] even when there is a certainty regarding its absence. [This leads to] the consequence of it being erroneous.

The point is this: although it is necessary for one who knows the error to have the cognition, "the mother-of-pearl and so forth, which lacks silverness, has been apprehended under the form of silverness," it is still possible for there to be a cognition having as its qualificandum the mother-of-pearl (which lacks silverness) and as its qualifier silverness; consequently, that person too would become a locus of the illusion of silverness. Now, [an objection might be raised]: since even the word *gaṅgā* possesses the capacity to convey the bank (*tīra*), it would follow that it is directly denotative (*śakta*) of the bank, which would result in the collapse of the very definition of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He avoids this by saying "nor... (*nāpi*), accepting the consequence as desired.

"Because it is common. The sense is that, in this way, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs there as well through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). By this, the objection that "the power of the word *gaṅgā* is not intended to be directed toward the bank and so forth, because there is an absence of a lexicon or other means for apprehending power there" is refuted; for linguistic usage, which is the crest-jewel among the means for apprehending power, is present. The distinction between primary and secondary (metaphorical) usage is to be established on the basis of what is well-known (*prasiddhi*) and what is not.

Now, one might object: since linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) does not grasp the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*), its occurrence would establish that words such as *gaṅgā* denote the bank and so forth; furthermore, this would contradict the maxim "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings. For this very reason, the word *gaṅgā* is not listed among the synonyms for "bank" in the lexicons. To this, he replies: "Moreover... It is not an auxiliary factor for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); that is, even when such a presentation [of the meaning] exists, because verbal cognition is not produced by that word for a person who has not grasped its primary power (*śakti*), it should be understood that such a presentation is not an auxiliary factor for that cognition.

"Produced by the capacity" (śaktijanyā) means "produced by the knowledge of the capacity"; this should be understood likewise in what follows. However, according to the view that "that which has its occurrence [in the primary sense] being known is the cause for the presentation [of the secondary meaning]," the literal reading itself is correct. Regarding the objection concerning "complexity" (gaurava): one might argue that since there is no conventional usage of terms like *gaṅgā* as denoting the bank (*tīra*) and so forth, it is improper to accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) there; therefore, another mode of operation called "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) must necessarily be admitted. And thus, there would be two causal relations...

The assumption of a complex conceptual relation (*kalpanā-gaurava*) is not a fault; to this he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*). Alternatively, it is beyond dispute that the capacity to produce the cognition of the bank, etc., residing in words such as *gaṅgā*, is distinct from the capacity to produce the cognition of the flowing stream. Thus, even in your own view, there is complexity in postulating a relation of "denotative power" (*śakti*) for the capacity to produce the cognition of the bank; however, since the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in a relation to the primary denotation, is already established, its postulation is not an additional burden. For I merely postulate that the representation produced by that [secondary function] is a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*); thus, there is nothing extra.

"Gaurava" (complexity); however, being a generator of cognition (*bodhajanakatātva*) is not "potency" (*śaktitva*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) since inference and other means also generate cognition. If one were to claim that potency is the state of being a generator distinct from those [other means], there would be both complexity and injustice; thus, he says "api ca" (furthermore) to show that there is no abandonment of the principle [of parsimony]. "Vyabhicāraḥ" refers to negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). He explains this with the words "śaktīti. "Avyeti" means: by way of the relation of immediate succession qualified by co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as constituted by inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) arising in Maitra immediately after the mental representation (upasthiti) produced by Caitra’s capacity also possesses a mental representation through the relation of "immediate succession" (avyavahitottaratva). Even though that [specific] representation does not exist within Maitra’s own self, the verbal cognition of Maitra is not subsumed under the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka), since it is not co-referential (asamānādhikaraṇa) with Caitra’s representation; for the possession of such a representation as a factor in the delimitor of the effect is based solely on the relation of co-referentiality (samānādhikaraṇya).

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, where a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arises—produced by an apprehension (*upasthiti*) generated by a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) that has occurred either at a prior time or a later time relative to the [compound's] occurrence—there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the moment immediately preceding that [verbal cognition] does not exist within its own self. Therefore, "immediately subsequent" (*avyavahitottaratva*) is adopted [as the relation]. Furthermore, the inclusion of "subsequent" (*uttaratva*) is intended so that a deviation does not occur in the case of such a verbal cognition produced at a time immediately preceding [the apprehension]; for [otherwise], there would be a deviation in the case of a cognition produced at a time separated [from the apprehension] by an interval.

The inclusion of the element of "immediacy" (*avyavadhāna*) is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the term "infinite" (*ananta*): the sense is that because the mental representations (*upasthiti*) are infinite, there would result an infinity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) due to their respective differences.

It should not be suspected that there is no possibility of an infinite regress because the relation between cause and effect can be established by just two causal relations: namely, that with respect to a verbal cognition characterized by an apprehension produced by the knowledge of *śakti* (primary denotative power), the cause is such an apprehension (*tādṛśopasthititvena*); and with respect to a verbal comprehension characterized by an apprehension produced by *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indicative power), the cause is likewise such an apprehension. This is because it is impossible to define "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) without first specifying the apprehension as a particular individual instance (*tattadvayaktitvena*). To explain: [The text continues: ...for indeed...

Immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*) consists in being the locus of the destruction of a moment that is itself the locus of its own destruction, while not being the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of its own destruction. This definition is common to both the second and third moments; for [the second moment] is not the locus of the destruction of the third moment—which is the locus of the destruction of the moment (the first) that is its own locus—and it is the locus of the destruction of the first moment, which is the moment that is its own locus.

The inclusion of the term "satya" (truth) is for the purpose of excluding [the cognition] of the fourth and subsequent moments, while the inclusion of the qualificand portion (*viśeṣyadala*) is for the purpose of excluding its own preceding moment. Here, the word "sva" (self) does not refer to the general class of such cognitions by way of being produced by a power (*śakti*) or the like; for every moment would then be the locus of the destruction of the destruction of some such cognition produced in its own preceding time, and thus there would be no absence of being different from that [moment] as delimited by those [preceding cognitions]. Rather, it refers to each specific individual instance of that cognition. Thus...

Due to the infinity of co-presences (*copasthiti*), the infinity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is indeed evident. There is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because even in the absence of one [co-presence], the other generates the co-presence. There is complexity (*gaurava*), due to the conceptualization of two distinct causal relations.

If it is argued that, by the aforementioned relationship, the cognition of the word’s power (*śakti*) is the cause for the presentation qualified by the cognition of that power, and likewise the cognition of the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted as the cause for the presentation qualified by the cognition of that function—in order to avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—then the meaning is that there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations. Indicating this, he says "as before" (*prāgvat*). Regarding the phrase "the word and its meaning" (*padatadartha*): it means by the distinction between the word and its respective meaning.

Regarding the claim that "there is complexity in the hypothesis": just as, according to the opponent's view, a cognition having the form of "the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object *ghaṭa*" (with the word *ghaṭa* as its locus) and a cognition having the form of "the word *kalaśa*, etc., denotes the same object" are causes for an apprehension delimited by having *ghaṭa* as its object, so too—in order to account for the arising of an apprehension of a cloth (*paṭa*) from the word *ghaṭa*, which is otherwise held to be produced by the knowledge of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—there must be a cognition having the form of "the word *ghaṭa*, etc., denotes the object cloth, etc. (with the word *ghaṭa*, etc., as its locus) as the cause for the apprehension of the cloth, etc.

Causality must be accepted; however, for one who accepts *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication), it need not be postulated that a cognition having the form "the word 'pot' etc. causes the understanding of the object 'cloth' etc. is the cause of the mental presentation of the cloth etc., since [the understanding] occurs through the power (*śakti*) [of the word] in conjunction with [the secondary indication]. The word "pot" etc.—[is the cause].

The meaning is: "because it generates the cognition of a cloth and so forth from a word. "Even for you" means even for you, the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*). Regarding "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*): the sense is that the verbal cognition of a cloth arises even without a cognition having the property of being the word "pot" as its locus and the quality of causing the cognition of a cloth as its mode; and it arises even without a cognition having the word "cloth" as its locus and the quality of causing the cognition of a cloth as its mode, because the verbal cognition of a cloth arises from a cognition having the word "pot" as its locus and the quality of causing the cognition of a cloth as its mode.

"Immediately preceding" (avyavahita) means that the delimitor of the effect-nature (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is constituted by the property of being immediately followed (*avyavahitottaratva*). Thus, one must accept that each specific cognition is a cause for an apprehension delimited by the nature of an apprehension qualified by a single cognition, through the relation of its own co-location (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) qualified by its own state of being immediately followed. Likewise, within the body of the delimitor of the effect-nature of each respective apprehension, the qualification by that respective apprehension must be included via the aforementioned qualified relation; otherwise—

The sense is that this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the term "sutārām": the suffix denoting excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*) is used to indicate that the resulting excessive burden (*gaurava*) arises because, due to the infinity of such cognitions, there would be an infinity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the error regarding [the word's] power" (*śaktibhrama*): even for one who does not accept that all words denote all objects, since it must be admitted that even the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), when accompanied by an error regarding its power, can bring about the cognition of a "cloth" (*paṭa*), one must necessarily accept that the cause for the presentation of the cloth is the knowledge of the power of the word "pot" as residing in the word "pot" itself. Thus, the meaning is that because the resulting infinite regress of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—where each specific word would have to be included for each specific object—is equal [in both views], this [theory] is untenable. Regarding the phrase "the function of indication" (*lakṣaṇākārya*).

The meaning is: [the causal relation] consisting of the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the causal relation [between the word and its object]. "Precisely as the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a cognitive operation" means: precisely as the presentation produced by the cognition of a cognitive operation; by the word "precisely" (*eva*), there is an exclusion of [the status of being] a cause [of verbal comprehension] in the capacity of being a presentation produced by the cognition of denotative power (*śakti*) and in the capacity of being a presentation produced by the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "It must be stated by me" implies: likewise, in my view as well, there is only one single causal relation, so there is no complexity (*gaurava*); this is the sense. "As a cause of verbal comprehension" [is the phrase to be supplied].

The compound *śābdabodhahetuścāsau padārthopasthitiśca* is a *karmadhāraya*; the meaning is "of that which is the relation between word and object, which is conducive to such an [appropriate] presentation of the object. The term "conducive" (*anukūla*) is included as a qualification of the relation in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the case where the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) exists between the word and its object in the form of the ether (*ākāśa*), since that inherence is also conducive to the presentation of space; thus, the aforementioned fault would remain, and for this reason the qualification "cause" (*hetu*) is applied to the presentation.

"Because it is more cumbersome" means that, compared to the nature of *śakti* (denotative power) as the capacity to generate verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the nature of *vṛtti* (the relation between word and meaning)—which consists in being either *śakti* or *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function), distinct from each other—and the [definition of verbal cognition] beginning with "verbal cognition," etc., possess a more complex (cumbersome) body. "Of the occurrence of the presentation of the word-meaning" refers to the property residing in the presentation of the word-meaning, which serves as the delimitant of the causality for verbal cognition and consists in being a presentation produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti*. "Because of the impossibility" means...

The meaning is as follows: "being conducive to verbal cognition" means being a cause of verbal cognition; and since that [causality] is difficult to grasp when its delimiting property (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-rūpa*) is not known, and because the aforementioned delimiting property of causality is difficult to ascertain, the apprehension of the relation of cause and effect is impossible. "In my view as well"—the word "in the opinion of" (*mate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of this phrase. "Precisely by way of the knowledge of *śakti*"—that is to say, not by way of the knowledge of *śakti* nor by way of the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā*. "Causality"—[refers to the status of being a cause].

The meaning is that [the knowledge of the denotative power] is the cause with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) and with respect to the presentation of the word-meanings conducive thereto. Thus, even in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, the relationship of cause and effect is singular; this is the intended sense. Regarding the view that "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the presentation of the non-denotable based on the denotable," indication is not constituted by the denotative power (*śakti*), because indication is simply the presentation of the bank and so forth caused by the actual denoted meaning of the word "Ganges" (the current and so on). Nor is the aforementioned cognition useful for the presentation [of the indicated meaning]; therefore, he says: "consisting of a relation to the denotable."

In this context, the entry of *śakti* (denotative power) occurs precisely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and not as a mere incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that the cause for the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) is a cognition in the form "the bank related to the flow which is the denotation of the word *gaṅgā*," and not one in the form "the bank related to the flow. The final sense is that since there must be a requirement for a cognition whose object is that [power]—namely, its entry—to be the cause of an apprehension whose object is that [power], it follows that the two must have the same objective domain (*samānaviṣayatva*).

Regarding the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—namely, "the bank is that which is related to what is denotable by the word *gaṅgā*"—or the cognition of indication in the form "the bank [is understood] from the word *gaṅgā*" where the relation is the connection between the denotable and the indicated: although such a cognition has the bank as its object, it does not have the denotation (*śakti*) as its object in respect to the portion consisting of the bank. Consequently, it is impossible for it to function as a facilitator for the presentation of the bank by way of being a cognition of denotation (*śaktijñāna*). Here, the phrase "between the cognition of denotation and the presentation of the object" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood to mean "between the cognition of denotation and the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)."

He states the objection [to not including] the condition of having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Regarding the phrase "non-apprehension of the relation" (*saṃbandhāgraha*): at the time when that [relation] is not apprehended, it is indeed accepted that the cognition of the bank arises from the knowledge "the word *gaṅgā* has the current as its primary meaning" (*pravāho gaṅgāpadaśakyaḥ*); therefore, the pursuit of that [condition] is necessary. Now, one might object: "One should accept that the cause for an apprehension (*upasthiti*) and so forth having a certain object is the knowledge of the primary power (*śakti*) having that same object, and not in the form stated [above]. Thus, there would be no way to account for the knowledge of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the like, because that [knowledge of secondary indication] also has the bank as its object. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the aforementioned application of the primary power [to the bank], because that [primary power] does not have the bank as its object. Anticipating this doubt, he says "moreover" (*api ca*).

He followed the first cognition as having the sentence "bring the jar" as its object, in order to ensure that the subsequent recollection would have the jar as its object and be produced by the word. Then, in order to ensure that it had the elephant-driver as its object, he followed [the cognition] as having the elephant as its object. He says "he remembers" because a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) having both the elephant and the sentence as its objects is impossible.

In reality, however, there is no insistence on the unity of memory; rather, since perception of a sentence composed of multiple words—which themselves consist of multiple sequential phonemes—is impossible, recourse is taken to memory. For this very reason, even the opponent (the *hastin*) accepts that same [memory-based] view, due to the parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*). Regarding the phrase "being produced by a linguistic function" (*vṛttijanyatva*): the meaning is that it exists because it is produced by the knowledge of the expressive power (*śaktijñāna*). It should be understood that the mention of "being produced by a linguistic function" is intended to reveal a flaw even in the position that [verbal cognition] has as its cause an apprehension produced by a linguistic function (*vṛttijanyopasthiti*). By the word "by this" (*etena*),...

By means of the refutation consisting in the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) occurring for the elephant-driver (*hastipaka*) in the aforementioned instance: [Objection] It must be admitted that the cause of a verbal cognition is such an apprehension (*upasthiti*) by way of the relation of a locus of a content (*viṣayatā-saṃbandha*), where the content is delimited by the state of being prompted by the knowledge of the word’s expressive power (*śakti-jñāna*). Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition of the elephant-driver arising from the aforementioned collective recollection (*samūhālambana-smaraṇa*), because the content residing in the elephant-driver is not delimited by the state of being prompted by the knowledge of the expressive power of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa-pada*). However, since the content residing in the jar *is* delimited by the state of being prompted by the knowledge of the expressive power of the word "jar," [the verbal cognition] is established.

If it is argued that the jar possesses the status of being an object of verbal cognition because the subjectivity residing in the bank and so forth is also an undamaged delimitor of the state of being produced by the knowledge of the power consisting in the lakṣaṇā of the word *gaṅgā*—and thus the appearance of the bank from the word *gaṅgā* accounts for the bank’s status as an object of verbal cognition—this is not so; for even the subjectivity residing in the elephant-driver would be a delimitor of the state of being produced by the knowledge of the power having the word *hastipaka* as its locus, and consequently, in the aforementioned case, the occurrence of its [the driver’s] verbal cognition would be unavoidable.

[Objection: "But surely, one should include in the definition the property of being the delimitor of the state of being prompted by the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) directed toward each respective word; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. To this, he says: "of the state of being prompted" (*prayojyatvasya*). [He explains: "not exceeding" (*anatīti*). The point is as follows: For a person who possesses the apprehension of potency in the form "the word *ghaṭa* has potency for the jar," when there is the presentation of the jar from the word *ghaṭa*, there would result the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the ether (*ākāśa*), which is presented through its inherence in that very [jar], becomes the object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the word *ghaṭa*. This is because even in that case, the aforementioned presentation exists by virtue of the relation of being the object-delimiter (*viṣayatā-sambandha*) of that which is delimited by the state of being prompted by the apprehension of the potency of the word *ghaṭa*.

Nor is it accepted that verbal cognition has as its cause a cognition characterized by a qualificand residing in the meaning (artha), which is itself determined by a qualifier residing in the word (pada), and which is in turn determined by a relational objectivity (sāṃsargika-viṣayatā) delimited by the property of "power" (śaktitva). This is because, in a cognition where the word is the qualifier and the meaning is the qualificand—whether through the relation of power (śakti-saṃbandha) or the relation of the "power-possessor" (śakya-saṃbandha)—power functions as the relation (saṃsarga). Furthermore, since the pervasion (paryāpti) of the delimitation residing in the property of "power" is not introduced [as a requirement], cognitions where the word is the qualifier via the relation of the "power-possessor" are also included.

However, the state of being obstructed by a certainty whose qualifier is the absence of a word—where the counter-correlativity is delimited by a relation with its denotation (*śakti*)—does not apply to a cognition in which the word is the qualifier and the relation with its denotation is the relational content (*saṃsarga*). This is because the relational objectivity residing in the power (*śakti*), as determined by the qualificative objectivity of the word, lacks the property of being determined by the objective predication (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning. [Such obstruction applies] only to a cognition whose qualifier-ness resides in that [meaning], which is determined by the relational objectivity residing in that relation, which in turn is determined by the objective predication residing in that [meaning].

This is because the certainty of the absence of that [object], whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its connection with the possessor of the true property (*saddharmika*), acts as an impediment; otherwise, even the cognition of the possession of a jar through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) would not occur when there is a certainty of the absence of the jar through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

And thus, it should not be argued that there is the undesirable consequence of postulating that the knowledge of a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇājñāna*) is a separate cause for verbal cognition; nor that there is the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition occurring for the elephant-driver from the aforementioned collective recollection; nor that there is the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition occurring for "space" (*ākāśa*) in the aforementioned instance. For it would be unavoidable that space and the like would result in verbal cognition from a cognition having "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and "cloth" (*paṭa*) as qualifiers and "space" as the qualificand, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with the word "cloth" existing at the same time as its power (*śakti*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because such a thing is never experienced.

However, a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) is not accepted by the elders as a basis for indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for this very reason, the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* stated: "There is no connection with the result [if there is sublation]. Otherwise, since a mediated relationship—in the form of inherence in that which is conjoined with itself (*svasaṃyuktasamavetatva*)—exists even in cases such as coolness and purifying power belonging to a riverbank, the aforementioned statement would clearly be inconsistent.

[Objection: "But surely, even in the view of the opponent (the Naiyāyika), there is no room for the aforementioned complexity; for where the cognition of the bank arises simply from the knowledge of a possible relation, the Grammarian must necessarily postulate that the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* is the cause, in order to account for the cognition established by universal experience. [Reply: This is not so, because even in that case, it is accepted that the verbal cognition of the bank has as its cause a distinct cognition, namely: "The word *gaṅgā* denotes the bank. Nor is there any complexity in postulating such a specific instance of cognition, because such complexity is not a fault when it is "aimed at a result" (*phalamukha*).

Others, however, maintain that in reality, from the moment deep sleep ceases until the moment it arises again, a perceptible quality of the self must necessarily be admitted; for this very reason, a period distinct from the time of deep sleep and devoid of such a quality is called the state of fainting (*mūrchā*). Thus, since cognition and so forth are indispensable during such a time, they argue that this [quality] itself is postulated in place of other forms of cognition, and therefore where is the burden [of complexity]? This is the summary; intending this, he says: "This has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. (37)

Thus, regarding the view that the power (*śakti*) is the cause of comprehension: according to the position that "the power is the will of God" (*īśvarecchā*), power consists precisely in the will as qualified by the relation between each respective word and its object. Consequently, although the will "let comprehension of a jar arise from the word *gagarī*" is necessary for comprehension to arise from the word *gagarī*, that will is not postulated as having the nature of a relation to the word *gagarī*.
