Since there is an absence of supporting factors such as lexicons (*kośa*), etc., there is no contingency of power residing in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). The point is that even in the view that "power is a distinct category" (*padārthāntara*), it is not postulated in that case [of corrupt forms].

"In two ways" means in two manners: one manner is the non-acceptance that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) possess direct denotative power; the other is the admission that they do indeed possess denotative power. The distinction is that the first resolution is according to the view of the Naiyāyikas and others, while the second is according to his own view. "Having inferred" means having remembered. For this very reason, he will later state: "Their utility lies solely in the recollection of the correct words (*sādhu*). Now, if this is so, its status as a denoter is untenable, since being a denoter consists precisely in possessing direct denotative power; therefore, he says: "The denoter is the communicator."

"Direct denotative capacity" (sākṣāttadvācakatvam) means that its denotative capacity consists in being the direct communicator of that [meaning]. "Having accepted identity with it" (tādātmyam upagamyaiva) means having grasped the identity with the object in words such as *gagara* and so forth. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used to indicate that this grasping is erroneous; by this, their lack of denotative capacity is implied, for it is only that which is truly denotative of something that one accepts as being identical with it.

By this, it is also indicated that cognition arises from that [corrupt word] due to an error regarding its expressive power (*śakti*). Nor should it be asked: "If common people do not grasp the expressive power, how can there be an error regarding that power? For when a person hears the word *gagarī* and understands it through the recollection of the correct [Sanskrit] word, even though he understands, a bystander might mistakenly think, "This person's understanding was produced by the word *gagarī* itself. Thus, while the first person has an error regarding the expressive power, it is possible for others to have an error based on that [initial error]. This is what is meant by "not by the learned" (*na śiṣṭaiḥ*).

The construction is: "By the learned, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) are not followed, just as synonyms (*paryāyas*) [are not used together]. The meaning is that they are not included within the collection of synonyms. Regarding "nayataḥ": this refers to the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) which conveys the meaning; the ellipsis is "the attainment of the comprehension of the meaning occurs through its mere recollection. "Baṃbaṃba" [is an example].

When a child being trained speaks indistinctly, saying "baṃ baṃ be," for those who know—that is, for those who understand correct words—when there is clarity, meaning the correct pronunciation, there arises certainty, which is to say, the determination of the meaning. The sense is that because an incorrect word has the same phonetic nature as a correct one, it brings that correct word to mind through similarity. In this context, the reading "baṃ baṃ be" alone is appropriate, and not "ambāmbe," because the latter is itself a correct word.

He explains the preceding verse with the words "Thus, in the case of correct [words] (*sādhau*). "Separated by the correct" means preceded by the recollection of the correct form. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "from usage, etc.," the inclusion of the speech of trustworthy persons (*āptavākya*) is intended. Regarding "equivalence of synonyms": the meaning is that just as all various synonyms are denoters of a single object without distinction, so too are corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). He points out the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration with the words "of those" (*teṣām*); that is, of the synonyms. "Because of their oneness" (*ekatvāt*).

For this very reason, there is a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*); otherwise, the expressive power (*śakti*) would be established only for that synonym which is well-known in all regions—this is the sense. Likewise, there is unity across all regions, because those [synonyms] are not differentiated by differences of location; it is for this reason that it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Where speech forms diverge, that is considered a different region. The phrase "otherwise" means: in the case where corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) were non-expressive.

The sense is that if those [words] were denotative, then in order to exclude them, something else entirely different would have to be stated. Nor is there a failure to include words used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), because even they possess denotative power (*śakti*) in some instances; or rather, the meaning of that [term "denotative"] should be understood as simply possessing a function (*vṛttimat*). [This applies to] "the ignorant" (*aviduṣām*).

The meaning is: "of those who lack the apprehension [of words] as signifiers of their respective objects. And thus, even if there has been a prior experience [of the word] as having such-and-such a word-form (*śabdatva*), the desired conclusion is not established; for although such recollection is possible for those who have had that experience, it is useless for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), since only a recollection [of the word] as a signifier of its respective object is useful. This is the intended sense. With this very intention, he says: "of them" (*teṣām*). The meaning is "of the common folk" (*pāmarāṇām*); "common folk" refers to those who are proficient only in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*).

Is the delusion regarding the power (*śakti*) of the form of being a signifier (*bodhakatva*), or rather regarding that which is of the nature of intention (*icchārūpā*)? It is not the former; thus he says, "of being a signifier" (*bodhakatvasya*). This means: of the capacity to produce the cognition of this or that object. "By non-sublation" (*abādhenā*) means: by the absence of a certain sublation such as, "This is not a signifier of that object. "Due to the absence of sublation" (*bādhābhāvāt*)...

Since even from words such as *gagari* there arises the cognition of an object in the form of a jar (*ghaṭa*), the will of God must necessarily be of the form: "Let the jar become the object of the cognition produced by the word *gagari*. Otherwise, because the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word *gagari* residing in the jar would not be within the scope of God's will, it would be impossible for that will to have all things as its objects. Nor can it be maintained that the will has, with respect to the jar, the property of having the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word *gagari* as its qualifier, simply by virtue of that [state] being a pure objecthood (*viṣayatātva*), and not by virtue of [the object] being the object of a cognition produced by that specific word.

It should not be argued that its status as having all things as its object is untenable even on that account; for although it does not apprehend [the property] by virtue of being a constituent of the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of the qualifierhood (prakāratā) determined by the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the jar, it is admitted that it apprehends it independently within the aspect of the cognition.

Power (*śakti*) is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) as related by the relation of being the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the property of being the objectness of a cognition produced by the word "tattva. Since this is the case, such [power] is not possible there [in the word *gagari*]. Alternatively, it should not be argued that power is the will of God characterized by the property of being a relation between a word and its referent, and since the characterization of that [will] by the property of being a relation of the word *gagari* is not admitted, power is not possible there; for even from that [word], the experience of the arising of a cognition [of the jar] occurs, and thus [power] exists there as well.

The intended meaning is that one must necessarily admit that the desire possesses the property of having that [the jar] as its qualifier (tatprakārakatva) by way of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "gagarī," or else one must necessarily accept the specific relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consisting in the relation between both the word "gagarī" and the jar.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of the specific words and word-meanings": since *śakti* (denotative power) is defined as a desire whose objective is a meaning that possesses a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) consisting in being the object of a cognition produced by a particular word, the *śakti* for the word *gargarī* is simply the desire whose mode is "being the object of a cognition produced by the word *gargarī*" and whose qualificand is a jar. In the present case, this [desire] is what is to be denoted. If it exists, then there can be no error regarding it; if it does not exist, then even more so, an error regarding it cannot be established, because an error consists precisely in a cognition of something well-known in one place occurring with respect to that which lacks it.

Now, one might argue that the desire (*icchā*)—which has a specific word as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and has the property of being a generator of the cognition of a specific meaning as its qualifier (*prakāra*)—is also [the basis of] *śakti*, because there is no restrictive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*). Furthermore, since such a desire, which has the property of generating the cognition of a jar (*ghaṭa*), is well-known to exist with respect to the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), it is possible for an error (*bhrama*) to occur whereby this desire is attributed to the word "gagarī. If this is argued, we say: no. Because a desire characterized merely by the property of making a jar known does not constitute *śakti*, an error regarding it is useless [for establishing the meaning]. [The term] "defective" (*viguṇeṣu*) refers to those words that lack proficiency in the rules of correct derivation (*vyutpatti*).

"Among speakers"—that is, among those who speak. "Confused"—meaning altered, that is to say, corrupted into *apabhraṃśa*. Regarding the phrase "but for those who perceive [words] as non-eternal": the sense is that according to the view that "words are produced," the capacity to convey meaning is understood through the scriptures alone; thus, since there is no means of apprehending it within the scriptures regarding *apabhraṃśas*, the delusion arises that only correct (*sādhu*) words are expressive, and not the corrupt ones.

Since the status of being a denoter (*vācakatva*) is not restricted by differences among individuals, it is incorrect to say that "those [words] are correct but non-denoters"; therefore, he says: "non-denoter" means "non-cognizer. Now, one might object: "Power (*śakti*) is simply the desire whose qualifier is the state of being the object of a cognition produced by that word; likewise, there is the desire whose qualifier is the state of being the generator of a cognition of that meaning. The former consists of the word and not the meaning, while the latter consists of the meaning and not the word. Thus, in the case of words such as *gagarya*, the latter [desire] exists through a relation of a distinct objective determination (*viṣayatā*)."

Anticipating the objection that such an error is indeed possible, he says "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). "In all cases as one" (*sarvatraikatvena*) means "in a uniform manner throughout the regions suitable for the movement of Mahārāṣṭra speakers"; by this, there is no deficiency even if [the word] is absent in Yavana and other lands, because the Sanskrit word is likewise absent there. "As in the case of synonyms" (*paryāyeṣviveti*).

The meaning is as follows: just as various word-final forms (*niṣṭhā*) and various sequences (*anupūrvī*) are accepted as delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) according to their respective capacities, so too should those [forms] ending in corrupt words (*apabhraṃśa*) be accepted as delimiters of expressive power, since there is no distinction between them. This applies only to correct words (*sādhu*), not to every denotative item (*vācaka*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Bhāṣya*: "When the comprehension of meaning is equal [whether] by means of words and corrupt forms (*apaśabda*), there is a restriction of merit (*dharma*) by means of the *śāstra*. In that context, "equality" consists in not being preceded by the recollection of another word; otherwise, the inclusion of that [qualification] would be purposeless as it would lack the power of exclusion (*avyāvartaka*).

Furthermore, the causal efficacy of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) is naturally perceived to be exactly the same as that of corrupt forms, and not mediated [by something else]; this would be subverted if one were to admit that the corrupt form is non-expressive (*avācaka*).

Nor does this contradict the discussion regarding Āryas and Mlecchas; for in that context, it was established that while Āryas employ the word *pīlu* for a specific tree and understand it as such, and non-Āryan Mlecchas employ that same word for an elephant and perceive it as such—likewise, the word *yava* refers to long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*) and its opposite, *kaṅgu* (millet)—nevertheless, because the usage of the Āryas is more authoritative, the conclusion was reached that the word *pīlu* has its denotative power (*śakti*) only in the tree and not in the elephant, and the word *yava* only in long-awned barley and not in *kaṅgu*. Thus, [your position] would contradict that.

It must be stated that because the consensus of the Āryas is more authoritative, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that in the Veda the word *yava* refers exclusively to the long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*) and not to the millet (*priyaṅgu*), even though the latter sense exists—must be maintained. Just as words such as *śavati* have restricted domains according to the Mahābhāṣya and the Nirukta (e.g., "The root *śavati*, meaning 'to go', is used only among the Kambojas; the Āryas use it only in the sense of 'decay'"), it is appropriate to assume that the word *yava* in the Veda has precisely that [restricted] referent. Thus, the [independent] denotative power (*śakti*)...

Furthermore, it remains awake in both cases, because there is no evidence for an intention [to convey] either a meaning well-known among the non-Aryans, or incapacity, or incorrectness. Jaimini also formulated a sūtra: "In those cases, since no contradiction is observed, the conflict should be equal. The meaning of this is that, because the word *yava* conveys two meanings, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Because for those who abide by the scripture, that [scripture] is the cause [of determination]."

"Of those established in the scriptures"—that is, of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) who are proficient in the scriptures; "in the meaning of words," the remainder being "in the Veda. Their "uninterrupted tradition" (*smṛti*) is their memory; the meaning is that regarding words and Vedas, those learned ones are the authority for the preservation of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Precisely because corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) possess denotative power, the example from the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, "māedharova araṇam" (*mātar eva araṇyam*), which illustrates how a denotator can also function as a suggestor (*vyañjaka*), is easily reconciled with the authors of that work. Enough of this elaboration. [End of section] on the production of merit.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ": "A single word, correctly understood, well-employed, and consistent with the scriptures, becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadhuk) in the heavenly world. The ancients maintain that this is Śruti; others hold it to be Smṛti. [The phrase] "giving rise to sin" [is used].

The prohibition "one should not speak barbarously" (*na mlecchitavai*) is intended to convey that the employment of improper words produces demerit; the sense is that through a prohibition, one is made to understand the undesirable nature of the prohibited act. Furthermore, it is clear from the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Bhāṣya* and other sources that this prohibition applies specifically to ritual acts (*yājña-karma*), as was already established previously in the discussion on the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*). Regarding the phrase "producing merit": the meaning is that the capacity to produce merit consists in its being essentially fit for such production; the same applies in the subsequent cases. In the expression "in the lexicons, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used to include the speech of authoritative persons and so forth.

In the phrase "grammar and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including analogy (*upamāna*). Lexicons (*kośa*) and the like are mentioned first because they directly convey the expressive power (*śakti*) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and because the apprehension of that power generally occurs through lexicons and such sources. Regarding the statement "there is no fruit for a Brāhmaṇa": in the sentence "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," since the word "king" (*rājan*) denotes a Kṣatriya by its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), a Brāhmaṇa lacks the qualification for it; therefore, the meaning is that when [the sacrifice] is performed by him, there is no production of the result. Regarding the statement "there is no correctness (*sādhutva*) in [using it for] horses and so forth."

"Because correctness (*sādhutva*) is based on a specific meaning. "It is concluded" means that Apabhraṃśa words are not correct because they are not derived (*vyutpanna*) for that [Sanskrit] meaning; this is the intended sense. "Of the secondary (*gauṇa*) [words]" means, for example, in cases such as "The boy is a lion," words like *siṃha* (lion) have come into use—i.e., are applied—to a person due to their association with qualities such as cruelty; [this is indicated by the suffix] *aṇ* in the sense of "come to that" (*tatra āgataḥ*). "In the quality" refers to a property such as "cowness" (*gotva*).

"By way of that" means by way of those respective attributes (*dharmas*), that is to say, by the superimposition (*āropa*) of the attribute that serves as the delimitor of possibility (*śakyatāvacchedaka-dharma*). The cause for this superimposition, however, is the connection with qualities such as cruelty; the sense is that in cases such as "The boy is a lion," the boy and so forth appear in the form of "lion-ness" (*siṃhatva*) and so on. This is likewise the case in "The hamlet is on the Ganges" and similar instances. And this is clear in the *Kāvyapradīpodyota*.

However, this [explanation] does not hold in the view of those who accept the cognition in the form "the boy is cruel" (*krūraḥ māṇavakaḥ*), because words such as "lion" (*siṃha*) do not directly denote cruelty (*kraurya*). If one attempts to reconcile the present text by taking it to refer to quality-denoting words like "white" (*śukla*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include examples such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*). The term "modern" (*ādhunika*) means those indicative words (*lākṣaṇika*) whose intention is to convey a meaning through a form distinct from the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). [The phrase] "even by indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is ungrammatical" (*asādhu*)...

For this very reason, the grammatical prescription of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others in relation to *karman* (object) and so forth is purposeful; this has been explained at length elsewhere. Even though corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), they do not receive the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem), because grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) also serves as the delimiting condition for the object of the rule. For this same reason, the author of the Vārttika stated: "The relationship between word and meaning being established, and the use of words being prompted by worldly usage, the treatise [grammar] effects a restriction regarding merit (*dharma*)," and it is likewise stated in the Bhāṣya: "In this treatise, which is an instruction on correct forms (*sādhvanuśāsana*)."

Thus, one should not raise the objection: "Since the knowledge of grammatical correctness (*sādhutvajñāna*) is the cause of verbal cognition, or since the certainty of incorrectness (*asādhutvaniścaya*) is its inhibitor, how can there be cognition for those who possess the apprehension of correctness from such [words]? This is because verbal experience occurs even for those who lack the knowledge of correctness and who possess the certainty of incorrectness; for the knowledge of correctness is the cause, and the certainty of incorrectness is not an inhibitor. Having this in mind, he says: "In detail" (*vistareṇa*). || 38 ||

Regarding the term *atirikta* (additional): the meaning is "additional to a particular desire" (*icchāviśeṣa*). Furthermore, that [relation] may consist in the nature of being a generator of cognition (*bodhajanakatā*), or it may be a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). Regarding the phrase "the relation is the object": it means the object of the comprehension produced by that [relation]. Thus, in the expression "the relation in the word 'relation'," the meaning is "the relation denoted by the word 'relation'"; in this same way, the meaning of "fitness" (*yogyatā*) and so forth should be understood. He states the utility of demonstrating the meanings of the words "relation" and "fitness" for the present context with the passage beginning "the word 'jar'" (*ghaṭapada*) and so on.

In this context, "suitable" (yogya) means suitable for the object that is the form of the jar; that is to say, capable of generating a cognition having that as its object. "Related to this" (etatsambandhin) means related to the jar; "that" refers to the capacity (śakti). Thus, the initial apprehension of capacity arises from the aforementioned linguistic usage, and therein the apprehension of the word's capacity for the relation and so forth is required; therefore, the demonstration of that meaning has been made. In this regard, the example is "mother."

In the reading "yogyavat," it means that [the relationship] is appropriate for the mother and so forth—being non-distinct because it is correlative to them—and that it is exactly as it is apprehended from worldly usage; however, the reading "yogavat" is indeed correct.

Others, however, maintain that in the case of a word whose meaning is a relation (*sambandha*), the relation itself—characterized as identity (*tādātmya*) with respect to fitness (*yogyatā*), which consists in the property delimiting the capacity to produce a cognition—is what constitutes fitness. And this fitness is innate; it is ascertained from the convention of God (*īśvara-samaya*) as apprehended through the conventional usage of elders such as ourselves—a usage which is synonymous with an beginningless succession. This is just as the relation between mother and son, characterized by the state of progenitor and progeny, is ascertained from conventional usage.

The meaning is "so it is," but they say that fitness (*yogyatā*) is not merely the state of being a producer, because there is the conventional usage: "this is fit for the production of this. In this interpretation, the term *saṃbandha* (relation) in the phrase "the word for relation" (*saṃbandha-śabda*) should be understood as follows: it is derived from the root *bandh* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), thus meaning "that which is related"; the meaning is that words such as "pot" are related to their respective objects. The construction of the verse should be understood as: "the word for relation is related to fitness; [therefore], fitness [is established]."

Alternatively, the meaning of the word "relation" (*saṃbandha*) in the phrase "this word is related to this meaning" is as follows: thus, the word *saṃbandha* is formed with the abstract suffix *ghañ*; its meaning is "the object of fitness," that is, fitness itself. This is the general direction of the argument.
Thus ends the determination of power (śakti). 6.

By the statement "the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is what is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*)," the intended meaning is that only the meaning of the negative particle itself is being demonstrated, and not the meaning of the compound as a whole; this is expressed by the phrase "he states the meaning of the negative particle. Here, the connection [of this discussion] should be understood as one of incidental relevance (*prasaṅga-saṃgati*). He states the meaning of the word *apara*: "of the meaning of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadārthasya*). "Precisely for this reason"—that is, precisely because of the requirement that the meaning of the subsequent member be predominant. Regarding "the state of being superimposed": the meaning is that the state of being superimposed—such as being a Brahmin—is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words like "Brahmin," and it is this that is indicated by the negative particle within the word *abrāhmaṇa*.

Otherwise—that is, in the absence of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*)—it would be as in the case of *atisarva*. Just as in the sense of "one who has surpassed all" (*sarvam atikrāntaḥ*), when a compound is formed by the rule "prefixes such as *ati* [are compounded] with a word in the second case in the sense of having surpassed, etc.," the word *sarva* lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) because it is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) and thus not included among the words beginning with *sarva*, so too here, if the negative particle (*nañ*) were to signify difference, then in the sense of "different from all" (*sarvabhinna*), forms such as *asarva* would not exist; and consequently, there would be no justification for usages such as *asarve* and *asarvasmai*.

[The objection: "But surely, under the view that [the negative particle] has the meaning of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), if that [non-existence] functions as a qualifier of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) by means of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*), then the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound] would be established. Anticipating this, he says: "In cases such as 'there is no jar' (*ghaṭo nāsti*)," etc. "Of that" refers to the non-existence (*abhāva*). "Only as the qualificandum" (*viśeṣyatāyā eva*) means: because the cognition whose form is "the non-existence of the jar is the locus of existence," or "the absence of existence having the jar as its agent," is established by experience.

Anticipating the objection that "in this case, the universal experience of understanding 'non-pot' (aghaṭa) as 'distinct from a pot' cannot be denied," he says: "And according to our view. The point is that since the superimposition of "pot-ness" upon what is actually distinct from a pot occurs, the cognition "distinct from that [pot]" is established by the very nature of the thing; thus, there is no denial of it. The intention is that while the perception of it being "verbal" arises because it is prompted by words, that perception is merely an error.

Regarding the phrase "being the object of superimposition" (*āropaviṣayatva*): its connection is with the meaning of the subsequent word, such as "Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the superimposition is understood as having precisely the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as its qualifier. Thus, from the word "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the cognition arises that "the Brāhmaṇa is the object of superimposition. And in the case of the co-occurrence with the negative particle (*nañ*), it is only a Kṣatriya or similar person who is denoted by the word "non-Brāhmaṇa"; [in this case], Brāhmaṇahood and so forth are cognized through the relation of superimposition, where the relation is inherence (*samavāya*).

Thus, the cognition having the form "this is a Brāhmaṇa" as its object of superimposition (āropa) is not untenable; for it is indeed possible for some person to have such a superimposition even at that time, so there is no inconsistency. This is clear from the very commentary on this Sūtra in the passage beginning with "due to doubt or from faulty instruction. Alternatively, the meaning of "being the object of superimposition" is "having the cause of activity (pravṛtti-nimitta) residing in the object of superimposition"; thus, there is no harm even if the superimposition exists at a later time, since the superimposed state of being simultaneous (tatkālitva) is not required as a factor.

The manifestation of the object of superimposition (*āropa*) as both a qualifier (*prakāra*) and a relation (*sambandha*)—just like the manifestation of ownership (*svatva*) and other meanings of the genitive case in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*)—is not contradictory. From expressions such as "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), there arises the cognition "one who possesses superimposed Brāhmaṇahood. Since the state of possessing Brāhmaṇahood qualified by being superimposed exists only in one who is different from a Brāhmaṇa, the word "non-Brāhmaṇa" is not applied to an actual Brāhmaṇa. He states the concise meaning: "the meaning is merely superimposition" (*āropamātram arthaḥ*).

The meaning expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*) is either indicated or denoted; and that [meaning] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the object following it through the relation of being its object (*viṣayatva*). Thus he says, "but the relation is objecthood" (*viṣayatvaṃ tu saṃsargaḥ*). And so, the intention is that in this view there is concision (*lāghava*) compared to the previous position, as this is the final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*) within this alternative.

However, the view accepted by the *Bhāṣya* is the very first alternative stated with "Or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth; and that first [alternative] is correct, while the last is not. For even if superimposition (*āropa*) were denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*), there would be the abandonment of the primary meaning of words such as "Brāhmaṇa," which would result in the contingency of the relationship between word and meaning being non-eternal. In the middle alternative, however, there is no fault, because just as one who possesses Brāhmaṇahood through a primary relationship is the referent of that term, so too is one who possesses it through a superimposed relationship; the negative particle (*nañ*) merely serves to determine the intention toward the latter meaning. This indeed is what is called the "indicative function" (*dyotakatva*) of the negative particle.

It is for this very reason that the linguistic convention of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) is applied here, and the meaningfulness of the compound is also established, because the specific sequence [of the constituent words] serves as the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) through the inclusion of the indicated meaning within itself; thus they say, as is explained in detail elsewhere.

Others, however, say that in expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the word "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) denotes the object of the superimposition (*āropa*) of being a Brahmin through the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*), while the negative particle (*nañ*) serves to determine the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇāyaka*). Thus, in the case of "This is a non-Brahmin," the cognition is: "This is the object of the superimposition of being a Brahmin. They further state that this very same cognition is expressed by the phrase "a superimposed Brahmin. In this context, the superimposition must be understood as having a qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) that is not distinct from a Brahmin; therefore, even though the status of being an object of a collective superimposition (*samūhālambana-āropa*) exists in a Brahmin in the case of "These two are Brahmins," the term "Brahmin" is not applied [to the individual who is not actually a Brahmin].

[Objection: "But surely there is no harm even if we accept that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses a meaning already stated; for since 'superimposedness'—in the form of being the object of superimposition, or the state of being superimposed, or the superimposition itself—can function as a qualifier of the subsequent word-meaning through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-saṃsarga*), the desired predominance of the subsequent word-meaning is established. To this, [the author] says: "The mention of its being indicated" (*dyotyatvokti*). The point is that such a statement is made in accordance with the established doctrine that particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*); it does not mean that there is any flaw in accepting expressiveness (*vācakatva*) in the present context.

In fact, they argue that since the fault has already been stated regarding the view that [the word] denotes the expressed meaning (*uktārthavācakatvapakṣa*), it is more appropriate to hold that it merely indicates the previously mentioned meaning (*prāguktārthadyotakatva*). Otherwise, after the verbal cognition "one who possesses superimposed Brahminhood" (*āropitabrāhmaṇatvavān*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of a further cognition: "he is a Kṣatriya, distinct from a Brāhmaṇa. Similarly, following the verbal cognition from the sentence "there is no jar on the ground"—namely, "existence (sattā) residing in the locus of the ground, having as its agent a jar that is superimposed"—there occurs a mental cognition of the absence of such existence. Therefore...

The cognition of existence (*sattā*) having the jar as its agent and the ground as its locus is obstructed. It is not a rule that only a preceding non-cognition of absence acts as an obstacle to the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); rather, it does so even by coexisting with its effect. Therefore, at the time of the arising of the cognition of absence, there is no arising of the cognition of the counter-positive. Even in cases such as "there is no color in the air" (*vāyau rūpaṃ nāsti*) or "the conch is not yellow" (*śaṅkhaḥ pīto nāsti*), what is superimposed (*āropita*) is the existence having the air as its locus and color as its agent, and the existence having the yellow conch as its agent.

The cognition [arising from the sentence] is as follows: the well-known excellence is indeed brought about by mental imposition (*āhārya*). It culminates in the superimposition (*āropa*) of the locus of air upon the existence whose agent is form, and the superimposition of the agenthood of the conch-shell upon the existence whose agent is yellow. It should be understood that the description of the cognition as "an existence of such a kind that is superimposed" is intended on the basis that the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the action (*kriyā*) itself, which is the primary element. || 40 ||

"Due to the intention regarding that" means: due to the intention (*tātparya*) regarding that—namely, when non-existence (*abhāva*) is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). "In a general manner" means: even though non-existence is what is expressed by *nañ*, its status as either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is postulated in accordance with the respective cognitions [of it]. Alternatively, even for the meaning indicated (*dyotya*), its status as a qualificand arises from that very same [intention]; or else, in the view where *nañ* is expressive (*vācaka*), it is the qualificand, while in the view where it is indicative (*dyotya*), it is the qualifier. Therefore, one should understand that this does not violate the rule established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *hetumati ca*, which states that meanings indicated by particles are invariably qualifiers.

He states the meaning of the word *nivṛtta* (exclusion) with the phrase "having non-existence as its meaning. Regarding the term *adhyāropita* (superimposed): the meaning is "those in whom Brahminhood has been superimposed. Regarding the phrase "because it is the expressed meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*"): the point is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and common worldly usage, the expressed meaning of *nañ* is simply non-existence; however, in cases such as "Devadatta is a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇo devadattaḥ*), the compatibility (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) experienced through Devadatta and so forth is understood to be established by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) upon the substratum.
"Otherwise"—that is, even if the experience [of compatibility] could be explained otherwise, if one were to maintain that what is expressed by *nañ* is one who possesses superimposed Brahminhood.

"Also because of similarity and so forth" means that since similarity and the like are also perceived in expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), they would consequently have to be considered denotable meanings (*vācya*). Regarding "sinless" (*apāpa*): here the cognition is of the absolute absence of sin. From "horseless" (*anaśva*), the cognition is of "other than a horse. The distinction in the case of "non-Brahmin" is that there is a cognition of otherness as a constituent of the similarity [with a non-Brahmin], rather than a cognition of mere otherness; this is because, according to the view that similarity is a distinct category of meaning (*padārthāntara*), difference (*bheda*) does not exist therein.

In the expression "anudarā kanyā" (the girl with no belly), the understanding is "a girl with a small belly. In "apaśavo vā" (or, they are non-animals), the understanding is "animals that are not praiseworthy. In "adharma" (non-dharma), what is cognized is a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) opposed to dharma, and not merely its simple negation. Regarding the "implied meaning" (*ārthika-artha*): after the verbal cognition such as "an imposed Brāhmaṇa," there occurs a mental cognition of similarity and so forth. In cases like "anudarā," because of the proximity of the negative particle (*nañ*), there is an imposition of the absence of a belly caused by factors such as smallness; through this imposed cognition of a belly, the final rest (*viśrānti*) lies in the smallness and so forth rooted therein. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well.

Desiring to dispel the objection that—since the absence which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be a qualifier distinct from its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there would result by implication the impossibility of compounds such as *abrāhmaṇa* (non-Brahmin), and furthermore, the impossibility of the cognition of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) regarding Brahmins and the like—he says "pratīti" (cognition).

The difference (*bheda*) is a qualifier by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*) as delimited by "Brahmin-ness" (*brāhmaṇatva*) and so forth; however, if its status as a cognitive mode (*prakāratva*) is experienced, its inclusion [within the qualificandum] must be admitted. Even though the mere counter-correlativity of difference is present in the case of a bare negative (*kevalānvayin*), such counter-correlativity of difference does not possess that same status [as a qualifier]. Thus, in the verbal cognition "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), where the Brahmin is the counter-correlative of the difference, the cognition of the difference having the Brahmin as its counter-correlative is implied (*ārthika*). This is also the case in "the cloth is non-pot" (*aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ*).

The understanding is that "the jar is the counter-correlative of the difference from the function of cloth. Since *nañ* is a particle (*nipāta*), its meaning—the absence—is not incompatible with the co-referential connection (*anvaya*) of the name-meaning "cloth" through the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatva*). When one says, "Bring the non-jar," the bringing of a jar does not occur; this is due to the force of employing *nañ*, because it is only after the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has arisen that the possibility of such an action is perceived in that which possesses the difference having the jar as its counter-correlative. This is the intended sense. As for cases such as "Devadatta is a non-Brahmin," [this is explained] either by the very point just made or by a lack of satisfaction [with that explanation].

It should be understood that "or the qualified [substantive]" (*viśeṣya*) refers to the adoption of an alternative position. He states the purpose of the position in which the meaning of the final member is predominant (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*) with the word "aneka" (more than one). This alone is the primary purpose of the position that the compound is *uttarapadārthapradhāna*. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "Furthermore, this [rule] also includes the predominance of the meaning of the final member; what is it? 'Aneka'. What is included here? The singular number (*ekavacana*). This refers to the restriction regarding the singular number.

The intention is that since a single entity divided [into parts] is manifold, there would only be dual and plural endings, and not the singular; thus, with the view that the rule *dvayekayoḥ* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), the word "restriction" (*niyama*) was stated. Now, one might object: the meaning should not be understood as "the singular ending is restricted by the word," because if that were so, it would imply that in other cases there is no such restriction, which is not tenable, since the singular ending would remain unestablished in cases where the prior member of the compound is predominant (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānya*) or where another member is predominant (*anyapadārthaprādhānya*).

Regarding the phrase "the status of being a *tatpuruṣa*": the sense is that, when possible, even the predominance of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*)—though it is merely common—is appropriate for a *tatpuruṣa*. He states "otherwise" because if the predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) were accepted, the established distinction of [the cases of] *puruṣa* and so forth would not be tenable. The phrase "just as... [is used].

Just as in the case of "your absence" (*tvadabhāvaḥ*) or "my absence" (*madabhāvaḥ*), because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the second-person pronoun *yuṣmad* or the first-person pronoun *asmad*, neither the second-person nor the first-person personal endings occur; rather, only the singular form of the third person occurs. Similarly, in the cases "you do not become" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*) and "I do not become" (*anahaṃ bhavāmi*), if it were admitted that the referent of *yuṣmad* and so forth functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), then dual and plural forms such as "you two do not become" (*ayuvāṃ bhavathaḥ*) and "you [all] do not become" (*ayūyaṃ bhavatha*) would also not occur, because the absence of the agent (*kartṛ-abhāva*) is a single entity. This is the meaning.

He establishes the systematic arrangement of *puruṣa* (person) and so forth according to his own view with the words "In our view... (*asmanmate ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). "Coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means coreferentiality with [words such as] *yuṣmad* (you) and so forth. Coreferentiality is simply the denotation of the number residing in the referent of *yuṣmad* and so forth; and it is argued that this is possible even under the view that the meaning of the preceding word is predominant (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānyapakṣa*). However, this is not correct, because the term "coreferentiality" lacks the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) to convey the aforementioned meaning, and furthermore, because the distribution of the [grammatical] numbers (*vacana*) remains unaccounted for even in that case.

"Regarding the phrase *pratiyoginīti*: thus, from the expression 'a non-Brāhmaṇa is a Kṣatriya,' the cognition arises that 'a Kṣatriya is distinct from a Brāhmaṇa. Now, one might object that in this case, [the application of] *idam* (this) and so forth would be unestablished; anticipating this doubt, he says: 'The point is as follows. Even in the case of being secondary (*gauṇatve*)—that is, even in the state of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatve*).”

One might object: "Even if [the word] is subordinate (*upasarjana*), the rule 'not in a compound with a negative particle' (*anañ-samāse*) is purposeful so that the elision (*lopa*) of *su* does not undesirably apply in cases such as *aneṣo dadāti* (he gives these) or *asaḥ śivaḥ* (that Śiva), because the word *tat* is present there. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that this rule is redundant because *su* is prescribed for elision only when it expresses the number belonging to the meaning of *tat*, whereas in a compound where the prior member is predominant, such an expression of number by *su* is impossible. This objection is invalid, because there is no evidence that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has such a relation as its meaning; rather, one must supply the immediately preceding word [from the context].

Having established this, since it is appropriate that the meaning of the rule be "the elision of *su* immediately following *etat* and *tad*," and because it has been explained as such elsewhere, he says "of those not having *ak*" (*akor*). The point is that by means of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) of those accompanied by *ak*, it is appropriate to understand those two [pronouns] only as being *sarvanāman* (distributive/possessive) when they are eligible for *akac*; for, just like association, dissociation is also established as a cause for the cognition of a specific quality, as in examples such as "Hari without the conch and discus" (*aśaṅkhacakro hariḥ*).

And likewise: when, according to the stated method, only those two pronouns (*sarvanāman*) are taken [as the basis for the rule], this is merely an illustration; it should also be understood that even if only the words *etad* and *tad* were taken, the rule would be redundant because in compounds such as *atitad*, the elision of the final vowel by Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*) would be unavoidable due to the absence of the status of being a pronoun (*atva*) in the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Regarding the term "indicative" (*jñāpaka*): the meaning is that it serves as an indicator for the application of grammatical operations triggered by the predominance of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*), even when there is predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*). The implication is that by this, the establishment of person (*puruṣa*) and voice (*vacana*) is also accomplished.

"Because of conformity with the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). The meaning is as follows: it is only when the qualified object has a different number that the suffix *suP* expresses the number residing in the principal member of the compound; however, when such a qualified object is present, a multi-word compound may end in the dual or plural case endings.

If it is objected that, by this same logic, in the case of *a-varṣā hemantaḥ* ("the winter season without rain"), there would also follow the use of the singular number in accordance with the gender and number of the qualified object (*hemanta*), we say no. For the *Mahābhāṣya* itself provides the solution: "The gender and number of quality-words depend upon their substratum" (*guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni*). In that context, since the substratum in the form of the qualified object is the correlate (*pratiyogin*), the correlate itself is understood as the substratum. Thus, it is accepted that in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the gender and number sometimes belong to the subordinate member (*anuyogin*) and sometimes to the correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, there is no fault.

This is because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Now, one might object: "Just as when *pratyayaḥ* is carried over in rules such as *tavyat-tavya-anīyar*, there is a change in number (from singular to masculine), and just as when *dhātoḥ* is carried over in rules such as *nandi-grahi-pacādibhyaḥ*, there is likewise a change in number; let that same [change] apply here to the word *subantam* as well. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). Regarding the phrase "of many": the construction is "the *bahuvrīhi* compound of many would not be established. Or, it is the general rule (*autsargika*).

The intention is that the singular number [is used] according to the rule *ekavacanaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.22), which prescribes the singular when there is no desire to express oneness, duality, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the second member" (*uttarapadārtha*): the point is that one need not maintain the predominance of the meaning of the second member in accordance with the usage *sevyate 'nekayā* ("she is served by many"), because the use of the singular ending can be accounted for otherwise. "For this very reason" means precisely because of the predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārtha*). "Easy to establish" (*sūpapāda*) refers to this.

The suffix *khal* is applied after the causative form of the root *pad* (*padi*) in the sense of "capable of being produced easily" (in the object). However, if the meaning of the subsequent member were predominant, the use of the plural ending for the word *aneka* would be untenable. One might argue that this is possible through *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), as in the sense "many chariots, horses, and elephants. But this is not so; since the single word *aneka* can convey the entire meaning, there is no occurrence of *ekaśeṣa* involving two words, *aneka* and *aneka*. Consequently, the separate application of different case-endings and other words such as *ratha* and *aśva* occurs.

The point is that since the application of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is unnecessary—because the connection [of the pronoun] with multiple words is possible through the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of a single word—and because even when they are indicated by a *dvandva* compound, the connection is possible for only one [pronoun] within the collective whole.

Now, an objection is raised: "In the rule *etattadoḥ*, the mention of *anañ* (not preceded by a negative particle) has already been stated as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) applies even when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant. Thus, although forms such as *asaḥ* are established, the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) remains untenable in cases like *atvaṃ bhavasi*. He dispels this doubt with the phrase "in cases such as *atvaṃ bhavasi*," and explains: "And thus, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*)."

By means of the distinct referent of *yuṣmad*—that is, by the meaning of the word *yuṣmad* which is distinct from "you"—the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) for the word *yuṣmad* is established even without the technical rule (*lakṣaṇa*), because the inclusion of the negative particle (*nañ*) serves as an indicator of the grammatical operation triggered by the non-predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member, even when there is no non-predominance of the meaning of the prior member. Therefore, according to others, there is no violation of the rule that the meaning indicated [by a particle] must function solely as a qualifier. Regarding the phrase "the absence of the productive urge" (*bhāvanābhāva*), the word "of this" (*asya*) connects to the phrase "understanding in this manner" (*iti rītyā bodha*).

Now, one might object: "By accepting that there is an understanding of the non-existence of an action qualified by all its causal factors (*kāraka*), it would follow that [the cognition 'the ground is without a jar'] could neither be sublated nor be a sublator with respect to the cognition 'the ground has a jar. This is because, even when the form of the cognition is the apprehension of such a superimposed existence, the former [cognition] does not have the absence of the jar as its object, and the latter does not have mere absence as its object. If this is argued, we reply: this defect persists even if one accepts the cognition "the jar possesses the absence of subsistence on the ground. Alternatively, [we maintain the position] on the strength of experience.

If the state of being sublated and the state of being a sublator are admitted for the cognition [of absence] as stated above, then those two must likewise be admitted for the two cognitions stated above. If it is argued that the sublation and so forth of the aforementioned cognitions are accounted for by accepting a mental cognition of the absence of a jar based on the locus of the ground immediately after the cognition of the absence of occurrence in the ground, then that very path is adopted; enough with excessive detail. [The phrase] "only in the case of action" [is used].

The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is also an indication for "quality" (*guṇa*); for this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Nañ-sūtra*: "Having first applied [the negation] to both action and quality, it subsequently effects their cessation. The meaning of this is that after having enjoined (*prasajya*), there is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of that [enjoined element]. By this, even in the cognition of the absence of a quality, it is understood as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). An example of a quality, however, is: *na na ekaṃ priyam*. Here, *naḥ* is the genitive plural ending.

For here, by the negation of one beloved, the perception of many beloveds arises. And in such instances as "no doubt," the absolute absence of doubt is perceived, because doubt is [here treated as] a quality (*guṇa*). In the previous example, singularity is a quality in the form of number; its negation consists in the sense "there is not even one beloved for us," and thus it results in the negation of the number one.

This has been stated by Kaiyaṭa: "In this case, precisely by the force of the single negation (*ekapratiṣedha*), there is the cognition of an object endowed with a different number. Nor should it be argued that because of the ellipsis of the verb *asti*, the existence of a single substratum as the agent is what is negated, and thus this is merely an example of a verbal action (*kriyā*); for the intention is that, according to the authority of the aforementioned Bhāṣya, it is the quality (*guṇa*) alone that is experienced as being negated therein. In this view, even in the definition of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—"where the negative particle is connected with an action"—the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a quality.

This is what must be understood. However, according to the *Bhāṣya*, the inclusion of the term "negation" (*anañ*) [in the rule] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the predominance of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*), because it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*). Thus, the very explanation stated by Kaiyaṭa in his *Bhāṣya* commentary—that [the compound] has its own word-meaning withdrawn (*nivṛttapadārthaka*)—is indeed correct. In that case, under the view of the predominance of the second member, if the absence of the second member's meaning were to be conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*), then the predominance of the second member would be destroyed; therefore, it must be accepted that the negative particle there is meaningless (*anarthaka*). Furthermore, properties such as being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of an absence do not serve to distinguish [the meaning], and thus are not [intended].

With the intention that [the term] can function as a qualifier, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), the apprehension that the bringing of any Brahmin whatsoever would follow is removed by the statement beginning with "This is not a fault" (*naiṣa doṣaḥ*). Just as in the case of "Bring the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), where a man qualified by the king is understood, so too here, a Brahmin qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is meant, and not a Brahmin alone; thus it is said, "The bringing of one qualified by the *nañ* will take place. Thereupon, [the question is asked]: "But what is this [person] whose substance has ceased? (*kaḥ punarasau nivṛttapadārthakaḥ*)?

This is because the commentary (bhāṣya) adopts the expression "that in which the category of being a Brāhmaṇa has ceased," and because the subsequent passage of the commentary also establishes that the very meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa*—as indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense that a Kṣatriya or other caste member who possesses superimposed Brāhmaṇahood is an *abrāhmaṇa*—is precisely this. Furthermore, under the view that the meaning of the prior member of the compound is predominant (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānyapakṣa*), if the meaning were "one who is different from those [Brāhmaṇas]," the dual ending would be inappropriate in the form *itau* (as in *itau abrāhmaṇau*); likewise, if the meaning were "those who are different from them," the plural ending would be inappropriate in the form *te santi* (as in *te abrāhmaṇāḥ*).

Furthermore, under the view stated in the Bhāṣya that the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*) is predominant, there would be the undesirable consequence of a singular number; yet this cannot be accepted as an intended consequence, because it is improper to accept such a consequence when it results in a difference between the outcomes of the two positions. This is because, just as the singular number in the word "anekam" [is explained by the predominance of the subsequent member], it has already been largely established that in the present case, the dual number and so forth likewise result from the predominance of the subsequent member; therefore, it is incorrect to resort to a non-distinct substratum based on the cited usage.

Although, by the rule *etattadoḥ*, even when there is predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha-prādhānya*), the forms *itau* and so forth are established through the extension of grammatical operations conditioned by the predominance of the subsequent member (*uttaraprādhānya*)—thereby accounting for the dual number and so on in *dvivacanādiḥ* and the singular number in *anekam*—nevertheless, the sense is that the assumption of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*) is superior due to its simplicity (*lāghava*) compared to the postulation of such an extension (*atideśa*).

Regarding the term "aneka," the use of the singular number is not established; however, it is not correct to argue that the singular is used merely to conform to the gender and number of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), as there is no grammatical rule stating that the number must conform to the qualified object even when a different number exists within the word itself. Nor can this be resolved by the rule *aśrayato liṅga-vacane* (gender and number are determined by the substratum), as is the case in the expression *avarṣā hemantaḥ*.

Because here the substratum (*āśraya*) in the form of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is grasped, and because the cognition of the counter-correlate is relied upon for the sake of the cognition of the absence (*abhāva*); for this very reason, as in the case of the view that the other member of the compound is predominant (*anya-padārtha-prādhānya-pakṣa*), the defect consisting in the occurrence of the gender and number belonging to the substratum in the form of *hemanta*—as in the example *avarṣā hemantaḥ*—is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya under the view that the preceding member is predominant (*pūrva-padārtha-prādhānya-pakṣa*). This is because it is accepted that "just as qualities (*guṇa*) take on the gender and so forth of their substratum, the meaning of the compound takes on the gender and so forth of that substance (*dravya*) which is resorted to by it as its counter-correlate."

This must be stated: because accepting the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule beginning with "of words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanānām*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because it would result in a discrepancy caused by the difference in the substrata (*āśrayavailakṣaṇya*) between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). This is the general direction of the argument.

By the phrase "anyonyābhāvatva, etc.," the inclusion of *dhvaṃsatva* (the nature of destruction) and *prāgabhāvatva* (the nature of antecedent non-existence) is intended. Now, one might object: "It is more appropriate for the [word's] denotative power (*śakti*) to reside in that which is delimited by *abhāvatva* (the general property of being an absence), as this is parsimonious (*lāghava*), rather than in those delimited by various properties such as *atyantābhāvatva* (the nature of absolute non-existence), because that would involve complexity (*gaurava*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "because there is cognition in those respective forms. This means that cognition in those respective forms is established by experience (*anubhavasiddha*).

At the time of the destruction of the prior absence of a jar, by the cognition "there is no jar here," both the prior absence of the jar and the destruction of the jar are made objects of awareness as being characterized by the nature of the prior absence of the jar and so forth; however, they are not made objects as being delimited by the nature of absolute non-existence. This is because, according to the school of Prācīna-Tārkikas, there is an incompatibility between prior absence or destruction and absolute non-existence, and thus absolute non-existence of that jar does not exist there at that time. This is the intended meaning.

Modern logicians, however, maintain that the word "not" (nañ) has its denotative power (*śakti*) only with respect to what is delimited by absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), but not with respect to what is delimited by antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, because there is no evidence for such a claim. They argue that at the time of antecedent non-existence and the like, the cognition "the jar does not exist" apprehends only the absolute non-existence of the jar, since there is no evidence for any contradiction between antecedent non-existence and the rest with absolute non-existence.

Is it not the case that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*) is the state of being a permanent absence of relation, while mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) is the state of being an absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by the relation of identity? Thus, since mutual non-existence is simpler than absolute non-existence, it is more appropriate to postulate the primary denotative power (*śakti*) as residing in that which is delimited by mutual non-existence, rather than in that which is delimited by absolute non-existence.

If it is argued that, because the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)—defined as being an absence possessing a counter-positive whose origination is empty of origination—and the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—defined as being an absence possessing a counter-positive whose origination is not empty of origination—are more complex than mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), it is improper to postulate a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for those [terms] as delimited by such natures; we say no. For the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*) and so forth is simply a specific kind of "locus-ness" (*anuyogitā*) witnessed by cognitions such as "it does not exist," and not the aforementioned form. If it were otherwise, since the nature of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) would be difficult to define, the nature of absolute non-existence—which is constituted by it—would likewise become indefinable. To explain:

First of all, relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*) cannot be defined as that which is the object of a cognition produced by the superimposition (*āropa*) of a relation; for since the superimposition of the counter-positive's relation is a cause only for the ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) of absence, this definition would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to absences that are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Nor can it be defined as an absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by a relation; for even mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) has counter-positivehood delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), and thus the definition would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to it. Nor can one avoid this fault by inserting the qualification "other than identity" into the relation, [as the following shows].

It must be stated that even so, there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the case of the absolute absence of a conjunct (*saṃyogin*), which has a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of conjunction; for that [absolute absence] is not distinct from it, since it consists in the identity (*tādātmya*) with the conjunct, which is of the nature of conjunction. Likewise, the nature of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) is not the state of being an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of identity; for this would fail in the case of the absolute absence of a conjunct whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of conjunction, as well as in the case of the absolute absence of an inherent (*samavāyin*) entity whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

This is the direction regarding the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*); indicating this, he says, "the details are elsewhere," meaning that the full exposition should be seen in the *Dīdhiti* and other such works.
Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

Regarding the phrase "in [expressions] such as *īśvaram anubhavati*": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as *prajayī* are included. The word "etc. in the compound "*anubhavādi*" is intended to include superior victory (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) and other such states. It is not the meaning of the verbal root—that is, it is not that which is expressed by roots such as *bhū* (to be) and the like. He states the reason for this in the words "in the case of *bhavati*. Thus, the meaning is that it is not denoted by those respective verbal roots. He dispels the objection that, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) and the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it should rather be the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) itself, by stating "it is not the meaning of the prefix."

The meaning is that [the meaning of the prefix] is not to be expressed by the prefix itself. Now, one might argue: let it be postulated as a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meanings as related to either the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) or to the meaning of that with which it is uttered in proximity; and there is no such complexity (*gaurava*), because there is no loss of parsimony (*lāghava*) in assuming that the root expresses those respective meanings rather than assuming the prefix to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*). To this, he states another objection: "in cases such as *anugacchati*," and so on, ending with "and because of the consequence of [the prefix becoming] a suffix."

If it is argued that since the prefix *an-* is accepted as denoting "experience" (*anubhava*), it is postulated that the co-occurrence with specific verbal roots acts as the regulator for the cognition of that specific experience through those respective prefixes—then it is more appropriate to postulate that the prefix functions as a *dyotaka* (indicator) while the verbal root itself, already established as denoting meanings such as "existence" (*sattā*) and so on, conveys the cognition of experience and the rest. This being the case, the etymological rule "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*) would not need to be restricted; this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "not a qualified meaning" (*na viśiṣṭārthaḥ*) [is used].

The meaning is that [the action] is not denoted by those respective verbal roots as qualified by prefixes (*upasarga*). "Due to complexity" (*gauravāt*) means that because the qualified entity possesses a dual nature, it would involve the conceptual complexity of postulating a denotative capacity for both [the prefix and the root].

If it is asked, "Why not simply accept that in the word *prajayati*, victory (*jaya*) is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) while excellence (*prakarpa*) is expressed by the prefix (*upasarga*)," listen: because excellence, being the meaning of a noun (*nāma*), cannot logically connect with victory, which is the meaning of the verbal root; for it is unestablished in linguistic usage (*avyutpanna*) that the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root can connect directly through a relation of difference (*bheda*). The point is that if one were to include "being distinct from a prefix" within the definition of a noun, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

[Objection: But how can there be a cognition of experience there without a *vṛtti*? To this he says, "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This means: because, according to the reasoning stated, it is impossible for either the verbal root (*dhātu*) or the prefix (*upasarga*) to denote experience. [He adds: "of that which denotes existence and so forth."

This is a qualification of the verbal root (*dhātu*) that contains the reason [for the following argument]: since the verbal root denotes existence and so forth—as is evident from the cognition of its meaning in expressions such as "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*)—it is precisely the verbal root that can possess *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the form of a relationship with its primary meaning (*śakyasaṃbandha*). The meaning is that because a prefix (*upasarga*) is never used alone and thus does not express any meaning by itself, it cannot possess *lakṣaṇā* in the form of a relationship with a primary meaning. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the traditional doctrine that prefixes are merely "illuminators" (*dyotaka*), he says: "with regard to the intended meaning" (*tātparya*).

Thus, in the case of the word "pratiṣṭhate," the cognition established by experience as being of the nature of "going" must be accounted for solely through the metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of the verbal root (dhātu). It should be understood that if one were to accept a primary denotative power (śakti) in the absence of a prefix (upasarga), then even if the rule of grammatical derivation—"the meaning of a noun [is connected] with the meaning of the verbal root"—were restricted, the resulting cognition would be only in the form of the "absence of the cessation of going," and not as "going" itself.

Others, however, say that since the root *ji* already possesses a capacity for victory (*jaya*), it is the root itself that has the capacity for "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*). The state of being preceded by *pra* (*prottarajitvam*) is the delimiting factor of that capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). This very thing is what is called the "contextual capacity" (*aupasaṃdānikī śakti*) of prefixes. For in this context, the meaning of the term "contextual" (*upasaṃdāna*) consists precisely in the entry [of the prefix] into the delimiting factor of the capacity. They maintain that this is exactly the case in expressions such as *anubhavati*. Regarding the phrase "its own meaning" (*svārthe*): the construction is that since the root *ās* does not denote a result in the form of "worship" (*upāsanā*), the status of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*)—in the form of "its own meaning," etc.—would not otherwise follow.

Nor should it be argued that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) should consist simply in denoting an operation that has a different locus from its result, and that there is no need to include "denoting its own meaning" (*svārthatva*) therein; for even if the prefix (*upasarga*) denotes the operation, the root would still unimpededly denote an operation whose locus is distinct from the result which constitutes that [operation]. This cannot be said, because since the mere property of denoting an operation with a locus distinct from some result leads to over-extension (*atiprasañjaka*), it is necessary to include "denoting its own meaning" within the result. [The reason given is] "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*).

This is an illustration: since a specific [root] is not included in the *bhvādi* class, it would fail to attain the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). If one were to argue that its inclusion in the list should be postulated, even then, the systematic application of rules regarding reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the augment *āṭ* would fail to obtain. As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "In the grammatical treatise, the separate postulation of the root and the prefix is for the sake of establishing the system of augments such as *aṭ*; however, in reality, the root itself is of such a nature."

It should be understood that this same principle applies even in cases such as "idamanubhavati" (he experiences this), where one must assume the denotative power belongs to the qualified [complex]. Anticipating the objection that even if the verbal root lacks transitivity (*sakarmakatva*), the *lakāra* suffix might still arise in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*)—as in "upāsyate"—the author states: "In the case of 'dṛśyate,' the word 'in the objective' (*karmaṇi*) is to be supplied. The point is that if the *lakāra* were in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), the usage "hariharāv upāsyete" (Hari and Hara are both worshipped) would be untenable. || 42 ||

"Denoting that respective meaning" means denoting such meanings as the activity conducive to a perception possessing a worldly object-domain (*laukika-viṣayatā*). If one accepts *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the meaning of "non-denotative-ness" (*avācakatva*) should be understood as "causing cognition" (*bodhakatva*); however, if one posits a primary power (*śakti*), the literal sense alone is correct. In some places, however, the reading is simply "causing cognition. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, by the same logic, if one posits a power here [for the root], then for [the root] *anubhavati*—

It is likewise appropriate to assume that words such as *tyad* (and similar pronouns) possess the capacity to denote experience (*anubhava*) and so forth; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* on the *Paspaśāhnika*: "In cases such as ‘the teacher is worshipped’ (*upāsyate guruḥ*) or ‘happiness is experienced’ (*anubhūyate sukham*), since the suffixes denoting the object (*lakāra*) would be impossible unless the verbal root has the sense of a transitive action, its status as a direct denoter (*vācakatva*) is established. In the expression ‘it is adorned’ (*alaṃkriyate*), the meaning of the verbal root is a specific activity conducive to beauty. Otherwise—if one were to resort to the status of being transitive based on some incidental meaning, even when there is a different intended meaning—it would lead to over-extension.

The phrase "it would also be so here" means that since the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is observed to be transitive in the expression "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), it would follow that it is also transitive in cases such as "the wind undergoes transformation" (*vāyur vikurute*). This is not an acceptable consequence, because if it were, one could not have the impersonal (bhāve) verbal suffix in forms such as "it is transformed by the wind" (*vāyunā vikriyate*) or "it is transformed by the Saindhava horses" (*saindhavair vikriyate*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the mention of the teacher (*guru*) and others as the object (*karman*) of actions such as "direct realization" (*sākṣātkāra*) would not be possible through the verbal suffix (*lākāra*), because direct realization and the like lack the status of being the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); for only that which is the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning possesses the status of being the object. Nor is there even the possibility of [the teacher] being the object of the verb *karoti* (to do), since that is sublated in the case of what is already established (*siddha*) and eternal (*nitya*). The doubt might arise either because the word is identical despite a difference in meaning, or because—despite a difference in words—there is an imposition of non-difference based on the similarity of the words in the form of a transitive verbal root (*sakarmakadhātu*). The answer is that a difference in words follows necessarily from a difference in meaning. This is because it accords with the natural sense of the lexicon (*kośasvarasa*).

Although a dictionary does not establish the denotative power (*śakti*) of a word in contexts such as meditation (*upāsana*), nevertheless, by virtue of the authority of dictionaries such as: "The word *sākṣāt* denotes directness and similarity," "The word *alam* expresses ornamentation, sufficiency, capability, and prohibition," and "The word *vā* may be used in the sense of option, comparison, the meaning of *eva*, and also conjunction"; and because the *Nirukta*, beginning with "Now, the particles (*nipātas*) fall upon various meanings," states that particles possess those very meanings, the sense is that even the word *upāsana* is to be understood as having that [same] meaning.

He dispels the doubt that if the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes merely the operation (*vyāpāra*), it would not be transitive according to the method previously stated, by the words "svasva... (its own...). "Sva" refers to the root, and "that" refers to the particle associated with it; the meaning is that the denotation of an operation distinct from those two [the root and the object] belongs to one or the other of them. Regarding the phrase "by way of example": in both cases, the status of the teacher and others as the object (*karman*) is established even without the particle having a signifying function (*dyotakatā*). [The opponent objects: "This is not a proof."

In the aforementioned instances, the mention of the teacher and others as the direct object (*karmatva*) of realization and so forth by means of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is proof for the fact that the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses a qualified meaning, and it is proof for the fact that the particle (*nipāta*) functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*).
