The phrase "of the connection alone" (*anvayasyaiva*) means "of the connection alone through the relation of favorability" (*anukūlatā-sambandha*); the sense is that the previously cited lexicons and other sources are justified by taking into account the indicated meaning (*dyotyārtha*). "Its connection" (*tadanvaya*) refers to the connection with the meanings of words such as "of what kind" (*kīdṛśa*). [This is] because they are to be resolved in the same manner, and so forth.

"By the same"—meaning by the same reason of being meaningless, because [the objection] can be resolved in the same way. Now, one might argue that there is no fault in the analogy or the case to be illustrated, since we accept the following causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*): "for the cognition of a nominal meaning as a qualifier (*prakāra*) through non-difference, the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by something other than a particle (*nipāta*). To this, he says: "Moreover... [and] "because connection through difference is impossible."

This is because it would contradict the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that [the term *nāmārtha*] refers to "the meaning of a noun" (*nāma-artha*); furthermore, there is an absence of the cognitive presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a cause that is a cognition having as its qualifier a noun-meaning characterized by difference or relation. However, in the view that [case endings] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), since each respective nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself possesses the qualified meaning, there is no fault precisely because there is no [incompatible] syntactic connection (*anvaya*). The statement "without the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth" is intended to convey the sense that: "When those [case endings] are present, a distinct connection between the meanings of two nouns is possible either through the meaning of that [case ending] itself, or through the relation that is the meaning of the case ending."

In the phrase "the sixth case-ending and so forth" (*ṣaṣṭhyādika*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the second case-ending and others. Otherwise—that is, if one were to accept the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns even without the sixth case-ending and so forth, which amounts to not accepting the grammatical rule that "the meaning of a noun [is connected] with the meaning of another noun"—[the compound would not be formed]. The phrase "and so forth" implies this; it does not mean "the *dhava* tree and the *khadira* tree. || 43 ||

Regarding the term *sādṛśya* (similarity): to prevent the misconception that it is a word ending in the suffix *-āp*—as in the case of *vācā* or *niśā*—he says *sādṛśyena*. Since similarity in some form is possible even when not in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), he specifies "by one in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*). This means: by that which is expressed by a word in apposition with the word expressing itself; or, by that which has as its locus a property-limiting factor (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) co-located with a property-limiting factor residing in itself; or, by that which is related to itself through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

With the intention that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between such two word-meanings is possible through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), he says: "by way of non-difference" (*abhedena*). [He further specifies] "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) and "co-referential" (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*). That is to say, [it refers to] two words that possess identical case-endings or are devoid of conflicting case-endings.

The meaning is "of the two meanings of the nominal stems. The point is that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) at all, because a connection consists in the relation between two things that have been presented separately. "The fault does not arise" means that the fault stated—namely, that one would instead say "of the *dhava* and of the *khadira*"—does not apply; for the rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) concerns objects presented separately, whereas in the present case, the conjunction with the *khadira* is presented by the word *khadira* itself. This is precisely why the restriction of the rule of usage to "the meanings of nominal stems" (*nāmārthayoḥ*) is necessary.

Regarding the term "figurative" (*lākṣaṇika*): if there were a restriction [to a specific meaning], the postulation of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be entirely purposeless, because it is possible for the jar to be construed with the negative particle's meaning (absence) through the relation of having a counter-correlativity delimited by jar-ness.

Now, it might be argued that the Naiyāyikas’ attempt to justify the syntactic relation of non-difference by accepting a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of the word "pot" as having the pot as its counter-positive is not tenable; for even if that were the case, the authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others accept that when there is an intention (*tātparya*) in the sentence "There is no pot on the ground," there arises a cognition of the absence of subsistence-in-the-ground in the pot. And thus, in that instance, the grammatical rule "between two nominal meanings" (*nāmārthayoḥ*) would be violated.

Likewise, in the case of "Caitra does not cook," because the absence of an effort conducive to cooking is construed with Caitra, it is the same there as well. Similarly, in the case of "The pot is not a cloth," because a difference having the pot as its counter-correlate is understood through the relation of substratumhood, it is the same there as well.

If the negative particle (*nañ*) were merely indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) like an absence (*abhāva*), it would follow that its primary meaning could hardly ever be attained; furthermore, even if one accepts the cognition of the connection of difference (*bhedānvayabodha*) with an absence, since there is no additional complexity in the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), it is more appropriate to accept the cognition of the connection of difference itself. This is clear in the *Vyutpattivāda*. Moreover, raising the objection that rather than postulating a power of conjunction (*samuccaya-śakti*) for many words, it is more reasonable to postulate it for only a few particles, he says "api ca" (furthermore). [He explains: "rasasadṛśān" (those similar to rasa).

In the phrase "et eṣām udicyānām," these [words] function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatva*). Here, "karaṇam" (instrument) refers to the action of rescuing the king belonging to the northern region (*udagdeśīya-rāja-uddharaṇa-kriyā*). Regarding the phrase "even though the similar thing (*saddaśasya*) is the instrument": even though it is possible for that which is similar to the *usra* (bull) to function as the instrument in the action under discussion by being a qualifier of the arrow through non-difference (*abheda*), [the following is said]. "Of that" means of the similar thing. "By this" means by the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyā-pratyaya*) following the word *usra*. Regarding the phrase "not as the base form (*aprakṛtyā*)," the word "of the similar thing" (*saddaśasya*) is to be supplied here.

The collective meaning is as follows: likewise, in the case of the word *sadṛśa* (similar), it is impossible to express instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) by means of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) following the word *usra*, because this would contradict established grammatical rules such as "suffixes [denote their own meaning] as connected with the meaning of the base" (*pratyayānāṃ prakṛtyarthānvite*). This is due to the impossibility of the third case; for while a third case expressing instrumentality is impossible, even though all case-endings may be elided after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), that [third case] would be meaningless, since the meaning of a particle (*nipāta*), which primarily denotes a case-meaning, cannot function as a factor of action (*kāraka*) to enter into syntactic relation.

But surely, even that [meaning of the particle *eva*] may be construed as a *kāraka* (participant in an action); for this very reason, in the *Dīdhiti* on the passage "smell exists in earth alone" (*pṛthivyām eva gandhaḥ*), having accepted the construction of the meaning of the particle *eva*—which is other than the locative sense denoted by the elided seventh case—as being the "locatedness" (*ādheyatva*) in earth, and having admitted its construction with the other meaning of the word *eva*, namely "absence," the resulting cognition is described as: "smell is inherent in earth and is not inherent in what is other than earth. And thus, the instrumental case following the word *eva* has the sense of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*).

Anticipating the objection that [the formation] is indeed possible, he says: "It would indeed be possible. Regarding the term *kṣavaṇa*: the point is that if its referent were construed as an agent (*kāraka*), then because it would lack the status of denoting a substance (*asattvārthakatva*), it would not be a particle (*nipāta*); consequently, it would not attain the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Since the elision [of case endings] by the rule *avyayāt* would thus not apply, there would be the occurrence of case-endings (*sup*) in *kṣavaṇa*. For this very reason, it has been stated by authoritative scholars that the author of the *Dīdhiti* does not place full reliance on this point. And so, the previously mentioned cognition is to be justified by accepting that the word *eva* has the sense of "inherence" (*ādheyatva*).

Regarding the statement "and the hearing of case-endings" (*supām ca śravaṇam*), he says that the word "and" (*ca*) has a distinct function, meaning "and the hearing of case-endings. Now, one might object: even if *tasi* has the sense of existence (*sattva*), its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*; thus, there would be no occasion for the hearing of case-endings. To this, he states that the word "and" is included in the root text to indicate what is to be conjoined: "from the word 'and'."

And thus, there would also be the ungrammaticality of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*). For even when there is a difference in gender and number, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) exists; however, the case-ending remains one and the same. The point is that the rule composed by the Sage [Pāṇini], "of the standard and object of comparison," simply does not exist. [The phrase] "for the sake of mere grammatical correctness" (*sādhutvamātrārthā*) means this.

The point is this: by the rule that "the *prakṛti* alone [is not the stem]," the case-ending (*vibhakti*) applied must appropriately be of the same class as the case-ending of the word expressing the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Otherwise, there would be no cognition of the relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*), because the absence of conflicting case-endings and so forth is the governing factor (*tantra*) therein. The compound "usrasadṛśaśarāṇām" is a three-membered *dvandva*. [The phrase] "by way of difference" (*bhedenānvaya*) refers to this.

The meaning is that the connection of the object "cow" with the similarity—which is a part of the object "similar"—by means of the relation of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*), or the connection of the similar object by means of the relation of being the correlate (*anuyogitva*) of a similarity residing in itself, is contradicted. And thus, in expressions such as *ghanaśyāma* ("dark as a cloud"), the word *ghana* (cloud) is used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean something similar to a cloud; this remains the case even when analyzed as *ghana iva śyāmaḥ* ("dark like a cloud"). For this very reason...

Since both the compound formation and the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) are established naturally through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), otherwise—by the force of the explicit statement—if one were to accept a compound even in the absence of coreferentiality, there would be a contradiction with the context; furthermore, even so, the masculine substitution would not apply. As for the argument that the usage is sustained by intending to express the mere genus (*jāti*), like the word *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer's milk"), this is clearly untenable when another alternative exists, as stated by Kaiyaṭa on this very sūtra.

The status of being subordinate to comparison (*upamāna*), however, is established either by resorting to the usage of a bystander as "cloud" (*ghana*) based on its prior existence, or because even when the word has the sense of "something similar to a cloud," it possesses the sense of "cloud" itself as a qualifier. Thus, the cognition in both cases is "one who is similar to a cloud is dark. There is no harm in accepting that even the "similar" (which is suggested) can be the substantive (*viśeṣya*) due to the force of experience; for the rule is that the suggested meaning functions as a qualifier of the expressed meaning only where the two are presented separately.

Because of the acceptance [of this view], when there arises an expectation for a qualifying property (*prayojaka-dharma*) regarding similarity, the quality of "darkness" (*śyāmatva*) becomes an object of mental cognition as that qualifying property; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding the phrase *usrābhinna*: the meaning is that when there is a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) of the *usra* (bull) with the "similar," there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the non-difference of the "similar-to-the-bull" with the reed (*śara*); whereas when there is a non-difference relation of the "similar" with the previously mentioned reed, there is the relation of the *usra* with the reed that is non-different from the similar.

Others, however, maintain that certain particles possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) in accordance with actual experience; for this very reason, the cognition of absence is not experienced from them alone, and a desire to know "of what [is there an absence]" is observed, just as in the case of the word *abhāva*. Furthermore, since in passages such as "From the great heaven, from the mountain... (*ā no divo bṛhataḥ parvatādā*), there is the cognition of meanings such as "having come from before the mountain," their denotative power is necessary. Thus, in the third section of the first chapter of the *Nirukta*, beginning with "Prefixes express meanings" (*upasargā arthān nirāhuḥ*), it says: "The modification of meaning... (*arthavikaraṇam*).

This is clear from the statement "ityavargārthe" (in the sense of excluding the *ava*-group). For if [the particle] were merely indicative (*dyotaka*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) characterized by connection with a direction (*digyoga*) would be untenable, and it would also function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). For this very reason, in the rule "striyām," the impossibility of the expression was resolved by resorting to the view of indication (*dyotakatā*), given that the feminine gender (*strītva*) is the primary element. For this same reason, in the Bhāṣya on the rule "hetumati ca," it is stated that under the view of indication, the word "hetumatī" functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Hari also said: "Particles are indicators; some express independent meanings."

"Like certain scriptures (*āgama*s), they may be expressive of a meaning when combined. Here, the word "certain" (*kecit*) applies to both [the preceding and following clauses]. He explains this by saying "like certain scriptures," the meaning of which is that some are expressive words denoting distinct meanings, while others are meaningless. It should be understood that the *Prātiśākhya* treatises, such as "noun, verb, prefix, and particle," also serve as authority in this regard; this has been established in the *Mañjūṣā*.

Similarly, in cases such as "śarair usrābhir iva," even under the view that [the particle *iva*] functions as a dyotaka (indicator), the meaning "by arrows resembling the sun's rays" is not tenable; for, according to the principle stated above, that which conveys the dyotya (indicated) meaning must necessarily function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, in this way, in compounds such as "ghanaśyāma" (dark as a cloud), where the word *ghana* (cloud) in both the analytical statement (*vigraha*) and the compound refers to something similar to a cloud, the rule "upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ" (comparisons are compounded with words expressing common properties) would apply. This rule means that words denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), when they convey the sense of being a standard of comparison through their reference to something similar to it, are compounded with words denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*) that are co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and qualified by a common property (*sāmānyadharma*).

There is no non-application [of the rule], because that [term] refers to the object of comparison (*upameya*) and lacks reference to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Furthermore, the principle of "referring to what has occurred previously" (*bhūtapūrvagati*) is not applicable here; for even in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), that term refers to the object of comparison. Even though in the expression *ghanena tulyaḥ* ("equal to a cloud") it refers to the standard of comparison, it does not constitute an analytical sentence (*vigraha*). Therefore, it is appropriate to understand the denotation of the standard of comparison as residing in both the compound (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vigraha*) due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). However, the aforementioned sentence is not an analytical sentence; otherwise, in the case of *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle as a deer"), the masculine form would not apply.

In the case of the expression "mātā darśanīyā" (the mother is beautiful), the masculine form [of the adjective] is prevented because, both in the analytical compound (*vigraha*) and the formed compound (*vṛtti*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the condition for the application of the masculine form. However, when words such as *ghana* (cloud) are used alone, it is difficult to establish that they denote something qualified by the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Likewise, even if the meaning of the first member is construed with the meaning of the second member through the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*), the application of the masculine form remains untenable. Furthermore, since the word *śyāma* (dark/black) refers to the object of comparison (*upameya*), it cannot be construed with the word *ghana*; therefore, its...

Due to the qualification by a common property (sādhāraṇadharma), it is untenable for [Devadattā] to possess the status of a standard of comparison (upamāna), which consists in delimiting this [subject] from that [standard]. As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "If the analysis is 'Devadattā is dark like a knife' (śastrīva śyāmā devadattā), then 'darkness in the knife' would be the required correlate; if the analysis is 'Just as the knife is dark, so is Devadattā' (yathā śastrī śyāmā tadvad devadattā), then 'darkness in Devadattā' would be the required correlate."

The teacher Kaiyaṭa also states: "And there is no repetition of the word [itself] by which it could express blackness as residing in both [the object of comparison and the subject of comparison]. From this, the conclusion was established in the Bhāṣya: "In that case, both reside in that very [thing]"—that is to say, in the object of comparison (*upameyā*).

Because of the identification based on similarity (*sādṛśyamūlakābhedādhyavasāya*), it is possible for the word *upamāna* (the standard of comparison) to also refer to the object of comparison (*upameya*). For the sake of establishing that similarity, one must accept—through the principle of *tantra* and so forth—that the quality such as "darkness" (*śyāma*) mentioned in relation to the object of comparison is also connected to the standard of comparison. Furthermore, by virtue of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), even an unmentioned attribute such as "having a pleasing appearance" becomes the basis for the simile in expressions like *candramukhī* ("moon-faced"). Thus, how could that which is heard in relation to the object of comparison not also touch upon the standard of comparison? This is clearly stated right here in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary.

Even though repetition [of the word] is possible, this very position was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya on account of the requirement for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Regarding the connection of "darkness" (*śyāmatva*) and so forth with both [the individual and the universal], the Bhāṣya states subsequently: because darkness is connected with both, and not with many; "samāna" means "commonality" (*sāmānya*), and "sāmānyavacana" means "denoting that [commonality]," which is to say, "denoting a property associated with many."

Anticipating the objection that this [the word *śyāmā*] might not exist [as a common term], the proponent (siddhāntin) stated: "Since the quality of darkness (*śyāmatva*) exists in both [the woman and the night] and since the word *śyāmā* denotes the qualities residing in both, it expresses a universal; thus, it too is a word denoting a universal. Here, by the phrase "because it denotes the qualities residing in both," it is indicated that the common property has a verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) with both.

It should be understood that if, according to the actual state of things, the word were intended to denote both qualities, then since blackness exists in many things as well, the statement in the text—"it is not necessarily that [word] alone is expressive of the universal"—would be entirely inconsistent. Furthermore, the resulting cognition is: "Devadatta is black, non-different from the object of comparison (the dark cloud). In the analytical exposition (*vigraha*), the word *iva* indicates the object of comparison; however, in the compound (*samāsa*), its manifestation occurs through the process of unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* also accepts a cognition in which [the object] has the mode (*prakāra*) of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), since he stated: "Although words such as *yathā*, *iva*, and *vā* are qualifiers of the standard of comparison, it is precisely that [object] which is understood as the standard of comparison. Intelligent readers should reflect upon how the consistency of the aforementioned *Bhāṣya* passage and the consistency of the *Prakāśa* text are maintained by accepting the meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) as: "That which is the standard of comparison in reality is compounded with its designator."

In cases such as "As Hari, so Hara," however, since the denotation of that which possesses a differentiating attribute is accepted by the author of the commentary on the rule *prakāravacane thāl*, the cognition arises: "Hara possesses the same attributes as those possessed by Hari. Following this, by means of the words *yat* and *tat*, there is an apprehension of the identity between those two attributes. Taking that attribute which serves as the common mode (*prakāra*) as the basis, the resulting cognition is that the object of comparison (the *upameya*), Hara, is non-different from the standard of comparison (the *upamāna*), Hari. According to the school of rhetoricians (*ālaṃkārika*), this [final] cognition is also verbal in nature.

It should be understood that this refers to the cognition of coolness, purity, and so forth, which is produced by the *vyañjana* (suggestive power) rooted in *lakṣaṇā* (indication). This is clearly stated in the *Mañjūṣā* during the discussion on the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), at the point of analyzing the non-existence (*asattva*) of the action denoted by a verb ending, as well as in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works on the rule "yathā sādṛśye."

If the property of having "similarity" (*upamānatva*) as its qualifier were admitted by the initial cognition itself, then in the case of the passage, "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hateful enemy," one would have to accept that same status in the initial cognition there as well. This would lead to a contradiction with the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Pāṇini Sūtra* (2.1.56), which states, "There is no comparison expressed by a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*). Enough of this excessive elaboration.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of "The man is brave like a tiger," a compound would be untenable because the qualifier "tiger" would also depend on the qualifier "bravery" within the cognition of the stated form; for since the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—consisting in the delimitation of the other by virtue of possessing a common property—is necessarily dependent upon the aspect of the common property, it is untouched by this fault. A compound certainly occurs when the principal element is dependent, as the principal can be connected with multiple qualifiers, as in "Devadatta... [and so forth].

This is like the expression "dhanī sundaraśca" ("wealthy and handsome"). By this, the objection that the *bhāṣya*—which states that the rule "sāmānyāprayoge" (Pāṇini 2.1.57) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that a compound occurs even when the subordinate element depends on the principal element, because the nature of being comparable (*upamitatva*), which consists in being delimited by the possession of a common attribute, also depends on [that] constant dependence—is refuted. This is because the *bhāṣya* is not at fault, as it intends to convey a meaning established by the logic stated by Kaiyaṭa; or else, as stated in the *Samartha-sūtra-bhāṣya*, constant dependence is not the cause for compounding, but rather intelligibility (*gamakatva*) alone is.

This is clear and has been explained in the *Mañjūṣā* under the discussion on compounds (*samāsavāda*). Thus, since the capacity for conveying meaning (*gamakatva*) of a compound whose primary member is dependent [on another word] is observed in examples such as "the king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ*), the possibility of compounding would arise even in the case of "the man is brave like a tiger" (*puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ*). To prevent this, the *bhāṣya*—which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by stating "when the general term is not employed"—also intends precisely this point; thus they say, and the details are found elsewhere. (45)

Regarding the phrase "the definition would result in being over-narrow (*avyāpti*)," it means that because the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) lacks the status of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the impossibility of forms such as *asaḥ* was not raised [as a fault]. As for the phrase "due to the absence of predominance (*prādhānya*)," the sense is that since predominance is defined in relation to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is impossible when the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is devoid of meaning (*nirartha*). Regarding the phrase "of the preverb (*upasarga*)," the word "preverb" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for particles (*nipāta*) in general; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*: "from preverbs and so forth."

Alternatively, in order to indicate that—according to the manner previously stated—not all particles (*nipāta*) are indicators (*dyotaka*), but only some, the word "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*) alone was used [in the rule]. Regarding the phrase "taking only the indicated meaning": the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*) consists in being a generator of a cognition characterized by a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualificandship (*viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in the meaning of the other member. In this context, by the term "meaning of the other member," all three types of meanings—the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the indicated (*dyotya*)—are included; thus, there is no loss of the knowledge of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member. "That very same"—meaning only the indicated meaning. "Because of its having meaning" (*arthavattvāt*).

The point is that in the *arthavat-sūtra*, "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) is defined as being the object of a cognition that generates the understanding of meaning; it does not consist in being a generator of the understanding of meaning through a linguistic operation (*vṛtti*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency.

But surely this is incorrect, because in cases such as "dhanaṃ" and "vanaṃ," each individual phoneme would incur the designation of *prātipadika*, since they too are objects of the cognition that generates the understanding of meaning. Nor should it be argued that even if they possess the status of *prātipadika*, no case-ending (*sup*) arises due to the absence of number, objecthood (*karman*), and so forth; for if that were the case, the arising of case-endings from particles (*nipāta*) would also be untenable. And this is not an acceptable consequence, because in examples such as "pragacchati," the rule "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.28)—which prescribes the low pitch accent (*nighāta*) for a finite verb following another finite verb—would fail to apply due to the absence of a word (*pada*) preceding it.

Because [rules] such as *jaśtva* and *rutva* would fail to apply in cases like *udgacchaty uccaiḥ*, he says "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). Regarding the statement "the production of the suffix *su* occurs by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*)," the meaning is that even in the absence of *prātipadika*-hood, the production of *su* occurs due to an indicator. Regarding the phrase "of a particle" (*nipātasya*): in this view, since all particles lack meaningfulness in the form of conveying a meaning through syntactic function (*vṛtti*), the present Vārttika would apply; however, others hold that because of the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"the mention of 'meaningless' (*anarthaka*) will not be made"—the rule applies to that [particle] even when that word [from the Bhāṣya] is omitted.

Since there is an absence of verbal action (*kriyāyoga*), the designation of "motion" (*gati*) or "prefix" (*upasarga*) does not even arise; thus, by the rule *adhiparī anarthakau*, the designation of "karmapravacanīya" is prescribed for *adhi* and *pari* in order to prevent their being designated as *gati* or *upasarga*. However, if one maintains that this Vārttika is unnecessary—on the grounds that it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even meaningless particles (*anarthaka-nipāta*) possess the capacity to trigger grammatical operations when used in a meaningful context—then, by relying on that very principle as a general indicator that meaningful operations apply to particles, their status as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is established. This is the intended meaning.

He states "kṛttaddhita" [Pāṇini 1.2.46] because, since the status of being a nominal stem (prātipadika) is already established by the rule itself, there is no need for this Vārttika. However, others maintain that particles (*nipātas*) possess meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) by virtue of their function as *dyotaka*—a term synonymous with *vyañjaka*—which conveys meaning; thus, their status as nominal stems is established. For this very reason, the Vārttika, which contains the word "anarthaka" (meaningless), becomes consistent. Furthermore, since there are some particles such as "tu," "ha," "sma," and "vai" for which even a signified meaning (*dyotya-artha*) does not exist, Kaiyaṭa explains that the word "anarthaka" was stated in the commentary to indicate that this [Vārttika] is intended for them.

They say: he states the consensus of the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* regarding the nature of indication (*dyotakatā*) with the words "And it has been said. Regarding the phrase "in the fourfold [category]": this refers to that which consists of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). As it is stated in the *Nirukta*: "There are four classes of words: nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. He states the reason why doubt does not arise regarding these two with the words "of those two. Now, one might object: if this is so, then the statement by the elders (*vṛddha*) in the passage beginning with "by the prefix" (*upasargeṇa*)—which asserts that the prefix alone possesses the power of indication—is contradictory. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the prefix... and "the other... [is...].

It is delimited by a form other than the form specifically indicated [by the word]. Therefore, there is no defect even if the "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) perceived in the expression *prajayati* is non-different from "pure victory" (*śuddhajaya*). || 46 ||

[Objection: But if those [kṛt suffixes] were denoters (*vācaka*), would there not be the undesirable consequence of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) involved in postulating a primary expressive power (*śakti*) for them? To this, he says: "because they are indicators" (*bodhakatā*). By the phrase "of tiṅ and so on," the inclusion of kṛt suffixes and the like is intended. One should not suspect that if a kṛt suffix were merely an indicator (*dyotaka*), its meaning would necessarily become a qualifier; for this is contradicted by experience, and by the traditional dictum, "Nouns (*nāman*) have being as their primary sense," the meaning of a kṛt suffix—even when functioning as an indicator—[is established as the principal].

This is because [the author] intends [the term] to mean "being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatva*); in this way, it should be inferred even for *san* (the desiderative suffix) and so forth. [Objection: This would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). [Response: It is not an acceptable consequence, because it contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*); such is the underlying intention. However, others hold that if verbal suffixes (*suptiṅ*) are merely indicative (*dyotaka*), then an acceptable consequence does indeed follow. For this very reason, the time, agent, and so forth denoted by them function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the fact that time is what is indicated (*dyotya*) is accepted even by Kaiyaṭa and others; for this very reason, the agent is understood from forms such as *pacati*.

However, they say that suffixes such as *kṛt* do not possess indicatory (*dyotaka*) power, because their meaning would otherwise result in being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor does the meaning of such a suffix become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) even if it is indicated; for, according to the reasoning already stated, it is more appropriate to accept the position that these suffixes are denoters (*vācaka*) in those cases. The phrase "of presence and absence" (*anvayavyatirekayoḥ*) means "when those two exist. Thus, the intended sense is that just as verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like are denoters based on presence and absence, so too are particles (*nipāta*) denoters.

The construction of the root text is as follows: "That which is the opinion of others is precisely what is not tenable for us. And thus: "And if particles (*nipāta*) were denotative" (*vācakatve*). Regarding the phrase "likewise" (*tathā*): it means "likewise, [the rule] concerns objects other than particles"; furthermore, the other defects have already been raised previously.

This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa); the previously mentioned state of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*)—beginning with the rule "in the case of a particle joined with its own [verbal base]" (*svasvayuktanipāte*)—should be understood. By this, there is no fault in cases such as *anubhavati*. Even in the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of the term "suffixes" (*pratyaya*), one must include the property of being construed with either the meaning of a particle co-occurring with the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*) or the meaning of the verbal base itself. For this very reason, there is no deficiency in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, even though the prefix (*upasarga*) expresses motion (*gati*).

However, if one accepts that a prefix denotes only the result while the verbal root denotes the operation (*vyāpāra*), then this [distinction] need not be respected, because the meaning of the suffix would then be construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) itself.

It should also be understood that, for the sake of explaining verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) characterized by the relation between a name, its object, and its specific mode, one must accept that the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by either an inflection (*pratyaya*) or a particle (*nipāta*). Nor is there any excessive complexity (*gaurava*) here; for once it is established—by the reasoning already stated—that these [particles] denote their respective meanings, such complexity must be accepted as unavoidable due to the lack of any other recourse. For this very reason, they say that the cognition of negation is accomplished by the mere word *na*, since in that case, without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another word, it would be impossible for [the particle] to function merely as an indicator (*dyotaka*).

If it is objected that if these [prefixes] were denotative, there would be the undesirable consequence of their being used alone, we say no; for while some are restricted by the rule "they [occur] before the verbal root" (*te prāgdhātoḥ*), others such as *na* and so forth are accepted as being [denotative] in that way. Furthermore, even if others are denotative, this is logically consistent—just as a base or a suffix may appear alone—as has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:

It should not be suspected that—just as a suffix (*pratyaya*) requires a governing factor (*niyāmaka*) when it follows another element, so too here, even in the absence of such a factor, the use of the particles alone is impossible because their connection with a relatum is untenable without a sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*) and the like; and that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of forms such as *śobhanaśca* instead of *śobhanaḥ samuccayaḥ*, or *ghaṭasya ca* instead of *ghaṭasya samuccayaḥ*—because, due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*), they are eternally dependent and present their own meaning only as qualifiers of something else, and thus neither of those two consequences arises.

Alternatively, there is no fault because one may assume that the cognition of the relation denoted by the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyartha-sambandha) and the cognition of the connection with other qualifiers depend solely upon the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by words such as "and" (*ca*) expressing conjunction (*samuccaya*). Or rather, since the word "and" (*ca*) has the power (*śakti*) to denote conjunction, there is no defect; furthermore, the complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from assuming a power in the substratum (*dharmyaṃśa*) is accepted because it is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇikatva*). As it has been said: "For when there is the expression of what is conjoined, there is no [logical] exclusion (*vyatireka*). This should be understood. [The term] "useless" (*vyartham*)...

In the view that [prepositions] are indicators (*dyotaka*), since all of them would be devoid of meaning (*nirarthaka*), there would be nothing to exclude; this is because their meaning is already clear. As for the phrase "of that which is meaningless" (*anarthakasya*) in that context, it is intended to indicate that words whose purpose is merely to fill out the meter (*pādapūraṇa*) are not meaningful in any way whatsoever. As for the phrase "because it has been rejected" (*pratyākhyātatvāt*): the rule "the prepositions *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless" (*adhiparī anarthakau*) was rejected on the grounds that it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that even a meaningless word may take the suffixes prescribed for meaningful words. The mention of the plural number (*bahuvacanam*) refers to the Mīmāṃsakas.

The sense is that the plural number is used because there are many Mīmāṃsakas due to the distinctions between the Bhāṣyakāra and others. He presents the Mīmāṃsaka view with the words "kevala" (only). Regarding the phrase "tātparyagrāhakatvena" (by way of being a grasper of intention): the sense is that since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*), they do not serve as the graspers of *śakti* (denotative power). Regarding "lakṣaṇāgrahe" (in the absence of the apprehension of secondary signification): the meaning is "when the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verbal root [ji] in the sense of 'excellent victory' and so forth has not been apprehended. Regarding "kārya" (effect): the meaning is the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the apprehension of secondary signification and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

"Of the apprehension of the power as well. Here, the phrase "the causal relation is necessary" is to be supplied. "Both" means both denotative power (*vācakatva*) and indicative power (*dyotakatva*). "Precisely for this reason" means precisely because of the acceptance of both denotative and indicative power. || 47 ||

Now, if both the *prādi* prefixes and the *cādi* particles were denotative, there would be the complexity [of postulating] that the properties of being a prefix (*upasargatva*) and being a particle (*nipātatva*) serve as the delimiters of their expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*); therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "mūle-nipātatvam" (in the root [text], it is *nipātatva*): the meaning is that since *nipātatva* (the status of being a particle) is common to both the *prādi* and *cādi* groups, there is no complexity in the aforementioned sequence. Alternatively, because there is no single property common to both the apprehension of dyotakatva (suggestiveness) in prepositions (*upasarga*) and the apprehension of vācakatā (denotative power) in particles like *ca*, the apprehension arises as delimited by *upasargatva* and delimited by *nipātatva* respectively; thus, if both *upasargatva* and *nipātatva* are related [to the function], why should dyotakatva and so forth be postulated as being delimited solely by *nipātatva*?

He dispels the doubt—namely, "What is the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) in [the claim] that [this is so] not by being delimited as *upasarga*-hood?"—with the words "But furthermore" (*param tu*), and so on. Even though *upasarga*-hood exists, its being a universal (*sāmānyatva*) does not follow from its being a pervader (*vyāpakatva*), because the state of being a pervader consists in such things as not being the delimiting factor (*anavacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that is co-extensive with itself; therefore, he says: "Because it is a pervader, because it is a universal."

And thus, the intended meaning is that "pervasion" (*vyāpakatva*) in the present context refers to that which is qualified by the aforementioned non-limiting nature (*anavacchedakatva*), consisting in the property of subsisting in a locus where its own absence exists—that is, the form of subsisting in a wider domain (*adhikadeśavṛttitva*). He dispels the charge of deficiency [in the definition] by stating that "the state of being capable" (*śaktatā*) is a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). || 48 ||
Thus concludes the determination of the nature of particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and so forth. 8.

"Because it has the sense of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)," meaning that the statement of the *Vārttika*—that is, a statement in the form of a *vārtika*—has the sense of the suffix *tva*. [The phrase] "by Hari": the point is that they have the misconception that what was stated by Hari (Patañjali) is itself a *vārtika*. [The author says] "of *tva* and *tal*" because, by specifying these two particular suffixes, there might arise a doubt that *imanij* and others have different meanings; therefore he says "of *tva* and *tal*. [The word] "abstract" (*bhāva*): this refers to what is about to be explained. "Meaning" (*artha*): the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*). "States" (*vadati*): the meaning is "makes known" (*bodhati*). "Is not possible": [this concludes the sentence].

In that view, since the relation is not a qualifier (*aprakāratva*) in the cognition produced by compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, the intention is that in the expression *rājapuruṣatvam*, the suffix *-tva* has "difference" (*bheda*) alone as its meaning.

Thus, according to the view that the meaning of the compound is the person who, in reality, possesses a connection with the king by way of the form "puruṣa" (person)—in this case, the meaning of the suffix *tva* is simply "personhood" (*puruṣatva*). The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is then construed there through the relation of being a superstratum (*ādheyatva*) whose nature is determined solely by that individual. For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) would be necessary under this view. Such is the process of syntactic understanding; such is the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Even in the case of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, since there is the existence of a power (*śakti*) [to denote both meanings], and because the relation between two meanings that are presented as distinct objects of cognition is itself the *anvaya* (syntactic connection), it would follow that the literal meaning is inconsistent; however, its status as verbal (*śābdatva*) is established there by the experience "I am expressing it through words," as is explained in detail elsewhere. But according to the view that "the relation between two presented [meanings] is *anvaya*," let it remain exactly as stated in the literal text. As for the phrase "in an invariable relation" (*avyabhicaritasaṃbandhe*), it refers to the case where the relation between offspring and the progenitor is an invariable relation.

The point is this: just as the relationship between "being" (sat) and "existence" (sattā) is never subject to deviation, so too is the relationship between these two; for the relationship exists from the very moment of the being's birth until its destruction, and likewise, the aforementioned relationship [of the child] exists from the moment of the offspring's birth until its destruction.

The intended meaning is as follows: by the statement "the *gotra* together with the [Vedic] practices," even a descendant (*apatya*) is understood to possess the status of a genus (*jāti*). Consequently, because the relationship of non-difference from the genus is obscured, the genus itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) there; thus, it is that very genus which constitutes the meaning of the suffix *tva*. The word "but" (*tu*) is used to indicate an alternative view: that only the grammatical operation (*kārya*) conditioned by the genus is extended [to the descendant], and not the property of being a genus (*jātitva*) itself. Regarding the phrase "occurring in another sense": the meaning is that examples such as "Aindratvam" (the state of being Indra's) should be cited as instances where a *taddhita* suffix denotes a deity or similar referent. The phrase "even though it ends in a *taddhita*" [is used to address this].

For this very reason, there arises the contingency that [the suffix] would signify a relation. Regarding the phrase "because of the cognition of non-difference": the rule for the elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix *matup* is intended to prevent the undesirable usage of forms such as *śuklavān* (possessing whiteness), since the conventional distinction between quality and the possessor of quality—as in the expression *paṭasya śauklyam* (the whiteness of the cloth)—does indeed exist. Regarding the phrase "only in the case of a genus (*jāti*)": because the relation of difference is obscured by the worldly-established cognition "this is that," there is no cognition of a relation; the same applies to cases such as "white" (*śukla*).

In the case of "the cook" (*pācaka*) and similar terms, however, since it is precisely non-difference that is perceived through the action, and because there is deviation [from the rule], the application of the word to the substance is rooted solely in the ignorance of its connection with the action; the same applies to "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and so forth, where it is that specific relation itself [which is the basis].

The meaning of the suffix *tva* and similar affixes is the respective subsequent state (*uttarabhāva*). In cases such as "the potness of a blue pot" (*nīlaghaṭatvam*), the suffix *tva* denotes potness (*ghaṭatva*) as it exists in the blue pot and so forth; it does not denote it as being identical in form with the qualifying relation (*saṃbandhiviśeṣaṇa*), because there is no relation between the meanings of the preceding and succeeding words other than that of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Potness alone is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "blue pot," though by virtue of qualifiers such as "blue," it is [cognized] in the form of potness.

When a particular blue object or the like is manifested, it is precisely the "potness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth, which is co-referential with that blue, that appears as the basis for engagement or withdrawal; since the distinction [of potness] arises from the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there is no room for the objection: "How can 'potness'—being over-pervasive—be the basis for the application of words such as 'blue pot'?"

Regarding expressions such as ‘*dhavakhadiratvam*’ (the state of being a *dhava* and a *khadira* tree), they say that what is denoted is a collection (*samudāya*) of universals (*jāti*); it should be understood that when the parts of the collection are not manifested (*anudbhūta*), the singular number is used, whereas when the parts are manifested (*udbhūta*), dual or plural numbers may also occur. To indicate this, he says “*dig*” (the direction/point). The logicians (*tārkika*), however, have stated that the suffix following a *karmadhāraya* compound expresses the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two property-delimiters (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), such as "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

"Qualified by the meaning of the base" means that, in reality, [the object] is qualified by a staff and so forth through a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). In that case, since the conjunction and so forth appear by virtue of the relational scope (*saṃsargamaryādā*), there is no expressive power (*śakti*) for them; rather, the power resides in the staff for the base, and in the substratum for the suffix. By the word "only" (*mātra*), relations in the form of conjunction and so forth are excluded; for this very reason, even in cases such as "cook" (*pācaka*), the relation is not denotable. And it has been said by the Bhaṭṭas: "The root *pac* itself expresses the cooking, and the single suffix expresses the agent."
"Furthermore, the agent must be expressed as being endowed with the capacity [to act], not as any single individual.

Nor is it impossible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) regarding infinite substances; rather, this is possible by taking a single property such as "stickness" (*daṇḍatva*) as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) through a traditional lineage (*paramparā*). This should be understood according to the method explained in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*. The word "of the Mīmāṃsakas" requires the supplement "in their view. "Its denotation" refers to the denotation of the relationship.

One might object: "In cases such as *dāmodaratvam* ('the state of being Dāmodara'), the word *bhāva* (abstract state) denotes a specific property residing in Dāmodara and the like; thus, that [property] is not denoted [by the suffix]. However, in cases such as *daṇḍitvam* ('the state of being a staff-bearer'), the abstract state is simply a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, what obstacle is there to its being denoted? To dispel this doubt, he states the reason beginning with the words *prakṛti*.

For this reason—because the state of being that which has been spoken of (uktatva) is denoted by the suffixes such as *-tva* and *-tā*—it follows that in the expression *daṇḍitvam* ("the state of being a staff-bearer"), according to your view, there would be no denotation by the suffixes *-tva* and *-tā*, since the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) lacks the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) in the cognition produced by the word *daṇḍin*. This is the meaning. He states the distinction between the two words in sequence with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). "Otherwise" means if only the property (*dharma*) were the referent of the word *bhāva*. "Of substanceness, etc. (*dravyatvādeḥ*).

Since that [number] also inheres in the jar, it does not denote [the jar] by virtue of being subsequent to the word "jar" and so forth, because it lacks the status of being the primary object (*prakāratva*) in the cognition produced by the word "jar. This applies to the staff and other such things as well.

Because that [stick] is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), yet there is no inherence (*samavetatva*) in Devadatta or others who are merely conjoined with a staff, the word "staff" and so forth is not denoted by the suffix *-tva* in the expression "staff-ness" (*daṇḍitva*). Here, "inherence" does not mean existing by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); for if it did, then since "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) and "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) do not inhere [in the pot or absence], they could not be expressed by the suffix *-tva*. Rather, it consists in existing in that [locus] by means of the relation that serves as the delimitor of the qualifierhood (*prakāratāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

The meaning is as follows: "Relation is the qualifier (*prakāra*). Thus, since there is an absence of the status of being a qualifier in the cognition produced by words such as *dāmodara*, just as there is no expression of a relation by a suffix following that [word], so too in cases such as *daṇḍitva*, there would be no expression of a relation by that [suffix]. This is the collective sense. Regarding the expression *daṇḍitva* and so forth, having restated the argument stated by the Mīmāṃsakas concerning the expressibility of the relation, he refutes it with the words "when... (*yadā*). "Inhering in itself" (*svasamaveta*) means inhering in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*).

"Expressible" (*vācya*) means expressible by the base (*prakṛti*), that is to say, the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by the base; or alternatively, it means expressible by suffixes such as *tva* and so on, that is to say, fit for being denoted by them. For that which is the locus of the "mode-ness" (*prakāratā*) belonging to the cognition produced by the base is indeed fit for being denoted by them. Regarding the phrase "the relation is expressible": the meaning is that even the relation inherent in itself, which is the mode of the cognition produced by the base, is posited as being expressible by suffixes such as *tva*. And this has been explained in detail. The point is this: in cases such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), if the relation were not expressible—

Even in the case of *daṇḍitvam* ("the state of being a staff-bearer"), the denotability (*vācyatva*) of the relation would not [be necessary], since its cognition is established in exactly the same way. If it is argued that the denotability of the relation must be postulated because otherwise suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would become redundant (*vaiyarthya*), we say no; for in cases such as *ghaṭatvam*, the requirement is met by the very power (*śakti*) residing in the already established delimitors of the referential object (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). As for the rule "after a *kṛt* or *taddhita* [suffix], [the final vowel is elided]" (*kṛttaddhite*) and so forth, it would only lead to a forced assumption regarding Hari (Pāṇini) or the Sage (Vyāḍi). If it is argued that the assumption of the power of suffixes like *tva* and *tal* with respect to the relation is made in accordance with experience (*anubhava*), we say no; for rather than assuming a further power (*śaktyantara*), it is more parsimonious to assume that the relation resides within the already established power of the suffixes themselves, just as the property (*dharma*) does.

Since it is logically possible for [the relation] to be established as the object (*viṣaya*), it is improper to postulate a separate power (*śakti*); for if that were the case, the cognition of it would be possible through the very power that delimits the already established category of the entity, as has been elaborated therein. This is the point of dissimilarity: the meaning is that in cases such as "Dāmodara-ness" or "devotion," the relation is not denoted (*avācya*), whereas in cases such as "staff-bearer-ness" (*daṇḍitva*), it is denoted (*vācya*). Regarding the term "to be mentioned": it means that which is both "to be mentioned" and a "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Others, however, maintain that although a word such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) does not directly express the relation [between the staff and the person], its application occurs only through the cognition of that relation; thus, since the relation itself serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it is possible for the relation to be the denotation (*vācya*) of the suffix *taddhita*. This is because [the suffix is applied] when there exists such a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) as "in this regard."

With the intention that "in the base [meaning], there is the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) of the non-inherent meaning (*aprakṛtyartha*)," the word "is attained" (*apannam*) is to be supplied as a remainder; thus he says: "appearing as a qualifier. The meaning is that because it is a qualifier—because *ghaṭatvatva* (the property of potness) is a qualifier—it would follow that it must be denotable by the suffix following the word *ghaṭatva*. Regarding the phrase "mere property" (*dharmamātram*): they say that it is denotable as a property (*dharmatvena*), but not in its specific forms (*tattadrūpeṇa*), for fear of the consequence of an infinite number of linguistic capacities (*śakti*).

Nor can it be said that there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the sense of the "heavy property" (*gurudharma*), because the preference for brevity (*lāghava*) applies only to *śakti* (primary denotative power), not to *lakṣaṇā*; this is the intended meaning, as there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā*) [to the contrary]. In fact, however, there is no such heaviness at all; thus he says, "the individual," etc. Others, however, say that in the case of "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*), the referent is a specific property belonging to ignorance (*avidyaka*), and not a form such as "not inhering in anything other than a pot," because of the resulting heaviness. Regarding the stated definition having the meaning of "and so forth" (*ādi*), he cites the agreement of the author of the *Vārttika* with the words beginning "And it has been said," etc.

Intending that the word *guṇa* in the phrase "of which quality" (*yasya guṇasya*) refers to that which is auxiliary (*upakāraka*), he says "by way of being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatayā*). And it is stated in Kaiyaṭa’s work: "By the word *guṇa*, whatever differentiator dependent on another is included here—be it a genus (*jāti*) or anything else. He explains "from existence" (*bhāvāt*) as "because of being the substratum" (*āśrayatvāt*). He explains "in the substance" (*dravye*) as "the qualificand" (*viśeṣya*). [He then states] "in the quality" (*guṇe*).

From words such as *guṇin* (possessor of qualities) and *śukla* (white), which primarily denote the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the suffix denotes the quality (*guṇa*); however, from those same words when they primarily denote the quality, it should be understood that the suffix denotes the genus (*jāti*) residing therein. Since words such as *aṇu* (minute) always primarily denote the possessor of qualities, the suffix after them denotes the quality consisting of dimension (*parimāṇa*) itself. Regarding the statement "Dimension is fourfold: minute, large, long, and short," its meaning should be understood as: "that which resides in the minute and so forth [is dimension]."

Regarding the phrase "jātivācakānām" (of those denoting universals), the meaning is "of words such as 'ghaṭatva' (potness) and so on. The phrase "the individuals themselves" means that these [individuals] possess the status of being the delimiters of the denotable (vācyatāvacchedakatva) through the relation of subsisting in themselves (svavṛttitva). Having thus explained the meaning of "tva" and so on in various instances, he states the resulting verbal cognition (śābdabodha) with the words "tathā ca" (and thus).

In the expression ‘ghaṭatvam’ (pot-ness), the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) functions as the qualifier through a relation consisting in its inherence in its entirety while being non-inherent in anything other than itself; thus, by this much, the property (*dharma*) denoted by the suffix acquires the status of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). It was precisely with this intention that [the author] stated that there is a cognition of "uncommon property" (*asādhāraṇadharma*); however, the word does not have a direct denotative power (*śakti*) toward it as an uncommon property, because such a definition—consisting in its subsistence in the entire extension of the base-meaning while being qualified by non-subsistence in anything else—is too cumbersome (*gaurava*).

Alternatively, in reality, that which is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is what relates to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) by way of the relation of being a superstratum (*ādheyatvasambandha*); therefore, in the case of *ghaṭatvam*, there is no appearance of *dravyatva* (substancehood) and so forth. The phrase "even though it serves as the indicator of that" means: for the purpose of indicating that *vārtika*.

The word *api* is for the purpose of indicating an alternative position; the word *yadvā* (or) serves to include the meaning [of that alternative]. By the phrase "having the purpose of indicating the Vārttika," the suspicion of its lack of authority—that this position was stated in the Vārttika—is dispelled. He states the commentary on the Vārttika as expressed in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*: "They exist" (*bhavanti*). [The phrase] "by way of denotative power" (*vācakatvena*) means "by the relation of being a denoter. The ellipsis is "they function with respect to their objects. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *bhū* here has the sense of "functioning" (*pravṛtti*).

And "functioning" (*pravṛtti*) in this context consists in the form of application (*prayoga*). Thus, he says "bhāvāḥ" (the states), meaning that the word *bhāva* is that which makes the word itself known. Here, he says "by its own form," where the word "own" (*sva*) signifies the self (*ātman*); "he" refers to the self of the word, and "of them" refers to those words. He explains the meaning of the final term *bhāva* found in the Vārttika as "the state is the ground for the application [of the word]."

One might object: "How can a word have a basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)? For that status belongs only to a qualifier (*prakāra*) residing in the denotable object (*śakya*. To dispel this doubt, he says, beginning with "The point is this," and so forth: "some [object] is denoted by each [word]. Since the object is not presented in its specific form, it is impossible to grasp the word's denotative power (*śakti*) as being delimited by a specific property such as "being a *nala*"; therefore, it is [grasped] only in its general form.

Cognition must be admitted [as the result], because there exists a grasp of the word’s expressive power (*śaktigraha*) consisting of a general inference such as: "This word is expressive in some sense, because it is a word, specifically because it is a correct word. The term "urbanites" (*nāgarika*) is used to indicate that for them, there would be the consequence of non-cognition; for they generally lack knowledge of the specific forms, and since a grasp of the expressive power in its specific form is possible [for them], whereas for forest-dwellers (*gāramauna*) knowledge of the specifics is possible, there is no lack of cognition [in their case]. Thus, "urbanites" is stated.

And that [cognition] is ultimately characterized by a lack of specific knowledge; therefore, there is no inconsistency even if some cultured person (*nāgarika*) has an understanding of it in a specific form. "In this very way" means: it is of the nature "denoted by this word," and not as those various universals (*jāti*) and so forth—the term "experience" (*anubhava*) is to be supplied here. For this very reason, the view that Nala and others appear in their specific forms because the apprehension of their power (*śaktigraha*) occurs in a specific form due to the force of impressions (*saṃskāra*) from another birth is rejected.

They say that because there is no specific experience [of all particulars], there is no evidence for postulating infinite latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); furthermore, it would follow that those [particulars] would be remembered specifically even without hearing their respective denotative words. Nor is it correct to claim that there is no memory due to a lack of an awakener (*udbodhaka*), for if verbal cognition were established by that alone, the status of latent impressions and memory as causes would be untenable. "Both are the delimiters" means that both the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, as well as the word, are the delimiters of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

In that context, the property of being the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) belongs to the word itself through the relation of *śakti* (denotative power), whereas it belongs to the universal (*jāti*) and so forth through their respective relations, such as inherence (*samavāya*). Likewise, the apprehension of *śakti*—that is, the apprehension of *śakti* in the form of the universal and so on—is likewise characterized by the word as its qualifier (*padaprakāraka*). The sense is that the difference in the cognition arises from the difference in the apprehension of *śakti*. And thus—namely, when the word also functions as a qualifier in verbal cognition—the word too [is a qualifier]; the particle "api" serves to include the universal and so forth.

However, in the view of those for whom the word itself is the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the word is the primary meaning; whereas in the view of those for whom the meaning consisting of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth is the ground for application, they say that such [the universal] is its meaning.

The base (*prakṛti*) has word-ness (*śabdaparatva*) as its secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*); or else, the meaning of the suffixes beginning with *tvā* is "that which is expressed by words" (*śābda*), such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth. The meaning of the base—the word—is construed with the meaning of the suffix through the relation of being the qualifier (*prakāratva*) in the cognition produced [by the sentence]. For this very reason, word-ness is accepted as the meaning of the base; otherwise, it would be impossible for the meaning of the base, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), to be construed with the meaning of the suffix, which is of the nature of a word, because in that case neither inherence (*samavāya*) nor any other relation is possible. Furthermore, the aforementioned relation of "being the qualifier in the produced cognition" would also be impossible.

It should be understood that although the relation of *śakti* (potency) is possible [in some cases], it is impossible in the case of *paṭatva* (clothness) and so forth; therefore, the word itself (*śabda*) alone is accepted as the basis. However, others hold that in the Bhāṣya, under the rule "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*), the possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to meanings such as intention (*abhiprāya*) was avoided by the Vārttika "by the presence of which quality... (*yasya guṇasya bhāvāt...*). Their intention is that by the word "state" (*bhāva*) in the present sūtra, the property (*dharma*) that serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is intended, and not intention or the like.

Immediately following that, there arises the objection that in expressions such as *ḍitthatvam* (the state of being Ditttha), the suffix *-tva* and so forth would be untenable, because the word *ḍittha* and the like denote only the individual (*vyakti*). Having resolved this by accepting that the individual itself can function as both the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*prakāra*), and that the meaning of the suffix consists of an individual qualified by the state of being a qualifier, an alternative resolution is provided by the Vārttika beginning with "Or rather, all entities [are denoted] by their own... and so forth.

This is its meaning: here, the word *sva* (self) refers to "one's own. A word has two kinds of meanings: the denoted object (*vācya*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, and the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). When either of these is expressed, the suffixes *tva*, etc., are used. Of these, the latter occurs in cases such as *ghaṭatvam* ("jar-ness"). In that instance, the base (*prakṛti*) refers exclusively to the object, because the object—such as the jar—is capable of being construed with the meaning of the suffix, which consists of a universal (*jāti*) and so forth.

In examples such as *kutvam* and *ḍitthatvam*, the former [type of word] applies; there, because the meaning of the suffix is untenable, the base (*prakṛti*) refers solely to the word-form itself. From a base that refers to the word-form—such as the word *kvādi*—the suffix occurs in the sense of an individual entity (*vyakti*). Thus, there is synonymy between *ḍitthatvam* and *ḍittha-śabda*, between *kutvam* and *kuśabda*, and between *padatvam* and *padaśabda*. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *vṛddhi* rule: "Why does *kutva* not occur [in the word *padasya*], given the rules *coḥ kuḥ* and *padasya*?"

Thus, because [the word *bhāva*] is a *bha*, how can it have the designation *bha*? It has been stated that "words such as *ayasmaya* [occur] in the Veda (*chandasi*). And in this way, the meaning of the word *kutva* and so forth is simply the *ka*-class (the gutturals) and so on. This being the case, one must maintain that the pronoun *tat* in the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ* refers to the word-form itself; yet, for that same pronoun when it recurs in the rule *guṇavacane*, one must rely upon its referring to the meaning. In this manner, there is no occurrence of the cumbersome complexity resulting from the abandonment or adoption of the meaning.

They have stated that action is neither possible nor perceived for a word, since in expressions such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), it is observed that the word *tat* refers solely to its own meaning; however, the relationship between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the denotable power (*śakya*) of the entire aggregate consisting of the initial and final elements.

Thus, the determination of the meanings of suffixes such as *tva* and others is completed. Following the context, he states the meaning of the *taddhita* suffixes whose sense is "deity" and so forth in the rule *sāsya devatā*. Although the [suffix] denoting "offspring" (*apatya*) was mentioned first, it is set aside here because the meaning of the suffix in that case—namely, offspring—is a single entity; and since in that instance, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is easily understood as being a qualifier through a relation of distinction, such as the relationship between the produced and the producer.

However, it should be understood that regarding a *taddhita* suffix whose meaning is "deity" (*devatā*), because multiple interpretations are possible and thus the matter is difficult to grasp, great care must be taken in determining its precise meaning. The phrase "qualified by the deity" (*devatāviśiṣṭam*) means qualified by the deity either through the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) or through the relationship of being the object of a renunciation (*tyāga*) intended for that deity. For this very reason—that is, precisely because the *taddhita* suffix under discussion conveys the aforementioned meaning—it is "the offering of the subject matter" (*viṣayārpaṇam*) of that very same *taddhita* suffix.

The meaning is this: since the pronoun *asya* (of this) conveys a specific [object], the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) attached to its referent is likewise restricted; thus, when there arises the desire to know "what is that specific [object]?", the proximity of the word *āmikṣā* leads to the cognition that the specific object is of the nature of *āmikṣā*. Regarding the phrase "from the mere [word]":

the construction is "the secondary derivative expressing the deity, arising—that is, manifesting—from the mere word *agni*, is not capable of establishing a deity associated with another [deity]. The sense is that if [Agni] were a deity only in dependence on another, it would lack the semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) required for the application of the secondary derivative suffix, and thus the formation of the word itself would not occur.

For this very reason, since the term *āgneya* is not applied to the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice and the like, the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) enjoined by the sentence "He divides the *āgneya* into four parts" does not apply; for in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) resides collectively only when there is mutual dependence between the two members. This was established in the first section of the third book of the *Pūrvatantra*. Furthermore, it was indicated by the statement "not that which has Agni as its deity when joined with another," etc., that [the term *āgneya*] is capable of denoting a deity consisting of Agni alone; thus, there is a supporting consistency.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *devatā*": the authors of the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*, however, maintain that just as in expressions such as *āgneya*, the dative case merely indicates that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—which is already obtained from the base itself—is the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), so too here the suffix indicates both deityhood (*devatātva*) and the state of being a sacrificial offering (*pradeyatva*). Deityhood has the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) with respect to the offering; the meaning of the base has the relation of being contained therein (*ādheyatva*) with respect to that [deityhood]; and the state of being an offering is the meaning of the suffix only in its capacity as a related entity, and not otherwise.

[The deity is understood] by way of its specific form consisting of curd and so forth; for this very reason, there is the grammatical coherence of such usages as "curd for Indra" (indraṃ dadhi). The expectation for a specific [deity] is fulfilled by the word *āmikṣā*. Thus, in the case of *āgneyī*, the cognition is that it is the specifier of the status of being a deity residing in Agni. Now, an objection:

"In that regard, the connection with the deity is established either by a taddhita suffix, or by the dative case, or again by the wording of a mantra; among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding."

If it is argued that the weakness of the *taddhita* suffix as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas is untenable, we say no; for while the relationship with the deity is obtained from the sentence (*vākya*) through the dative case, in the case of the *taddhita* suffix, the relationship with the oblation—which is presented by a separate word—is obtained precisely through the direct word-hearing (*śruti*) within the same compound term. Thus, the superiority of the *taddhita* suffix is logically established.

Alternatively, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is simply that which is to be offered (*pradeya*). The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with the meaning of the suffix by way of the relation of being the specifier of the deityhood (*devatātva*) residing in itself. By this much alone, Indra and others acquire their status as deities. Since the purport of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) lies precisely in the cognition [of the deity] through a relation constituted by deityhood—and not in [the cognition] having that [deityhood] as its qualifier—there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule; for its purport indeed resides in the cognition of deityhood itself, and not merely in [the cognition] characterized by it.

They say that the intended meaning is that even the cognition of the aforementioned relation necessarily has "deityhood" (*devatātva*) as its object. And deityhood—according to the commentary on the sūtra *devāt tal* [Pāṇini 4.2.24], which states that a deity (*devatā*) is derived from the root *div* in the sense of sovereignty—is the state of being the substratum of a fruit other than the fruits such as heaven produced by the relinquishment of an oblation (*havis*) performed with a mantra as the instrument, as well as the state of being praised by a mantra; this is established in the *Anukramaṇikā*.

It has also been stated that "he whose word [it is] is the seer (ṛṣi), and that by which it is uttered is the deity. For this very reason, there is the establishment of the two-fold usage in the mantra dedicated to Indra as "indrasya haviḥ" (the oblation of Indra). Furthermore, the fruit residing in the deity is simply the cognition consisting of the desire, "May this fruit be his. Regarding the mantra beginning with "ka idam kasmā adāt," which produces for the recipient the sense of ownership and results in the cessation of anxiety, the qualification "having a mantra as its instrument" is applied to the oblation and the animal victim.

In the *darśa* and other *śrāddha* rites, the inclusion of "being the object of dedication" (*uddeśyatva*) is for the purpose of precluding wives who have died from being [independent] deities. Nor should it be argued that they lack a connection to the fruit of the rite; for by such texts as "One should not give separately to women," their connection to the fruit is indeed established. Furthermore, even in *śrāddhas* performed by Śūdras and others, there is no inconsistency regarding the status of their ancestors as deities, because there exists a mantra in the form of a salutation (*namaskāra*).
