This is because of the *Gautama-smṛti*: "A salutation is permitted as his mantra. The details of this and other points are explained elsewhere at length.

"Even by way of non-difference there is concomitance (*anvaya*). The word "even" (*api*) is used to indicate that concomitance through the relation of difference is not possible, because that [relation] is sublated. Alternatively, the word "even" is employed to exclude concomitance through the relation of possessing the property of being a deity residing in itself (*svavṛttadevatātvarūpadharmavatva*). || 53 ||

"By means of the word *lakṣmī* itself": the meaning is that words such as "fire" (*agni*) and so forth are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the deity Agni and so forth. "Only with respect to what is to be offered": the particle "only" (*eva*) serves to exclude the deity. "Conventional" (*nirūḍha*): the meaning is that it is a conventional metaphorical function (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) possessing beginningless intentionality (*anāditātparya*). By this, the cognition [of the deity] is consistently maintained in the form of being a deity. "Established": established in the treatises of the Mīmāṃsakas and others. "In that case, there is direct denotative power" (*śakti*): "in that case" refers to the substance to be offered.

Even though there is no denotative power (*śakti*) for the substance itself—which is already obtainable from words such as "curd" (*dadhi*)—it is possible to obtain a qualified meaning through the connection of the deity, which is obtained by the suffix, with that substance via a relation such as being the qualifier of the deityhood residing in itself. The phrase "from the cognition of that" means from the cognition of the substance. And [the phrase] "and because of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) implies that, in accordance with the requirement for the connection of non-difference (*abheda*), the denotative power of the suffix in that context is necessary; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the connection of the deity through the aforementioned relationship is not tenable, as it would contradict the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that [the suffix] does not denote the meaning of two non-nominal bases (*anāmārtha*). Nor should it be argued: "Since the substance qualified by the deity is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), let there simply be a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*); what is the need for postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) of the suffix with respect to the offering-substance (*pradeya*)? For if that were the case, the offering-substance would fail to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the primary base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), because there is a rule that the meaning indicated (*dyotya*) by a suffix must necessarily be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Otherwise, even in cases such as *aupagavaḥ*, the suffix would result in being merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

"Otherwise"—that is, if one does not admit a denotative power (*śakti*) in the *pradeya* (the substance to be offered) in order to conform to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). "It would not be established" refers to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), and so forth. "Only the deityhood" (*devatātva*): rather than postulating a power in the individual deity, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate the power in the property of deityhood itself; the idea is that the property of deityhood will then be construed through the relation of being its own qualifier (*svanirūpakatva*). "Expressibility like that of the agent" (*kartṛvat vācyatvam*): [this means that the deity is expressed by the suffix just as the agent is].

Just as in the Mīmāṃsaka system, the agent is not the denotation of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), but rather the *bhāvanā* itself due to parsimony (*lāghava*), since the substratum is obtained from another word and because the cognition qualified by agency is possible through the very connection of the agency—which is of the nature of *bhāvanā*—with that [suffix], so too here, since the specific [object] is obtainable through the connection of the deityhood (the meaning of the suffix) with the offering-substance (*pradeya*) obtained from another word, the capacity of the suffix for the offering-substance would not be established.

This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because by the statement "āmikṣā [is] connected with the deity," the capacity [of the word *āmikṣā*] is understood by them with respect to the substance to be offered (*pradeya*). If, in this case, the assumption of capacity with respect to the substance to be offered is made out of deference to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) would likewise have to denote the agent, on account of the experienced coreferentiality between the agent and Devadatta in the sentence "Devadatta cooks. This refutation is to be understood according to the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokana-nyāya*).

[Objection: Surely, since the deity Agni and others are obtained through primary denotation (*śakti*) itself by the word "Agni" and so forth, what is the purpose of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? [Reply: To this he says, "the nature of being a deity" (*devatātva*). He states the meaning of the term *nirūḍha*: "due to the impossibility [of the literal sense]" (*anupapatti*). Even in the absence of knowledge of the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there is the possibility of knowledge of the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparya*); thus, having raised the doubt regarding inconsistency, he says "beginningless" (*anādi*). The meaning is: being delimited by that beginningless usage which occurs with respect to the indicated object (*lakṣya*). And the status of the usage as a delimiter is by way of the relation of being the object (*karmatā-sambandhena*).

"At the root" means that this is the very direction and this is the very method. Regarding "in this [context]": [it refers to] the *dāṇḍa* and other [derivatives] ending in the suffix *ṇa*, as taught by this sūtra.

In the word *śabda*, the phrase "qualified by a weapon" (*praharaṇaviśiṣṭa*) is to be construed with the word "its meaning" (*asyārthaḥ*). "Meaning" (*arthaḥ*) refers here to the meaning of the suffix *ṇa*. In that context, the stick (*daṇḍa*), which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is construed non-differently (*abheda*) with "weapon" (*praharaṇa*), which is one part of the meaning of the suffix *ṇa*—namely, the play qualified by a weapon. One who cannot accept this partial construal (*ekadeśe'nvayam*) asserts that there are separate powers (*śakti*) for "weapon" and "play" individually. In this alternative view, the "weapon" conjoined with the stick is construed with "play" through the relation of being its locus (*āśrayatva*).

For the sake of brevity, he says "mere play" (*krīḍāmātram*). By the word "mere" (*mātra*), striking (*praharaṇa*) is excluded. The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), such as "staff" (*daṇḍa*), is construed with the suffixal meaning through the relation of being the specifier of the state of being a striking that resides in itself. Alternatively, in this view, it should be understood that the word "staff" has a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) for "striking with a staff. Others, however, say that the state of being a striking (*praharaṇatva*) is the meaning of the suffix, as is "play"; the relation here is that the meaning of the base is the locus (*ādheyatva*) within the state of being a striking, and that [state] is the specifier (*nirūpakatva*) of the play.

The meaning is that, by this connection, the word *praharaṇa* (weapon) found in the sūtra serves to indicate the intended sense (*tātparya*) regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). [Regarding the sūtra] "that is his residence" (*so'sya nivāsaḥ*): *sughoṣa* is the residence—that is, the locus of residence.

*Bhūto'sya straughnaḥ* (The full moon day occurred in this [month]). Here, as before, three alternative interpretations (*pakṣa*) are to be inferred; the cognition [of the meaning] begins with "that which is related to the locus of residence non-different from Strughna," and so forth. *Sāsmin paurṇamāsī* (That full moon day occurs in this). The meaning of this rule is that an affix occurs after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of "that full moon day occurs in this. The word *iti* is for the purpose of ensuring that [the formation] applies when there is a name (*saṃjñā*); that is to say, provided that the aggregate of base and suffix is conventionally established as a name. An example is *caitro māsaḥ* (the month Caitra).

In this context, for the sake of brevity, the meaning of several unmentioned secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) is being examined. The word *caitrī* and others are feminine forms ending in the suffix *ḍīp*, derived from bases ending in the secondary suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "time joined with a non-nakṣatra [constellation]" (*anākṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*). In that regard, words such as *citryā* (from *citryā*) refer to the moon as conjoined with the respective nakṣatra [such as Citrā] which serves as its own referent; otherwise, since all nakṣatras exist at all times, there would result the undesirable consequence of such usages as "Today is Caitra" occurring at all times.

In this case, only the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is appropriate, and not time as well; for, by parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more fitting that only that which is an actual entity (*vastusat*) serves as the cause for the production of the suffix, and because such [time] can be obtained through words such as "day" (*ahar*) and so forth. Thus, the cognition produced by words such as *caitra*—meaning "conjoined with the moon when the *citrā* constellation is present"—is as follows: the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) following the word *caitra* has as its suffix-meaning the fact of being the locus of the full moon (*pūrṇimā*). Here too, as before, the three possible positions (*pakṣatraya*) are to be inferred; the resulting cognition is: "the locus of such a full moon."

Even though there is no fixed rule regarding the conjunction with specific constellations such as Citrā on each respective full moon day, in expressions such as "the Caitrī full moon," it is precisely the *yogyatā* (fitness or potentiality) for conjunction with those respective constellations that is intended. This is because the usage "Caitrī full moon" occurs even when there is no actual conjunction with that constellation, and because of usages such as "Caitra" and "Vaiśākha" [which name months regardless of the lunar day].

And "suitability" (*yogyatā*) consists in being conjoined with one or another of the constellations adjacent to its own; for the months from Caitra to Śrāvaṇa, conjunction with any of the pairs beginning with Citrā is the cause for such conventional usage. For Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja, it is conjunction with any one of the triad beginning with Śatabhiṣaj or Revatī. For the months from Kārtika to Māgha, it is conjunction with any of the pairs beginning with Kṛttikā. For Phālguna, however, it is conjunction with any one of the triad beginning with Pūrvā-phālgunī—such is the distinction. And so it is stated in the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*: "When there is a full-moon conjunction with the pairs of stars beginning with Citrā..."
"The months beginning with Caitra are to be known as having three [nakṣatras] each, ending with the sixtieth [day];
and elsewhere: "The last two [months] are to be known as having three [nakṣatras] each, and Phālguna is considered to have three;
the remaining months are to be known as having two [nakṣatras] each, according to the arrangement starting from Kṛttikā."

The last two [months] are Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja. Since the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of terms such as "Caitra" is accepted as referring to the aggregate of thirty days beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight and ending with the new moon (*darśa*), there is no risk of the term "Caitra" being applied to any arbitrary collection of thirty days that merely includes the full moon of Caitra.

However, there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the entire collection beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), because such a meaning is not widely established therein. Furthermore, since a month comprised of the full moon is lunar (*cāndra*), and according to traditional law (*smṛti*)—such as "The lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon" (*darśānta*)—as well as due to the abundance of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), it is proper to accept only that which begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon. They say that the usage [of the term "month"] for the period beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight and ending with the full moon is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Mādhavācārya, however, maintains that because both the *darśānta* (ending with the new moon) and *pūrṇimānta* (ending with the full moon) systems are seen in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, there is an equal option between them; yet the followers of the Atharva Veda, in the section on creation, record only the creation of months and fortnights within the creation of the year and the southern and northern solstices: "Prajāpati is indeed the month; his delight is the dark fortnight, and the bright [fortnight] is his life-breath. In this context, the fact that the dark fortnight is mentioned first is a *liṅga* (indicative mark) for the month beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*).
[As it is said: "In the month of Bhādrapada, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, at midnight..."
"The constellation of Prajāpati is known as Jayantī. Thus it is remembered.

The Smṛti passage situated in the section on Jayantī is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "One should perform the Śrāddha day after day during the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja. Furthermore, the Smṛti passage situated in the section on Mahālaya is an indicative mark for the fact that [the rite] begins from the first day of the bright fortnight; otherwise, since that fortnight would fall within the month of Bhādrapada, it would lack connection with Āśvayuja, resulting in an inconsistency. The specific practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is also an indicative mark, as is the duty of ascetics (*yati-dharma*).

In the *Prakaraṇa*, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "They have their hair shaved during the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtusandhi*). However, ascetics (*yati*) shave only on the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*) and not on the new moon day (*darśa*); otherwise, they would perform the shaving on that [new moon] day as well. They say that the settled rule regarding the performance [of the rite] is determined by specific scriptural injunctions and the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). According to this view, it is understood that the conventional usage of terms such as *Caitra* applies to both the end of the new moon and the end of the full moon; enough of this excessive detail.

In expressions such as *gomān* ("possessing cows"), the suffix *matup* is applied according to the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup*. In this context, the meaning of the suffix consists of both the related object (*saṃbandhī*) and the relation (*saṃbandha*), as well as the substratum (*āśraya*). Here, the present tense is intended by the word "exists" (*asti*); otherwise, if the cows were past or future, the form ending in *matup* would result in being grammatically incorrect. Thus, the word "cow" (*go*) and so forth refers to its own meaning as possessing present existence. Consequently, the cognition produced is: "one who possesses a relation with cows that have present existence."

In cases such as *gomān-as-ī*, however, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain in their treatises that there is no inconsistency, because the word *gomat* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the object of the usage of that [derived] word. "Pāṇinīya" means "proclaimed by Pāṇini. Here, "being proclaimed" (*proktatva*) does not mean "made manifest through teaching," for if it did, the form *sauśarmaṇam* would result for the *Kāṭhaka* when taught by Suśarman. Nor does it mean "composed," because if that were the case, this rule would be redundant since the formation would already be established by the rule "after a name for a work that is composed" (*kṛte granthe*).

If it is objected that since the Veda is eternal and thus lacks the quality of being "composed" (*kṛta*), expressions such as *taittirīyam* (the Taittirīya) or *kāṭhakam* (the Kāṭhaka)—which imply authorship—are untenable, we say no; for the objection is resolved in the Bhāṣya itself: "Even though the meaning is eternal, that which is the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is non-eternal."

If it is argued that—because at the time of dissolution there is no person to utter [the Veda], the sequence [of sounds] perishes; yet, upon its re-emergence, the sages, through the excellence of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), remember the meaning of the Vedas and compose the arrangement of words—and that even though the meaning remains the same, the usage of terms such as "Kaṭha" and so forth is based solely on differences in sequence; and therefore, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement, "Kaṭha and others are the authors and the proclaimers of the Vedic sequences"—we say: no, for "proclaimed-ness" (*proktatva*) means being first made manifest, and that [status] is common to both what is composed by oneself and what is composed by another.

And thus, since Mādhura composed his commentary (*vṛtti*) after [the text] had already been first published by him, the application of the term *mādhurī* is justified because the rule "proclaimed by him" (*tena proktam*) is necessary [to derive that name]. However, as Suśarman did not first publish the *Kāṭhaka*, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the very sūtra "proclaimed by him," where it is indicated that in the phrase "the sequence of phonemes" (*varṇānupūrvī*), the word *varṇa* refers to the word (*śabda*), and therefore there is no identity with the individual words [of the text]. Accordingly, the traditional law (*smṛti*) states:
"In every Manvantara, this Śruti is ordained in another form."
"This Blessed One is the Self-Existent Veda sung by you in ancient times;
from Śiva down to the sages, they are its rememberers, not its creators."
"At the end of the age, the great sages, having been authorized by the Self-born (Brahmā), recovered through austerity the Vedas along with the Itihāsas that had been hidden away.

These two Smṛti texts, however, are justified because their subject matter is not eternal; this is explained in detail elsewhere. "The fifth" means that which completes the group of five; here, [the suffix] *tasya*...

By the rule *pūraṇe ḍaṭ*, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied; by the rule *nāntād asaṃkhyādeḥ*, the augment *maṭ* is added to it. The relation [of the base-meaning] to the meaning of the suffix is the state of being the completer (*pūraṇatva*) of the number five residing in itself. The resulting cognition is: "the completer of the number five residing in itself. Completer-ness (*pūraṇatva*) is the state of being the cause for the completion of that specific number residing in itself. As for the objection that this would lead to the application of the term "third" and so on to the second and subsequent [members], that is not accepted by him [the author of the rule]. For this very reason, [the rule] "A grammatical operation concerning words applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*) is placed at the beginning of the eighth chapter.

This conventional usage is dependent upon a limit established within the intellect; thus, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. For example: "As is Hari, so is Hara. Here, the suffix *thāl*—by the rule "the suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a manner" (*prakāravacane thāl*)—expresses the sense of a manner (*prakāravat*), because of the requirement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and because of the inclusion of the word "expression" (*vacana*). However, this does not constitute an exception to suffixes such as *jātīya*, for we see the usage of the suffix *jātīya* in the *Bhāṣya*: "of that same kind" (*tathājātīyakaḥ*).

In this context, a *prakāra* (qualifier) is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that differentiates a generality. Thus, the cognition is: "Hara possesses those same specific attributes that Hari possesses. When the identity of the two attributes is understood through the pronouns *yat* and *tat*, the similarity of Hara to Hari results as the final meaning. Now, one might object: let "similarity" itself be the meaning of the suffix; in this way, the verbal cognition established by experience—namely, "Hara is similar to that which is similar to Hari"—would be explained as having "similarity" as its qualifier. This is not so, because such a meaning is not perceived in cases such as "otherwise" (*anyathā*) or "in another way" (*itarathā*). Furthermore, [the suffix is used] in expressions like "grapes are like molasses" (*guḍakalpā drākṣā*) and "full of molasses" (*bahuguḍo*).

In the word *drākṣā*, by the two rules—"The suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are used in the sense of slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*)" and "Optionally, the suffix *bahuc* follows a nominal stem (*sup*), but it may optionally precede it"—the suffixes *kalpa* and *bahuc* occur in the sense of denoting something slightly incomplete; the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is for the purpose of allowing these suffixes to apply even after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*), where they have scope. The word *guḍa* refers to that which resembles molasses (*guḍasadṛśa*), while the suffix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). Therefore...

Thus, the feminine gender in "guḍakalpā drākṣā" (grape slightly like molasses) and the masculine gender in "bahuguḍo drākṣaḥ" (grape with much molasses) are both accounted for; this is because it is an inherent property of suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) whether they deviate from or do not deviate from the gender and number of the base word (*prakṛti*). However, if similarity were the meaning of the suffix, then in the case of "bahuguḍo drākṣaḥ," there would be the undesirable consequence of the feminine gender belonging to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) [since the suffix would be feminine]. Here, what is perceived as the basis for the similarity is the sweetness and so forth that completes the word-meaning (*padārtha-samāptatva*); therefore, the suffix does not arise when there is only slight similarity. The understanding is "the grape is similar to molasses," and thus a comparison (*upamā*) is conveyed.

Others, however, maintain that because of the similarity [of the grape] to molasses, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the nature of molasses (*guḍatva*) upon the grape; and since the universal of molaseness (*guḍatvajāti*) is actually absent from the grape, one says "the nature of molasses is only partially present in the grape. Thus, they claim that the resulting cognition has the nature of molasses as its qualifier (*prakāraka*). According to the author of the *Mañjūṣā*, however, the cognition is that "the grape is non-different from the molasses which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)."

Others, however, hold that the meaning of the suffix is the completion of the word in the form of similarity (*sādṛśya*); and because of the superimposed non-difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality, the syntactic connection with "grapes" (*drākṣā*) and so forth is established. Alternatively, the meaning of the suffix is "that which possesses similarity," or the two meanings [of the compound] are the substrata of that similarity. As for the objection regarding the unaccountability of the usage "grapes with much molasses" (*bahuguḍā drākṣā*), it does not apply; for according to the explanation in the *vibhāṣā*-sūtra—whereby, through the repetition of the word "purastāt" (beforehand) as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), it is understood that "everything occurs only before"—those [elements] which were seen prior to the production of the suffix [are what is intended].

Only these two—gender and number—are [the meanings]; and the word *tu* is not intended to exclude the status of being "subsequent" (*pratyayaparatva*) by accepting that the application occurs "before" the base (*prakṛti*), because that is already established by the very fact that this rule serves as an exception (*apavādaka*). Nor should it be argued that since the word *vibhāṣā* is connected with the phrase "before" (*purastāt*), there would be an option regarding priority, and consequently, posteriority might also occur; for the purpose of excluding that, the word *tu* has a restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇārtha*). This is because, unlike the case of "udaśvito 'nyatarasyām" where posteriority is optionally applied, here priority is not subject to optionality.

They say that, according to the maxim "because qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another," and because it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the suffix itself is postulated due to its predominance, [the suffix *kan* applies]. In examples such as *pācakakaḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *kutsite* to the word *pācaka*, which denotes an object qualified by contempt; the resulting cognition is "one who possesses a contemptible act of cooking. However, when contempt regarding the primary ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is impossible—as in *aśvakaḥ* and similar cases—the suffix is motivated by contempt directed toward other properties associated with that [primary ground]. In cases such as *kutsitakaḥ*, [the suffix is applied to the word *kutsita* itself].

The suffix is conditioned by the state of being contemptible (*kutsitatva*) and the cause of that contempt; its state of being contemptible is not intrinsic, but rather the contempt is attributed to it by enemies out of hatred. Alternatively, the suffix occurs only when the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is indeed a contemptible quality, in order to convey a necessary connection with contempt. Furthermore, since the contempt applies to the complete meaning [of the base] itself, the suffix *kan* is added directly to the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because the contempt pertains to the very meaning expressed by that word ending in a case-suffix.

The contempt residing in the substance, the gender, and so forth, is conveyed by the suffix *kan*. In this regard: in the case of "paṇḍitaka" (pseudo-scholar), there is contempt for the ground of application (*pravṛttinimitta*); in "śuklakaṃ rūpam" (white color), there is contempt for the substance; in "paśya gāṇḍīvadhanvānaṃ viddhi koravakān striyaḥ" (Behold the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; know the Kauravas as women), there is contempt for the gender; and in "putrakaḥ śatam" (a hundred sons), there is contempt for the number one, because of the realization that the suffering involved in supporting a hundred is the same as that involved in supporting only one—this is the general direction.

In the case of *aśvaka* (a small horse), the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *ive pratikṛtau* ("the suffix *kan* is used after a word ending in *iva* when it denotes a likeness"). The resulting cognition is either "this is non-different from one similar to a horse" or "this is non-different from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) which is a horse. In the latter case, the cognition arises from the nominal stem ending in the suffix (*pratyayānta*), namely *upamānāśva*. Its connection with the object of comparison (*upameya*)—which is the referent of the word *tasyeda* (belonging to that)—is based on a superimposed identity rooted in similarity. In the case of images, paintings, banners, or statues of venerable beings, there is only the cognition of non-difference from Śiva and others; since there is no perception of the meaning of *iva*, the suffix *kan* is not used.

This is clearly stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* during the discussion on *rasa*: "In that context, [it is said] ‘Rāma’ is apprehended by the intellect as being present in the actor," and so forth. In the compound *kākatālīya*, the latter member (*tāla-patana*)—which refers to the falling of the palm fruit—is used as a point of comparison (*upamāna*) co-referential with the previously mentioned meaning of the former member (*kākāgamana*), which refers to the arrival of the crow. There is no inclusion of the former member’s referent within the referent of the latter member; rather, such a formulation is intended solely to convey that the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has the referent of the former member as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, there is no lack of syntactic expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*).

When the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), such as "crow's coming" (*kākāgamana*), stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a portion of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then—either in the latter case, the relation consisting of that coreferentiality [is present] in the substratum (*dharmin*); or precisely because of this presence of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), the formation of the compound is justified. It is not correct, however, to argue that the subsequent member refers merely to the falling and so forth inherent in its own primary meaning, and that there is no inclusion of the coreferential element within that meaning, since the semantic capacity is established by the possibility of a relation between the meanings of the prior and subsequent members in the form of coreferentiality; for coreferentiality itself lacks the status of being a relation.

For this very reason, in expressions such as "Caitra’s brother" (*caitrasya bhrātā*), a relationship denoted by the genitive case is not possible [if it were simply co-residence], because if that were the case, a relationship would exist between two travelers who happen to stay together for one night in the same place; and consequently, the usage "Yajñadatta’s Devadatta" would also occur there. Anticipating this objection, it is resolved in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* that the meaning of the genitive is a conceptual relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*).

However, for two travelers (*pānthau*), such a relationship cannot be postulated, because no such usage exists. By this, the view that "precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), a compound occurs even in the absence of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*)" is refuted; for, according to the method described above, semantic competency is indeed possible. The aggregate term *kākatāla* refers to the object of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, the cognition produced by the compound is as follows: "The arrival of Devadatta, which is coreferential with the arrival of the beloved, is non-different from the falling of the palm tree, which is coreferential with the arrival of the crow (the standard of comparison)."

In the cognition of the relationship between the qualified subject (*upameya*) and the qualified object (*upamāna*), that [cognition] culminates in the [recognition of] the qualifiers and the qualificands; the co-occurrence with the respective words denoting the subject is the regulator. Consequently, when a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is present, the meaning of the compound is that object of comparison, namely: the falling of the palm fruit (*tāla-nipatana*) which is coreferential with the crow’s arrival (*kākāgamana*), and the meaning of the compound is non-different from the enjoyment of the palm fruit split by the crow acting as the agent—which serves as the object of comparison—whereas the object of comparison is the meeting with Devadatta, which is coreferential with the beloved woman’s arrival.

The resulting cognition is that "the enjoyment of the beloved has Devadatta as its agent. In both cases, a non-difference based on similarity between the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameya) is determined; this is just as, in the expression "dark as a cloud" (*ghanaśyāma*), the relationship of being the instigator and the instigated between the referent of the term *ghanaśyāma* and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is understood through the power of the collective denotation (*samudāyaśakti*).

Others, however, hold that the first member of the compound is metaphorical (lākṣaṇika), resembling the flight of a crow (*kākāgamana*), and that the relation [of the compound] is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two indicated meanings; or else, the first member itself is metaphorical, being coreferential with that which resembles the flight of a crow, and thus the relation between the two is simply identity. Consequently, the cognition produced by the compound is: "that which is coreferential with what resembles the flight of a crow is similar to the falling of a palm fruit coreferential with the flight of a crow. Then, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "like" (*iva*); this is the case regarding the function of the word ending in the suffix *cha*.

The term *kākatāla* possesses a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) directed toward the event brought about by the meeting of the crow and the palmyra fruit. This brought-about event is understood—depending on the context—to be either the crow’s consumption of the palmyra fruit or the crow’s being killed by the palmyra fruit, due to its co-occurrence with words denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*). The brought-about event is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the similarity. The resulting cognition is: "Devadatta’s enjoyment of his beloved is similar to that which was brought about by the meeting of the crow and the palmyra fruit. Furthermore, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) arises through the suddenness of the occurrence, by virtue of the co-occurrence of the specific words denoting the object of comparison; [this involves] the delimitor of the state of being the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedaka*)...

Alaṃkārikas accept that there is a simile based on the cognition of non-understanding (*abodhapratyaya*) in the form of "the enjoyment of palm fruits by such a crow" or "the killing by such [a person]," provided that the definition of a sentence is not accepted; however, they state that if the definition of a sentence is not accepted, then—as before—there is a conventional metaphor (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) other than that [primary sense] of the word *tāla* itself, which is to be applied as previously described. This should be inferred in other cases as well. The details, however, should be sought from the *Mañjūṣā* and similar works; enough with this elaboration.

This follows from the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (P. 2.1.1). The sense of the rule *tasyāpatyam* (P. 4.1.92) and others is that a suffix is introduced when the meaning is "the offspring related to that. Thus, even though a suffix would not apply to the word *upagu* in the intended sense "the offspring of Upagu belonging to Caitra" (*vastram upagoḥ apatyaṃ caitrasya*), the Paribhāṣā regarding semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) must necessarily apply even in the case of *taddhita* suffixes; this is the underlying point. The phrase "by a specific power alone" (*viśiṣṭa-śaktyaiva*) means by the power of the whole [word] residing specifically in the meaning of the respective base and its relation.

Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of secondary suffixes (*taddhita-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "without division" (*avibhāgena*): the meaning is that all numbers appear in the form of the universal property of number (*saṃkhyātva*). Regarding the phrase "having abandoned its particulars" (*parityakta-viśeṣam*): in this view, there is the appearance of the universal of number alone in the form of the universal property of number, and not of its particulars; this is the distinction from the previous position. Although this is impossible because a universal cannot exist unqualified by its particulars, there is no fault, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpātmaka*) is possible—just as in the cases of "the son of a barren woman" or "the head of Rāhu. As it has been said: "For a word produces a cognition even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent."

In both views, regarding the expression "rājapuruṣa" (the king’s man), the cognition is that of one related to the king who possesses number. Regarding the "portion of the universal"—that is, the nature of number—the operation [of the word] is its manifestation in that very form. "By means of the exclusion of difference" (bhedāpohena) means: by means of that exclusion of difference which is the negation of what is other than itself (atadvyāvṛtti); it exists by that, meaning it manifests in that form. The intended meaning of the universal is precisely this exclusion of what is other. [The phrase] "not grasped" [is explained as follows]:

Just as a form (*rūpa*) is perceived from a distance as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and not as "whiteness" (*śuklatva*) and so forth, so too it is the universal (*sāmānya*) itself that appears as "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*); thus, in some way, there is an analogy. In the phrase "not white, etc.," the word "by means of whiteness, etc. (*śuklatvādinā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. For this very reason, even though it appears through the form of "form-ness," there is no inconsistency. Alternatively, the meaning of "white, etc. (*śuklādi*) is "qualified by whiteness, etc. (*śuklatvādiviśiṣṭa*); thus, there is no need to supply the word "iti. Previously, it was stated that "that" is the nature of the exclusion of difference (*bhedāpoha*) which conforms to a specific number.

Now, the distinction is that it consists of the manifestation (*saṃbhāra*) of all differentiated things; [this refers to] "of that"—namely, of the number whose nature is non-dual unity. The term "the number of non-dual unity" is used as a designation for a number from which differentiation has dissolved. He states another view regarding the cognition of that [number] as one: "of that," meaning as a single entity—that is, as being one. "As in the case of the *kapiñjala* birds," etc.

In the injunction "one should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds," only three are indicated by the plural number because they are the first to be presented in the act of counting; likewise, in the present case, the meaning is that oneness in the form of non-dual unity appears as oneness. The phrase "in that form" means "precisely in the form of three. The meaning is that plurality is simply the form of three and so forth. He refutes the view that the number of non-dual unity appears in the compound (*vṛtti*) with the words "but in reality."

The appearance of that [number] in the form of oneness (*ekatva*) is utterly improper; rather, it is as number (*saṃkhyātva*). Otherwise, the aforementioned inquiry would not arise in cases such as "the king's servant" (*rājapuruṣa*). Nor can one accept this as a desired conclusion, for it would entail the maxim: "While you desire the interest, even your principal is lost. It has been stated in the section on compounds (*samāsa-prakaraṇa*) that in cases such as "the king's servant," one or many individuals appear in the function (*vṛtti*) by way of their respective property-delimitors (*tattat-padārthatāvacchedaka-rūpeṇa*), but not as possessing number.

It should not be argued that this [objection] is inconsistent because, although a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) characterized by specific attributes arises from words such as "brāhmaṇa," one does not admit that the word [itself] is denotative (*vācaka*) of that [attribute]. For in that case (the former instance), there is no necessary arising of the desire to know, whereas here (the latter instance), there is a necessary arising of it; thus, the intention is that if no other means of presenting that [attribute] exists, denotativeness would be required for its presentation. In reality, however, the emphasis lies precisely in the absence of such a desire to know, and this is not a flaw in the present argument. The details should be sought in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa* and other works. || 56 ||

Thus concludes the determination of the number "one" as non-differentiation. Regarding the statement "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine is that in such cases, the act of cleansing is enjoined with reference to the cups (*grahān*)—which are already established by other sentences—and therefore the qualification residing in the object of reference (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant; consequently, the cleansing of all cups is not established. This [Mīmāṃsā position] cannot be accepted by the Grammarians, because it would lead to inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) in rules such as *dhātoḥ* ("after a verbal root"). The sense is that if unity were not intended to be significant there, then suffixes would result even after a collection of verbal roots (*dhātusamudāya*).

He states that even the authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* agree that the singular number is intended in the rule *dhātoḥ*, saying: "it would arise" (*utpadyeta*). Regarding the phrase "arising from a *dvandva*": just as when a case-ending arises from a *dvandva* compound, all the constituent members of that *dvandva* are qualified by the number and other meanings of that case-ending, so too, if a suffix were to arise from a collection of verbal roots (*dhātu-samudāya*), then as many root-meanings as there are would be connected with the meaning of the suffix. This is the sense.

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication); it should also be understood that when the designation "member" (*aṅga*) applies to a whole (*samudāya*), then the *aṭ* augment and so forth would belong to that [whole]. Now, one might raise the objection: "By the force of the previously mentioned counter-argument (*bādhaka*), even if there is a desire to specify the qualifier of the thing restated (*anuvādya*) as conveyed by the affix (*pratyaya*), there would still be a desire to specify that which is conveyed by the base (*prakṛti*), since there is no counter-argument against that. He dispels this doubt with the words "of the *ārdhadhātuka*."

Alternatively, if one accepts the meaning as "an affix [occurring] after that which is the locus of the pervasion of non-dhātu-hood," then because the entire aggregate lacks the status of being the locus of the pervasion of dhātu-hood, there would be no occurrence of an affix after an aggregate of roots; thus, the intentionality (*vivakṣā*) regarding singularity would have no utility in that context. To this, he says: "of the *ārdhadhātuka*. [The result] would not be obtained. Nor can that be obtained through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), for in that case, prolixity (*gaurava*) would result; and it is exactly so.

And [the author] has done this because of the extreme brevity [attained] by not employing the suffix *kṛt*; it is like the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). Just as in that instance, having referred back to the sacrifice already established by another sentence, the singularity residing in the animal is intended to be significant; for that very reason, since the performance of a sacrifice using multiple animals does not result in the attainment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the rule established in Mīmāṃsā—that an attribute residing in the thing to be enjoined is indeed intended—is not present even in the view of the Grammarians (*śābdika*). He states the reason for this with the words "from *radābhyām*."

[Objection: "But surely, because of the use of the word *ca* (and) there, it is understood that the author of the Sūtras intended a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) itself; thus, the acquisition of two *na*s is entirely unimpeded. To this, he says: "In the case of *ādguṇaḥ*," etc. [He adds: "Because of the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyāpatti*). The sense is as follows: if the qualifier of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇa*) were necessarily intended to be significant, then since only a single substitute—such as a *guṇa*—would be established for the single locus consisting of both the preceding and following sounds, the inclusion of the word *eka* (one) would clearly be redundant. Therefore, Pāṇini’s intention is indeed [that the qualifier is not always significant]; the restriction [that it must always be significant] is not what he intends.

Likewise, it should be understood that there is no fixed rule that something must necessarily be unintended (*avivakṣā*). For instance, in the sūtra *upeyivān*, we observe that while *upeta* is unintended, the negative particle (*nañ*) and other elements are intended. This refers to what is intended and what is not intended within a given system (*tantra*), which amounts to saying "intentionality and non-intentionality" (*tātparya-atātparya*). Intention (*vivakṣā*) is the desire to communicate; it is the cause for whether a number is intended or not intended, based on conformity with the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). [This is illustrated by the example] "resting upon a single rib."

For in that case, by virtue of the proximity of being conveyed by the same suffix (*samānapratyayopāttatva*), number is construed with the *kāraka* which is the meaning of the suffix; there, according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the meaning of the suffix first connects with the action, and subsequently with the meaning of the stem. Thus, the cognition arises: "The sacrifice has both the animal and the singularity as its instruments. When the question arises—"What is the substrate of this singularity?"—it is stated that there occurs a subsequent mental cognition (*pāṣṇika-mānasa-bodha*) to the effect that "the animal is one."

If the singularity of the cup (*graha*) were intended to be expressed, there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in enjoining both the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) and the singularity with reference to the cup. To explain: if one were to enjoin the cleansing by way of restating the cups already prescribed in such sentences as "The cups dedicated to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyā grahāḥ*), the verbal formulation would have to be "he cleanses the cup and that [cup] is one," which is clearly a syntactical split. As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"But the cups are enjoined elsewhere individually with distinct numbers, such as 'nine cups for Prajāpati' and other such variations."
"When the subsidiaries have been understood as such, how could the number mentioned in the instruction regarding the primary acts be intended [to be restrictive]?

Others, however, argue that because the number nine and so forth is heard in the originative injunction (utpattivākya), it is understood through the injunction itself and is conveyed by words such as "nine. Thus, its...

Because the number is intended to be expressed, the planets perceived as qualified by that very number are denoted by the word "planets" (*graha*). Consequently, when their oneness is conveyed by a case-ending in the recollection—which is qualified by that same number—there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the sublation of the number present in the initial statement. It is clearly stated in Helārāja’s commentary on the *Hari-kārikās* that this is precisely what is meant by the "syntactical split" mentioned by the Mīmāṃsakas.

Alternatively, because there is a contradiction between the number mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) and the number mentioned in this [subsequent] injunction, the two sentences would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Nor should it be argued that while the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is enjoined with reference to the cups (*graha*), the singularity is enjoined with reference to the cups being cleansed; for it is impossible for two things presented by a single word to stand in the relation of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), and because it is impossible for the act of cleansing to enter into the category of the subject. They say that the fault of syntactical split remains as it was. (57)

"Because of the consequence of an infinite series of *yakāra*s and so forth. This means that in examples such as *sudhyupāsya*, the rule *iko yaṇaci* would result in an infinite sequence of *yakāra*s and other substitutions. He resolves the previously mentioned objection regarding the redundancy of the mention of "one" (*eka*) with the words "one [substitute] for what precedes" (*ekaḥ pūrva*). As for the phrase "due to the difference in substitutes," this is merely a description of the intention of the author of the Sūtras.

In this context, just as when two heaps of grain are being made into a single mat (*kaṭa*), there is the cognition of a single mat connected with a result qualified by duality, so too—by the mention of the *dvandva* compound "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*)—there is the prescription of a single [element] such as a *guṇa* substitute for both in a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatayā*). Consequently, there is no contingency of multiple *guṇas* and so forth, because there is no reason to disregard the number inherent in the element being prescribed. This has already been refuted at length in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ," as is clear to those who know the texts of the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa, and others.
Regarding the phrase "vākyabheda etc.": as for *vākyabheda* (splitting of the sentence), it is as follows:

It has been described. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), through the accusative case in "the cup" (*graham*), the predominance of the cup—characterized by its being the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*)—is understood. And thus, according to the maxim "the repetition of a subordinate element follows each principal element," and because there is no determining factor [to restrict it otherwise], and because the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) which serves the purpose of removing the soma-drops is required by all the cups, the cleansing is established everywhere; hence, the reason consisting in the absence of any intended result is adopted, just like the qualification "animal" (*paśu*) and so forth, since there is an absence of being a constituent part of the action (*kriyāṅgatva*).

The sense is that there is no resulting deficiency in the ritual action caused by a deficiency in those [subsidiaries] either. Master Jaimini also composed the sūtra for the final conclusion (siddhānta)—"It is common to all because it is the characteristic mark"—following the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) which stated, "It belongs to one alone, because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement regarding oneness."

The meaning of that [statement] is as follows: the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of all [the vessels] must be performed because the genus (*jāti*) "cupness" (*grahatva*) serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for the substance; that is, since it makes the substance known, it is the defining characteristic of the substance, and by the word, the individual instance (*vyakti*) is implied through the genus being expressed. Thus, the final sense is that there is a cognition of all individuals because there is no distinction [between them]. "Not established in the source" (*anākara*) means not proven in the original treatises (*ākara-grantha*), or else contrary to them.

One might object: "In the case of *dhātoḥ* in [Pāṇini 3.1.91] *grahaikatvavat*, and in rules such as *ārdhadhātukasyeṅvalādeḥ* [6.4.24], there would likewise be a lack of intention (*avivakṣā*) regarding singularity, the quality of beginning with *val*, and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he says: "qualified by singularity" (*ekatvaviśiṣṭam*). He adds: "as the subject" (*uddiśya*). Thus, the meaning is that in those instances, because it is possible for the reference (*anuvāda*) to be qualified by singularity and the like, there can be a lack of intention regarding singularity and so on. || 58 ||

If it is argued that when singularity is intended to be expressed, the suffix should arise from only one verbal root and not from another root, we say: no. This is because each of all [the roots] possesses singularity individually; thus, in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), it is possible for the suffix to be established as arising even from other individual instances. The manner in which the expression of singularity regarding the "cup" (*graha*) is possible according to the stated method has already been explained.

Others, however, argue that since the desired result can be achieved simply by the meaning "an affix occurs when there is a locus possessing the property of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) in its entirety," there is no need to intend singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*). Furthermore, if this were the case, the affix would occur after only one particular root and not after other roots; moreover, the phrase "of all" (*sarveṣām*) and so forth would be inappropriate. For if that were so, in a sentence such as "one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa," it would follow that multiple Brāhmaṇas must be fed. The details should be sought in the commentaries on the *Samartha-sūtra* and related sections.

If it is asked, "What is the authority for the intention to express the number residing in the predicate (vidheya)? the Mīmāṃsakas reply: By virtue of the proximity of being expressed by the same suffix (*samānapratyayopāttatva*), the number connects only with the *kāraka* (the factor of action), and not with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*).

Furthermore, according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the meaning of the case-ending functions as a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The sacrifice has both the animal and its singularity as its instruments. The notion "one animal," however, is merely a secondary, mental [cognition]. Consequently, since singularity is understood through the word itself as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, its expression is necessary.

Others do not accept this, because grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) resides only when the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is construed with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and not when it is construed elsewhere; furthermore, since the *svādi-sūtra* forms a single syntactic unit with rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and "for one or two [things]" (*dvayekayoḥ*), it is clearly the case that if the meaning is "the singular second case is used for a single object," then its grammatical incorrectness is evident whenever number (*ekatva*) is construed elsewhere. Moreover, rather than construing [number] with an action expressed by a different word, it is more appropriate for it to be construed with the meaning of the base itself, since it is observed that only that which is so construed requires an action.

[Objection: "Granted that even if the three sūtras beginning with *svaujasamauṭ* form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*), it is not appropriate for singularity and so forth to be qualifiers of the object (*karman*) and other case-roles; rather, they must be the primary elements as things to be enjoined (*vidheya*), according to the maxim *guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt* (and because subordinate factors exist for the sake of another). Consequently, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would take the form: 'from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), when there is an object and singularity, [the suffix] second-case singular,' and not the other form. Thus, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the relation of the factorhood (*kārakatva*) with the object-role. [Reply: This is not so.

Thus, by the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is established in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works that the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) teach the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those two [the base and the suffix] precisely when they convey a meaning that is mutually connected; furthermore, it is established that the meaning of the suffix (*vibhaktyartha*) functions solely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Therefore, in cases such as "one should lead the animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), it is logical that the singularity is intended (*vivakṣita*), because since the qualified entity is being enjoined (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), there is no possibility of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Since the scripture teaches that the qualified [entity] is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, it is established that—just as in the case of a deficiency in qualifiers such as "animal-hood"—there is also a deficiency in the sacrifice due to the non-performance of the qualified [act] when there is a deficiency in [the number] "one.

Jaimini also stated this in the *Pūrvapakṣa*: "In that case, oneness is not a subsidiary of the sacrifice, because it is subordinate to the object," and then, in response, [he concluded]: "It is perceived as being like the word itself."

Regarding this, the *siddhāntasūtra* has been formulated: "For upon its arrival [in the cognition], its knowledge is seen to be like that of others," just as in the case of a word (*śabda*). Its meaning is as follows: "Just as it is perceived such that it is not understood through the word alone; for when there is its arrival—that is, the arrival of the singular number (*ekavacana*)—the knowledge of its being a subordinate factor (*aṅgatva*) is seen to be like that of others, namely the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) such as 'animal-ness' (*paśutva*) and 'redness' (*lauhitya*) presented by the word. Thus, even for Jaimini, the intention is precisely the cognition of the object as qualified by number. Hari also says:
"In the statement 'one should sacrifice with an animal' (*yajeta paśunā*), even though the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is possible..."
"By which [the suffix], the genus (*jāti*) as well as oneness (*ekatva*) is understood as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Helārāja explains that, according to the principle "the base (*prakṛti*) alone [is not meaningful]," although it is possible for the case-ending (*vibhakti*) to serve the purpose of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), its status as a means of accomplishing an action (*kriyāsādhanatva*) belongs to it just as it does to the genus; the meaning is that only the qualified [entity] (i.e., the base plus the suffix) is presented [to consciousness].

Moreover, since number is formless (*amūrta*), it cannot directly serve as a means to an action; therefore, rather than postulating its status as a means through indirect connection with the action—given that such a postulation would require the aforementioned logical arguments—it is more appropriate to assume its connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). As for the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), however, because it is the meaning of the verbal root, its status as an instrument of purchase can only be established indirectly due to the lack of any other alternative. Thus, every qualifier of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant, as there is no reason for non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*). Furthermore, since the sacrifice is accomplished by a single animal alone...

The immolation of another animal in the interval would be useless; nevertheless, if another animal were immolated in the middle, there would be a sublation of the promptness of performance understood from the injunction of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vidhi*). For it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:

"If an action [performed] with a single individual were to complete the genus (*jāti*) residing in each substratum, then the sacrifice could not be accomplished by means of a single animal; yet such a completion [of the genus] does not occur."
But when an action has already been established by one [means], if another animal were to be taken up because of its possibility, that taking up would be purposeless.

"Just as the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) is useless for a woman who is already pregnant, so too is another animal useless when [the sacrifice] is already accomplished by one. This is the detailed explanation regarding those who maintain that the number inherent in the object to be enjoined is intended to be significant.

Thus ends the determination of the non-intentionality of number regarding the *ktvā* suffix and others. Although it is stated in the root text (*mūla*) that "the *tumun* suffix and others [denote action]," nevertheless, because there is much to be said concerning the *ktvā* suffix, the phrase "the *ktvā* suffix and others" was used to highlight its primary importance. Regarding the phrase "according to the Vārttika": the authors of the Bhāṣya, having established in the rule *tumarthe* that "the meaning of *tumun* is action" (*bhāva*), and subsequently accepting the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *tumartha*, reject the view that "kṛt suffixes added to indeclinables denote action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*). Instead, they maintain that the *ktvā* suffix and others denote action alone.

However, the meaning of suffixes such as *ktvā* and *tumun* is indeed a state (*bhāva*) that has not yet become a substance (*asattvabhūta*), because, as in the case of "pāka" and similar forms, there is no experience of gender or number; thus, it follows that suffixes such as *tumun* merely restate the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). What, then, is the [proper] interpretation?

If it were accepted that the *ktvā* suffix signifies merely the abstract action (*bhāva*), then since [properties] such as having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) could not possibly be its meaning, their inclusion would result in redundancy; therefore, the meaning of the *ktvā* suffix must be stated as the substratum of the agency of that action. For this very reason, in the sentence "Having cooked the flatbreads, I shall eat," the third case ending does not occur after the word "I" (*asmad*), because the agent of the cooking is already expressed by the *ktvā* suffix.

The attainment of "having the same agent" (samānakartṛkatva) results from the connection of the agent of cooking with the act of eating and so forth, through the relation of being the qualifier of the agency residing in oneself. Alternatively, this question may be raised with the intention that "having the same agent" might be the meaning of the suffix itself; however, it is argued that the status of being a dyotya (indicator) for "having the same agent" and so forth is redundant, because one does not experience such a quality as a qualifier or a qualified within the meaning of the base (prakṛti). Since "having the same agent" and so forth exist as objective facts, they would merely serve as the regulator of the grammatical correctness (sādhutva) of the suffix *ktvā* and others; hence he says: "This is the intended meaning."

"This" refers to what is about to be stated. "Established by all experience" means established by the experience of everyone. "Otherwise" means even in the absence of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), when there is a single sentence—as in "He eats while he walks. In this case, the cognition whose primary objects of predication (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) are two actions—"an eating action occurring at the present time with a single agent" and "a walking action occurring at the present time with a single agent"—is established by experience; however, a unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) consisting in having a single primary object of predication is not established by experience therein.

Even in the case of "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), if one accepts a cognition consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*)—namely, that both the eating and the going have a single agent—then syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is untenable. However, if one accepts that the agent is expressed by the suffix, then syntactic unity is indeed possible, as in "he cooks and exists" (*pacati bhavati*), because there can be a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the agent denoted by the *ktvā* suffix (the eater) and the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). This is because even in the sentence "Caitra goes after having eaten" (*caitreṇa bhuktvā gamyate*), one accepts the cognition that the object of the going has as its agent Caitra, who is non-different from the agent of the eating.

For this very reason, there is no expressive power (*śakti*) regarding the aspect of non-difference that constitutes the "single agent" (*samānakartṛtva*), because it would be fruitless; furthermore, as shown by the aforementioned method, the possibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) exists therein. Nevertheless, one should be satisfied knowing that the author himself will state that the denotability of the agent (*kartṛvācyatva*) is not obtained from the Sūtra.

With the intention that not only "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) and "occurring in prior and subsequent time" (*pūrvottarakālikatva*), but other relations as well, appear as *saṃsarga* (relational content) and are expressed by suffixes such as *-ktvā*—since the phrase "of the two [cases of] having the same agent," etc., is intended as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative instance)—he says: "being produced" (*janyatva*), and so forth. However, others say: since there is no evidence for it being an *upalakṣaṇa*, and because it is cognizable through other means of knowledge, it is not expressed by *-ktvā* and the like. [The term] "that which produces eating" (*bhojanajanikā*) [is used].

In the expression "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*), the relationship between the two actions of eating and cooking—namely, the relation of producer and produced—is indicated by the suffix *tumun*. This is because it is stated [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] that "the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is for the sake of another action. The point is that this "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) consists precisely in the relation of producer and produced. Furthermore, just like "being for the sake of," the fact that the two actions have the same agent also appears as a relation between them due to the very nature of linguistic capacity (*śabdaśakti*). For this reason, the expression "he cooks in order to eat" is not employed when there is an intention to refer to two actions having different agents.

Others, however, hold that "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), which consists in being the specifier of the object-to-be-achieved (*uddeśyatva-nirūpakatva*) and is indicated by the suffix *tumun* and others, appears as a relational factor (*saṃsarga*). This [tādarthya] is the state of being the object of a desire dependent upon a [prior] desire. Furthermore, because the word "in the future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is understood to carry over from the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām kriyārthāyām*, futurity is also indicated by it. Thus, the cognition is: "Cooking performed by one who cooks, having as its object-to-be-achieved a future meal. However, the suffix *tumun* does not denote the agent, because it is stated that "gerundives formed by *avyaya*-suffixes denote the action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*), and thus the rule *kartari kṛt* does not apply here.

Since this [rule] applies to cases where the meaning is not explicitly specified, by this very argument the following view is refuted: "Co-occurrence with a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is not the relation [between two verbs], because there would otherwise result the undesirable consequence of such usages having as their purport two distinct actions performed by different agents, given that the agent of the infinitive ending in *-tumun* and the agent of the finite verb are construed as non-different from one another. Furthermore, this is because such a relation is impossible in examples such as *bhoktuṃ pacyate* ("He cooks in order to eat") and *bhoktuṃ sthīyate* ("He stands in order to eat").

Nor should it be argued that even in that case there is no inconsistency because the word ‘Devadattena’ is supplied (*adhyāhāra*), and thus the meaning of the instrumental case—the agent—is construed as non-different from [the action]; for it is established by experience that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs even without such a supply. This is the general direction. However, the suffix *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule ‘tumun-ṇvulau’ (Pāṇini 3.3.10) applies only to the agent, according to the rule ‘kartari kṛt’ (Pāṇini 3.4.67). The relation between the two actions is exactly as previously stated. Thus, they maintain that from the sentence ‘kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti’ (‘He goes to see Kṛṣṇa’), the cognition is: “A present-time going, whose agent is the seer, which has as its purpose a future seeing whose object is Kṛṣṇa.”

And this is logical: for even when the sight of other people on the road arises during a journey whose intended object is the sight of Kṛṣṇa, there is no usage such as "he goes to see people"; rather, we have usages such as "he goes to see Kṛṣṇa, and not the Yavanas and so forth. For this very reason, the modern logicians (navyatārkikas) accept that the meaning expressed by the suffix *tumun* is the state of being the object of a desire qualified by having the agent as its agent.

For this very reason, in the *Vyutpattivāda* regarding the fourth case (the dative), it is stated that the meaning of the suffix *-tumun* in "to bring" (*āhartum*) is "bringing" (*āharaṇa*) which is connected to its own object, which in turn is connected to the purpose of its own meaning as it relates to the action expressed by the word with which it is uttered. Without the denotability (*vācyatā*) of the state of being a purpose for its own meaning, the aforementioned connection would be inconsistent.

Otherwise, because that [relation] would not be a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), a counter-correlativity delimited by that relation would be unestablished; consequently, it would be impossible to convey the absence of a perception whose counter-correlate is barley and so forth as qualified by such a counter-correlativity. Nor can it be maintained that what is conveyed by the nominative case-ending is simply the absence of being a locus of going qualified by a perception of barley and so forth through the aforementioned relation, for this is untenable in cases such as "One stands in order to see Kṛṣṇa, but not barley and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument.

In the system of the Grammarians (Śābdikas), however, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency, because they accept that in all cases the cognition consists precisely of the action qualified by all its qualifiers as the primary qualificand. In expressions such as "he desires to eat" (*bhoktum icchati*), the suffix *tumun* is applied according to the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu*; the meaning of that rule is that *tumun* is added to a verbal root when there is a governing word (*upapada*) expressing an object whose agent is the same as the agent of the action denoted by the root which serves as the base for the *tumun*.

This [rule] is for the purpose of excluding cases where there is no *upapada* that expresses an action or purpose. In the view of our own school (*svamatam*), the suffix *tumun* serves as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) when the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with the desire (*icchā*) through a relation qualified by having the same agent as that which has the object-domain of the *tumun*-meaning. However, in the opinion of others (*paramate*), since the denotation of that [suffix] is that [desire], the relation of "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also included among the relations in order to prevent the usage "he desires to eat" (*bhoktum icchati*) from occurring in the case of a desire to eat whose agent is someone else.

In expressions such as ‘śaknoti bhoktum’ (he is able to eat), ‘dhṛṣṇoti paṭhitum’ (he dares to read), and ‘jānāti paṭhitum’ (he knows how to read), the suffix *tumun* is applied according to the rule: “*tumun* is used after the roots *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, *jñā*, *glā*, *ghaṭ*, *rabh*, *labh*, *kram*, *sah*, and *arh* in the sense of the root *as* (to be). In the first case (*śaknoti*), the relation of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) between the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) and the meaning of the verbal root—which is the capacity (*śakti*) synonymous with capability (*sāmarthya*)—is what is illuminated by the suffix *tumun*. In the second case (*dhṛṣṇoti*), the relation is either the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*) of the doubt that constitutes the lack of timidity (*prāgalbhya*), or it is the status of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) in relation to the aforementioned lack of timidity. In the third case (*jānāti*), the relation of being the object (*viṣayatva*) is quite evident.

In this case as well, the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) must be included in the relation [between the infinitive and the finite verb]. Here, whatever the relation is, according to the view of others, that is what is expressed by the suffix. Here, within the meaning of the root *śak* (to be able), the respective meanings of the verbal roots with which it is co-uttered (*samabhivyāhṛta*) must be incorporated; for instance, the function of the root *śak* consists in an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to an action resulting in contact below the throat (*galādhaḥ-saṃyoga*). In that context, there is a primary denotation (*śakti*) regarding the capacity, while in the other case there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In this regard, the base of the *tumun* suffix, such as *bhuj* (to eat) and so on, serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*).

In such a sense, the function [of the root] occurs only in the case of an object-terminating suffix (*karmapratyaya*) and not in the case of an agent-terminating suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*), due to the absence of purpose. Therein, the operation (*vyāpāra*), which is conjoined with the power (*śakti*) through the relation of being instigated (*prayojyatva*), is construed with the aforementioned action through the relation of being produced (*janyatva*). Because rice and the like possess a fruit in the form of such an action, they have the status of an object (*karman*). And thus, from the expression "rice is able to be eaten" (*śakyate odano bhoktum*), the understanding is that there is an action residing in the rice, which is conducive to the conjunction of the throat and the lower parts of the body, produced by an operation instigated by the power.

In the system of the logicians (tārkika), however, the cognition is that "the rice-gruel is the locus of such an action. Furthermore, in the Mīmāṃsā system, potency (*śakti*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*); in the Nyāya system, it is the collection of uncommon causes conducive to their respective effects, such as, in the present case, contact with the blazing gastric fire and so forth.

"There is," "exists," or "is found" [to eat]. Here, in the sense of existence (*sattā*) whose agent is the non-determiner (*anirūpaka-kartṛ*), the meaning of the base of the *tumun* suffix is construed through the relation of being a producer (*janakatva*). Alternatively, in the sense of possibility expressed by "there is" and so forth, it is construed through the relation of being an object (*viṣayitva*). "Sufficient to eat," "skilled to eat," "proficient to eat. Here, the *tumun* suffix is used according to the rule: "In the case of words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*), when they have the sense of 'able' (*alam*)."

The meaning of *paryāpti* is "sufficiency. Its purpose is that the suffix *tumun* occurs when the governing words (*upapada*) expressing that [sufficiency] do not convey the capacity [of the agent]. In this context, the agency (*prayojakatva*) or objecthood (*viṣayitva*) of the root-meaning, residing in [the agent's] skill (*kauśalya*) and so forth, is what is illuminated by *tumun*. In examples such as *paryāpto bhoktum* ("capable of eating"), words like *paryāpta* signify "capacity" (*samartha*). If the first word [of the rule] were not included here, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [applying *tumun*] in cases such as *alaṃ bhuktvā* ("enough of having eaten").

In this context, regarding the word *alaṃ* in the expression "Kṛṣṇa is capable (*alaṃ*) of killing Kaṃsa," there is the possibility [of its application] as a term signifying "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*). If the second word [in the compound] were not employed, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he eats sufficiently" (*paryāptaṃ bhuṅkte*), where the word *alaṃ* is understood; however, when that [second word] is employed, no such fault arises, because what is conveyed there is specifically the sufficiency consisting of an abundance of the object to be eaten, and not mere capability. Thus, enough [with further elaboration].

"Kālaḥ," "samayaḥ," or "velā" [mean] "it is time" to eat. Here, the suffix *tumun* is used according to the rule: "In the sense of time (*kāla*), occasion (*samaya*), and opportunity (*velā*), *tumun* [is applied]. Here, the relationship of eating, characterized by suitability (*yogyatā*) and residing in time, is expressed by the *tumun* suffix. Since the mention of "command" (*praiṣa*) and so forth continues [from the previous rule], *tumun* is used only when there is an intention to express command and the like, not in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)—as in examples such as "Time cooks the elements. Enough with this excessive detail; let us return to the subject at hand. He states the cognition produced by the sentence "Having eaten, he is satiated" with the words "generated by eating" (*bhojanajanya*).

The meaning is that it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that satisfaction (*tṛpti*) produced by eating; for the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... [Pāṇini 3.4.72]. Now, one might object: let there be the manifestation of only immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) as the relation (*saṃsarga*) in that case; what is the point of accepting the manifestation of "being produced by a heavy body" as the relation? To this he says: "For this very reason. This means: precisely because the manifestation of "being produced" (*janyatva*) is accepted as the relation. "There is no usage" [means...]

The sense is that satisfaction produced by food lacks the quality of being produced by drinking water.
