Regarding the phrase "identity of agent as well": in the case of "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), when the occurrence [of the action] in the locus of eating is manifested in the act of going, the identity of the loci of the two actions is also established by implication; for the sharing of a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be untenable without such identity.

In the verse, "She cursed you, saying, 'O son, without having propitiated my progenitor, you shall have no offspring,'" there is no inconsistency in the use of the suffix *ktvā*, because the word "remaining" (*sthitasya*) is supplied, whereby there exists the identity of agent with the action of remaining.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being prior and posterior": this means the aggregate of occurring at a prior time and occurring at a subsequent time. If one does not accept that this [aggregate] appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*), then even though going occurs at a prior time, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*). If one does not accept that coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) functions in that way, then there would be the consequence of such usage even when intending two such actions performed by different agents; therefore, both are pursued as relations.

Even the aspect of non-interruption (*avyavadhāna*) must be included in the relation of priority (*pūrvatva*) and posteriority (*uttaratva*). Otherwise, taking as the basis for the current year both the eating at the father-in-law’s house that occurred in the previous year and the journey [occurring later], there would result the undesirable linguistic usage: "Having eaten at the father-in-law’s house, he goes" (*śvaśuragṛhe bhuktvā vrajati*). However, non-interruption is to be understood according to the intended meaning (*tātparya*): in some cases by a moment (*daṇḍa*), in some cases by a muhūrta, and in some cases by a prahara or other duration, as appropriate.

And "obstruction by a staff" and so forth means being the locus of the prior absence of that which is the locus of the prior absence of the staff and so on; here, "itself" (sva) refers to the specific action such as walking mentioned in close proximity.

Thus, "immediately preceding" (avyavahitapūrvatva) is a property residing in time, consisting in being the locus of the prior absence of that action qualified by such non-intervention. In cases where walking occurs after eating or after taking up a staff, there is no occurrence of such usage [as "he eats" or "he takes up a staff"] because the moment that is the locus of eating, etc., is not the locus of the prior absence of the walking, nor is it the locus of the prior absence of the staff. By including the qualificand portion [of the definition], there is no unwanted consequence of using the expression "he eats" (*bhokte*) with the intention of referring to eating after walking.

In reality, at the time of that departure, there is no over-extension of the definition because of the absence of "subsequent-ness" (uttaratva)—which consists in being the locus of the destruction of the locus of the action of eating; therefore, that [condition] need not be included. In cases such as "having eaten today, he will go tomorrow" or "having married in Mārgaśīrṣa, he went to Kāśī in Pauṣa," what is intended is the absence of the aforementioned interval measured by days, months, and so forth; thus, there is no inconsistency.

However, if prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not accepted—then "being prior" (*tatpūrvatvam*) consists in being the counter-positive of a destruction that arises at a moment which is the locus of that [object], while not being the counter-positive of a destruction that arises at a moment which is the locus of the staff; whereas "being posterior" (*tatparatvam*) consists in being the counter-positive of a destruction that arises at a moment which is the locus of that [object]. But it should be understood, as before, that this inclusion is unnecessary in the present context. [This concludes the section on] "particular time" (*kālaviśeṣa*).

The meaning is that pervadedness (vyāpyatva) consists in a relation of co-existence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) characterized by having as its qualifier [the property] "having the state of having the mouth wide open" (mukhavyādānatva), which is not a delimiting factor (anavacchedaka) for the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) residing in its own locus (svādhikaraṇa) as delimited by that specific time. [This refers to the phrase] "delimited by a particular time."

In this context, "time" (kāla) should be understood as subtle time, such as a moment (kṣaṇa) and so forth; it does not refer to being pervaded by gross time. Therefore, there is no risk of the undesirable consequence that one would use the expression "having opened his mouth, he sleeps" with reference to a specific instance of sleep occurring at a time when the mouth is not open, following a period when it was open. For this very reason, the usage "he remains having studied" applies only to one who has been engaged in continuous study, and not to one who studies only occasionally; thus, the established rule is logically justified.

In that case as well, since the aforementioned state of being pervaded (vyāpyatva) appears as a relation, there would be no occurrence of such a usage when a person who lacks continuous study is present, because the state of being pervaded by study would be absent [in him]. However, in the expression "co-located with itself" (svasamānādhikaraṇa), the word "self" (sva) should be understood as denoting the generality of the state existing at a time devoid of sleep and so forth belonging to that particular person; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not remain.

In the case of the expression "having opened the mouth" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya*), however, by the word itself, that specific individual instance of opening is to be understood; thus, it appears that there is no possibility of such usage at a time devoid of opening, nor is there any impossibility of such usage at the time of opening. The verbal root *sthā* (to stand) and others are likewise intended to denote being delimited by such states of standing and so forth; therefore, there is no inconsistency in the connection of such pervasion as delimited by the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Although the admission of *sāmānādhikaraṇya* as a relation is redundant—since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is already ruled out by the very manifestation of such pervasion (*vyāpyatva*)—nevertheless, it is stated that "and *sāmānādhikaraṇya* is the relation" in order to indicate that pervasion, which is constituted by *sāmānādhikaraṇya*, must be accepted as the relation. Alternatively, it is more elegant to take the text literally, as it stands, meaning that *sāmānādhikaraṇya* need not be included in the aforementioned pervasion.

Alternatively, the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "conditioned by a specific time" (*kālaviśeṣāvacchinna*) is simply that the relation is pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) as delimited by a temporal relation. And thus, since even the persistence of a person who performs study only occasionally would be a locus of the aforementioned pervasion as defined by the study of another person, the usage "having studied, he persists" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) would result; therefore, co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also put forward as a relation.

Regarding the phrase "co-referential with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*): since the word *sva* (self) has exactly the same meaning as previously stated, there is no room for the aforementioned defect. If it is argued that—due to parsimony—it is appropriate to accept the connection [of the action] with the delimitors such as "the state of being so situated," which are co-referential with [the agent] by virtue of being simultaneous with that specific time [of the action], then such usage would be desired only in cases where there is frequent yawning at the time of one's own sleep, or frequent study at the time of one's own hunger, and not when these occur only occasionally at the time of one's sleep and so forth.

It appears that the pursuit of the manifestation of pervasion (*vyāpyatvabhāna*) has been stated here in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding such cases as the opening of the mouth.

However, if that usage is indeed authoritative even in the aforementioned instance, then this [interpretation] alone is appropriate; or let it be that the intention of the present treatise also lies precisely here. Furthermore, since the relationship of "prior time" (*pūrvakālatva*) and so forth exists because of the existence of the state of sleep even after the opening of the mouth for study, there is no lack of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) for the suffix *ktvā*. And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that, in order to exclude the usage "he eats while eating" (*bhuñjāne bhuṅkte*), one must accept as the criterion only a priority relative to the entire set of actions conducive to the specific result co-occurring with that [eating], and thus how—according to the aforementioned method—the usage "having opened his mouth, he sleeps" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*) could be possible; for in that case, by postulating a difference in the results, there is no fault, since it is possible for the opening of the mouth to be preceded by a general activity whose results include a particular pleasure and so forth occurring after the opening of the mouth.

Because it follows the usage "having eaten, he eats," the expression "having eaten at midday, he eats at night" is indeed accepted and is justified by the manner described above. When there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), even in the case of a single meal, people say, "Having eaten rice, he eats flatbread."

On this point, some Naiyāyikas maintain that "prior temporality"—consisting in existence at a time delimited by prior non-existence (prāgabhāva)—is the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*, and that the agent is also [part of its meaning]. In that regard, the denotative power (*śakti*) resides either in the prior temporality, specifically in the prior time or in the prior non-existence which constitutes it; whereas with respect to the agent, there is either denotative power (*śakti*) or conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). In the first alternative, the state of existing at a prior time is construed with the meaning of the base (such as "eating") by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatva*).

In the second alternative, the relation is the locusness (ādheyatva) of the prior time, delimited by the temporal relation (kālika-sambandha). In the third view, there is the role of qualifier (prakāratā) in the antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) through the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva); and the act of eating, which is the meaning of the verbal root, functions as a qualifier of the agent—the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*—through the relation of being the determiner of the agency residing in itself (svaniṣṭhakartṛtvanirūpakatva).

In the case of *vrajati* (he goes) used with that meaning [of "having gone"], since the agency (*kartṛtva*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is not intended as the primary focus here, it functions as a qualifier. Thus, the cognition is: "The locus of the agency of going is one who possesses an effort conducive to eating, existing at a time delimited by the prior absence of going. However, in the case of *paktvā bhujyate odanaḥ* (Having cooked, the rice is eaten), the agent of the cooking—denoted by the suffix *-ktvā*—is construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the root *bhuj*, through the relation of being the specifier of the agency residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhakartṛkatānirūpakatva*).

And thus, the cognition is as follows: "The rice is the locus of an action conducive to conjunction with the throat, produced by an operation whose agent is the agent of cooking occurring at a time delimited by the prior absence of eating.

Because it is accepted as a rule of grammar (*vyutpatti*) that the specific action instance in which the agent of the *ktvā*-suffix is construed—either directly or through the mediation of agency—is precisely that action instance which is construed with the prior absence denoted by the *ktvā*-suffix, there is no risk of the usage "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*) applying to one who is the agent of eating occurring after a departure performed by another agent.

In the sentence "Caitra, having eaten, goes" (*caitro bhuktvā vrajati*), however, Caitra is either the qualifier or the qualificand by virtue of being non-different from the agent of the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*, which is itself construed with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). In the sentence "The going of Caitra after eating" (*caitrasya bhuktvā vrajanam*), the cognition is that the going has as its agent the same person who is the agent of the eating that precedes the going. In this case, the relation in the act of going is the state of being the counter-correlate (*nirūpakatva*) of the agency residing in oneself (the eater), belonging to the agent of such an eating.

In the sentence "Caitra does not go after eating" (*caitro na bhuktvā vrajati*), the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys in Caitra a difference from one who is the agent of eating at a time prior to the act of going, which is qualified by being the current agent of going. Consequently, when such a usage is justified—namely, when it intends a person who has never performed an act such as going after eating—the expression "he does not go after eating" (*bhuktvā na vrajati*) is also logically established.

By this, the view that one must accept a cognition of the absence of being the present agent of going in the eater of the aforementioned kind—who is non-different from Caitra—is refuted; for it does not account for the aforementioned instance. This is the direction [of the argument], they say.

Furthermore, the logicians have described it as follows: the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the object to be brought about by the agent. In the case of prior non-existence, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with it either through the relation of occurring in its own locus-time (*svādhikaraṇakālavṛttitva*), or through the relation of occurrence delimited by temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*). The prior non-existence, which is already construed with the meaning of the verbal root, functions as a qualifier of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) in relation to the subsequent action, by means of a relation consisting of being a part of the agent (*kartṛkadeśa*), being conducive to the action (*kṛtimukūlatva*), and being the object of cognition (*viṣayitva*).

The relation of being the non-qualifier of the agenthood residing in oneself (*svaniṣṭhakartṛtānirūpakatva*) belongs to the agent of the first action with respect to the subsequent action as a constituent of its qualifier-role; by this much alone, the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is obtained. Thus, from the sentence "Caitra, having eaten, goes," the cognition is: Caitra is the possessor of the agency of that going which is the counter-positive of a prior absence (or, alternatively, which resides in the eating), that [absence] residing in the time-base of the eating (or, alternatively, residing in the eating) whose agent is the same as the agent of the eating that is non-different from Caitra.

However, when there is no co-utterance with a word ending in the nominative case (prathamāntapada), the cognition has the agency of going as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). But in cases such as *caitreṇa bhuktvā vrajanam* ("Having eaten, Caitra goes"), that cognition has the act of going, etc., as its primary qualificand. Because of the rule that the two meanings of the suffix *ktvā* must both conjoin to a single individual action, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such a usage being applicable to a person who eats at a time subsequent to his own act of going, which occurred prior to the act of going performed by another person.

"In the case of 'Caitra does not go after having eaten,' the cognition is that Caitra possesses the absence of being the agent of such going. He states that such views are not worthy of adoption, saying "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). "Thus" means when priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) and so forth are presented as relations (*saṃsarga*). The sense is that since these can appear by way of relation even without a verbal function (*vṛtti*), because they are obtainable from other sources; otherwise, one would have to admit a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for mere syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

In the first alternative, if one accepts a cognition such as "the agent of eating which is prior to going," one must also observe the flaw that it contradicts experience; for experience establishes a cognition in which the subsequent action is the qualificand (viśeṣya) and the preceding action is the qualifier (prakāra). For this very reason, the authors of the *Maṇi* [the *Śaktivāda*] stated the following objection: "If the state of being prior (*pūrvakālatva*) were the denotation [of the suffix], the resulting cognition would have the preceding action as its qualificand, and not the subsequent action; thus, there would be a contradiction with experience. Having stated this objection, they subsequently accepted that the suffix *ktvā* itself is the denoter of that [state].

Nor can one object that even if priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) is denotable, the cognition established by experience is indeed accounted for by accepting its connection with the subsequent action through the relation of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*). Anticipating this, [the author] argues that in the case of "having eaten, he does not go" (*na bhuktvā vrajati*), it is impossible to convey the relation of being a qualifier. For if one were to accept a cognition of an absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva-sambandha*), there would result the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using such a negative construction even when the agent goes after having eaten.

However, they also asserted that the absence of "immediacy" (ānantarya), whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being the locus (āśrayatva), can indeed be conveyed. Furthermore, it was stated by the venerable teachers (*gurucaraṇa*) in the *Caṣaka* that even contemporary logicians accept that properties such as "occurring at a later time" appear precisely as relations [of the absence], since they are obtainable through other means; thus, enough of this prolixity.

[Objection: But in that case, there would be an inconsistency with the established Mīmāṃsā doctrine that the sentence "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma" enjoins the Soma sacrifice as occurring after the Darśapūrṇamāsa, because time cannot be the expressed meaning [of a word]. [Reply: This is not so; for there is no flaw, since we accept that what is enjoined is the qualification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa by its relation to a subsequent time.

Even by that much, the result of their established doctrine is proven: namely, that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in performing the *soma* sacrifice prior to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; for this is established in the section concerning the *darśa* (Jaimini 5.4.1) and in the section concerning the non-performance of the *soma* (Jaimini 6.2.31). Regarding the term "the base and the meaning" (*prakṛtyartha*): it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the base" (*prakṛti*) and "the action" (*artha*). Alternatively, the "base" (*prakṛti*) refers to the verbal root and the suffix that is co-occurrent with it; thus, there is no inconsistency. Regarding the phrase "expressed by its own word" (*svaśabdenopātta*): [it means expressed by the word itself].

Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of "he eats first, then he goes"? The introduction of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as "by its own word," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "when [the meaning] is to be indicated" (*dyotye*): by this, it is clearly indicated that suffixes such as *ktvā* serve only to indicate (i.e., suggest) priority in time, posteriority in time, and so on, but do not denote them; thus, the sense is that Kaiyaṭa’s intended view is that [the relation] exists solely as a semantic connection (*saṃsarga*). He refutes the view of the author of the *Parimala* and others with the words "as for what [they say]," and so forth. [The phrase] "from the Sūtra" refers to...

The meaning is that the expression *samānakartṛkayoḥ* refers to the properties (*dharma*), while the dual number is based on the superimposition of duality upon the two substrates (*āśraya*) consisting of the two actions. Alternatively, it may refer to the property-bearers (*dharmin*) themselves, since the property-bearers in the form of the actions are already obtained from the verbal roots; the sense is that, by the force of the rule, the expressive power (*śakti*) is postulated as residing in the agent (*kartṛ*) itself when there is identity of agent. Or, let it be that the expressive power resides in the identity of the agents of the two actions in accordance with experience; in the case of *bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten, he goes"), the eating is construed as having the agent as its locus.

He states the refutation of its being inexpressible with the words "otherwise. Regarding the phrase "by the third [case-ending]": the sense is that the agent is not denoted by the *ktvā* suffix. He says "and not," having accepted a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) based on the rule that the third case-ending does not occur when [the agent] is already denoted. The phrase "even though the agent of the action is not denoted" means "even though there is a denotation of that which is qualified by being the agent of the action"—this is the final meaning, as it refers to the power (*śakti*) of being the agent of the action; for otherwise, the literal reading would result in an inconsistency, namely, that there is only one agent for two actions.

This is the meaning of [the rule] *evam agranimasyāpi kriyākartuḥ* (likewise, even for one who is not the agent of the action), because it relies upon *paryudāsa* (exclusion). However, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the meaning would be "it does not exist when [the agent] is already expressed"; since the capacity for agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*) would have been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the occurrence of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the form *mayā* (by me) would follow. But when relying on *paryudāsa*, the meaning is "it exists when different from what is expressed"; thus, by taking up the capacity for agency as defined by the act of eating which is not expressed, the occurrence of the third case is indeed firmly established—this is the sense. For the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), relying on *paryudāsa* alone is appropriate.

For in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), one would have to resort to either an *asamartha-samāsa* (an inefficient compound) or a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). He states the purpose for resorting to that [negation]: "of the locus of the action" (*kriyādhikaraṇasya*). [The word] *adhikaraṇa* is derived from the root *√sad* with the prefix *adhi*, meaning "that in which something settles," using the suffix *ghañ* according to the rule *'halaśca'* (Pāṇini 3.3.121). The phrase "of the locus of the action" is to be explained in the same way as "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*). This is clear in the *Bhāṣya*. [The rule] begins with "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) and so forth.

In reality, however, according to the established position (*siddhāntapakṣa*) that the suffix *ghañ* denotes the capacity (*śakti*) to be a means (*sādhanatva*), since the capacity as determined by the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is not denoted [by the suffix], even though the seventh case (*saptamī*) is prohibited when that [capacity] is the expressed meaning, there is no prohibition when the capacity for being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva-śakti*) as determined by the action of sitting (*āsana-kriyā*) is the expressed meaning. Thus, the establishment of the seventh case in the expression "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) is entirely unimpeded. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s *Uddyota*. And so, the truth is that here one resorts to the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) precisely because of parsimony (*lāghava*). He concludes with: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

Regarding the phrase *sāmānakartṛkayoḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is the two actions, meaning "those two actions which have a common (*samāna*) or single (*eka*) agent. Regarding *pūrvakāla* and so forth: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose time is prior (*pūrvaḥ kālo 'syeti*). Thus, the meaning of the rule is simply this: between two actions that have a common agent, the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the verbal root (*dhātu*) that denotes the action occurring at the prior time. And so, the point is that the agent is not obtained as something directly expressed (*vācya*) in any way whatsoever.

Anticipating the objection that "surely this is indeed obtained by the method previously stated," he says: "otherwise. It should be understood that when the agency of the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended to be expressed according to the sequence mentioned before, the inclusion of the term *samānakartṛke* (in the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*) serves to indicate that the agent of the action denoted by the suffix *-ktvā* is to be construed as non-different from the agent of the action expressed by the co-occurring verb, according to the aforementioned method. [The phrase] *nyāsaḥ syāt* means "the placement [of the word] would have been made. Furthermore, it should be understood that the description of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) according to the previously stated method is not correct.

One might object: "Surely the very absence of the third case-ending (instrumental) will serve as the proof for the agent being the expressed meaning (*vācya*), by way of postulating the previously mentioned sense. Anticipating this, he states that the non-appearance of the third case is established otherwise, beginning with the words "But the introduction of the third case... etc. The two verses beginning with "Of the primary and the other" have been explained previously. It is clear from the *Śekhara* and other works that these two verses of Hari are restatements of the meaning found in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *svādumi ṇamul*.

Now, one might object: "Why is it described in this way? Let it be accepted that the suffix *ktvā* and others have their denotative power (*śakti*) solely in the sense of the agent, for the very purpose of excluding the third case [the instrumental]. It is precisely for this reason that the author of the Sūtras’ statement, ‘[when there are] two actions having the same agent,’ is purposeful. Otherwise, just like the relation of being produced by the suffix *ḍa*, this relation too will be obtained simply through the force of experience; thus, that statement would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*), meaning "by another method."

Even if one accepts that the *śakti* (potency) resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) after the word *odana* (rice) would still be unavoidable, because the object is not denoted [by the verbal suffix]. However, if one were to accept that the *śakti* resides in the object (*karman*) as well, there would be both unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*). But if one follows the aforementioned method, since the *śakti* of the object—defined in relation to the primary act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅ*)—is denoted by that *tiṅ*, there is no occurrence of the accusative even though that same *śakti* defined in relation to the subordinate act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) is not denoted; such is the collective intended meaning.

Moreover, on the view that [the suffixes] denote [action], there would be the undesirable consequence that *ktvā* and other such suffixes would have multiple meanings, such as being produced (*janyatva*) and being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*). If being produced and so forth were the denoted meaning, they would—by virtue of being the meaning of the suffix—become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and consequently, in the case of "having eaten repeatedly, he goes" (*abhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati*), the doubling [of the word] required by the rule "doubling occurs when frequency is to be expressed" (*ābhīkṣṇye dve vācye*) would not apply. This is because the primacy of the action (*kriyāprādhānya*) would be lost. If, however, one accepts that the application of that rule depends upon taking the action that has become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhūta-kriyā*), then the same undesirable consequence would arise even in cases such as "cook" (*pācaka*).

In this way, there would also be the undesirable consequence of subverting the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding the connection between verbal roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the connection mediated by the meaning of the suffix remains intact. This is because, in examples such as "He cuts [repeatedly]—he cuts indeed," we observe a direct connection between the meanings of two verbal roots; and since the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*) is carried over from rules such as *yathāvidhyanuprayoga*, its purport is determined to be precisely this direct connection. Consequently, it is certain that mutual connection does not constitute its intended meaning.

Out of deference [to the tradition], he states—"let the elaboration suffice"—indicating that even out of respect, one cannot claim that [the suffix *ktvā*] signifies a lack of mutual connection between those meanings. Others, however, hold that based on the meaning of the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle ktvā*, among two verbal roots having a common agent, the suffix *ktvā* denotes the time prior to the other; thus, "prior time" is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the *ktvā*-suffix, while "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is the relation that constitutes the qualifierhood of such a base-meaning with respect to the meaning of the other root.

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* addresses the objection regarding the suffix *ktvā* in the example "he eats first, then he goes" (*pūrvaṃ bhuṅkte paścādvrajati*), resolving it with the statement: "In this context, the word *pūrva* has the sense of prior time, but the verbal root does not function there [in that sense], because its own meaning has already been expressed by the word itself. However, this does not mean that the rule is intended to apply only to words whose meaning has already been expressed; for if that were the case, the subsequent *Bhāṣya*—which raises the objection, "Why does [the suffix] not occur here in the form *āsyate bhoktum*?"—would be rendered incoherent.

In that case as well, since the suffix *tumun* indicates a relationship consisting in having that [action] as its purpose, it expresses the state of being prior in time (*pūrvakālatva*) with respect to the sitting (*āsana*), and thus [the suffix *ktvā*] does not apply there. If the priority in time were not understood there, how could a doubt even find a footing? As for the derivation by means of the present tense (*laṭ*) according to the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), that is another matter. Kaiyaṭa’s text states: "But when the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the root *ās*, then the suffix *tumun* does not occur after the root *bhuj*, because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*)."

In the case of the expression "having first eaten, he goes afterwards," the sense is that "having eaten before other eaters, he goes after other goers"; thus, since priority in time is understood only in relation to the action of another means of accomplishment (*sādhanāntara*), this is not the subject matter of this sūtra, but rather of the rule *vibhāṣāgre prathame*. This is clear from the Bhāṣya on this point.

However, in the case of the expression "by means of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices," there is no fault, because through the relation of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the qualification of being prior in time (such as the *darśa* sacrifice) is understood in reference to the *soma* sacrifice. Thus, they say that "prior in time" (*pūrvakāla*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound; and likewise, it can be maintained that the suffix *-ktvā* and others, like the genitive case, denote relations such as having a common agent.

Here, "priority in time" means being a time delimited by antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); and this antecedent non-existence is construed with the act of going (*vrajana*) by way of the relation of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the specific individuality (*tattadvayaktitva*) of that particular action.

And "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) consists in occurring at a moment that is the locus of the destruction of the time [of the action] which is the locus of that [action], while being qualified by not being the locus of the destruction of a muhūrta or other period that is the locus of the destruction of that same time. By this, the previously mentioned fault does not arise; for in the case of the statement "the Lord remains having known," since the destruction of the Lord's knowledge is unestablished, its destruction is not included in the definition of immediacy.

The essential point here is this: in the expression "having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes," the suffix *ktvā* is used everywhere by taking the state of being prior in time relative to the action of going (*vrajanakriyā*) as its limit, but not by taking that [state] relative to actions such as eating (*bhojanādi*).

That being the case, just as in expressions such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), where the singular number and so forth are not intended to be significant, so too here—in the rule "of two [actions] having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*)—even if the duality expressed by the dual suffix is not intended to be significant, when it is said, "Let these Brahmins be brought first," it is the very first of all who is brought, and not some intermediate one; likewise, in this instance as well, the *ktvā* suffix would apply only to the root *snāti* (to bathe), and not to *bhuj* (to eat) and the others.

And thus, the connection of the acts of bathing and drinking is only with the act of going, and not of bathing and so forth with eating and so forth; for this very reason, even the reversed usage "having eaten or having drunk, he goes" is justified there, as is clear in the Bhāṣya. May there be auspiciousness! || 60 ||
Thus concludes the determination of the meanings of the suffixes -tumun, -ktvā, and others.

Regarding the term "siddhānta" (the established conclusion): the meaning is that he states the final conclusion—that the *sphoṭa* alone is the expressive agent—in order to suggest that the analysis of the meanings of stems, suffixes, and so forth discussed previously is unreal. Based on the etymology "that from which the object (*artha*) bursts forth or is manifested," it follows that the *sphoṭa* is the word that conveys the meaning. [He says] "it is meaningless" because, since other types of *sphoṭas* are also accepted, this [term] would not serve as a differentiator.

*Durarthakam*—this refers to that which establishes the exclusion of non-denotative phonemes (*varṇa*), *sphoṭa*, and so forth. He states the conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) which serve as a constituent of the investigation, beginning with the words "sādhuśabda" (correct word). A *vipratipatti* is a statement that brings to mind all the possible alternatives (*koṭi*) of a doubt, but it is not merely a sentence that generates doubt; for the modern logicians (*navyatārkika*) do not accept that a word can be a generator of doubt. However, in the view of those who do accept that, let that very [statement] be what is conveyed by the term *vipratipatti*. [This concerns] those phonemes such as the letter *gha* which are not included among correct words (*sādhuśabda*).

Since even opponents admit that the components of words such as *ghaṭa* and *ati* possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is no partial *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already accepted) for the Grammarian school when proving denotative capacity by delimiting it to being included within correct words (*sādhuśabda*). Nor is there a shift of subject matter (*arthāntara*) or partial sublation (*bādha*) when proving [denotative power] through non-prohibition; therefore, "being included within correct words" is adopted as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). "Others" refers to the ancient Naiyāyikas and others.

[Objection: "Granted that the exclusion of *bodhakatva* (the capacity to convey meaning) has been established for the phonemes that do not constitute a correct word (*sādhuśabda*), yet the exclusion of *vācakatva* (the capacity to denote) has not been established. To this, he says: "Those which convey [meaning] are the denoters" (*bodhakā vācakāḥ*). The term *vācakatva* is obtained from the word *bodhaka*. To the question "How so? he says: "Of that very [thing]" (*tasyaiva*). This means: "of that very *bodhakatva*."

Even according to the view that "potency (*śakti*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*)," it should be understood that since potency is postulated on the grounds that the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*) would otherwise be inexplicable, this potency is co-extensive with the capacity to convey meaning. Consequently, when the absence of the capacity to convey meaning is established for those words not included among correct words (*sādhuśabda*), the absence of potency is also established by implication. He introduces the opponent's view in order to refute it with the words "As for [the claim] that... (*yattu*). "Of them" (*teṣām*) refers to the substitutes such as *tiP* and others; "by virtue of their plurality" (*bahutvena*) means by virtue of their being more numerous than the substituenda (*ādeśya*) such as *l* and so forth. "By an infinity of potencies" (*śaktyānantyena*).

It should also be understood that in this position, the status of being the delimiting factor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedakatva*) must be postulated for the numerous serial orders (*ānupūrvī*) residing in the various substitutes; this too is a defect in this view. Furthermore, even in the view that the substituend (*sthānin*) is the expressive unit, there is no room for parsimony (*lāghava*) when one must postulate multiple recollections prior to the verbal cognition; therefore, he states another defect with the example "edhāṃcakre. Here, by the rule "āmaḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix.

"Of the nature of non-existence" (*abhāvarūpasya*) is a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha-viśeṣaṇa*). Since it is of the nature of non-existence, its capacity to sublate [an object] is impossible; the sense is that because it is grounded in existence (*bhāva-niṣṭhatvāt*), no cognition whatsoever can be produced by means of non-existence. It is clear in the authoritative treatises (*nivandheṣu*) that in the case of *edhāṃścakre*, the temporal and causal relations are understood precisely through the suffixes heard after the root being subsequently employed (*anuprayujyamāna-dhātu*).

Although the connection with that meaning and time occurs only in the sense of the root *kṛ* (and others) being subsequently employed, nevertheless, by way of non-difference (*abheda*), its appearance as an additional factor (*ādhikya*) is indeed possible even in the sense connected with that [original] meaning. This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra. For this very reason, it is stated in the Kaumudī on the sūtra "And *kṛ* is subsequently employed": "Because those [periphrastic forms] express general action (*kriyāsāmānya*) while the original bases (*prakṛti*) express specific [actions], there is a connection of non-difference between their respective meanings."

The relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) is as follows: verbs such as *edh* (to increase) have as their meaning an operation conducive to their respective results; the root *kṛ* has as its meaning an operation conducive to origination (*utpatti*); and the roots *bhū* and *as* denote operations conducive to existence (*sattā*). Since proximity (*pratyāsatti*) dictates it, origination and so forth reside solely in the result that constitutes the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*). Thus, they say that from the sentence *aidhāṃcakre* ("he increased"), the understanding is: "an operation conducive to an origination in the remote past, which is non-different from an operation conducive to growth, having a single agent."

Thus, even in the view that *ādeśas* (substitutes) are expressive (*vācaka*), there is no fault here; for this reason, the word "brahma" is followed [as an example]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as "vāri," "paca," "yā," and "apācī" are included. Nor should it be argued that even in those cases, by the maxim "that which remains [is what is intended]," the base (*prakṛti*) itself possesses the meaning of the elided suffix; for the intention is that, rather than postulating a power (*śakti*) and so forth in the base, it is more appropriate to assume the recollection of the suffix, which is already established elsewhere as the signifier.

He states that even in the view that the *ratha* and *nara* [phonemes] possess denotative power (*vācakatā*), there is simplicity regarding the delimitors of that power (*śaktatāvacchedaka-lāghavam*), by saying "of the quality of *la*-ness" (*latvasya*). The point is that its status as a universal (*jāti*) is established because it serves as the delimitor of the production of the dental-vocalic air-conjunction (*danta-vāyu-saṃyoga*) and because it accounts for the occurrence of a uniform cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*). In the opponent's view, however, the multiplicity of the serial orders (*ānupūrvī*) which serve as the delimiters of power is quite evident.

He states another argument as well—beginning with "avyabhī" (non-deviation)—meaning that in the substratum of the knowledge of the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, there is necessarily the existence of the knowledge of the *l*-suffix at the time preceding that knowledge. Thus, in his own system, there is no deviation regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). However, he states that such a deviation exists in the opponent's system with the words "of the substitutes" (*ādeśānām*): that is, by way of being distinct—possessing mutual opposition—which means by way of being manifold.

Nor should it be argued that understanding would likewise arise from "bhū-la" [the substitute form]; for we accept that a specific co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) is the cause [of linguistic cognition]. Otherwise, even in your own view, understanding would result from forms such as "bhū-ati. As for the understanding of those devoid of knowledge of the original substituend (ādeśin), it is accounted for through a misconception regarding the expressive power (śakti-bhrama), since such a postulation is made in the case of corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa). This is the intended meaning.

Now, if it is argued that in cases such as those ending in *śatṛ* (present participles), there would be no cognition of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), because in your view the *lakāra* suffix denotes only the action (*kṛti*) and the state of being an object (*karmatva*), we say: no. For even though the *lakāra* denotes only the action and so forth, it is accepted that the *śatṛ* and other suffixes denote the agent and so forth, according to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "the *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). Furthermore, in order to ensure the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of the nominal stem and the case-suffix, the agent and other meanings belong to the *lakāra* itself; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

And thus, because the capacity to denote is absent in that which functions merely upon being heard, they explain as follows: if substitutes (*ādeśa*) were the denoters, then in cases such as "arāmaḥ," the *visarga* would be established as the denoter of singularity; however, if remembered [original] forms were the denoters, there would be no such fixed determination.

For instance, regarding the word "rāma," should the *visarga* be remembered as *su*, or as *ru*, or as *si*? For the followers of Pāṇini it is *su*; for others, *ru*; and for those versed in the Kālāpa-tantra, *si*. However, for one who is versed in all the grammatical systems (*tantras*), due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) and the resulting conflict, there would be no remembrance of any one of them at all. But that is not tenable.

Just as, even when there is knowledge of many scripts, there is no obstruction to the presentation of the word *namaḥ* at a single time, so too for one who is proficient in all grammars, there is no obstruction to the recollection of the substitutes (*ādeśin*). Rather, it is accepted that the recollection of all [substitutes] occurs, and through that, the presentation of the meaning is indeed non-distinct (*avilakṣaṇa*). For this very reason, a non-distinct cognition is established even from multiple synonyms such as *ghaṭa*, *kalaśa*, and so forth; therefore, he explains it otherwise with the words beginning "tathā hi" (for instance). [The phrase] "from the cognition" (*bodhāt*)...

And thus, the sense is that here the very non-arising of cognition is the meaning of the term "non-establishment. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of proof": the sense is that because the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is not sublated there by the arising of cognition. Anticipating the objection that, due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), the denotative capacity might belong to all substituends (*sthānin*), he says: "of all. And indeed, there is even a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

And thus, the meaning is that those two defects—which led to the abandonment of the position that substitutes (*ādeśa*) possess denotative power—are indeed difficult to avoid even under the position that the original bases (*sthānin*) possess denotative power. Anticipating the objection that this position involves excessive complexity (*gaurava*) compared to the other because of the multiplicity of substitutes such as *ti*, *p* and so on, he says: "And thus... [He explains] "primary" (*mukhya*): primariness consists in the independence from any other means of grasping the expressive power (*śakti*) when the apprehension of that power is to be produced.

However, grammar and the like do not possess that same status; for it is said: "In the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) of suffixes such as *aṇ* (in the rule *tasyāpatyam*, etc.), the apprehension of the power of words such as 'offspring' (*apatya*) is required. If that [apprehension] occurs through another word, and the apprehension of the power of that [other word] likewise requires yet another word, then by accepting this, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Therefore, the meaning is that grammar is required only insofar as it facilitates the apprehension of the power of words such as 'offspring' through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). The phrase "those very ones" refers specifically to the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth. By the restrictive particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of the nominal suffixes (*syat*), the *nibhūta*-suffixes, and the case-endings (*lakāra*).

One might object: "Even though the expressive power (*śakti*) is perceived in the *tiṅ* suffixes through linguistic usage, it is established as residing in the substitutes (*ādeśin*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and not in the *tiṅ*s themselves due to complexity (*gaurava*). This is just as the expressive power, though grasped in the sentence through usage, is attributed to the individual words due to parsimony. Anticipating the objection that the complexity of postulating multiple recollections is not a fault because it is "aimed at the result" (*phalamukhatvāt*), the author states another proof in the root text: "by the principle of 'that cause' (*taddhetunyāyataḥ*). The compound *taddhetunyāya* is a *karmadhāraya*. In the commentary, he asks: "Furthermore... (*kiñca*).

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "he states another proof for this. Alternatively, it should be understood as an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous section) of that which stands in the preceding paragraph. He explains the logical principle (*nyāya*) with the words "of the letter *l*" (*lakārasya*). The meaning of "in such a cognition" is: a cognition in the form "an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*), occurring in the present time and having a single agent. The phrase "the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) even with the word *pacati*" means: the co-occurrence consisting of the word-form *pacati*, which is qualified by the verbal root *pac* and qualified by the suffix *ati*, through the relation of being immediately followed [by the other element].

The term *vācakatva-śaktiḥ* means the power in the form of denotative capacity. Although it has been established that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) [of phonemes] possesses denotative capacity, the author states "And thus... (*tathā ca*) and so forth, in order to dispel the doubt that this is not established with respect to each individual phoneme as delimited by its being a constituent of a correct word (*sādhuśabda*). The phrase "it is established" (*sidhyati*) means that, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*), the denotative capacity of the phonemes occurring in co-occurrence is also established.

Others, however, maintain that because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary], and because [the property] resides neither in each individual [letter] nor in the collection [as a whole], it is the phonemes as uttered together alone that possess denotative power. They argue that it is not possible for something to reside in the collection while residing in each individual—just as with duality—since even duality is accepted as residing in each individual.

The author of the *Peṭaka* [the Bhāṣyakāra] states: "Even though the capacity conducive to movement does not exist in each individual wheel, it exists in the chariot which is the aggregate of them. Regarding this, in the *Arthavatsūtra*, it is said: "For the existence of the purpose of the possessor of a quality is seen through a quality that does not itself serve that purpose; just as, for instance, the wheels of a chariot, when disassembled, are individually incapable of the action of moving, yet their aggregate, the chariot, is capable"—this has been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya—and the same possibility applies here as well.

They say that, in the absence of any determining factor (*vinigamanā*), it is more logical to maintain that even the phonemes uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*) possess denotative power. It should be understood that since denotative power is accepted as residing in the totality of the phonemes uttered in proximity, there is no possibility of the cognition of a specific meaning arising from each individual phoneme constituting that sequence. Regarding the phrase "the agent and the bhāvanā": the meaning is that the distinction—that the suffix *kṛt* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) while the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) denotes the *bhāvanā*—would not hold in your view. [The phrase] "it would not hold in your view" [is the conclusion].

The point is that it is impossible for the *kṛt* suffixes, such as *śatṛ* and others, to denote the agent (*kartṛvācakatva*), because they—just like *la*-suffixes—are equally incapable of denotation; furthermore, the *lakāra* (the verbal root-suffix) which serves as their original base (*sthānin*) denotes only the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). [Regarding the phrase] "due to lack of expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣatayā*), the word "in respect to the meaning" (*arthāṃśe*) is to be supplied. [Regarding the phrase] "of this [rule] 'kartari kṛt'," the meaning is "of the rule *kartari kṛt*. [Regarding the phrase] "because it does not apply," the point is that it is only appropriate to enjoin what is required by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣita*). || 62 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to such coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): this means that, in examples such as these, it is because of the requirement of coreferentiality, and because of the requirement of non-difference (*abheda*) in the syntactic relation. If the agent were not the meaning of the suffix *śānac*, then in cases such as *caitraḥ pacamānaḥ* ("Caitra, while cooking"), there would be no syntactic connection, because non-difference would be contradicted. This is because a connection between two nominal stems (*nāman*) through the relation of locus and located is impossible, as it would contradict the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*). The phrase "it would have the status of denoting the agent" refers to the beginning of the passage starting with "of the *tiṅ*-suffixes," etc.

In the case of "pacatitarāṃ maitraḥ" (Maitra cooks very well), since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) conducive to the action conducive to excessive softening is the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāma*), it cannot be construed as non-different from Maitra. Consequently, the verbal suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*) would have to denote the agent itself; however, this is undesirable according to the opponent's own doctrine—this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "there is the same consequence here as well": one should not suspect that because the primary power (*śakti*) of the suffix *-śānac* is not determined elsewhere, secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—defined as a relationship with the primary meaning—is impossible.

For, just as in the case of a verb not co-occurring with a word ending in the nominative case, it is possible to determine that the suffix *śānac* in the expression "one who is cooking" (*pacamāna*) also possesses the power to denote the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Alternatively, it should be understood that there is a transfer of meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) from the *l*-suffix, which is the substitute for that [suffix], to that [activity].

Furthermore, in the grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) "of the meanings of nouns" (*nāmārthayoḥ*), the word "noun" (*nāman*) does not refer exclusively to those [words] whose primary meaning is a substance (*sattva-pradhāna*); since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) expressed by suffixes such as *-tara* and *-kalpa*, which have verbal roots as their base, is indeed non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), there is no fault. Moreover, according to the derivation beginning with "of the meanings of nouns," the core principle is that the connection (*anvaya*) occurs only between the two qualificands (*viśeṣya*) produced by the cognition generated by nouns, and that [connection] must be through identity (*abheda*). Consequently, even in your own view, how could there be a connection of Devadatta in such cases as "Devadatta cooks better" (*pacatitarāṃ devadattaḥ*) or "Devadatta cooks somewhat" (*pacatikalpaṃ devadattaḥ*)?

If it is argued that, according to your view, the connection [of the agent] is with the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) which has become a qualifier, and that there is a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of grammatical usage (*vyutpatti*) in that regard, it must be replied: "I too follow that [restriction]. This is because the intention is that the term "noun" (*nāman*) refers either to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone or to the inflected word (*suvanta*) alone, and there is no evidence for a rule such as that the connection applies only between the object of the cognition produced by a noun and its own qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Nor should it be argued that if such a restriction is not accepted, the sentence "the pot is impermanent" would incur the fault of being authoritative because the term "permanent" could then be construed with "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva). For since "pot-ness" is but a part of a word-meaning, its construction there is impossible due to the conflict with the linguistic rule that "a word-meaning is construed with a word-meaning [and not with a part thereof]"; thus, the aforementioned sentence does not incur the status of being authoritative.

Since the agent (*kartṛ*) is not a part of the meaning of the word [itself], the syntactic connection in cases such as "Devadatta cooks somewhat" (*pacatikalpaṃ devadattaḥ*) remains entirely unimpaired. Therefore, since only the phonemes (*varṇa*) uttered together possess denotative power, the *varṇasphoṭa* is established beyond dispute. Now, one might object: "If the substitutes (*ādeśa*), such as *ti* and so on, were the denoters, there would be a contradiction with grammatical rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), because that rule teaches that the original bases (*sthānin*) alone possess denotative power. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The rule *laḥ karmaṇo*... Thus concludes the exposition of the *varṇasphoṭa*.

"Of the phonemes that are co-uttered"—this means of all the phonemes that constitute each respective word. "When the denotative capacity is established"—the meaning is this: without the denotative capacity of those [individual] phonemes, the denotative capacity of the word, whose nature will be described hereafter, would not be possible; therefore, the establishment of the word's denotative capacity is dependent upon the establishment of the denotative capacity of those phonemes. In this way, the relationship between this section and the preceding text as one of dependence (upajīvya-upajīvaka-bhāva) is indicated.

One might object: "Even so, let it be granted that denotative power (vācakatā) rests in each individual letter; yet this does not establish the desired conclusion that 'the word (pada) is the denoter. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In each letter" (*prativarṇam*). [He explains: "In the form of co-utterance" (*samabhivyāhārarūpā*) means "in the form of a collection" (*samudāyarūpā*). And [he adds]: "lest there be the undesirable consequence of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth. As for the non-occurrence of the audible suffix (*sup*), it is not brought forward because, since the letters are parts of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of a collection, the elision by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* is possible.

Regarding the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*): since this serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that "only when there is a mutual connection between the word-meanings and such a collection of meanings possessing [those meanings] occurs, then it is [the case of] a compound"—the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for the present collection is established without obstacle. According to the author of the *Pratīpoddyota*: because there is no number or meaning of number associated with each individual phoneme, the case-ending that expresses that [number] does not arise; for the production of number occurs only in such instances [where a meaningful unit is present].

Furthermore, number is the meaning of the aggregate alone, not of the individual phonemes, according to the natural drift of the *bhāṣya* on the *aiuṇ* sūtra, which states: "Unity is the meaning of the combination. Accordingly, the *bhāṣya* there says: "Because the aggregate has a single meaning, there is an absence of case-endings (*sub*), as in the case of [the word] *varṇa*," and so forth. Although there may be transposition or addition of phonemes within the stem portion (*prakṛti*), since no other number is perceived, the intention is that number is the meaning of the aggregate alone.

Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*), the singular number is unavoidable; for although such a construction may be postulated on the authority of the *Bhāṣya* only when the meaning is devoid of number, its application to meanings endowed with number is not fit for postulation because it would lack denotative power (*anabhidhāyakatva*), as there is no evidence for it. Furthermore, such a postulation occurs only when there is an indicator (*gamaka*). Thus, since these [indeclinables] do not possess "stemness" (*prakṛtitva*) in the form of being the basis for the introduction of suffixes, the maxim "not when isolated" (*na kevalāḥ*) does not apply. Consequently, they maintain that there is no contingency of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth.

Thus, since it would lead to the recollection of meanings contrary to actual experience, and because no other meaning of the verbal root is perceived in cases such as *tarku* and *rajjū* despite the presence of letter-transposition or insertion, and due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*), it is more appropriate to maintain that individual letters do not possess meaning. This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the *aiuṇ* sūtra. The phrase "and this" means the establishment of the denotative capacity [of words] through co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). The phrase "only the final letter" means only the final letter constituting the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

However, there is no potency (*śakti*) residing in the first letter alone, because it would follow that the meaning is cognized merely from the utterance of that single letter; furthermore, since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the subsequent letters has not yet arisen at that time, it is impossible for the experience of the first letter to have the experiences of the successive letters as its auxiliary causes.

The point is this: if the cause [of word-meaning cognition] were the impression produced by the experience of the first letter, assisted by the impressions generated by the experiences of each subsequent letter, then—due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*)—it would follow that the expressive power (*śakti*) must reside in the entire collection of those letters. Regarding "subsisting collectively" (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*), this means being pervasively present across multiple letters. The reason given is "for want of proof": since the comprehension of meaning arises only after the experience of the final letter, the expressive capacity (*vācakatva*) is exhausted in that very [final letter].

[Objection: But in that case, the cognition of meaning would result even from the utterance of the final letter alone; therefore, he says: "each preceding [letter]. For this very reason, there is no pointlessness of the other letters. Because the refutation of this position is intended precisely as a target for refutation—meaning, it is for the sake of refutation alone—it is struck down by the previously mentioned defects. [The phrase] "only of the sequence" means: not of the particularity (*tadvyaktitva*) residing in the final letter alone, and so forth.

If it is objected: "In words such as *ghaṭa*, since the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*)—consisting of the property of being preceded by *gha*, followed by a vowel, followed by *ṭa*, followed by a vowel—resides only in the final phoneme, it does not reside in the collection of all phonemes; therefore, how can your intended position that the word (*pada*) is the signifier (*vācaka*) be established? We reply: No, because this objection does not touch upon the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain that sequential order is a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*).

Even on the view that "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*) consists of the aforementioned form, there is no loss [of the definition], because the property of being a letter immediately following [another] resides in the subsequent letter, while the sequence consisting of the property of being a *gha* letter immediately preceding it and so forth rests upon all the letters constituting that word. If it is argued that these [sequences] cannot serve as the delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) due to their multiplicity and resulting complexity, we say no, for they must be accepted out of necessity; or else, because sequence is the nature of a collection of successive letters joined with each preceding letter by the relation of "immediate succession."

Alternatively, let it be accepted that the *ānupūrvī* (sequential order) itself is the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedikā*), by virtue of its being the counter-correlative of a subjectivity (*viṣayatā*) that pervades the subjectivity whose object is the sequence resting solely upon the final phoneme. Thus, even though the constituent phonemes differ according to the difference between words, one should intend that the subjectivities regarding the phonemes—by virtue of their being subjectivities whose objects are delimited by [the universal] *gha*-ness and so on—are pervasive of such a sequential subjectivity; consequently, there is no fault such as non-pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*). Enough with this prolixity.

[Objection: "But surely, since such a sequence (tādṛśānupūrvī) is sufficient to prevent the aforementioned over-extension simply by virtue of being a cooperative factor (sahakārin), there is no need to postulate it as the delimitor of capacity (śaktatāvacchedaka). To this, he says: "The direction [is as follows]" (*dig iti*). The meaning of that is as follows: because the aggregate (samudāya) lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), it would fail to attain the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); furthermore, even if one were to accept the status of a nominal stem for the aggregate merely on the basis of its being a cooperative factor in the production of the cognition of meaning, then the final phoneme alone would also possess the status of a nominal stem, and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of suffixes arising after that as well.

In this way, just as for the final phoneme alone there would be no application of the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) with respect to its referent, because it is not the base (*aprakṛtitvāt*); so too, even if the aggregate were the base, since the meaning of the base is not presented through its occurrence therein, it would lack the status of being that [aggregate's] meaning.

Furthermore, if there were no expressive power (*śakti*) in a composite word such as *paṅkaja* (lotus), the distinction between derivative (*yaugika*), etymological-cum-conventional (*yogarūḍha*), and so forth, would result in total collapse. For instance, if one were to utter "pāk" followed by "aka" with an interval—such as a pause of a few moments—between them instead of saying "pācaka," there would still arise the cognition that [the speaker] is an agent of cooking (*pākakartṛ*). Consequently, it would be impossible to assert that "a word is derivative (*yaugika*) when the constituent parts [of the compound] alone possess the auxiliary function (*sahakāritva*) [in producing the meaning]."

Now, is it not the case that a word is *yaugika* (derivative) when it presents its meaning through the power of its final phoneme alone, as in the case of words such as *pācaka* (cook)? And a word is *kevalarūḍha* (purely conventional) when it presents its meaning through the power of its final phoneme alone, as in the case of words such as *ḍittha*?

If it is argued that such a classification is indeed possible—where a term is *yogarūḍha* (based on both etymological derivation and conventional usage) when there is a mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between two meanings presented separately by the power (*śakti*) of the final phoneme of its own constituent base (*prakṛti*) and so forth, and the power of its own final phoneme, as in the case of words like *paṅkaja* (lotus)—we say no. For in a word such as *pācaka* (cook), since the property of being the final phoneme of itself exists even in the final phoneme of the suffix (*pratyaya*) that constitutes the word, it would follow that the aforementioned definition of *yaugika* (etymologically derived) could not possibly apply.

In this way, there would be no case of mere conventional usage (*kevalarūḍhatva*) for the word *gopada*; for its final phoneme, because it is non-different from the final phoneme of the suffix that constitutes it, there would be no presentation [of the meaning] by the power of its own final phoneme alone—this and similar points are to be understood. || 64 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the defined word" (*paribhāṣitapadasya*): the meaning is "of that very [word]. The intention is that this excludes stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), which are intended to be meaningful words [only when combined]. This is because linguistic usage occurs only with items ending in *sup* (case endings) and so forth, and it is precisely there that the apprehension of expressive power (*śaktigraha*) takes place. Others, however, say that the meaning is also "of a word as defined by convention. He provides a proof for the fact that such a word must be the denoter (*vācaka*), otherwise it would be inexplicable, by citing the root text's example "with a jar" (*ghaṭena*) and so on. He explains that: "in 'with a jar' (*ghaṭena*) etc."; and "not... the suffix."

The word "asya" (of this) is to be construed with "vibhāgasya" (of the division). Thus, the construction is: "because it is impossible to know the division. This means because a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) is impossible. [This is stated] because specific knowledge is possible: in the view that "there is a substitute for two phonemes," a doubt arises from the uncertainty as to whether the substitute in the form of *e* is the prior member or the subsequent member; thus, that doubt is possible. However, in the view that "all [phonemes] are substitutes for all words," the meaning is that—just as in the case of *vasnasā* and so on—a knowledge of the division is not possible at all due to total confusion (*saṃpramoha*).

The statement "it is undifferentiated" (*aviśiṣṭa*) is said because the cognition that "there might be some base-portion (*prakṛti-bhāga*) here" is indeed possible; however, the meaning is that there is no possibility of the cognition that "this is the base-portion and this is the affix-portion" (*pratyaya-bhāga*). As for the phrase "the division is possible": the point is that just as even for grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) such a knowledge of division is not possible in cases like *vatnasā*, so too it is not possible in cases like *rāmeṇa* under the view that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words" (*sarve sarvapadādeśāḥ*).

In this view, it should be understood that even according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra—who prescribes the substitution of *nā* in place of *ṭā*—it is not easy for grammarians to have knowledge of the [phonetic] divisions. Nevertheless, the point is that since the cognition in the form "the agent is non-different from Rāma" arising from the word *rāmeṇa* would otherwise be inexplicable, one must accept that the word, consisting of a nominal stem (*su-anta*) and so forth, possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*).

They say that the expressive power (*vācakatva*) belongs to the word itself in cases where the conceptualization of divisions such as stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is impossible; however, in cases where such conceptualization is possible, the expressive power belongs to the stem and the suffix alone. But those who know the intent of the *Bhāṣya* say: "In such instances, since the expressive power of the word has already been established, the expressive power must belong to the word in all cases; otherwise, one would fall into the error of the 'half-old woman' (*ardhajaratīya*) principle, and because the apprehension of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*) occurs precisely there [in the word] through common usage. This same pair of views should be understood to apply to the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*) as well.

Regarding this, he says: the meaning is that it expresses the status of being a designator (*vācakatva*). "Of the two words" (*padayoḥ*)—in the view that there is a substitution (*ādeśa*) of phonemes (*varṇa*), this means "of the two phonemes that are constituents of the word. However, in the view that "all [phonemes] are substitutes for all words," the literal reading itself is correct. "Its division" (*tadvibhāgaḥ*) refers to the division into the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). By the phrase "in *hareva*" and so forth, examples such as *viṣṇo'va* and *kṛṣṇeva* are included. There is no removal by substitution of the portions consisting of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), as in cases such as *lihaṃ*, *lihau*, and *liha*.

To the objection that even in that case, the power of the whole (samudāyaśakti) must be admitted, he says: "In this way, regarding the *prakṛti*," etc. In the root text, it says "the *sphoṭa* of the sentence. "Sentence" (*vākya*) means the signifier (*vācaka*). Now, one might object: "Even if the status of being a signifier is established for that sentence where no analysis into parts is possible, its establishment does not follow for all sentences. To this, he says: "In reality," and so forth. Just as an object such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) is conveyed by words—namely, nominal stems like *ghaṭa* or by inflected forms (*subanta*)—so too is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) conveyed by sentences such as "The jar exists" (*ghaṭo'sti*).

It is understood; however, it should be noted that through the discrimination between what is already established and what is not yet established, that power culminates in the relation of connection (*saṃsarga*).

As for the authors of the *Peṭikā*, they hold that since the relationship of action and factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is expressed by the case-ending itself, even though the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) is impossible regarding that portion, the power of the sentence resides in the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva*).

Although the status of being a qualifier residing in the meaning of the base (prakṛti) of an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*) may be the denotation (*śakyārtha*) of that ending, it should be understood that the status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), which resides in the qualificandum and is counter-correlative to the status of being a qualifier of the meaning of another word, is its denotation. This is because the manifestation (*bhāna*) of the objective relation (*viṣayatā*) is also necessary in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* "arthavat... (Pāṇini 1.2.45), as well as from the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* "prātipadikārtha... (Pāṇini 2.3.46) and the *Sūtra* "ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe" (Pāṇini 2.3.50).

For in that context—regarding such examples as "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*)—it has been stated that "the sentence-meaning is that surplus [of meaning] which consists in the relation between qualifier and qualified. Regarding the term "surplus" (*ādhikyam*), they say that the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (i.e., as a nominalization). He states the objection to not postulating a primary expressive power (*śakti*) in the sentence: "otherwise," etc. "Such an understanding" (*tādṛśavyutpatti*) means: for one who lacks the knowledge that a sentence such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) generates the cognition of bringing the pot as the object. "The consequence of cognition" (*bodhaprasaṅga*)... [refers to the unwanted result].

There would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the bringing [of] the pot as its object" (*ghaṭakarmakam ānayanam*). The phrase "for one who possesses the grasp of the word-potency for 'pot' and so forth" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Thus, the meaning is that just as in the case of "bring the pot," here too there is the undesirable consequence of such a cognition because the causal complex consisting of the presentation of word-meanings and so forth is present. Since such a cognition is indeed desired for one who possesses that specific linguistic proficiency, the author follows the path of excluding those who lack such proficiency.

Now, one might object: "The sentence *'ghaṭaḥ karmatvam'* (the pot is the object-ness) is inherently incapable [of producing cognition], so no understanding arises from it; for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in the presence of the word *am* in the word *ghaṭa* by the relation of being immediately preceding, the presence of the word *ghaṭa* etc. in the word *am* by the relation of being immediately following, the presence of the word *ānaya* in the letter *a*, or the presence of the letter *a* in the word *ānaya*. And such expectancy is absent in cases like *'ghaṭaḥ karmatvam'*."

Since the property of having the word *karman* (object) as its co-occurrent (*padavatva*) does not constitute expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the case of the word *ghaṭa*, because expectancy is defined solely as a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) that generates verbal cognition, he says: "just as in the case of *ghaṭam ānaya*" (*bring the pot*). Here too, the phrase "of one who lacks such linguistic proficiency" (*tādṛśavyutpattirahitasya*) is to be supplied. And [he adds] "due to the absence of cognition. The meaning is that if the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) were not admitted, then since all other causal factors for cognition would be present, verbal cognition would result [even in the absence of expectancy]. "In that very case" means precisely in the case of *ghaṭam ānaya*.

The construction is: "from the awakening of one who possesses such knowledge. [The phrase] "the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose meaning is a jar" includes words such as *kalaśa* and others. [The phrase] "denoting the objectness (*karmatva*)" is for the sake of clarity; for there is no deviation from its denoting objectness in the case of the accusative suffix (*am*) following words like *ghaṭa*. In some places, the reading is simply "of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting objectness," by which both the dual (*au*) and the plural (*śas*) are included as being case-endings that denote objectness.

The sense is that, likewise, there is no multiplicity of cause-and-effect relations due to the difference between words such as *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*, nor due to the difference between verbal suffixes such as *am* and others. Immediately after the word "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), it should be understood in some places as "of the vikaraṇa. However, the inclusion of "the vikaraṇa" is not universal, because it is absent in cases such as *odanaṃ papāca*.
