Although in cases such as "ānaya" (bring), the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is likewise not explicitly heard, and the process of mental supplementation (*anusandhāna*) is identical in both instances, nevertheless, for the sake of bringing the meaning of the suffix to mind, such supplementation is necessary; however, because the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational sign) is devoid of meaning, its supplementation is not required. With this intention, the term "of the *vikaraṇa*" was not mentioned immediately after "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*). Alternatively, the *vikaraṇa* was not mentioned to indicate its subordinate status, characterized by its lack of meaning. [The phrase] "that knowledge also" refers to this.

The knowledge of such a causal relationship is also [the cause]. Thus, since it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the cause is simply the knowledge of such an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the point is that there is no evidence for the existence of a denotative power (*śakti*) in the sentence itself. "The sentence-sphoṭa is established" means that the capacity of the sentence to denote meaning is established. "In the cognition of the specific sentence-meaning" means in the cognition of a particular sentence-meaning; that is to say, in a cognition of the form "the bringing of a pot as the object. "Co-occurrence of words" (*padasamabhivyāhāra*)...

The meaning is that this is a sentence consisting of a collection of words possessing the previously mentioned relation of antecedence and sequence; and this is stated with the intention that comprehension arises precisely from a sentence such as "Bring the jar."

If, however, such a cognition is established by experience even from a reversed sentence such as "bring-the-pot" (*ānaya-ghaṭam*), then for this very reason, it should be understood that—as stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*: "In a sentence, the connection with either [word] occurs according to one's wish, as in 'the king’s man' (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) or 'the man of the king' (*puruṣo rājñaḥ')"—just as with the aforementioned co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), the grasp of the capacity to convey the intended meaning of the sentence residing in that [word], based on a co-occurrence with a reversed finite verb (*tiṅanta*), also functions as a cause for such a cognition.

[Objection: Surely such a knowledge of the causal relation between [the word and its object] must be admitted; otherwise, from a cognitive state (*vṛtti-jñāna*) whose object is a jar, there would arise the undesirable consequence of a cognition whose object is a cloth or something else. Thus, since it is necessary that the causal relation differs according to the difference in objects, even if one posits causality in this way, how is it established that the word possesses a denotative power (*śakti*)? To this, he says: "that which presents the meaning" (*arthopasthāpaka*). The meaning is as follows: that word which is the object of the knowledge that presents the meaning—causality with respect to that [knowledge] is what belongs to it (the word).

The phrase "that which brings about the apprehension of the meaning" (*arthopasthāpaka*) is included in order to exclude from the definition of *śakti* (denotative power) the cognition that [the word] is the cause of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning—consisting of the bringing of a jar—as residing in the sentence "Bring the jar. This means "that which brings about the apprehension of the relevant meaning. By this, the aforementioned defects do not persist. Thus, the intention is that what is called *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) in the view of the opponent is, for us, simply *vākyaśakti* (sentence-power); therefore, there is no redundancy.

One might object: "Since the cognition of the *vṛtti* (the expressive relation) regarding a particular object is the cause for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of that same object, and since there would be no purpose [for postulating a separate power] if one were to postulate a causal relationship by including the 'relation' itself as the object, it is possible to account for the cognition of that [relation] even without admitting a *śakti* (power) in that respect. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And this is reasonable," and so forth. [The phrase] "by way of the relation of objecthood" (*viṣayatā-sambandhena*).

And thus, since there is no multiplicity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the diversity of objects, the point is that if one does not admit a power (*śakti*) in the aspect of the relation itself, the comprehension of that [relation] cannot be accounted for; therefore, the acceptance of power is not necessary. Now, if it is argued that "there would be an infinity of powers due to the infinity of co-utterances (*samabhivyāhāra*) such as 'bring the jar' and 'bring the cloth'," [we reply: even in your own view, there would be an infinity of causal relations due to the difference between those respective co-utterances, and thus the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) is equal.

If the cognitive presentation (upasthiti) generated by the case-ending following a word denoting "pot" is the cause for a verbal cognition delimited by having "pot" as its qualifier (*ghaṭaprakāraśābdabodhatva*), then the delimiting relation between the effect and the cause is the relation of qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*). Likewise, the cognitive presentation generated by the word preceding the case-ending denoting "objectness" (*karmatva*) is the cause—by way of the relation of qualificandumhood—for a verbal cognition delimited by having "objectness" as its qualifier (*karmatvaprakāraśābdatva*).

This is the case when one accepts that "objecthood" (*karmatva*), which is the meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). However, if one accepts it as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then a general causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—where the verbal cognition has objecthood as its qualificand through the relation of being a mode (*prakāratā*)—must be accepted everywhere. If you argue that in that case, by accepting a sentence-meaning power (*vākyaśakti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of such powers, then in my view as well, only a single power residing in all sentences such as "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) and "Bring the cloth" (*paṭam ānaya*) is accepted.

However, since the relation such as "being the object" (*karmatva*)—which is determined with respect to the sentence-meaning—is unitary, there is no possibility of the cognition of a cloth as the object in the case of the sentence "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), precisely because the cloth is not presented by the word. In reality, however, it is necessary to postulate a specific causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) by including each respective word, such that the presentation generated by the accusative suffix following the word "jar" is the cause for the verbal cognition having "jar" as its qualifier.

Otherwise, it should be understood that when the word "ghaṭa" (pot) presents the object "pot" without requiring further expectation, there would be the undesirable consequence of understanding arising from the sentence "kalaśam ānaya" (bring the jar) for a person who has not grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word "kalaśa. It is precisely to avoid this that the *Bhūṣaṇa* uses the word "yadi" (if) in the phrase "yadi ghaṭaprakāraka... (if [the cognition] has the pot as its qualifier). However, if that [word "yadi"] were stated while including each specific term, the aforementioned undesirable consequence would not arise; for only the presentation produced by each specific term, conjoined with the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) involving that term, is included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

If it is asked, "Even so, what is the proof that the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the sentence?"—understand that it is the otherwise inexplicability of the manifestation of the relation (*saṃbandha*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is because the objective content (*viṣayatā*) of a verbal cognition must be the objective content of the word-generated presentation (*padajanyopasthiti*) through a *vṛtti* (relation of meaning). For one may postulate a general causal relationship between verbal cognition and word-generated presentation by including the object itself as the locus of the relation of objective content, rather than specifying the relation. However, the property of "belonging to a particular person" (*tatpuruṣīyatva*) should be included within the scope of the limiting condition (*avacchedaka*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even a person for whom another person is present [in the vicinity] would have verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding an object that is empty of that other person. If one were to posit a causal relationship between those two based on a relation residing in the self (ātmaniṣṭhapratyāsatti) by introducing the object [as a relatum], then because objects are more numerous than persons, there would result an excessive number of cause-and-effect relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even a jar or similar object presented to the eyes and other senses from a word like "jar" whose expressive power (śakti) has not been grasped would give rise to verbal cognition.

If it is argued that the causal relation is accepted only through a relation that is a distinct objective content (*viṣayatā*) other than the relational objective content (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*), and therefore there is no necessity to admit a power (*śakti*) in the relation itself—here they reply: because the objective content, which is of the nature of cognition, is one and common to all three (the qualificand, etc.), it is impossible to introduce [the causal relation] in such a manner.

Even in the view that there is an additional objective relation (*atiriktaviṣayatā*), since that [relation] can be accounted for as being one alone, the threefold nature of objective relations is not accepted. Furthermore, although a threefold nature is possible in the view that objective relation is the very nature of the object (*viṣayasvarūpa*), it should be understood from the *Bhūṣaṇa* that this is because it would involve the cumbersome postulation of distinct objective relations for the relations between relations (*sāṃsargikaviṣayatā*). With this in mind, he says: "And this has been analyzed in the *Bhūṣaṇa*."

Others, however, argue that if the capacity of the sentence [to convey] the inferential relation (*anvaya*) is not admitted, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I am cognizing that through verbal testimony," because such a reflective awareness has as its object only a cognition connected with a word. If it were held that being produced by a word alone is the regulator of such a reflective awareness, then there would be the undesirable consequence of such a reflective awareness even regarding an inference of fire based on the mark of smoke presented by the word "smoke," since that too is produced by a word.

If it is argued that the universal *śābdatva* (verbalness) itself is the cause of such a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), and that this universal exists only in a verbal cognition produced by a causal complex consisting of the knowledge of expectancy and so forth—not in inference—therefore no such undesirable consequence follows; even so, the common usage "these two sentences are mutually connected" would be undermined, because, given the acceptance that the connection between words occurs only through their meanings, the two sentences themselves lack such a connection.

Nor should it be argued that a connection between two sentences is indeed possible by way of their objects being the cognition of a purposeful form; for such a connection lacks the capacity to regulate linguistic usage regarding relatedness.

Otherwise, even in the absence of relations such as producer-produced (*janya-janakabhāva*), there would result the linguistic usage "these two are connected" with respect to a person from Mathurā and a person from Pāṭaliputra—since a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of "conjunction of the conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*) and so forth exists between them, and since the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) residing in themselves also exists [in the other]. Enough of this; thus they say, and let us stop this prolixity.

This, however, must be understood: although in many instances the *padasphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) and *vākyasphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa) are established, wherever the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sentence alone is prescribed by the treatise, the comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence itself and not from the word—as, for example, in "ṣaṭ santaḥ" and so forth. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the rule "ḍaḥ si dhuṭ," the doubt as to why the augment *dhuṭ* and others were not made "endings" (*pūrvānta*) was resolved by the application of the rule for the substitution of *ṣṭu*.

Otherwise, due to the resulting difference in the *ānupūrvī* (sequential order) that delimits capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), the comprehension of the primary meaning from the word "asantaḥ" would be untenable; thus, since the status of being "preceded by *par*" is necessary, they argue that such an investigation would lead to inconsistency. In every case, only the *ānupūrvī* as it is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇa*) serves as the delimiter of capacity, and not the *ānupūrvī* as it is remembered (*smaryamāṇa*), because the experience of comprehension arises only from what is heard, and because those who lack knowledge of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) are unable to remember it.

By this, the objection—that in the case of "ṣaṭtsantaḥ," the mere sequence devoid of traditional authority (āgama) is the delimitor of the capacity for those respective meanings, and that for this very reason the word "santaḥ" within the sentence "santaḥ pūjyāḥ" yields the presentation of its own meaning and so forth, and thus there is no inconsistency with the discussion in the Bhāṣya—is refuted. In the same way, in cases such as "ghaṭena," the verbal cognition occurs only preceded by the recollection of the suffix *ṭā*; for it is precisely that [suffix] which is postulated in accordance with forms such as "matyā" and "goduhe."

Furthermore, the objection that the substituend (*sthānin*) is never heard anywhere—just as the *lakāra* and so forth are not themselves expressive (*vācaka*)—must also be refuted. This is because for one who lacks knowledge of the relationship between the substituend and the substitute (*ādeśa*), comprehension arises from the substitute itself as it is heard; thus, its status as the expressive unit is necessary. This is the general direction of the argument. As for the term "because of being unprecedented" (*apūrvatvāt*): this means it is unknown prior to every verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency even if such knowledge of it occurs in some cases through the sense organs.

The impossibility of grasping that [relation]: the impossibility of grasping the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Regarding the phrase "acceptance of the debate" (*vādābhyupagama*): since that which has unapprehended potency is of no use, the term "acceptance" was stated; thus, in this view, a lack of firm conviction is indicated. For this very reason, another alternative view is stated in the root-text. He introduces that with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*). The phrase "like the word-meaning" (*padārthavat*): because the locative case is seen in the form of the suffix *-vat* when the object of comparison is a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), as in the rule regarding the locative case. "Even in the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthe’pi*) means even in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaye’pi*).

*Tad-grahaḥ* means the apprehension of the word’s power (*pada-śakti-graha*). Regarding the phrase "let it be [the case] with respect to the word and also the meaning," there would be an inconsistency if the particle *api*, occurring after the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the compound *vākyārtha-pada*, were intended to conjoin the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), because the apprehension of the power with respect to the word-meaning has not been rejected; therefore, he says: "the *api* follows the word *pada*. *Tad-agrahaścediti* means: "if there were an apprehension of the power with respect to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)."

By this much of the text, it was previously stated that the apprehension of the word’s power (śakti) occurs first with respect to the individual word-meanings; then, once those word-meanings have been presented [to the mind], the apprehension of the power with respect to the relation—presented subsequently by the mind—occurs. Now, however, he says "But in reality... to show that the apprehension of the power occurs first with respect to the sentence-meaning itself by means of the mind assisted by the observation of linguistic usage (vyavahāra), and only afterwards does the apprehension of the power of each specific word for its respective meaning occur through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa). Here too, the phrase "observing the linguistic usage of elders" is to be supplied as a complement.

Therefore, there is no harm even if the word-meaning (*pada-śakti*) is grasped prior to the grasp of the sentence-meaning (*vākya-śakti*) from a lexicon (*kośa*) and similar sources. In some cases, by means of instruction (*upadeśa*), the grasp of the power [of meaning] determined by a specific sentence-meaning occurs first in the sentence, and subsequently the grasp of the power of the words constituting that sentence. In such instances—as in "six cows" (*ṣaṭ-gāvaḥ*) and so forth—they say that the rule that "the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is preceded only by the knowledge of the word-meanings" is violated.

In some cases, when the meanings of the words have been presented by the individual words, the sentence-meaning is presented through the assistance of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); at that very moment, there is the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) and the comprehension. Since the presentation of the underlying sentence-meaning lacks the quality of being produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), it is not considered a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Nor should it be argued that since the power of the words themselves is sufficient to account for their own meanings as related (*anvita*), it is redundant to postulate a power in the sentence; for even if one accepts a power in relation to the connection (*anvaya*), one must still admit that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) is the cause of that specific comprehension of the connection, in order to account for the cognition of a particular instance of that connection.

Likewise, since the capacity of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) is unimpeded, one must accept that the apprehension of that [sentence] is also a cause in order to exclude the cognition of one who does not apprehend its causal nature; furthermore, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a power (*śakti*) in the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of words. This and more is explained in detail elsewhere.

Now, if it is objected that in this way the meaning of a sentence would be merely a memory (*smṛti*), like the meanings of individual words, and not a direct experience (*anubhava*), the reply is as follows: because the cognition of the sentence-meaning lacks the nature of direct experience—for even one hearing of heaven and so forth does not have the realization "I am experiencing heaven"—but rather, "verbal-ness" (*śābdatva*) is a specific genus (*jāti*) subsumed under the genus "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). || 66 ||

The two positions mentioned are: that the word (*pada*) is expressive, or that the sentence (*vākya*) is expressive. He clarifies the untenability [of these positions] with the words "because of their production" (*utpatteḥ*). According to the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced, [the expression is] "because of their production"; according to the view that they are eternal, however, it is "because of their manifestation. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility at all times": if their production were to occur only occasionally, then there would be perception [of them], just as there is of color, taste, and so forth, which are produced simultaneously.

Thus, if the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of various phonemes (*varṇa*) were to occur simultaneously, then the perception of a word (*pada*) and the perception of a sentence (*vākya*) would be possible; however, that is not possible at one time. Because the conjunctions of air with their respective articulatory locations (*sthāna*), which serve as the manifestors (*abhivyañjaka*), are successive, and because it is impossible for sequential things that perish very rapidly to coalesce, the perception of a word or a sentence—which consists of a collection of those many phonemes—is untenable. This is the collective meaning. In the phrase "in that" (*tasmin*), it refers to the subsequent phoneme. "Presented" (*upasthita*) means remembered (*smṛta*).

"Having the same preceding phoneme" (*pūrvavarṇavattva*)—this connects with the word "easy to grasp" (*sugraha*). "The second letter qualified by the presented [first]" (*upasthitaviśiṣṭa*) means: that second letter which is qualified by the first letter that has been presented.

In this manner, at the time of the perception of the fourth and subsequent phonemes, the property of being qualified by the second [phoneme] as qualified by the first [phoneme], and so on, is easily grasped; thus, the perception of the final phoneme comes to have all the phonemes constituting the word or sentence as its object. Consequently, there is no inconsistency in the cognition of word-meanings or sentence-meanings—this is the meaning of the section. The phrase "just like the status of being a word" (*padatvasyeva*) refers to this.

Even if the expressive power of a sentence (*vākyaśakti*) is not accepted, the denotative capacity of a word (*pada*) is certainly admitted; therefore, the occurrence of a perceptual cognition characterized by the nature of being a "word" (*padatva*), which is necessary for the establishment of that [denotative capacity], must be accepted precisely through the aforementioned method. Likewise, on the view that accepts the expressive power of a sentence, a perceptual cognition characterized by the nature of being a "sentence" (*vākyatva*) is also established by that same method—this is the meaning.

It should not be suspected that this cumbersome method [of postulating a sphoṭa] is unnecessary because the meaning can be understood from letters mounted upon a single memory; for since the understanding of meaning is impossible without knowledge of the sequence [of the letters], and since there is no rule that memory must necessarily follow the order of experience, an identical cognition would result even in cases such as "saro" and "rasa. || 67 ||

Now—at the time immediately following the determination of the *sakhaṇḍapada-sphoṭa*. Thus, it is indicated that "occasion" (*prasaṅga*) or "opportunity" (*avasara*) constitutes the connection (*asaṅgati*). He states the position of the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) [sphoṭa]; the words "on account of parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) are to be supplied as the remainder. [Objection: But surely, the statement "there are no parts in letters" is irrelevant to the present context; to dispel this doubt, he says "by way of an illustration" (*dṛṣṭānta*). The meaning is: "by means of the guise of an illustration. "Just as they are not [parts] even though they are perceived," and so forth.

That cognition, however, is merely an error caused by the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the pitch (*svara*) of specific sounds which manifest those respective phonemes (*varṇa*) through their particular modes of utterance; therefore, it does not establish the [existence of] the object. For if one were to postulate constituent parts in [phonemes] such as *e* and *o*, it would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). The phrase "as it were" (*iva*) means "only as it were. The meaning is that the reading is "parts in the phonemes. In this reading, the status of the example is quite clear. He explains the meaning of the word "discrimination" (*praviveka*)—namely, "difference" (*bheda*).

Following the meaning of the verbal root *vi-cir* in the sense of "separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*), the intended meaning is that the word *praviveka* signifies "distinction. He dispels the doubt that the very fact that the perception of the letter *ka* and so forth is distinct [from other letters] would otherwise be inexplicable—by stating "the production of those respective phonemes," etc. This means: it resides in that conjunction of air which is measured (or delimited) by its being the producer of those respective phonemes. Regarding the phrase "of the status of being a generator" (*janakatāyāḥ*): the meaning is that it possesses that delimiting-ness (*avacchedakatva*) which is either defined by the status of being a generator (*janakatā*) or defined by the status of being a manifester (*vyañjakatā*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in cognition": the meaning is that the *sphoṭa* manifests in the form of *ka*-ness and so forth, which reside in the conjunction with air; thus, cognitions such as "the letter *ka*" and "the letter *kha*" are accounted for as distinct. In the *Bhāmatī*—that is, in the work of Vācaspati—it is said: "it is superimposed upon the phonemes (*varṇas*). For this very reason, the cognition and linguistic usage regarding a single phoneme as being "high" (*tāra*) or "low" (*manda*) are possible; otherwise, since two contradictory properties cannot arise in one [entity], it would follow that there is a difference between those respective phonemes.

The conventional usage that even within a single phoneme (varṇa) one is "higher" (tāra) in relation to something else and "lower" (manda) in relation to something else is indeed established for all people. However, this fault does not arise if one accepts [the difference as] a superimposition (āropa), because it is only a non-superimposed connection with two contradictory properties that necessitates a difference in substrates. Regarding the phrase "perceived through direct perception" (pratyakṣopalabhyamāna): it means that which is perceived by direct perception as being qualified by "k-ness" (katva) and so forth—that is, the object of a direct perception whose qualifier is "k-ness" and so forth.

Thus, the *sphoṭa* is necessary in accordance with the experience expressed as "I hear [it]"; for conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot be grasped by the sense of hearing. The phrase "that very thing is this" is to be construed with the word "perception" (*pratīti*) in the compound "of the perception of the triad beginning with that. The meaning is: "by means of a perception having the form 'this very word is that same [word]' and so forth. Nor should it be argued that, despite the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), this perception is based on similarity (*sājātya*), just like the perceptions "this very medicinal herb is that one," "this very nail is that one," or "these very hairs are those ones."

Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such conventional usage as "this word belongs to that same class," and so forth. Nor can this be accepted as a desired outcome, for it is precisely the conventional usage "this is that very same word" that is intended. In the same way, the cognition that "this is a single sentence" should also be understood as establishing [the existence of the sentence as a distinct entity]. Nor should it be argued that the unity is logically established because it has a single aggregate as its object—like an army, a forest, or a heap of grain—for we accept that forests, heaps, and the like are indeed entities distinct from their constituent parts.

Moreover, although such a cognition as "one heap of grain" is possible because it refers to a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—such as its occupying a single location—which is itself unitary, in the present case that is impossible, as no such limiting adjunct can exist.

Nor is it the case that being the cause of a cognition whose primary qualificand has a single meaning constitutes [the definition], because this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to both the expanded (*vyāsa*) and the contracted (*samāsa*) forms taken together. Furthermore, if one were to include "being qualified by some meaning of a word-part" in the sense of *ca* (conjunction), this would result in under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding compounds. Moreover, there would be over-extension regarding the stem-portion (*prakṛtyaṃśa*) of the word "ghaṭa. Additionally, since oneness is established by virtue of being the cause of a cognition of a single meaning, and the status of being the cause of a cognition of a single meaning is established by virtue of that oneness, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Finally, even in the absence of a cognition of meaning, when hearing a word with an unfamiliar meaning, there arises the perception that "this is one word."

Nor should it be argued that there is no such cognition as "this word has a single object of a unitary cognition, a single substratum, and a single agent," for even in the case of an utterance by multiple agents, the intended cognition—"this is one word 'ghaṭa'"—would be untenable. Nor should it be argued that because the status of being the object of a unitary cognition is absent there, it is simply not accepted in that case; for this is established by the Bhāṣya on the *Sārūpya* Sūtra, which states: "The very same word 'Indra' manifests in various sacrifices," and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that being the object of a cognition of a single class (*ekajātīyabuddhi*) is the cause [of the unity of the object] there; for the uniformity of cognitions is dependent upon the unity of their objects—such as the form of a cloth—and the unity of the object is itself based on the uniformity of the cognitions, resulting in a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). If it is argued that "uniformity" means having a single form (*ekākāratva*), and that this is possible even without the unity of the object, so that there is no circular argument, then it would follow that even a whole (*avayavin*) such as a cloth, which is distinct [from its parts], could not be established.

Even regarding the linguistic usage "one cloth," its status as the object of a single cognition is established by the collection [of threads] itself; if you maintain that this usage of "one" proves the existence of a distinct whole (*avayavin*) because that status as the object of a single cognition is not otherwise perceived there, then in the present case, that [usage] is not blocked. Nor should it be said that the phrase "one *indra* word" means "an *indra* word of a single type," for it is more appropriate to assume the oneness of that very [word] rather than postulating multiple words.

Furthermore, because they share the same genus (*ekajātīyatva*), there would arise the undesirable consequence that even for five or more jars, one would have the cognition "one jar. Moreover, we do not employ such expressions as "the Indra-jar" or "the Candra-jar" [to refer to individual jars]. Enough of this prolixity. Regarding the phrase "of the phonemes alone" (*varṇānām eva*): the meaning is that the perception (*pratyakṣa*) whose object is those very phonemes has already been established above. Regarding "because there is no absence of being distinct from the *sphoṭa*" (*sphoṭātiriktatvābhāvāt*): the meaning is that the *sphoṭa* itself is what appears through the universals (*gatvādi*) residing in the conjunctions with the manifesting air (*vyañjakavāyu*).

Having raised the alternative as to whether the denotative capacity belongs to each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) or to their collection (*samudāya*), [the author] states that the first is not the case: "of the phonemes individually. He states that the second is not the case: "but of the collection. This is to be construed with the phrase "the knowledge of this" (*etasya jñānam*). Regarding the term "arising very rapidly" (*āśutarotpannānām*), the word "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) is supplied, and it is to be construed with "of that collection. The phrase "arising very rapidly" is also an elliptical expression for "perishing very rapidly" (*āśutaravināśinām*).

By this, the statement that "the cognition of objects—even those produced rapidly in succession and persisting for a long time—is indeed possible" is refuted as being inconsistent with the claim that it is "impossible. Likewise, [it occurs] only in succession. Thus, on the view that phonemes are produced (*janya*), their collection is impossible, and therefore the cognition of them is impossible; on the view that they are eternal (*nitya*), even if their collection is possible, the cognition of them remains impossible—this is the sense. [The phrase] "by means of a latent impression" (*saṃskāreṇa*)...

This auxiliary factor (*sahakāra*) is to be understood as occurring either in the auditory organ or in the experience of the final phoneme. Thus, the experience having the final phoneme as its object—either by virtue of such a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) or by virtue of the memory produced by it—comes to have all those phonemes as its objects. This is because the experience of the final phoneme, assisted by such a latent impression, [produces] through the medium of the latent impression it generates, a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) whose objective domains are co-extensive (*samaniyata*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no lack of distinction because the sequence in which the object appears in experience is the very same sequence in which it appears in recollection; for such a rule is unestablished, since it is an empirical fact that recollection occurs even in a sequence contrary to that of the experience. Nor should it be argued that such a restriction applies only to the experience and recollection of phonemes, for there is a lack of evidence for this.

If it is argued that such a [distinct entity] is postulated because the difference in the cognition of meaning in cases such as "saro rasa" must be accounted for, we say no; for that [difference] can be explained even by the postulation of a distinct *sphoṭa*. Furthermore, there is the experience of recollecting the words and so forth in a sequence contrary to the order in which three, four, or more words were initially perceived. This is what is meant by "in the alternative."

If each [phoneme] were individually manifesting, then since manifestation would be accomplished by the first phoneme alone, the other phonemes would be redundant. However, it is impossible for them to be manifesting collectively; and even if the final phoneme were the manifester, the preceding phonemes would still be redundant. If, on the other hand, it is the experience of the final phoneme—conjoined with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experiences of each preceding phoneme—that constitutes the manifestation, then let that very [experience] be what conveys the meaning; there is no need for the postulation of a separate *sphoṭa*. This is the intended sense.

Others, however, argue that the demonstration of the possibility of word-knowledge (*pada-jñāna*) according to the stated method is not tenable, because expressions such as "this is prior" and "this is posterior" would be impossible; and in the absence of such expressions, the grammatical rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* would result in inconsistency, making it impossible to accept [the opponent's] position.

In my view, however, just as a cloth or similar object appears with various color-impressions produced by various dyeing substances, so too is the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of the *sphoṭa*—possessing the unity and other properties inherent in each respective phoneme—brought about precisely by the sequence of articulated phonemes. It is in that very [manifested *sphoṭa*], which is the object of cognition, that the linguistic usage of priority and posteriority is possible. For this reason alone, the distinct apprehension of different meanings in cases such as "sara" and "rasa" is accounted for; otherwise, since it is impossible to speak of a relation of "immediately following" between what has perished and what exists—just as it is impossible to speak of a temporal relation [between them]—such a distinction could not arise.

By this, the following is refuted: that just as there is the conventional usage "this person is prior" and "that person is posterior" regarding a man who has perished and one who exists, so too here the usage based on priority in time and so forth is justified. For even so, the impossibility of a relationship between those two remains evident, and it is impossible to speak of such a thing, just as in the case of a temporal relationship.

Likewise, even if the word were produced at each individual phoneme, it would be impossible to have a cognition of that word as the substratum of its own function (*vṛtti*), because the word does not exist [as a whole] there; and if one were to admit that something can be a substratum even when it is non-existent, then the cognition "the past jar contains water" would result [as a valid perception], since that cognition would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) by virtue of having an uncontradicted object.

[Objection: "But surely, even though it lacks the status of being a substratum for a linguistic operation (*vṛtti*) at the present time, its status as a substratum for such an operation delimited by a prior time is perfectly possible there, just as a past jar is a substratum for color and so forth. [Reply: No, because a word (*pada*), which consists of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa-samudāya*), did not exist even previously. It is clear that since the jar existed previously, its status as a substratum for color and so forth at that time is indeed established.

Indeed, it might be argued that the cognition "the past jar is swift" cannot be produced, because the possessive suffix *matup* denotes only a present relation, as is taught by the rule *tadasyāstyasmin* (Pāṇini 5.2.94). However, in this way, there is no obstacle to accepting that a word—consisting of a collection of phonemes which are objects of cognition—is the locus of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, the usage "I know the past jar" is logically justified.

If it is argued that otherwise, since a past jar lacks the status of being the locus for present cognition and so forth, its [existence as an object] would clearly be untenable—this is not so; for even in that case, due to the absence of words and sentences, there would follow the loss of the very relationship between word and meaning. As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"If the meaning of a sentence were non-verbal, then the meaning of a word would be likewise."

The point is this: just as there is no sentence in the form of a collection of words, there is likewise no word in the form of a collection of phonemes, because the relation to meaning is absent in both cases. Furthermore, it has been established that the cognition "this very word *kṛṣṇa* is a single sentence" would be untenable. Moreover, in this way, it would be impossible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) in words that are distinct due to differences in pronunciation, because under the theory of individuals (*vyaktivāda*), there would be the consequence of infinite regress and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The direction [of the argument] is that one should understand there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule that cognition arises only from a word-form whose power (*śakti*) has been grasped. Thus, they say that what Kaiyaṭa stated is indeed correct. Furthermore, among the fourfold speech consisting of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, the Sphoṭa is of the nature of the sound-component (*nādāṃśa*) of that which is Madhyamā-vāk. The details should be understood from the *Harigrantha*; this is clear in the *Mañjūṣā*.

And regarding that [word], in the view that it is an indivisible entity consisting of a single phoneme (*ekavarṇa*), although it is manifested by a single phoneme, nevertheless other phonemes are not redundant; for it is only that [word] as manifested by the final phoneme that serves as the cause of cognition. Nor should it be argued that even so, the redundancy of those other phonemes remains unavoidable; for the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme also act as auxiliary causes, and since these impressions are stable, the aforementioned logical justification is not impossible.

Furthermore, the experience at that time must be accepted as the basis [for the cognition]. Therefore, the objection that the meaningfulness of the phonemes *da* and so forth in words such as "Devadatta" is difficult to establish—on the grounds that impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of those same phonemes occurring at different times would still exist—is without merit. This is because the purpose [of the phonemes] is fulfilled by awakening the impressions, since only those impressions that have been awakened act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Nor does this render the *sphoṭa* useless, for the answer to that has already been given.

In the commentary on the sūtra "paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ," it is stated— in order to dispel the doubt that proximity and sequence are untenable for phonemes that perish as soon as they are uttered— that "the wise agent, whose intellect perceives reality, performs all actions having first formed them in the intellect;
having perceived the meanings to be expressed by means of words, he should establish their sequence within the intellect."

The sequence of words belongs solely to the domain of the intellect. Here, a person who acts with foresight perceives: "In this meaning, this word should be employed; first this word, then this phoneme, then that, then this. This is the method of truth—that which possesses knowledge of all objects.

The wise person—one possessing scholarship—having caused the activities [of speech] to be reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), that is, the internal organ, as sounds produced by the operations of striking the throat and other parts; and having seen those sounds, along with their co-occurring denotative meanings, within the intellect during the act of instruction (the instrumental case in "by means of sound" [*śabdena*] is used in the sense of accompaniment in this context); he should then establish the usage of sequence (*paurvāparya*) therein—that is, its meaning is that one should apply the convention of priority and posteriority to those very objects within the intellect. The phrase "an object of the intellect" (*buddhiviṣayam*) means "having as its object the word residing in the intellect."

It should be understood that the demonstration [of the letters] as residing in the speaker's intellect by means of the words "this which... and so forth is because the scripture proceeds solely for the sake of the speaker, and because the fruit of its merit is heard by him alone. However, it is not correct to say that this Bhāṣya intends merely to superimpose the sequence existing in the intellect onto the phonemes; for even in the case of cognitions, since they arise sequentially and perish instantly, a [real] priority and posteriority is impossible.

In this way, even the impossibility of the expression "this" (*idam*), which refers solely to an object of direct perception, should be understood as a flaw if the *sphoṭa* is not accepted. However, if that [the *sphoṭa*] is accepted, its possibility is established by its being manifested through a subtle utterance that is audible only to oneself; such is the intended meaning. "Thus there is a flaw" means: a flaw consisting of a conceptual dilemma (*vikalpa*). He explains that [flaw] with the words "of each respective letter" (*tattadvarṇa*) and so on. "The capacity to manifest individually" means: if that were the case, the assumption of other conjunctions with air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) would result in futility; such is the intended meaning.

It should be understood that there is no impossibility regarding the occurrence of the various air-conjunctions (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) as they arise sequentially at their respective locations from the air rising from the region of the navel. Although each individual conjunction is a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), it is one particular conjunction that manifests the *sphoṭa* in the form of the phoneme *ga*, another in the form of *au*, and another in the form of the *visarga*. Thus, since it is only that *sphoṭa* manifested with such specific characteristics that conveys meaning, no air-conjunction whatsoever is redundant; this is the intended sense.

He provides the resolution: "each one indeed. For this very reason—namely, because the conjunctions of air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) are the manifestors [of phonemes] by means of their own inherent properties such as *ga*-ness (*gatva*) and so forth—even though there is no admission of anything additional to that—that is to say, even though there is no admission of anything distinct from the *sphoṭa*—the point is that if one does not accept that the conjunctions of air are the manifestors by means of *ga*-ness and so forth, then it would necessarily follow that one must admit a separate phoneme (*varṇa*) for the sake of such manifestation.

[Objection: But surely, since the conjunctions with the air cannot occur simultaneously according to the method previously stated, how is it possible for the *sphoṭa* to be manifested simultaneously in its various forms? [Reply: This is not so; because the air rising from the region of the navel is gross, it is possible for multiple conjunctions to arise simultaneously at various locations, and thus there is no room for the aforementioned objection. [Objection: Even so, in the absence of a word (*pada*), the claim that the cognition of a word is the cause of the understanding of meaning is utterly devoid of reason. He dispels this doubt with the words "If this is so... (*evaṃ ceti*).

The meaning is: "and upon the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* in the form of this or that [letter] through conjunction with the air. For the word "is apprehended" (*gṛhyate*), the phrase "wherein" (*yatra*) is to be supplied as a complement. Thus, the meaning is: "by way of being the cause of that word-cognition in which the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) appears in the letter *ṭ*. "Because there is no dispute" means: "because it is accepted by all schools of thought."

[Objection: Since the *sphoṭa* appearing as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth is eternal, it is impossible for it to possess "immediate succession"—defined as being produced in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of the moment which is the locus of the destruction of its own locus, while not being the locus of the destruction of the moment which is the locus of the destruction of its own locus. Therefore, he says: "But [this] immediate succession is [defined differently]. [He explains: "By its own cognition" (*svajñāna*). Here, "its own" (*sva*) refers to the *sphoṭa* appearing as "pot-ness" and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that the inclusion of such an "immediately preceding" relationship (*avyavahitottaratva*) has not been observed before, he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). He refutes the critique of the *sphoṭa* theory stated by Parimala with the words: "By this" (*etena*), meaning by the reasons already stated and those yet to be stated. "In the word 'ghaṭa' alone" means "in that which is manifested as the word 'ghaṭa' alone. "From the word 'kalaśa'" means "from that which is manifested as the word 'kalaśa'. "Because of the consequence of [simultaneous] cognition" (*bodhaprasaṅgāt*).

The meaning is that if the sphoṭa were a single entity manifested by the word "ghaṭa," then because the apprehension of its expressive power (*śakti*) would have already occurred therein, it would follow that the cognition of the object would arise even from the manifestation of the word "kalasa" (pot). However, this fault does not apply to the view that the word consists of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa-samudāya*), for in that case, the apprehension of the power of that specific sound is the cause for generating the cognition. Regarding the phrase "the cause of the cognition of the object": the manifestation produced upon hearing a synonym of that word, when conjoined with the apprehension of the power manifested by that synonym, becomes the cause of the cognition of the object.

The meaning is that, when the comprehension of the object is to be produced through the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* by means of hearing its various synonyms (*paryāya*), the apprehension of the expressive power residing in those synonyms is the auxiliary cause. He states the reason why it is appropriate for the apprehension of the power residing in each respective synonym to be the cause: "That being so," and "by the very fact of being the apprehension of power. This means: by the very fact of being the apprehension of the power residing in each respective synonym.

Alternatively, the meaning is that [the cognition] is [produced] with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of verbal cognition (śābdabuddhitva) through the relation of being its producer (upadhāyakatā), precisely by way of the apprehension of power (śaktigrahatva) through the relation of objectivity (viṣayatā). "And because of parsimony" (lāghavāt): the word "and" (ca) indicates a reason; the meaning is "because of the parsimony of the delimiting factor of causality" (kāraṇatāvacchedaka). "In that state" (tattve)—that is, in the state of being the cause. "'As stated in the Parimala'" means "as stated in the *Parimala* and so forth"; by "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *Anyāyarakṣāmaṇi* is included. "Because it is established for all" (sarvasiddhatvāt).

The meaning is that even in the view of those who do not accept *sphoṭa*, a difference in power (*śakti*) is established through the difference in synonyms. Now, one might object: "If there is multiplicity of *sphoṭa*, there is indeed complexity; but if it is a single entity, how can there be a difference in power? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the delimiters thereof" (*tadavacchedaka*). Thus, even though the *sphoṭa* is one, there is a difference in power due to the difference in the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) which serves as the delimiter of the power; the point is that this is like the difference [in powers] based on the difference in the delimiters of the denotable (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Since there is no existence of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are distinct [from the sphoṭa], defects such as "for one who has grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) only in the word *ghaṭa*" have no place. If it is objected: "Even if one does not admit distinct phonemes, the defect remains unavoidable—namely, the contingency of verbal cognition arising even from a sphoṭa manifested by the universal *kalaśatva* (jar-ness) for a person who has grasped the respective expressive powers only for a sphoṭa manifested by the universals *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), *ṭatva*, and so forth"—we reply: No.

They say that because the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) occurs with respect to a specific sequence, such a sequence-specified cognition acts as an auxiliary cause for the production of understanding through a cognition whose qualifier is that specific sequence. Even on the view that letters are admitted to be distinct entities, since the apprehension of the convention (saṃketa) regarding the meaning occurs only for that which is colored by the form residing in each respective letter, there is no possibility of an unintended understanding arising in a person who has grasped the power only in the word "ghaṭa" upon hearing the word "kalaśa."

And that word, whose essence is *sphoṭa*, although in reality one, assumes as it were a manifold form through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding each respective phoneme, appearing in their various reflected forms; thus it should be understood as having the form of every word. This has been confirmed in the commentary on the *Pāṇini Sūtra* "eoṅ" (P. 1.1.9), which states: "The *sphoṭa* itself is manifested by means of [phonemes] such as *ka*."

For in that system, since [the phoneme] is established as being of a different class—like a man-lion (narasiṃha)—the partial constituents of a phoneme are not grasped by the apprehension of the phoneme itself. Anticipating the objection that, consequently, the substitution of *l* for *r* (via the rule "kṛpo ro laḥ") would not apply in the word *klṛpta*, it is stated: "Alternatively, only the sphoṭa is indicated on both sides; the sound *r* becomes the sound *l*."

In this regard, the intention of the commentators is as follows: in reality, there is no phoneme (*varṇa*) whatsoever that possesses the nature of *r*-ness; rather, it is merely the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* in that form. Therefore, the meaning to be described is that when there is the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* as *r*-ness, there occurs the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* as *l*-ness. Otherwise, [the rule] would not apply even in cases such as *kalpate*. Similarly, because of the manifestation of the *repha* (the sound *r*) in *kṛpa*, the status of *l*-ness is established even in cases such as *klṛpta*.

Thus, there is no over-extension of the grammatical operation prescribed for short vowels to long vowels and the like, because in those cases there is an absence of the manifestation of shortness. However, the claim that this Bhāṣya is intended solely to provide a designation for a genus (*jāti*) common to both included and non-included [vowels] is not sound. This is because there is no evidence for the existence of the genus *ratva* (the "r-ness" of *ṛ*) within the [long vowel], and because it contradicts the accepted doctrine that "the letter is another [distinct entity], like Narasiṃha. This has been explained in detail by the masters in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works.

Furthermore, if the *sphoṭa* is not accepted in this way, then because the short vowel (*hrasva*) is produced by efforts of varying duration—whether fast, medium, or slow—the application of the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) would result in an unintended consequence: the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* (Pāṇini 7.1.9) would apply to one mode of articulation but not to another due to the difference in time. However, if it is accepted, there is no such flaw. For the perception [of the vowel] occurs for a long or even longer duration in the medium or slow modes of articulation, due to the modified sound (*vaikṛtadhvani*) that arises immediately after the manifestation of that [sphoṭa].

Furthermore, it can be argued that the difference in time pertains only to the perception (*upalabdhi*) and not to the *sphoṭa*, because there exists a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as, "This person has pronounced that same [word] quickly, while another [pronounced it] slowly. In the case of short (*hrasva*) and long (*dīrgha*) vowels, however, such recognition does not occur; thus, even when the *tapara* rule is applied, there is no occurrence of an operation conditioned by a short vowel in the case of a long vowel. It should be understood, moreover, that if phonemes (*varṇa*) were produced entities, their acceptance as being subject to extremely rapid destruction would make their prolonged perception impossible.

This was stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya on the *tapara* sūtra, and in another commentary (*vṛtti*), in order to dispel the doubt that "there would be no occurrence of *ais*" [in cases like *ai*]: "If this is so, then the *sphoṭa* is the word (*śabda*), while the sound (*dhvani*) is a quality of the word. How so? Just as when someone strikes a kettle-drum, one person walks twenty paces [afterward], another thirty, and another forty, the *sphoṭa* remains exactly the same; the increase is caused by the sound. Both sound and *sphoṭa* belong to words, yet for some it is only the sound that is perceived as small or great; both of these [sizes] are due to their own nature. Thus it is said.

"Sphoṭa is sound" (śabda). The category of reality named *sphoṭa* is that which is perceivable by the sense of hearing (*śrotrindriya*). Here, the term "sound" (*dhvani*) refers to the modified sound (*vaikṛtadhvani*) that arises following the manifestation of the *sphoṭa*. And because it serves as an auxiliary to the word consisting of the *sphoṭa*, that [modified sound] is a quality (*guṇa*). Regarding the phrase "having struck the drum," the ellipsis is "perceiving that sound. In the expression "produced by sound" (*dhvanikṛta*), the word "sound" also refers to the modified sound (*vaikṛtadhvani*). In the phrase "sound and *sphoṭa*," the ellipsis is "exist" (*stah*).

Regarding sounds—the sound-connection is *dhvani*. However, it is observed that for some [sounds], the modified *dhvani* (*vaikṛtadhvani*) is slight and produces cognition for a short duration, while for others it is great and produces cognition for a long duration. He provides the proof for this: "Both of these [are so] by their very nature. The word "establishment" (*siddhi*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Hari also says:

"Of the *sphoṭa*, which is of undivided duration and conforms to the duration of the *dhvani*, [the distinctions of] short, long, and protracted [vowels] exist by its very nature, because it is eternal."

"The time of the *prakṛti* (the manifesting sound) is metaphorically attributed to the word (*śabda*)."—this and more is explained in detail elsewhere. He states the argument from the *Kaustubha* for establishing a distinct *sphoṭa*: "In the *Kaustubha*, however... [etc. Regarding the phrase "in the series of phonemes" (*varṇamālāyām*), it means in the collection of phonemes. This is because there is the cognition "this is a word" (*padam iti pratīteḥ*). This is an elliptical expression; it also includes the cognition "this is a sentence" (*vākyam iti pratīteḥ*). It must be something distinct—that is, distinct from the phonemes—because a whole (*samudāya*) is distinct from its constituent parts (*samudāyin*). Otherwise, cognitions such as "this is a word" would be untenable, since individual phonemes do not possess the nature of being a word.

Furthermore, according to the reasoning stated, the cognition "one word" would otherwise be untenable. "Otherwise" means: in the absence of accepting a distinct *sphoṭa*. Regarding the phrase "distinct from the potsherds": if the cognition "word" is explained as having for its object merely those phonemes present in the intellect, then the cognition "jar" could likewise be explained by the potsherds themselves—which are accepted as being inherent in the jar—without requiring anything else. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the jar and so forth, as postulated by the opponent, would remain unestablished. This is the meaning.

The consequence that a pot distinct from its atoms would be unestablished has not been stated [here], because if that were the case, perception would be impossible due to the absence of magnitude (*mahattva*). This is also an illustration of the consequence that even the shards and so forth, being distinct from the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the rest, would likewise be unestablished; enough with this excessive detail.

Thus—when the acceptance of the *sphoṭa* alone as the expressive agent is asserted. "By the lack of authority of the treatise" means by the lack of authority of the grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). "By the end of [the phrase] 'for the sake of understanding that which is to be attained'"—this conceptualization, namely the conceptualization of base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth, is for the sake of understanding that which is to be attained; here, a change of number and a change of gender are to be understood. The meaning is: "by that which has this form as its end. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied from what follows.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: for whatever reason, the means (*upāya*) intended for the attainment of the goal (*upeya*) become unstable. "Of the goal" (*upeyasya*) means of that which is to be attained; "attainment" (*pratipatti*) means reaching or knowledge—that is the meaning. He establishes [the point] with the words beginning "like the five sheaths," etc., by stating "this is the sense," and so forth. In the *Bhṛguvallī*—a specific Upaniṣadic section—and in the *Ānandavallī*—another specific Upaniṣadic section—the compound "food, breath, etc. (*annaprāṇa*) is a *dvandva* ending in the word *ānanda*, followed by the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of abundance and so on.

It has a connection with each [term] individually, according to the maxim "that which is heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound [is connected with each member]. Thus, the meaning is: the exposition of the pentad of sheaths (*kośas*) consisting of the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*. Regarding the word "real" (*vāstava*): it means for the purpose of making known that "tail"—the Brahman which is the support of the universe—which is real, being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.

By stating that this [Self] is real, the unreality of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) is indicated; and this is indeed clear from the Śārīrakabhāṣya and other works. On this point, some explain it as follows: "For instance, Bhṛgu Vāruṇi asked his father Varuṇa about Brahman. Varuṇa said: 'Food. Having observed its origin and so forth, [Bhṛgu] asked again. Then [Varuṇa] replied: 'Life-breath (prāṇa) is Brahman.'"

After determining that it was not that [Self], he asked again, and [the teacher] replied: "Mind. Since its origin is heard in the Śruti—“The food that is eaten becomes threefold: that which is coarse becomes feces, that which is middling becomes flesh, and that which is subtle becomes mind”—he asked again, and [the teacher] replied: "Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). Having understood that this too is not the [Self] because it is conditioned by mental modifications (*vṛtti*), he questioned once more.

Therefore, [the opponent claims] that after it was stated, "Brahman is bliss," Bhr̥gu remained having attained the reality of the thing itself. That is not correct, because the fifth [sheath] is not a means there, and because it is not a sheath (*kośa*). Consequently, the *Bhr̥gu-vallī* is not the example; rather, it is the *Ānanda-vallī*, because all five [sheaths] therein serve as means. For the term *ānandamaya* there conveys Brahman as the ultimate (*mukhya*), and for this very reason, the word "tail" (*puccha*)—which signifies being the support of the universe—is appropriate.

Because the primary meaning of the word *lāṅgūla* (tail) is contradicted in that context, the *Vyāsasūtra*—"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition"—must be reconciled by taking the term *ānandamaya* there to refer to the word *brahman* heard in the remainder of that passage; this and more has been elaborated upon by the venerable Śaṅkarapāda and others. With all of this in mind, only the *Ānandavallī* has been cited here.

In some manuscripts of the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*, a passage beginning with "in the Bhṛguvallī" (*bhṛguvallyām*) is seen; however, that is not correct for the reasons already stated. Alternatively, precisely because of the aforementioned lack of satisfaction [with that view], one should adopt the interpretation that the presentation of the *Ānandavallī* follows immediately after the presentation of the *Bhṛguvallī*. [Objection: But surely there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) regarding the knowledge of *sphoṭa* arising even without the knowledge of grammar; therefore, he says: "And thus, by grammar... [The term] "distinctness" (*vaijātya*) is postulated. And so, because there is a difference in the delimitors of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there is no inconsistency.

He recites a mantra. The sense is that since the Mīmāṃsakas postulate a specific "extraordinary nature" (*vaijātya*) in the memory of an object produced by a mantra—intended to exclude the possibility of deviation (i.e., that such memory might arise through other means) on the grounds that "the memory of an object occurs through a mantra even by way of another method"—so too should it be here. The phrase "produced by a mantra" means "that which delimits the state of being produced by a mantra. "Vedānta," etc., refers to that which delimits the state of being produced by hearing that [Vedānta].

The sense is that, otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since the knowledge of Brahman could arise even from listening to grammatical treatises (*bhāṣāgrantha*); therefore, the Vedāntins postulate a specific difference in kind (*vaijātya*) in that case. "And of that knowledge" means: of the knowledge of *sphoṭa* produced by the study of the scriptures. "Usefulness for the purification of the body and so forth" means that, in this way, the scripture is not rendered useless. "Or indirectly" means: by way of the performance of sacrifices and other such rites.

He cites the *Vākyapadīya* as authority for the stated meaning—“it has been said. The sense is: “wherein healing (*cikitsā*) is proclaimed. The final meaning is: “it is the cause for the removal of those things rooted in speech. Regarding the term *adhividyam*: this is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of a case ending; the final meaning is: “pervading all sciences. Regarding *atīta-*: the sense is “that from which error or delusion (*viparyāsa*) has passed away. *Kevalām* refers to the speech known as *parā*. [The question] “How is it real? is posed.

The point is that, since it is never observed that the perception of a real thirst and so forth is produced by an unreal mirage of water, the cognition of a real *sphoṭa* cannot possibly arise through the postulation of an unreal nature (*prakṛti*) and so on. Regarding the phrase "because it will be stated later": this is because, in the passage beginning with "manifested by many individuals" (*anekavyaktyabhivyaṅgye*), its distinction from the category of "existent reality" (*sadrasa*)—like that of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth—will be indicated. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the phrase "the five sheaths and so forth" (*pañcakośādi*) is intended. || 66 ||

"Of the classes of phonemes (*varṇajāti*)" means of the classes such as being the state of being a phoneme (*varṇavṛttitva*) and so forth. "It would not be produced" means that the cognition [that "the letter *ka* has been produced"] would not occur. The statement that the classes are eternal is for the purpose of refuting the view that the cognition "the letter *ka* has been produced" and so on is accounted for by taking the class—which serves as a qualifier—as its object, just as in the case of the expression "the crested one (*śikhī*) has perished. It should be understood that this is also an elliptical indication (an *upalakṣaṇa*) of the cognition "the letter *ka* has perished."

In the view that "birth" (*jāti*) is a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) produced by ignorance (*āvidyaka*), the aforementioned inconsistency of perception does not arise; therefore, [the author] says: "due to contact with air" (*vāyusaṃyoga*). Regarding the phrase "even by others" (*parairapi*): in the root text, the word "others" (*para*) refers to the Mīmāṃsakas. In the root text, regarding the phrase "for others [accept] even accents, length, etc. (*svaradairdhyādyapi hyanye*), the first instance of the word "others" (*anya*) also refers to them. In the term "accents, length, etc. (*svaradairdhyādi*), the word "accent" (*svara*) should be understood as referring to tones such as the acute (*udātta*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "destruction, etc. (*vināśādi*), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is included.

Because of its unity—meaning, because the phoneme whose essence is *sphoṭa* is one. And thus, the coexistence of multiple contradictory properties such as acute (*udātta*) and so forth would be untenable. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction between the acute and other accents; for if that were so, there would be no justification for the cognition that "the letter *a* in 'agni' is grave (*anudātta*)" or "the letter *a* in the position of 'yajñasya' is acute (*udātta*)," and so on. Anticipating the objection that its impermanence is admitted and therefore the aforementioned cognitive inconsistency does not arise, he says: "And because of its permanence."

"And it is not delimited by *g*-ness (*gatva*). Thus, although there is a mutual difference between the *ga* sounds occurring at the earlier time and the present time—wherein the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by their respective individualities (*tadvyaktitva*)—there is no difference delimited by *g*-ness in the *ga* sound as delimited by *g*-ness; therefore, the absence of such a difference remains intact. This is the intended meaning. "Its object" refers to the object of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this very same *ga* sound [is the one previously heard]."

The meaning is that since there is no contradiction in the multiplicity of phonemes (*varṇa*) in this way, there is no impossibility of the cognition of [qualities] such as acute accent (*udātta*). Regarding the phrase "the absence of difference from the individual" (*vyaktyāśābhedasya*): the meaning is the absence of a difference—wherein the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the nature of that very individuality—between an individual occurring at this time and an individual occurring at a past time. Regarding the phrase "because of the impossibility of abandonment" (*tyāgāyogāt*): the meaning is that otherwise, all entities would necessarily be momentary, whereas recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is established precisely in the manner described above. Regarding the word "experience" (*anubhava*):...

The intended meaning of the statement "the letter *ga* has arisen" (*utpanno gakāraḥ*) is that the letter *ga* has been manifested; this is the purport. Now, one might object: "Just as in the cognition 'the jar has arisen,' the object of the cognition 'the letter *ga* has arisen' must be said to be origination itself—defined as existence characterized by prior non-existence—for it is improper to assume that two cognitions of identical form have different objects. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).

In response to the objection that "the state of being uttered" (uccaritatva) is simply the state of being produced by the contact of the palate and lips, and thus the cognition of its production remains intact, he says: "And the state of being uttered... [and so forth]. "Indirectly" (paramparayā) means through a further relation consisting in being manifested by its own substratum. By the word "etc. in "of production, etc.," destruction is included; however, for that [destruction], the relation to be understood is the state of being manifested by its own counter-positive. "Residing in the phoneme" (varṇaniṣṭhatve) means because it is accepted as residing in eternal phonemes.

The meaning is as follows: since the non-difference between what was previously experienced and what is now being experienced is established in this way, the eternity of the phonemes (varṇas) is indeed proven by the maxim: "Who could destroy this [entity] later, which has persisted through all that time? Regarding the phrase "in the aspect of direct relation": the intended sense is that the defect consisting of error remains in the cognition regarding the aspect of direct relation—namely, the cognition that "the letter *ga* has been produced" based on a direct relation such as origination. Regarding the phrase "in the aspect of the non-difference of the individual": [the same applies].

The meaning is: regarding that cognition which apprehends the non-difference between individuals—namely, the perception "this very same letter *ga* [is present]"—in its aspect of non-difference. "Just as [the cognition] is erroneous for you" means: just as that cognition is considered erroneous in your view, so too, in my view, the cognition of production and so forth through direct relation is equally erroneous. The final sense is that the defect consisting in the consequence of a single cognition being erroneous is common to both systems.

One might object: "If the defects are equal in both positions, then the disregard for the position that letters are eternal and manifold is without foundation. Anticipating this, he says: "But rather... (*parantu*). [The word] "for me" refers to the proponent of the eternality of letters. "Simplicity (*lāghava*) excels" means that the other's position is disregarded because of the aforementioned complexity (*gaurava*); this is the sense. He raises a doubt with the words "if not" (*na cet*), intending to show that if there were a necessity of *dhvani* (sound-manifestation) in the case of letters, then the production and cognition [of letters] could be accounted for through a mediated relationship; however, there is no proof for the existence of *dhvani* in that context.

Anticipating the objection that the very impossibility of accounting for cognitions such as "the letter *ga* has arisen" will serve as the proof in this matter, he says: "Because of the absence of the causal complex that produces those [sounds]," and so on. The point is that such [cognitions] are impossible because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the sounds; for it is not merely the impossibility of another explanation (*anyathānupapatti*) that brings about the production of an effect, since even a hundred instances of such impossibility have never been seen to be capable of producing an effect without the causal complex.

He explains: "by the utterance of the letter *ka*, etc. This means: when there exists the effort (*yatna*) and so forth that are capable of having the nature of the utterance of the letter *ka* and so forth. "Slightly apart" (*īṣadantara*) means: when there is a slight separation. "The tongue" (*jihvā*) means: that which is produced by the contact called "impact" (*abhighāta*) between the tongue and its respective place of articulation (*sthāna*), namely the contact of the air with the throat (*kaṇṭha*) and so forth. "In being the producer of sound" (*dhvanijanakatve*) means: because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one postulates that the aforementioned contact of the air with the place of articulation and so forth is the producer of sound.

"Of that"—meaning, of such contact with air and so forth. "Because of its existence": the sense is that since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) exists, the production of sound (*dhvani*) remains unimpaired even in the case of the production of phonemes (*varṇa*). He raises an objection—namely, "for you alone"—suggesting that because the causal complex for the production of phonemes acts as an inhibitor, the production of sound is impossible in the case where a phoneme is produced. "In this way"—that is, according to the stated manner, if phonemes were eternal and unitary—"even length and so forth": the word "even" (*api*) includes production and other such properties as well.

Likewise, the point is that properties such as length (*dīrghatva*) and so forth, like [the notions of] production (*utpatti*) and the rest, do not reside in the phoneme (*varṇa*), because of contradiction. As for those—the Mīmāṃsakas—it should not be suspected that the inference of the speaker’s possession of negligence (*pramāda*) and so forth from a word uttered preceded by negligence is untenable; for in this view, even if a specific difference (*vaijātya*) in each particular uttered word cannot serve as the inferential mark, there is the superimposition (*āropa*) upon the phonemes of a specific difference residing in the contact of the palate, lips, and so forth, which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being produced by negligence and the like.

This is because the inference [of their non-eternality] based on their being produced by negligence and other causes is logically sound; for it is observed that the inference of fire occurs even from another object known as smoke. Nor can it be argued that these [musical compositions] must be eternal on the basis of recognition such as "this is that same *gurjarī*" or "this is that same *dīpakalikā*. It must be said that *gurjarī* is a specific musical mode (*rāga*). Since its status as the counter-positive of destruction is established by other means of knowledge, one must—due to the lack of any other recourse—accept that such recognition is either an error or is based upon a commonality [of the type].

If letters were a single entity, then in the case of *aghaṭika*, the suffix *ṭhan*—which is conditioned by a word having two syllables (*dvyajlakṣaṇa*)—would have to be justified by superimposing the number two, belonging to the repetition [of the vowel], onto the single letter. Similarly, in cases such as *ghaṭena*, the acute accent on the case-ending (*vibhaktyudāttatva*) prescribed by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* would also have to be prevented by the sublation of the singularity [of the vowel] through the number two belonging to the repetition. All of this is clear from the Bhāṣya and other works in the section on *pratyāhāra*; let this elaboration suffice. Thus, the answer is by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*).

The sense is that in some cases even a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) may serve as a valid reply; for in such instances, if the counter-argument were not accepted as a reply, it would result in the collapse of one's own established doctrine (*parasiddhānta*). Regarding the word "five": there are three types of *sphoṭa*—those of the phoneme (*varṇa*), the word (*pada*), and the sentence (*vākya*). Since the latter two are each twofold, being either with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) or without parts (*akhaṇḍa*), the sense is that there are five varieties of the individual *sphoṭa* (*vyaktisphoṭa*). || 70 ||

Thus concludes the exposition of the *vyakti-sphoṭa*. Now, following the method of Bopadeva, he states the *jāti-sphoṭa* with the words "Just as in the case of denotability" (*śakyatva iva*). An objection is raised: since the proponent of the indivisible *sphoṭa* (*akhaṇḍa-sphoṭa-vādin*) does not admit the existence of phonemes (*varṇa*), a universal (*jāti*) cannot exist without a substratum; therefore, the view that the universal is the signifier (*vācaka*) is untenable.
