To dispel this doubt, he says, "The sense is as follows," and so on. The phrase "by the aforementioned method" means by the method already stated—that is, the admission of the *sphoṭa* accompanied by the non-admission of phonemes. Now, in this view, the cognition "this is the letter *ga*" and so forth is indeed accepted.

In the Advaita system, [the opponent] says "this is not the letter *ga*" (gakāro'yaṃ na), just as one might say "this Devadatta is Yajñadatta. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the cognition 'this is the letter *ga*, not the letter *ha*' is logically possible by relying on a superimposed difference, just like the perception of mutual difference among individual souls (*jīva*) in the Vedānta school? Anticipating this, the author states another refutation with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). Regarding the phrase "the universal of *ga*-ness" (*gatvādi*): the meaning is whether or not a non-superimposed *gatva* (the universal of being *ga*) must be admitted. This is because the opponent also accepts that *gatva* can be superimposed; therefore, it would be inconsistent with the literal sense [of the argument] if it were not so accepted.

"That very [universal]" means "the universal of being *ga*," and so forth. He states the reason for the universal of being *ga* (*gatva*) having the form of the letter *ga*, etc.: "the eternity of phonemes" (*varṇanityatā*). "Distinct" (*atirikta*) means "distinct from the phoneme. "Because of the non-acceptance of the universal of being *ga*" means "because of the non-acceptance of the universal of being *ga*," and so forth. For the acceptance of a distinct genus (*jāti*) is indeed for the sake of a recurring cognition (*anugatapratīti*) among multiple individuals. However, in the view that phonemes are eternal, since there is no possibility of a lack of recurrence due to the identity of the individual *ga*-phonemes and so forth, the acceptance of a universal of being *ga* distinct from the *ga*-phoneme would be purposeless; this is the sense.

And likewise: "In the case of the sphoṭa, and in the acceptance of *gatva* (the universal 'g-ness') and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Or, if the letter *ga* and others were of the nature of *gatva*, etc. Regarding "a distinct sphoṭa": the meaning is "in the postulation of a sphoṭa distinct from *gatva* and so forth. Regarding "complexity" (*gaurava*): the meaning is "the complexity of postulating a substratum (*dharmin*) in the form of a distinct sphoṭa. Regarding "in the latter"—that is, in the position where *gatva* and so forth are not accepted in the sphoṭa. Regarding "contradiction with experience" (*pratītivirodha*): the meaning is that in the absence of *gatva* and so forth, the aforementioned experience characterized by the qualifier *gatva* and so forth would be untenable.

Regarding the phrase "having superimposed, thus [arises] the cognition": the sense is that even though the property of being a *ga*-sound (*gatva*) and so forth does not reside in the *sphoṭa*, there is no sublation (bādhaka) when one superimposes such properties as *gatva* which actually reside in the contact with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) and so on. The construction of the word "having superimposed" (*āropya*) is justified by supplying the word "remaining" (*sthitasya*). Otherwise, the suffix *-ktvā* would be untenable because it requires a common agent for both the action of superimposing and the occurrence of the cognition. However, the pursuit of a superimposition occurring at a later time is justified because it accounts for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) rooted in such a cognition.

And thus, the meaning is that there is a linguistic convention regarding the two cognitions. Alternatively, let the word *pratyaya* (cognition) retain its literal sense, namely that simultaneity appears as the relation in the arising of the cognition. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "the conjunction with air alone," the *sphoṭa* is excluded. Regarding the phrase "the letter *ga* also": the meaning is "that which is also the object of such a cognition. And in this way, there is no possibility of the cognition being erroneous. By the word "also" (*api*), the objects of cognitions such as "the letter *ka*" and so forth are included.

The meaning is as follows: regarding that conjunction with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*), its being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*) is a defect. This is because one must admit that for the perception of a conjunction, the perception of all its substrata is a necessary cause; otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of perceiving the conjunction between a jar and space (*ghaṭākāśasaṃyoga*). Thus, since air is imperceptible, the conjunction of air with its respective locations is also beyond the senses, and consequently, the perception of [sounds such as] "the letter *ga*" and so forth would be impossible. The phrase "like a property" (*dharmavat*) means like the tactile sensation (*sparśa*), which is a property of air.

The point is this: just as air, though beyond the reach of the senses, has the touch of air as an object of tactile perception, so too will the conjunctions of air with the palate and other [articulatory organs] be perceptible by the senses; for it is accepted that in the case of a perceptual cognition of conjunction produced by an external sense organ that grasps a substance, the perception of all its substrata is a necessary cause.

Alternatively, just as in the case of "sound in the sky," let there be a sensory perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) regarding the universal *ga*-ness (*gatva*)—which has the conjunction as its qualifier and is presented by that very conjunction—with the individual *ga* as its qualificand. This is because, in the case of a sensory perception of a conjunction, the perception of all its substrata is a necessary cause. The point is that this single perception is expressed by the word "the letter *ga*" (*gakāra*). In this view, the phrase "like a property" (*dharmavat*) should be explained as "like a property of something supersensible (*atīndriya*), such as the sky."

The Sphoṭa has been refuted—the sense being that there is no need for a Sphoṭa, since the comprehension of various meanings is accomplished by the respective conjunctions with air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) alone. The core point is that the collection of those very conjunctions is the object of the cognition "this is one word" and so forth. However, in reality, they say that the postulation of a distinct Sphoṭa is necessary because this cognition cannot otherwise be explained. This has already been examined previously.

Regarding the phrase "in the Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa": for there, it was stated that because of [the faults of] infinity and deviation, the individual (vyakti) is not the denotation of a word, but rather the genus (jāti). Similarly, the acceptance that the genus alone is the denoter when accompanied by the word is appropriate, as the reasons are equal; this is the meaning. Now, raising the objection that since the genera residing in the phonemes (varṇas) are also manifold, how can the status of being a denoter be maintained, he says: "This is 'harī'... and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for the Tantrikas, the establishment of a universal (*jāti*) is not accepted on the basis of a uniform cognition (*anugata-pratīti*), but rather by virtue of being a delimiting factor of causality (*hetutāvacchedakatva*) or a delimiting factor of effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedakatva*)? To this, he says: "because of the presence of the letters" (*varṇopasthiteḥ*). The meaning is: "by virtue of being its delimiting factor" (*tadavacchedakatayā*), that is, by entering into the scope of the delimiting factor of causality (*hetutāvacchedaka*). [The opponent] objects: "The uniform cognition can be accounted for simply by the sequence of letters (*varṇānupūrvī*); let that alone be the delimiting factor of causality. What is the use of accepting an additional universal?"—this is the doubt expressed by "na ca" (and not). [The response is: "Because it would result in the fallacy of being otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhyāpatteḥ*).

The point is this: since the universal *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and so forth would not be established—because the uniform cognition "this is a pot" and so on can be accounted for by clay and other materials as qualified by a particular conjunction, and because the status of the stick and other tools as causes can be explained as being restricted to clay and the like as delimited by a particular conjunction—likewise, even the composite whole (*avayavin*) such as a pot would not be established; the meaning is that the cognition "this is a pot" and so on is satisfactorily explained as having as its object clay and the like as qualified by a particular conjunction.

*Ākāra* is a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is common [to all instances]. If it is argued that the admission of universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is necessary because the conjunctions of parts are not common [to all pots], and likewise—given the multiplicity of parts qualified by specific conjunctions—if the cognition "this is a pot" were to have those [specific parts] as its object, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) and the impossibility of the cognition "this is one pot"; therefore, one must resort to [the universal] "pot" and "pot-ness"—then, with the intention that this is equally applicable to the present case as well, he says: "Therefore," meaning: because a universal must be accepted according to the reasoning already stated.

Now, if it is argued that if the genus (jāti) residing in the word and so forth alone were the denoter, then the property residing in that [genus]—characterized by being inherent in all words such as "pot" while not being inherent in anything other than the word "pot" and so forth—must be accepted as the delimitor of denotative capacity (vācakatāvacchedaka), and thus there would be excessive complexity (gaurava)—to this he replies: "by way of identity" (tādātmyena).

The term *avacchedikā* means that which delimits denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedikā*). The sense is that even though identity (*tādātmya*) is not a relation that regulates occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), there is no inconsistency in its being the delimiter of a delimiter (*avacchedakatāvacchedakatva*), because what is essential for delimitation is simply being connected to its own locus (*svādhikaraṇasaṃbaddhatva*). Regarding the phrase "because of the existence of two universals" (*jātyoḥ sattvāt*): the meaning is that since the phonemes themselves, which serve as the substrata, exist in both words, and since there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to prefer one over the other], there is no difference in the presence of two universals in either single word.

Since the word *vā* would imply an alternative (*vikalpa*) and thus result in a lack of coherence, he says: "Or (*vā*) in the sense of 'but' (*tu*). And with the intention that in this context "but" signifies restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he says: "That very [consciousness] alone. [The phrase] "difference as the cause" means...

And thus, although there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*) in both cases, because a difference in sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is clearly present, one and the same universal (*jāti*) is manifested by that specific sequence in the one case, while a different universal is manifested in the other. Therefore, due to the difference in the cause—which consists in the cognition of those respective universals—the production of distinct cognitions in the form of "saro" and "rasa" is logically accounted for. Regarding the phrase "vyañjiketi": the word "iti" indicates the reason; the construction is "the difference in the cognition which has become the cause."

"An over-extension (atiprasaṅga)" means that there would be an over-extension regarding cognition that lacks distinguishing characteristics. "Caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)" means that being uttered with great force and so forth are the limiting adjuncts in that case; the meaning is that, just as there is a difference in the cognitions "high-pitched" and "low-pitched," so it is here. || 71 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the universal" (*jāteḥ*): it refers to the universal that is intended to reside in words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*). He states that the word *sphoṭa* refers to the signifier, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "that from which the object becomes manifest (*sphuṭati*), i.e., becomes the object of cognition, is *sphoṭa*"—this is what he means by "by way of its etymological meaning" (*yogārthatayā*). As for the phrase "rejected" (*apāstam*): although the universal exists at all times, there is no fault in the aforementioned [position], because the universal is not a signifier when it is merely present; rather, the intention is that only the universal as qualified by manifestation (*abhivyakti-viśiṣṭā*) is the signifier.

[Objection: Even so, the cognition of meaning from two or more individual phonemes that constitute a word remains unavoidable, since the universal (*jāti*) qualified by manifestation exists [in them]. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because it is accepted that the manifestation of the universal occurs only through all the phonemes constituting the word; for if that were the case, one would arrive at the *pada-sphoṭa* or the *vākya-sphoṭa*, and in this view, the doctrine of the *varṇa-sphoṭa* (phoneme-sphoṭa) would result in total abandonment. To dispel this doubt, he says: "The point is as follows."

The "stated fault" (*kathitadoṣa*) refers to the fault consisting in the unintended consequence of understanding a meaning from any arbitrary letter. In the phrase "not in either of the two positions" (*pakṣayoḥ na*), the expression "the stated fault" is carried over [from the previous context]. Therein, "subsisting collectively" (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*) means subsisting in the entire collection of letters that constitute a word or other unit. However, in the position of *varṇasphoṭa* (the phoneme-sphoṭa), it is not possible to say this; for since [the sphoṭa] does not reside in each individual letter, it is impossible for it to reside in a collection of letters that is not distinct from those [individual letters].

The point is that if the whole (*samudāya*) were something additional [to its parts], then only the word-sphoṭa or the sentence-sphoṭa would be established, not the phoneme-sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*). Regarding the two positions of the word and the sentence—the phrase "of those two, by the evidence grasping the substratum" (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) means this: the property (*dharma*) is the universal (*jāti*), and the evidence grasping it consists of such things as the uniform cognition "this is the word *hari*. Since [the sphoṭa] is established by that, the intention is that in this view the phoneme-sphoṭa is not accepted because it is defective. In the root text, the phrase "only the individuals of this [universal]" refers to this.

The phrase "of this" [refers to] the genus (*jāti*); the word "manifesting" (*vyañjikā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The meaning of the remainder is the meaning of the latter half-verse beginning with "by some... expressed" (*kaiścid vaktavyā*). In response to the inquiry as to why the term "sound" (*dhvani*) is used there for the individual phonetic manifestations (*varṇavyakti*) because they manifest the *sphoṭa*, he says: "For it has been stated," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that which manifests the *sphoṭa*": the meaning is that the term "sound" (*dhvani*) is applied there to the individual phonetic manifestations because they manifest the *sphoṭa*. || 72 ||

In the Advaita Siddhānta, having raised the objection—given that according to such scriptural passages as "All this is indeed the Self" (*ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*) and "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*), every entity other than Brahman is unreal, how can a universal (*jāti*) be real?—he says: "Brahman itself, qualified by each respective individual. The sense is that Brahman itself, conditioned (*upahita*) by each respective individual through the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā-sambandha*), constitutes the universal; thus, its eternity is not untenable. An *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) is that which distinguishes [the substrate] and does not connect with the predicate that connects with the substantive.

A qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which is connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is connected with the predicate (*vidheya*), and serves to differentiate. In the statement, "The auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space delimited by the ear-canal," the ear-canal functions as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it is not connected with the predicate, which is the nature of being an auditory organ (*śrotratva*). Conversely, in the statement, "A pot qualified by color is impermanent," color is a qualifier because it is connected with the predicate. In the present case, however, each individual instance (*vyakti*) is merely a limiting adjunct, as it is not connected with the predicate, which is the nature of being a universal (*jātitva*). This is to be understood as follows: "Existence itself, though differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in its relata..."
It is called "jāti" (the universal), and within it all words are established.
They declare that [Bhāva] to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self (mahān ātmā), and it is that which suffixes such as -tva and -tal express.

—Thus it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. Regarding the phrase "asatyā" (unreal): this was stated by Kaiyaṭa in his commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *Paspaśāhnika*, taking up the statement "substance (*dravya*) is eternal. Regarding the phrase "the very reality of Brahman": this passage from Kaiyaṭa is found in the *Pratyāhārāhnika* on the verse, "The expanse of Brahman is to be known as adorned like the moon and the stars. Regarding the phrase "thus says Kaiyaṭa": this passage of Kaiyaṭa’s also should be understood as being located in the *Paspaśā* section of the *Bhāṣya* on the statement "the form (*ākṛti*) is non-eternal. Regarding the term "avidyā" (ignorance).
In the phrase "herein lies a distinction of dharma," the term "distinct from the genus" (jātiriktah) is to be supplied. This is clearly stated in the Kaustubha. || 73 ||

At the beginning—"Nirañjana" means free from ignorance (*ajñāna*). "Samārambha" refers to the commencement—that is, the production—of entities, namely perceptible objects such as jars and the like. "Anādi" (beginningless) means that which is not the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). By the term "śāśvata" (eternal), the state of not being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is expressed. Thus, permanence is obtained as the nature of not being the counter-positive of destruction, qualified by the state of not being the counter-positive of prior non-existence. "Maṅgalam at the end of the accumulation."

This means at the end of the work titled *Kārikāvalī*. The meaning is that he performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) at the conclusion of the book, based on the practice of the learned and the statement of authoritative scholars: "One should perform an auspicious rite at the beginning of a work, in its middle, and at its end. Regarding "praise and salutation": by the word "namas," salutation is expressed; by the phrase "to the Perfect One" (*saṃpūrṇātmane*), praise is conveyed. Perfection (*pūrṇatva*) consists in having unimpeded will, or, due to the fulfillment of all desires, being free from desire (*niricchatva*).

He desired, "May I become many; may I procreate. Since this desire therein is indeed non-superimposed (*anāropita*), there is no contradiction. Alternatively, fullness (*pūrṇatva*) consists in being other than the desire for one's own pleasure. This is clear from Gadādhara’s *Gadādharī* commentary on the *Dīdhiti* in the passage "To the full Supreme Self"; thus, enough of this excessive detail. May there be auspiciousness. || 74 ||

There was one who was perfected within the circle of the wise, who attained mastery over the essence of the ocean of the Vedas, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, and who was always honored by the lords of the earth;
he was the illustrious Keśavadīkṣita, whose every purpose was fulfilled through service to the dust of the feet of the venerable Bhairavaśaṅkarī; his son was Hari.
This *Kāśikā*, the excellent work of the venerable [Vāmana], was indeed composed by him in the city of Śiva known by the name of glorious Kāśī, which is protected within by Rāma and Śiva;

it, whose body consists of service at the feet of the illustrious Bhairava and which delights in the feet of Śrīkaṇṭha, may it long bestow joy upon the virtuous scholars who possess true reasoning and have attained wisdom.
The illustrious younger brother of Dhanarāja, born from the womb of Queen Sakhī,
has provided this commentary on the *Bhūṣaṇa* according to his understanding for the sake of attaining Śiva.
When a year equal to the number of the Yugas, the elements, the directions, and the lords of the quarters had passed,
on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Monday.
While the moon was situated in Rohiṇī and the sun was in Scorpio, this book reached its conclusion; may Śiva be pleased with us because of that.
